column1: # The known limits, gaps and bad results of this release, one row each. docs/limits.md tells the larger ones in prose and docs/limits-further.md the lesser ones. Pages and source comments cite rows by id, for example SO-15.7. To read one row, search for its id at the start of a line; from the repository's root: grep -P '^SO-15\.7\t' docs/limits-all-rows.tsv

# Many of the tests and readings that this repository reports were not made on the released programs, but on programs built from other sources; some, the tests with deliberately cheating provers among them, on programs that also held test-only code. The compiled programs differ too; the machine code that differs is not shown equivalent and has not been read. Two of the five tests of weight hiding have run on the released programs: the first at small size on synthetic weights and at full size, once on synthetic and once on a real model's public weights, and the fifth once, at small size on synthetic weights. One of the fifth's two audits, the audit of a commitment, also ran on them at full size, in the timed runs (row LIM-63.2, line 5). At full size the first test has also run on other programs, and the fifth's two audits have run together only on other programs. The second and the third ran on test builds of other sources, which hold the code that injects a fault, and the fourth on programs of other sources that held test-only code. (What was run on which programs, and by what rule these pages tell it: docs/limits.md#what-was-run-on-these-programs.) "The released programs" are `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` and `cp_verify` as the sources in this repository build them (the production build). The programs that made the runs that these pages tell as runs on the released programs, or on a test build of these sources, were built from sources that differ from these, in what is told at docs/limits.md#what-was-run-on-these-programs and in nothing else, and these pages say of them that they were "built from these sources"; what has run on programs built from exactly these sources is told there too. The runs told on these pages are of these kinds: runs on the released programs (the timed runs are among these); runs on other programs (what "other programs" and "other sources" are: docs/glossary.md#other-programs and docs/glossary.md#other-sources; row HW-678), test builds among them; and, told apart, the calls of the Lean verifier (docs/limits.md#what-was-run-on-these-programs). Most rows rest on readings of other sources and on runs on other programs, and have not been checked on these sources or on the released programs; the sixth column says whether the note holds of the released programs. A run that is told without a mark ("on the released programs", "not on the released programs", "on other programs", "on test builds") and is not told as made "in the timed runs" (what these are: docs/limits.md#the-timed-runs) is to be taken as not made on the released programs, unless the note says that it was, or it is the planning call at the default's file (this head's line "The columns"). A test of the public table (SUITE.md; a row gives the test's name there, such as `blocks.tests`, mostly behind "the public row" or "the public test") is told apart: 171 of its 173 rows have run on programs that each test run built from these sources (most run test programs or scripts, not the three released programs themselves; eight run `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` as test builds: docs/limits.md#what-was-run-on-these-programs). The words "production build", in whatever form, are no such mark: other programs were built so too, and a run that is told of such a build, with no more, comes under this rule. A fault of the code, told in the present tense, holds of the released programs, unless the sixth column says otherwise. Count a leak found not on the released programs as a leak of the released programs, unless a page says that these sources do not have it. "On test builds" adds that a fault, a test switch or a test seed was built in.

# The columns. "kind": the property or the use that the row bears on. "the note": the limit, the gap or the result. "what you can do": advice, where there is any. "basis": how the thing is known. "run": a program was run and its outcome checked; "run, not on the released programs" says so of the run outright. "run (the public test …)": what ran is the named row of SUITE.md. "read": the code was read, and nothing was run; unless the note says otherwise, take it as read in other sources (sources that these pages do not tell as this repository's: docs/limits.md#what-was-run-on-these-programs). "reported": taken from an account of a run or a reading, whose files were not checked; of which code was read, the same holds as for "read". "reasoned": worked out from the design, the code or a configuration, not observed. "proved": a theorem under lean/, checked by Lean's kernel, under its own assumptions and in the model that it names. "argued on paper": a written argument that Lean has not checked. "not examined": it has not been run, read or tried. "as the note tells": the note gives the basis of each thing that it tells. "nothing checks it" (row L43 only): nothing in this repository shows or checks it. A figure that bears the bracket "reckoned by a planning call …", or is told "by the planning call", has that call for its basis, whatever the basis told beside it says of the rest. Such a figure is the released programs' own accounting, and the rule on unmarked runs does not touch it: at the default's full-size parameter file the released `cp_verify` has made the call, and it printed the figures that these pages give as its own (by report). "run in a trial" (L rows only): a program was run on the Lean library, but not as a run of record; "run in a trial, not over the files of this repository": the same, over Lean files that differ from this repository's. A run is to be taken as made at the default setting only where its row, or a row that it names for that run, says so (of the timed runs row P1 says it); the same holds of what a row gives as read, reasoned or argued on paper, where it depends on the setting. docs/limits.md, "Kinds of evidence", says the same at more length. "does it hold of the released programs?": whether the fault, gap or limit is there in the released programs. Its values: "yes", which goes by the evidence that the basis names; "yes, of the runs and readings that the note reports": the answer is given of what was run or read, as the note tells it, and of no more (rows LIM-63 and P1.3 add that these were not, or nearly all not, on the released programs); "yes, by report; not checked again"; "yes, by its parent row; not checked by itself"; "in part", where only part of it holds (two rows say which part); "not known", which means that the matter has not been held against the released programs; "not known: not compared with the released programs"; "seen, not on the released programs; not seen in the timed runs", which means that the timed runs, made on the released programs, did not show it, and not that these programs are free of it; "seen, not on the released programs; not tried on them"; "not tried on the released programs"; "no: these sources do not have it"; and in one row "as the rows named at docs/limits.md#the-verdict tell". A few rows leave the cell empty. The fifth column says on what a note rests; the sixth, whether it holds of the released programs. A gap that was read in other sources and is marked "yes" is to be taken as a gap of the released programs. The last column names a page that covers the matter, where one does.

# For binding, what has been run on the protocol is this, all at exact match, and most of it not on the released programs. At the default setting, at full size: the published out-of-domain answers and the commitment IDs of honest commitments, recomputed by value and found equal (also at small size, and on a real model's public weights), and a real model's commitment ID remade; altered copies of honest key files, leaf files and proofs, all refused, among them alterations inside the out-of-domain answers, and calls under a false commitment ID; hostile copies of the stored full-size example, all refused; and one comparison of the default's parameter file with the technical report's setting by a planning call, which checks no proof. At the small example's setting: the 23 lies of a lying committer's build, refused in every whole call; edited committers' tables altered within the distance that the verifier allows, whose proofs were accepted as the bound allows, each held true by a count of how far its table was altered (a reading; no decoder was run), and other altered tables refused, some far inside that distance: there is no threshold; among these, three further commitment IDs under which one leaf table's proofs were accepted, by design (that such tables decode to the same weights is an argument on paper, not tried); eleven cases with a stored table that is another matrix's, in whole or in one row, or close to it, all refused, and four false replies under one of them, refused at the leaf file's check; and an illustrative committer written in Lean, which agreed in values with `cp_commit` on one example, which a reader cannot repeat. Apart from one cheating committer's false leaf file (a false copy's file) at full size, tried once through a form of the executable `verify` that is not in this repository and through a C++ verifier built from other sources (row HW-678), and rejected by both, in `verify` at that file's own check, by report (lean/GAPS.md, 14 (i) and 33), no lying or edited committer has been put to the verifier at the default setting at full size. That file was tried over Lean files that differ from this repository's; no such trial has been made on this repository's files. Every run, with its bounds: rows LIM-63 to LIM-63.2, HW-747, M1.4, LIM-47, SO-7.2, SO-15.5, SO-15.7, LIM-2, LIM-14.3 and lean/LIMITS.md L61.

# Measured figures. The prover has been timed in the timed runs (docs/limits.md#the-timed-runs): runs of the released programs, made within three hours of one day. Six kinds of run at full size were made 3 times each, each kind's three on three machines: at the default setting, on a third party's public 4-bit files of Llama 4 Maverick a commitment with one request, and services at 24, at 64, and at 8 and 1 requests a batch; on synthetic weights of that shape a commitment, its audit and services at 24 (cp_verify's timed calls are part of these runs); at that setting with a clipped-gap policy, on the public files, sessions with every reply token checked and like sessions that check none. A clipped-gap example was made once, and one call and one service at 64 on synthetic weights were each run once; the call and the service failed. Of the public tests (173 rows), 172 were in four test runs and one in a test run of its own (row RES-22); two of the 172 did not run. The tests ran on programs that each test run built from these sources, and none was timed. Every other time, rate, size or memory peak is marked as not on the released programs (row RES-6), or as on them and not made to be timed (row RES-9), or is a figure of the runs that timed the serving scripts' check, by itself and beside a serving cp_prove, on the released programs, in one of which a constant of the scripts is not this repository's (row RES-32). All of it was got at the default setting, at that setting with a clipped-gap policy or on the small examples, or involves no prover. All that ran on a GPU, on one kind of GPU. No other time, rate, size or memory peak has been measured (row RES-6).

# First letters of an id. SO: soundness. H and HW: weight hiding. C: completeness. M: the model. P: speed, size and scope. R: running the programs. T: tests. E: evidence. L with a number: what Lean proves, as a short form of the entry of lean/LIMITS.md that the last column names (the terms: lean/TERMS.md). PS: where the programs differ from the protocol as written, and what the written arguments do not reach. LIM: an entry of docs/limits.md, or a part of one, in full, where that page tells it in short; the last column names the entry, and in these rows "this page", "this entry", "above", "below" and "the table" (of figures) mean docs/limits.md and that entry. LF: what adds to the row that the note names. RES: further limits and results.

# "Hiding" and "weight hiding" are plain names for a goal: clients and the public learn nothing about the weights beyond the list in docs/what-is-not-hidden.md. The cryptographic property nearest to it is index privacy (docs/glossary.md#index-privacy; lean/TERMS.md). What is claimed of the protocol is close to that property, not the same: it has batches, and as the programs run it, it is weaker in several ways. Where a row says "hiding" of a theorem or a written proof, it means what that text states, not the goal. In rows PS-59 to PS-61 and PS-67 "index privacy" is the name that a technical report that is not public and not refereed gives to its own statement. Hiding one client's request from another is a different property. "OOD answers" are the answers to out-of-domain (OOD) sampling on the committed tables: masked sums of the weights, which a commitment publishes (docs/glossary.md#record). The programs, their files and the format pages say "the record" for the published answers, as in the parameter line `record 1` and the printed field `record=1`.

# Many rows mention tests. `SUITE.md` lists the tests that the test suite runs, and more test files are in this repository without an entry there. A test or a file that a row names and that is not in this repository cannot be run or inspected by a reader. Other terms: docs/glossary.md.

# Words for tests with faults. A production build is what the build script makes unless a test build is asked for, and it accepts no test options. A test build has test options, such as a fixed test seed. Most trials ran on test builds, which are assumed to apply masks as the production build does. An injected fault is one that was put into a copy of the programs on purpose; a forced fault was brought about from outside, or by overwriting memory in a running program. No way for a client to cause an injected fault is known, but none has been looked for. No fault has been injected into the released programs, which have no option for it, and no broken duty has been tried on them, unless a row says so: what a row says of a fault or a broken duty is read or reasoned, unless it tells a run. A fault went unnoticed if the file verified and nothing stopped it. It was stopped if a self-check did. A self-check is a check that `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` runs on its own work in every run (one, `cp_commit`'s worst-case check, is skipped under a test seed: row HW-744).

# These rows tell or bear on bad results, that is, trials in which a fault went unnoticed, or something of the weights or of a request came out: HW-71, HW-308, HW-331, HW-340, HW-441, HW-660, HW-689. Other rows say "a bad result" in their own words.

column3: The error bound behind a YES is computed by the programs themselves and has not been checked independently. It is not a security level. For one request's proof with its key file and leaf file at full size, at the default setting: each single round has an error of at most 2^-128 only with its proof of work counted (71 rounds hold only so, of 67,383 entries of the plan, 62,421 of them with a verifier's message. Two of the entries, named `RECORD`, are the draws of the tables' OOD seeds and are no rounds: 67,381 rounds; without the work the least round has 96.23 bits), and all rounds added give 119.38 bits with the work and 92.42 bits without (reckoned by a planning call: `cp_verify -plan accounting` at the default's parameter file; the programs' own accounting, not a security level). Where the parameter file declares proof of work, every call of `cp_verify` that ends in `YES`, `WITHIN LIMITS`, `PART PASSED` or `NOT-A-VERIFICATION` prints both numbers: with the work and without it. Where it declares none, the two are one number. A sum is not a bound on everything that can go wrong, and a figure for one round is only an input to the bound with hash computations counted (docs/limits.md#the-soundness-figure). Of the plan's entries 62,417 bear an error (the two named `RECORD` among them; the four steps that seal a hash chain bear none: read in the programs' source and closed by the counts). The error of 8,853 of these rounds, every round with fewer than 152 bits with its work counted among them, was derived a second time from the statements of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, and at 8,843 the derived figure is the plan's to nine decimals; at the other ten, of five late stages, the plan claims less, by 0.010 to 0.018 bits (the cautious side), and has at least 128.00 bits at each; nowhere does the plan claim more than the derivation gives. The other 53,564 rounds were not derived a second time; the least of them has 152.4 bits by the plan. 8,003 of the 8,853 are two kinds of round with the error 1/|E|; 541 have a formula with more in it; 284 are one number of the plan over |E|, 25 the range check's. The integer that sets each distance and the numbers of positions are taken from the plan. The derivation compares a planning call's numbers with the report's formulas, not the programs' source, and says nothing of a checking call; it has not been checked independently; at no other parameter file has it been done, and its record is not in this repository. At any parameter file but the default setting's, none of this has been checked.

column3: None of the figures for single rounds counts a malicious prover's hash calls. Against a prover that computes N hashes in all, the bound is below about N/2^126 at the default setting; at the default that is with the work counted, and below about N/2^96 without. After 2^64 hash computations that is one in 2^62 with the work counted, and one in 2^32 without. The figures follow from the largest round error that the programs calculate. `cp_verify -plan accounting` prints 126.21 bits "as one number", and at the default 96.23 bits beside it for the work counted for nothing. N counts the verifier's own hash computations too (at the default setting 839,115 calls by the planner's count, which is no proved ceiling: it plans every opening at its largest and leaves out some hashing outside the rounds; in a checking run of a stored full-size proof on the released `cp_verify` the verifier counted 794,273, fewer than planned; hashing of public files and tables, and words that a draw skips, are planned nowhere, so no rule keeps a run's count at or under the plan; on the stored sets it stays under, because the plan counts every opened path whole and paths share vertices). For a cheater who computes nothing the underlying bound at the default setting gives 2^-108.3 with the proof of work counted, 2^-76.5 without crediting it, at the planner's count, calculated from the planning call's prints; printed by no program; not a security level. The same call says in its prints that the rounds' errors and the bound are cited from published work, some of it not peer-reviewed, or argued on paper in a technical report that is not public and not refereed; they are not proved for these programs (the Lean library proves its own verifier's bound, not this one). At the default setting every figure in this row is the programs' own, from one planning call (per round; the rounds' errors added; the compiled bound), or, where the row says so, calculated from that call's prints (reckoned by a planning call: `cp_verify -plan accounting` at the default's parameter file; the programs' own accounting, not a security level). A test of the verifier's suite, verifier/tests/kit_rounds_second.py, computes the proximity tests' round errors a second way, per round, from the formulas of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, at this file among others; for the weight table's rounds it uses the programs' formulas (a second arithmetic, not a second derivation: SO-1.6). That script covers the proximity tests' rounds only, about a third of the stored lines, and checks no sum of errors (prover/examples/TARGET-KITS.md; SO-1.6). The figures in bits that the report gives for this setting are not printed, and are not set beside the programs', figure by figure. The figures in this row have not been checked independently. There is no margin. At the default setting, with the work counted, these meet the target by under 0.01 bit: 68 rounds: 25 of the range check and 43 with a closeness term, out of 67,383 entries of the plan, 62,421 of them with a verifier's message. Two of the entries, named `RECORD`, are the draws of the tables' OOD seeds and are no rounds: 67,381 rounds. 71 rounds hold only because their work is counted.

column3: The figure for all rounds added is no bound over all error events: in some rounds the error that is counted is the largest of several events' chances and not their sum, as the program's own output says. Each round's error is compared with the target by itself, so the largest single round's error decides; the stricter sums are printed and decide nothing. What moves the sums is how many rounds only just meet the target, not their number alone. That follows from the provider's configuration files; no condition of the standard parameter form caps it, though the parser bounds every driver (28 blocks of layers, eight stages after a group's first, 256 parts), so under other files that pass every check the sums can come out lower than under the shipped ones.

The error of the round that tests that committed cells are small counts one column: the first that no column of small integers explains, which is fixed before the draw. That one column suffices is argued on paper, in a technical report that is not public and not refereed (the written proof has not been checked independently). Counted by a union over all columns, a stricter count that is not due by that report, the round would read 113.44 bits at the default setting (reckoned by a planning call: `cp_verify -plan accounting` at the default's parameter file; the programs' own accounting, not a security level). There are 25 such rounds in one proof. The program prints both readings.

column3: The one number that `cp_verify` prints, 126.21, already takes in the calls on the second hash function (blocks/numbers/accounting.h); no separate figure is owed for that hash. The number rests on the same footing for the closeness rounds as the number without the work: the theorem on codes, taken as given, and the binding of the weights rests on that theorem too. It is no floor. The figure has not been checked independently. Three steps behind it stand only in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, argued on paper and not checked independently: that interleaved rows need no extra factor, that a fold of 2^v rows costs v closeness terms, and that a repeated mask code costs one list size more; so does the step that a session's shared rounds are charged with one run's error, with no factor for the number of requests: of the shared rounds one term alone keeps that factor, one of the two terms at the shared point, and the rounds that are each request's own (its first message; its own proximity tests) carry the factor, as that report's theorem states; that step is argued for requests that share one weight table and its OOD answers (a lemma and a proof of the report's, not checked independently).

The program says of its own count, in its printed accounting, that the round errors and the compiled bound are cited from published work, some of it not peer-reviewed, or argued on paper in a technical report that is not public and not refereed; they are not proved for these programs (the Lean library proves its own verifier's bound, not this one). They have not been checked independently. By the head of blocks/numbers/accounting.h the shape of that bound is that of Ben-Sasson, Chiesa, Spooner, "Interactive Oracle Proofs" (Cryptology ePrint Archive 2016/116), as sharpened for round-by-round soundness in Chiesa, Yogev, "Building cryptographic proofs from hash functions". Lemma 3.2 of the first paper states the guarantee of the extractor for Merkle commitments in the random-oracle model. In the first paper the verifier's next message is a hash of the instance and of the current value. Here (blocks/chain/chain.h) the statement enters the chain's first query alone, and a round's query holds the value before it and the prover's whole message of the round, roots included. Whether the cited analysis carries over to these differences has not been shown. How the trees here (blocks/tree/tree.h), with salted leaves and pruned paths for a list of positions, stand to that lemma's hypotheses has not been compared with the paper. The Lean library proves its own statements on the trees it uses; nothing of that lemma is assumed there. These are that library's own trees; no theorem ties them to the programs' (row PS-43).

A shipped test (verifier/tests/kit_rounds_second.py) computes part of `cp_verify`'s printed accounting a second time, from the formulas of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, for two example configurations and one of the tests' own: the rounds of the proximity tests, and not, among others, those of the sub-proofs' sumchecks and lookups. It compares each round's figure to two decimals, so terms that change no digit are not checked, and it checks no sum of errors and does not read the line `work:`. By the script's own comment, three things in it were changed after a first comparison with the stored lines; some choices and shapes, not error formulas, come from the programs' headers, with one exception: for a weight table the two distances, the numbers of columns and the rounds RECORD, LIN point, LINK point, LINK and LOC (table, columns) are computed by the formulas of blocks/numbers/blocks.h, not the report's: there the second count is a second arithmetic, not a second derivation; and it uses the theorem on codes (ePrint 2025/2055, Theorem 4.6), taken as given (row SO-2), as the report restates it, which agrees with the restatement in the programs: whether the two restatements are independent is not known, and neither was compared with the full version of the paper for this script, so an error in the restatement would show in neither computation.

By the programs' own calculation, at the default setting and full size, every round of one call reaches the target of 128 bits, some of them only when up to 32 bits of proof of work are counted. Counting it is a step which is assumed, not proved, for the programs' hash chains. (The figures for a whole call are lower: the whole bound as one number, 126.21 bits with the work counted and 96.23 without; all rounds of one key file's, one leaf file's and one request's proof, added, 119.38 and 92.42; for one call and a cheater who computes no hashes, 108.32 and 76.55, calculated from the prints: rows SO-1 and SO-1.1; docs/limits.md#the-soundness-figure.) Without that work the weakest round has 96.23 bits (reckoned by a planning call: `cp_verify -plan accounting` at the default's parameter file; the programs' own accounting, not a security level). The truth of an accepted request and the binding of the weights both rest on the theorem on codes, and, at the default setting, both lean on counted proof of work in the rounds that draw positions. The bound rests on a theorem from the full version (ePrint 2025/2055, Theorem 4.6: not in the proceedings; that version gives an outline of its proof) of a paper published at STOC 2026, taken as given in a technical report that is not public and not refereed and in the programs' accounting. A statement on codes held to follow from that theorem, in its case of two words, is proved in this repository's Lean library, by way of another formalization's theorem and a comparison of bounds; the paper's own form of the bound is not proved there, and that the library's statement follows from the paper's, and that these programs' parameters meet the theorem's conditions, rest on reading, not on a proof (lean/LIMITS.md, L15; lean/THEOREM.md, "What it rests on"; what has been checked of it, and what has not: docs/limits.md#what-the-theorem-assumes). By that reading the parameters meet the conditions with no bits to spare. The bound rests too on further steps argued on paper in that report alone, which have not been checked independently. A round's bits are not the chance of a forgery: that chance grows with every hash computed, the verifier's own included, and even the figure without the work still rests on results that are cited or assumed and on the hash, taken as a random oracle. These figures are a calculation, not a security level, and no theorem is about the three programs (what they are worth (docs/limits.md#the-soundness-figure)).

column3: On every ground the bounds also rest on proofs in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, after public works (preprints among them). The printout names two such bounds. The first (beyond a third of the distance a fold's round has no factor for the number of interleaved rows) is stated, more generally, in a public preprint's abstract (ePrint 2026/891). By the abstract, that statement has no factor where the challenges are drawn from no more values than the field has elements. A fold's round combines by one challenge from the field over which the code is read, so by a reading of the abstract it is such a case. Only the abstract was read, which does not define its error term, and no bound rests on the preprint: the lemma rests on the report. For the second (a fold of 2^v rows counts v closeness terms) a published work (Bordage, Chiesa, Guan and Manzur; ePrint 2025/2051, CCC 2026) has the step for mutual correlated agreement, at its Lemma 4.4, and results of the same form, and the report gives a form of its own with the count of the theorem on codes; the two have not been compared line by line (this sentence rests on the report's own citation: that work's version of February 6, 2026 was read, and statements were restated from it); none of that work's proofs has been checked, its last revision, of May 19, 2026, has not been read and its proceedings version has not been compared; the report follows ePrint 2024/1399 and ePrint 2024/1351, which blocks/numbers/codes.h cites second-hand, not checked against the papers. The report's proofs have not been checked independently, and but for a few named steps they are not machine-checked. The program itself says in its prints that the bounds are cited from published work, some of it not peer-reviewed, or argued on paper in a technical report that is not public and not refereed; they are not proved for these programs (the Lean library proves its own verifier's bound, not this one).

The bound e = max(a/|E|, 1/(|E|-1)) in the proof library's step that sends oracle messages is argued in three lines of the source, which the file's writer wrote down itself. Where the argument in the file comes from is not known. The file cites a lemma of the paper that this protocol builds on for the bound. The public paper (ePrint 2026/391, version of February 25, 2026, Lemma 9.3 with its proof) has, by a reading, the same bound, by the same two cases, with one answer and one pad. The argument owes a credit to that lemma. Parts of the library were compared with the paper point by point, not line by line (PUBLISHED-WORKS.md, "The paper that this protocol builds on"); on the last step, and on the blocks that call these steps (`split.h`, `line.h`, `batt.h`, `batt_shown.h`, `lkp.h`, `rng.h`, `wf.h`, `lin.h`, `member.h`, `req*.h` and `laid.h` in blocks/iop/; prover/; verifier/), differences were not looked for; unknown differences may exist. Of the known differences (PUBLISHED-WORKS.md lists some, and marks where one is not told; the fold's: docs/limits.md, "Cited soundness"; the masking's: row H1.1), some: the code switch has a second form that stops before the batching; it carries kept rows; and it has further oracle messages in the same prover message. Oracle messages are sampled wherever a prover sends them, not only the new oracle of a code switch; a fold's fresh mask and the last step's masking oracle are not sampled; and the sample's weights are multilinear on one cube. Whether the cited analysis carries over to these differences has not been shown.

With several answers to a sample the same step takes the bound to the power of their number, s. The source's printed comment states the bound for s answers and argues only the case where they differ in pads alone; for s above 1, which the three programs refuse (row SO-6.3.2), so that none of their bounds rests on it, the bound e^s rests on a split on what differs outside the pads (each answer whose pad agrees contributes at most a/|E|, each whose pad differs at most 1/(|E|-1)): a derivation by cases with exhaustive checks over small fields, which has not been checked independently.

That a parameter file meets the hypotheses is the planner's own check with the reading of the report, not a theorem, and the frame that goes round by round is a theorem of the paper that this protocol builds on, which that report cites and does not prove. The binding of the weights rests on the theorem on codes too, with no margin to spare, and, for the committer's files, on two further steps that the report argues, with its own step for the repeated mask code (that combining the rows of an interleaved word costs nothing more, and one list size more for the repeated mask code beyond a third of the distance); these steps have not been checked independently. In a like corollary and proposition without proof of work (row LIM-14.3), sentences were false as worded and one printed upper limit was too low; the report's text corrects them, by its own account; a further correction in one proof has been read only by whoever wrote it.

Carrying the bound to the subcodes that the protocol uses (over this field, only the copied mask rows) is one lemma of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, proved there (the proof has not been checked independently); for rounds that count beyond unique decoding it is the theorem on codes itself, not its reach, which the programs' accounting takes as given (what this repository's Lean library proves beside it, and what rests on reading: row SO-2).

The default setting counts proof of work. In one run at the small size, at one of the default's files (target_small_f2_roomy's), on synthetic weights, under a seed that `cp_commit` drew, not on the released programs (prover/examples/TARGET-KITS.md), there were 121 proofs, each accepted in a whole call of `cp_verify`, and 83 altered files and calls, each rejected. What else has run is told in docs/limits.md#what-has-run. (See also docs/limits.md#soundness and row SO-15.7.) The library has an example of the same lines without a model's, blocks/frame/examples/record.f2.txt; none of the three programs can take that library file, because it has no lines on a model, and two CPU tests only size and plan it. At the library's level one shipped test makes and checks a whole leaf file with six counted bits of work, at toy length (blocks/frame/tests/check_entry_test.cpp).

The errors of the rounds other than the closeness terms are derived in a technical report that is not public and not refereed for its protocol or, for three kinds of round (the fold's, the code switch's and the last step's), cited from the paper that this protocol builds on and restated without proof. For the programs' own forms they are argued in the head comments of the library's sources; these arguments have not been checked independently. A lookup's padding is covered in that report for its protocol; where a key map reads places that count as padding that report has no statement, so soundness there is not known, and that does not happen at the full-size example's vocabulary. In the source's head comment the programs' lookup with padding is argued, and "not proved" is that comment's own word of itself.

Where one sub-proof hands a committed matrix on to the next (the request matrix to attention; the residual stream from group to group and to the head), the tie is the code switch with kept members: the old code words are spot-checked at drawn positions against the message sent again. Its soundness is argued on paper: a theorem of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, whose written proof has not been checked independently (a hypothesis of that theorem had a fault, which is corrected in the report; the correction has had single readings only: row PS-35.1); that the programs' switch meets that theorem's hypotheses has not been compared by name, and for the programs' own form the source's five steps have not been refereed. No Lean theorem is about the C++ programs' switch. At the default setting the 25 rounds (12 + 12 + 1), in which a switch with kept members draws its positions, are priced at 128.26 bits with their proof of work counted (108.26 from the positions opened, 20 from the work: verifier/tests/known_answers/kit_rounds/target_full_f2.txt) and no factor for the list of 54 candidate code words; with such a factor they would stand near 122.5 with the work, 102.5 without (by a reckoning); that none is due rests on the report's theorem on the switch, which pays the list in the sample's round. That the model's links keep 12 and 3 rows, as the plan counts them, has not been compared with the layout file.

The theorem on codes, on which every closeness round rests at the default setting, is stated for a plain Reed-Solomon code; so is the second source, the bound within a third of the distance (row LIM-11), on which rounds rest with parameter files other than the default setting's. That their counts carry over to a mask code that is read several times (a repeated code) is argued on paper in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, not in these two sources. It needs the theorem's mutual form: from plain correlated agreement no way beyond unique decoding is known.

The programs run one output head, the scored one, under every policy. A technical report that is not public and not refereed computes its figures for both heads. As to the scored head: how that head's cells are placed is written, but that report's theorems are shown for no whole configuration with it. By a reading it is a gap in what that report shows, not a known fault. That report's figures and the programs' are figures of two objects: the protocol on paper, under numbered statements, and the programs' planner, under none.

The provider's parameter file decides how much proof of work is counted and, through its numbers, on which source some closeness rounds rest (row T7.1.13). No condition of `cp_verify` looks at either choice, but for one cap (it rejects a file that counts more than 32 bits of work in a round: `policy-work-most`), and for counted work when the caller passes `-no-proof-of-work`. The default combines the theorem on codes, in every closeness round (no round's bound at the default setting rests on the lemma proved within a third of the distance; that count is reached for two mask codes and read by no round), with counted work up to the 32-bit cap; a provider's file can count 32 bits in every kind of round where the default counts 20 / 28 / 32, and set the numbers of row SO-4; the last line shows none of it; the work and accounting lines do. These choices move what the bounds rest on, not the target: every round must still meet it by the bound that belongs to its ground. The line `proof of work:` and `result-v1` show the work. Only the printed line on the grounds shows on which ground a request's rounds rest; neither the last line nor `result-v1` does.

column3: The second computation of the round errors, a script that shares no code with the programs (some choices and shapes in it, though no error formula, come from the programs' headers; the weight table's rounds are computed by the programs' own formulas: a second arithmetic, not a second derivation: row SO-1.6), takes the theorem on codes (ePrint 2025/2055, Theorem 4.6), taken as given (row SO-2), in the form in which a technical report that is not public and not refereed restates it, which agrees with the restatement in the proof library. Whether the two restatements are independent of each other is not known, and neither was compared with the full version of the paper for that script: an error in the restatement would show in neither computation. "Shares no code with the programs" means only that a script includes and imports none of their files. Where a page, a comment or a printed line says that a script was written from the specification or the format page alone, that does not hold of its text of BLAKE2b.

All printed figures are for one key file, one leaf file and one request's proof. By a reading of the source (nothing run; a reading not made on this question), the programs' chains bind every hash call of a request's own rounds to that request's digest, as those of a technical report that is not public and not refereed do, and a proof's first chain also to the request file's own words, which are in its first query byte for byte, under BLAKE2b. That report models both hash constructions together as one random oracle; by a reading, with no formal proof, the form of the proof's first hash makes that unnecessary for soundness against a prover, with the public files fixed beforehand; which four tables, bit for bit, a parameter file names hangs on the second hash function alone (row SO-14.1.1). On that report's footing, by its bound, the compiled bound and the one number are for any number of proofs; only the bound for a cheater who computes nothing weakens with a batch: at the default setting it is 2^-102.32 with the proof of work counted, 2^-70.55 without crediting it, at the planner's count of the verifier's own calls (no proved ceiling: row SO-1.1), for 64 whole calls, calculated from the planning call's prints; printed by no program; not a security level. The compiled bound and its one number bound the chance that a cheater who makes N hash calls gets any false proof accepted, however many proofs it puts out; a batch enters only through N, which counts the cheater's own calls and the verifier's on all the proofs, together. The figures below for a full batch (each of a request's own rounds read 6 bits lower at 64, in general by the logarithm of the batch's size; the sums for 64) are stricter readings of one pass of the interactive protocol, counted jointly; they are no bound for a cheater that hashes and no part of the compiled bound. All rounds added, counted jointly for a full batch of 64, give, at the default setting, with the proof of work counted 113.91 bits, calculated from the planning call's prints, and without it 92.36 bits, calculated from the planning call's prints (neither is taken from a run, and neither is a security level); these come from a calculator that is not in this repository; no program in it reckons a batch's joint count. A key file or a leaf file is judged once for all clients: the verifier draws nothing of its own, so a false file for which its maker has found favourable challenges, by tries on its own machine, passes in every client's run (by reading, not run).

column3: The programs' count of errors added over all rounds is for one call: one key file, one leaf file and one proof. It is no bound over all the leaf files whose proofs a client checks: each further leaf file adds its own rounds, so over several leaf files the total reads lower. The error of a single round does not move with the number of leaf files. Neither sum has a term for the number of responses a provider serves, and the fall of the stricter reading with the batch's size has no stated floor.

At full size 297 rounds at the default setting (reckoned by a planning call: `cp_verify -plan accounting` at the default's parameter file; the programs' own accounting, not a security level) are priced, in part or wholly, on a number that no check ties to the run at that round (at a lookup's rounds that number and the field's size are the formula's only inputs; at a batching the number of rows is compared at the round). The count covers only plans that the library's own planners make. At nine of the fourteen rounds in which one element's powers batch rows the plan and the run take the number from one source, so the comparison holds the form and not a second count. The rounds are counted by hand-set marks; some have been found too favourable, only those that were pointed at have been corrected, and there is no reading of all the marks, so the count may be too low.

Bad results on the proof library's own accounting, not on the released programs, on plans written out line by line, or made by the planners from a hand-chosen table size. The routine that says whether every round of a plan meets the target accepted, at a target of 128 bits, a round that samples positions (one column) or a random matrix and is given the error 0: under the mark that says that the round counts nothing, and under three further marks, under which the round also showed in no count of the rounds that rest on the caller's word; and the second routine that gives this verdict, the one behind the printed accounting, did not look at the mark at all. See rows SO-5.1, T7.1.11 and RES-51, and docs/limits.md#false-claims-in-test-programs. column3: `cp_verify` admits parameter files under which `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` cannot make files (the table's numbers in wider ranges). There are no honest files there, so no altered file and no malicious prover has been tried there, and whether a YES can be reached there has not been traced. Attention's list of lookup calls is one such freedom. The list is public data (the parameter file's lines callA: name, kind, segments). `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` take one list alone: KR {RM, RD}; KFD {FM, FD}; R16 {WL, IX}; WH {WH}. No parameter file in this repository has another list, and no proof has been made or checked under another. A run under another list that the verifier accepts can end YES all the same: no condition of the standard parameter form fixes the list. For some of the lines by which a writer could choose a laxer count of the error the standard form has a condition, for others it has none. By the source's own comment the lines on proof of work are an exception by design; by the same comment the key file's and the leaf files' closeness rounds rest on the theorem on codes, taken as given (row SO-2), and a call can still end `YES`. The parser holds the line rowcost at 1; it has not been shown that the conditions cover every other such line. For one such rule (what combining the rows of an interleaved word costs) the parser takes one choice, the laxest, on our own short argument, unrefereed (`blocks/numbers/setting.h`).

`cp_verify` admits more shapes of a weight table than the provers can make. `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` take 4 to 18 column variables and an odd number of random entries; the table's line names no radius, the committer's tests can run up to the Johnson radius, and these two programs' test on the numbers of opened columns does not run (read: the count of opened columns against what a row's random entries hide runs at a start and at each opening; no other cap on these numbers was found in the provers' sources or the proof library below 2^32); `cp_verify` takes 1 to 20 column variables and whatever sizes the proof library can lay out. For the wider shapes no honest files exist, so no altered file and no malicious prover has been tried there.

The released provers reject such a file themselves. With a `group omega` whose message has one entry, a planning call ends in a plain rejection (`NO: parameters-not-admitted`, status 1). No shipped file is such a file (at full size 202,048 is a multiple of 64).

No configuration of the programs, shipped or not, is known to meet all hypotheses of the theorems of a technical report that is not public and not refereed: the verifier's own tests do not imply them all, and the list has not been gone through for a configuration of the programs. The theorems are stated for every choice of public parameters that meets their hypotheses, so that report's protocol at another choice of parameters is covered in kind; the programs, at any shape, only through the comparison of programs and report. That every file which the verifier admits meets the hypotheses is not shown: that report's own table names forms of files that the verifier admits and for which it has no statement. No figure has been evaluated for a shape other than the full-size example's (they were evaluated at the default setting's own parameter file: row SO-1 says how far). One lemma of that report is the middle ground: the programs' constants and the verifier's tests on a parameter file's free lines together imply the size conditions of the theorems on the model's conditions, for every file under which the verifier accepts. Its hedges: but for one clause, which only completeness uses; at one point it does not apply to the programs to the letter; it is about inequalities only, and says nothing on lookups or range checks; that the verifier makes these tests is a reading.

The shipped full-size configuration is meant for synthetic weights. Its table of scales holds constants: each of its fields of scales has one value in every layer, as the file shows. By the project's own records, which are not in this repository, they were set down by hand. That none of them was picked with a fit to Llama 4 Maverick in view is not shown, and two sets of ranges were known when these constants were set down: ranges from fits to Llama 2 7B, and a second set, whose origin is not established (it is not known whether Llama 4 Maverick's weights had a part in it); the table's attention shift very likely stems from Llama 2 7B (inferred). Single values in the example files and in other files depend on Llama 4 Maverick's weights (that the weight files were public ones is likely; which files the fit read is not known), or were chosen with a model of Meta's in view, or may have been (THIRD_PARTY.md, "What depends on Meta's models"). A real model needs scales and some lines of the parameter file that are fitted to its own weights, so every proof about a real model runs under a configuration other than the shipped ones, for which the theorems' hypotheses have not been checked. For the commitment whose ID examples/maverick/expected.txt records, six of the route's eight stages (`needs`, `checksums`, `fit`, `commit`, `compare` and `prove`) were run one by one, on the real weight files, in three runs on three machines of one kind, not on the released programs, by forms of the script that differ from the shipped one and without the option `--width` (the route for files of 8 and 16 bits); `build` and `download` were not run, nor `all` (the script's one run with the released programs: docs/limits.md#what-was-run-on-these-programs). Two of the runs gave the same five values, byte for byte, the commitment ID among them (by report; not on the released programs); in the third, also not on the released programs, `compare` ended with exit code 0 against the `expected.txt` that ships, and `cp_verify` accepted its proof (by report). The two runs were not blind to each other: the values of one were at hand in the other while its `cp_commit` still ran (by the runs' account its commands had been fixed beforehand and contain none of these values); in the third run the five values stood beforehand in its copy of the repository. In the third run the peak while `cp_commit` ran was 310 GB and `bin/weight_sums` took 5.9 minutes, against 299 GB and under 5 minutes in each of the other two. That peak lies 10.8 GB above the larger of the other two, which is about one of the buffers of 10.74 GB that `cp_commit` holds while it checks the weights. When the check ended, 62 GB were freed in that run and 51 GB in each of the other two, which fits six buffers in that run and five in the others. That is inferred, not known: no count of buffers has been read, and the cause of the higher peak is not known. Plan by the 330 GB that the script itself asks for, a figure at which it has not been tried (row P5). While the script read the weight files in the third run, another process kept dropping their pages from the operating system's file cache. The fitted file's first 32 lines, which set the proof system, were compared with the default setting's on the file that two of the runs used, and they are the same; the file parts from the default's from line 33 on alone, in what the fit writes. An acceptance of a key file says that the committed word is close to one code word and that its entries meet the ranges and lookups that the public parameters name. Nobody checks that these are the right ones for a model, and neither the configuration's digest nor the commitment ID holds the routine that makes them: one has to judge the public files and the program's rule.

The commitment ID covers the configuration files, the commitment's first root and shape and the published OOD answers and the OOD seeds. Key files and leaf files travel with the proof and are checked against that root. That the sizing finds the least number of random entries, and the largest message length, is not proved under the Johnson rule, which the default setting uses; what it returns is always valid, so sizes may be larger than needed.

A no-overflow condition is a test on the public parameters, meant to ensure that an equation the proof checks modulo p also holds over the integers. A technical report that is not public and not refereed argues that its protocol's conditions suffice (the argument has not been checked independently); that the programs' conditions are the same, and that they suffice for the programs' equations, is not proved (SO-7, SO-9.1 say what they assume). For that report's own scored head, which differs from the programs' in points of form, so that its statements cover the programs' head only in part (row PS-16: the conditions as it writes them; not those the programs write otherwise, nor one identity), the lemma, theorem and corollary had one reader in the reading in shares that came nearest to reading that report whole (row PS-35.1), and no second set of readers. For the programs' output head no proof is known that its claims imply the statement over the integers.

The round called LINK is charged the larger of its two lists' errors, not their sum. That the larger is enough is argued on paper, in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, for its protocol, and has not been checked independently; for the programs' own LINK it is argued, and that argument has had no second reading. At the default setting LINK, as charged, has 129.57 bits with its proof of work counted (97.57 from the positions opened, 32 from the work: verifier/tests/known_answers/kit_rounds/target_full_f2.txt). Counted as a sum it would read between half a bit and one bit lower: at the default setting's full-size file still above 128 bits with the work counted; at its small example configuration, where LINK as charged has 128.77 bits (verifier/tests/known_answers/kit_rounds/target_small_f2.txt), it may read below 128 bits (about 127.8 if its two errors are equal there); the programs do not compute the sums.

The embedding's entries are proved by the key limb by limb only (each base-256 limb a signed byte, so a number within 32 bits), not within the 21 bits that the model states. The honest committer admits up to 2^30 - 1. What a prover gains from that downstream has not been examined.

A row of the stored weight table can have more message places than weight cells; `cp_commit` writes zeros there, but nothing shows that these places are zero in a table made by a malicious committer: the proof library's linear claims on the table stop at the last weight cell, and a leaf table is shown only to agree with the anchor there, so for a cheater these places are free coordinates, as the masks are (by reading). No test tries a table with these places filled (the cheating `cp_commit` of the tests that are not part of this repository can alter weight cells only), and whether they help a malicious committer or prover beyond what the code's dimension, which counts them, already allows for has not been examined for this protocol.

The masked sumcheck, the range check and the lookups inside a request's sub-proofs are, in the programs, a second implementation of what the library holds, so the library's tests say nothing about them; four error events of the sub-proofs have no round of their own. That the three are a second implementation is known from reading the source, and for `cp_prove` only from its files' head comments and includes; for the key file's proof of ranges `cp_verify` runs the library's own lookup.

The number of combinations in the test that committed cells are small comes from the parameter file's line tau. `cp_verify` takes it from the file, if it is one of the numbers that it serves (else hid-tau); `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` are compiled for one number and reject a file that has another (hid-tau). The library's plan has a number of its own: `cp_verify` rejects a file under which the two differ (plan-tau), `cp_prove` ends if the plan's differs from its own, and in both a guard of the library ends the run if a round draws a matrix of another number of combinations than its planned error is priced for. It has not been shown that these comparisons cover every way in which the numbers could part.

The lookup argument's chief error term, the number of keys over the field's size, is tight, not a loose estimate: with many equal foreign keys a false product identity holds at almost that many challenge values. Not known: whether a sub-proof's other checks allow a prover to present such keys.

Whether each of the verifier's checks is what stops some cheating prover has not been counted, but for one count, whose record is not in this repository, at the refusals of the kept calls (what a kept call is: row LIM-63.1) on the files of the committers edited to alter a stored table, which reached at most eight of the verifier's rejection names as a last line; at the other kept calls' refusals how many are reached has not been counted (row SO-15.7). That every planned round holds at the target is tested in one place, and no file or test has made that test fire on a sub-proof's round: a parameter file that asks for fewer than 128 bits is stopped earlier: a plain call under it is rejected (`NO: security-bits`), and only a call that itself asks for fewer bits gets past that test, to end NOT-A-VERIFICATION at best.

column3: Some digests are made by the second hash function, a fixed hash function built on BLAKE2b's compression function: a request's tokens with its two numbers and the public tables reach the proof's first hash call as digests under the second hash function. The request file's own words (the tokens, then the two numbers) go into that call, the first of the proof's first chain, as bytes too, as an item of their own, under BLAKE2b (read in the code; not run apart from one test). The statement's words themselves, all but the next token's, go in as bytes (the next token enters the chain in a round of its own) (read in the verifier's code; the prover's side was not read).

That another request (other tokens, or another range of checked tokens) gives another hash chain rests on BLAKE2b, and on the weak assumption that the second hash function does not disturb its standing as a random oracle, with the public files fixed beforehand: the request file's words are in the first hash call of the proof's first chain byte for byte (read in the code; not run apart from one test). The second hash function digests nine inputs of that call: the request file, whose own words stand there too, and eight public ones (the scale file, four public tables, three lists of look-up calls), none of which a prover can change after the commitment (docs/limits.md#what-the-theorem-assumes says what the theorems ask: public files fixed before the hash function is drawn): it is used as the fixed, public function that it is, not as a second random oracle; that it does not disturb BLAKE2b's standing as a random oracle is a weak assumption about the pair (by a reading; no formal proof); which four tables, bit for bit, a parameter file names hangs on the second hash function alone, on its collision resistance (docs/limits.md#what-the-theorem-assumes). A technical report that is not public and not refereed models both hash constructions together as one random oracle, which is argued nowhere, and its bound is stated under that assumption. The commitment ID and the digest that `cp_verify` prints as `configuration=`, and as `h_par=` in another written form, are not made by the second hash function. The hash that makes them binds the configuration files too. From reading the code, the second hash function's tree hash takes only the list, and no number or word that names its use: one list hashed for two purposes gives one digest. The digests of the four public tables and of the three lists are made by another call, which takes such a number; the four share one, the three another (verifier/HASHES.md). No exploit is known, and no search for one is known.

With the request file's own words in the first BLAKE2b query of a proof's first chain, and with the public files fixed beforehand, soundness against a prover asks of the second hash function only that it is a fixed, public function that does not disturb BLAKE2b's standing as a random oracle: it runs BLAKE2b's compression function under another counter word, so that is a weak assumption about the pair (row SO-14.1). One thing hangs on the second hash function alone: which four tables, bit for bit, a parameter file names, and so a commitment, since only their digests under the second hash function stand in the file. A verifier's verdict is about the tables that it computes itself and holds against those lines. Two verifiers, or a definition that takes the tables as data, speak of one function if their tables are the same; that both tables fit the lines shows this only as far as nobody can find two tables with one digest under the second hash function (collision resistance of the second hash function: an assumption of such a statement). That function is outside BLAKE2b's published analysis, and no attack on it is known.

No test was found that records under which domain-separation numbers a whole run of `cp_verify` really calls its two hashes (searched). `cp_verify` counts the compressions of both hashes and prints one total. As the programs are built, neither count is kept by number: the second hash function's source holds a count for each number, but it is compiled in only under a switch that nothing in this repository sets (read in the code; searched). The numbers are checked by value only: by known answers of single calls of both hashes; by second verifiers in Python, on toy files of the proof library; and by a reader written from the page on the format, which two tests in this repository have walk one honest proof of `cp_prove` each, at the tests' small configurations with and without proof of work. With its own copy of the numbers the reader forms each chain's first value and every round's query, tests the work, and opens the trees at the drawn positions. It is no verifier; it takes the parameter bytes of each chain's first query from a tool built on the programs' own code; and its functions for the request's item, which holds the digests made with the second hash function, were written from `cp_verify`'s source, so an error that the two share would not show there. No test has a reader of that kind walk a key file or a leaf file of `cp_commit` (searched).
