column3: Hostile tests on finished honest files ran on CPUs (not on the released programs), on synthetic weights, at small size but for one table of 40 rows, 32 of them hostile (a false commitment ID or a changed request, all refused; 7 honest rows accepted and 1 planning call), on the full-size example. The tests are of ten kinds of hostile act. Five are: a proof file altered item by item; single places altered in key, leaf and proof files; a request, a reply, or a reply changed to fit the altered request, beside an honest proof; files and parts of files crossed between honest sets; changed parameter files. The other five are: a false commitment ID; another honest request; a request with one token or one end of the covered range changed; one more token behind the checked range; a sixth line in `policy.txt`. `cp_verify` accepted only where a row is an honest call or, by the list's rule, reads byte for byte an honest call's files; and, the one case beside a file that is not honest, at 30 rows the partial check `-leaf` ends `PART PASSED: leaf` beside a key file in which later parts were swapped in from another key file: `-leaf` reads the leaf file and only the head, root and stored answers of the key file; the same swaps were refused by `-key` and by the full check; a partial check is no verification and never says YES. Not run in these tests: the largest round of other tests (key and leaf files altered item by item), hostile ways of calling, files grown to their size limits, and the rounds of other tests at full size. The lists that alter a proof item by item are thin: about 260 of some 303,000 items in each set were tried, all five sets at one configuration; a row is not always a different call; how many calls the hostile tests made in all is not told. Such edits show that items are bound, not that the protocol's equations hold against a lying prover. `cp_verify` refused all 703 calls that it was given on altered or hostile copies of the stored full-size example (`examples/full-size`, as it ships; not on the released programs; synthetic weights): one job on one CPU machine, run once, every call ending with exit code 1 and the last line that was expected for its kind (`NO: proof-refused`, `NO: key-refused` or `NO: entry-refused`; in the public test, the name that the test asks for); in each of the three parts the unaltered files passed the same calls. The three parts: the 23 altered sets of the public test `verifier.record_altered_sets.full`, one call each, the only part that ships (that row also passed in the runs of the public table: docs/limits.md#what-was-run-on-these-programs); 264 copies of the proof (202), the key file (48) or the leaf file (14), one whole call each: each opening of a file in turn (here: the opened columns of one tree after one round, with their salts and Merkle paths) left out, with the rest moved up (132), or left out and put at the file's end (129: a file's last opening put at its end gives the file itself back), and, once for each file, every opening that stands directly behind another left out together (3); and 208 leaf files, each given to the part-call `-leaf` and to the whole call (416 calls): 173 with a word that is no field element, 28 with a column's salt one byte too short or too long, 7 with a whole opening cut out. At least 8 of the 703 calls repeat another on the same bytes: those 7 files are the leaf file's 7 copies of the second part with an opening left out, and the leaf file has only one opening that stands behind another. The scripts that made the altered files of the second and third parts are not part of this repository, and they took the place of each opening from `tools/audit/cut.py`'s reading of the unaltered files. The job's log gives counts by exit code, last line and reason, not each call's own line. Such edits show that at full size the verifier does not pass over an opening that is missing or out of place, and that it refuses plain damage of these kinds; they are not a cheating prover's work (no hash chain and no Merkle path was made again in any of the 703), they touch one stored set alone, and they say nothing of soundness beyond it. A committer edited so that it alters a stored table behind the honest encoding (the edit is not part of this repository) made 70 lying commitments on one small synthetic model: in a table of 256 rows of 8,388,608 positions each (at the small example's parameter file as it ships (by its checksum in the runs' logs)) the symbols at a chosen number of positions, from 1 to all of them, were replaced in place. `cp_verify` was called 230 times on their files. The ending of each call was reckoned from arithmetic, which is no proved bound: a test that samples c columns of a table altered at d of n positions misses all of them with chance (1 - d/n)^c. `cp_verify` refused 175 calls and accepted 55. Some full checks accepted the files of a lying committer (not on the released programs; how the released `cp_verify` ends the kept calls: at this row's end): all 24 full checks on the 6 commitments that were altered at 1, 16 or 256 positions ended in YES. By that arithmetic such a check misses every altered position at least 996 times in 1,000; by a reckoning so few positions are also far inside the distance, 3,899,393 positions, below which a table is close to one codeword only, here the honest one; and in all 24 the request and the reply were those of the honest run. In 12 of the 24 the altered table was the leaf table (the second stored table, of which the leaf file speaks): they stood under the honest run's own commitment ID and key file, with a lying leaf file and a proof from an edited prover that follows the altered table. In the other 12 it was the anchor (the first stored table, of which the key file speaks), on 3 commitments: there the key file, the anchor's root and stored answers in it, and the commitment ID differed from the honest run's; and the four proofs, which the unedited prover made on each lying committer's files, came out byte for byte the honest run's: the same four proofs were accepted under four commitment IDs, the honest run's and the three (row LIM-2 tells these twelve checks, pair by pair). By the format's own pages a proof's hash chain takes the root and stored answers of the leaf table, as read from the leaf file, and neither the commitment ID nor the anchor's root; the leaf file's link ties the two tables by a sampled test. A look at the bytes of these four commitments' files, which ran no check, fits this: the four leaf files are equal in head, root and stored answers and differ only in what follows these, the link's proof, while the four key files' roots and stored answers differ; and the commitment ID reckoned from each key file by the format pages' own script is the one that lay beside it. By reading, not machine-checked, all 24 are the commitment's designed tolerance: a table that differs from the honest one at so few positions decodes to the same weights, so the accepted statement is true, and, where the altered table is the anchor, an honest proof verifies under such a commitment as under the honest one. That is a reading, and an argument on paper: this run did not test it (how that squares with these pages' claiming no binding for the programs: docs/limits.md, "Soundness, in short", the point "Accepted, though the committer lied"). The other 31 accepts were partial checks, which take no request and no reply, so no claim about an inference was accepted in them: 10 at small distances (where the anchor was altered at 1, 16 or 256 positions, the check of the key file and that of the leaf file, 6; where the leaf table was, that of the leaf file, 3; and 1 of the key file of a further commitment, in whose anchor each of the table's 256 rows was altered at one position of its own, so at no more than 256 positions); 15 of a key file that was byte for byte the honest one, because the lie was in the other table (3 of them at 1, 16 or 256 positions); and 6 of the key file alone at 113,239 positions, a distance chosen so that the 51 sampled columns miss every altered position half of the time (6 of 16 such commitments passed). Every call with a chance to pass of at most 2^-40 was refused, 121 of 121. So was every full check at 524,288 altered positions (one sixteenth of the table) or more, 104 calls on 26 commitments; for 24 of these calls, at up to 1,048,576 positions, the chance to pass was at most 1 in 700. In all 128 full checks the request and the reply were those of the honest run, so no false reply was tried in this run. In 60 of them the proof too was the honest run's, byte for byte; in the other 68 it came from an edited prover that follows the altered table, and the 56 of these that were refused were refused at the key file or the leaf file, not at the proof. `cp_verify` gave one reason for all 175 refusals, the table's proximity test (at the key file in 101, at the leaf file in 74), and the calls on one commitment meet the same key file and leaf file: the refusals fell on 43 different key files and 26 different leaf files, so they are not 175 different checks seen at work. The 43 and the 26 count files, not commitments: 57 of the 70 commitments were refused in some call, 45 at the key file (2 of these, in which both tables were altered, have byte for byte the key file of another of the 45, hence 43 files), 26 at the leaf file, 14 at both files; the other 13, refused in no call, are the 6 with full checks that ended in YES, the 1 in whose anchor each row was altered at one position of its own, and the 6 that passed at 113,239 positions. How many positions a commitment altered, and that no sampled column was altered in the 6 that passed, rests on a reading of the edit and on the edited program's own counts. Each setting was committed once, so every accept and every chance here is for one try: a committer that grinds, that is, spends work to draw new samples, was not built; against such a committer stand the bits that a technical report that is not public and not refereed counts for the rounds that draw the samples, proof of work among them: an argument on paper, not these runs. The honest commitments and proofs came from a build with test options. In this run 60 of the 260 rows (the 230 calls and 30 calls on commitments with no position altered) could end either way. A lie refused shows that this lie is caught, not that no lie passes: these are fixed lists, and no search was made for a lie that passes. Only `cp_verify` was tried outside test builds, and not on the released programs. Of an edited prover's 113 lies: `cp_verify` gave only two different reasons for the 113 refusals (109 and 4), both in the same stage, so they are not 113 different checks seen at work. Of five lying committers' 23 lies: 20 partial checks on such files passed; a partial check is no verification; for 17 of the 20, that the pass is right rests on a reading, which has not been checked on these files. One of the 23 is, by a reading, a consistent commitment to another matrix and not a false one: both partial checks passed it, and the one full check on it, with the honest proof, was refused. No false reply was shown to the verifier there and no proof was made to fit a lie: what a prover that cheats together with the committer could do was not tried in this run. (Row SO-15.5 tells runs with the same counts: 23 lies and 46 whole calls, and an edited prover's 113 lies; whether their lists are these is not known.) That each altered table behind the 24 accepted full checks is close to the honest codeword alone rests on arithmetic, an argument on paper and a run. A separate program, written after the format's pages and run on CPUs with none of the GPU programs, made the two stored tables of the honest run (the unedited committer of a build with test options): the anchor, of which the key file speaks, and the leaf table, of which the leaf file speaks. Its two roots, both tables' stored answers and the commitment ID are those in the honest run's files. By its construction each of a table's 256 rows is a Reed-Solomon codeword (8,388,608 positions, dimension 589,823, least distance 7,798,786) whose message holds, beside random masking values and zeros, the digits of the synthetic model's integer weights. Two further programs checked this. One took all 512 rows at all positions, out of the buffer that is hashed, and compared the polynomial through a row's symbols with the row's message at a random point (a row that is no such codeword passes with chance below 2^-41). The other reckoned each weight's place from the format's and the model's pages alone and found all 58,212,352 digits of the 28,844,032 weights at their places, and zero in every cell that belongs to no weight. With the rule of the edit put in, a copy of the separate program made the six altered tables: their roots are, byte for byte, the roots in the very key files and leaf files on which `cp_verify` had said YES. So, unless two inputs of BLAKE2b-256 collide, the table under each of the six roots is the honest table changed in exactly 1, 16 or 256 columns, and every one of its 256 rows differs from the honest codeword at exactly 1, 16 or 256 symbols. That is far below half the least distance (any count up to 3,899,392 is below it), so the honest codeword is the one nearest; every other codeword is at least 7,798,530 symbols away, beyond the Johnson radius (6,164,246 symbols), which bounds from above the radius that the verifier's test uses. This is a count of differing symbols; no decoder was run. By reading, not machine-checked, each of the 24 is a YES to a true statement. In all 24 the request and the reply were the honest run's, and the four replies are also those that this repository's integer model, a program by the prover's authors, gives on CPUs on the separate program's integers. The separate program is not independent. The synthetic model is defined by this repository's sources alone, and the program, like the check on the digits, takes in two of its headers (how a stored block is made, and how it becomes an integer weight), so a mistake there that the committer shares would not show; its writer knew parts of the programs' source; and the format's pages were themselves written from that source. Its integers are those that the prover's set-up rule gives; that the prover's GPU kernels compute with them is not shown. One seed; small size; synthetic weights. A committer built with the same edit made 80 further lying commitments on the small synthetic model. A further run made the six altered cases behind the 24 with newly built edited programs, beside three cases with nothing altered: all 162 public files of the nine cases came out byte for byte the same, so its 24 YES are the same 24, on the same bytes, and no new trial. In each of the 80, one stored table, the anchor or the leaf table, was altered behind the honest encoding at 257, 1,024, 4,096, 8,192, 16,384, 32,768, 65,536, 131,072, 262,144 or 524,287 of its 8,388,608 positions, in all 256 rows; by a reading of the edit, the stored answers and what the committer proves about the table followed the honest matrix. There were four commitments for each count and table, one under each of four test seeds, each made once. A commitment here is one run of the edited committer: a key file, from which the commitment ID is formed, and a leaf file. Where the anchor was altered (40 of the 80), key file, commitment ID and leaf file are the case's own, and the unedited prover of a build with test options made the proofs. Where the leaf table was altered (the other 40), the key file, and so the commitment ID, is that of the run with nothing altered under the same seed: what lies there is the leaf file, with proofs from a prover edited to follow the altered table. On each, `cp_verify` was called for four full checks (not on the released programs). The four meet the same key file and leaf file, and their four requests are proved in one batch, whose columns are sampled once, so they are one try; in all 80 commitments the four ended alike. `cp_verify` accepted 45 of the 80 (180 full checks said YES; not on the released programs; how the released `cp_verify` ends the kept calls: at this row's end), 22 with an altered anchor and 23 with an altered leaf table, and refused 35, at the key file, the leaf file or the proof. Of the 8 commitments at each count it accepted, in the order above, 8, 8, 8, 6, 8, 4, 2, 1, 0 and 0. There is no threshold: refusals begin by chance, far inside the distance up to which a table is close to one codeword only (3,899,392 positions). The least count refused was 8,192 and the largest accepted 131,072, which is 3.4 in 100 of that distance; both are the luck of these draws. That distance says what a YES means, not when a NO comes. Not the single endings but their chances were reckoned, from arithmetic that is no proved bound: with c = 102 in a full check for the anchor and 104 for the leaf table. By it 48 acceptances were to be expected; the 45 lay within the band of 35 to 61, and so did the number at every count (with 8 commitments a count those bands are wide and show little). In all 440 calls that met an altered table (the 320 full checks and 120 partial checks of a key file or a leaf file alone) the call passed if and only if none of its sampled columns was altered; how many were altered is the edited programs' own print, which no other program has counted. Every YES stood beside a reply equal to that of a run of the same edited programs with nothing altered. For every one of the 80 a separate counting program hashed the committer's stored leaf hashes up to the root in the public file and found them to differ from those of the run with nothing altered at exactly the stated number of columns; so, unless two inputs of BLAKE2b-256 collide, at most that many symbols differ in any row. And each altered root is the one that a copy of the separate CPU program told of above, with the edit's rule put in, gave from a table in which every row differs from the honest codeword at exactly that many symbols. The honest tables in that comparison are that program's: their roots are those of the edited committer with nothing altered at all four seeds, and of the unedited committer at one seed only; the check of every row at all positions was run at that seed only, and at the other three the rows are codewords by the program's construction alone. So, on the same condition, each YES was on a table that is close to the honest codeword alone, with every other codeword beyond the Johnson radius. One try each: a committer that alters, looks at the sampled positions and tries again was not built; against such a committer stand the bits that the report counts for the rounds that draw the samples, proof of work among them: an argument on paper, not these runs. Every committer and prover in these runs was a build with test options or an edited one. Small size; synthetic weights. Eleven cases put before an unedited `cp_verify` (not on the released programs) a stored table that is another matrix's, or lies 1 or 256 positions from it, and it refused all eleven, each at the check that was expected. In each case the other matrix differs from the committed one in one weight. In seven cases an edit replaced one of the 256 rows of the anchor (three cases), of the leaf table (three) or of both (one) by the other matrix's codeword, whole or but for 1 or 256 positions, while, by a reading of the edit, the stored answers and what the committer proves about the table followed the committed matrix: the four with an altered anchor were refused at the key file, the other three at the leaf file. All eleven ran on a cheating test build of the committer, which is not part of this repository, with an edit applied to it. In the other four the lie was named by that build's own test setting, and the edit altered no table. In three of the four the leaf table, its stored answers and everything that the committer proves about it followed the other matrix, under the key file and commitment ID of the run with nothing altered, and the cheating prover, set to change the same weight, made the proofs: the checks of the key file and of the request passed, and the check of the leaf file, which holds the link between the two tables, alone refused. In two of the three the committer also falsified its own side of that link, plainly (refused at the same check, one of them already at its opened columns); no link was built to pass. In the fourth the stored anchor and its opened columns followed the other matrix while, by a reading of the cheating build, its stored answers followed the committed one: refused at the key file. Behind the eleven cases stand seven different tables and nine different tries: the three hold one leaf table; and the fourth, the case in which the anchor's row is replaced whole and the case with both tables bear one key file, at which all three were refused. The roots of the seven cases' altered tables had been given before the run by a copy of the separate CPU program told of above, from tables in which that row lies 0, 1 or 256 symbols from the other matrix's codeword (a further checker counted this again). The fourth's anchor bears one of these roots, which was seen only after the run; the root of the three's leaf table equals that of a table which the CPU program made from their other matrix after the run. All these tables carry the honest table's own masking values and salts. In all eleven the reply was the one of the run with nothing altered. In the six cases that stood under that run's own commitment ID, cp_verify had accepted the same requests and replies under that ID, so what was refused there is a false table, not a false reply. The five with an altered anchor stood under key files and commitment IDs of their own; whether the reply is true of such an ID has not been reckoned. No reply known to be false was among the eleven. In all eleven the committer's own closing check, which calls `cp_verify` on the files that it has just made, had refused them too, and the edited cheating build went past that stop (by a reading, an unedited committer stops there). At most one try a case; one seed; small size; synthetic weights. One further run put false replies before an unedited `cp_verify` (not on the released programs). The liar was the first of the three told of above: its leaf table, that table's stored answers and its prover follow another matrix (one weight changed) under the key file and commitment ID of the run with nothing altered. The four requests were picked, out of 2,000, because on them, by this repository's integer model, the other matrix's reply differs (it did on 20 of the 2,000). A reply here is one token: it came out as 8, 235, 83 and 224 where the run with nothing altered said 228, 114, 114 and 452. cp_verify refused all four full checks, which are one try. Inside each, the check of the key file passed: it sees no reply, and the key file was the unaltered one. The check of the request passed each false reply with its proof: it holds a proof against the leaf table of which the leaf file speaks, and these proofs had been made over that false table. The check of the leaf file, which holds the link between the two tables, alone refused: every NO to this liar hangs on it. By a reading of the verifier's source that check sees neither request, reply nor proof, and key file and leaf file were byte for byte those of the case above, so this is no second trial of it. Beside the unaltered key file and leaf file each false reply was refused with the unaltered run's proof ("the proof is about another reply", 4 of 4): the one kind of call here in which the reply alone is false (that the files lay so is read from the runner; their checksums as they lay were not fetched). It was also refused there with its own proof (4 of 4: "a nonce does not give the proof of work that its round asks for"); the true reply with the liar's proof ended in the same words (4 of 4), so these eight calls are no trial of a false reply: they show that a proof made over one leaf table does not pass under another. That the four replies are false rests on two things, neither a proof: cp_verify accepted another reply for the same request under the same commitment ID, on files made by the same two builds with no lie set; and this repository's integer model, a program by the prover's authors, run on CPUs on the committed integers and on the other matrix's, had given all eight numbers. All GPU programs in this run, those of the unaltered run too, were the cheating test builds told of above: no released prover gave any of the eight numbers. One weight alone was changed, by one step of its stored code (from -44 to 44). Not run here: the two forms that also bend the link; a link built to pass; a prover that lies about the computation itself; a committer or prover that tries again. Small size; synthetic weights. No checksum of the parameter file was recorded for each commitment; for the eleven cases the jobs, not the cases, are tied to it. Not tried: a committer or prover that tries again until the sampled positions miss its lie; a link, key file or proof built to pass rather than made by the programs' own routines over false tables (no search was made for a lie that passes); a prover that gives a false value in a step of the computation under a cheating committer's commitment; a table that lies within the verifier's radius of two codewords, at this size; any run of a decoder; any of this at full size, on real weights, under another parameter file than the small example's, or with a production build's committer and prover. Not tried in these runs: another matrix that differs in more than one weight, or such a table under a second seed; the forms that bend the link, on a request whose reply moves; a false reply of more than one token; at 257 to 524,287 positions, both tables altered at once or some rows only; any count between 524,288 and all but 257 positions. No run, on the files of the 80 commitments, the eleven cases or the false replies, of a stand-alone program built from `verify-on-bytes` (row L14), which this repository does not build as one, is known. At toy size only (rows of 128 or 256 positions; the library's own test frame and its link check, not cp_verify; no radius and no proof of work priced) a first table of a link that agrees with each of two codewords at half of its positions was tried in 18 cases (not on the released programs); there the cheating committer did start again until the sampled columns suited it. Where the table's stored answers were one codeword's and the link followed the other, it was refused (6 of 6); by the cheating prover's own count the claim on the stored answers was the only false one, but the verifier's message names no claim. Where stored answers and link followed the same codeword it was accepted (6 of 6), and refused when a sampled column came from the other (6 of 6). 32 GPU tests with cheating programs, whose tables and scripts are not part of this repository, ran each once (not on the released programs), on small test models with synthetic weights. The default `cp_prove` runs in none of them: in 22 tests a cheating build of the prover makes the false proofs (in one of these on a cheating committer's files), in 10 a cheating build of the committer makes the commitment files (one of the 10 makes no false file and asks for no verdict), the honest files beside them come from a build with test options, and in the other 31 tests the verdict is that of an unedited `cp_verify`. A passed test shows that these particular false files were rejected once, and not that every cheat would be, and 11 of the 32 tests (among them 8 of the 10 in which the committer alone cheats) run at a parameter file for tests alone that asks for no proof of work, which the default setting counts; none of it has been checked independently. These 32 tests are, by report, the 32 rows that row SO-15.5 tells: the row on the joint lie, which failed there, by a reading through an expectation in its own script that did not fit and not through a fault of a shipped program, passed here in a changed form, in which the committer's lie reaches the OOD answers too: in each of its three scenes the request stage passed and the leaf stage rejected the joint lie; the two rows that were run by hand there went through the test runner here, and passed; 9 of these tests' own scripts and tables, the driver that 27 of them share among them, and the test runner differ between the two. At which parameter files the other 21 of the 32 tests run is not told. None of the runs that this row tells was made by an outside party, and none of their records has been checked independently. The released `cp_verify` was given all 2,720 kept calls (what a kept call is: row LIM-63.1): 2,672 ended with the exit code and the last line of standard output that the tests recorded, every call on the files of the committers edited to alter a stored table among them; 48, all on honest files with settings that the parser does not take, ended at the parser's refusal (`NO: parameter-range (policy)`), so they show nothing behind it; no call accepted what the tests' record refused. Of the tests that this row tells, only those with committers edited to alter a stored table are known to have calls among the 2,720 (the tests were not made on the released programs). 228 accepted calls are the four full checks on each of 57 kept sets of files (six of them, by the tests' records, a second making, byte for byte, of six others) in which an edited committer had altered one stored table at 1 to 131,072 of its 8,388,608 positions (in 29 of the 57 the leaf table: a lying leaf file, with proofs from an edited prover that follows it, under the key file and commitment ID of the run with nothing altered). By separate programs' counts of the changed columns (BLAKE2b-256 taken as collision-free), each of these tables lies far inside the distance (3,899,392 positions) up to which a table is close to the honest codeword alone, and each YES stood beside the reply of the run with nothing altered. Those counts measure from the table of the run with nothing altered; that this table holds the honest codewords was checked at all positions under one of the four test seeds only, under which 24 of the 57 stand. 72 passed checks of one part were of a key file or leaf file whose own table such an edit had altered, at up to 262,144 positions: 57 belong to the 57 sets of files, 8 to commitments whose four full checks were refused, at the other file or at the proof, and 7 to key files that were given no full check. A passed check of one part is not an acceptance. These grounds are those of the tests above, and their limits (small size, one try for each commitment among them) stand; the repeat adds only that the released `cp_verify` ends the calls on these altered tables as in those tests. The repeat's limits: these files only; of the verifier program's rejection names (304 in verifier/src/vf_rejection_names.txt; row T31.1 counts by another list, the project's own table of 309 names, which does not ship), at most eight, by a count whose record is not in this repository, are reached as a last line at the refusals of the calls on the files of the committers edited to alter a stored table; at the other kept calls' refusals how many are reached has not been counted; no hashed byte is shown unchanged on a path that no kept call walks; at the kept refusals it is blind, since those calls end just as a changed digest would end them. In a like repeat, not on the released programs, the same scripts, run with the `cp_verify` of those tests first, reproduced the kept endings; no such control is known for the released `cp_verify`. This shows only that the two programs end alike on these files. All of the files were made by other programs (row HW-678), on synthetic weights, or were written to the same bytes (in the like repeat each file was checked against a kept checksum); nothing was proved or committed again, and no cheating program was built from these sources or run. Where both programs accept, the test cannot tell whether either is right to.

column3: The masking is built in and on by default; a commitment made with the option `-public-weights` hides nothing. Where weight hiding stands: [docs/limits.md](limits.md#the-verdict). One search of public files ran, at small size, not on the released programs, and it is worth little by its own word: it found nothing, and on the first of its two sets its first look cannot see any fault of a pad at all. Hidden values did come out in other trials on other programs (row HW-678), as other entries here report. No theorem covers the programs, and `docs/limits.md` says what is proved about the protocol, and with which limits.

column3: The masking here differs from that of the paper that this protocol builds on, in at least these ways. Each variable of a sumcheck has a degree of its own and, in the programs, is summed in one of three ways (the hiding polynomial of blocks/iop/hp.h serves any linear functional): g(0) + g(1); (1 − z) g(0) + z g(1) at a public point z; or, for one further variable, g(0) alone. A summand may have any degree in the values shown at the sumcheck's end, and may also read, linearly, maps whose values are never sent. A map may also be one that is never sent as an oracle message but is a function of sent ones (a level of a product tree, a matrix times a vector). The masks on the values shown are carried by that further variable. A fold's fresh mask is an oracle message of its own, and the fold leaves it and the earlier masks as two separate rows. Where a mask row shares a tree with main rows, each of its symbols is copied into every leaf over its position; every leaf has a salt of its own. Also known: rows kept unfolded for a later step, and an out-of-domain sample for every oracle message but a fold's fresh mask and the last step's masking word. (The code of these forms lies, among others, in: blocks/iop/hp.h; blocks/iop/iopp.h and blocks/numbers/blocks.h; blocks/iop/psc.h and blocks/iop/summand.h; blocks/tree/.) Where this repository's files were not compared with the paper, more may differ. So the paper's results on hiding do not carry over by themselves. Lean proves statements on such forms, one block at a time, as Lean writes the blocks and under conditions on their parameters (lean/Cb/Ld/: the heads of LdHide.lean, LdPscZk.lean and LdSumZk.lean say what is proved and what is not). Not shown: that the blocks, put together as the programs run them, hide the weights. Lean's theorems on zero knowledge are about Lean definitions of the three provers, not about the programs' blocks, and a written proof of the whole, in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, is not settled (docs/limits.md, "The written proof").

The C++ types around mask entries guard that an entry is handed out once, and only after its message's sample has been answered. They do not see everything: looking at a slot's numbers does not use it up, so code can add one mask entry to two values. No honest run shows such a fault: every statement stays true, and what is lost is hiding.

Further things that the types around mask entries do not catch, by the header's own list: a slot taken in time can still be used after its ledger is closed; reading a slot's numbers does not use it up, so a prover's code can add one entry to two scalars, and a row can name a mask entry by its number without a slot; and a program that does not include send.h can define the access type itself (the type that lets only the sending routine issue the receipt from which a ledger is made). The sending routine cannot tell mask rows of fresh random values from mask rows that carry data, so whoever sends such a message must close its ledger; the routine that the header names as sending one, the switch from one code to another, closes it (read in the code) before the message joins its group. No honest run would show such a fault: both sides make the same calls, and the proof still verifies; what is lost is hiding. send.h adds that its access type stops mistakes, not intent: its routines are templates, so a program can hand them a channel of its own that swallows the answers, or specialize them; the real channel lets no round be closed while answers are owed.

A routine that makes masks or salts under a weight table's key ends the run if it is handed no key, or a key of 32 zero bytes (`own-test-zero-key`; exit code 4 in `cp_commit`, 9 in `cp_prove`). By a reading of the code, every host routine that hands a table's key to a GPU kernel goes through that stop before the key is used (`refuse_the_zero_key()`, prover/hash_commitment/hf_mask.cuh), and no kernel that makes masks or salts has a form without a key. On some roads a missing key ends the run before it reaches that stop, under another name: where the pads on the OOD answers are drawn, `own-test-pads` (row H47.8); where a table is opened, an internal check; the plain second implementation, which gets the key's second copy, aborts if it is handed none, and its callers fail their self-check before that (row H47.8). That every such routine goes through the stop is a reading. One run bears on the stop itself: a test that is not part of this repository hands no key to `key_for_a_launch()`, through which the others go, to `masks_of_rows()` and to two routines that only tests call, not to the routines that call these, and asks for that end; not on the released programs it has run once, compiled apart from the programs from a copy of other sources (row HW-678), on synthetic data, and every one of its 566 checks ended as expected; of three tests in that run that are not in this repository the runner marked two as failed, against wrong counts in its own table. Nothing but the sources ties that program to a build. No run of `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` has been seen to end there. The stop sees that a key is missing or all zeros, and nothing else about a key. Two calls pass a null pointer that does not stand for a table's key, and do not reach the stop: `mask_limit(nullptr)` asks for a number, and `hf_mask_columns()` without a key takes masks that were made under the table's key. That `make_table()` has one caller is, by the source's own word, a rule, weakly guarded.

Several things that depend on the weights or the requests are shown on purpose, among them the architecture, all sizes, the rough size of the largest weights, whether a request was served, and timing. The list holds only while what an operator sees (logs, causes, counts, `cp_commit`'s verdicts), and whatever an operator visibly does because of it, stays with the operator.

How many rounds occur, and whether time shows them, has not been measured. Parts of NVIDIA's CUDA Toolkit are linked or compiled into the GPU kernels (cuBLAS, cublasLt, CUB, cooperative groups, wmma, pipeline primitives). The requests that `cp_prove` proves in one pass over the weights share the GPU code's working buffers, but each has things of its own in GPU memory, among them a proof transcript object, allocated once at set-up, and a buffer that keeps its state between its turns. This index is not the place in the batch's hash tree, which a proof states. Which kernels take such addresses is not known: they have been neither listed nor counted.

The CPU code that builds the batch's hash tree indexes its arrays by each request's place in that tree, and the places are a random arrangement that is meant to hide the order of arrival (read in the code). So CPU memory addresses, and with them possibly time and cache traffic on the provider's machine, follow that arrangement; how much of it they show has not been measured. Each proof states its own place.
A threshold of a score policy that is measured on the model's own costs is a function of the weights, and it is published with the parameter file. What it reveals has not been worked out.

`cp_verify` does not check whether a mask is there, and for most masks it cannot: no run of a verifier, by a client or a third party, can check hiding. Only a program or machine fault loses a mask, but if that happens before the prover commits to it, the proof can verify with the value exposed. If it happens after that, by readings of the code the proof is false (argued, not proved), and `cp_prove` releases it all the same (rows H3.18, H26). At the default setting's small form, on more than one set of test builds of other sources, runs on one fixed sample gave the same outcome, loss for loss (one witness, not several; the table that is stored with the test is one of these runs' print; rows LIM-63 and LIM-63.2, line 3): of 165 losses injected in CPU memory 30 went unnoticed and after 12 more the files were byte for byte those of an honest run; all 130 in GPU memory were stopped by a self-check. That is no rate. No case of the sweep loses one of the pads on the out-of-domain (OOD) answers (masked sums of the weights). What an unnoticed loss exposes this test does not show. By two readings, made apart, about ten minutes each, of other sources, with toy computations and nothing run on the programs, none of the 30 exposes anything of the weights by itself, as long as every other random value is there, but for one case, the loss of a batch's salts: whether that exposes anything is not known. The written proof of hiding counts some of the 30, or values of their kinds, as random or fresh: a run that has lost one lies outside what that proof is stated for, and what that costs is not known. Not tried: a loss later than right after the draw; of a draw's parts any but its last cell. The test passes when every run ends as its stored table says, including the runs in which the proof verifies and no check notices the loss. So a pass records which check, if any, notices each loss; it is no sign that losses are caught.
