column3: In each sub-proof with weights one value has no mask of its own, and an entry of the request's table of masks covers it. By the code's own comment a proof made with that table's values lost between sampling and sending sends that value, a linear form in the weights, unmasked. A self-check looks for this loss; it has limits of its own, listed in this row, and the loss has not been tried on the released programs. The self-check looks at the whole table. By the code's comment the test on the weight table reads entries of the table as masks of sums that are linear in the weights. The check's limits (read in the code): it skips the places of one other mask, which a check of their own reads back; it does not see the copies of the table that were handed on for encoding before it runs; and it misses a fault that the sampling and its second implementation share.

In each sub-proof with weights one value has no mask of its own, and an entry of the request's table of masks covers it. Read in the code: nothing tests that mask for zero, on purpose by the source's comment; the self-checks compare it with the sampled value instead. The comment's first reason: a program that rejects a zero mask does not sample the mask uniformly, which is what the written hiding argument (unpublished) assumes. The comment calls this an argument, not a proof. Its second reason: such a stop would leave the GPU unusable, so that the wipe of GPU memory at the program's end would fail.

`cp_prove` compares every leaf's salt of the hash trees that its GPU engine builds, as it lies in GPU memory right after a tree is built, with the generator's values computed again, and ends the run at a difference (read in the code). It does not see a kernel that reads a salt wrongly, nor a fault in the code that the comparing and the drawing kernels share; the salts of the tree that binds a batch are not compared.
No self-check sees a mask that is there and wrong by the rule itself: a second computation by the same rule agrees.

The leaf tables' own random entries and salts mask the weights themselves. While `cp_commit` makes a table, it compares the random entries by value (samples against a second making, every entry against a second implementation) in its first pass over the table only, and compares no salt; in the routine that writes opened columns each opened column is made again from the key and must fit the stored hash tree, and its salts are compared with a second making, before any of it is written out (read in the code) (what is written comes from a second read: row HW-574). These checks do not see a fault that is alike in the kernels that make and that open a table, which would verify and leak, or a salt at a column under a stored hash-tree node below which no column is ever opened (an opening hashes all columns under the opened column's lowest stored node again and compares each of their salts with a second derivation: read in the code).

Some faults are no losses, and a self-check that computes a value a second time by the same rule agrees with them: a mask that is never generated, a value that is used twice, a rule shared by prover and verifier that masks too little. None of the three has been tried on the released programs. The public test that compares the two programs' readings (row H19.3) is of that kind: it holds what the prover's code derives from the three public files against what the verifier's code derives from them, and both sides reckon with the one proof library (blocks/), so a wrong number in that library's own reckoning of a shape is the same on both and is not seen (read in the code). Only one of the generators of random values ends a run in which a cell is drawn twice. Against numbers that mask too little, all three programs test ten conditions on the parameter file at every start and reject a file that misses one (read in the code). That test looks at numbers only: it does not see whether the places are filled, whether the ten are the right ones, or a rule in the code itself: against some rules of that kind the proof library has six run-time guards (read in the code), and a test at toy size with six faulty layouts made for it (blocks/tests/hiding/guards_test.cpp): `make test` runs only their valid counterparts; the faulty layouts are built only from a list that is not part of this repository, and they have not been run on the released programs.

A mask that is lost while `cp_commit` makes a commitment leaves a value exposed for as long as that commitment is in use. So both programs compare a table of masks (but for the places of the one-time masks in it), and the random bytes at its end, with what was drawn, right after they send it. `cp_prove` does so for each request, and `cp_commit` for both such tables of the key file. No such check has been seen to fire in the production build.

The zeros of the filler cells of a request's matrices are written twice and counted before committing. What set-up wrote is written again in every sub-proof's run by one kernel, k_fork_memory_repeat, which has eight kinds of launch. Of what it writes only the layers' shared list is written twice, and of attention's own list only the five matrices. What the launches for a sub-proof's own list, for the middle of a layer sub-proof's run and for a run's late part lay is written once: a buffer there that is read in part without being written would be a quiet place, in which a hidden value that the previous sub-proof had left can lie, and whether there is one is not known. Whether the released programs' checking and zeroing kernels could silently not run, where a kernel launch is swallowed and nothing notices, has not been tried (the tests that leave out a launch: row T11.3.1). By a reading of these sources that went by the kernels' names, not through every kernel: a check whose count must reach a value (the two counts of row H18.1.1) would see that its own launch was lost in silence, and so would a check whose values the CPU reads back and compares, unless that memory already held the expected values; a check that only raises a flag would not (the comparison of attention's cells, row H3.18.2; the forward pass's flags, which were not read one by one); and, the filler cells' zeros apart, nothing reads wiped GPU memory back in a production build. A check or a wipe of these last two kinds whose launch is lost does not run, and nothing says so. The count of the filler cells' zeros is the prover's check on itself: it does not see a write that comes after it (row HW-692), and a launch lost at these cells has not been tried on the released programs.

A fault in the generator of random values, or on the masks of the claims about the weights: whether the self-checks of the released programs would stop either has not been tried. Such a fault can strike every proof alike, and each proof then gives exact equations in hidden values (what that is worth: row HW-445). A bug or failing hardware might cause such a fault, and no one has looked for a way a client could.

In the test that injects the loss of random values (row H3.1), the list of samplings has lengths and no names, so it is not known whether every kind of random value was hit, and the sub-proofs' masks and the leaf tables' random entries, which come from other generators, are not in it.

The spot check on fresh random values reads four values of each sampling. It does not see any other value, whatever happens to the values later, or a wrong key. From reading the code, for a sampling of one element, which most are, it reads a temporary copy.
The search that looks at every value of a proof for zeros, small values and repeats cannot see a missing mask under a value of full size.

Every hash tree that the proof library or the GPU engine makes must give each leaf a salt of 40 to 64 bytes, or the program ends (for the proof library: `OracleTreeShape::valid()` in blocks/tree/opening.h, and blocks/tree/tests/tree_test.cpp, which asks that a shape with no salt is not valid). The programs enforce the length. Where the GPU engine does not keep the salts, the salt of a leaf that is never opened is looked at once at most: `cp_prove` compares every leaf's salt with the generator's values right after a tree is built, and only under the GPU's own generator (rows H3.3 and HW-344 tell this, from a reading of the code); no self-check looks at it later, and, from reading the code, `cp_commit` compares every leaf's salt of the hash trees that its GPU engine builds with the generator's values, computed again, once each tree is built, and judges the outcome before the key file's or a leaf file's bytes are returned (a tree that is made again gets no such comparison: row HW-558); of a stored table's own hash tree, whose salts the hashing kernel derives from the table's key and writes nowhere, it compares only the salts of the leaves that it computes again to open the drawn columns (these and their neighbours), and no others. A leaf table's tree has 40 bytes a leaf, and `cp_commit` makes every table under a key: a routine that is handed none ends the run (row H1.4: read, not run); under one injected fault a test build hashes the salts of a fixed public key into a table's leaves, not the table's own; the tree over a batch's requests must have 40 to 64 bytes a leaf as well. One tree hash of `cp_prove` has no salt. A search found it used only on a request's tokens and the two ends of its checked range, which are the client's own, and on the public configuration files. A routine that builds a hash tree without the library lies in the sources (`node()` in prover/common/hash_tree.cuh); a search found nothing that calls it (read and searched, not run).

No self-check of `cp_prove` looks at the CPU's fetched copy of a sub-proof's masks, which is the copy that the proof commits to. By the sources, after a loss in that copy every value still lies under the true masks on the GPU, and the proof is false: `cp_prove` runs no verifier, so the response is released, and it is a verifier outside `cp_prove` that rejects it (row H26). It is not shown that such a false proof, taken as a whole, gives away no pad. This row rests on a reading of the sources, not on a run.

In `cp_prove`'s layer sub-proofs and in its head sub-proof, two GPU kernels compute the sums from which the checks of the norms start, and store them with their masks already added. A test build can be told to skip these launches, as an injected fault; no test does, so no run shows how the released programs end when such a launch is lost. By reading, not run: a launch that the driver rejects ends the program; after a launch that is lost in silence the message keeps in those places what was there before (the source says so itself), so no sum goes out without a mask, but the sums that are sent are not the true ones. What those places held before has not been followed to the end (by a partial reading: zero, or a value that an earlier sub-proof had already sent), nor whether the sumchecks that start from these sums still mask all that they send after such a loss. Nothing in `cp_prove` stops such a response: where its proof is false, it is a verifier outside `cp_prove` that rejects it (row H26).

After the forward pass of each attention sub-proof, `cp_prove` compares that sub-proof's own cells of q, k, v and o with the cells that the layer sub-proof kept after committing to them; a difference marks that one request with a failed self-check (read in the code). No test of the suite runs this comparison on a changed cell: a test program with a mode that changes one such cell is run by no test, and one test checks, by text only, that the line with the comparison is still in the source. By comments in the sources, which were not followed into the verifier's code, if the comparison did not work, a stray write into these cells would give a proof that `cp_verify` rejects; nothing else in `cp_prove` would meet it, and the response would be released (row H26), where the comparison is meant to fail that one request. The check by text is part of this repository; the test program is not.

`cp_prove` compares each sub-proof's mask entries by value with two further derivations: one on the GPU, by the routines that derived them, and one on the CPU, separately written. Both look at the array of entries in GPU memory, the last time after the entries' last use; neither looks at what the masking routines did with an entry. So both pass a correct mask entry that is never added to the scalar that is sent, one that is added to two scalars, and one that a routine read before it was written: the sources' own list says so of the CPU comparison, and of the GPU one it follows from what it looks at (read in the code, not run; whether such a proof would still verify the comments at the two comparisons do not say; for a value that is sent without its mask entry, a GPU test that is not part of this repository expects `cp_verify` to reject it, in 20 cases: 13 at the first values of the first sumcheck of a place where values are sent, 5 at a sumcheck's end values and 2 at values that are sent alone). The sweep of injected losses, a test of this project that is not part of this repository, overwrites one random draw in each run, so its counts say nothing on two faults in one run.
`cp_commit`'s self-check on a key compares one 32-bit word that is derived from the key, not its 32 bytes: by the source another key passes about once in 2^32.

`cp_commit` derives each table's key and the key file's key a second time from the seed's file on disk and compares. A leaf file's key gets no such check: it is compared only with a second implementation that is fed the seed from memory.

The self-check that samples freshly drawn random values moves its middle sample places by eight bytes from the system's generator, drawn once in a process, so that other runs look elsewhere. If that call fails the bytes are zero and the places are fixed ones.

Hiding depends on duties of the operator that no program can check: one secret key directory, never copied, restored or rolled back; a machine or process that is never cloned or resumed; a sound random source that does not repeat; a local disk that honours fsync.
column4: Follow docs/operators-duties.md to the letter. Never run on this directory a program that opens a leaf table and does not count.

column3: If a batch's random values come a second time under other data, two messages under the same masks can be subtracted, and every proof still verifies; no program notices a repeat of the 32 bytes from which they come. By the source, the production build's `cp_prove` takes 32 fresh bytes from the operating system for each batch, never from a file, and derives the batch's key from them, the seed, the configuration and every request of the batch: so a retry, a restart or a rolled-back secret key directory does not bring a batch's own masks back, and under repeated bytes other requests get another key. (A leaf table's random entries are another matter: they serve many batches, only the directory's count of shown columns guards them, and a rolled-back directory rolls that count back.) A repeat therefore takes the same 32 bytes, the same secret key directory and the same requests in the same order, which needs a faulty random source or power over the machine, for instance a machine image or snapshot that runs on twice. Whether two such runs of the released programs can differ without a fault is not known.

That a process copied after it has drawn a batch's random bytes gives the same bytes as the original rests on three requirements: wherever parallel operations combine values, the arithmetic is exact; floating-point steps work on one element at a time, in a fixed order; and nothing that is computed depends on the order in which threads arrive. Other sources (row HW-678) were read for this once, and not all of them; as far as that reading went, the arithmetic was exact wherever parallel operations combined values, and of three kernels that give out places in a list in the order in which threads arrive nothing that was computed depended on the places; the rest of the code, among it the code that makes the weight table and its masks, the folded rows and the lookups, was not read for it, and the reading has not been made on the released programs: for them it is a requirement that has not been checked by reading. Where the two runs did differ, the same masks would lie over different data.
column4: Never let two runs continue from one saved state.

column3: If two runs under the same masks differ, the equations that go out would not be in the weights alone: what the part of a batch's proof that all its requests share commits to is a combination of whole rows of the leaf table, and a row holds weights and the row's random entries, which serve every batch of that table's life; so what is sent of it twice under the same mask entries, subtracted, gives equations in both. Such a loss cannot be undone: the weights do not change, a table's random entries are never renewed, and no counter sees it, because `cp_prove` counts only the opened columns of the batches that it begins. (Reasoned from the source's description of that message; how much could be read from such equations has not been worked out, and nothing was run.)

No program notices if one machine image or snapshot is started twice, or a running one is resumed, and the system's random source then repeats, because the seed and a leaf table's 32 random bytes, like a batch's, are tested only for being all zero (the seed also for being one of the tests' fixed seeds), and by the source no table's key depends on the weights. Both machines then build weight tables with equal random entries and salts. With the same weights, that is one table under two counters. With different weights under the same three configuration files, that is two tables under two roots, and whoever sees the same column of both (columns are shown in proofs and leaf files and, for the anchor, in key files and leaf files) can subtract the two and gets exact linear combinations of the differences between the two sets of weights, with no mask on them. If `cp_commit`'s random bytes repeat over other weights, the two commitments' public files alone give, for good, one exact linear equation on the two sets of weights for every row and stored answer (in the weights themselves, if one of the two sets is known), with no proof served. (Row H47.4; more: row HW-584.) Over the same weights, which is the case at a renewal, a repeated seed gives the same key file's table and the same ID again; where the leaf tables' own random bytes repeat too, the second commitment is the first again with its counts at zero, and its masks would then be used beyond the limit for which they were sized.
column4: Never let two runs continue from one saved state. See also docs/operators-duties.md#a-new-commitment, step 3.

column3: The only test on a batch's 32 fresh random bytes is that they are not all zero.

No verifier can see a breach of the committer's rule that the same randomness never goes under two roots: the committer's own program has to keep it. Nothing of the rule or of its reasons is proved; the reasons are argued on paper only. Tests look at how `cp_commit` keeps the rule, not at its reasons. One, which is not in this repository, reads `cp_commit`'s sources by patterns (ten rules on which code may draw the secret bytes from which a table's random values are derived, and which code may build a table, with injected breaches that it must see): that is a reading by patterns and no proof, and a writer who means to can go round it.

The rule that the same random values never stand under two roots is one of several that `cp_commit` must keep for hiding, and no verifier can tell from the finished files whether it kept them. One kind is an exception: `cp_verify`, like `cp_commit` and `cp_prove`, rejects configuration files that miss one of the conditions that hiding asks of a parameter file (`parameters-not-admitted`; read in the code); nothing in a proof itself would show a missed condition: it is the files that are tested. The sources' comments say of the keys and the random values that what was made with one of them broken is still accepted; of the other rules the same follows because `cp_verify` sees finished files only (reasoned). (But for the exception, read in the sources' comments; the routines behind them were not read for this; not run.)

The other rules that `cp_commit` must keep for hiding, as its sources' comments state them: in what order a run goes and what reaches the disk when (the seed is drawn only after the weights have passed their checks; no key file, leaf file or stored node is written before `cp_verify` has passed its bytes in memory); that a finished leaf table is never made again (a secret key directory that is set back or copied can lead to a second making, and no program sees that; `cp_commit` makes a commitment and its leaves in one call and rejects a call that would add a leaf to a commitment that stands); that a run which stops counts for nothing and is not continued: `cp_commit` takes away what an ended run has made and rejects a start beside what a killed one has left, and the rest is the operator's rule, which no program enforces; that every secret is drawn fresh from the operating system for one table or one file and serves no other; that every row has enough random entries for all that is opened of it, which all three programs test on the parameter file's numbers and the provider's programs alone on the running count, and with no margin for a table's opened columns; and that one seed serves one anchor, each table with a count of its opened columns that counts in one directory only. (Read in the sources' comments; not run.)

If a batch's random bytes repeat, a client can test guesses at its former neighbours' requests. A client that can fill the batch's other places with such guesses resends its request. Its new proof is made with the same random values, and so holds the same salted digests, exactly when every guess is right (this is reasoned from the key schedule and has not been tried). The bytes repeat when a saved state runs twice or the random source repeats, but how much of this a count that has moved on prevents has not been worked out. So the condition against running a saved state twice also protects clients' requests, even where the weights are public, as long as the seed is still secret (under `-public-weights` it is not, and nothing is claimed to be hidden in that mode). Under repeated bytes the leaf table is no fresh draw either: its number is computed from the same key, so with all else equal it is a fixed function of the list of requests (read in the code).
column4: Never let two runs continue from one saved state.

column3: What a batch's key takes in, and what it does not (read in the code). The key from which all random values of a batch are derived takes in the seed, the batch's 32 random bytes, the digest of the three configuration files, a number that stands for the state of `cp_prove` (`the prover's revision`), the number of leaf tables and the first one in use, every slot's request and, in a second step, the drawn leaf table's name. The four public lookup tables that `cp_prove` computes at its start with the machine's floating-point library enter it through their digests in the parameter file: where the file has these lines, a computed table with another digest ends `cp_prove` at set-up, and for a model with experts `cp_prove` does not start without them; only under a file without the lines do the tables stay outside the key. It does not take in the weight files as this run reads them, or the options by which a batch is run (how many requests share a pass over the weights, how memory is used, whether batches overlap), which are meant to change no byte of a proof. If the 32 bytes repeat for the same requests and one of these differs between the two runs, the same mask entries can cover different data (reasoned); whether one of `cp_prove`'s self-checks would catch that has not been examined; `cp_prove` runs no verifier. The key takes in which programs run only through that number and the format's version word. Whoever makes a change after which `cp_prove`, on equal inputs, sends another byte or draws its random values in another order or number has to raise the number by hand, and nothing in the programs or the tests checks that. Where it was forgotten, two states of the programs on one secret key directory would, under repeated bytes and equal requests, put the same masks under different challenges with no fault (reasoned; docs/format/COIN-KEYS.md, section 2, at `the prover's revision`).
column4: Never let one saved state of a machine or a process continue twice (docs/operators-duties.md, "Read this first", rule 3).

column3: On a rented machine you may not be able to know whether the host saves and resumes its state (snapshots, live migration). That case was not examined.

No program marks a commitment as given up. Where the counter file of a leaf table in use is missing, or is not a plain file that belongs to the serving account alone, `cp_prove` itself rejects: it serves none of the commitment's leaf tables, at every start and before every batch, for as long as the file stays so, and it never creates the file (read in the source; a test that is not part of this repository asks for these rejections). Where a counter was set back, or replaced by a shorter file that looks right, no program can see it and the directory is served: then it is for you alone to see that this secret key directory serves no further batch.
column4: Treat a leaf table whose counter is lost or doubtful as used up: switch off whatever restarts `cp_prove`, stop every `cp_prove` on the directory, wait until each has ended, and make no further call on it (docs/operators-duties.md, "If the count is lost or in doubt").

column3: Several machines need one commitment each. Which commitment serves a request is visible, so do not let that choice depend on anything that must stay hidden.

A machine that is booted afresh from an image is no case of a saved state that runs twice, if the system seeds its random generator freshly at every start and the image holds no secret key directory. No program can check the first condition, and an image can carry a saved seed file for the system's generator. "Booted afresh" does not cover a machine that is resumed from a snapshot of a running machine, a process that is restored from a checkpoint, or a clone that is made after the boot. A container shares its host's generator, so what matters is how the host was started. What a fork that comes from outside the programs, or a checkpoint of a process and a restore from it, does with the state that the C library may keep for `getrandom()` has not been examined for these programs, and for the sake of these draws no version of that library or of the kernel is asked. From version 2.41 on, and in some distributions' packages from 2.39, the GNU C Library may answer `getrandom()` without a system call, from a state in the process's own memory. For such packages in Fedora 40, Fedora 41 and CentOS Stream 10, CVE-2025-0577 records a fault: after a fork that runs concurrently with a call, a later call may return predictable bytes. The seed, the 32 random bytes of a leaf table's, the key file's and a leaf file's commit run, and those of every batch come from `getrandom()`. (What this says of the library, the kernel and the CVE's record has not been checked a second time.)
column4: Ask of your system, image or hypervisor whether it seeds the random generator freshly at every start: that was not examined here. Use a C library in which CVE-2025-0577 is fixed.

column3: `cp_commit` makes all leaf tables in one call and rejects every call on an existing commitment (read in the source), so to make one leaf table a second time under its number needs a call that it rejects. The code of the rejected call is in `cp_commit`'s source, with the rules that it was written to keep: a leaf table that exists is not made again; its kept leaf file is published, or the call is rejected by name; each making has masks and random values of its own. No test runs that code in the whole program, and by the source's own comment it reads a record that the key file does not hold; a program that allows the call rests on these rules, and no test for them is in this repository. Whether `cp_commit` could finish a key file or a leaf file a second time inside one call, from hash trees that it has kept, which, by what row PS-40 says of the protocol, would open further positions, is not known: its code was not read for it.

A leaf table serves a limited number of batches, and the programs count for each leaf table by itself: at full size up to 688,127 batches at the default setting (a batch opens 64 columns), by the planning call as the tree's pages print it. As soon as one leaf table has no room for a further batch, `cp_prove` takes no further batch on any; `cp_commit` cannot add a leaf table to an existing commitment, so the commitment must then be made again, with a new seed and a new commitment ID, and two commitments to the same weights have not been searched together. The count of opened columns leaves no margin: by the source a leaf table may show, over its whole life, exactly as many columns as a row of it has random entries (44,040,191 at full size, the 62 columns of its own link among them). These are the programs' own figures, for one leaf table. It is not proved for the programs that the counter keeps a table within its limit, or that staying below the limit is enough (what is proved about such a limit, and of what: guide/weight-hiding.md; docs/limits.md#what-lean-proves).
column4: Choose the number of leaf tables when you make the commitment so that they last, and make and publish a new commitment before any one of them is full. A further commitment to the same weights, under the same configuration files, lies inside the judgement on weight hiding, on thin ground and on [conditions of its own](limits.md#a-further-commitment): a count over two small commitments, not on the released programs, found no derived random value twice (a check for gross faults only), and no test has searched two together for leaks.

column3: A batch that fails, is aborted or is killed counts against its leaf table's limit too. The one exception is a batch that a power loss ends before its opening has begun, which may drop out of the count again, but such a batch has not shown anything. Every proof holds its table's number, so anyone who collects proofs can count a lower bound on each table's use. That count can show that a table is near or past its limit, but never that it is not.
column4: Read the limit `cp_commit` prints; plan the new commitment early. A further commitment to the same weights, under the same configuration files, lies inside the judgement on weight hiding, on thin ground and on [conditions of its own](limits.md#a-further-commitment): a count over two small commitments, not on the released programs, found no derived random value twice (a check for gross faults only), and no test has searched two together for leaks.

column3: A written proof of hiding, which its authors call "complete but not settled" (what that means: row PS-23), in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, covers a further commitment to the same weights only on conditions that no program checks, and it leaves some cases out for more than one commitment (row PS-40). That part speaks of a narrower prover than the released one: it does not take in one program run on all places of a batch at once, or a single proof withheld at a rare challenge. It asks of every commitment all that is asked of one, and among other things: a secret seed of its own for each, drawn independently; one configuration for all, the scales included; weights that were fixed in advance; and a count of its own for each, never copied or restored, which moves in every batch. No program checks these conditions. No test has searched two commitments together. A further commitment to the same weights, under the same configuration files, lies inside the judgement on weight hiding, on thin ground and on conditions of its own (docs/limits.md#a-further-commitment): a count over two small commitments, not on the released programs, found no derived random value twice (a check for gross faults only). (Among which matrices the written proof hides: row PS-28.)
column4: At a renewal keep the configuration files unchanged. Never copy or restore a secret key directory, and never let one saved state of a running machine run on twice, so that no seed serves two commitments. Keep every old secret key directory secret for as long as it exists.

column3: Past a leaf table's limit the opened columns give equations in the weights without masks (row H21.11); whether weights can be solved for from them has not been tried on the released programs (what such proofs give away: rows HW-544 and HW-584). No client can bring a crossing of a leaf table's limit about: it takes whoever writes the provider's parameter file before the commitment, whoever can write, copy or roll back the provider's secret key directory, or an accident: a disk or a repair that lost what a sync had promised, or a machine that was cloned. None of these ways to a crossing has been tried on the released programs.
column4: Read the line "the limit:" that `cp_commit` prints before you publish: `cp_commit` rejects only a limit of no batch at all. Let one account only write the secret key directory, and never serve from a copied, restored or rolled-back one.

column3: Across several commitments this is not hidden: how many there are, how many leaf tables each has, under which commitment a batch ran, when a commitment was first shown, that two commitments have the same public files, and whatever the answers themselves tell, since one request put under two commitments with the same configuration files compares the two sets of weights at that request. A provider that picks the commitment for a batch by something hidden (the size of the batch, a request that is not shown, the weights) gives that away.
column4: Do not pick the commitment that serves a request by anything that must stay hidden.

column3: A new commitment heals nothing: if more batches were answered on a leaf table than it bears, no statement of the written argument (unpublished) holds for those weights, also under a later commitment. And if one seed serves two commitments on changed weights, a single column that is read under both shows, without a mask, a piece of the encoded difference of the two sets of weights; no common column is needed: the two tables share their random tails, so the limit on opened columns holds for both together, and nothing counts them together. No column need be read: the two commitments' public files alone then give exact linear equations in the two sets of weights (row H4.2).
column4: See that an old secret key directory whose count is lost or in doubt answers no further batch.

column3: Hidden values stay unwiped in free GPU memory, and no exit of `cp_prove` wipes everything. Only a coding rule keeps such values out of a proof; one reading of the code of other programs (row HW-678) checked it for about a hundred kinds of buffer, and not for some thirty kinds of the committer's and those of four further files that the prover uses, and it holds only in a run without a fault.
column4: Give the service a machine and a GPU of its own; which reset clears GPU memory is not known.

column3: Before it exits, `cp_prove` zeroes, of the code that holds the weight table, the key of its masks, salts and pads (both copies), the rows' combination and the GPU memory that it was lent, but not any pads already made from that key, which during an opening lie in an ordinary host buffer that no step of the wipe reaches; the GPU and pinned buffers on its own lists; the keys and the seed: unless the wipe is skipped whole (a kill, a crash, an abort), is given up at its time limit, or a step of it fails or is skipped (rows R7, R7.1: after a GPU fault the zeroing of GPU memory fails). The wipe neither stops nor waits for the program's other threads: they run on until the process exits, so one of them can still write hidden values into host or GPU memory that the wipe has already passed, and the end then still counts every step as run. Nothing that they produce from then on can be released: the release of responses is blocked before the wipe's first step (read in the code). Where a self-check ends `cp_prove` in row R7.5's case, not every step of the wipe runs (by a reading of the code): hidden values may then stay in the process's memory until it ends. On none of its lists, and so left as they are after every exit: the copy of the weights in pinned host memory; each thread's page-locked buffer for uploads to the GPU (32 MiB a thread), which is never cleared and which, by its source, is meant only for lists that are no secret, a rule that the source names no check for; the memory of CUDA and its libraries, launch arguments included; during a batch's opening, in ordinary host memory that no exit zeroes, one exact sum for each row of the weight matrix and the opened columns' words; and whatever only a destructor clears, since `cp_prove` leaves by `_exit()`, which runs no destructor: the random generators' own copies of a key in host memory, and GPU tables that are derived from the weights and that only a destructor zeroes, stay, if the object is alive at the exit, unless a step of the wipe reaches them (read in the code). The pads of the leaf table in use: during an opening they lie in an ordinary host buffer that no step of the wipe reaches, also at an exit at which every step of the wipe ran (at a bad end a test build's last line then says `every step of the wipe ran: 1`; the default build prints no line `p258 not every step of the wipe ran: ..` before its last) (read in the code; inferred from the order of its lines, not seen in a run). With the published OOD answer that it masks, a pad gives one exact equation on a row of the weight table. The list is not complete, and no zeroing by the programs reaches memory that they did not allocate themselves. In an honest run too the proof library itself frees host memory that has held random values (mask rows, random tails, old one-time pads) without zeroing it; in `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` replacements for the global operator new and operator delete zero each block when it is freed, not before (prover/common/zeroing_heap.h; read in the code, and a search of the library's sources found no other way in which they allocate host memory; no run has looked at a program's freed memory). Not covered, by that file's own comment: blocks allocated directly with malloc() or aligned_alloc(), what precompiled code of the C++ standard library allocates and frees, and blocks not yet freed when the process ends; nor anything on a stack or in page-locked memory; of such vectors the library itself wipes only the one-time pads' copies in one routine (read in the code; no sweep over the library's sources for such vectors has been made). By a reading of the sources. For GPU memory that zeroing goes by the status that each CUDA call returns and never reads the memory back, so a call that reported success without having zeroed would go unnoticed (read in the code). The code has test modes that first fill memory with a pattern and afterwards count the bytes that are not zero (by the source's own comment `cp_prove` sets none of them: test programs that are not part of this repository do), but only for the zeroing between requests, at the end of a batch pass, of newly mapped scratch memory and of lent memory: the zeroing at exit has no such mode (read in the code). Where `cp_prove` ends through exit(), as after a failed CUDA call, the C library first runs the exit handlers that were registered later than the program's own (such as destructors of static objects constructed since), and the calling thread's thread-local destructors; the release of responses is stopped only after them, but still before the wipe's first step. In that time a response that was staged can still get its final name (read in the code; nothing was run). A stop that another thread raises, as after a failed CUDA call, while `cp_prove` reads a staged batch for its tags can miss the wait in which what is staged is erased: the exit then counts as not all wiped, and the staged files, on which no verifier has run, stay until a next start whose requests have the same length as those left in `work/`, or `cp_prove -clear` (row HW-480; read in the code; nothing was run).

Whether any reset of the GPU, or a restart of the machine, clears what the programs leave in the GPU's memory is not known, and which reset would clear what is written down nowhere in this repository. The programs themselves reset nothing: no shipped source or script calls a routine or a tool that resets a GPU or ends its context (searched). See also three studies, published from 2013 to 2017. Di Pietro, Lombardi, Villani, "CUDA Leaks: Information Leakage in GPU Architectures", arXiv:1305.7383, section III, says that the vendor tells nothing of how CUDA manages memory inside, so that it is open whether memory is cleared after a program has given it back. The other two are named here without a retelling: Lee, Kim, Kim, Kim, "Stealing Webpages Rendered on Your Browser by Exploiting GPU Vulnerabilities", IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2014; Hayes et al., "GPU Taint Tracking", USENIX Annual Technical Conference 2017, section 4.1.
column4: Do not pass the GPU on to anyone (docs/operators-duties.md).

column3: `cp_commit` never overwrites the host memory that holds the model's tensors. When interrupted, and after some failed exits such as a rejected model, it also leaves keys, masks, weights or weight-derived values unwiped on the host and the GPU. On Ctrl-C, `SIGTERM`, `SIGHUP`, a broken pipe or an abort it overwrites every file that the call has created and then removes it (row R3.2 tells what stays), and a weight-derived file made under `-worst-case-table` is removed only once the cleanup is armed. `cp_prove`, wherever it acts on a `TERM`, runs its wipe first; that wipe can itself fall short. `SIGKILL`, any other signal, a crash or a power loss leaves everything in place.
column4: Run `cp_commit` on a dedicated machine and GPU.

column3: On the provider's machine, whoever can list the secret key directory sees from the count files' lengths how many columns, and so batches, each leaf table has served, failed and killed batches too. Whoever can list the system's locks sees when a batch begins and when a table is being opened. `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` also pin the calling thread, and so every thread that it starts later, early in the run, to the CPUs that lie near the GPU, where the machine reports such CPUs (read in the code). By the operating system's usual rule any user of the machine can read which CPUs another user's process is bound to; that was not tried here. The set follows from where the GPU sits in the machine and from the CPUs that the process was allowed before, not from a request or a weight.
column4: Give the service a machine of its own.

column3: A prompt that drove an inner value out of its range would make the request fail, and "served or failed" would then tell a client one fact about the weights. Before it writes any file of the commitment, the production build of `cp_commit` bounds 18 kinds of inner values over all prompts and makes no commitment unless every one fits (it ends with exit code 7); the production build of `cp_prove` does not start without the line that a passed check leaves in the secret key directory, and no key protects that line, so whoever can write that directory can add it. Not shown: that the list of kinds is complete, that the bounds' mathematics is right, that the prover decodes the same integers. One reading of the code found every place where the prover raises such a failure bounded. With `-worst-case-table` a file with numbers computed from the weights is written before the verdict and stays after a failed check. What `cp_commit` prints after a passed check speaks of the sites that the check bounds ("every bounded site fits: at none of the sites that the check bounds can a prompt drive the value out of its range"), not of every place at which the forward pass tests a range (read in the code). Not on the released programs, the program printed a line that spoke of every site, which said more than the check shows (reported). The code that writes the file of `-worst-case-table` has "every site would fit" or "NOT every site would fit", in a line for other settings that a caller may pass; `cp_commit`'s one call passes none, so no run writes these words (read in the code); there too only the sites that the check bounds are meant.
column4: Nothing that an operator can do is known to help; the programs do not count or limit requests.

column3: The line `ranges` in the secret key directory's text file is added only by a call of `cp_commit` whose worst-case check has passed on the weights that, by the program's own comments, the same call then commits to, and `cp_prove` does not start on a randomly drawn seed without it; but the line holds a digest of the configuration files alone, nothing in it depends on the weights, no key protects that file, and nothing in a proof is tied to the check, so whoever can write the provider's secret key directory can put the line there; `cp_prove`'s opening still fails on other weights than the committed ones: at every opening each opened column is made again and must fit the stored tree (that it fails is run by two tests of this repository, `gpu.other_weights_nothing_leaves` (on a test build, at `prover/tests/configurations/pinned_no_proof_of_work`) and `gpu.one_changed_weight`, at a small size, on synthetic weights: other weights, and one changed bit of one weight, each end in an empty failure marker; how, is read in the code; it does not help where the committed weights themselves were never checked: a line copied from another commitment under the same files fits as well). The check's bounds on matrix norms assume that the GPU library computes the classical matrix product in IEEE binary64: the check sets the library's strict mode and tests the assumption in every run by two guards, whose failure counts as "does not fit". These guards are spot checks, not a proof.

No test makes the second guard of `cp_commit`'s worst-case check, the exactness check of the Gram matrix, fail where it is used, so the line that records that failure has run in no test. No test in this repository makes either guard fail (searched). Read in the code, not run.

One rare failure of an honest run is not independent of hidden values: an honest range check fails when a random combination of the request's hidden cells leaves its window, and how likely that is depends on those cells, and so on prompt and weights. The programs reckon an upper bound on that chance for each range check from the configuration's own numbers, taken at the worst cells that a client's request can bring about, and reject a configuration unless the chance, summed over all requests that a key can serve, stays below 2^-s for the parameter file's security target s. The bound's arithmetic was read, not derived again for this line.

`cp_prove` may answer some requests with a `.failed` file although a valid proof exists. A reading of other sources (row HW-678) says that the prover serves only inside ranges that are, in places, narrower than the ranges that a proof enforces. That reading has not been checked against the released programs. `cp_commit` exits with code 7 unless its worst-case check finds that, at the sites of the forward pass that it bounds, no prompt can drive a value out of its range (its bounds rest on an assumption about the GPU library's 64-bit arithmetic), and the production build's `cp_prove` does not start a service without the line that the check leaves, which is under no key; that no request then fails for a range is not fully established.
column6: not known: not compared with the released programs

column3: By the sources' own comment only two of the bits of a request's failure word can change the routing, because they put substitute values into the forward pass ahead of a router: a forward-pass value out of its range, and an index outside its table; that no other bit's substitute reaches a router has not been followed through the code. At least these further bits depend on the request's hidden values, by the sources' comments: the bit for the approximate range check, which requires every entry of its random combinations of committed columns to lie in an interval, and is set when one does not; the bit that says that the checked tokens exceed the parameter file's bounds (there, too, a substitute value is used, behind every router); the bit for a failed self-check, which also carries a check of the lookup argument that depends on weights and prompt; and the two bits on drawn challenges, rare events on values that are hashes over messages made from the hidden values.

`cp_commit`'s worst-case check bounds values of the forward pass only, and it works for the one kind of parameter file that the parser takes (`prof` 20, 12-bit cells); where it does not support a value of the lines eg, smax, rcl, dcl, gcl or xl, the production build's call ends with exit code 2 and makes no commitment (a test build under a test seed leaves the check out and commits). It does not touch the other way in which a request fails: the acceptance policy's own bounds on the checked tokens, which the sources call a result and not a fault, and which depends on the weights. A request names its own checked range. None of the programs counts or limits a client's requests: that is left to the provider's front end, and the example front end does not do it. So under exact match a client whose request failed can halve the range and ask again: about ten further requests at full size locate the first checked token that is not the model's top choice. A "failed" names no cause, so this needs other failures to be rare (read in the code; the halving is reasoned, not run).
column4: Let the front end set the checked range and limit each client's requests (docs/what-is-not-hidden.md, item 2, "What a provider can do", and "What a front end must do", rules 2 and 5). The example front end that ships does neither.

column3: The version of the GPU compiler that built the programs on which most tests ran has a published bug that can silently compute a wrong value, and a second one of the same kind, in no release note; a wrongly computed mask still verifies. The build requires a later version, in which the vendor lists the published bug as fixed. For the second the build does nothing against it; it tests for it on one small sample kernel: before every target that runs the GPU compiler it compiles that kernel and, where the machine has a GPU, runs it and stops at a wrong value. Compiled by that earlier version the sample gave wrong values on an H100, and by the required one all values were right, in every run of one series, not on the released programs: three forms of the program around the one kernel, with 66 different inputs in all; the build script's own stop has been seen once with a real compiler. Where no GPU is found, or it cannot be used, the build goes on with one line, and nothing was then checked by value; that is so in every test that builds, and there a test of its own runs the same program. No such bug has been found in the vendor's release notes, so it is not known whether the later version repairs it or only compiles this kernel differently. The sample does not show that the compiler makes no other mistake, or not this one in another kernel: no kernel of the prover runs in it.

column3: nvcc 13.0.88, the version of the GPU compiler which built most of the programs that were tested (not the released programs), has a published bug that can silently compute a wrong value, and a second one of the same kind that is in no release note; the build requires a later version, in which the vendor lists the published bug as fixed. A wrongly computed mask still verifies; `cp_verify` is built by g++ alone, so neither compiler bug can by itself make it accept a false proof; by NVIDIA's note the later compiler is the repaired one, which no test here has checked.

The build tests for it on that one small kernel only, and only where a GPU is present: it stops at a wrong value, and built by the required compiler version the kernel gave the right values in at least five runs, not on the released programs; beyond that it does nothing against it. column3: Besides the two compiler bugs that other rows tell, a third fault of the compiler of CUDA 13.0 did strike one of the prover's own kernels, in the transform that computes code symbols: the compiler left a loop out, and the kernel's results were wrong. The benchmark that showed the fault also checked nine shapes, all of which came out right; the fault showed only at two lengths at rates 1/2 and 1/4 (the benchmark's notes, which are not part of this repository; not run again). Nothing says whether the compiler release that the build requires has the fault.

The programs on which most tests ran were built with another compiler version than the build asks for: so they are not the programs that this build makes, and what was tested on them does not carry over to this build's programs unless it is repeated there.

NVIDIA lists the published compiler bug, which gives a wrong value without any message, as fixed in nvcc 13.2.86, which the build requires (release notes for CUDA 13.2 Update 2, "Resolved Issues", "CUDA Compiler"; present since CUDA 12.8). That fix has not been checked here by a test. The programs that nvcc 13.0.88 built (not the released programs) did not work around it, and whether it affects them is not known; a wrongly computed mask still verifies.
