column3: Every build of `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` but the production build rejects a model's files (read in the code), and the production build knows no test option. A test option here means one that only a test build accepts (docs/glossary.md#test-option). The production build does accept four other options that work on synthetic weights alone: `cp_commit -keep-for-the-audit`, and `cp_prove -keep-for-the-audit`, `-overlap` and `-overlap-two`. A check at run time rejects them on a model's files (read in the code; docs/limits-further.md#h9; rows HW-435, PS-53). A bad result, not on the released programs, by a reading of the code (no such program was run on a model's files): test options could meet a real model's files (`cp_commit` took a test seed there and called the result fit to hand out), and four of nine test build targets rejected a model's files nowhere.
column6: in part: these sources do not have the fault that the note tells as a bad result

column3: That no build with test options reads a model's weight files rests on a rejection at run time in each program (seen in a run of a test that is not part of this repository, not on the released programs) and, behind it, on the compile: in a test build the two calls that open a model's files are not compiled in, and the program ends with an internal error in their place (read in the code; no test brings a run to that end). `cp_prove`'s rejection and its loader ask two different variables; both are set from one line of isk.txt, and they agree. A test that reads the sources (it is not part of this repository) guards these lines by patterns, against careless edits, and can be evaded. Reported: weakened copies that gave the mode for synthetic weights a way to files were made twice, apart, and three of the one set and five of the other were not noticed by a form of the test; which form is not known, and no run of them on the test as it stands is known. By reading, the sources as they are give no such way; if a later edit opened one, a test build on a real model could make files that hide nothing, and no verifier would see that (the programs' own rejection says so).
column4: For a model's files use only the production build (prover/build.sh without an argument).

column3: No key protects the lines of the text file in the secret key directory. The production build does not start under an added line `seed test`; a test build takes its test options on that line's word, and it does so on synthetic weights only, by the same file's word. What follows from a changed line on the weights' source in that file was traced by a reading of the code: the prover then generates weights, opens no file of the model, and its first batch fails a self-check before anything is released (read, not run).
column4: Never add or strike a line in the secret key directory's text file.

column3: Destroying the secret key directory of a test or a measurement that used a test option, a test seed or test randomness undoes nothing that was already revealed. There is no tool that destroys one; backups and images hold it too.
column4: Keep such a directory as secret as the weights for as long as it exists, backups and images too.

column3: With `-overlap` or `-overlap-two` a service shows more than without. The time of a batch's release then also shows whether the next batch (with `-overlap-two`, the next two) stood ready and how long its first passes took, and so more of a neighbouring batch's size and arrival time, and that batch holds other clients' requests; and a cause that belongs to no single request, or an end of the process, costs one or two more batches their responses (`cp_prove`'s own first lines and a comment in the source; read, not measured). These are among the grounds that the source gives for rejecting both options on a model's files; the rejection is this project's own precaution.
column4: Do not plan on these two options for a real model: `cp_prove` rejects them there.

column3: No test of hiding covers overlapping batches.

`cp_commit -keep-for-the-audit` writes beside the seed the bytes that open every mask of the public files. `cp_prove` rejects every start while anything is in the directory where they are kept (a service that already runs goes on: the look is taken once, at a start); what that check sees is that nothing is there any more, not that the audit said yes. `cp_commit` rejects the option on a model's weight files, so no real model's masks can be exposed this way. `cp_prove`'s option of the same name keeps one batch's 32 bytes in the same directory, until that batch's audit, called with `--erase-kept-files`, gives a verdict; a rehearsal (`--rehearsal`) makes all the checks and erases nothing (the erasure itself can stop or leave the file as it is, which the audit then says; and "erased" reaches the file's present blocks and its name, not what a journal, a snapshot, flash or a back-up keeps).
column4: The audit works on synthetic weights only. There, run it to its YES before the first call of `cp_prove`.

column3: That a proof hides the batch's other requests is a requirement of the design. Of the programs it is not proved; a paper argument, which has not been checked independently and which covers no program, states it (what-is-not-hidden.md). As served it rests on the secret seed, and under `-public-weights`, where the seed is public, no argument that it holds has been made. Three readings of the code, which did not reach the bodies of the GPU kernels, found nothing of another request sent bare.
column4: Whether that evidence is enough is the provider's decision.

column3: A client does learn which proofs shared a batch, from timing roughly how many requests did and, through the experts' routing, something of their prompts; time is not hidden (docs/what-is-not-hidden.md, item 3). A little was measured, in honest runs not on the released programs, all on synthetic weights. On the weights themselves: two synthetic models were told apart by the model server's time to the first token, with no prover behind it. How much timing reveals in all has not been measured.
column5: run, not on the released programs

column3: One way to read how many requests shared a batch needs no clock: a client that keeps a full batch of its own requests waiting reads, from which of its proofs share a batch, how many places went to others (by reading; not run). `cp_prove` does nothing to see that each response reaches its owner only: that is left to a front end. The repository's example front end, a middleware for vLLM, lets anyone who has a proof ID (64 hex digits, sent in a header of the reply to the client that asked) fetch or delete the proof; where vLLM was given an API key, however it was given (the variable VLLM_API_KEY, --api-key, a config file), and the middleware can read it from vLLM's application, so that fetching and deleting ask for it (how it learns that key, and where it cannot: integrations/vllm/REFERENCE.md#the-operators-checklist), all clients share it, so between clients the proof ID is the only guard; where vLLM has a key that the middleware neither reads nor suspects, fetching and deleting need no key unless the variable VLLM_API_KEY is set (a fault of this kind that these sources do not have: a form of this middleware that is not in this repository (row HW-678) knew the variable alone, so that a key given to vLLM with --api-key alone did not cover fetching or deleting a proof: in one run at toy size, at a start with that option alone, a caller without a key was sent the list of policies and, on naming a job's proof ID, the job's state and its whole proof file, whole by its length: the bytes were counted, not compared; deleting, a guessed or a wrong ID and a token file were not tried in that run; integrations/tests/test_proof_middleware.py, which the public test `integrations.unit` runs, asks for the key with a stand-in for vLLM's application; row HW-275). The middleware has run under the pinned vLLM, not on the released programs, at toy size, and four times at full size, where the key was in `VLLM_API_KEY` alone and on the middleware's routes no call without it was tried. At toy size: at one start with `--api-key` alone, six calls without a key and one with a wrong key got status 401 on the middleware's routes, and four calls with the key were answered (the run at toy size: integrations/LIMITS.md#what-has-never-been-run). The six, each once: the list of policies; a job's state; its `proof.bin`; its `y.bin`; a `DELETE` of that job; the published `key.bin`. The wrong key: on the job's state. The four with the key (no `DELETE` and no `y.bin` among them): the list of policies; the job's state (so the refused `DELETE` had deleted nothing); its whole `proof.bin`; `key.bin`. Three more, each once: a POST with the policy's header and no key, and a published leaf file without a key: 401; an unknown proof ID with the key: 404. Three further starts, each once. With the variable alone: five calls on a job's routes without the key or with a wrong one: 401, and nothing was deleted. With no key at all: the routes answered without one, and the middleware's line that says so stood in vLLM's log, once. With two different keys, one in the variable and one in `--api-key`: the option's was taken and the variable's refused. At a start with `VLLM_API_KEY` alone, in the same run, the list of policies and a request with the policy header got 401 without the key, and the list got 200 with it. Not run behind vLLM: a `DELETE` or a fetch of `y.bin` with the key; a start with several keys or with a config file; a refused start; `layout.txt` with or without a key; an unknown proof ID without a key. Toy size; synthetic weights; each call once.
That the bytes of a single proof do not show how many requests shared its batch is the design's intent. No run has compared proofs across batch sizes for this, beyond their average lengths.

Some of `cp_prove`'s GPU memory is left out of the restoring between requests, because it is written once and then only read. By one reading of the source the launch descriptors in it have no field that can hold a value of a request, a weight or a random value; not every caller was traced. With the option `-overlap` one buffer for each opening is entered there too, and hidden values are in it during an opening: the opening zeroes it when it takes it and before it gives it back, and, being on `cp_prove`'s list of GPU memory, it is zeroed again when the program ends by itself, not after an abort, a kill or a crash (read in the code; not run). `cp_prove` rejects `-overlap` and `-overlap-two` on a model's files, in every build, so this happens in runs on synthetic weights only (read in the code; not run in a production build; the one test of that rejection uses a test build, on a stand-in with one empty model file: docs/limits-further.md#h9). No tool checks this memory, and a comment in the source says that such memory holds nothing of a request.
Whoever serves a client the leaf files learns which leaf table it asks for, and when; the table's number is in every proof of the batch.
Memory that is lent to the code that opens the weight table is zeroed at hand-over and before it goes back. Not every path after a failure was followed.

By reading, `cp_prove` zeroes the scratch memory that its sub-proofs share (between requests up to a bound, all of it at the end of a batch pass), restores most of the buffers on its own list of GPU memory between requests, and zeroes the memory that it lends to the code that opens the weight table, at hand-over and before it comes back. No test looks in a running `cp_prove` whether those bytes really are zero or restored: the sources have test switches that overwrite such memory with a marker byte and count the bytes that are not zero, and no test runs `cp_prove` with them switched on (one test that is not part of this repository switches one of them on in a test program of the code that loads the weights, where it overwrites released weight buffers and counts nothing); the production build has no such count, so a zeroing that fell short would go unnoticed there. By the source's own comment a request's proof reads what its own run has written; that is a coding rule, which holds only in a run without a fault, and the restoring bounds what a bug that reads old memory could get.

By reading, the separately compiled code that opens the weight table for `cp_prove` erases, at the end of each batch, both its copies of the table's 32-byte mask seed, its combination of the table's rows in host memory, and all GPU memory that it was lent, where an opening writes copies of weights, combinations of them, masks and other private random values; where CUDA reports that this zeroing failed, the process ends. It does not erase any pads already made from that seed: during an opening these lie in an ordinary host buffer (read in the code; rows H6.1, R7.1.1). It is handed no key of a batch; not erased, by a comment in its header, are the table's stored nodes, which stay in pinned host memory until the next table's are read over them (digests over salted leaves, which are in the secret key directory anyway and of which every opening publishes some), and the mask seed also goes to the GPU as a launch argument of kernels, which none of the programs' zeroing reaches. Host memory of the opening's own objects, such as the words of opened columns before they are handed on, is zeroed by the opening's own last step, not by this call; an exit during a batch's opening zeroes neither these words nor the one exact sum for each row of the weight matrix, which `cp_prove` then holds in ordinary host memory (read in the code; row H6.1); what an opening that is broken off before that step leaves in freed host memory is not known. GPU memory that this code has taken from the driver itself, outside an opening, is not zeroed by this call; what it holds was not followed. By a comment in the source an opening also puts one sum for each row of the weights into `cp_prove`'s GPU engine and has it commit to the combination of the table's rows, and the engine's GPU memory pool is not zeroed. No test looks at this memory after a batch: two GPU unit tests of this code, which are not part of this repository (a test build, synthetic weights, one small configuration) run several batches and, of the erasing, check only the return value of the call that is meant for the process's end. So a zeroing that silently fell short would go unnoticed, and the lent memory would go back as it is to the work on the next requests.
The written argument (unpublished) assumes that what honest clients ask next does not depend on bytes of a proof that the clients who act together do not see.

That each generator of random values is made only once under one key is a condition that the written hiding argument (unpublished) needs, and in a run the programs themselves check it nowhere, with one exception: the generator that draws the sub-proofs' pads in `cp_prove` ends a run in which its counter does not rise. In `cp_prove` the condition rests on the layout of the code: all generators of a batch are made in one block at the batch's head, from a key that is passed as an argument and wiped at the block's end (copies of its bytes stay in two other places until the batch's passes are over), and the compiler does not reject a second call of a routine that makes a generator inside that block. A test that reads the sources, which is not part of this repository, guards this layout, and it is weak: it missed most of the rewritten forms of the code that break the rule, among those tried; it also holds the block's lines to the letter (whether it would catch those forms is not known), and by its own head it does not see what the called routines do, a second way to a key under other names, or anything in `cp_commit`. In `cp_commit` each of the two callers (the key file's making, a leaf file's making) must see to it itself. The public test `gpu.coin_contexts.services.not_full` (SUITE.md) checks the condition in the runs that it makes (test build, synthetic weights, a test seed, not full size); by its script's own head it guards those runs alone (prover/tests/coin_contexts_listed.py). No run of `gpu.coin_contexts.services.not_full` lets a service take a further batch after one that is not full.

It is not proved that under one process key no two masks come from the same input of the generator (the source says so itself). What the programs do: a stream generator gives every draw a stream of its own by construction; the generator that draws the sub-proofs' pads keeps a record of drawn cells and ends the run if a cell is drawn a second time in one context (it sees a second draw, not a second use). The two kinds' records do not see each other, and only the label's word for the kind of object keeps their values apart (the numbers are fixed in the source); in a run the programs themselves do not check that no context is made twice under a key (in `cp_prove` a layout of the code stands in for that check: row H12). No test of the suite lists the draws of the generator of the sub-proofs' pads, and how far its record covers the arrays that the programs draw is not known.

A proof of the production build can be checked by value only where `cp_prove` was started with `-keep-for-the-audit`, which it takes for one batch, outside a service, on synthetic weights only. Such a check does not show where the program took the kept bytes from, or that a run without the option draws in the same way. A batch that a service made cannot be checked by value: its random bytes are kept nowhere. On a model's files that must stay hidden, two versions of the programs can be compared only in the reply and in the files that do not depend on the seed; on a model's public files, under `-public-weights`, the same call is meant to give the same commitment, so they can be compared in the commitment's files too (by the option's design). That holds between versions that form the commitment ID by the same rule.

How far evidence from the test build carries to the production build rests on two tests, neither of which is part of this repository: that the GPU code was the same function by function, but for two test functions that the test build's `cp_commit` holds more, and lists of the differing CPU source lines, which were read; these readings have not been checked independently. The CPU machine code has not been compared, a run under a fixed seed takes branches that neither test sees, and the CPU code, which differs on purpose, decides which GPU functions are launched, in which order, on which memory and with which arguments, the keys among them. Some code only the production build runs: the reading of a model's files, and the lines of the option `-public-weights`: no run of the test build executes them (tests of that option walk them). The comparison says nothing of a build that a provider makes elsewhere, and the test build has no record that ties it to a state of the sources. No other test program, those with an injected fault among them, is compared with either build; some of their scripts, which are not part of this repository either, hold theirs to the honest program by equal files where no fault is asked for.

The lists of differing CPU source lines, by which evidence from a test build is carried to the production build, show neither a line that changes in both builds alike nor common text that one differing line brings to life in one build only, nor some sixty lines of common text that act only under `-public-weights`, an option that only the production build takes, so that no run of a test build shows what they do; nor text that is compiled for the GPU only, the CPU machine code, or how a run with a test seed parts from a run without (branches in common text). The test is not part of this repository.

The comparison of the two builds' GPU functions looks at calls only, not at where a branch or a jump goes, and reads only what the vendor's tool dumps without its option for all embedded binaries. Equal code is not correct code: a fault that both builds have is not detected. It leaves out the PTX that the programs also hold, from which a driver can compile new machine code, and every library that is loaded at run time (cuBLAS, cuBLASLt, the CUDA runtime, the driver's library). The test is not part of this repository. The vendor's tool is NVIDIA's cuobjdump. For `cp_commit`, whose test build holds two functions more, a second test, which is not part of this repository either, compares the two builds' GPU images section by section. It goes by the sections' names, which by that test's own text are those that nvcc 13.0 gives (the programs are built with nvcc 13.2.86); by the same text NVIDIA's document "CUDA Binary Utilities" shows two of these names in a sample output of another tool, nvdisasm, and not the others.

All GPU code of the prover and of the proof library is in headers, and every unit test is one source that is compiled with its includes into a program of its own: no object is shared between a unit test and `cp_commit` or `cp_prove`. So a unit test of a kernel runs the same source compiled again, not the programs' machine code; the programs' own code is run by the tests that run the programs. One test does compare machine code across compilations: the GPU functions of the programs' two builds, and of two unit tests, function by function.

Hiding needs each entry of a sub-proof's mask row to hide at most one sent scalar. The one check of this on the whole prover is a separate test program: `cp_prove` compiled with counters, which counts in every sub-proof how often each place of the message array is written, and ends the run unless each is written exactly once, with a mask entry that is not zero, and none beyond them (the test that runs it is not part of this repository). The counting instruction is compiled into the routine through which the kernels write these places, so this program counts in other machine code than the code that a provider runs; the production build cannot be compiled with the counters, and no test compares this program's GPU functions with either build. Reported: one comparison, not on the released programs, found that 22 of 741 GPU functions differed between the counting program and the `cp_prove` beside it, and that the counting program had three kernels more; the functions that differed were those that do the masking. What ties the two together: in its counting run the program's output files must be those of the test build's `cp_prove`, byte for byte, under the same test random values. By the sources it is a regression check and no argument that anything is hidden; a write that bypasses that routine is not counted, and that the places written depend on the shape alone, not on a request's values, is known from reading only. It does not count the opening of the weight table, whose code is built without the counters, nor the scalars that the library's own blocks send, and of a sumcheck it does not check the form of a round or the number of end values (by the source such a fault would show as a rejection where `cp_verify` is run on the proof, and each sent scalar still has a mask entry of its own).

A fault that was built in for a test and was stopped shows that the comparison at that one place noticed it, on synthetic weights, in a test build under a test seed. No built-in loss that leaves a proof which verifies was tried at full size, and no test of the test table runs `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` at full size.

The CPU machine code of the test build and of the production build was not compared, and the code paths that a run under a fixed test seed does not take are the production build's own: under a test seed some twenty checks are off or milder (by a reading of other sources (row HW-678); not counted in these sources), so the evidence by value has not taken those branches, but for the audits of the production build's own files under a drawn seed (row LIM-63.2 tells them), and neither of the two tests that tie the builds together sees them.

The code that reads a model's weight files is executed by no run on which evidence by value was gathered. Both builds hold that code, but only the production build calls it: a build with test options rejects a model's files long before. It stages real weights in the machine's memory and in GPU memory. So the checks by value, and the runs with injected faults, say nothing on how weights that are read from files are buffered and wiped.

Three lists of the CPU source lines in which the test build and the production build differ (for `cp_prove`, for `cp_commit` and for the code that holds the leaf tables) are kept by a test, which like the lists is not part of this repository, and which makes them again and compares, so a new differing line cannot come in unseen. Every listed line was read with one question: can it change what is drawn, masked, sent, counted or wiped in a run without test options that both builds take? The answer for every line was no; these readings have not been checked independently. Of `cp_prove`'s list, 85 lines were read in a first reading only by their writer, and 6 by their writer and one other reader. Some 300 lines that came into the lists and some 60 that left them were read again in two further readings, made apart, with the same answer; the other lines were not read again. Some sixty lines of the option `-public-weights` are on no list: both builds have them, and they act only if the option is given. The code that reads a model's files is text that both builds hold and that only the production build can execute: no list shows it, and no run of the test build speaks for it.
A test build prints each failed request's cause and flags, which tell more than the one bit "failed".
column4: Serve with the production build only.

column3: The commitment of the stored example in examples/full-size-clipped-gap/ (made on a production build, not on the released programs; a drawn seed, synthetic weights, full size, the default setting with a clipped-gap policy in place of exact match) was audited once by the repository's own audit, `tools/audit/audit_commitment.sh`, before any call of `cp_prove`: it passed (exit status 0), and the directory of bytes kept for that audit was empty afterwards. It compared 10.20 % of the bytes of `ivk/key.bin` and `ivk/leaf/0.bin` by value; by its own output it did not check the pads of the stored tables' OOD answers (its output says "records"), the pads inside tables of real values, the stored tables' columns, or unopened leaves of trees that hold real values; no false kept bytes were tried. In the timed runs (docs/limits.md#the-timed-runs) the job that makes a set of files in the form of that example (row RES-23) audited its own commitment with the same script, once: full size, synthetic weights, a drawn seed, a production build, the default setting but for a clipped-gap policy's three numbers. By that run's own summary the audit ended with exit status 0 and a last line of the form of a yes, and no file was left among the kept bytes; of what it printed the last six lines were kept: by them it compared 10.18 % of the bytes of its key file and leaf file by value (635,248 of 6,237,384); an accept of an honest commitment is no negative test. Such a pass does not show that the weights are hidden.

**Both audits under a clipped-gap policy.** Both audits with the provider's secrets ran under a clipped-gap policy, on the released programs, with no test option, in one run, each once in rehearsal and once in earnest: at small size, on synthetic weights, on one commitment under a seed that `cp_commit` drew and two proofs, each covering 32 reply tokens. Both accepted the honest files: every random value that they compare by value was what the secret seed gives (in the batch's audit just under a fifth of the bytes of the two proofs, key file and leaf file). Under a false file in turn for each of three kept files, in rehearsal mode, the answer was no each time. `cp_verify` accepted both proofs as within the policy's limits. Bounds: one run; the batch's two requests have one and the same reply; no altered public file was put to the audits, and no false proof to `cp_verify`; such a NO shows that the comparison is switched on, not that one lost mask would be caught. The audit of a commitment ran once more on the released programs, at small size, at the same configuration and under such a policy, in the making of a small example: by the run's own account it accepted the honest commitment, which is no negative test. By the audit's own table a proof under this policy has no class of values that a proof under exact match lacks (the same 131 classes): so this is the exact-match check passed on such proofs, not a check of something that only this policy has. What the audits do not ask or compare: row LIM-63.2, line 5, and tools/audit/README.md, "What a batch's YES does not cover". It says nothing of what the policy's outcomes tell of the model's scores (row LIM-27), of full size, of a real model's weights, of a service, or of a batch with a failed request. It shows that the masks are there as derived; it is no search for a leak, and such a pass does not show that the weights are hidden.
column6: yes, of the runs and readings that the note reports

column3: Two tensor-core kernels end with hidden values in shared memory and registers, which nothing clears (sums and scale pairs in one; decoded weights, activations and sums, up to 231,936 bytes per thread block, in the other). These two are not the only ones: other kernels that multiply on the tensor cores also end without clearing their shared memory (by a count from the sources, not checked: twelve in all, in eight files).
column4: Give the service a GPU of its own; which reset clears GPU memory is not known. Timing is declared as not hidden.

column3: One kernel instance in the two tensor-core files in prover/weights_blocks/ has a stack frame. By one reading of its machine code, the frame holds two hidden routing values, an expert's first rank and the number of tokens routed to it. The same reading found four words computed from the thread's index, but no weight, activation or sum; that reading has not been checked independently, and no test has checked it. A test that is not in this repository requires every other kernel of those files to have no stack frame or local memory, and only prints this one.

In the kernel for the routed experts' product the time inside the launch follows how many tokens the router sent to each expert. The grid and the number of launches do not follow the routing only where the tensor's type is Q4_K or Q5_K and its shape fits that kernel (its number of lines is a multiple of the kernel's block); for any other tensor, so for every one of type Q8_0, F16 or BF16, the CPU code makes one library call for each expert that has tokens, and the number and the sizes of the launches follow the routing too. The other tensor-core kernel reads no routing table.

Audits apart (rows H13.7 and H13.8), no known test of hiding ran under clipped gap, the acceptance policy that scores tokens together, although one example configuration sets it. Under such a policy one client is enough to measure the model's hidden scores over many requests, because it chooses every token and no program limits requests. A search of the automated tests found only exact match; for runs outside the test suite, not on the released programs, no record of the configuration is known.
So under ordinary serving the model's hidden scores are not hidden from a client that sends many requests and chooses the checked tokens, and no statement bounds how much that tells of the weights.
column4: Under clipped gap, have your front end request proofs only for replies that you served yourself, and let it set the checked range.

column3: How a wider request, one whose proof is about more than the one token that follows the request's window, affects hiding is not known. A provider that proves a whole generated answer needs such requests.

The test runner confines its tests with Linux's Landlock. The confinement limits where a test writes, with holes (/dev/shm; whatever directory the variable BUILD names; truncation on older Linux kernels), and, on Linux 6.12 or later, which processes it signals. On Linux 5.13 to 6.11 it rejects, of signals, only one sent to every process of the account, and that level has never run on such a kernel. The confinement has a test of its own, which runs harmful commands against decoys at the one level that the machine's own kernel gives. For the levels of other kernels it runs no harmful command: it runs one harmless command through the tool with the kernel's answer set to each older level, asks the tool which level it would choose, and looks, among the rights that the tool would restrict, at two (linking or renaming across directories; truncation), and at whether signals are restricted. That the tool's rule for /dev/shm rejects a directory shows only where that test is run outside the test runner: under the runner the test's own confinement already rejects it (read in the test). A bad result: in one run of the public tests (155: row T45), not on the released programs, that test failed one of 19 checks, on one machine: two real-time signals were left ignored in a command that the tool confined. That was seen only where the tool ran inside a test that the runner had already confined; on another machine the same test passes. column3: Under root the test runner's confinement limits where plain files are written. It also lets no test make a block device file, or a character device file other than the inert node 0:0 (under any account; a device file already in its folder can still be used), refuses, as root, the opening of every pseudo-terminal for writing by name (the test's own too; reading one, and ioctl on one, stay possible: read in the tool, not tried), and gives each test /proc's system settings (/proc/sys and four more places) read-only and an empty /dev/shm of its own. The sandbox promises nothing about the inert character node 0:0: on one 6.18 kernel it was made inside the sandbox, as a plain file would be (not on another 6.18 kernel or on 6.12; tried as an ordinary account, not as root). Seen, not with the tools as released, as a true root and under sudo, on one kernel (Linux 6.18); of the five places /proc/sysrq-trigger was not seen (it does not exist on the test machines). Since a test then sees nothing of the machine's /dev/shm, the runner as root refuses at its start, with a sentence, settings that point into /dev/shm (seen for nine: five variables, BUILD, and a folder of PATH, PYTHONPATH or LD_LIBRARY_PATH). It is a guard against a test's mistake, not against a test that means harm: a test run as root keeps root's other powers. Seen: a device node that already lay in the test's folder before the confinement was set up still opens for writing; a device outside the test's folders cannot be opened for writing by its name, but for the few that the tool lets through: /dev/null, /dev/zero, /dev/full, with --gpu the GPU's own device files and, except as root, pseudo-terminals (read in the tool; seen with a harmless device, as root, under sudo and as an ordinary user, once each, on one kernel; that this holds of a disk too is by reading alone; opening a device for reading, and ioctl on one that is open, stay possible: read in the tool, not tried); and with --gpu either of two raw system calls gets past the read-only on /proc/sys: open_tree gives a copy of /proc that lacks it, mount_setattr clears it; behind each a setting opened for writing (nothing was written; the machine's own mounts did not change). By reading: chmod, chown and touch on any file are not limited; with --gpu a test run as root can write those files of /proc outside the five read-only places that root may write (any process's oom_score_adj, for example); on Linux 5.13 to 6.11 a test run as root can signal any process of the machine (only a signal to -1 is refused there). Seen on Linux 6.18: a signal from a test run as root to another account's process is refused. Where the machine refuses the new mount namespace (seen: root without CAP_SYS_ADMIN), tests without --gpu still run, with /dev/shm shared, so that another account's file there opens, and `confine.py --level` says so; tests with --gpu run only if those five places are read-only already (both seen once: refused, with status 125, while the five places were writable; run where they were read-only already). So there every test that runs, on CPU or GPU, runs with /dev/shm shared and can remove, overwrite or empty any account's files in it (seen once, in test machines, for tests with and without --gpu: as root without CAP_SYS_ADMIN a command behind the sandbox read one made-up file of another account's in /dev/shm, overwrote a second and removed a third; no container was run). The tool's line for that case says "/dev/shm is shared with whatever else runs here, so a command can remove, overwrite or empty any account's files there" (read in the tool). run_suite.py also says so in a line of its own, and confine.py started by hand says so in one line on standard error, which is lost where standard error cannot take it: the command still runs (seen, as root without the right to mount, not with the tools as released: through the runner a line of its own; by hand one line on standard error; with standard error closed, full, a pipe whose reader has gone, or a full pipe that nobody reads, the command still ran, status 0). That arises where root is refused a mount namespace of its own (root without CAP_SYS_ADMIN, as in Docker's and Kubernetes' containers by default, or a filter that refuses unshare) and a /dev/shm exists. By extracts of the container runtimes' public pages, the /dev/shm in question is then the container's own (Docker) or, under Kubernetes, the pod's, which the pod's containers share: so "any account's files" means files inside that container or pod, unless it shares the host's IPC or /dev/shm (not tried); on a plain machine it is the machine's. (The runner's first line was seen, not with the tools as released, to say so in both cases: where the namespace is set up, the level's words; where it is refused, that the machine refused it and that /dev/shm is shared.) Where a later step is refused, nothing runs (seen: status 125, with the step named). No test with a GPU was run as root: the rule of --gpu was tried on machines without one. Even at its best level a faulty test can still create, write and remove files in the repository's bin/ directory, in the run's shared directory and, if the test is one that builds, in the GPU programs' build directory; run by an ordinary account, also in /dev/shm, another process's among them.

The test runner's confinement does not cover, at any level, among other things (the head of tools/confine.py has the list): reading and running files; a file's mode, owner and times; the network; with a GPU, what the account may write under /proc.

The test runner sends a test that has begun to use the GPU no signal: not at its time limit, not for programs that the test left running when it ended by itself, and not when the runner itself is stopped by a signal. One case is ended all the same, because it is safe: a test that the runner starts as a whole behind the GPU's lock file and that is still waiting for that lock. If the runner can take the same lock itself within ten seconds while the test's wait has not ended, nothing of the test has run on the GPU; the runner ends it, as it ends a test without a GPU, while it holds the lock, and the test counts as failed. A test that takes the lock only for single programs is never ended this way. Otherwise, if the test's process group still lives, the runner names it in capitals and leaves it running: its programs, and what it would remove at its end, are left until it ends by itself. The runner then starts no further test on the GPU, finishes the others, and ends with exit code 1 (or 3 if a test accepted something false). The reason: a program killed while one of its kernels runs can make the GPU's driver take the whole machine out of use. For a test without a GPU the processes still in its group get SIGTERM and, twenty seconds later, SIGKILL; a process that has left the group can stay behind. One way to leave the group is known: GNU timeout makes a process group of its own unless it is given --foreground, so a program that such a test starts under timeout can live on after the runner has ended the test, until that timeout's own limit. It was seen with synthetic tests and harms no file.

column3: `cp_commit` does not create, rename or remove a listed name by its whole path: it works through handles on its two working directories and their parents, which it keeps open to its end, so that somebody who can write a parent directory (since `cp_commit` walks the paths at its start, that is root, another process of the caller's or, under sudo, the account that typed sudo; in a sticky parent another account can only put something under a free name: row R2.6.1) and renames a working directory during the run, or puts a link or another directory under its name, does not turn what the run writes or removes onto another directory. A public CPU test, `commit.exchanged_directories` (SUITE.md), runs such an exchange on `cp_commit`'s own routines; the whole `cp_commit`, which needs a GPU, has not been run so on the released programs (a reported test on a test build: row R2.7). There are gaps, by the source's own list: each of the two last renames happens only if the working name still leads to the run's own directory, and between that look and the rename lies a gap; and what the run only reads is looked up by its whole path. (What such a redirect did without the guard, and 32 cases with the guard, neither on the released programs: row R2.2.) Before a file of the public key directory, or that directory itself, gets its final name, `cp_commit` lists the directory and stops if it holds any name other than key.bin, the directory leaf and the files <number>.bin in it; the files may also end in `.making`. It does not list the secret key directory at these moments, and it does not list the public key directory again between a listing and the renames that follow: a name that appears in that stretch is published with the rest. Read in the code; no test of this repository runs it on the whole `cp_commit`.

column3: In `cp_commit`'s clean-up a name is recorded before the thing is created, with two exceptions: the empty directories of the try at its start, which the try removes itself (row R11.1), and the file named with `-worst-case-table`, which is created early and listed only when the cleanup is armed (rows R11, H31). Below its two working directories names are looked up inside a directory of mode 0700 that the run has made, where only its owner and root can change a name; each working directory that the run has opened is itself removed only while its name still leads to the directory that was opened, and between that look and the removal lies a short gap; one that is listed and not yet opened, or whose opening failed, is removed by its name without that look, which can take only an empty directory.

A bad result, not on the released programs: a hostile second account that could write to the directory in which `cp_commit` works could turn what it wrote and removed onto other files, also when it ran as root; in tests this harmed the caller's files. With `cp_commit`'s guard against that, 32 cases were run, not on the released programs, as root and as a user: the 22 attacks that had done harm, 8 good calls and prepared cases, and the guard's own test twice. Nothing of the caller's was harmed; in 2 of the 22 only a directory's times moved. The runs drive `cp_commit`'s file-handling code through the tree's own test harness, not `cp_commit` itself, which needs a GPU. The guard is in these sources (row R2); the public test `commit.exchanged_directories` tries such exchanges on the same routines.

column3: `cp_commit`'s guard against redirected paths has one narrow gap. A working directory that the run has just made must be the caller's own, closed to others and empty when it is opened; if it is not, or cannot be listed, the run ends with exit code 4 and leaves it as it is. So between its creation and its opening only an empty, closed directory of the caller's own can still be taken for the run's own: at a bad end it is removed, at the good end it becomes the secret or the public key directory; nothing of anybody's can be inside it. A public CPU test, `commit.exchanged_directories` (SUITE.md), covers that case: a closed directory with a file in it, exchanged in between: exit code 4, nothing written into it, its file unchanged, not removed.

`cp_commit` rejects a working directory that holds files: a closed directory of the caller's own, with files in it, that a second account puts under the working directory's name between its creation and its opening is not taken for the run's own (the public test commit.exchanged_directories tries it: row R2.3). A bad result, not on the released programs: such a directory was taken, in 22 runs of a test driver around `cp_commit`'s file-handling code, not of `cp_commit` itself. No contents were lost, but after a run that succeeded the caller's directory was the secret key directory, with the caller's files inside it beside the seed and the key, and no line told the caller.

One case is told otherwise: where the name `<name>.making.making` is taken, under which a call that was killed in its first moment leaves an empty directory, the rejection's sentence says first that `rmdir` removes that empty directory, then offers two new names, without these looks (read in the code). column3: What `cp_commit` writes into its two working directories it reaches from handles that it keeps on these two directories, not by a whole path; the count of the anchor's opened columns is raised through the kept handle too. Below a working directory the rest of a name can have several parts (a leaf table's directory and its files), and these are looked up by path from the handle: a part that is exchanged for a link there would be followed, which only the account that runs `cp_commit` and root can do, since the run makes both directories with mode 0700. A fault that these sources do not have, by a reading of the code: where that count goes by a whole path, somebody able to exchange the name of the secret working directory while `cp_commit` runs can get the bytes that count these columns appended to another count file that belongs to the caller, so that the other count grows and this one does not. The unit test commit.exchanged_directories, which raises that count as `cp_commit` does, under an exchanged directory, finds another count file of the caller's untouched; the whole program has not been run so. What the run only reads is looked up by its whole path (the seed's file, read again for a comparison; the configuration that `cp_verify` reads); there a difference ends the run. Outside the two directories `cp_commit` writes one more file, the one named with `-worst-case-table`: it is created and removed from a handle on its directory, which `cp_commit` opens at its start, part by part, as it opens the parents of the two key directories (row R2.6.1); nothing is overwritten. Root, the caller's other processes and, under sudo, the account that typed sudo can still rename the file while the run goes on; a failed run, which removes the file by its name, then leaves it under the new name (read in the code, not tried). The file is computed from the weights; it is created so that only the account that ran `cp_commit` can read it.

column3: At its start, before a weight is loaded, `cp_commit` opens the directories in which it creates the two key directories and the file named with `-worst-case-table` part by part, as `cp_prove` opens the secret key directory. It rejects a symbolic link along the path, and a directory along it, the last one included, that belongs to an account other than root, the caller or, under sudo, the account that typed sudo, or in which group or others can write (a sticky directory such as /tmp is accepted, but not a part in it that belongs to another account): `cp-commit-path`, and nothing is touched. It does not walk the paths given with `-config` and `-weights`: whoever can write to a directory on one of these can point `cp_commit` at other input files. A directory along the path that belongs to root, the caller or, under sudo, the account that typed sudo, and in which group and others cannot write, is trusted: against what these accounts themselves do there the walk does not guard. The walk is made once, at the start: a later change of these directories' owner, mode or place `cp_commit` does not see (it does end the run at an exchanged working directory and at a final name that has been taken); once the run has ended, an older secret key directory of the same owner put where the new one stood is not noticed by it; `cp_prove` walks the path to the secret key directory again at every start. In a sticky parent another account can still put something under a name that is free, a final name too, but cannot rename or remove the run's directories. By the code nobody can read the seed or the weights in this way: `cp_commit` rejects a name that already exists, and accepts a directory that it has just made only if it is the caller's, closed to group and others, empty and no link. The seed's file, when it is read again, and the configuration that `cp_verify` reads are looked up by their whole paths. Read in the code, and seen in two halves, not on the released programs: the rule itself beside a second account, as root, in a test harness on the CPU; and that a built `cp_commit` applies it at the three options and at the parent, on a GPU, under one account, in a test build (it rejected a link at each of the three and a parent with mode 0777; a control without the rule rejected none). Not shown: root beside a second account on the built program; the production build. A CPU test of this repository (commit.walked_parents) tries the two routines without `cp_commit` itself.

column3: A bad result, reported, on a test build, not on the released programs; of its two ways the second is open to the run's own account. Reported: a test that is not part of this repository ran the whole `cp_commit` (a test build, a test seed, synthetic weights, one small configuration) beside a stand-in for `cp_verify` that exchanged directories during the run, under the run's own account. Through a link to the public key directory, put under the secret key directory's name, the run wrote there, and then removed what it had written; and where a leaf table's unfinished directory was replaced by a link to the public key directory's directory of leaf files, that table's kept files were written there, `cp_commit`'s listing of the public key directory noticed them, and no leaf file was published. By reading, the first way is closed: `cp_commit` writes and removes through handles on its two working directories, which it keeps open, and a public CPU test, `commit.exchanged_directories` (SUITE.md), makes such exchanges on its file routines. The second is closed only against other accounts: below a working directory names are looked up by path, inside a directory that only the run's own account and root can change (the source says so itself), and the CPU test has no such exchange in a run that makes a commitment. There a table's stored nodes and its 32 random bytes could be written into the public working directory; the same listing comes before a leaf file is published and ends the run, the cleanup then overwrites each of these files with zeros, if it is a file that the run itself has created (it knows them by device and inode), and unlinks them by the same path, and the public key directory gets its final name only in the run's last step (by the source's own comment, if that step fails, or a caught signal comes right behind it, what has its final name is renamed back or removed again: docs/faults.md, "A killed or failed cp_commit"). Whoever has that account can read the secret key directory anyway; the risk is a mistake, or another program of that account. Beside that reported test and the trial of row H21.13, no run of the whole `cp_commit` beside such exchanges is known.

column3: After SIGKILL or another signal that it does not catch, `cp_commit` removes nothing: it leaves directories whose names end in `.making`, one of them with the seed; if the call died in its very last step, what it made is under `<isk>` and `<ivk>.making`, or, partly or wholly, under both final names (docs/faults.md, "A killed or failed cp_commit"). After Ctrl-C, SIGTERM, SIGHUP, a broken pipe or an abort of its own it removes everything that the call has made, from the moment when the cleanup is armed, overwritten first; a file that it cannot overwrite keeps its name (row R3.2 tells what the printed line then says). Before that moment the file named with `-worst-case-table` can stay (rows R11, H31). A signal that was ignored when the program started, as under `nohup`, stays ignored.

column3: When the end of a `cp_commit` begins on a second thread (by the source's comment: that thread's own abort, or a signal from outside that the system delivers to it), its last line can say that everything was removed while the empty public key directory is left (in test programs, 2 to 4 runs in 1,000 to 3,000); by the source's own comment a file or a new name can be left as well. In the test build a call for fewer than all leaf tables ends with exit code 0 and leaves a commitment that no later call can finish.
column4: After any call of `cp_commit` that did not end well, look into the output directories yourself and do not rely on its last line.

column3: When `cp_commit` stops early and takes back what it has made, it first writes zeros over every file on its own list of the files that the call has created (kept by device and inode) and syncs it: first those of at most 32 bytes (the seed, each leaf table's own random bytes and, with `-keep-for-the-audit`, the kept bytes), then the large files of stored hash-tree nodes and the file named with `-worst-case-table`, which is computed from the weights. The overwriting has limits: the cleanup goes by the names that the run gave, so a listed file that another hand has moved away from its name is not overwritten; a file that cannot be overwritten keeps its name, and a line says so (at an abort or a caught signal without naming the file); a file with a second hard link is not overwritten: its name is removed, and nothing is said; so is what is no regular file, what cannot be examined (that may also be left), and a file whose device and inode numbers are no longer those that were noted at its creation; and on flash, on a copy-on-write file system or under snapshots the old bytes can outlive the zeros. Overwriting the large files takes seconds for each gigabyte, and a call that is killed meanwhile (as by a scheduler that sends SIGKILL some seconds after its first signal) leaves the rest as it is (read in the code; a CPU test that is not part of this repository tries the overwriting on `cp_commit`'s file routines in a harness, for files of 32 bytes, for larger ones and for one that cannot be overwritten, not with the whole `cp_commit`).
column4: Keep everything that `cp_commit` writes on an encrypted disk. If a disk has left your hands, assume that these files have been read.

column3: `cp_commit` sets the times of last access and last modification of the public files that it writes to 0. The time of the last status change, which the system sets, stays and still tells when a file got its name; the times of the public key directories are not set. That the two times are 0 is tested on `cp_commit`'s routines in a CPU harness that is not part of this repository, not on the whole program; on the whole program a test (a test build, a small configuration, synthetic weights) checks the modes of the seed's file, of the files kept for the audit and of the worst-case table's file, and of no public file. No test checks on the whole `cp_commit` which names an honest run leaves, that the published bytes are the ones that its own run of `cp_verify` passed, or what it does when that run says no.

The removals in `cp_commit`'s cleanup make only system calls, and overwriting takes time: if one of these calls never returns, as on a dead network disk, only a signal that the program does not catch, such as SIGKILL, ends the process (the source's own word; read in the code).

column3: After a failed call `cp_commit` overwrites a file only if it is a file that this run made: a regular file, with one name, whose device and inode numbers are among those that this run noted. Where that look fails, or the file at that name has other numbers, is not regular or has a second hard link, it writes no zeros, the name is removed all the same, and no line says so. This was shown for the routine alone, by one small test program with other numbers noted at a file's creation: the seed's file was unlinked with all its bytes as they were, under the same printed line as after an overwrite. No file system on which a file's numbers change is known, and none has been tried; by a reading of the code, every call that writes such a file notes it before its first byte.
column4: Keep everything that `cp_commit` writes on an encrypted disk. If a disk has left your hands, assume that these files have been read.

column3: For the anchor and for each leaf table, the secret key directory holds a file, `hcnodes.bin`, with one level of that table's hash tree. Each entry is a hash over a run of neighbouring columns of the masked table. Each column is hashed together with a 40-byte salt of its own, which stays secret until that column is opened. `cp_commit` creates the file readable by its owner only, and no program publishes it. Otherwise the programs do not treat it as a secret. Every opening of the table sends some of these hashes, or hashes computed from them, beside the opened columns. `cp_prove` leaves its copy in memory when a batch ends. What someone who got the whole file could learn from it has not been examined, by a test or by a reading. No written statement covers what all the stored digests together tell somebody who holds the whole file. This row reports no finding: the file is not known to give anything away.
column4: Let no other account open the secret key directory, and copy or hand out nothing from it (duties 1 and 4: docs/limits.md#the-conditions).

column3: The routine by which `cp_commit` would sweep what a dead call has left of an unfinished leaf table only unlinks it, its 32 fresh bytes too, without overwriting them. No call reaches that routine: it belongs to a call on an existing commitment, which `cp_commit` rejects. So no program removes a dead call's leavings, and nothing overwrites the seed or the fresh bytes in them. A call that ends by itself, or at a signal that it catches, overwrites every file that it has created before it unlinks it (row R3.2 tells the limits of that).

column3: `cp_commit` has a routine that, under a lock, keeps two calls on one existing commitment from setting back the two numbers in the secret key directory's text file that say which leaf tables are in use (how many there are, and the first that is still in use); a lower second number would put a retired leaf table into use again. No call reaches that routine: `cp_commit` rejects every call on an existing commitment. A CPU test that is not part of this repository runs the routine by itself, with one call paused at a chosen moment, and it does not show: calls that meet without a pause; two machines on one directory; a file system that does not enforce flock(); a text file that is edited by hand; a clean-up call beside a call that is at its rename; that another account cannot hold the lock; or that `cp_commit` calls the routine at all. By the source's own comment, of calls from two machines one can still take another's number back where a shared file system grants the lock to each machine by itself.

The audit's helper programs run beside the seed. audit_commitment.sh and audit_batch.sh keep them in a directory that they close to everybody else, and start python3 so that no PYTHON* variable and no user site-packages decide where it looks for modules. Ways by which foreign code could run there: both scripts trust the rest of the caller's environment, in which PATH, LD_*, BASH_ENV and other variables can name code; and every other python3 start of tools/audit/, in play.sh or by hand, honours a PYTHONPATH that the caller has set; audit.py started by hand also loads libfield.so from where AUDIT_LIB points, or else from the tool's own directory, without checking whose it is.
column4: Start the audit through audit_commitment.sh or audit_batch.sh, not through audit.py; give the script a work directory that does not exist yet; start it from a shell whose variables you have set yourself; unset PYTHONPATH before play.sh.

column3: prover/build.sh does not build `cp_verify`: it takes the program that it finds at the verifier's build path, and `cp_commit`'s check of its public files relies on that copy. `cp_commit`'s production build rejects, before anything is made, a `cp_verify` that was not built from the sources that are there (what this does not catch: row LF-15), and looks at its copy once more; a test build takes what it finds. `cp_prove`'s build looks at no `cp_verify`: a new `cp_prove` can stand beside an older `cp_verify` with nothing saying so.
column4: Rebuild the verifier before each build of the prover.

column3: For `cp_commit`'s production build prover/build.sh rejects a `cp_verify` that does not hold, in its bytes, the digest of the verifier's sources as they are (the word that it would print as `build=`), and `cp_commit`'s build record carries the copy's SHA-256 (the line `verifier-beside`); `cp_prove`'s record names no verifier. The script searches the file for that word and does not run it; the word covers the sources only, neither the compiler nor its options; and any file that holds the word passes. For the tests' build nothing is asked.
No program compares the digest of the sources for the reader, and the tests, but for one file, lie outside that digest.

Once it has begun to read secrets, the production build's `cp_prove` says why it ended only by a fixed word in its last line; an ending for which it has no word ends in a bare line, and so does a crash, unless a word was set before the crash: then that word is printed, with exit code 9 after a failed self-check. Status 0 also ends a run whose answers are all "failed", and it never says that a proof verifies.

column3: An abort of `cp_prove` skips the wipe; under the production build a line before the last ("p258 not every step of the wipe ran: ..") then says so, if the program has begun to read its secrets (the line is shown by a unit test on the host, which is not part of this repository, on the code that ends the program; on a GPU only its absence at complete wipes has been seen, not on the released programs). A wipe can also run and fail: after a kernel's illegal memory access or trap every later CUDA call fails, the zeroing too, so weights and masks may stay on the GPU; the last line does not tell the operator that, a line before it does, wherever the program can still print (read). That the zeroing then fails has been seen, on a test build, not on the released programs, in three runs of one test on a small synthetic model, under NVIDIA's compute-sanitizer, which reported an internal error of its own; after an illegal memory access `cp_prove` printed that GPU memory could not be zeroed, and its last line said that not every step of the wipe had run. The production build's line has not been seen in such a run. Where the fault is first met inside a call of the code that holds the weight table, that code's own zeroing is skipped as well, and its mask seed, any pads already made from it, and the combination of its rows stay in host memory too (row R7.1.1 tells that case). A zeroing that has not finished after 600 seconds, as when the GPU no longer answers, is given up, and the program ends with the name not-all-wiped; after exit code 9 the last line does not say so: a line before it does. By the source's own comment the limit does not help while the program's main thread sleeps uninterruptibly in the kernel, as with a dead driver or a hung disk: the process then hangs and prints nothing until it is killed. This limit has been tested only on CPUs with stand-ins, not on the released programs, and never on a GPU.

At every exit at which it can still print, under every name and status, the production build's `cp_prove` prints a line before its last (`p258 not every step of the wipe ran: ..`) if a step of the wipe failed or was skipped, a crash included once the program has begun to read its secrets. Where, after the line `p258 closed`, the last line is printed without it, the program has counted every step as run, which is less than that nothing is left: a staged file that could not be overwritten earlier, when a request failed together with its batch, has been deleted all the same, and the ending that follows need not count as not all wiped (row H26.1; all read in the code); and the memory that no exit wipes is as before. Where nothing at all is printed (a kill; a loss of power; a stack overflow; a fault inside the handler) nothing is known. The line is shown by a unit test on the host, which is not part of this repository, on the code that ends the program; on a GPU only its absence at complete wipes has been seen, not on the released programs, on 21 screens of four tests. A test build prints at each end whether every step of the wipe ran; that speaks of the wipe's steps, not of all memory: the GPU engine's pool is wiped at no end. One cause of a wipe in which not every step runs is known from the source: where an end begins in the opening that a batch's requests share, which runs on a thread of its own, one step of the wipe is left out on purpose, the erasing that the code which holds the leaf table does itself, because a call of that code is still under way; by the source that holds of every end that comes during such a call, whichever thread began it. Until the process is gone a moment later, the leaf table's 32-byte mask seed, from which the masks, the salts and the pads are made, a second copy of it, any pads already made from it, and the combination of its rows, which is an exact linear image of the weights, of the masks and of the pads, then stay in the machine's memory; by reading, the GPU memory that this code was lent is zeroed by the wipe's next step, if CUDA still responds and the wipe is not given up at its time limit; that was read in the code for each of the three places that lent memory comes from: the sub-proofs' scratch memory and the weight stream's GPU buffers, in both of which copies of weights lie for a while, and, with `-overlap`, a buffer that `cp_prove` allocates for the part. The thread that is still inside that code can write to this memory again afterwards, and the GPU memory that the part allocates for itself at set-up is zeroed at no exit. The source allows other causes: if the zeroing of the GPU's memory itself fails, weights and masks may stay on the GPU, and that it was this step only a line on standard error says, which the production build does not show; and in a service the last step, which overwrites and removes staged files, can itself fall short, and then staged files that were not released stay under out/.tmp/ until a next start on that directory whose requests have the same length as those left in `work/`, for any commitment, overwrites and removes them (rows HW-480 and R18.2). Under the first two causes nothing stays on disk.
column4: Where that line is printed, or nothing at all, treat the GPU and the machine's memory as not wiped; after exit code 9 do so in any case. After every other exit both still hold what no exit wipes (R7).

column3: A public file that fails a guard of the shared planning code ends `cp_prove` at its planning step, before a request is taken; whether that end runs the wipe has not been traced (blocks/base.h: a guard wipes only where the wipe has been armed in that part of the program). By then the seed has been read and the weights are in memory (the host's, the GPU's or both, by the setting).

By a reading and a search of other sources (row HW-678), a production build has no switch that skips the zeroing of memory buffers. Such switches as `skip_zero_shipped` and `skip_zero_turns` are in test builds, but in a production build each is a constant, so no code can enable one and the compiler can drop what depends on it.

The verifier's code is linked into `cp_commit` behind one entry routine. That it opens no file there, works only on bytes that are handed to it, and never reaches its forking, piping and printing parts rests on that routine's text and header: the routines that it calls have not been traced.

At an ending of `cp_prove` that comes while the service's thread is inside a call of the unit that keeps the weight table, such as a failed guard there, that unit's own wipe is left out. By a reading, host memory then keeps that leaf table's 32-byte making key, twice, and one vector, for the moment until the process is gone. That is so through the whole of a batch's shared chain: the chain runs on a thread of its own while the service's thread waits inside that unit, so every self-check that ends `cp_prove` on that chain (own-test-fold-mask, own-test-mask-rows and own-test-lin-mask among them) ends it in this way, wherever the check itself stands in the code; a test build's last line then says that not every step of the wipe ran (under the production build a line before the last does: row R7.1). Memory adds nothing to the disk here: `cp_prove` makes that key at each batch's head from files that are in the secret key directory for the commitment's life. A wipe in which every step ran is no clean bill either: further copies of the key on stacks, the weights' pinned host copy and the GPU engine's pool stay then too.

Neither abort() nor a signal runs an exit handler, and the stops of the proof library and of the GPU engine end by abort(), running out of GPU memory among them: in a run of a `cp_commit` that caught no signal, not on the released programs, the seed's file stayed on the disk under its temporary name (mode 0600). These sources do not have that fault (prover/hash_commitment/hf_commit_making.h, "The cleanup at five signals"): `cp_commit` catches five signals, SIGABRT among them, and, from the moment when the cleanup is armed to the run's good end, removes by name what the call has made; one stretch is not covered (an abort, or a signal from outside, on another thread in the middle of a write). Two tests, which are not part of this repository, ask for it: one, a harness on the cleanup's source file and not `cp_commit` itself, has passed on CPUs, not on the released programs; the other, which signals a GPU program in mid-work, has not been run on the released programs. After SIGKILL, any other signal, a crash or a power failure what was made stays, with the seed.
column4: After a killed `cp_commit`, treat what is left under the two working names as secret; the next call's rejection says whether a call is still running there and which two directories an interrupted call has left.

column3: Test scripts do shell arithmetic on words that they read; a crafted word would run a command unless the script first checks that it is all digits. By one reading of 102 shell scripts, not all as released (33 of them are part of this repository, which has at least one that was not among them; nothing was run in that reading; for two of the scripts in this repository a test or a trial, not on the released programs, has shown that a word with a command in it is rejected), every such word that comes from a file which the script did not write itself is checked in this way before it is used (read by eye for the 33 scripts that are part of this repository; sorted by program for the others); of the 42 words that are checked, 19 have a check of their own, and 23 are checked only by the pattern of the sed or grep that fetches them (8 of these in scripts of this repository); several scripts read a word of a parameter file so. One of them, prover/tests/serving_first_run.sh, was tried, not on the released programs, with four crafted parameter files, as root and as a user: rejected 8 of 8. Five variables in four scripts are not checked: one is read from a file that the script has itself just written (prover/tests/refused_at_the_start.sh, the only one of the four in this repository); the others come from the caller's own arguments or from a line that a test program prints. Not read: shell text inside other files (the commands in SUITE.md's rows, Makefiles, Python tests).

column3: The scan for file names that a script could misread (a blank, a colon, a quotation mark, a dollar sign, a line end, a leading dash) is a test that is not part of this repository. It looks at every name below the tree's top directory; it does not look at the name of that directory or of any directory above it, and it checks a symbolic link by its own name without following it (read in the test). So it says nothing on the place where a user unpacks the tree. The test runner admits a work directory only if its whole path consists of letters, digits and / . _ - alone, but asks nothing of the kind of the tree's own path, which it hands to the tests; ten rows of the test table put that path into their commands without quotation marks, where the shell splits it at a blank (read; what follows from it is reasoned, not run). Some scripts stop by themselves under a path with a blank. tests/new/run_new.py refuses to run under a path that holds [, ], * or ? (read in the script). No test in this repository was found that runs anything from a tree that lies under a path with a blank or a colon (searched); one test that is not part of this repository does so with blanks, for the opening checks of one build script alone, which is not part of this repository either, in a small tree that it makes for itself.
column4: Unpack the repository under a path of letters, digits and / . _ - alone.

column3: Some of the tests that ship run malicious provers or committers with code of their own, but only at toy size: they show that a check rejects each of them, not how small the soundness error is. The malicious provers and committers that were built from the library's and the programs' own sources under a switch are not part of this repository, and the code under that switch is not in these sources, but for hooks that do nothing and lines behind them that can never run, and but for one test variable of `cp_commit`'s test builds, which can get a committed integer past the range scan (row E29.1). Of the 57 lying proofs tried at full size (row LIM-63.1), at least three, by their makers' labels, aimed at the lookups (a key in no row; a count at another row) and at a digit's range (the 24 made for false replies have records that name no kind); these three were refused at the check that the proof's masked message fits the linear claim, before any check of a lookup or a range was reached, so no refusal at the lookup checks themselves has been seen (by the testers' record, which is not in this repository; row LIM-63.1). No test that ships runs a copy of `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` or `cp_verify` that is weakened or made to cheat; where the tests that ship do cheat, they do so in test programs of their own. No test that ships injects a fault into the running state of the three programs. No test of the table runs `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` at full size, and none of the table's tests puts a malicious prover's full-size files before `cp_verify`. Public tests have `cp_verify` check the stored full-size example, an honest prover's files on synthetic weights, made at the default setting, and require that the proof is accepted (where that example's three large files are not in the tree, the three rows leave it out, or run nothing, and end with status 77, which the runner counts as passed in part: SUITE.md): the row verifier.call_accounting.examples by a call of its own, which goes on only at exit code 0, the row integrations.cp_verify through integrations/check_proof.py (where python3 has no pytest the row runs none of this and counts as not run, not as failed; where pytest's temporary directory lies below a place that another account can change it runs none of this either, and counts as passed in part), and the row verifier.record_altered_sets.full, which asks for `YES` on the honest files and then has `cp_verify` reject, each by name, 23 altered sets of them, in whole calls and in the part-calls `-key` and `-leaf`; where other tests of the table call `cp_verify` at the full-size configuration, they do so on synthetic key, leaf and proof files, or in planning calls, which judge no proof. None uses a real model's weights.

Some tests would not notice the fault that they are there for, and most tests that were written for other programs (row HW-678) are not in the suite, most of the apparent guards of hiding among them (92 of 111). Some 2,150 more such tests are not in the suite either, and which kinds of cheating no test tries, or which rules of hiding no test guards, has not been mapped.

The rules that the tests in row T2 checked apply to these programs (no stretch of random values drawn twice; the record of what an attempt reveals; salts of openings; memory lent to several requests), and what checks them has not been traced, test by test.

That each planning routine reads its sizes once, so that nobody can change them between two reads, is checked by a test for 18 of the 22 places. A second test, which is not part of this repository, weakens each place by itself and runs the first test on it, under two compilers: 36 of the 44 runs were noticed; the four places that are not seen are ones that the planner passes on once, to a routine that copies them first. A copy that allocates memory is itself not made in one step (a list is copied entry by entry, a struct member by member), so code of the caller's that runs in the middle of a planning routine can change the original during the copy; by that second test's own argument the copy is then an object that the caller could have passed in, and a round's bound and what is stated with it still come from the copy alone.
