column3: The range check's own text in the verifier is tested claim by claim at toy lengths only, by one unit test (verifier/tests/tail_twin_test.cpp: its source is in this repository, and no row of SUITE.md runs it). Two of eleven kinds of altered prover are not in that test (one of ten runs at tau 24 and one of four runs of repeated tries at tau 8): they need the library's prover to go on past a false claim, which only a cheating build allows, and these sources cannot make one. That test does not walk the place where values are sent, the link's closing or the proximity tests, which another test walks on a synthetic equation. Of the weakened copies of the sources that it must catch, in a control that is not part of this repository and was not run on the released programs, nearly all (21 of 23) break the honest prover too, so they show little beyond what an honest run shows.

The range check's own code in `cp_verify` has a unit test that goes claim by claim, at toy lengths. It judges each claim by itself on the prover's data: the step that hands the sub-proof's one batched equation to the proof's chain, the segment's closing and the proximity tests are not run there (another unit test runs these, on a synthetic equation). Its control, which is not part of this repository and was not run on the released programs, makes 23 scratch copies of that code with one step changed: 21 of them break the honest prover too, so they show little; under the last two the honest prover passes, and the test fails only because a malicious prover is accepted (in one run under the one, in two under the other).

No test of `cp_prove` and `cp_verify` together tries a prover that commits to cells which are not small numbers and fits everything else to them, so that the range check alone stands in its way. A cell that everything follows is tried only in a unit test of `cp_verify`'s range-check code (verifier/tests/tail_twin_test.cpp: its source is in this repository, and no row of SUITE.md runs it): at toy lengths, with 8 combinations in the place of 128 (for 2^18 also with 24), for cells of 2^18, and for cells that hold half of a small odd number in the field; for cells of 2^17 + 5,000 too (shown on a cheating test build; no test that ships repeats that run); no test is known with cells that are arbitrary field elements.

A bad result, not on the released programs: in a control of the unit test of `cp_verify`'s lookup code, one weakened copy of that code went unnoticed: the one in which the claim that the multiplicities add up to the number of keys was dropped. The unit test falsifies that claim by itself, and with that all 23 weakened copies were noticed (reported, not on the released programs); that the list of weakenings is complete is not shown. The unit test is part of this repository; the control that makes the weakened copies is not.

At one small example configuration (target_small_file_f2) a proof passed the `cp_verify` that the program of that run started itself, not on the released programs. Two GPU tests ask for the verifier's last line there: one, under the option for public weights only, is handed that configuration and two other small ones; the other makes a commitment, once under a seed that `cp_commit` draws and once under the option. Both are rows of the public test table (`gpu.public_weights` and `gpu.record_on_public_weights`), and passed on the released programs (the first with a test build in four of its calls: docs/limits.md#what-was-run-on-these-programs).

Some shapes of the protocol occur at full size only, so no test at a small configuration reaches them: rate 1/8 in every middle stage of a closeness test (at the small configurations in 5 of 28 middle stages); the main code deciding every middle stage of two of the tests (there the first of four in each); and the code lengths of a request's and a batch's messages, 2^21 to 2^24 (there 2^17 and 2^18; only the key file's message on the ranges has a long code there, 2^22 against 2^23). No test of the test table runs `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` at full size. One branch of the GPU encoder is reached by no configuration file.

Three test programs lack a full race check: on one the checker did not finish in 30 minutes, on another it watches the first 400 kernel launches only, and a third runs under three of NVIDIA's checkers and never under the race checker. That checker looks at shared memory only, so no tool looks for races on global memory. One run of a memory checker, on a served batch, is told in T3.1. On the whole programs of the released design, by the records that were read, the checker for uninitialised memory and the checker of synchronisation have not run, and the race checker has come to its end in no run. So, but for the reports on a served batch that T3.1 tells, which have not been explained whole, no run has shown whether these programs read uninitialised GPU memory. By the same records, on programs of the released design no checker has watched a run with the prover's own overlap option (off by default, and refused on a real model), nor a configuration with proof of work, which the default setting has. No checker of NVIDIA's, on the whole programs or on a unit test program, has run on a GPU on the released programs, by the records that were read. And a pass says little. The runs under NVIDIA's checkers were test builds, synthetic weights and small configurations. Inside the large allocations from which the programs carve many of their buffers, and which they zero when they take them, memcheck sees no read or write that runs from one buffer into the next, and the checker for uninitialised memory no read of a buffer that nothing filled. Neither of these two, nor the checker of synchronisation, notices a read of an unwritten slot of a kernel's local memory. Where the race checker watches the first 400 kernel launches only, it has said nothing about any later launch of that test, or about the launch shapes and branches that only the test's five other small shapes reach; which kernels are among the first 400 was not counted, and why the whole run does not finish under the checker is not known. The runs under NVIDIA's checkers are tests that are not part of this repository, nor are their records.

On one unit test in which two threads use the GPU engine at once, not on the released programs, the checker for uninitialised memory reported reads of unwritten memory in 50 of 148 runs; for 28 of 30 such runs, which were of a test build with print lines added, the reports that the tool printed are explained as false alarms; the reports that it counted and did not print (it printed 1,800 of 11,332), the other runs, one report in the programs' own kernel among them, and one illegal memory access are not explained. A memory checker reported reads of uninitialised GPU memory in a served batch, in both runs of one test, not on the released programs, at a small size; a one-line fix to the warm-up removed the reports seen, but it was never shown that all those reads came from the warm-up, and no test replays the check.

The unit test of the routines that open a weight table (a GPU test that is not in this repository) is not run under NVIDIA's checker for uninitialised memory. By report, in runs not on the released programs, that checker called every read of the 32-bit sums that a cuBLAS product had written a read of memory that was never written, while the test's results stayed right; this is assumed to be writes by the library's kernel that the tool does not follow, which has not been confirmed from NVIDIA's documents. No check in these sources shows that the GPU library's products write every word that is read afterwards: a check under a test switch, which filled each product's result with a fixed byte beforehand and stopped the program at a word that held it afterwards, is not in these sources. A second unit test, not in this repository either, which does run under that checker, fills the same buffers with a fixed byte before the calls and compares every result with slowly computed sums, which a place that is read before it is filled would spoil, at small sizes; by report it passed, not on the released programs, with no report from the checker. But a buffer filled in this way counts as written, so in these buffers the checker could not have found anything. If such a read were real, old GPU memory would enter the values of an opened column; from reading the code, with nothing run, the node of the stored hash tree above each opened column is recomputed from these values and compared with the stored one (self-check hc-own-node) before any of the column is handed on.

Most GPU unit test programs run under no sanitizer at all; those that do include no test of the two tensor-core kernels in prover/weights_blocks/. On the whole programs memcheck has run as one test (not part of this repository), at one small configuration of the tests' own (the folder prover/tests/configurations/pinned_no_proof_of_work; it has no proof of work): `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` on one request and `cp_prove` on six requests in batches of two (without the prover's own overlap option), in test builds of programs that ran a check before release, under a test seed, on synthetic weights, with that check switched off by a test option. It passed in three runs on test builds (by inference at the parameter file as it is in this repository). So memcheck has watched the making of published OOD answers in at most three runs, one of them a trial. A pass means that the tool found nothing in the three cases and did find the fault that a control program commits on purpose (row T3.3.1). The test has not been run on a test build of the released programs' sources. No sanitizer can watch the production build: it starts a second time with a reduced environment, where no tool follows (by a reading of the code; no run is known that tried a checker on a production build). Of the eleven GPU kernels that can decode weights stored in 8 or 16 bits nine are launched by test programs (not part of this repository) that have run under the race checker on such weights, synthetic, at small shapes: six runs in one session on one H100, with CUDA 13.2's libraries and CUDA 13.0's checker, not on the released programs: 0 hazards (reported). Of the 178 sources from which these test programs are built, 13 differ in code from the other sources that they were compared with (row HW-678), none in GPU code; no such count has been made against these sources. The text of the eleven kernels and of every device function that they reach is the same in those other sources and in these, token for token (compared by program; the built programs were not compared). That the programs launch the nine was seen in separate runs under a launch counter, not in the checker's own runs. Only two of the nine, qblocks::k_cells_wide and hf::k_slab_cells, have shared memory of their own, which is all that this checker watches. The other two of the eleven have not run under it: wb::k_embedding_cells and fold::integers<int>. No race check has watched any of the eleven kernels at `cp_prove`'s own launch shapes.

The GPU code that opens the weight table (prover/hash_commitment/hf_open_side.cuh) is compiled into `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` and works on values computed from the weights or from the masks (the source says so itself); no race check has finished on its released sources. A test that is not in this repository gives NVIDIA's race checker 30 minutes on that code's unit test (toy sizes, random cells, a test build). In three runs, not on the released programs, the checker was stopped at that limit with no report up to then, which says nothing either way, so that test failed in each of the three, while the checkers for memory errors and for synchronisation found nothing on the same program. By reading: that header's own three kernels declare no shared memory, which is what this checker watches; of the headers that it includes directly, two declare some (what those include was not followed), and tests that are not in this repository put their own unit tests under the race checker, at those tests' sizes (what those runs found is not told here). What a race in this code would do to a proof, and which self-check would notice it, has not been tried.

Before a test program runs under one of NVIDIA's checkers, a test script first runs a small control program that commits a fault on purpose, which the checker must report; else a silent checker would show nothing. For the checker of synchronisation that fault is a barrier which part of a thread block never reaches: such a kernel need not end by itself, and killing it can put a shared GPU out of use, so it is committed only in one test of its own, which wants a GPU that nobody else uses and has not been run. The other runs under that checker say themselves that they have not shown that it finds a fault. These tests are not part of this repository.

Two builds of the same sources need not give the same program files, though in the pairs that were compared their machine code was the same (row R19.1.1). The word `build=` that `cp_verify` prints covers its source files only, comments included, not the compiler or its options, so two verifiers with the same word can differ; and `cp_verify` gets no build record.

Speed was measured at the default setting (the sessions with whole replies checked: under a clipped-gap policy), in the timed runs for some jobs only and for the rest not on the released programs, in three whole runs of each job at most; on one H100 at a time, on shared machines; with requests of 1,024 tokens; in few serving sessions, of five or six batches each. The plain baselines behind the overhead rows were not measured in the timed runs. Of the services at 24 requests a batch on the public files: in the timed runs the six services of this job, at the same setting, lay between 110.07 and 112.04 tokens/second steady; not on the released programs six such services lay between 100.81 and 111.55 tokens/second, and three of the timed runs' six lie above that range (the timed runs' six are counted by another rule, every interval between two batches: row RES-4); the widest difference between two services at 24 requests a batch that ran one after the other on one machine, card and commitment was 0.7 % in the timed runs (108.44 and 109.23 tokens/second, in the like job on synthetic weights; the slower under the faster), and not on the released programs it was 6.3 % (104.56 and 111.55 tokens/second); a gap between two rows of the figures no larger than the larger of these shows nothing about the programs, an option, the weights or how busy a machine was. docs/figures.tsv gives the figures, and for each set of runs its conditions. column3: `cp_prove` does not reserve all its GPU memory at start-up (some buffers' sizes follow which of the verifier's drawn positions coincide), and its alarm for memory that grows, which every build prints at most once in a process, does not look at the GPU engine's memory pool and so can miss late growth, which was observed, not on the released programs: in four full-size services the whole GPU's memory in use grew after the first batch; whether it was the pool that grew was not looked at, and the reason is not known. With other buffer sizes, not on the released programs, the pool could rise by steps of 32 MiB (seen: 160 MiB over six batches in one full-size service, and not in the next); how far it can rise on the released programs has not been measured, and the growth was not looked at on them. If memory runs out, `cp_prove` exits and every client in the batch sees a failure, and one allocation's size depends on memory content that may include tables made from the weights (P3.3).

column3: Of the GPU engine's memory pool no buffer's size was found to follow a hidden value (by a reading of other sources (row HW-678)); but for the largest buffer that changes from batch to batch the cause has not been shown. For the prover's other GPU memory the source says that this has not been shown for all allocations.

If GPU memory runs out, `cp_prove` ends. The ending process answers nothing: the requests that it held stay in the spool directory, and the next start answers "failed" to each, which every client of the batch then sees. The alarm for memory that grows does not see, by the source's own list: what the CUDA runtime and vendor libraries take; the GPU engine's own pool; the buffers for streamed weights; two tables of the program's own book-keeping; what the separately compiled code that holds the weight table allocates; a buffer that fits in memory that is already mapped; and a later allocation that stays at or under the earlier peak. It can also go off without a fault, and is never taken back while the process lives. Not on the released programs, a pass with more requests than the first set this alarm off for the rest of the process. Whether a pass with more requests than the first sets this alarm off on the released programs is not known: by the source's own comment a later pass with more requests than the first can allocate more (concluded from reading the code; not tried on the released programs), and no test asks for the alarm's line by name or forbids it by name. Two GPU tests in this repository compare what `cp_prove` prints after its line "p258 closed:" with a list of allowed lines, and the alarm's line is on that list, so that comparison passes with the line and without it. Of the tests that are not part of this repository one holds that list to the sources, and one requires an exact number of printed lines of a run of one batch, so it would fail if the alarm came there; neither looks for the alarm (searched; read in the code, not run). On the released programs no test runs a service whose first pass holds fewer requests than a later one. The alarm is one constant line for the operator and costs no request its files. Whether it appears depends on how many requests a pass holds compared with the first pass; that it does not also depend on how tokens are routed to experts, and so on weights and prompts, has not been shown (the source says so itself).

column3: One size of `cp_prove`'s GPU memory is known to follow content. At the end of the set-up the GPU memory on `cp_prove`'s own allocator's list, but for the weights, the buffers into which they are streamed and what is declared as written once, is sorted in pieces of 256 KiB, and every stretch that is not all zeros gets a second copy: on the GPU only for stretches of at most 16 MiB, 1 GiB in all, else in host memory. Tables made from the weights may be among these stretches; whether any are, and which, has not been traced: two of three readings of the source could not trace what that memory holds; the third found only values from the configuration files for one of the two kernels, and could not finish for the other.

`cp_commit` fills the GPU on purpose while it makes the key file: before the range proof it takes nearly all GPU memory that is free at that moment as a cache of packed weights, whatever the model's size. A smaller GPU or a neighbour on the GPU gives a smaller cache, or none. Where memory then falls short while the cache is held, the program ends by an abort or with "GPU fault: out of memory", a file and a line; before an abort it first prints how many bytes were asked for and how many the driver calls free. Once the cache has been given back, at the two places where it then sizes its large buffers a shortage is told in a plain sentence, with exit code 2; later allocations still end in one of the two ways above.
column4: Give `cp_commit` an empty GPU. `-gpu-memory <GiB>` makes it take less.

column3: `cp_prove` and `cp_commit` look once, at their start, at how much memory is in use on the one GPU that they will use, their own share counted in, and refuse to start if it is more than 2 GiB (`gpu-in-use`; `cp_commit`: exit code 2, nothing read of the configuration or the model, nothing drawn, and nothing written but the early try's empty directories, which it has made and removed again by then (row R11.1); `cp_prove`: no key was drawn). The look does not see a program that starts later, or one that has not yet taken its memory; it does not show that there is enough memory; a small neighbour passes. Only a build with test options goes on, under a test option. It guards against running out of memory in the middle of the work. It is no guard of hiding on a shared GPU.
column4: Give each program a GPU of its own.

column3: `cp_commit`, for the host memory in which it holds all the model's tensors, and `cp_prove`, for the host memory in which it holds the streamed weights, ask the system for huge pages (madvise, MADV_HUGEPAGE) only with the option `-huge-pages`, which is off by default; for its weight-table keepers' buffers `cp_prove` never asks. Without the request the machine's own setting (/sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled) decides whether the memory gets huge pages. Either way the programs zero that memory at once with up to 16 or, in `cp_commit`, up to 32 threads (read in the code; a test that is not part of this repository reads the sources for the two requests and their flags). At a start on a model's files both programs then page-lock that memory and read the files into it through the system's file cache, which leaves a second copy of what was read beside the locked one. Each program asks the system to drop that copy (posix_fadvise, POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED) once it holds a whole tensor, and `cp_commit` under `-public-weights` also once it has computed a file's SHA-256; until then the cached bytes of up to one tensor for each reading thread (one in `cp_prove`, eight in `cp_commit`) stand beside the locked copy, and during the check of the SHA-256 values, before any memory is locked, those of up to one whole file. The request is advice: pages that lie only partly in a tensor's range stay, on some file systems larger units of the cache at a range's edges too, read-ahead can bring a dropped tensor's first bytes back, and the system may keep others, so at worst the two copies still stand together: up to twice the files' size. What it frees at full size has not been measured. Its price: whoever reads the files next, `cp_prove` after `cp_commit` or a service that is started again, may have to read them from the disk again, and `cp_commit` under `-public-weights`, which reads every file twice, may have to read it from the disk both times. No option turns the request off, and neither program looks first at how much host memory is available (read in the code). Seen on a machine shared with other work, at full size, not on the released programs: starts that took markedly longer than the like start of different programs on another machine of the same kind. The programs of those starts asked for huge pages at every start, as a start with `-huge-pages` does. By `cp_commit`'s own print the time went into preparing and locking fresh host memory, not into reading the files; meanwhile the kernel reported memory pressure and stalls for compaction, which neighbours on the same machine feel too (seen at each of three starts on one machine). Two causes are candidates: the request for huge pages on fragmented memory (likely, not shown), and plain want of free memory (measured once). On machines with plenty of free, unfragmented memory no slow start was seen at full size (not on the released programs). Some full-size figures were taken, not on the released programs, with `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` asking Linux for transparent huge pages for their large blocks of host memory at every start. The released programs do so only with `-huge-pages`, so a run of theirs without that option is not the run that was measured there. A run with the option is nearer to it, but not the same. Those other programs (row HW-678) also requested huge pages for some of `cp_prove`'s other buffers, and even with the option `cp_prove` does not. The released programs have not been timed with the option at full size.
column4: Before a start at full size look at the machine's free memory, by NUMA node, and do not run `cp_commit` at full size beside other people's work on one machine. Against the first cause: leave `-huge-pages` out. What the option gains or costs at full size has been measured once, as a pair of runs, for the start and the exit, not on the released programs. Without huge pages `cp_commit`'s start took longer to lock its memory, and each program took longer to exit (the exit's times: prover/docs/ends-in-short.md). Whether the option changes a steady rate has not been measured.

column3: On the option `-huge-pages` of `cp_commit` and `cp_prove`: From reading the code, nothing that the programs print says that it was given, or whether the system granted the request. Without the option the machine's own setting, `/sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled`, decides whether that memory gets huge pages: under `always` it can get them unasked, and under `madvise` or `never` it gets none.

`cp_verify` sets itself no limit on time or memory, and it parses and plans the configuration before it compares the commitment ID, so a hostile configuration is processed first. At the default setting, with 24 threads, `cp_verify`'s largest process in the timed runs took 3.53 GB on real public weights and 3.53 GB on synthetic weights (each the largest of 3 runs, each run's own figure being the largest resident set of any one process, the larger of two calls; docs/figures.tsv, rows verify-memory and verify-memory-synthetic).
column4: Take the configuration from whoever vouches for the model, or run `cp_verify` under a memory and time limit of your own.
column5: run: the two figures told of `cp_verify` in the timed runs; reported

column3: `cp_verify` bounds single numbers of the parameter file (no code is longer than 2^32: `parameter-group-shape`, `parameter-stages-shape`, `parameter-table-shape`), but not the sizes that follow from them: with only the line `table` of the full-size example changed (`table 20 32 3000000000 44040191 0 20`), a planning call plans, without the remark that the file is not in the standard parameter form, a key file of up to 3.9 x 10^9 and a leaf file of up to 7.7 x 10^9 bytes (the largest of sixteen tries; no search for a maximum has been made). This call (`cp_verify -plan accounting`) only counts: it reads no key file (run once, not on the released programs). In a whole call the lengths of the request and of y are tested before a byte of them is read, so that a regular file of many gigabytes in the place of either is rejected and not loaded; no such look was seen for the key, leaf and proof files.

`cp_verify` reads the key file, the leaf file and the proof file whole, whatever their size, before it tests their lengths: a file far too large can end the call with exit code 5, or get the process killed by the system, never with YES.
The option `-j` sets the threads of the request's stage only: two more processes run beside it, each on an eighth of that number of threads.

column3: By the last line of the audit of a commitment with the kept bytes, a yes does not cover pads inside tables of real values, the leaf tables' columns, or unopened leaves of trees that hold real values. (Audits at the default setting, and which of them ran on the released programs: row LIM-63.2.)
The audit is to be run only after `cp_commit`'s good last line, and one audit at a time on a directory. It prints its digests and the commitment ID once: nothing prints them a second time.

column3: No way is known by which a client's request passes the prover and is rejected by the verifier. `cp_prove` would not learn of it and would serve on; at the vLLM integration's check it would cost the whole batch, and put on hold the policy under which the batch was proved; where that hold can be written, only a person lifts it (row H26). One such way, a parameter file with theta = C and a cap of 1 or more, is rejected at the programs' start. That there is none is not shown.

By design every published value that depends on the weights is masked, apart from what is shown on purpose (the reply, for one, is in the proof file without a mask: see the page on what is not hidden); a reading of other sources (row HW-678), kind of record by kind, found no other published value that depends on the weights without a mask. That reading, whose record is not in this repository, counted 53 masked kinds: by that reading (nothing was run for it), in real service the programs compare the mask value by value for 25, sample it for 16, compare it only through a hash where it is used for 3 (the stored weight tables' columns) and compare it with nothing for 9; the released programs have further self-checks, and the count has not been made on them.

The programs hold three checks on a pad's write. The first speaks at a lost write. The second reads every pad back, after each sampled message is sent, at a place that is worked out a second time, and compares it with a copy kept at the draw. The third compares it also with the value that a second, separately written derivation gives for that draw, so that a pad lost right after its draw, which is in the copy and in the table alike, is meant not to pass. Unseen by these checks: what strikes both derivations alike (their innermost routines go back to the same public reference texts, so the comparison cannot show an error of that reference); a pad overwritten after the look (the answer is then bare; the proof does not verify: `cp_commit`'s own run of `cp_verify` then stops the file, but `cp_prove` releases it, so there the check of duty 6 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions) is what keeps it from a client); the copies that the engine has encoded by then; entries that are written later, or when a table is moved, which only the engine's own look covers; a fault in the one formula through which a pad's place is both written and looked up, so that "worked out a second time" holds of the engine's address, not of the index; a mask written beside its place at one spot of the library, which passes the read-backs; most of the random values drawn on the CPU that are no pads (some have checks of their own: two tables of masks and their tails, and, by two self-checks, the masking words of the proximity tests' last steps and the mask rows of the test on the weight table at its two own sendings).

A report of the audit's comparison by value says that a value is not what the rule gives, not whether something is bare; and the tool has blind spots of its own (pads inside tables of real values; unopened leaves). What a provider has is a commitment's audit, and the audit of one batch made for the purpose: in a proof that a service made nothing sees a loss of a random value in CPU memory that the self-checks miss, nor in the files of a commitment to a model's weight files, for which the audit's option is rejected.
column4: Audit a commitment before its public files leave the machine, where that can be done: on synthetic weights only.

column3: A further self-check guards against a fault of machine or code: in the last step of every proximity test the prover holds the three masking vectors that are made in CPU memory against the values that a second, separately written derivation gives for their draws; a value lost between its draw and this look ends the run before the masked words are formed. A second such self-check holds the mask rows of the test on the weight table, but for the one-time pads' places, and their random tails against a second derivation, right after each of that test's two own sendings. At stake at the loss of a batch's salts (row H3.1) is a test of any guess at what of the weights enters a failed request's part of a batch, for whoever holds its neighbour's proof. In small computed examples a prover that fills that part without fresh random values leaked fully. That the released prover fills it freshly and hands out nothing of it rests on brief readings of the code of other programs (row HW-678), with nothing run (what goes out for such a request in these sources: prover/common/slot_flags.h; row C3.1.1). In the examples some pairs of losses did leak. None of this is proved or checked. Not seen by the second check: the other sending in that test, of the folded row's message and the mask that goes with it; the proximity tests' own sendings. Not seen at the first check's step: the main row's random tail (in the programs the GPU engine draws it and, by two readings of the code, holds it against a second working-out; the library's CPU engine has no such look); a generator that numbers no draw; a fault that strikes both derivations; a loss after the look. By a reading of the library's sources, the routine behind these self-checks, which compares a sent message's mask rows and random tail with what was drawn, is also called at every opening, for every message with mask rows in the tree that is about to be opened (own-test-mask-rows), except in a context that did not itself send the message, and except the committed table's columns, which another routine opens, where this comparison is not made. There it compares the random tail of every such message, and the mask rows themselves only where the code that drew them has noted the draw's number: four callers do; the callers in three further source files (blocks/iop/foldeq.h, req.h, rng.h) do not, and by the source's own comment no message that `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` sends keeps mask rows drawn there. `cp_prove` compares one further message, a request's index-mask message, whose mask it draws itself, by a routine of its own. The fresh masks of folds are compared wherever the library's provers send one: coefficients and random tail, against what was drawn (own-test-fold-mask); not the table that is built from the coefficients, nor the copies from which the sum and the rounds are computed. A message that is never opened, a generator that numbers no draw, the engine's own copies and the code words are seen by none of these; and where nothing is compared the routine's result is the same as where nothing differs, and nothing reports that.

Of a fault that begins only after the start-up self-checks have passed and then turns every sub-proof pad into zeros: that without the second derivation the proof would be released and accepted is known, of the released programs, from reading the code alone. Every scalar that the sub-proofs send then goes out unmasked.

For pads that are written into tables in GPU memory (read in the code): in the production build and the test build the GPU engine reads each such write back and compares it with what was sent (own-test-entries-written), and the proof library reads every pad back at an address that is worked out a second time and compares it with the value as drawn and with a second derivation of that draw (own-test-pad-kept); a difference ends the program. Not seen, by the sources' own comments: a fault in the one formula for a pad's index; a fault that the draw and its second derivation share; a pad overwritten after the check (the answer is then unmasked; the proof does not verify: `cp_commit`'s own run of `cp_verify` then stops the file, but `cp_prove` releases it, so there the check of duty 6 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions) is what keeps it from a client); a value drawn once and used again; the copies that the engine has encoded by then; entries that the engine's other writing routine writes later (it reads nothing back); entries that are written again when a table is moved (there the engine's read-back alone, which uses one list of places for writing and reading); and a moved table that is refilled without its mark.

`cp_prove` keeps two counts in GPU memory for each request: how many of the sub-proofs' mask entries were found to be the values that the batch's key gives, and how many filler cells were found to be zero; with any other sum than the expected one the request gets no proof. Requests of one shape have equal sums, so each request's counts start at one of 255 values, taken in turn, which the CPU subtracts at the end, so that a count left over from an earlier request does not pass for this one's (read in the code). No test that can run on the released programs runs a case in which that matters: one test (`guards_stand.py`) checks, as text only, that the line which sets the start value is in the source. Were the start the same for all requests, a count that was neither reset nor made would hold just what the CPU expects, and both checks would pass without having been made (the test's table says so); the mask entries are compared by value on the CPU as well (own-test-slot-pads), while the filler cells are not fixed by the verifier, so for them the count is the only check: without it a request in whose filler cells an earlier sub-proof's bytes have stayed gets its proof, with those bytes committed to. No test of the released programs (searched) puts a byte that is not zero into a filler cell (padding that the forward pass does not write) and looks whether the request then gets no proof: the count of zero filler cells is made for every request, but no test makes the comparison fail; one test checks, as text only, that the line which compares the count is in the source.

The value at which `cp_prove`'s two self-check counts start differs from request to request. After 255 and more requests in one process a start value is used again (read in the code). By the source's comment a value does not come twice within one pass over a batch, which has at most 64 requests.

All three programs reject a parameter file that misses one of ten named conditions for hiding; whether these are the right ten has not been shown, and a pass proves nothing by itself (how far the sources have been held against what the written proof asks of the code: row HW-296).
column4: None for a client. A provider whose parameter file is fitted to a real model relies on these ten conditions as the programs test them.

column3: The programs compute and print no bound on what a proof reveals, so there is no security level for hiding. Two of the ten conditions that they test at their start count over the whole life of one commitment's key: the chance that an honest range check fails, which the source counts as part of the zero-knowledge error, is summed over all requests that a key can serve (the requests of a batch, the batches of a leaf table, and as many leaf tables as the anchor's random entries allow links to) and must stay below 2^-sec, where sec is the parameter file's target; and a table's random entries must cover its one-time openings and all the batches that its counter admits. The whole bound, which also grows with the number of batches, leaf tables and commitments, and anything over several commitments together, no program computes.
column4: Do not read the target `sec`, or a passed start-up test, as a level of hiding.

column3: At their start `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` and `cp_verify` test the configuration files against ten named conditions under which hiding is argued, and reject files that miss one (read in the code). A pass proves nothing by itself. Whether the ten are the right ones is not shown; `cp_verify` tests the files, and cannot see whether the prover really drew and placed as many random values as the files ask. The argument itself is on paper, in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, which calls its proof of hiding complete but not settled (what that means: row PS-23). The readings of it have missed real errors, and it has not been checked independently. It covers no program. (Among which matrices the written proof hides: row PS-28.)
column4: Do not read a passed start-up test as a level of hiding.

column3: How much room the default's file has above the 128 bits that the hiding condition on range checks (`range-checks`: it bounds the chance that an honest prover fails a range check, over all requests that one key can serve) needs is not known: it meets the condition, since `cp_verify`'s planning call admits the file. Fewer opened columns, in a batch and in a link, mean more batches and more leaf tables, and each doubling costs about 2 bits, in steps. It is no fault: whoever changes that file later must know it.
column4: If you change the number of columns that a batch opens, run a planning call: a file that misses a condition for hiding is rejected there by name (`parameters-not-admitted`, with the condition's name).

column3: That `cp_prove` and the verifier test the hiding conditions on the same range checks is compared by the public test `gpu.frame_readings` (SUITE.md), on test builds, at six small stored configurations (eight folders, two of them copies) alone, none of them at full size, and that test passed, run once; no proof fails if they differ, and for a provider's own configuration nothing compares them unless that test is run on it. `cp_commit` builds a weight table by the verifier's reading of the public parameters, and `cp_prove` counts the table's use by a reading of its own; the lists enter no first query of a proof. The test is a script (prover/tests/frame_readings.sh) that runs a tool (prover/tests/frame_as_the_verifier_reads.cu); it needs a test build and a GPU, and makes a commitment to synthetic weights for each configuration that it is given. The script calls the tool twice for each configuration: plainly, and with `-turn-one-bound`, which adds 1 to the bound of the verifier's first range check; that call must name the check as differing. This shows that the comparison sees that one number changed, and no more: not that the comparison of the parts that are compared byte for byte can fail, not the other numbers of a range check, and not that the list which it compares is the list on which `cp_prove` tested its hiding conditions. `cp_prove`'s own tests of the hiding conditions run at its start.
column4: Run that test on your own configuration files before you serve.

column3: Weight hiding is computational at best, because the programs derive every private random value from a short key. The commitment and the proofs stay public. So if the generator that derives the values is broken later, anyone who kept those files could remove the masks after the fact, and the provider can do nothing about it. The step from derived to uniform values is an assumption and has no bound.
A leaf table's salt is not uniform, on purpose: it loses 1 bit for each element.

Whoever can write the secret key directory, or name a directory of their own as the directory of weights, may learn about the weights from how starts end. `cp_prove` is given no commitment ID, and compares the secret key directory with nothing from outside it. The commitment ID that the check of duty 6 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions) gives to `cp_verify` is compared with the configuration files and, of the key file, the anchor's root and shape and its OOD answers only: it covers no line of the secret key directory's text file (the line on the weights among them), no count file and not the seed's file, and no file of the secret key directory has a keyed tag. Of what writers of the secret key directory read from how starts end, no trial on the released programs is known.
column4: Let nobody else write the secret key directory. Give the check of duty 6 the commitment ID from a record of your own that nobody who can write the secret key directory can change, never from that directory. Keep `fs.protected_hardlinks = 1`, set before the weight files are put in place. Count whoever sets a container's mounts as a reader of the weights, and keep no other weight file of the model's shape where the service can read it.

column3: Somebody who can write the secret key directory can point its line on the weights' directory at a directory of their own, and learns about the weights from how each start of `cp_prove` ends; the commitment ID does not cover that line. A search for another route by which a plain client could learn the same is not known.

Someone on the provider's machine, never a client, who cannot read the weights but can pass their own directory as the weights' directory can swap a link in a loop. `cp_prove`'s checks on links in the weights' directory are, in the source's own words, "not a reliable barrier" against a link that is switched in a loop; what closes that road is `fs.protected_hardlinks = 1`, or no right for others to create a name on the weights' file system. `fs.protected_hardlinks = 1`, set on every host that mounts the file system, stops only accounts that neither own the weight files nor can both read and write them. The seed's file, each leaf table's random bytes and each count file must be the service account's own and have one name; a second name that is created and taken away between two looks is not seen. The production build's checks look only at what kind of entry a file is: not a symbolic link, a regular file, no second hard link (looked at twice; a name that is made or switched between the two looks or after them is not seen). They do not ask whose the directory or the file is, and `cp_prove` takes the directory's name from the unprotected line in the secret key directory and each tensor's exponent from a text file of that same directory (read in the code). So a weight file that comes into another directory as a regular file with one name, moved there or made visible there by a bind mount, would pass them beside somebody else's text files (reasoned from the code, not run). The guard is who may write the secret key directory, the weights' directory and the mounts, not the code that reads the weight files.
column4: Keep `fs.protected_hardlinks = 1`, set before the weight files are put in place.

column3: Whoever can write the secret key directory can undo every guard that lives in it. `cp_prove` asks of the seed's file, each leaf table's random bytes and each count file that it is a plain file, the service account's own, under one name, with no permission for group and others. A second name that is created and taken away between two looks is not seen.

A weight file's header that names more entries than it holds, or in which an array or a string gives itself more length than it has, can lead the programs' parser on into the tensors' bytes: where the run ends then depends on weights' bytes, and so does the entry's number in the printed line, at the places that reject an entry of the tensor table. That line holds a fixed sentence, the file's path and there that number, and no name or string that was read. A second reader of the same files (prover/weights_blocks/gguf_source.cuh), which of the three programs only the production build of `cp_prove` uses, has two rejections whose text holds numbers that were read in the header (how many layers the model has and their width; how many bytes a tensor has): by then `cp_prove` has sent its standard output to /dev/null, and that text goes there too (read in the code). Such a header is a damaged file's, or the work of somebody who can write into the weight file. `cp_commit` prints that line on standard error; in the production build of `cp_prove` it goes to /dev/null, and the last line says only "p258 end 1 cp-weights-files". (The test build rejects a model's files, so it never parses such a header.) By reading.
column4: Keep `cp_commit`'s standard error on a model's files as secret as the weights; let nobody else write into the weight files.

column3: Whoever can set the environment of `cp_prove`'s or `cp_commit`'s first start, or the system's preload file, runs inside the program; starting a second time with a reduced environment does not protect against a library that is built to hide itself.

An unprotected line of a text file in the secret key directory names the first leaf table in use. So anyone who can write that directory, even without reading it, can send every batch to one leaf table, whose counter then stops the service. Hiding is at risk if the counter is also shortened, which only the service account or root can do, because the table then shows more columns than its masks cover and the proofs verify. The commitment ID does not cover the counter or the line that names the first leaf table in use.

`cp_prove` takes a leaf table's count afresh at every batch, from the length of its counter file, and keeps no earlier length. So if that file is cut short, even while the service runs, the table goes on serving past its limit, and `cp_prove` says nothing. Only an account that can write the file on the provider's machine can cut it: the service account itself or root, and no client. That rests on one reading of other sources (row HW-678). It has not been tried on the released programs under a running service. Past its limit a table gives equations in the weights without masks.
column4: Record each counter's length outside the secret key directory. Treat a table whose counter is shorter than your record as used up. Let only the service account write the directory.

column3: A failing append and a failing lock on a leaf table's counter file are tried on the file routines alone, in a unit test on the CPU, never inside `cp_prove`. That test is not part of this repository.

The unit test of the counter's file routines, which is not part of this repository, runs them on the CPU, on directories that it makes itself. By the comment at its top it does not cover `cp_prove`'s use of these routines, a file system that does not keep appends, locks or syncs, or a directory that is copied or rolled back.
column4: Keep both key directories on a local disk that honours fsync (docs/operators-duties.md).

column3: The tests of this repository look at a leaf table's counter file (`count.bin`) only for whether it changed and for its length: none reads its bytes.

Someone who can write on the provider's machine can do this, and it was not tried on the released programs. The trial used other programs (row HW-678): a production build that could add a leaf table later, a call that the released `cp_commit` rejects. An attacker racing the operator's `cp_commit` call redirected the new leaf table's five `isk` files in two ways, 3 of 3 times each. They were written to a directory of the attacker's choice (exit code 0, no warning) or to the public key directory that is handed out (exit code 2, the files stayed). Those files include the table's random bytes but not the seed file, and everything ran under one account, so the attacker's lack of direct access was only assumed.
column4: Give both key directories a parent only you can write.
column5: run, not on the released programs
column6: seen, not on the released programs; not tried on them

column3: A leaf table's counter is the length of one file, and nothing ties that file to its table. So an account that can write the leaf tables' directories could exchange two tables' counter files by renaming: both are the service account's own, so the check at opening passes, and one table's count falls. What is in the way is the directories' mode only: `cp_commit` makes the secret key directory and all beneath it with mode 0700, `cp_prove` looks at the owner and mode of the secret key directory itself, once, when it opens it, and of a count's own directory when it appends; nothing looks at those of the directory that holds the leaf tables.
column4: Let one account only write the secret key directory, and leave its directories' modes as `cp_commit` made them.

column3: `cp_prove` opens the secret key directory once, at its start, and keeps it open to its end: the last name of the path must be a directory and no link, the caller's own, with no permission for group or others, or the start is rejected. What it writes below that directory (a leaf table's count; with `-keep-for-the-audit` one file) it reaches from that handle, name by name, without following a link, so that another directory or a link put under the path after the start moves none of its writes. An exchange of the directory after the start did not move the count (4 of 4, as root and as an ordinary user), and a link at the last name was rejected (5 of 5), not on the released programs. The path is also walked from the root at each start, part by part: a name that does not begin with / is rejected, no part may be a link, and every directory on the way must be root's or the caller's and closed for writing by others, or sticky; under sudo the account that typed sudo is trusted on the way too. What these guards do not stop: whoever is trusted on the way can put another closed directory of the caller's under the path before a start: `cp_prove` is given no commitment ID, so another commitment's is taken up as it stands, and an older copy of the same secret key directory that is put under the path before a start brings its lower counts; `cp_prove` sees neither, and no program sees the older copy; the configuration and the leaf tables' files are reached by path; nothing looks at the owner or mode of the directory that holds the leaf tables.
column4: Never copy a secret key directory in order to serve from it; let one account only write the secret key directory and the directories above it; name the directory itself with `-isk`, not a link to it.
column5: read; run, not on the released programs

column3: A directory that you made with a plain `mkdir` under umask 002, which some Linux systems set for ordinary accounts, can be written by its group, so `cp_prove` rejects it on the way to `-isk` or `-spool`. The rejection names the directory, the permission and the fix. The printed routes make closed directories of their own and pass. The like test, on the mode's bits alone, is made by `cp_commit` on the way to its output directories and by scripts of this repository for a directory that you name (read in the code: the verifier's build script for a named output directory, `scales/calibrate.py` for `--out`, `integrations/vllm/end_to_end/end_to_end.py`). In a clone that itself has such a mode the verifier's build script lets its default output directory through with a note (verifier/README.md). The programs make no exception for a user's own private group.

A fault that these sources do not have; it needs no fault of the machine. The routine that pins a thread to the CPUs near its GPU (prover/common/numa_pin.h) asks the system which CPUs the thread may use. In a form of these sources that is not in this repository (row HW-678) it did not clear the 128 bytes on its stack that take the answer, and did not read the call's result, so that, where that call failed, what stood in these bytes before decided, one bit for each CPU of the GPU's NUMA node, the thread's CPU mask, which threads made later inherit and which, as far as is known, other accounts on the machine can read, and a count in one printed line. `cp_prove` calls the routine before it has read the parameter file, and `cp_commit`'s first call comes before a configuration or model file is read and before the seed is sampled: nothing hidden could stand there. `cp_commit` calls it again for each table that it makes, when the weights lie in host memory and the seed and the keys are drawn; what those bytes held is not known. No client, no public file and no proof holds the mask or the count. In these sources the routine clears these bytes first and, where the call fails, gives up without pinning and prints nothing (read in the code; the public test `prover.numa_pin_test` makes the call fail, with stand-ins for the system's calls). By the Linux manual page sched_setaffinity(2) the call fails where the kernel's CPU mask is larger than the 1,024 CPUs that the set has room for; no machine on which it fails is known, and on such a machine nothing was run (read in the code).
column4: Run `cp_commit` on a machine that no other account can use, and keep its output as secret as the weights (both are operators' duties already).
column6: no: these sources do not have it

column3: In these sources each of a fold's hiding coefficients is a random value of its own (one call of the generator each), and no code of the library or the programs makes one value serve for two of them (read in the source, not run). If one value did serve for two, a client that knew which two could compute one linear combination of the entries folded, with factors that it knows: a fold sends as many values as it has hiding coefficients (reasoned on the protocol, not run). The rest of the fold's own mask would not cover that combination, nor would one mask row among the folded messages; only random entries among those folded that nothing else has used up could. Whether such entries are left, and so whether the combination would tell a client anything of the weights, is not known for any fold of the released programs.

The range test inside the key file is masked by mask rows that are made in CPU memory in one draw; a key file stays public for good. `cp_commit` has a self-check (own-test-ranges-mask) that, right after the message is committed and before a byte of the key file leaves the process, compares every value of these mask rows and of the random entries that are encoded with them, except the pads' places, with the values that were drawn, and ends the run at a difference; the key file's index-mask message is compared in the same way, but for its pads' places (own-test-index-mask), and the pads have a self-check of their own (own-test-pad-kept) (read in the source). Not covered, by the source's own comments: the copies that are handed on for encoding, which are made before the comparison, and the encoding itself; the fold mask that goes with the message has a self-check of its own (own-test-fold-mask: its coefficients and the random entries that are encoded with it, against what was drawn; not the table that is built from them, nor the copies from which the sum and the rounds are computed; read in the code); the check also returns "nothing differs" where nothing is compared, and rests on `cp_commit`'s own test that its generator numbers its draws; and a fault that both writings of the generator's rule share passes. No self-check on random values has been seen to fire in a production build, which has no option for injecting a fault.

Every build of `cp_prove`, and `cp_commit`, disables core files and makes itself non-dumpable before any key is chosen or any weight is read, and ends if that fails. A debugger that starts the program, one that the same user attached before that step, or one that root or a process with the right to trace others attaches, still works. Neither step reaches a dump of GPU memory that the CUDA driver makes on its own under a variable of the environment; every run in which something is hidden, of `cp_prove` and of `cp_commit`, starts a second time with all but a few named variables dropped; that keeps away a setting made by accident or habit, not a library that was preloaded on purpose. No test reads the flag, and obtaining a core dump or a driver's dump of GPU memory has not been tried. `cp_verify`, on Linux only, makes itself non-dumpable at its start and ends without a verdict if that fails; it sets no limit on core files itself; that no core file of it is then written is by the system's rules, and was not tried. Who may attach, and that an attached debugger stays, are the system's rules (the Linux manual pages ptrace(2) and prctl(2), under PR_SET_DUMPABLE); no run that tried them is known.
column4: Give nobody else root, the right to trace processes, or the service's account; run no debugger.

column3: `cp_verify` sees files before they are public: `cp_commit` has it judge key and leaf files that are not published yet, and the check of duty 6 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions) has it judge responses that are not handed on yet. On Linux it marks itself as not dumpable at its start (as the second act of its main routine; nothing of a file has been read by then) and ends without a verdict if that fails; the stages that it forks inherit the mark. By the source's own comment the mark is set because a limit on core files does not hold where dumps are piped to a program. That no core file and no piped dump is then written, and that a debugger attaches only with the right to trace other processes, follows from the system's rules (the Linux manual pages core(5), prctl(2) and proc(5)); it was not tried.
column4: Give nobody else root, the right to trace processes, or the service's account.

column3: `cp_prove` asks the system to keep the page that holds its copy of the seed out of swap space, and does not look at the answer: where the system rejects, for instance under a low limit on locked memory, it goes on and prints nothing (read in the code). `cp_commit` goes on too in that case, but prints a warning. What reaches swap space can be read by someone with access to the provider's machine or its disk, not by a client.
column4: Use no swap, or encrypted swap, and give the service account a limit on locked memory (ulimit -l) under which `cp_commit` prints no such warning.

column3: No test shows that a whole `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` runs its second start with the reduced environment (searched). The running program has marked itself as not dumpable, so by the system's rules another process of the same account cannot read its environment under /proc (reasoned, not tried). What there is, read in the code: the routine that makes the second start passes on only a few named variables, and in the second start it goes on only if it finds no entry beyond these. Two tests that are not part of this repository run that routine in small test programs of their own, not in `cp_commit` or `cp_prove`: one, on the CPU, links a stand-in for the CUDA driver's library, which prints the environment that it finds each time it is loaded, and compares the two starts; the other checks on a GPU that CUDA still works after such a start.

Gaps in the verifier's self-checks: nothing compares the plan with the statement afterwards; how the code that called a lookup uses the points that it hands over (which coordinate goes into which claim) is tested in no run: a run compares only the points' lengths and, where several calls share one table, the shared coordinates; the order of heads in two arrays is taken as given.

Not covered by the verifier's self-checks: the terms inside one claim, and whether a coefficient that was handed out was really multiplied in (but for the range check's claims, part of whose weights a self-check computes a second time in every run: row SO-17.3.1); an index that strays to another tensor, layer, limb or digit inside the same table; and no value carries its kind as data, so a run cannot tell from a value which kind it is. From reading the code, the self-check's bound is a table's whole length, which takes in the filler features that round a matrix up to whole columns: an index that strays to their entries passes too.

That each linear claim of the sub-proofs reads the entry of the reads' vector (`U3`: docs/format/FORMAT.md, 11.1) that it is meant to read has not been checked entry by entry: a claim pointed at an entry of equal value, or at filler, would not show in an honest run. Where the verifier's test build that compares its weight vectors with a prover's, array by array whatever the entries hold (row SO-17.3), has been run, a mismatch between the two programs would show there, on every committed array of the segment, `U3` among them (the coefficients on hidden values and the constant are not compared, and the build skips trees that its list does not name: by a trace, only trees with empty names, none of which bears a weight); such a comparison has been made once, on test builds (the prover's side: the build of a cheating prover, run without its cheat; `cp_verify`, not on the released programs, accepted its proof), at a small test configuration with one OOD answer a row and no counted work, on synthetic weights under a test seed: the vectors agreed at all five links (by report); of one at the default setting's own files nothing is known. That both programs mean the cell that the format pages and the model mean, no run shows; it is held only by reading.

Two guards of `cp_verify` ask that every sub-proof's check ran to its end. No input can trigger them, because a rejection inside a sub-proof ends the run earlier, and no test builds a copy of the program in which a sub-proof is skipped.

In `cp_verify` most weights of the sub-proofs' claims have no second computation in a run. The exceptions: where a row's weights are a product over the bits of its index, the product form is compared with the vector written out (internal-row-form), and part of the range check's weights are computed twice (row SO-17.3.1). That the others have none has not been checked claim by claim. A checker under verifier/tests/ (forest_lookup_check) compares the coefficient vectors that the verifier's lookup routines compute with those of the prover's lookup routines. It does so outside any proof, on arrays that the two test programs set up themselves: in the public GPU test gpu.forest_lookup_test, on ten synthetic groups of lookups. A test build of `cp_verify` that makes the same comparison in every sub-proof of a whole proof, with the files of a prover's test run, is not part of this repository, and neither are the tests with a malicious prover for which it was made (what has been run with it: row SO-17.1.1); it skips trees that its list does not name. By its own comment the comparing code does not compare the equation's coefficients on hidden values or its constant. A fault in this part of the code could let a false statement pass, or could reveal something that is meant to stay hidden.

`cp_verify` computes the public coefficients of the range check's claims itself. For one half (ties; the multiplicity bits' tree) a self-test holds them against an independent second computation. For the reads' half, `cp_verify` computes the reads' weights on the digits' columns a second time in every run, with loops of its own, from the same sizes (mz, NM), places (ix) and list of functionals as the first, and with them the power of the batching element under which each read stands whose weights are not all 0 (by the source's own comment, in the head's sub-proof of a request on the last position alone three tables' reads have weights 0, add nothing, and no self-test compares their powers); a mismatch ends the call NOT CHECKED. It does not recompute the reads' weights on the tables' entries, their constant terms, or that a claim's index into a table meets the read's: for those there is one computation only. A slip on that side that honest data leave invisible, in the verifier alone or shared by prover and verifier, would let every honest proof pass and could let a false statement pass. Not run: such a slip, planted; a weakened text of the first computation at full size.

After a run `cp_verify` reads back five words of the finished statement, but not the plan's output position or its ranges of tokens, so a programming error could make it check other positions than those that its YES names.

Nothing checks how attention heads are ordered inside the value and output weight matrices, or which key-value head serves a query head. The verifier's code and the committed weights are both assumed to follow one convention of the converting programs, so a commitment made with other tools can describe another function than its maker meant.

The round in which the range check's matrix is drawn has its error only if the cells and the reads are fixed before the draw: otherwise a prover could add to a read a vector that the matrix maps to 0, and every equation would hold for a read of cells that are not small. `cp_verify` checks that order before the draw, and ends `NOT CHECKED` (exit code 5) under the name `internal-f-matrix-order` if it is wrong. By the source's own argument a failure is a fault of the program, not of a file: at which moment an array is sent follows from the program's own lists, and layout.txt chooses only the message within that moment. Whether some layout.txt could after all bring the wrong order about is not shown by any test. Not shown: the wrong order inside `cp_verify` and `cp_prove` themselves; the check's branch for an array of an earlier link, which honest calls only reach.

The error 2^-N of the round in which the range check's matrix is drawn is argued in a comment of the source (blocks/iop/rng.h, "Error of this round"). By that comment the step was argued on paper: by one comparison part of it rests on Lemma 2.5 of the first work that the comment cites, its argument has the shape of the proof of that work's Lemma A.1, and what it adds is not in that work; a form of the argument that takes packing and reads apart has a hole, and the comment's form takes the two together; it rests on readings and on exhaustive searches at toy sizes, and has not been checked independently. By one unchecked reading of Lyubashevsky, Nguyen, Seiler, ePrint 2020/1448, Lemma 2.5 is the statement on which the count rests (at probability 1/2 its bound is 2^-n, with the same factor 2 between what the verifier sees and what it concludes), and the proof of Lemma A.1 has the argument's shape (one coordinate taken out, the others held fixed, independent rows). What is added here (cells that are sent packed and through reads; digits that a lookup checks) is not in that paper. Lemma 3.4 of Gentry, Halevi, Lyubashevsky, ePrint 2021/1397, has not been compared; by one unchecked reading of that work the step is found, at least in part, in its section 3.4; that reading did not set the work beside the code line by line.

The range check's error of 2^-N for N random combinations is attained, so it has no slack: cells that hold halves of odd numbers survive each combination with chance one half. In every parameter file under prover/examples/ the line sets N = 128 (the line `tau`) for a target of 128 bits and counts no proof of work in that round, so the bound meets the target exactly; `cp_verify` rejects a file whose `tau` is not the number that the target calls for (`NO: policy-tau-hb`, `NO: plan-tau`).

Where `cp_verify` computes the public weights for a run of consecutive table keys, it takes a shortcut that is right only if every aligned run of keys is placed on an aligned run of places. Both programs take the same shortcut; what a failure of its condition would show as has not been traced. By reading the code, no parameter file that the program admits can make the condition on the stretch's first key fail: in two of the shortcut's three uses the stretch begins at key 0; in the third the run's length is the first key itself, and a file with expert layers is rejected unless that number is a power of two. By numbers it has not been counted on this repository's set of parameter files with model lines. No check at that place and no test asks it, so a YES rests on that reading.

That every place of every lookup key's formula is fixed by some claim is argued only in single sentences at the claims, in the source's comments, and for no host as a whole; it is neither proved nor tested; one unfixed place would free its whole group. A key's formula may contain scalars that the prover sends, for example the first scalar of a sumcheck that proves a part of the key. A sent scalar that only the join constrained (the group's one claim that ties its keys to the committed cells) could be set by the prover to whatever makes the join true, and then the join would say nothing about any call of the group. The verifier's test that every slot but the merge's end value has a non-zero coefficient in the sum of all the sub-proof's claims (internal-g-free-slot, internal-a-free-slot, internal-h-free-slot; a slot stands for a sent scalar or, for a sumcheck's round scalars, for the committed mask entry) would not notice it, because the scalar has such a coefficient in the join. Three separate readings, of other sources (row HW-678), found no sent scalar of a key's formula whose only constraint is the join, in any of the four hosts (read, not run; not proved). For the layers' one sent scalar the second constraint is parted from the join by a single challenge drawn after both (an argument from the order of messages, read in the code; written nowhere in the tree; by an argument on paper, in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, the case is covered by a lemma on early reads; the forms have not been derived a second time). From reading the code, only packed entries are committed before a lookup's challenge; cells follow from them only once the range check, which runs later, passes. No text that was found defines a cell for an entry without a small unpacking.

`cp_verify` rejects a parameter file under which a lookup call would consist of padding alone (an acceptance would say nothing about such a call), and asks this in four places where it makes its plan. No parameter file is known that reaches this rejection, so no run of the unaltered program shows that the four places ask; without them a checking call asks all the same (the fifth caller, at the head of the routine that reads a sub-proof's lookup); only planning calls without a proof do not.

The routine of `cp_verify` that arranges the segments of a lookup call in columns splits each segment's length into powers of two and looks only at bits 0 to 40 of that length; it does not test that no higher bit is set. Of a segment of 2^41 columns or more, only the part that the low 41 bits give would get places of its own, and every further column would keep place 0 (read in the code). What keeps the lengths small is the tests on the statement's shape, which `cp_verify` makes before both calls of the routine: the model's width and its inner width are at most 2^20 each, query and key-value heads together at most 64, the experts at most 4,096 and the vocabulary at most 2^24, so every length that the routine is given stays below 2^27 (reasoned from the code, not run). No test calls the routine by itself (searched), so that it never meets a longer segment rests on that reading alone.
The step that rewrites a weight claim summed over a tensor's indices as weights on the committed matrix's rows and columns, by the layout's rule, has no written proof.

In a layer sub-proof `cp_verify` compares the sizes of the run's lookup with those from which the plan sized its matrices and counted its slots, and ends under the name `internal-g-forest` if they differ. The runs of the output head and of attention make no such comparison: for the output head the like name, `internal-h-forest`, stands only where the plan is made, and for attention there is no like name (read in the code: `verifier/src/vf_layers_check.inc`, `verifier/src/vf_output_head_plan.inc`; by separate readings and a search for the three names; a like comparison under another name was not looked for). What a difference there would let through has not been traced.
A YES says nothing about positions that the request does not cover.
column4: Build the request file yourself, from the tokens that you sent and the reply that you received, with the range of positions that you expect to be covered; never use a file that came with a response. Then read the line `covered:`.

column3: Where a request's range ends before the last position, `cp_verify` requires the next-token file to hold 0 and otherwise ends `NO: statement-range`; this rule is tested by name only on its routine alone, in a unit test that is not part of this repository. By a search of the tests, none gives the whole `cp_verify` an honest proof of such a request with another value in that file: the nearest whole call in a shipped test pairs such a request with another request's token and proof and asks only for some NO, so that NO need not come from this rule.

An accepted proof does not show when it was made, for whom, or that it was made in answer to the request at hand. One commitment ID does not mean one key file. Accepted proofs are not unique, by design: a proof holds the prover's own random values, so two honest proofs of one statement differ, and both are accepted.
column4: Do not use a proof as a token of when something was computed.

column3: A proof names no client, time or nonce: a valid proof verifies for anyone holding the same request, ID and configuration, now or later; freshness is the client's to bind (its own nonce in the prompt).

Whether a third party can alter a proof's bytes and still have it accepted for the same true statement has been tested in part. By field, the sweep over a real proof's fields stops at the first answer to a draw of positions, so the fields behind that point are not walked one by one; by place, a test that ships overwrites words spread evenly over a whole real proof and asks that each is rejected, and other shipping tests alter a proof's bytes too (one of them on the library's toy verifiers, not on `cp_verify`, at a low error target of 32 bits). What is untried is a field-by-field walk of the later part of a real proof, not its later bytes as such; and any such sweep at full size. The sweep alters the first and the last symbol of the first opened position and one bit of that position's salt. By a reading of the hash chain's code, every item that a prover sends either enters the next hash query or is checked against a root or the work test; that reading does not cover the second text of the sub-proofs' rounds in the verifier. Such a proof would state nothing false.
column4: Do not treat a proof's bytes as a fingerprint of one response.
