column3: The number of leaf tables is bound by nothing, and retired leaf tables are accepted for ever. `cp_verify` opens only the leaf file whose number is in the proof's head, so a false leaf file beside it is not looked at; and any further true leaf table that is linked to the anchor is accepted. Every further true copy that is accepted and linked to the anchor spends from the same column budget as the first.
A leaf file holds no number, and the key's directory does not say how many leaf tables exist.

Some places of the committed table hold no weight. What is in them is up to whoever makes the commitment, and no part of a proof shows that it is 0; a client who trusts a commitment ID therefore learns nothing about their content. A committer that fills these places has not been run on the released programs. What filled places would do to hiding has not been looked at: no test of hiding in this repository fills them. Where such places lie in a row's memory, the honest `cp_commit` zeroes that memory before it writes the weights into it (read in the code, whether it keeps the table whole in GPU memory or builds it in pieces); the other such places were not followed. That whoever fills these places is the committer, whose own weights are the hidden ones, so that it would harm only itself, is an argument, not a test.

Axes are padded to powers of two, so committed cells exist beyond the true width, vocabulary or number of entries, in attention and in a layer too. Why such a cell cannot carry a false value is argued axis by axis, not tested: in attention no rejection compares a table's index with how many entries are real, and for the layers the protocol leans on a claim that is not proved.

Of the committed table's places that hold no weight this much is proved or read: padding lines of the matrix are bytes, like every line. Lines of the table beyond the matrix enter no claim, by reading: the statement's claims address cells by the place that the layout gives each tensor, so a line outside all these places is read by none. Whether the cells of a padding column can enter a claim has not been followed.

The argument for the hash mode is taken from a published analysis, with no separate proof and no referee: by the mode's own page the published result is for the whole 512-bit output under an ideal cipher, the cut to the digest's length is, in that page's words, "a one-line step of our own", the cited proof asserts three conditions of an earlier paper in one sentence, and its simulator asks about q^3 times, so a strict count needs an argument of its own.

Nothing checks the rule by which public weight files are converted, a commitment cannot be recomputed from files only (but under `-public-weights`, where the seed is a published file and nothing is hidden), and how close the integer model is to the original model has been measured with a Python implementation of the integer model that is not this repository's (the figure, with its conditions: docs/limits.md#the-integer-model) and, once, in coarse bins, not on the released programs. That share has not been measured on the released programs.

The floating-point pass behind the scales, the meaning of the tensor names and the rotary pairing follow a public library's source text; their outputs were never compared with that library's on the public model, and the converting programs accept any architecture name.

How often its top choice differs from the token that a floating-point implementation served was counted once, in coarse bins (96 greedy replies, not on the released programs); the result carries over only if the release commits to the same fitted scales. That distance also decides which bounds of a score policy would tell the model's own replies from another's.

column3: `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` have a mode for public weights, `-public-weights <file>`, in the production build only. In it the commitment's seed is derived from that file's 32 bytes, so whoever has the file can work out every mask of the key file, of the leaf files and of the leaf tables' columns that proofs open: the weights are not hidden. No claim of hiding is made for anything in this mode. The public files carry no mark of it: the key file, the leaf files, the commitment ID, proofs and responses look like any other commitment's, and `cp_verify` cannot tell.
column4: Use the mode only for weights that are public. If you rely on a provider's weights being hidden, you cannot learn it from the public files.

column3: `cp_commit` takes a model's matrices in any of seven storage types (F32, F16, BF16, Q8_0, Q4_K, Q5_K, Q6_K); `cp_prove` takes less. The routed experts' matrices must be Q4_K, Q8_0, F16 or BF16, or Q5_K for the routed down projection only, and their number of rows a multiple of 4, as must that of every other matrix that `cp_prove` keeps as blocks. `cp_commit` tests four of `cp_prove`'s conditions beforehand, because no commitment to such files could be served, but not these two. So a model whose routed matrices have another type, or rows not in fours, is committed whole, after its hours, and `cp_prove` then rejects it at every start. Nothing false is proved, and no proof is made: the time is lost, and the commitment cannot be served. The same holds of two kinds of parameter file that a user can write. `cp_commit` accepts a file in which a line `lmS`, `lmh`, `lmo`, `lmbA` or `lmq` is below 11, and `cp_prove` rejects it at every start (verifier/docs/parameter-file.md gives the limit). `cp_commit` also accepts a file whose line `work field` has a first number other than 0; by a less sure reading `cp_prove` then ends at an internal check in its first batch. What happens with a file in which only the second or third number is not 0 has not been followed in the code. No parameter file under examples/ or prover/ is of either kind. This is known by reading; nothing was run.

column3: Two stops can end an honest run with a negligible chance (a challenge that cannot be used), and the retry of a draw is live code. No whole program and no GPU kernel is driven into the second try of the generator for the leaf tables' random entries, which a table of full size meets.

An honest proof is rejected (`NO: coin-zero`) if one element that is sampled in a sumcheck of a feed-forward segment is 0: a chance of about 1 in the size of the extension field for each such segment.
column4: After `NO: coin-zero`, ask for a new proof.

column3: One further cause gives the same "failed" and is no fault: a challenge drawn from the transcript that cannot be used. A search that finds no nonce fails a guard and ends the process. No run is expected to meet either.

Prover and verifier include the same basic headers of the library blocks/ (field, hash, transcript chain, code, plan), among them the reader of the parameter file's first part, the lines on the proof system. They share more than the library. The rounds of each kind of sub-proof are listed in one text for both: headers under prover/ (prover/prover/plan_rounds.h, prover/attn/plan_rounds.h, prover/head/plan_rounds.h, prover/hiding/token_plan.h). And cp_verify.cpp is compiled a second time and linked into `cp_commit`: it rejects the configuration files that that code rejects, takes its limits and the plans of the key file and the leaf files from what that code derives from these files, and compares its own table's sizes with that code's. A fault in a shared text is shared by both sides, and no comparison between the two can show it. There is no second, separately written prover.

What exists as a second implementation of the code that prover and verifier share: known answers from separately written Python programs for what is hashed and written; verifiers written a second time in Python for toy-size files (toy files alone, none that `cp_commit` wrote; where the public test second_writings.honest changes the first OOD answer in a toy key file and in a toy leaf file, the altered answer is refused at a proof of work, before the equations that tie the OOD answers to the table are checked); a second computation of the blocks' round errors inside a test: not of the OOD sample's, of the two tests on the committed table only at distances named in positions, and not of the factor for interleaved rows; by the test's own comment its formulas were written from the library's comments and code, not from a source outside it, so it does not show that a formula is right; and, in Python, a second computation of the proximity tests' round errors for two example configurations and one of the tests' own, with formulas from a technical report that is not public and not refereed and not from the programs' code; the weight table's rounds are computed by the programs' own formulas: a second arithmetic, not a second derivation (verifier/tests/kit_rounds_second.py; row SO-1.6). In C++ the audit tool has the field and the code written a second time (for the programs' one field; for a second field, for which the library cannot be built, it was typed from library functions, statement for statement); no second C++ implementation of the headers for chain or plan exists.

The Python checker of a proof file derives no parameter: plans, codes and shapes come from files that the C++ tool wrote, so its ACCEPTED means only that the proof passes under the given parameters. It reads toy-size files only and has never been given a proof that `cp_prove` made.

Second implementations that serve as checks are less independent than their names say. Count their agreement with the programs as a guard against a slip in one text, not as a second reading of the rule: least of all for the key schedule, the field's rule on which random words are rejected, and the weight table's masks.

The second implementation of the rule for random values and the programs follow one statement of that rule (a protocol document that is not part of this repository), so a misreading of it that both share passes their comparison; the other second implementations rest on the format's pages, on a technical report that is not public and not refereed or on the programs' own sources (the audit tool for the order of the draws, the key schedule's header for its table), so an error there passes them too; one header of the second computation was not made independently of what the programs put out; and the audit tool takes the order of the random draws from the prover's source.

One check from outside the programs removes blinding and looks at what remains: at the last step of each proximity test the audit tool takes the mask that it has derived itself off the masked main message and compares what is left with the committed row, at the positions of that row that the file opens and at no others. That tool unblinds no other blinded value, and reaches this step for the key file and the leaf files only in the commitment's audit or under a test seed, and for proofs only in a batch's audit or under test coins. The audit tool, in Python, derives the private random values from the seed by a text of its own and compares by value those published values that depend on the secrets and public data alone (not all: its comments name exceptions), on synthetic weights only; whether a mask is applied to the value that it should hide it asks at that one step alone, at the opened positions; everywhere else it does not ask (its independence: E2.1, E2.7). `cp_commit` compares with a second implementation (prover/second_writing/) every mask of each weight table, but only the first time that the table's making computes it (later passes derive all masks again and are not compared), and of the salts only those of the tree leaves that an opening makes again; each before a byte of the file built with them leaves the process. That implementation is not fully independent of the programs: see E2.8.

Three decoders of the weight files' storage types agree, but they are less independent than three: the Python decoder uses the format's reference package, the whole decoders of the C++ tool and of the committer are adapted from one public library's code (ggml), the tests' own expected values follow it too, and the Python package is of the same project, so that an error taken over from that library does not show; and the committer takes its exponents from the sums file. For the types Q8_0, F16 and BF16 the C++ tool's decoder follows that Python package.

Where the second implementations are not independent of the programs. Of the seven headers that the programs compile as a second implementation of the rule for random values, the key schedule's follows the table in the head of the programs' own key schedule, and the plain BLAKE2b and ChaCha20's quarter round are adapted from the same public reference code as the programs' own, through the same intermediate texts. The two ChaCha20 block functions are different texts around the quarter round, but both go back to one public reference text: the second implementation's in whole, the programs' in the quarter round and the order of its eight calls. So a comparison of the two can show an error made in adapting that reference, or in what the programs have of their own around it; it cannot show an error of the reference, and a misreading of the rule that is in both texts passes unseen. The field-dependent part of the second generator of random values is not independent of the library's generator. Every text of BLAKE2b's compression function in this repository, the Python ones among them, is adapted from the one public reference implementation, so none of them is an independent second text, and their agreement cannot show an error of that reference or a misreading that they share. What holds the function from outside is the standard's test vector alone: one message of one block, without a key, and it reaches three of the texts: that of blocks/hash/blake2b_f.h (in blocks/hash/tests/functions_test.cpp and older_test.cpp), that of prover/common/blake2b_f.h (in prover/tests/hash_test.cpp) and that of verifier/tests/known_answers/blake2b_f.py, which holds itself to the vector in a self-test that no row of SUITE.md runs. `cp_verify`'s own text (verifier/src/vf_earlier_hash_f.h) is not among the three. What holds the texts of verifier/src/vf_earlier_hash_f.h (`cp_verify`'s own text), blocks/hash/lanes.cuh and docs/format/format_rules.py to a value, other than that whole programs and scripts agree with one another, has not been established; by the comment at the head of the first a test that does not ship compares it with the vector; readers cannot rerun it. The tests also compare with the BLAKE2b of Python's standard library, which is taken to come from the same reference or to descend from it (CPython 3.14 has other code, HACL*, in its place): that is no check from outside. That library's BLAKE2b takes no argument for the compression function's counter, so a comparison with it does not reach calls of the function with other words than 0 in the counter's high half; among the routines that make such calls are `compress64` in blocks/hash/blake2b_f.h, `C` in prover/common/blake2b_f.h and `earlier_hash_c` in verifier/src/vf_earlier_hash.h. The standard's test vector does not reach such calls either. Among what reaches them is a stored file, verifier/tests/hash_vectors.txt (44 states and 13 tree hashes), with which tests compare the texts of blocks/hash/blake2b_f.h (all 57), prover/common/blake2b_f.h (the states; the tree hashes in a test that needs a GPU) and scales/policy_tables.py (the first half of each state); a Python text of this repository prints it (verifier/tests/known_answers/format_hash.py), so that is one text of this repository beside another of the same origin; for scales/policy_tables.py, whose Python text is the same translation as the one that prints the file, it can show an error of copying alone, as the test's docstring says. No test in this repository puts `cp_verify`'s own text to that file. Of the texts that the standard's vector does not reach, the comparison with Python's library is what holds tests/s8_model.py, scales/policy_tables.py (in scales/tests/test_policy_tables.py) and prover/tests/coins_second_text/format_hash.h (in prover/tests/coins_known_test.sh, on four lists). prover/second_writing/blake2b_plain.h is compared, inside the programs, with the first derivation of the key schedule, which runs on blocks/hash/blake2b_f.h. integrations/vllm/integer_model/integer_model/tables.py is compared with scales/policy_tables.py, which has the same Python text, so that the comparison can show an error of copying alone, as the test's docstring says (integrations/vllm/integer_model/tests/test_parameter_file.py). ChaCha20's block function, from which every mask, pad and salt is derived, stands in thirteen files of this repository. Nine of them are adapted from one public source, D. J. Bernstein's chacha-merged.c: the programs' own three texts, every other C++ text that a self-check or a test compares these with, the audit tool's, and a test's in Python (prover/tests/public_weights.py). Agreement among the nine cannot show an error of that source, or one made alike in adapting it. The other four are Python scripts that, by their own heads, follow RFC 8439 itself. From outside this repository the function is held only by values that the RFC prints, six blocks and two quarter rounds, and unevenly. In the self-tests at a program's start its own texts meet one block or all six. `block()` of prover/hash_commitment/hf_mask_ref.h, with which the masks' text is compared, meets one block. `second::block()` of prover/tests/longrow/made_key.h, with which a test compares prover/common/coin_chacha.h, meets none. One test also holds two blocks that OpenSSL 3.0.13 gave; whether OpenSSL's text follows the same source has not been looked at, so that is not counted as a check from outside. No value that a standard prints reaches the BLAKE2b of prover/second_writing/blake2b_plain.h, which is tested only through the keys that it helps to derive. The routine around BLAKE2b's compression function, which feeds it the blocks and finishes the hash, is shared too: the programs' (`HasherT`, blocks/hash/hash.h) is adapted from the reference's `blake2b_update` and `blake2b_final` as the second implementation's plain BLAKE2b has them. So in the comparison of the two key schedules the whole hash, not the compression function alone, is one text in two adaptations. A slip in that rendering which the programs' routine took over passes the comparison unseen, unless it bites in one way of feeding alone (the programs feed the string piece by piece, the second implementation whole) or a known answer made with Python's standard library meets it: for the key schedule's own strings these are seven keys, from strings of 117 to 347 bytes, none of which ends on a block's border.

The self-test that the programs run at their start is no blind trial. Five conventions in the program that makes its known answers are not independent of the programs' own lines, so an error in these five that the programs share passes unseen. The self-test's cases are also not independent of a list of faults that were injected into copies of these sources (prover/second_writing/README.md), so those faults are no blind test of it.

`cp_commit` and `cp_prove` turn a stored weight into its committed integer by two methods: one multiplies by the tensor's power of two after the product, the other before it. The two agree unless a single-precision result overflows or is subnormal; that they agree on every input is not proved. A GPU test, which is not part of this repository, compares them on synthetic blocks at edge values. Where they differed, `cp_prove` would compute with other integers than were committed. `cp_commit` itself uses both methods: the first in its checks, its tables' trees and its openings, the second for most lookup keys of the range proof. Where they differed there, the key file would fail the `cp_verify -key` that `cp_commit` runs before it writes the key file (for a leaf table: `-leaf`), and no commitment would be made (reasoned; not tried).

Some parameters reach the audit tool through the verifier's own code; the production build writes no list of its draws, so their order is checked only through the compared values; and a comparison by value cannot see a word of a random value's label that is zero, or equal to another, in every run that is compared.

For the weight table's masks, the reference header, the second implementation and the Python that gives the known answers were not made independently of one another, so three agreeing texts count as one. And on eight points the protocol document records what both texts do: there the two agree by construction, not as two readings.

The second implementation's own tests compare it with a table of known answers that was made with the programs: so a value has passed from the programs to these tests, and their agreement is not that of two sides that never met. The lines of the second implementation that compute random values were not changed to meet that table.

One difference between the second implementation of the rule for random values and the programs is known, and by a reading of the sources it holds at two places: the retry word of the generator of random values behind the sub-proofs' pads and the try word of the draw that picks a batch's leaf table are counted in 32 bits without a stop, so there the programs would go on modulo 2^32 where the second implementation stops with an error. At the two other generators that have such a word the programs stop as the second implementation does: the proof library's generator ends the run when no retry word is left, and the generator of a leaf table's masks ends the run after try 2^32 - 1. By arithmetic on the source, not by a test, no run reaches the case: it takes 2^29 rejected values in a row, or 2^32 rejected tries.

Four lines of the second implementation of the rule by which the programs derive their private random values were each changed by itself, and four CPU tests of it all passed, so they reached none of the four (reported: one run, not on the released programs). By a reading of the sources, with nothing run: the first, the retry word after a rejected value, has a test of its own, which is not part of this repository (no run of it is known) and which forces rejections through a stand-in for the block function; it checks the second implementation alone, not the programs' own generators. The second and third, the number under which the upper levels of a tree hash are hashed (`coins::tree_hash()` in prover/tests/coins_second_text/format_hash.h) and a salt's index within its stream (`salt_cell()`), are in routines that no program and no test runs: a fault there changes nothing that `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` compares, and no test would notice it. The routine with the fourth, the number of requests in the list under a batch's digest, is not in these sources.

No test of the suite looks at a proof of `cp_prove`'s for what it gives away; the runs that did so are outside the suite. The proof library's exact tests of hiding, which are part of this repository, compare two witnesses' views of whole proofs and key files at toy size, on the CPU, with the library's own CPU engine: none of `cp_prove`'s GPU code runs in them (what these tests pass without seeing: `blocks/tests/hiding/README.md`, "What these tests do not show"). No test runs `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` at full size. A GPU test that passes is a regression check on synthetic inputs; none is an argument that anything is hidden (the test table's own head says that a pass shows nothing more about hiding). No test uses more than one GPU: by its usage text a call of `cp_commit` works on one GPU, the first that it sees, `cp_prove` selects GPU 0 (read in the code), and the test runner knows of one GPU.

No test of the suite searches by value what a run leaves on disk, or the published files and the responses, for secrets (the seed, keys derived from it, a batch's random bytes, the leaf tables' random entries and salts), so the tests would not catch a stray copy of a secret. The tests nearest to it go by file names, not by values: which files are new after a run that a self-check stops, what lies in the responses' directory after a signal, and where a file of the seed's name lies when `cp_commit` is killed. All of them look when a run has ended or has been killed: no test lists which names appear in the spool directory or in the secret key directory while a service runs (some GPU tests, which are not in this repository, watch a running `cp_prove` only for the first staged file, or for the count file's growth, as the moment to send a signal).

A test option can write a proof's internal values and masks to a directory, but only someone running a test build on the provider's machine could reach it. From reading the source, a production build compiles neither the variable's name nor the branch behind it. Two tests check that the name is not in the program and that, with the variable set, nothing is written, the second (the public test `gpu.serving_first_run`) on a commitment made under a random seed; that a test build reads the variable's name is checked there only in the source text. The rejection at start-up of any run that is not on synthetic weights under a test seed and a test build's rejection of a real model's files are also tested. The writing code's own flag has never been tested, nor has the second kind of synthetic weights (`-weights generated`), nor has the test build's rejection on a commitment that was really made under a random seed: the test removes a line from a commitment made under a test seed. That the name is not in the program is checked by a step of `prover/build.sh` behind `cp_prove` and `cp_commit`, which prints nothing when it passes and without which the script writes no build record; and, on all three programs, by a test that is not part of this repository. The tests of the two rejections have not run on the sources as they are in this repository, and cannot: they need two test programs that are not part of this repository.
No test runs a weakened key reader that forgets the claims which the range proof leaves on the weight table, so that these claims are needed is shown only by reading.

After SIGKILL or another signal that it does not catch, a crash or a power failure, `cp_commit` leaves two working directories, whose names end in `.making`, one of them with the seed, which nothing overwrites (if the call died in its very last step, what it made is under `<isk>` and `<ivk>.making`, or, partly or wholly, under both final names); no program removes them: there is no tool for it. The file named with `-worst-case-table` stays then too; a call that fails by itself normally removes it, overwritten first, except at exit code 7, where it stays; an exit of the program's own, an abort or a signal early in the run, before the cleanup is armed, can leave it behind, empty, partly written or complete (read in the code).
column4: Keep them as secret as the secret key directory, and see docs/faults.md, "A killed or failed cp_commit".

column3: At its start, before a weight is loaded, cp_commit tries in the parent of each of the two key directories what the run needs there later: it makes one empty directory under the working name, opens it, checks its owner and mode, locks it, renames it without replacing anything, syncs the parent and removes it. If a step fails, the call is rejected (`cp-commit-file-system`, status 2) with the step and the reason, so that a run does not fail there late, after its long work; a creation or a rename that fails because the name is taken is rejected under `file-there-already`, with status 2 too. The try shows each step once, on one empty directory: a file system that fails later, or only sometimes, is not found. Ctrl-C, TERM and HUP are held back during the try. After SIGKILL, a crash or a power failure in that moment, and after a rejection whose line says that something is left as it is, one empty directory can stay, under `<name>.making` or `<name>.making.making`; the next call with the same names is rejected and says what to do. A last part of `-isk` or `-ivk` of more than 241 bytes is rejected. No file that was there before the call is touched: the run creates under free names only, replaces nothing, and removes only names that it has entered on its own list and the try's own empty directory, which it knows by device and inode. Read in the code; a CPU test of this repository (commit.walked_parents) tries the routine, with failing calls that the test puts in, not on a real file system without locks.
column4: Make the commitment on a local disk.

column3: Cheating provers that choose a message after they have seen the challenge that should come after it are run only on the library's toy-size proofs, not on the three programs; one such prover, which would fit a lookup's multiplicities to its challenge, cannot be run at all, and that order rests on the form of the code.

Thirteen orders of messages, claims and comparisons must hold, or a false proof goes through for certain. That the library keeps each of them has not been shown. By one reading of the sources and tests, order by order (a row of this table tells each of the thirteen; the one on a lookup's first challenge stands apart from the others, beside the row on provers that choose a message after its challenge): for four of the thirteen there is no malicious prover. Three of these four are held by other tests (known answers; a comparison at the very edge; a parameter file with a lowered target), and one, that a lookup's roots are shown before the point that joins the claims on them, by no test of this repository. Of the other nine, six are broken only in part: in one of the two protocols in which the order applies and not in the other; for a mask entry, by a prover that changes its own copy of one entry behind its challenge, which breaks the binding to the committed entry and moves no message, while none sends a mask's message late (there tests show that the wrong calls do not compile, or end the process, the latter tried on the prover's side only); by a prover that keeps a message out of its own hash chain and fits nothing to the challenge; or, for a lookup's first challenge, for two of the three things that must come before it, since a prover that fits the third, the multiplicities, cannot be run. The thirteen were counted on other sources of the library (row HW-678): they are no whole list of the orders of the library. All these malicious provers ran on test builds, on the library's toy-size proofs; through `cp_commit` and `cp_verify` three of the thirteen orders have a test, of which two are part of this repository. None of the malicious provers that the rows on the single orders tell of is part of this repository: they stood under test-only switches, and their code is not in these sources, so a reader can neither read nor run them. Another count had four orders that rest on reading only and that no test breaks; the two counts have not been compared.

The range proof in a key file never sends the keys of its lookups, so it says something about the committed weight table only if the claim that each part of each lookup leaves on its keys reaches the test on that table; without it a committer that runs the whole range proof on invented keys inside their ranges is accepted for certain. In the library wf_rows_verify() makes each such claim a pending claim on the matrix, check_key_under() hands all of them to the one-time test in the same chain, and the process ends if a caller drops them. Cheating provers at toy size run the range proof on another matrix that is in range (WF_OTHER_MATRIX, KEY_OTHER_MATRIX) or falsify one part's claim (WF_KEY_CLAIM_LIE, KEY_PART_CLAIM_LIE); in the lookup by itself, where keys are sent, one runs it on invented keys that are in the table while other keys were sent (LKP_INVENTED_KEYS); the same two lies through `cp_commit` and `cp_verify`, at one small configuration of the tests' own, are in a test that is not part of this repository, and no verifier weakened by leaving the pending claims out has been tried. The names in capitals are names of test switches; these switches and the code under them are not in this repository and cannot be built from it.

In a key file the vector that ties the range proof's claims to the table (the row weights times the matrix) must be fixed before the shared point of the one-time test is sampled; chosen afterwards, it could be fitted to the point, and the test would show nothing. In check_key_under() the first chain holds the index-mask message, the range proof and that vector with its sample's answer and ends in a seal; the seal is the one leaf of a binding tree whose root is in the first query of the shared chain, and the last chain's first query holds both seals. Cheating provers change the vector by one that vanishes at a shared point seen in an earlier run (LIN_W_AFTER_POINT, MEMBER_W_AFTER_POINT), in the tests of a batch's requests at toy size; none goes through a key file. The names in capitals are names of test switches; these switches and the code under them are not in this repository and cannot be built from it.

A mask entry must be committed before the first challenge under which it masks a value: a mask chosen afterwards can be fitted to any false value. In the library, by the rules of its types, a mask entry can be taken only from a receipt that the sending routine makes once the sample of its oracle message has been answered (SampleReceipt, MaskLedger), and the range proof and the lookup end the process if a message that gives masks has no answered sample (wf_start_check(), lkp_mask_messages_check()). One malicious prover picks a mask entry after its challenge: in whole toy proof files it changes its own copy of one index-mask entry behind the challenge that multiplies it, so that the two claims that are left over hold on its copy, but not on the entry that it committed to (one claim, whose value it has sent false, stays false), and it must be rejected in a proximity test of the request's second chain (SEAM_C_CHANGED). No message moves there: what that prover breaks is the binding to the committed entry, not the order of messages. None sends a mask's message late: there tests show that the wrong calls do not compile or end the process, all of them on the prover's side (the verifier's routines make the same two checks, by reading), and PSC_OTHER_W, PSC_OTHER_C and FOLD_OTHER_MASK use another mask than the committed one, in time. The sources name ways round the types' rule for a caller who means to: a claim can name a mask entry by its number. The names in capitals are names of test switches; these switches and the code under them are not in this repository and cannot be built from it.

Each request's claim and its vector on the weight table must be fixed before the point that all requests of a batch share is sampled; otherwise a prover reads the point first and commits to a vector for which both of its claims are true. In the library the vector and its sample's answer are sent on the request's first chain, which ends in a seal; the seals are the leaves of a salted binding tree whose root is in the shared chain's first query (lin_bind_shared()), a verifier works that root out from its own seal and a path (lin_binding_root()), and that the claim itself is a function of what the first chain has taken in before its seal is, by the source's own word, the calling code's duty. Cheating provers: LIN_W_AFTER_POINT, and LIN_TARGET_AFTER_BATCHING, which names the claim's value after the element that batches two false claims; neither has a control inside its test: for the second, a row of a list of tests that is not part of this repository (`lin-target-on-the-chain`) asks that a copy which does not send the claim's value on the first chain accept it, and no run of that row is told; neither prover is part of this repository. The names in capitals are names of test switches; these switches and the code under them are not in this repository and cannot be built from it.

Every element of a verifier's message must come from words of its own of the hash's answer; otherwise the coordinates of a point would not be independent, and the error counted for the round would be untrue. In the library each sampled value takes the next words of the round's answer, none twice and none skipped (draw_F_from(), draw_E_from(), ChainT::next_word(); rule R6.1 of the format's page). No malicious prover can break this, since it is the verifier's own computation, which prover and verifier compile from one file: what holds it are known answers from a separately written Python implementation of the rules.

The folded row of a weight table must be sent, and its sample answered, before the table's columns are sampled; a prover that knows the columns first fits the row's random tail to them and gives the row any content. foldeq_verify() (a key's or a batch's test) and Link::steps_verify() (a leaf file) receive root, seed and answer in one call and sample positions only afterwards, and the channel samples no positions while a sample is open. A malicious prover fits a leaf table's folded row to columns seen in an earlier run (LINK_ROW_AFTER_POSITIONS); in a batch's test there is only a prover that keeps the folded row's answer out of its own hash chain (CHAIN_ANSWER_OUTSIDE_AT), which fits nothing. The names in capitals are names of test switches; these switches and the code under them are not in this repository and cannot be built from it.

LINK_ROW_AFTER_POSITIONS (a test switch that is not in this repository): the further table differed in one entry. The prover made a proof, noted the drawn columns, and made it again. This time it sent, for the further table, a row with the first table's entries before the cut, pads fitted to the OOD answers and a random tail fitted to the columns that it saw. This succeeds with certainty if the positions do not depend on that row; here another row gave other positions. Control: the fitted row agreed with every column seen (shown on a cheating test build; no test that ships repeats the cheating run). Negative control (`chain-takes-messages`), which no test of this repository runs: a copy of blocks/ whose hash chain leaves the prover's messages out of its queries must accept the proof.

In the test on a weight table the vector that holds the matrix times the equality vector of the shared point must be sent, and its sample answered, before the point on the matrix's rows is sampled at which it is compared with the folded row. lin_shared_verify_on_shape() receives that vector and then samples the point. No malicious prover fits the vector to the point: LIN_OTHER_OMEGA sends a wrong one in time, and CHAIN_ANSWER_OUTSIDE_AT, which keeps one sample's answer after the other out of the prover's own hash chain, this vector's among them, fits nothing. The names in capitals are names of test switches; these switches and the code under them are not in this repository and cannot be built from it.

A weight table's root and its OOD answers must be fixed before the point at which the table is folded; a committer that knows the point first makes a table whose difference from the true one folds to zero there. Root and OOD answers are the first item of the statement in the first query of every chain that folds the table or leaves a claim on it: a key's first and shared chains (bind_one_time_chain(), lin_bind_shared()), a batch's chains and, for both tables, a leaf file's chain, which Link::verify() starts itself (link_bind()). A malicious committer fits a leaf table to a fold point seen in an earlier run, with an accepting control (LINK_TABLE_AFTER_POINT); in a batch's test there are only OOD answers fitted to the point (FOLDEQ_RECORD_AFTER_POINT), which bears on every parameter file, and a stored key file with another table's root written over its own, which the library's check of a key must reject. The names in capitals are names of test switches; these switches and the code under them are not in this repository and cannot be built from it.

In a lookup the roots of the multiplicities' bit planes must all be shown before the point that joins the claims on them into one is sampled; a prover that knew the point could show false roots whose weighted sum at that point is the true one, and every honest proof would still pass. The library sends no arrays of roots: lkp_run(), one routine for both sides, shows each root under a mask in a chain of sumchecks without variables and samples the point behind the last. No test of this repository breaks this order: LKP_WRONG_ROOT and LKP_FITTED_ROOT show wrong roots in time. The names in capitals are names of test switches; these switches and the code under them are not in this repository and cannot be built from it.

Every comparison of a round's error must in the end be with the number of bits that the verifier's own call asks for, not only with a line of the parameter file, which the provider writes. The library compares each round with the file's own target (its line `sec`) and knows no number of the caller's; `cp_verify` adds the second comparison: each of its three stages rejects with `NO: security-bits` unless the target under which the plan was made is at least the bits asked for (`-bits`; 128 if not given). No prover's bytes reach these comparisons; a test lowers a configuration's target to 96 and requires the two part-calls (`-key`, `-leaf`) and the whole call to reject at 128; that each of the three stages makes the comparison is read.
column4: If your own program calls the library's checkers, compare the configuration's target with the bits that you rely on: the library does not.

column3: A batch's test and a leaf file's link count each opened column by a bound that is true only of a table whose one-time test ran at the same distances and target; otherwise the split table comes back: one root over a word that is one matrix at some positions and another at the rest. The library holds these together at run time: plan and run each say which test on the table they are, or the process ends (require_table(); check_key_under() says the one-time test), and a later test takes only a table that the check of a whole key file or leaf file has handed out, at the same distances and setting (TestedTable, foldeq_columns_verify()). `cp_verify` checks key file, leaf file and proof in separate processes, where by the library's own contract the second comparison compares a value with itself, so there the order rests, by reading, on each process deriving its sizes from the same three configuration files; by a search of the tests, a word that holds two matrices has not been put before `cp_verify`. The caller says which test it runs, the plan says for which it was priced, and the two are held together where the point and the columns are drawn (blocks/iop/lin.h; LIN_KEY_PRICED_AS_LATER). The names in capitals are names of test switches; these switches and the code under them are not in this repository and cannot be built from it. That the caller states which test it runs, and where that is compared with the plan's, is told in blocks/iop/lin.h, in the comment on the parameter `test` above `lin_shared_prove_on_shape()`; the name LIN_KEY_PRICED_AS_LATER stands in no source of this repository.

A weight table has out-of-domain (OOD) answers (masked sums of the weights). In a test of the library's that is not part of this repository, on a split table (one root over a word that is one matrix at some positions and another at the rest), the half that disagreed with them was rejected (INDEX_TWO_TABLES: toy size, three columns, the table declared tested by the test itself); shown on test builds; no test that ships repeats it. No test puts a word that is two matrices before a key file's one-time test that is sized as the library sizes it at the full target. The names in capitals are names of test switches; these switches and the code under them are not in this repository and cannot be built from it.

Whether a closeness term may be counted by the lemma that is proved within a third of a code's distance hangs on a strict comparison. In the library at_distance() takes that lemma only where three times the whole number of positions that may differ is less than n - k: strict, and by one stricter than a distance of n - k + 1 would allow; beyond it the count rests on another source, which the accounting prints. No prover's bytes reach this comparison; a unit test asks at the very edge that the largest admitted number of positions counts by the lemma and the next one does not. No round's bound at the default setting rests on the lemma proved within a third of the distance; that count is reached for two mask codes and read by no round.

The lookups inside a request's sub-proofs do not run the library's lookup routine: `cp_verify` has a second implementation of its verifier's side (verifier/src/vf_lookup_argument.h). By that file's own head, nothing in it enters the multiplicities' planes, what the keys are read from or the mask row into the hash chain, so that these are committed and sampled before the lookup's first challenge is the calling code's duty; and that the claim on the keys was added is checked by a mark, which does not see what was added. The calls that add these claims were found in the sub-proofs' code and not read through; the malicious provers on these lookups alter counts, keys and sent values (none of these is in the public test table: verifier.forest_twin_test makes honest proofs only and alters what the verifier's routine is given; the others are not part of this repository, and their tests cannot be repeated from it), and none chooses a message after its challenge.

The ten of the thirteen orders that no malicious prover breaks, or only in part. There is none for four: that each element of a verifier's message is sampled from its own words of the hash chain's answer; that a lookup's roots are shown before the point that joins the claims on them; that a round's error is in the end compared with the bits that the verifier's own call asks for; and the strict comparison by which a closeness term may be counted by the bound within a third of the distance. Six are broken only in part: that a mask entry is committed before the first challenge under which it masks a value (one prover changes its own copy of an entry behind the challenge; none sends a mask's message late); that the vector which ties a key file's range proof to the table is fixed before the shared point (tried in a batch's requests, not through a key file); that a lookup's first challenge comes after everything that it tests (keys and table are fitted to it, the multiplicities cannot be); that a table's folded row is sent before the table's columns are sampled (fitted for a leaf table; in a batch's test only kept out of the prover's own chain); that the vector compared with the folded row is sent before the point on the matrix's rows (sent wrong in time, or kept out of the chain, never fitted); and that a table's root is fixed before the point at which it is folded (fitted for a leaf table; in a batch's test only OOD answers, a case which bears on every parameter file, and a stored key file with another root).

By a search of the tests' lists of malicious provers, which are not part of this repository, and of weakened verifiers, no test has a prover that hashes a digest of a sent message into the proof's hash chain in place of the message itself, and none gives files to a copy of `cp_verify` that hashes so. The nearest cases are on the proof library at toy size: there are malicious provers that keep a sent scalar, root, answer or sum out of their hash queries, and a test that requires them to be rejected (neither is part of this repository), and, in a test that is not part of this repository, a copy of the library whose chain leaves the prover's messages out must accept a fitted false proof.

One PSC with three variables on a false target. In a cheating build of blocks/iop/tests/psc_chain_test.cpp the prover's chain leaves mu', the hiding polynomial's sum, out of its query, so psc_prove() learns the next challenge, eps, first and fits mu' to the false target. The verifier's chain hashes mu'. Any proof by this build's prover is rejected, because the two chains differ: the rejection shows that the verifier's eps depends on mu'. A scratch copy whose verifier's chain left mu' out too accepted the fitted sum once; no build of this test repeats that (shown on a cheating test build; no test that ships repeats the cheating run).

A lookup's first challenge must come after everything that it tests: the multiplicities, what the keys are read from, and the table. In the range proof one call, wf_rows_verify(), receives the multiplicities and the answer to their sample and only then lets lkp_run() sample the challenge, so that a caller cannot change the order; the lookup's table and the committed weight table are fixed by the chain's first query. Cheating provers fit two keys, or two rows of the table, to a challenge learnt in an earlier run, or show a root that fits in the place of the keys' own (LKP_KEYS_AFTER_ALPHA (no control inside its test: one would need a hash chain that leaves out the message's root), LKP_TABLE_AFTER_ALPHA, LKP_FITTED_ROOT); a prover that fits the multiplicities to the challenge cannot be run, and that part rests on the form of the code. The names in capitals are names of test switches; these switches and the code under them are not in this repository and cannot be built from it.

The order of a proof's rounds is fixed by a plan that prover and verifier derive with the same code. No test holds the plan of a whole request, with the model's sub-proofs, to a separately written rule or to a stored list. So a slip in the order of rounds that prover and verifier share would pass every honest proof and every counting test.

The separately written reader of a proof file checks the file's form, each round's proof of work and, for every round that draws positions, that at least one tree's opened columns lead to that tree's root (a tree that does not open is passed over, not rejected), and no claim of the protocol, so a file that it reads to its end need prove nothing; and a misreading of the format that it shares with the programs does not show. It does not know which trees a given round must open: it reads a file to its end even if the second opening of a tree that is opened twice has been taken out. It stops where positions are sampled and no tree opens after them, and asks at the end that every tree has been opened at least once.

In the attention sub-proof each value that enters a lookup's key must also be tied to the committed cells by a claim of its own. That the verifier's list has all these claims rests on reading and on a count of claims; no test goes through the values one by one, and no malicious prover sends such a value so that the lookup holds and only the tie is false.

No lookup has attention's output as its key: its bound, on which a no-overflow condition of the layer relies, is meant to follow from the other checks together: an argument in five steps, read from the source, says so; it is not in this repository and has not been checked independently; the source's own comment says only that the attention sub-proof is meant to show it, and no test shows it. In the feed-forward and head parts too, a lookup key has no committed cell of its own, and sums are left to a sumcheck.

Where a lookup key has no committed cell of its own, it is computed from committed cells and from claims on the weight table, so these lookups are only as good as those claims and the table's opening. No circular dependence was found; that there is none has not been shown. This holds for every lookup of a group, those on plain committed cells too (in the output head's group: the final norm's and every checked token's digits): the group has one joining claim, so all of its lookups stand only if the head's weight claim and the table's opening are true.

No known answer shows a verifier's draw in which the real hash gives a word that the field rejects; that path is tested on given words, under a doctored hash, and in whole runs with a changed rule. Those whole runs do not reach the cap on how many words are rejected one after another, or an element that must not be 0 and is: these two paths are tested on given words on the CPU only, and no whole program has taken them. A word is rejected about once in 2^32 (the field has p = 2^64 - 2^32 + 1 elements, and a 64-bit word that is not below p is rejected), so a test run almost never meets a rejection, while a service will in time (reasoned). What happens then, read in the code: the rejected word is skipped and the next word is taken, by one source text that all three programs compile; the message may need a further hash call, every later draw of that message moves by a word, and on the GPU a kernel leaves its fast path for a function that it otherwise almost never enters. If prover and verifier parted there, `cp_verify` would reject an honest proof. The tests on given words and under a doctored hash are part of this repository and run on the CPU only. The whole runs with a changed rule are a test that is not part of this repository: it builds the three programs from a copy of the sources whose rule also rejects one word in 32, and asks that they agree on one batch of two requests (a small configuration without proof of work, synthetic weights, a test seed). So no test has a GPU kernel of the unchanged programs meet a rejected word of a verifier's message (searched).

The field's arithmetic is tested against slow arithmetic written in the same test program; values from a separately written program exist only through codes and whole toy proofs. No test runs the program that compares the field routines on the GPU with the host's, and that program is not part of this repository.

`cp_commit` and `cp_prove` read the GPU's error status before they release anything, but on CUDA 13.0 a successful `cudaFuncSetAttribute()` reset that status. So they read the status right before each such call, and a source-scanning test, which is not in this repository, reports any call where they do not. The programs require CUDA 13.2, where that is untried (row T11.4.2 tells one run), and the source-scanning test checks only listed release points. Whether a kernel launch that fails because GPU memory runs out when its code is first loaded shows in the error status that the programs read has not been tested, and no text of the vendor's is known to say so. A unit test, also not in this repository, tries one kind of rejected launch (a block that is too large), but no test makes a launch by `cp_prove` or `cp_commit` fail.

No test makes the driver reject a GPU kernel launch inside a whole `cp_prove` or `cp_commit`: tests that did so cannot run on the released programs. One unit test of this repository does it for one routine that `cp_prove` compiles: it asks the routine that fills a buffer with random values for a grid that the driver rejects, and requires that the program ends with exit code 1 and does not go on (prover/tests/coin_fill_gpu_test.cu; read in the code). That the error status is read before anything is released is checked by a test that only reads the sources and is not part of this repository.

A check that fails in a GPU kernel sets a bit in one word on the GPU, and the bit counts for its request only if every side stream that works for the request has been joined before `cp_prove` takes that word. `cp_prove` waits for its registered side streams at both places where it takes the word, but only a test that reads the sources checks that these waits are there.

A failure bit that a kernel sets after its request's failure word has been taken counts as the next request's or as no request's; in the second case the whole batch loses its files. Where a late bit lands in the next request's word instead, that request is answered "failed" without a cause of its own and the request whose check failed keeps its files; what kind of proof it then has, and whether `cp_verify` rejects it, depends on the check that failed (a proof with a lost mask, for one, still verifies) and has been neither followed nor tried.
No test looks at two failing requests in one batch, and none looks at the batch that follows one in which a request failed.

The test that reads the sources for the rule "read the GPU's error status before anything is released", which is not part of this repository, checks the hand-overs on its own list only, and does not read the verifier's code that is linked into `cp_commit`: a new hand-over that is not put on the list is not checked; the test does report a new caller of the routine that stages an answer, and a new place that starts a thread.

A GPU kernel launch, thread block or store that is lost without an error is noticed only by its effect. Lost data should give a false proof, which `cp_prove` releases like any other (row H26), and a lost mask or salt can expose a hidden value in a file that a verifier may accept. By a rule of the code, which a test that only reads the sources, and is not part of this repository, checks, a launch that the driver rejects should be noticed before anything is released. No run shows that on a whole program (T11.1), and the rule assumes that no call resets the GPU's error status, and one call is known to reset it (T11.4). A rejected launch that went unnoticed would set no failure flag and would not end the process, and the memory that the kernel was to write would stay as it was. One buffer, for a norm's multipliers, is pre-filled so that a run with its launch lost stops, but other launches or copies that are silently lost go unnoticed.

The GPU launch that computes the normalisation's masking sums is left out by no test: the four tests that leave out a launch do so elsewhere (two at the sub-proofs' pads, one at the tables' random entries, one at a generator's draw). Of lost sub-proof pads among several requests that are proved together: of the copies only one is lost there, the one that the CPU fetches to commit to, after whose loss the proof is false; in these tests `cp_prove` itself ran `cp_verify` and withheld the batch (a batch of four; a service with batches of two); the other copies are lost in a batch of one request only; none gives one request's place another's pads; a loss in a process's second batch only is tried in two small services (a lost draw; the fetched copy), and in no other way. The released `cp_prove` runs no verifier, and releases such a batch (row H26: by reading, not run). These tests are not in this repository, and no passing run of them on the released programs is known.

The rule "read the GPU's error status before anything is released" assumes that no call of the CUDA runtime, the driver or cuBLAS resets the thread's error status. One is known to: a successful cudaFuncSetAttribute() resets it, which without a read before it would let a rejected launch go unnoticed; so the programs make that call through two macros only, each of which reads the status directly before it, and a test that reads the sources, which is not in this repository, reports any bare call. The assumption was tried in part, on one machine, not on the released programs: after a rejected launch the error stayed across each call to cuBLAS in 64 of 64 trials, and a test follows a rejected launch by each function of the runtime and of the driver that the sources call by name (95 rows, as expected; one kind of rejection alone, a block that is too large). The cuBLAS manual does not speak of it, and no vendor's text is cited for the reset. The trials that are written up were made with a CUDA other than 13.2, with which the released programs are built; of one run with the program built by that compiler, only the outcome is kept (row T11.4.2).

column3: The test that follows a rejected launch by each function of the CUDA runtime and driver that the sources call by name compares its table with the sources. That comparison misses a name behind a macro, token pasting or dlsym(), a function that is called through a pointer, a call inside a library, cuBLAS and cuBLASLt among them (these two are assumed not to clear the status), and a call that the toolkit's headers make under another name. It does not compare a row's arguments with those in the sources; it does not evaluate #if, so code in every branch counts; where a name is a macro of this repository it is counted though the call goes to a function of this repository; and it reads neither prover/build.sh nor verifier/src/cp_verify.cpp. The test is not part of this repository.

`cp_prove` records steps of its sub-proofs' lookup arguments as CUDA graphs: a step's first run is direct, the second is recorded and launched, and later runs launch the recording (read in the code). That these recordings fit the rule "read the GPU's error status before anything is released" rests on a supposition: a kernel launch that is rejected while a graph is being recorded either spoils the recording, so that the process ends where the recording ends, or marks its thread's error status like any other rejected launch. One row of a GPU test program that is not part of this repository supports it: a launch with a block that is too large went into a recording; the call that ends the recording failed and left an error of its own in the status, which the programs' check at that call would find. The runs of that program that are written up were on one kind of machine (an H100) under CUDA 13.0, while the released programs are built with CUDA 13.2 Update 2; of one run on such a machine, with the program built by the compiler of CUDA 13.2, only the outcome is kept: all rows as expected (reported); and it tries one kind of rejection. No test rejects a launch inside a recording in `cp_prove` itself (searched), and no such run is known.

column3: Under a clipped-gap policy a pass says less than under exact match: it does not say that the reply agrees with the model's greedy reply at any position. Where a token of the request was judged under such a policy, which the caller has to name, the last line is `WITHIN LIMITS: clipped-gap ..`, not `YES`. The provider also sets the reply's length, and the allowance grows with it.
column4: Know which policy the parameter file sets before you rely on a pass.

column3: What a pass under the clipped gap allows. An acceptance policy that scores the checked tokens together. At most `cap` of their costs may exceed `C`. Each cost is then clipped to `C`, and the clipped costs must average at most `theta`. A proof accepted under this policy does not show that the reply is the model's own. Up to `above-clip` of the checked tokens can be any token at all (the line `covered:` prints that number). Every other token costs at most `C`, which rules out nothing when `C` is large or the model's scores lie close together, and a verifier cannot tell when that is so.

Two runs under a clipped-gap policy are told at the row's end, another in row T43, and one, on fresh replies, in `integrations/LIMITS.md`, all not on the released programs. The clipped-gap limits fitted to a real model are not published. The fact that honest replies get a proof does not show that the limits tell models apart, or that a reply that passes was served by the committed model (docs/limits.md#within-limits). One small example configuration sets a clipped gap: its limits were fitted on replies of a small floating-point model exported from synthetic weights, fit that example only, and say nothing about a real model's thresholds. A second one, at full size (prover/examples/target_full_f2_gap), sets limits that were fitted to no model or reply: they were chosen so that what passes follows from the policy's definition (with m = 2^sh = 256, the cost of a first choice, theta is 2 m, C is 101 m and cap is 1). They show how the policy works, are no pattern for a provider, and say nothing about a real model's thresholds either. One of the two runs, on real weights, made a commitment and ran one serving session of five batches of 24 under a clipped-gap policy, with every token of each reply checked; the replies are stored ones, and no inference engine ran; a session's 120 requests come from 48 different ones, by report the same 48 stored replies as in the runs of row T43, so it adds no new kind of reply or prompt; all 120 got a proof, and a separate call of the verifier accepted all of them (not on the released programs). The 48 are reported to have been chosen because the integer-model package's scoring expected them to meet the limits; so that all of them got a proof says nothing about how often honest replies do. That the parameter file's first 32 lines were the default setting's rests on how the run's script writes them; the file that ran was not looked at, and it was not kept. The run measured speed and tested nothing about hiding. The other was one run at full size, on the real, public weights, at the default setting with a clipped-gap policy in place of exact match, not on the released programs; no inference engine served anything in it. Its stored replies, limits and expected outcomes were not regenerated; the request files were built from those replies by the same rule: so this is no second sample and no rate of acceptance. Weight hiding was neither checked nor tested in it, and under this policy which requests get a proof tells something about the model's scores (row T43 tells its counts).

How often another model's reply would pass under a clipped gap has been measured for a real model for one smaller model of the same family alone, not on the released programs: in a scoring run without proofs few of its greedy replies met the limits (row SO-26.1.1), and in a run with the prover, at full size, under limits fitted during the run, none of 24 of its greedy replies got a proof. That model was served from a third party's public copy of the checkpoint. That the copy's weights are Meta's was not checked; that the files served were the copy's, unchanged, rests only on the publisher's name, the revision's first eight digits and the counts of files and bytes. That result is narrow (one model, few replies, and no one tried to deceive) and says nothing about other models. In the scoring run most replies that the same model sampled at another setting still met the limits. Altered replies of a real model were scored in a run without proofs: against limits fitted to a 16-bit engine's honest replies on Llama 4 Maverick's public weights, 27 of 32 replies with one token at a random place replaced by a random one still met the limits, and so did 49 of 96 replies sampled at temperature 1 (one run, not on the released programs; its counts whole, and where it broke off: row LIM-5.3; that run tested no cheaper model and no model with altered weights; the run of row SO-26.1.1 tested no model with altered weights either). On small synthetic models it was measured too, and two results are bad: in one run, on a CPU, with a demo, not on the released programs, all 64 replies of a slightly altered model met the limits, and so did 1 in 13 replies with one token replaced at random. At the small example that sets a clipped gap, 47 of 64 replies of a nearby model, which applies the router's score twice, met the limits when served in bfloat16, and 54 of 64 in float32 (by the run that the example's page prints, not on the released programs), and so did 3 of 64 and 5 of 64 replies with one token replaced; none of 64 replies set after another prompt did, and none with 4 or 16 tokens replaced.

On a scoring run on real weights, with the limits of row SO-26.1 (one run, not on the released programs; replies of up to 500 tokens that continue text from WikiText-2, scored and not proved; the run did not check the loaded weights against their checksums, and it ended at its time limit, with two further sets of replies unscored): under the limits fitted to the 16-bit engine and to the FP8 engine, 86 and 70 of 96 of Llama 4 Maverick's own replies sampled at temperature 0.7 met the limits, 85 and 65 of 96 sampled at temperature 1 with top-p 0.9, 4 and 2 of 96 greedy replies of Llama 4 Scout, a smaller model of the same family, and 0 of 96 of Scout's replies sampled at temperature 1. So these limits hardly tell another sampling setting of the same model from greedy serving. How loose they are depends on the single worst of the 48 replies that they were fitted to. A tighter threshold has a price. With the threshold at the third-worst instead of the worst fitted reply, none of Scout's 96 greedy replies met either set of limits. Of the sampled replies, 30 and 53 of 96 (temperature 0.7) and 21 and 34 of 96 (top-p 0.9) still did. But the limits fitted to the 16-bit engine then also reject 5 of 96 honest replies of that engine, and 11 to 17 of 96 honest replies of an FP8 engine. The limits did tell Scout's replies apart, but that result is narrow. Scout is one model, of the same family and with the same tokenizer. The 96 prompts come from one collection, and the limits were fitted on the other half of the same prompts. Each count of 96 adds up two sets of limits, where a provider publishes one. With so few replies, the true rate behind 4 of 96 could be about 1 to 10 in 100, and 0 of 96 still allows about 4 in 100. How long the four replies were is not known. No one tried to deceive in this run, and in the run of row SO-26.1 most replies with one token replaced met the limits. The result says nothing about other models.

column3: In the full-size example configuration the acceptance policy bounds the gap between a checked token's logit and the largest logit, not a log-probability (verifier/docs/parameter-file.md calls its table the step table).
A cap that is at least the number of checked tokens limits nothing.
column4: Choose the clip, the limit and the cap yourself, and say why.

column3: `cp_verify` rejects a few policies by their numbers alone (`NO: policy`), among them one kind that bars no token (theta = C, and cap not below the number of checked tokens). That kind is not the only one. A policy that it does not reject can still let every token through, and such a call ends WITHIN LIMITS with exit code 0: how much a policy excludes depends on the model's logits, which a verifier does not see; and a theta at or above 2^sh plus the largest logit gap that any committed weights can produce excludes nothing whatever the weights are. By a reckoning on paper such a theta fits into a policy line at the small example configurations; whether one fits at the full-size default has not been shown either way (nothing was run; the reckoning has not been checked independently). No parameter file of this repository sets such a theta. No soundness hangs on it: the claim that is proved is true; what it touches is what a WITHIN LIMITS is worth.
column4: Read the limits in the parameter file that the commitment ID covers, decide before you send a prompt whether you accept them, and pass them with `-policy`; if you cannot assess the numbers, accept only exact match (docs/limits.md).

column3: With large policy values nearly everything passes (a theta just below C, a large cap), and no program judges the values beyond four empty cases that it rejects. A threshold that excludes nothing can fit the file's line: how large a token's cost can be is set less by the width than by the final norm's two exponents (the lines MF and KF); at the full size, with a difference MF − KF of 11 or less, no token costs more than 3 · 2^30 whatever the weights, so a policy with a larger threshold bars nothing and no program rejects it; the programs accept every difference from 0 to 14; the shipped full-size file has 14; in Lean's model, at the library's written copy of the shipped full-size files, every policy with a threshold below C, and C below 2^32, bars something: under some weights, built for the proof, some reply with scores fails it (`VerifierAndGoals.AtFiles.every_output_at_meets_iff`, lean/Johnson/Goal/Files/MeetsPolicyAtFiles.lean); of the programs' files that has not been shown (both reckonings are Lean theorems about Lean's model: lean/Policy/Front/MeetsPolicyIdleAtScales.lean; Lean's kernel has checked them; their statements have not been checked independently; the programs' side from reading their code; nothing was run). At a very small width a threshold at or above the programs' own bound on a gap bars nothing either, and is not rejected; the example and full-size configurations have d = 512 or 5,120; two files with d = 64 ship, a toy's and a test's: the toy's is rejected at its first line, and under the test's, which has no clamps, no call ends with YES.
column4: Accept only under values that you have chosen or examined yourself, the parameter file's lines MF and KF among them (`cp_verify` prints these two in no line): name the policy's values in the call with `-policy`, and compare the line `covered:` with them.

column3: A plain YES can say nothing about the next token: a request that ends before the window's end with no next token can get a YES whose line `covered:` says `y=no`.
column4: Read the line `covered:`. For a request that asks only about the next token (r = T - 1 and e = T), pass `-next-token`: with any other request the call then ends in NOT-A-VERIFICATION at best.

column3: The proof system has no notion of an end-of-reply token: a reply that was cut short verifies as a shorter reply. Under a score policy a false end token counts as one wrong token, and is limited only as much as any other wrong token. One script, integrations/check_proof.py, says of itself that it checks the end token.
column4: Check yourself that the last checked token is one of the model's end tokens and that no checked token before it is. Where the provider gave you no end token, append it and cover one more position: under exact match a provider that cut off the reply cannot prove that position.

column3: A provider who may choose the key after it has seen the prompt can make a small model that gives the answer it wants, commit to it and prove honestly. A provider that gave different clients different IDs could serve them different models, and only a shared, public ID makes that visible.
column4: Fix the commitment ID before you send the prompt.

column3: `cp_verify` opens every file by name, at the path that it is given, and follows symbolic links.
column4: Give it files in a directory that only you can write.

column3: `cp_verify` reads only regular files. A file that the caller names and that cannot be opened or read whole ends the call with a line `input-unreadable-<role>`, exit code 2, and no verdict; the line names the file's role, not its path. Two exceptions: a configuration directory without any layout.txt ends `NO: plan-layout`, exit code 1; and in a whole call the leaf file, whose number the proof names, ends `NO: cp-entry-missing`, exit code 1, if it is missing or unreadable. In calls with links to private files in every role, a marker word in these files was found in neither output stream; no control showed that the search would have found it. A planning call with `-plan id` prints its hash of the three configuration files, and the commitment ID, only after the scan and the plans: a call on files that are rejected there prints no digest of them.
