column3: Where a parameter file declares proof of work, as the default does, its bits count toward a round's bits, and every call of `cp_verify` that ends in `YES`, `WITHIN LIMITS`, `PART PASSED` or `NOT-A-VERIFICATION` prints both numbers; at the default every response passes only with its work counted. That g bits of work lower a round's error by the factor 2^-g is, in the program's own print, assumed for this program's hash chains, and proved for another setting in a published work (ePrint 2021/582, Theorem 6). The step is argued on paper, in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, for that report's own chains (what the Lean verifier's own bound counts of the work: row LIM-58). No theorem ties the chains of that report or of Lean to the programs' chains (what is known of how Lean's hashing differs from the programs': row PS-68; lean/GAPS.md, 22; lean/LIMITS.md, L21). In the interactive protocol there is no event that the proof of work bounds, and no round's stated error has a term for it; the work enters only in the compiled argument, where a lemma of the report counts it for that report's own hash chains; for the programs' chains it is assumed. Whether work should count toward a security figure at all the release leaves to the reader, with both numbers printed.
column4: Read both printed numbers: what the opened positions give, and what the work adds.

column3: `cp_verify` accepts a response that passes only when proof of work is counted, just like any other response that passes: whether work counts is the client's decision, which only the client's own call of the verifier shows.
column4: Call the verifier yourself and read both printed numbers.

column3: The default leans on both at once: on counted proof of work in its position rounds, which rests on an assumption about grinding the programs' hash chains that is argued, not proved, and on the theorem on codes in its closeness rounds, the commitment's included. The truth of an accepted request and the binding of the weights both rest on the theorem on codes, and, at the default setting, both lean on counted proof of work in the rounds that draw positions. The bound rests on a theorem from the full version (ePrint 2025/2055, Theorem 4.6: not in the proceedings; that version gives an outline of its proof) of a paper published at STOC 2026, taken as given in a technical report that is not public and not refereed and in the programs' accounting. A statement on codes held to follow from that theorem, in its case of two words, is proved in this repository's Lean library, by way of another formalization's theorem and a comparison of bounds; the paper's own form of the bound is not proved there, and that the library's statement follows from the paper's, and that these programs' parameters meet the theorem's conditions, rest on reading, not on a proof (lean/LIMITS.md, L15; lean/THEOREM.md, "What it rests on"; what has been checked of it, and what has not: docs/limits.md#what-the-theorem-assumes). By that reading the parameters meet the conditions with no bits to spare. The bound rests too on further steps argued on paper in that report alone, which have not been checked independently.

The bits that `cp_verify` prints for the least round without its work belong to one round, the one with the largest error when the work is left out. What decides is an exact comparison of a round's error with 2^-sec; the printed bits are that error cut to two decimals, and were not compared. The round can be of any of the five kinds that the parameter file's lines `work` name.
column4: Do not compare the printed bits with 128 yourself: they are a rounded print.

column3: A rare value of the challenges can cost an honest run, in four ways among the causes that the sources name. A sampled column of the range check's matrix is all 0, or its combination vanishes: the prover sees it itself, that one request is answered "failed", and batch and service go on. A weight of a batched equation vanishes, or two coincide: the prover has no test for it, `cp_verify` ends NOT CHECKED under one of eight names, and `cp_prove` releases the proof like any other; the vLLM integration that ships hands on nothing of that batch (narrow exceptions, none open to a client: integrations/LIMITS.md), and `driver/measure_rate.py` and the example scripts show no byte of that proof or of its token. The first challenge of one sumcheck is 0: `cp_verify` says NO, at the vLLM integration's check too: nothing of that batch is handed on, and the batch is wiped (narrow exceptions, none open to a client: integrations/LIMITS.md). A coordinate 0 in the prover's own sumcheck code, or a search that finds no nonce: the process ends. None of these endings is an acceptance; but it has not been shown that no file can reach one of the eight guards, so a dishonest server may be able to turn a NO into NOT CHECKED. These four ways were gathered by reading the sources; it has not been shown that the list is complete.
column4: A client that gets "failed" may send the request again once the service runs: once, not in a loop, and under a new nonce (docs/service.md says why, and what no written statement covers). A provider: a rejection by the check of duty 6 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions) can, very rarely, be an honest run's bad luck; it costs one batch; nothing tells that from a bug or a hardware fault: stop serving proofs on that machine, and do not restart there until you know the cause (duty 8).

column3: The rare values by which `cp_verify` ends an honest proof NOT CHECKED: a slot's coefficient is 0, or two coefficients that are meant to differ are equal. For these no figure is settled: a weight may also depend on scalars that the prover sends, and no bound on the chance is proved. An all-zero column of the range check's matrix has the chance 2^-tau for each column; a column that is not all 0 whose combination vanishes is rarer. The list of causes is not shown to be complete.

`cp_prove` runs no verifier on what it releases; the vLLM integration that ships hands on no proof, and nothing of its response, before `cp_verify` has passed every proof of its batch (narrow exceptions, none open to a client: integrations/LIMITS.md); `driver/measure_rate.py`, which hands nothing to anybody, has the proofs checked once `cp_prove` has ended, and reports no rate unless `cp_verify` has accepted them all; each example script checks its one request's proof before it shows the answer. So where `cp_verify` ends NO on an honest proof, for a cause of row C2, the integration wipes that batch, and once the wipe is done and a person has lifted the hold its clients get `no_proof` (narrow exceptions, none open to a client: integrations/LIMITS.md); where it ends NOT CHECKED, the batch stays back, nothing is wiped, and the check is tried again: at the second such try the policy goes on hold. A front end of your own must do the same, or the proof reaches the client, whose own call of `cp_verify` is then the first to show it. Each of those causes is a rare value of the challenges; no run tells how rare, and no page gives a rate for all of them together. What a rejected proof can show of the weights: row H26.

The name `internal-stage` can be the program's fault as well as the machine's: a failed guard of the library, a failed check of the C++ library or of the hardening flags, an uncaught exception and, in places, lack of memory all end a stage by an abort, and the parent process cannot tell them apart.
column4: Do not read it only as "try again, the machine may have run out of memory".

column3: A last line that begins `NO: internal-`, with exit code 1, is no rejection of a proof: it says that the program met a fault of its own. It can come from a planning call, and from the first steps of a checking call, before any stage has begun. A stage's fault of that kind ends the checking call `NOT CHECKED`, exit code 5.
column4: Do not count such a line as a verdict on the proof.

column3: `cp_prove` starts no `cp_verify`: nothing of a verifier's output stands in what it prints. Its last line can name the class of a cause. A test build prints more.

Beside row C2's four ways, two more rare ends that the sources name: a random draw's retry loop that runs out (blocks/coins/coins.h: the guard "no retry word is left"), and a guard on challenge vectors in prover/engine/wf_heavy.cuh. The process ends.

Most faults that `cp_prove` finds in its own work end the process and its whole batch. A failed self-check on secret random values or keys ends the process, mostly with exit code 9 and a name, in a few cases with exit code 1, in two of these with no name (two stops of the generator of random values behind the sub-proofs' pads; prover/docs/ends-in-short.md lists the names); nothing that had no final file name at that moment is handed out, with three exceptions, the first two of which arise with `-overlap` or `-overlap-two` alone (read in the code). One the source states: an earlier batch whose responses are being read for their tags, or are getting their final names, at that moment gets all of them: whether the release is closed is read once, before that reading. The second: for six of these self-checks the result travels as a flag: the release of responses is blocked as soon as the process is ending or the service has read the failed check's result, which for those few is at the end of the request or, for checks in the shared chain, after the batch's second chains; until then an earlier batch's responses can still get their final names. The third: where the self-check ends the program through exit(), the release is stopped only after the exit handlers that were registered later, so in that time a staged response can still get its final names (row HW-583). The end takes back nothing that has its final names by then. By default the service gives a batch its final names before it proves the next (it takes the next batch's requests before that: row PS-53), so when a self-check fails in one batch, the batch before it already lies in `out/` under its final names, where whoever reads `out/` can take it. The next start of `cp_prove` removes of it only the responses whose requests still lie in `work/`, those that were named and not yet synced, and answers them "failed" (docs/service.md); once their requests have left `work/`, no start of `cp_prove` and no `cp_prove -clear` removes them. A failed self-check can be the first sign of a bug or a hardware fault that began earlier, and that batch came from the same process just before: the check says nothing of that batch itself, so it may hold unmasked values, and nothing shows that it does (duty 8: docs/limits.md#the-conditions). The serving scripts that ship hand it on only once `cp_verify` has accepted every proof of it (narrow exceptions, none open to a client: [integrations/LIMITS.md](../integrations/LIMITS.md#narrow-exceptions)); that does not clear it: no verifier sees a lost mask in a file that verifies. A few other checks answer "failed" for a request or a batch, and the service goes on.

A whole batch can fail while the service goes on. A cause that belongs to no single request (the batch's test on the weight table; a flag raised between two requests; a table of set-up constants that a run has changed) costs every request of the current batch its files, and with `-overlap` it can cost the other batches in progress theirs. By the source's own comment such causes can depend on hidden values. So every client of that batch learns one thing, that its batch failed, and that can depend on the weights or on another client's request; it cannot tell whose cause it was. The batch is proved to its end, on substitute values where necessary, through the same stages, and the process does not exit; within a stage the GPU launches can differ, and whether the running times are equal has not been measured. (From a comment and a search of the sources; not traced, not run.)

No statement, written or in Lean, covers what a prover computes or sends in a run that breaks off; it may depend on the weights. When a range check fails for one request while `cp_prove` proves a batch, not all of that request's values are replaced by fixed ones: the kernel marks the request and goes on with the very value that left its range, and cuts its digits from it, so values that depend on hidden ones go on through the same stages; by the source's own comment the batch is proved to its end, "on substitute values where necessary". None of that request's proof is handed out: neither its token file nor its proof file is written; its response is an empty file <id>.failed (in a spool with a file <id>.tag). What goes out all the same: the answer "failed", with a tag for the front end that is computed from the request's id and a key derived from the request's own nonce, and from nothing of the forward pass; and, in the proofs of the batch's other requests, the failed request's leaf of the tree that binds the batch: a salted hash (a salt of 40 bytes) of the value in which the first hash chain of its proof ends, bare to at most one neighbour, under inner nodes to the others, and through the root into the challenges of the chain that the batch shares. All this is read in the code; nothing was run for it. That no part of such a request's proof leaves by another way was traced in the code, from the mark to every write, on seven ways through the program (several requests; overlapping batches; a batch of one; with and without a spool; a run of `cp_verify` before release, which the other sources that were read (row HW-678) have and these sources do not; a process that ends on the way; what is printed), in one reading. For the salted leaf a technical report that is not public and not refereed has a written argument that the salt alone hides what is under it, for a prover that it specifies (complete by its own account, but not settled; it has not been checked independently). That `cp_prove` is such a prover has not been shown. By three readings, made apart, no message of a shared round takes in a claim or value of any request, so, beside the batch's key, which takes in every request's tokens, the salted leaf is the one thing that the batch's other clients get which depends on the failed request's hidden values; that nothing which a request leaves in the batch's one GPU engine enters another request's bytes is inferred, not read. That a failed check costs one request alone supposes that every rejection by `cp_verify` that depends on data is mirrored by a flag in `cp_prove`. That is shown nowhere: where it fails, the response leaves `cp_prove` as served, and a verifier outside it rejects it (rows H26 and HW-580). A comparison of the two programs, line by line, not on the released programs, found no such rejection at two of the shipped shapes, and one outside them: with an inner dimension of 116,509 or more (those two have 16,384 and 1,024, and a third shipped shape, target_small_file_f2, has 2,048) and weights chosen for it, a 32-bit sum in `cp_prove` could wrap. From reading the code, `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` reject a parameter file with an inner width of 2^16 or more (row C5.1), which shuts that case. That comparison did not read `cp_commit`'s worst-case check, the routed experts' kernels, attention's products or the aborting guards inside the verifier. Not known: whether a client can bring such a rejection about at will.

A few of `cp_prove`'s self-checks, all of them on data and none on secret random values or keys, do not end the process: they mark one request or one batch as failed, and the service goes on (read in the code). For those that share a flag with a check of the lookup argument, the source's own comment says that this is on purpose: that check depends on the weights and the prompt, so stopping on the flag would give a client one bit about a request of its choice, and a way to end the service at will.

What is supported: one full-size model shape (that of Llama 4 Maverick), with the default parameter file, or one that differs from it in the acceptance policy's three numbers alone (these three set how much a pass says: with large ones almost any tokens pass, and the project recommends no values: row SO-25.1), a window of 1,024 tokens, replies that are the integer model's first choices or that meet a clipped gap, seven storage types of weight files (no run on a real model's files has read an F16 file), one kind of machine (Linux, one H100 with 80 GB). Only one platform is recorded as tried, not on the released programs: Ubuntu 24.04 with g++ 13.3.0, one NVIDIA H100 80GB, driver 570.195.03, CUDA 13.0, code compiled for sm_90a. The build requires a later CUDA compiler than that: but for the trials under CUDA 13.4 that row P4.5 tells, builds have been made with nvcc 13.2.86, with which far less has been run. A later toolkit is not supported: the version check lets it through (row P4.5 tells what is known of one).
Only version 18.1.3 of the `clang++` compiler has been tried, not on the released programs (row RES-43), so a build with any other version is untested.

What `cp_commit` takes as a model's files (read in other sources (row HW-678); not run). Only the production build takes them: a test build rejects a directory of weights (`tests-build-on-a-model`, exit code 2). `-weights` must name a directory that holds at least one file `*.gguf` (the files are read in the order of their names), `wsums.txt` and `fold.txt`. In a call that makes a commitment every rejection below comes before the seed is drawn and before a file of the commitment is written. (1) Status 2, with a line on standard error that begins `gguf:`: a model file that is a symbolic link, has a second hard link, is not a regular file or cannot be opened; a file that is not GGUF version 3; a header that is cut short, names more entries than the file has room for, or has a string longer than 2^20 bytes, an unknown metadata type or an alignment that is not a power of two; a first file without `general.architecture`, `embedding_length` or `block_count`; a tensor with fewer than 1 or more than 4 dimensions, with a dimension of 0 or above 2^30, or with 2^61 or more elements; rows of a tensor of type Q4_K, Q5_K or Q6_K whose length is not a multiple of 256, or of type Q8_0 whose length is not a multiple of 32; an offset that is not a multiple of the alignment; a tensor that reaches beyond the end of its file; a tensor name that occurs twice; two tensors that overlap in a file; a tensor that is needed and is missing. (2) Status 2, with a sentence of its own: a width other than 5,120 or a head dimension other than 128; a number of layers, or dimensions of a tensor, other than the parameter file gives; a committed tensor that is not of type F32, F16, BF16, Q8_0, Q4_K, Q5_K or Q6_K; a committed tensor of type Q8_0, F16 or BF16 whose rows are not a multiple of 256 long; a normalization tensor that is not F32 or has not the length of its matrix's input; a `wsums.txt` that cannot be opened (a link counts as that), has a malformed or repeated line, names a tensor that the files do not have or gives it another number of elements, has no line for a committed tensor, lists another number of tensors than the parameter file's layout has, or does not end with `END` and the number of its lines; a `fold.txt` without the lines `eres <whole number>` and `qkrows asis`, each exactly once; an exponent outside 0 to 40, or above 24 for a layer's matrix of type Q4_K, Q5_K, Q8_0, F16 or BF16 other than the router's; a multiplier (a normalization weight times a fixed constant) that is neither zero nor of magnitude 2^-64 to 2^64. (3) Status 3: in the conversion to integers a value is not finite, an integer is above 4,095 in magnitude (2^30 - 1 in the embedding), or a multiplier is not zero and below 2^-100. Status 6: the SHA-256 sums of the integers are not those of `wsums.txt`. Status 16 (`integer-out-of-range`): an integer lies outside the range that the parameter file declares for its kind. Status 7: the worst-case check has not passed. (4) Two options: `-keep-for-the-audit` is rejected on a directory of weights (`cp-commit-kept-on-a-model`, exit code 2), and with `-public-weights` each model file needs a file `<name>.weights-are-public` beside it that holds its SHA-256 (`cp-public-weights-marker`, exit code 2).

An inner node of a hash tree is hashed from the configuration's digest and its two children only: nothing of the tree, the place or the run, the same for every tree under one configuration but one: the tree that binds a batch's requests hashes its inner nodes under another number. What one collision, once found, would reach is not narrowed by the inner nodes; for trees made in a run it is narrowed through the leaves.
That a hash tree's number is used once holds by construction for the trees of a run only; for stored trees and the trees that tie a batch together it is not stated.

Four public tables are computed with the platform's floating-point library. Where the parameter file holds their digests, a table with another digest ends the run; without the digests the verifier has nothing to compare its tables with. That every faithfully rounding library gives the same tables has not been shown. So a NO can be false of an honest proof: on a machine whose floating-point library rounds otherwise a table's digest differs, and the run ends NO under that table's name. This is reasoned, not run.

column3: The digests with which `cp_verify` compares the four public tables are written by the provider, so a passed comparison does not show that they are the format's tables.

On a platform whose library rounds differently `cp_verify` rejects every honest proof: a wrong NO. That another library gives the same tables was computed for one set of parameters only. From reading the code, `cp_commit` compares them too, on its own machine: before its long work it runs the verifier's code, compiled in, and a planning call of `cp_verify`, and it ends where a table's digest differs.

This is what the tests do, before `cp_verify`, to the parameter file's lines with the digests of the four public tables. One test in this repository, in planning calls, which read no proof, alters one bit in a word of each digest, leaves out the last line or all of the lines, exchanges two lines, and moves the lines behind the first call line; it requires the rejection's name each time (without any of the lines: that the condition is printed as not met). Only a test that is not part of this repository writes a line twice, or exchanges the optional line xl with the first of these lines, and requires the rejection's name. No test was found, in this repository or among the tests that are not part of it, that requires an answer of `cp_verify` to a number too large for 32 bits in these lines, to zeros in front of one, or to an optional line behind all of them (searched). A stress test in this repository does hand a build of `cp_verify` under sanitizers, again in planning calls, numbers of 11, 20 and 4,000 digits in three of these lines, and the same exchange of the line xl; it counts only crashes, the program's internal faults, time and memory, and a changed file that was planned would be listed for a person and not counted. column3: `cp_prove` runs no verifier: it releases a batch's responses once all of them are staged, and nothing in it tests a finished proof as a whole. In an honest run on a sound machine no case is known in which a verifier has anything to hold back, but for the rare hash outputs at which `cp_verify` does not accept an honest proof (row C2.2); that there is no other has not been shown (row HW-580). What stands between a bug or a hardware fault and a client is `cp_prove`'s own self-checks on masks, pads, salts and keys, and the proof library's guards on the prover's own steps (exit code 1, name `guard`): where one fails the process ends, mostly with exit code 9, and nothing that had no final file name at that moment is handed out, but for the exceptions that row C3 tells. Which bugs and hardware faults they stop, and which they let through, has not been sorted. What has its final names by then the end does not take back (row C3). After a bug or a hardware fault that they let through, `cp_prove` can release a response that `cp_verify` rejects. Nothing in `cp_prove` notices that: it goes on serving until a self-check fails or a person stops it. A response that `cp_verify` rejects can hold hidden values unmasked: by one reading an exact linear form in the weights; no upper bound is known for any cause. A client that is sent one learns from its own `cp_verify` that the proof is false, but it then holds the file. It also concerns whoever can read the provider's output and staging directories, or a place where a front end keeps rejected responses. Cases that are known, all by reading, none run, among them: rows H3.18, H3.18.1, H3.18.2, H45, H45.2, T11.3, HW-245, HW-458, HW-491 and HW-746; and a scalar that is sent under another's mask entry, or unmasked, past the three self-checks that hold scalars to mask entries. So `cp_verify` must accept every proof of a batch before anything of that batch leaves the provider (duty 6: docs/limits.md#the-conditions): a rejected response for what it can hold, and the rest of its batch because a bug or a hardware fault that spoiled one proof may have cost another its mask, in a file that still verifies (reasoned, not shown). Of what ships, the vLLM integration hands on no proof, and nothing of its response, before `cp_verify` has passed every proof of its batch (narrow exceptions, none open to a client: [integrations/LIMITS.md](../integrations/LIMITS.md#narrow-exceptions)); `driver/measure_rate.py`, which hands nothing to anybody, has the proofs checked once `cp_prove` has ended, and reports no rate unless `cp_verify` has accepted them all; each example script checks its one request's proof before it shows the answer; a front end of your own must do the like. At a rejection the vLLM integration withholds the whole batch, overwrites and deletes the batch's proofs and token files (but not what a wipe that breaks off, or cannot begin, had not reached, nor a response that looked malformed and was passed over at the second look, nor one that turned up under the batch's time after its check had begun: [integrations/LIMITS.md](../integrations/LIMITS.md)), lays failed responses in their place, and lays a hold that only a person lifts (where nothing can be written at a rejection, only the memory of the server process that saw it stops the policy, and another server process, or the same one after a restart, knows nothing of it: [integrations/LIMITS.md](../integrations/LIMITS.md)); where its check gives no verdict, or a response looks malformed, no proof of the batch that has not yet passed leaves, and nothing is overwritten unless another proof of the batch was rejected, so `out/` then holds unchecked files; and a batch that no client asks for is not checked ([integrations/LIMITS.md](../integrations/LIMITS.md)). The check of duty 6 holds back only what a verifier rejects: a faulty file that the verifier accepts passes it, and that is the main risk (docs/limits.md#the-main-risk). A rejected response's opening is counted like any other's: every opening of a weight table is counted in that table's counter file, by its planned number of columns, when it begins, whatever becomes of it, and `cp_prove` writes none of a batch's replies or proofs to a file before the batch's count is on disk. The same holds of a key file or a leaf file that `cp_verify` rejects inside `cp_commit`; such a file is written nowhere, and the call then removes all that it has made, the counter files and the seed among them (all of this read in the code, not run). The count is only the planned number of columns, taken before the columns are made: it does not look at what they hold, and whether a faulty run can open more columns than were counted has not been looked at. So it is no bound on what a rejected file shows.
column4: Let no response leave you before `cp_verify` has accepted every proof of its batch. Use a `cp_verify` built from the same sources as your `cp_prove`, and keep it where the service's account cannot write. After a rejection give out nothing of that batch, and stop serving on that machine (duty 8: docs/limits.md#the-conditions). The rejected response and the rest of its batch have their final names in `out/`: once their requests have left `work/`, no start of `cp_prove` and no `cp_prove -clear` removes them, so see that your front end can never hand them on. The vLLM integration overwrites and deletes the files of a batch in which `cp_verify` rejected a proof, but not what a wipe that breaks off, or cannot begin, had not reached, nor a response that looked malformed and was passed over at the second look, nor one that turned up under the batch's time after its check had begun ([integrations/LIMITS.md](../integrations/LIMITS.md)); where its check gave no verdict, and no other proof of the batch was rejected, they stay. Keep every place where a rejected response, or what the verifier printed about it, is stored as secret as the secret key directory. Never hand out what was staged, and leave its removal to the program's next start (which start removes it, and what to do if none comes: row HW-480). After a call with `-out` that ended with an exit code other than 0, or was cut off by a kill or a loss of power, run `cp_prove -clear` on that directory, and on no other.

column3: At an ending that `cp_prove` makes itself, staged answers and proofs are overwritten before they are removed, unless a thread that writes a response still holds the lock after a wait of about two seconds: then what is staged is left. The ending then counts as not all wiped, as it does if the ending itself could not overwrite or remove a file. A file that could not be overwritten earlier, when a request failed together with its batch, is deleted all the same; the program then ends with the name `write-failed`, and that ending need not count as not all wiped (read in the code; not seen in a run). What is deleted without having been overwritten stays in the file system's free blocks, or under its second name if somebody had given it one, where neither the next start nor `cp_prove -clear` reaches it (read in the code). An ending that `cp_prove` makes itself also clears the staging directory itself at its end, by the routine that a start and `cp_prove -clear` use, and what that leaves counts as not all wiped (read in the code; not seen in a run). In a spool directory it goes by their rule on names: only a directory named by 64 lower-case hex digits counts as a staged response's, and every other entry at the top of out/.tmp is left as it is. Unlike these two, which touch nothing while an entry of another name is there, the ending still clears the staged responses (that an ending drops what is staged while a stranger's file in a response's directory stays is tested on the spool's own code on a CPU, by the public test `prover.spool_clear_test`; the rule on names at the top of out/.tmp by a test that is not in the public table; neither seen in a run of `cp_prove`). The price: an entry in the staging directory that `cp_prove` did not make ends an otherwise good run as not all wiped. After a kill, a crash or a loss of power it stays whole too, under `out/.tmp` in a spool directory or `.tmp` in the directory named with `-out`. In a spool directory a next start on that directory whose requests have the same length as those left in `work/` overwrites and removes it (by reading the code: row HW-480). From reading the code, for a single batch the next call with the same `-out` takes the directory if it holds nothing but `.tmp` with a well-formed `mark.txt`, as a killed batch leaves it that had released nothing, and overwrites and removes what was staged (what it cannot overwrite, or did not make, stays, and that call fails); until then, or until somebody runs `cp_prove -clear` on it, what was never released stays there. What a file system or a disk keeps of overwritten blocks is beyond the program's control.
column4: Never hand out what was staged. After a call with `-out` that ended with an exit code other than 0, or was cut off by a kill or a loss of power, run `cp_prove -clear` on that directory, or, after a kill, make the same call again, and name no other directory (R18.4). Treat the disk under these directories as secret for good: encrypt it, or wipe it before it leaves your hands.

column3: The file of the weights' sums in the model's directory (`wsums.txt`) holds a plain SHA-256 of each tensor's integers, with nothing secret or random in it: whoever gets the file can test any guess of a tensor against it, offline and without limit. The tools that write it create it so that only the account that made it can read it. The exponents in the file give each matrix's largest absolute value (after its norm's gains are multiplied in, where it has a norm) within a factor of two, and the number of bits does the same for the embedding.
column4: Keep `wsums.txt` as secret as the weights.

column3: What holds of the file of the weights' sums holds of every other hash or checksum of the weights that has nothing secret in it: whoever gets it can test a guess at the whole model offline, without limit. The operators' page names examples from outside the programs (a download's list of sums, a backup's content hashes). The digest of the weights' sums, which this repository's vLLM integration takes, serves the same test, and that page does not name it: it stands on the command line where an operator passes the digests themselves, or in a file where an operator passes a file of them; the example script passes neither, and the loader takes the digests in memory (read in the code; not run with vLLM).

Like `wsums.txt` itself, the digest of `wsums.txt` lets anyone with a candidate model test whether it is the served one. It stands on vLLM's command line, and so in the process list and in vLLM's log, if an operator passes the digests themselves with the option "sha256". The example script passes the path of the directory of reference copies instead ("reference_directory"): the loader takes the digests of the copies there, in memory, and looks at no modes or owners there, though `wsums.txt` itself lies there. Whoever has only the digests can pass the path of a closed file ("sha256_file"), and by a comment in the sources the loader's error messages name no digest, on purpose (read, not run). `fold.txt` holds no hash of the weights, but one of its two lines is e_res, a setting that can be fitted to the weights.
column4: Keep `fold.txt`, that log and the process list as secret as the weights.

column3: Of ordinary (pageable) memory `cp_prove` locks only the seed's against swapping, and it does not read the result of the call that locks it. `cp_commit` locks the seed and four further blocks of secret bytes (each table's key with its second copy, the fresh bytes of the copy that is being made, one more block of 32 bytes, the record of its second derivation's state); where a lock is rejected it prints a warning and goes on. All other pageable memory, with keys derived from the seed and short-lived copies of the seed itself, can reach swap, where someone with access to the provider's machine or its disk could read it; a client cannot.
column4: Run the service with no swap, or with encrypted swap. Encrypt every disk that holds the secret key directory, the weights or the spool directory: removing a file does not overwrite it.

column3: The files in memory through which `cp_commit` hands a key file or a leaf file that is not checked yet to `cp_verify` are not locked, so they can reach swap space. Both programs mark themselves as not dumpable at their start (`cp_verify` as the second act of its main routine, so there is a short time before it), and `cp_commit` closes its own file descriptors as soon as the child is started; whether another process of the same user can still open these files under /proc while the child lives was not tried, and the programs' own documentation speaks both ways: one page says that it can; two others say that, by the system's rules (the Linux manual pages), from that mark on only a process with the right to trace others can read such files under /proc.

Whatever else reads or hashes the secret key directory, to compare it before and after a run, say, reads the seed too, holds it in ordinary memory, neither locked nor cleared, and does not mark itself as not dumpable, as the three programs do.
column4: Let no other tool read the secret key directory.

column3: A process that shares a processor with the proving process can learn something of its branches and memory accesses through what the two share (caches, branch predictors, performance counters) without reading its memory; another user of the machine also sees the GPU memory in use and the GPU's load. Of these channels no measurement is told on this repository's pages. Time is a side channel too, and it was measured, not on the released programs, on synthetic weights, in runs that were not repeated, and did show something: two synthetic models were told apart by the model server's time to its first token, with no prover behind it. It makes no difference under which user or in which virtual machine the other process runs: what counts is the physical machine: caches, branch predictors and performance counters serve whatever runs on a processor (reasoned from these channels). So it is a condition of weight hiding that no untrusted code runs on that machine at all, and that whatever runs under the service account, a front end too, is trusted as the service is: it can read the seed and the weights (the operators' page says both).
column4: Give the service a machine of its own.

column3: The service neither tests nor reserves disk space: no call that asks for free room or reserves it stands in the sources. By a reading of a service's code in other sources (row HW-678; not tried; no such reading has been made of these sources): with room for at least one response and for less than a whole batch's, whether a batch's responses are written depends on how many of its requests failed, so a client's own response could tell it something about the other requests' failures; by one reading the same reaches the clients of the batch before and of the batch after. A client can bring such a disk about by leaving its responses unfetched. A write that fails while a batch's responses are staged ends the process before any of them gets its final name; the requests that are left are answered "failed" by the next start (read in the code; not run with a full disk).
column4: Keep ample free space on the spool's disk.

column3: What an audit's YES leaves out. A proof made under a random seed can be audited only if its whole batch was made for that (`cp_prove` -keep-for-the-audit: one batch, one audit); of every other batch the random bytes are kept nowhere, and there only the leaf tables' salts are checked. The tool rejects a model's files, as does the option that keeps the bytes for it: on a real model nothing can be audited. The salt of a leaf that nobody opens is out of reach of any audit that does not rebuild the trees from the data. The readings of the audit tool were of other sources (row HW-678), but for the one with which row E4.9 opens.
column4: Read an audit's YES together with tools/audit/README.md, on what a YES covers and does not cover.

column3: The audit can find a bug that shows in every run. Whatever it compares by value it compares on synthetic weights alone: the tool rejects a secret key directory of a model's files, and both programs reject -keep-for-the-audit on them. On synthetic weights it can check one run's masks by value only if that commitment or batch was made to be audited (-keep-for-the-audit, which `cp_prove` rejects in a service) or was made by a test build under a test seed and test coins. Of any other run on synthetic weights, a served batch among them, it can compare by value only the salts of the weight tables' opened leaves (--drawn, with the secret key directory; read in the tool's code, not run on a served batch). So an accident in a run on real weights it never sees by value, and of an accident in a served batch on synthetic weights it sees by value only what strikes those salts.

The audit does not check the stored weight tables' columns, or leaves that no opening reaches in trees that hold real values. Nor does it compare the random values that fill the rest of a proximity test's main rows behind the folded row: it lists these draws (each one's number in the order of the draws, and its length), so that the draws behind them keep their numbers, but computes none of their values and holds them against nothing; and in an audit of a production build, which has no list of draws, nothing checks them or the lengths of their draws (read in the tool's code).

The audit tool does count, from outside the programs, at how many different columns each stored weight table is opened in the files that one call is handed, and compares that number with what the rows' random entries hide and with the table's own count file. The repository's test of the tool hands it one key file, two leaf files and the four proofs of one batch; a second batch on the same commitment is audited in a call of its own, on its own two proofs (whether that call makes this count was not followed). So no test adds up a table's opened columns from outside over more than one batch, and a table's limit is a limit over all its batches; the tool's own page says that this way of calling it is written for one batch. Of these two comparisons the test asks only that nothing is reported: no test makes either of them report. A third, which the commitment's audit alone makes (the count file against what the key file and the leaf files have drawn), must report in one case, after a prover has run on the directory. No test makes this count on proofs, or makes any of the three report, at another configuration or under a drawn seed: the same test audits a second commitment, made under a drawn seed at a second small configuration, on its key file and one leaf file alone, and there nothing may be reported. (Test build, synthetic weights; but for that second commitment, the small example configuration and a test seed, under which nothing is hidden.)

No test looks from outside a whole `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` at the random entries of the stored weight tables as they lie in GPU memory, the audit with the secret key does not reach these tables' columns either, nothing outside the programs recomputes a stored or opened line of such a table from the weights, and no test of the whole programs injects a single wrong random entry (one test of the routine alone injects one wrong column; the tests of the whole programs inject whole losses).
No test of this repository runs the audit on files of a program with an injected loss (one such trial outside it, on test builds of other sources, with its conditions: row LIM-63.2, line 3).
The repository's test of the audit tool takes the test build, which lacks the production build's check on HOME and TMPDIR, so it never meets that rejection (seen in two runs side by side).
A batch that a service made cannot be audited with the kept bytes, nor one on a model's files; and no injected fault has been tried on a batch that the production build made for the audit.

By a reading of the code, no option of the audit tool in this repository writes a seed, a key, a mask, a pad, a salt or a value computed from them to disk: `--report=` and `--ledger=` write names, counts, lengths and places, and `--erase-kept-files` writes zeros. The tool's own test, play.sh, leaves a test's seeds and random bytes in its work directory. Only the two audits' own calls (`--commitment`, `--batch`) try to shut out core files and swap; a direct call with `--drawn` does not (the tool rejects a secret key directory whose text file does not name synthetic weights). One whole reading of a form of the audit tool that is not in this repository (row HW-678) found three faults that needed a change; under one option its public audit wrote masking pads and bare values to disk. All three were changed there; no run of the tool so changed on honest files, and none of its self-tests, is known, and whether the tool in this repository is that tool as changed is not known. Honest files have gone through a form of it at full size once at the default setting, on synthetic weights, in one commitment's audit and one kept batch of two proofs, reported, not on the released programs (row LIM-63.2; tools/audit/README.md, "What has been run").

column3: With `-worst-case-table`, which every build takes, the production build on a model's files too, `cp_commit` writes a file that is computed from the weights. A call that fails removes it with everything else that it has made; it is overwritten with zeros first, like the call's other files (row R3.2 tells what stays). It stays at the good end and at exit code 7, where the table is the answer that the operator asked for; after SIGKILL, a crash or a power failure; and where an exit or a signal comes in the short stretch before the cleanup is armed. That only its owner can read or write the file (mode 600) is read in the code, and a GPU test of the suite, `gpu.cp_commit.small`, requires it at the good end and at exit code 7 (test build, small test configuration, synthetic weights). That none of the table's numbers is also printed is known by reading only: `cp_commit`'s one call of the routine that writes the table hands it the file and no stream for its short form. No test of the suite compares what the program prints with the file, so a number that did get printed would be in the operator's log, outside that file's protection, and no test would show it.
column4: Keep that file inside the provider. Keep `cp_commit`'s log as private as that file.

column3: Every acceptance that the documentation reports comes from a check on the prover's own machine, with the prover's own copy of `cp_verify` and the prover's own files and commitment ID: it is a measurement, not a verification.
column4: Check a proof on a machine of your own, with a `cp_verify` that you built and a commitment ID that you did not get from the prover.

column3: `cp_commit`'s runs of `cp_verify` are each started by a small supervisor, with a fixed time limit of 30 minutes; the supervisor kills the run's process group when `cp_commit` dies or when a time limit of its own passes. There are gaps. A `cp_verify` that cannot be killed, because it is stuck in a system call, is left behind. A supervisor that is itself killed outright leaves its `cp_verify` running, and if `cp_commit` is killed at the same moment that run goes on to its own end. The next `cp_commit` looks for no check that was left behind. At a terminal set to `tostop`, the first line that such a run prints to the terminal stops its process group until the time limit passes (in `cp_commit`'s planning run standard output goes to a file in memory, so only a line on standard error reaches the terminal there); `cp_commit` starts a check of a key file or a leaf file that was killed at the limit once more, so it can wait twice 30 minutes; the planning call at its start is run once, and if that is killed at the limit `cp_commit` ends with `cp-commit-judge-plan`, exit code 2, in words that do not say that the limit was reached (read in the code; no terminal was tried).
column4: Before the next call, make sure that no check of the last one still runs. At a terminal, leave `tostop` off, or send both of the programs' output streams to a pipe or to a new file that only you can read.

column3: If `cp_commit` is killed outright, the checks by `cp_verify` that it had started, and their children, end with it: each is started by a small supervisor, which kills the check's process group when `cp_commit` dies or when a time limit of its own passes. A public CPU test, `prover.gate_children` (SUITE.md), kills a small substitute that calls as `cp_commit` does, which starts a substitute for `cp_verify` through the same routine, and finds no process left; in its control, without the supervisor, four processes still run two seconds later. On a GPU the same routine was shown to work once, in another program than `cp_commit`, not on the released programs, with a substitute for `cp_verify` (reported). Not shown on a GPU: that the true `cp_verify`'s own children end too; a production build; full size. After a loss of power a request can in one case be taken into a second batch. `cp_prove` rejects a spool directory that a running `cp_prove` holds (by a file lock, flock). That lock has not been tried with two machines on one shared file system, or on a file system that does not enforce such locks. That the directory is never restored or copied is left to the operator: no program notices a restored or copied one, which has the same `mark.txt` (row R13.1.1). That the checks end with `cp_commit` is tested only on a CPU, with small substitutes for both programs (the same test).
column4: Never restore, copy or share a spool directory between services.

column3: mark.txt in a spool directory says that the directory is `cp_prove`'s. One that `cp_prove` wrote names no commitment: it writes 64 zeros in the place of the ID, takes any well-formed mark, and a front end takes that mark as any commitment's. So `cp_prove -spool` starts on a spool directory that another commitment's front end has marked (what such a start removes there: rows R18, R7.1.1 and HW-480), and where `cp_prove` marked it first, every commitment's front end takes it (R40): requests of the right length are proved under the commitment that it was started on, use up a leaf table's count of openings, and the first `cp_verify` that is given the right commitment ID notices. A copy or a restored backup of a spool directory has the same mark, and `cp_prove -clear` clears any marked directory. The mark guards against a mistake, not against someone who can write in the directory. A request of another length is never served or removed: in in/ it is left where it is; in work/ it makes `cp_prove` refuse to start, before anything is removed.
column4: Keep one spool directory for each commitment and policy.

column3: One `cp_prove` at a time runs on a secret key directory, as a service or for one batch: at its start it takes an exclusive lock (flock) on the directory, without waiting, and holds it until the process ends; a second start is rejected (`cp-isk`), and so is a start while the call of `cp_commit` that creates the directory has not ended. What the lock does not see: a process on a copy of the directory, or on another machine, unless the file system applies flock() across machines; it may also miss one that reaches the directory by another route on the same machine (through a container's layer, from a virtual machine, or by a second mount); `cp_prove -clear` and the audits do not take it. Where the lock call reports an error, `cp_prove` does not start (read in the code). Nothing at that step looks at the kind of file system, and some network and guest file systems may report no error and grant a lock for that machine alone (from general knowledge of such locks; nothing was tried).
column4: Keep the secret key directory on a local disk, and never copy it to get past that rejection (docs/operators-duties.md, "Backups and restored copies").

column3: The self-check that the GPU's tables of constants are unchanged at the end of a pass compares one 64-bit sum for each table, which is no cryptographic hash: a change that leaves the sum the same is not found.

Whoever can make a hard link to a weight file can make an honest `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` reject its own weights: a denial of service. Directories whose files have second names for honest reasons (hard-link copies, deduplicating stores) are rejected too.
column4: Keep `fs.protected_hardlinks = 1`, store the weights where no other account can link to them, and copy the real files.

column3: Only the system tool `flock` keeps two calls of prover/build.sh from building the programs into one directory at the same time; on a machine without it there is no lock and no warning, and one call's program could come to be beside the other's build record. Other targets build each in a work directory of its own.
column4: Do not start two builds into one directory at once.

column3: Some tests fail now and then, and the cause has not been found. The CPU test of the serving loop has failed several times in one of its checks: in one whole run, in 1 of 52 repetitions (not on the released programs), and more often where the machine was short of CPUs; each time it passed when run again. Readings of the code lay the failure on the test's own fixed clock and not on the program, but no failing run was caught with its numbers, so an occasional fault in how the service orders a batch's steps is not ruled out. One GPU test waited for the GPU's lock beyond its own limit.

column3: Little has been run on requests that cover more than their last position. Row LIM-3 tells the run behind examples/full-size-clipped-gap/.

Any token below the vocabulary's size may fill a request's window up to its length, and by the model's definition no checked position depends on the filling. But the model's range checks run at the filled positions too, so with some fillings a request gets no proof at all. This fits what was read of `cp_verify` (the sub-proofs' lookups and range conditions run over all positions of the window); no run has shown a filling that costs the proof.
column4: If a request gets no proof, client and provider may agree on another filling and send it as a new request. Whether a window gets a proof can depend on the weights, so each such try tells the client something (docs/what-is-not-hidden.md, item 2). A provider should not search for a filling on its own: the filling that it picked would then tell of the weights.

column3: The client forms the request file itself, tail included; a client that takes the file from the provider takes the tail from it too. By the model's definition no position reads a later one; in the checks as `cp_verify` makes them, a reading of the code found the attention's mask enforced and the routing and every feed-forward claim tied at one position each, without walking every claim with that one question. So the tail cannot change a checked token's logits by the definition, and by the code as far as it was read; it can only make a request unprovable.

The service gives no guarantee of availability. A client that leaves its responses unfetched can fill the disk; a write that fails then ends the process, and every later batch ends the same way until room is made. Any number of request files can be put into the spool directory, and a client can use up a leaf table's batches: a batch that was begun counts whatever becomes of it.
column4: Put a front end before the service that limits each client, and that deletes a response once it is delivered, or when its owner has not fetched it within a time that you set.

column3: Each time the service takes requests it scans at most 100,000 request names in `in/` and reads only the oldest files of the right length, up to the largest batch plus 1,024 (a file of the right length that is not the service's own, or lacks its owner's read bit: each scan that reaches it tries to open it and closes it at once, and reads nothing of it). Beyond the first bound requests are served out of order, and the alarm `cut-short` is printed at most once in a process. A file of the right length that a scan tries to open and the system refuses (`EACCES`) is left where it is too: that scan neither moves nor removes it, nothing is answered under its name, and each later scan tries again, and the alarm `unreadable-request` is printed at most once in a process. A file of a wrong length is left where it is, gets no response and does not count against the scan; in the production build nothing tells the operator how many there are: only `in/` itself shows them. Beyond the second bound no build prints a line that says that files were left unopened: if the oldest files, up to that bound, all cannot be served, one such scan answers or removes them and takes no request, and a request behind them waits for a later scan. So whoever can bring many such files into `in/` delays other clients' requests, and the operator is not told (read in the code; not run for this line).
column4: Let the front end check each request's length, limit how many requests wait, and keep a record of its own with a time limit for each request.

column3: Under a parameter file whose clipped-gap policy has theta = C and a cap of 1 or more, `cp_verify` answers a request that covers at most cap tokens with NO: policy (what such a request would cost: row R9). `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` reject such a parameter file at their start (`prover-only-policy-says-nothing`), as they do one whose C or theta is below the least cost of a token. No test in this repository holds the verdict of `cp_commit`'s and `cp_prove`'s own reader of the parameter file against `cp_verify`'s (searched). Read in the code, not run. No example configuration has such lines.
column4: If you write a clipped-gap policy of your own, do not set theta = C with a cap of 1 or more.

column3: The test that scans the repository's text for calls that can delete or signal the wrong thing (tests/dangerous_calls_test.py) misses several spellings, which the head of the test lists.

At its start `cp_prove -spool` cleans the directory that it is given: it removes an empty file `stop`, overwrites and removes what an earlier process has left under out/.tmp/, and removes files in work/ that have the form of a request's name and are not that request, and the responses in out/ of requests that were left in work/. A file of the user's own under such a name is removed without a question. `cp_prove` starts only on a directory that is empty or has a well-formed mark.txt, any commitment's (R18.1), so that can happen only to a file that the user has put into a spool directory, or to an empty file `stop` in a directory that counts as empty (R18.1).
column4: Give `-spool` a directory that is used for nothing else.

column3: If `cp_prove -spool` is given a directory that is neither empty nor has a well-formed mark.txt, it does not start and touches nothing that is there. A directory counts as empty if it holds only what a front end may put there before the first start: in/ with nothing in it but .tmp/ and request files, an empty out/ and an empty file `stop`; these directories must be the caller's own, with mode 0700. So an empty subdirectory of a spool directory, named with `-spool` by a slip, counts as empty too and is marked; and the top directory of a file system, which holds lost+found, never does. If it finds a `stop` that is not an empty regular file, or a name of an unknown form in work/ or out/.tmp/, it does not start and removes nothing. That holds for what lies at the top of these two directories, which is looked at before anything is removed. Where something that `cp_prove` did not stage lies deeper, inside a staged response's own directory under out/.tmp/, the start fails only after an empty `stop` and the staged responses that could be removed have gone; the foreign file itself is never removed, and the rejection says so and names `cp_prove -clear`, which lists what is left. While the service runs, a file in in/ of a request's length and name that is no request, or whose ID it already has, is removed with no response. In a marked directory, besides what R18 tells, narrow kinds of the user's own files do go at a start: files named proof, y or failed in a directory under out/.tmp/ whose name is 64 hex digits (and an empty directory of such a name), with the directories that are then empty, and a file in work/ that has a request's name and length, of which the start tells (tried by test drivers on the routine that opens a spool, not on the released programs, on a build without the mark, in which regular files of these names went too, not by `cp_prove` itself). A foreign name holds a start off, and nothing is removed, with two exceptions, read in the code: an entry named .tmp; and a file or a link whose name is 64 lower-case hex digits. The look that comes before anything is removed passes over the name .tmp, and of the others it looks at the letters of the name alone; so an empty `stop` and the staged responses go first, and the start fails only then. For the same reason an entry named .tmp in work/ is never looked at, and the start goes on.

column3: A client's true request can vanish with no response at all: a file in work/ of a request's length whose bytes do not fit its name is only removed, and so is a request whose file cannot be opened or read. A start under another window length removes nothing: `cp_prove` refuses to start, and the requests in that spool directory get no response unless a service for their own commitment is started on it. A bad result, not on the released programs: such a start removed what an earlier process had taken.
column4: A client sets a time limit of its own. Before it changes the window length, a provider lets the service answer every waiting request.

column3: A spool directory whose mode lets the group or others in (0750, 0755) is rejected at `cp_prove`'s start.

`cp_prove -clear <directory>` removes files. It overwrites with zeros and removes the responses that an earlier `cp_prove` staged under out/.tmp or .tmp in that directory and never released. It touches nothing unless a mark.txt says that the staging directory is `cp_prove`'s: the named directory's file for out/.tmp, the file in .tmp itself for a single batch. So if a slip names another closed directory of the user's own, nothing goes there. The call is given no commitment ID, so it clears any commitment's marked directory. In a marked directory it knows what was staged only by names: one level down, entries named y, proof or failed go, with the directories that are then empty or were empty. Which directory counts as a staged response's also goes by its name: below out/.tmp only a name of 64 lower-case hex digits, and any other name there stops the whole call; below a single batch's .tmp any name of 1 to 64 letters, digits, _ and - (read in the code). An ending of a running service goes by the narrower of these two rules in out/.tmp too: it leaves every other name there as it is and clears the rest (row H26.1); in the directory out/.tmp/<id>/ of a response that is still staged it removes every entry that is not a directory, whatever its name (read in the code). A running service does the same in the middle of a run, and prints nothing of it, whenever it turns what is staged for a request into `failed`: when the batch gets no proof (read in the code). `-clear` leaves every other entry in a marked directory, and lists up to twenty of them; mark.txt itself is kept and not listed. If an entry at the top of a staging directory has a name that `cp_prove` never uses there, up to twenty such entries are listed and nothing at all is cleared. A directory of `cp_prove`'s that has lost its mark.txt is cleared by no call: what is staged there stays. Before anything is touched the named path is walked part by part, as at a start; the directory, out and the staging directory must be the user's own, closed to others and no links; and no `cp_prove` may be running there. Under sudo the directory may be the account's that typed sudo. A relative name is rejected, as at a start. Tried, by two test drivers on these routines, not on the released programs, on a build without the mark, in which a regular file of these names went too, and not by `cp_prove` itself, as root and as an ordinary user: what went was bounded by these names, but any short name of a directory one level below .tmp served; nothing of another name went, no file that stayed was changed, and nothing outside the named directory was touched. With the mark, the public test prover.spool_clear_test drives the same routines: `-clear` and a start, each with the right mark.txt, a wrong one or none; it passes. It does not run `cp_prove`'s main(), and tries nothing under sudo and no network file system. One run of it, not on the released programs, with a test and routines that differ from these, was made on a machine without a GPU, as an ordinary user, and tried nothing as root. `-clear` says what it left, not what it took: where nothing else lies there it ends with exit code 0 and the words that nothing that `cp_prove` staged is left, so the caller is told nothing of files of these names that went.
column4: Name only the directory that you gave `cp_prove` with `-spool` or `-out`, by its full path, from /.
column5: read; run (the public test prover.spool_clear_test); run, not on the released programs; reported

column3: If the directory named with `-out` already holds a file under a response's name, the new response is not given that name: nothing is replaced, the staged copy is removed, and the call ends with exit code 0 and tells no fault. `cp_prove` makes that directory new, or takes over one that holds nothing but .tmp with a well-formed mark.txt, and it walks the path to it before its creation and after it; from reading the code, it rejects any other directory that exists already, and touches nothing in it. So such a file can be there only if root, another process of the caller's or, under sudo, the account that typed sudo puts it there while the batch runs. An operator could then hand out the old file as this run's. In a service the same rule is what makes a start after a cut-short end safe: a response that was named before stays as it is.
column4: Give `-out` a new name below a directory that only you can write.

column3: `cp_prove` gives a finished response its name in out/ by a call that replaces nothing (renameat2 with RENAME_NOREPLACE). Where the kernel or the file system does not support that call, it looks whether the name is free and then renames: a file that another process puts under that name between the two steps is replaced, and nothing says so (read in the code; not tried).
column4: Let no account but the service's own write the spool directory, and keep it on a local Linux file system.

column3: The test runner builds the verifier into the repository's own directory for it, over what the user has built there, and the test `weight_sums` builds `bin/weight_sums` in the repository too, over an earlier one; everything else it builds into a build directory inside its own work directory, unless BUILD names another. The `cp_verify` that it puts at the verifier's build path is an honest build of the sources; the prover's build copies from that path.
column4: Run the tests in a checkout of their own; serve only with programs from the production build's own directory.

column3: prover/build.sh builds no cheating program, and refuses to install one under `cp_prove`'s or `cp_commit`'s name. With the word `tests` it builds `cp_prove` and `cp_commit` with the test options under the true names, in the sub-directory hc/test_build/ of its output directory, inside the directory hc/ that holds the production build's programs; what it builds outlives the run unless it is in the run's own work directory. No script of this repository builds the library's or the programs' own prover code in a cheating form. Where a test that ships cheats, it does so with code of its own, in its own test program, and none of these programs is `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` or `cp_verify`. Every `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` but the production build's holds test hooks that can inject a fault (row E29.1); no test that ships sets a variable by which they inject a fault, except to see it refused or dropped (by a search). Every `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` but the production build's is marked: it rejects a model's files and prints that it was built for tests only; the `cp_verify` beside them is a copy of the one verifier. Only the production build's two programs carry a build record.
column4: Serve only with the programs that are directly in the directory hc/ of the production build, never with one from hc/test_build/ or below it.

column3: A rebuild does not give the same bytes. Two production builds of one checkout, made into one directory on one machine, gave one and the same `cp_verify`, but a `cp_prove` and a `cp_commit` with other SHA-256 sums (seen once, not on the released programs; what differed in that pair was not looked at). For another pair, not on the released programs, one set of sources built twice in two directories on two machines, it was looked at to the last byte: every GPU function's machine code and every CPU function's code were the same, and what differed were eight hexadecimal digits that the compiler puts into names internal to a source file, sizes and offsets that shift with them, and the linker's build id; no time was seen in the files. A path does stand in them: the programs hold the path of the toolkit's library directory on the machine that built them (in a note of NVIDIA's tools inside one GPU image and, where the build script sets a run path, in the host file too); in that pair both sides had one toolkit path, so nothing showed. In a third pair, two builds, not of these sources, on two machines, one of them from the files of the repository alone, with the tree, the output directory and the toolkit at the same paths, every loaded byte came out the same: the whole files differed in 6 to 12 bytes, the name of a temporary file of the compiler's in a symbol table that is not loaded. So what moves the programs' loaded bytes from one build to the next seems to be the paths at which one builds. A provider's `cp_prove` or `cp_commit` therefore cannot be checked by building the sources again and comparing the whole files; whether a build at the provider's own paths would give the same loaded bytes has been seen in that one pair only, and no tool in this repository compares loaded bytes; the tools that compared the code function by function are not part of this repository. What ties a program to its sources is the build record beside it, which is the builder's own word. (What building the released programs again gave: docs/limits.md#what-was-run-on-these-programs.)

Of eight more stops only the definition of their names stands in the code, three of them on labels of random values by the comments beside them. For the other ten self-checks and these eight stops, whether each guards something that exists in the released programs is not known.

The released programs do not compare, at every start, how many random entries each masked row gets with a second, separately written rule. All three programs test ten named conditions on the parameter file's numbers at every start; those on random entries count the opened positions a second time, by other code but from the proof library's own plans and shapes, not by an independently written rule: among them that the random entries of every main row and of every mask row cover all draws at which the row is opened (not known: whether the ten are the right ones). That is arithmetic on the parameter file, the plans and the shapes: whether a kernel is handed these numbers it does not ask. The self-check by value compares the values that are there: it would not notice a kernel that later reads fewer of them, nor two rows of a table that use one row's random entries, and it shares the generator's two core routines with what it checks.
Whether the released programs' self-checks would stop a changed copy of the programs that stores zeros in the last forty random places of every line of a table has not been tried.

column3: After a restart `cp_prove` withdraws the response of every request that it still finds in work/ and answers "failed", also a response that a front end has already delivered.

An answer "failed", a stop of the service and the withdrawal of a response can also be brought about from outside the programs: by the provider, by whatever passes the files on, or by a restart. Clients see such an act, and the programs cannot see why it happens: it is the provider's duty that it follows nothing hidden, such as what waits in the spool's staging directory (out/.tmp/), a log, a count or an exit code. The duties page says so for the staged files and for a hold of the service, and the list of what is not hidden for `cp_prove`'s last line, exit code and alarm; no page has a sentence for the general case (read). A client can also lose a response that was already released: its request stays in work/ in the spool directory until a background thread has synced the response to the disk, and if the process is killed, the power fails or that sync fails before that, for instance during a later batch, the next process removes the response and answers "failed" (read in the code).

column3: Several rules on what the GPU programs read, write and print, and on how they end, are checked by tests that read the source text, and such tests can be evaded. Faults put into copies of the sources on purpose went unnoticed by these tests: a guard's condition replaced by another (guards are counted by file); __builtin_trap(), assert(), err() and an endless pause as ways to end; secrets printed under the names of a batch's keys. A write or an exit behind a macro in a shared header is noticed in part: it appears once in the test's table, at the header, and not at the places that use it. No trial of these faults on the released programs is known.

The source-reading tests on inputs, writers, ends and the CUDA status, none of which is part of this repository, start from a list of files of their own, and nothing compares that list with the build script's commands. One other test holds every compile and link command of the production build, word for word, to a second list, on copies of the build script with stand-ins for the compilers, not in a real build; a further test reads what the listed commands name; and nothing compares the two lists; the test of what is printed lists only calls that name a word such as seed, key, mask or salt, so a hidden value under another name passes.

That the production build's build record covers every compiled file is checked only by a search of source text that builds nothing. That the production build takes no test option is checked in the same way, and was also tried, not on the released programs, on built programs on a GPU, at small configurations, on synthetic weights: they rejected the six that were tried; other test options exist and were not tried there. Besides, every production build searches the finished program's printable strings of four characters or more for any that equals a line of a list, the five `-test-` options among them (so it cannot see the list's one line of three characters, `LIE`), and installs no program that has one (prover/build.sh; prover/tests/serving_build_words.txt; read in the code). That altered sources cannot build the production build holds only for copies into which a test script has written its marker, and was seen once, outside the test runner, for one unit. The test that lists what the programs read searches only for names that it already knows, and that every hidden value which a sub-proof sends leaves through one file is checked, by a search of the source text, for the sub-proofs' own kernels only. The one test that reads the sources for what a sub-proof sends does not look at what the proof library's protocol steps send when they run on the GPU engine, with masks and routines of their own (it says so of itself); no other test by text that does was found; and that test does not read the separately linked code that opens the weight table. The searches of source text are not part of this repository.

In the sources, single compile-time switches of test programs move settings that hiding depends on. One lets an environment variable lower the threshold at which the mask generator rejects and redraws. One gives a test build the sparse output of the production build, which prints next to nothing once it has begun to read secrets; that test build says in its first line of output that it is a test build, and it runs only with random values from a test's file (read in the code). Neither compiles together with the production build's own switch (read in the code), but nothing in the sources ties them to particular test targets. A `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` compiled with either is not the production build, and every build of these two programs but the production build rejects a model's files (read in the code). Two more names, meant for tests that hand in keys, are read by no code: they occur only in lines that stop the compile. After a build, only the default `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` are searched for a kept list of the names and sentences of test code. The test builds of the two programs are searched only for the start-up lines of cheating programs and for one marker of the shared library's test switches, and neither the switch that lowers the mask generator's threshold nor the one for the sparse output leaves such a line. The model maker and the test programs are not searched.

`cp_commit` ends where a cause is found, and some causes depend on the weights or on the seed. Its exit code, its printed lines, its timing and what it leaves on disk show them. By what it prints this was seen, on test builds, where the attacker could write on the provider's machine: with sums of their own placed beside the model, `cp_commit` printed how many tensors matched (0, 1, 3, 37 and 38 of 38) and wrote nothing unless all did: to whoever reads that output a test of equality tensor by tensor (by run, on test builds; by a reading of the code the production build prints the count too). After a fault of the machine or of the program, whether a key file appears at all can depend on a hidden value: `cp_commit` writes the key file only if none of its failure flags is set and `cp_verify` accepts the bytes, and one of the flags is raised by a weight that, as it is read again for the range proof, lies outside its range (read in the code and reasoned from it; not run). What an onlooker could learn from that over many runs has not been examined. Four of its exit codes follow from the weights: a tensor cannot be turned into integers, the integers are not those of the sums placed beside the model, the worst-case check does not fit, or a committed integer is outside its range (read in a comment of the source). One printed line of a run that finds no cause depends on the weights too: in every run that gets that far, `cp_commit` prints whether the embedding is wider than the width that the parameter file gives for it (`wb_emb`) (read in the code).
