column3: A wrong table value that every pass of `cp_commit` reads alike is committed to unnoticed while it stays in its range. It is a fault of the committer's integrity, not of the verifier's soundness: that no proof of a false statement about the committed model follows from it is argued, not shown.

Every walk of `cp_commit` copies and decodes the weights again, and no documented step compares the cells between the walks. What it can cost, under a fault of the machine or a hostile host, is `cp_commit`'s own assurances: its scan of the weights before it commits, and its worst-case check. `cp_commit` keeps each tensor once in host memory as the model's file stores it and turns it into the committed integers again in every pass: one pass for its checks, one or more for each weight table's hash tree, the passes that make the range proof's lookup keys, and a first and later passes whenever a table is opened for the key file or a leaf file. Two separately written decoders read the same Q4_K, Q5_K, Q8_0, F16 and BF16 blocks. The slower one tests every value for finiteness and range and serves the checks, the trees and the openings (fold::value() under fold::integers() and stored_integer()); the faster one tests neither (only a lookup key outside its table is flagged where it is written, which ends the run) and makes the lookup keys of the tensors in such blocks, most of them straight from the blocks (k_block_keys(): by the source's own figure 96 % of the matrix and more at full size; for blocks of Q8_0, F16 and BF16 the kernel is k_block_keys_wide()); of the rest, a layer's tensor of kinds 1 to 11 comes through decode_planes(), and every other one through the slower decoder, with the decoder's own checks on each value; tensors stored as 16-bit or 32-bit integers are copied with no check. No step compares the integers of two passes directly, and the file of the weights' sums (`wsums.txt`), where there is one, is compared in the checking pass alone. Within one call, one self-check compares two passes indirectly: before opened columns leave the process, each is hashed up to the lowest level of the table's tree that is kept and compared with the node kept from the pass that built the tree (show_columns()). A difference between the lookup keys, or the pass that makes the folded row, and the committed table would be noticed only by the `cp_verify -key` or `-leaf` that `cp_commit` runs on the bytes in memory before it writes the file; and a stored byte that changed after the checking pass and is read alike by all later passes would be committed to unnoticed, as long as the weight stays in its range. All this is the committer's own integrity, not the verifier's soundness: that a wrong pass gives an honest key of another model, and never a false proof that is accepted, is argued, not shown.

`cp_commit`'s own scan of the weights' ranges before it commits (by its source, there so that no commitment to a weight outside its range is published by mistake) has been tried on the whole program with one injected weight only, 5,000, far outside the range: neither the largest magnitude that the scan admits nor the first that it rejects has been tried (4,095 and 4,096 outside the embedding; 2^30 - 1 and 2^30 in the embedding). A unit test tries 4,095, 4,096 and -4,097 on another routine, the one that writes the range proof's lookup keys, and not in the embedding; neither test is part of this repository.

No test injects a fault into `cp_commit`'s faster decoder (searched). In a test build the hook that replaces one committed integer makes `cp_commit` read that tensor through a pass and not straight from its blocks, writes the value after the decoding, and is rejected where the tree is built from the stored tensors in cuts, as at full size; the malicious committer's hook alters a lookup key's digit after it is decoded, no listed case uses its other form, which alters a byte of a stored block, on the lookup keys (searched), and the cheating build runs the lookups through other kernels than the honest program. What speaks for the faster decoder are honest comparisons on synthetic data, in tests that are not part of this repository. For Q4_K and Q5_K blocks: its two whole-matrix calls against the rule on the CPU, also at the full-size shapes, and the lookup keys made both ways at a small configuration. Q8_0, F16 and BF16 blocks are read by kernels of their own. For these the two calls were compared with the rule on the CPU at small shapes only, not at the full-size shapes, and the lookup keys were made both ways at a small configuration, in test builds whose synthetic model is stored in these types (two products that take such blocks were compared with sums on the CPU as well): in one session on one H100, where each ran plain, under a launch counter and under NVIDIA's four checking tools, and passed (on test programs built from other sources (row HW-678)).

`cp_verify` leaves several things to its caller: to bring a commitment ID of its own (`cp_verify` compares it with the files' once the caller passes `-id`, and a call without `-id` cannot end in a pass); to compare the request's range with the positions that the client expects, the next token with the one that was served, and the end of the reply with the model's end tokens. One script in the repository, integrations/check_proof.py, by its own description makes such comparisons against values that the caller states (the commitment ID, the checked range, the end token and the acceptance policy); it reads them from the verifier's line for programs (`result-v1 ..`). Its own tests run it on a substitute for the verifier and, in fewer cases, on a real `cp_verify`; that it makes each comparison has not been traced independently. It has an option that rejects a pass which counts proof of work (`--no-proof-of-work`: exit code 14); `cp_verify` has `-no-proof-of-work`: where some round meets the target only with its work counted, the call ends at best in NOT-A-VERIFICATION (exit code 14); where no round leans on work it can end `YES`; a whole call prints both numbers either way (a part-call under a parameter file that declares no proof of work prints one).
column4: Pass only values of your own (commitment ID, reply token, positions, the policy's numbers) and compare the printed fields with them; copy a provider's call into no client's example.

column3: `cp_verify` also leaves it to its caller to compare the acceptance policy with the values that the client accepts, and the fields of the line `covered:` with the request and the parameter file, and to make the token ids with the model's own tokenizer. The middleware that ships passes `cp_verify` the parameter file's own policy, and a provider's own check may do so too: right for a provider's filter and wrong for a client.

A part-call of `cp_verify` (`-key`, `-leaf`) without `-id`, like the planning call `-plan id`, prints the commitment ID that it computes from the very files that it was given (in a part-call: the line "computed commitment ID: .."). That value says nothing about who published it: whoever copies it into `-id` of a whole call gets a YES about those files and no others.
column4: Take the commitment ID from whoever vouches for the model, never from a call's own print.

column3: A request's proof by itself opens too few columns of the weight commitment to tie the root to one set of weights; that tie comes from the one-time checks of the key file and the leaf file under the same commitment ID and settings. `cp_verify` says YES only in a whole call that has made those checks; a part-call (only `-leaf` or `-key`) never says YES, and `-leaf` counts only beside a passed `-key`.
column4: Rely on a whole call's YES only.

column3: `cp_commit` prints one line that begins `commitment ID: `, as soon as the key file is made and before it makes any leaf table; lines that begin `computed commitment ID: ` repeat the digits. If a later step fails, the call removes all that it has made (a file that it cannot overwrite keeps its name: row R3.2), but its output still shows that ID (read in the code). An ID from a call that did not end well names a commitment that does not exist.
column4: Take the commitment ID only from a call of `cp_commit` that ended with exit code 0 and its closing line (docs/operators-duties.md).

column3: The next token is bound by the hash chain before every challenge that its own part of the proof meets, not from the proof's start: it is in no chain's first query, and is sent in a round of its own right before the first message of the output head's part. It has no influence on what is drawn in the earlier parts. In the published work on such arguments the whole statement enters from the first challenge on.

A malicious prover can also put many attempts for one request under one batch tree, of which a verifier sees one place only, and finish the luckiest. The bound counts such tries as hash calls, not as whole proofs; how much they save has not been worked out.

Because the next token enters the hash chain only before the output head's part, a malicious prover can reuse everything that it sends before that point for each false token that it tries, and a further try costs only the rest of the proof. Such tries are among those that the bound's count of hash calls covers; the bound has no factor for the size of the vocabulary.
One of the two planning tools (blocks/frame/cp_frame.cpp) can print a bound for a plan that the verifier would reject: it goes by the account only, and prints that the check is not made.
column4: Quote a figure only from `cp_verify -plan accounting` on the files that you use.

column3: The hash term's constant (17/2, from 16 hash values in one call) is the count of a technical report that is not public and not refereed for its own chain construction, which the programs' chains are read to be; no count was made on the programs' format itself, blocks/hash/MODE.md lists a strict count among the points that it does not decide, and the program prints the term as argued, not refereed. At best half a digest's bits can follow from any such term. `cp_verify` rejects a call that asks for more than 128 bits, because it counts a digest of 256 bits as 128 by the usual convention.

`cp_verify` computes its four public tables (SiLU, sigmoid, rotary, softmax) with the platform's floating-point library. A fifth table, the head's table of exponentials, it makes by an integer recurrence, from constants in the source; that one has no digest. The parameter file holds the tables' digests (no call can end YES under a form without them), and a table with another digest ends the call with `NO: table-digest-<name>`, though the proof may be honest: on a platform whose library rounds differently, an honest proof is rejected.
column4: If you meet that ending, verify on another platform before you conclude anything about the proof.

column3: The answers to the verifier's queries (opened columns, salts, paths) enter no query of the hash chain: only the trees' digests hold the columns, so a prover with two columns under one digest could choose between them with every coefficient in hand under which they are combined.
The value `h_par=` that `cp_verify` prints is a digest of the three configuration files; `cp_verify` compares it with nothing.
column4: Compare the commitment ID, never `h_par=`; a planning call also prints `configuration=`, the same digest written another way.

column3: There is no proof of a "no": a request above the policy's bounds gets the word "failed", as does a request that met a fault, and as would one that the provider chose not to serve.
column4: Never read "failed" as a statement about the reply.

column3: The arguments for soundness and for hiding both take the hash as a random oracle. If that model fails, at any later time, neither argument applies, and commitments and proofs that were released before are affected too: nothing can be withdrawn. In that model every party can only query the hash, and the extractor is given the committer's list of queries. The programs use BLAKE2b, and nothing is proved about it.

Some self-checks of `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` are themselves tested only by reading the source and by tests outside the programs (some of them part of this repository, some not): at the start, the known answers of the masks' generator, of the random-value routines that draw the sub-proofs' pads and of the key schedule; while a key file, a leaf file or a table is made, the comparison of masks, salts and keys, and of the key file's key, with a second implementation.

What the self-test at the programs' start (own-test-coins) cannot see. Before a seed is drawn or read, each program runs the routines that lead from a seed to its keys, and its generators of secret random values, under keys that are written in the source, and compares with known answers. No verifier can see whether a secret random value is what its key gives: the test narrows that gap and does not show that anything is hidden. Its third part runs a kernel of its own, not the three kernels that write random values into tables, and one of the generators that it tests is one from which `cp_commit` draws nothing. (This comes from a description of the test that has not been compared with the code.) By the comments of the part that tests the generator of the sub-proofs' one-time masks (read in the code), that part also does not detect: an error that shows only in a longer sample or a larger launch than the test's, whose sizes have not been compared with any example configuration; a wrong or stale key at a request, or wrong stream numbers; an error in the copies of the masks that are added to the values that they hide; an error that depends on the real key or arises after the start; a correct value that is then left unused. The test's third part compares one block and the first 32 elements of one stream. A value that is written correctly and then used twice or overwritten is not caught by the comparison of sampled values at run time either. The cases of its table of known answers are not independent of a list of faults that were injected into copies of these sources. That the test stops those faults is therefore no blind trial of it (prover/second_writing/README.md).
Clients who send fast, or flood the service, can steer with whom and when they are batched, and so aim the declared leaks (time, shared failure, which proofs share a batch) at one client.
column4: Put a front end before the service that limits each client.

column3: On what a client who steers its batching can see of another request in a proof: by the lines that were read, in three readings of the code, which did not take in the bodies of the GPU kernels, a neighbour reaches a proof only as a salted leaf at a randomly drawn place of the tree that ties a batch together, and through the batch's key. That the part which a batch's proofs share takes nothing of a request but one hash rests on reading alone, and no test of this repository compares one client's files under two different sets of honest neighbours. A batch's time does show something of the other requests.

Clients who act together can count, and not only estimate by time, how many places of a batch the others held: two proofs show whether they shared a batch, and a batch holds at most the number of requests that the operator has set (at most the parameter file's public line `slots`), a number that they can find as the most of their own proofs that ever share a batch; so if they keep so many requests waiting that every batch is full, the number of their own proofs in a batch tells them how many places the others held (a request that is rejected before a batch is formed holds none). Reasoned from the code; not run.
column4: Limit how many requests each client may send and have waiting (docs/what-is-not-hidden.md, "What a front end must do", rule 2).

column3: If the secret key directory ever leaks (the seed and each leaf table's random bytes), every column of a weight table (the anchor or a leaf table) that a key file, a leaf file or a proof has shown, and every published OOD answer of a table, turns into exact linear equations on the weights, and a guess of the weights can be tested against the key file, for all proofs ever handed out; for the anchor, the first weight table, the seed alone is enough; nothing that is done later takes that back. Where `cp_commit` was called with `-keep-for-the-audit`, the kept bytes open, together with the seed, every mask in the key file and the leaf files, and no program destroys them but an audit that ends with YES; where `cp_prove` was called with the option of the same name, one batch's kept bytes open, with the seed, every mask, pad and salt of that batch's proofs until that batch's audit has erased them. Both programs reject that option on a model's files, so kept bytes exist only beside synthetic weights.
column4: None after the fact: a new commitment under a new seed stops further loss and withdraws nothing. The judgement on weight hiding (docs/limits.md#the-verdict) does not cover a commitment that is in doubt. The one that replaces it may be covered alone, on [conditions of its own](limits.md#a-further-commitment), but for these weights as a whole that judgement does not speak. It does not cover what the old one may already have shown. Before: follow the duties on the secret key directory, and follow them when a commitment goes out of service: the seed and each leaf table's random bytes stay as secret as the weights for as long as the weights are secret. Go on guarding them for as long as they exist.

column3: That a past batch's random bytes do not follow from the seed or from a leaf table's kept bytes rests on a property of the generator (a secret input under a known key) that has not been examined.

The hiding argument takes the hash as a random oracle that has nothing to do with the generator of the masks, although BLAKE2b and ChaCha20 share a design; no argument that the two may be idealised together is known; nothing is known against it, and no search for anything against it is known.

`cp_commit` zeroes the access and modification times of its public files, but not their change times or the directories' times, and a first read of a file can set its access time again. The differences between the files' change times are the durations of the run's steps, and it is not shown that the time of a committing run is independent of the weights and the masks. Only someone who gets the metadata can read these times: for example if the operator shares the directory that `cp_commit` wrote or hard-links its files, another account on the provider's machine that may list the directory, or whoever holds a backup or an image of the disk. A copy never carries a change time; a copy with its times, and an archive, do carry the directories' modification times and an access time that a read has set again. A client who gets copies of the bytes alone sees none of them. `cp_commit` leaves the public key directory readable only by its owner, so publish copies, without file-system metadata.
column4: Publish copies of the bytes (an upload of the files; an archive only with its times set to zero), not the files' metadata: do not share the directory that `cp_commit` wrote, and do not hard-link its files.

column3: At each start `cp_prove` decodes every weight on the GPU and tests it against its range: these kernels compare a weight's size and raise a flag by an atomic operation only if one lies outside (read in the code). The decoding itself branches on a block's scale bytes and on how each weight rounds, and for a tensor stored as F16 on each weight's exponent field (read in the code); whether the compiled kernels take a different time for that was not looked at. In `cp_commit`, GPU kernels add to a memory cell that a weight's byte or digits choose, one scan skips the weights that are zero and counts and sums the others by size, and where a weight table is built a cell of a weight that is zero skips a multiplication and an addition, so how long they run can follow the weights (read in the code). Of the released programs only `cp_commit` includes that code. For other kernels of `cp_prove`'s start whose addresses follow a weight, the three directories that hold the loading of the weights and the commitment were searched, not the whole prover. How much the duration of a start of `cp_prove`, or of a run of `cp_commit`, tells about the weights has not been measured.
column4: Give the service a machine of its own, and do not tell clients when a start or a run of `cp_commit` begins.

column3: The list of what stays visible (docs/what-is-not-hidden.md) names, under time, how long a batch of `cp_prove` takes; how long a run of `cp_commit` takes is not among its items; it can depend on the weights' values, and whether it does has not been measured, on the released programs or on others (read).
column4: Do not let others see when a committing run begins and ends.

column3: Any list of what the tests do not cover is itself incomplete: a gap that nobody noticed is not on it, and nothing was run to compile it.

`cp_verify` counts a sub-proof's length twice, in its plan and in its walk; that the two counts agree under every parameter file that it admits is not proved, and a mismatch would reject an honest proof.

`cp_prove`'s options that change its schedule or its use of memory, and the amount of GPU memory that is free at its start, are meant to leave every byte of every proof unchanged. No test compares the files that `cp_prove` makes under its different `-memory` and `-in-step` settings or under two memory plans. That the bytes stay the same is argued, not proved; a reading of other sources (row HW-678) did not settle parts of it, and no such reading has been made of these sources. Of the five keywords of `-memory` that concern the weights only one, tensor-rooms, is used in any run of the whole `cp_prove` by a test, through the preset `lean`; the four others (one-room-for-experts, experts-by-layer, experts-rooms, rest-by-turns) are tested for their spelling alone, by a test that is not part of this repository either. The sources hold a test switch that overwrites with a fixed byte, before each use, the GPU scratch memory that `cp_prove`'s memory plan treats as no longer needed by a sub-proof. A test program that can turn it on for that scratch memory is only built by this project's tests: none runs it and compares the proof files, and neither the program nor those tests are part of this repository (read in the sources and in the test table).

The engine of the lookup argument has several settings that are meant to change its speed and not its results. No comparison was found across the number of lanes, their width, their memory for sums or small tail launches.

A shipped small configuration, meant for tests on a model's files, takes its lines on proof of work, groups and stages from the other small configurations, which were made for another small model's arrays; of its first 32 lines only the line on the table is its own. The planning call accepts it, but these groups were not chosen for it.
Each parameter file, and so each acceptance policy, needs a commitment of its own, and nothing public shows that two commitment IDs belong to the same weights: only the provider's word says so.

For soundness, no theorem relates two keys for the same weights, so renewing a commitment is not covered: after a renewal the new commitment ID is on its own, and nothing carries over from the old one.

If a leaf table's count file is missing, replaced, not owned by the account that runs `cp_prove`, or shorter than it was, what that leaf table has shown is unknown: treat the table as spent; hiding for it may be lost, and the commitment has to be made again. (An honest loss of power can shorten the file by batches that were begun and not yet opened, which have shown nothing; the rule is kept whole all the same, so that nobody has to judge how much may be missing.) The judgement on hiding (docs/limits.md#the-verdict) does not cover a commitment that is in doubt. The one that replaces it may be covered alone, on conditions of its own (docs/limits.md#a-further-commitment), but for these weights as a whole that judgement does not speak. It does not cover what the old one may already have shown. The programs reject only a file that is missing, a link, not a plain file, under a second name, another account's, or open to group or others; a file that was shortened, or replaced by one of the right kind, is served, and no program can see it. A count that was set back is served: no program can see it, and columns shown beyond the limit lay combinations of weights bare. Where the programs do reject, the production build prints only the rejection's name, not this advice.
column4: Never create the count file again, and never put a copy or a backup of it in its place. Stop whatever restarts the service, stop every `cp_prove` on the directory and wait until each has ended, and make no further call on it. Treat such a file as a sign that somebody else writes into the secret key directory.

column3: No program sets a floor on how many batches a leaf table may serve: `cp_commit` accepts any configuration whose masks cover one link and one batch, so under a parameter file of your own a commitment can be used up after a single batch, and one full leaf table stops the whole service.
column4: Read the limit that `cp_commit` prints before you publish a commitment. The leaf table of each batch is chosen at random and the service stops at the first full one: count on fewer than M times a leaf table's batches in all, and plan the renewal earlier.

column3: No test covers the one line of `cp_prove` that closes the output directory before memory is wiped at an exit; without it proofs made from wiped memory, so with lost masks, would be released, and `cp_verify` would accept them.

A local-memory test, which is not in this repository, requires twelve GPU kernels that take a key to have no stack frame in local memory, which no code can clear. By report it passed, not on the released programs; on a different set of other programs (row HW-678) two of these kernels had such a frame, of 64 bytes each (what it held, by a reading: row H39.3). Nothing checks kernels that the test does not list, including any that takes a key other than by value. The same test prints, without checking it, the frame of one instance of a tensor-core kernel, which by one reading of its machine code holds no weight, activation or sum. It does hold two hidden routing values that depend on the prompt and the weights, an expert's first rank and the number of tokens routed to that expert, and no test checks either reading; neither has been checked independently. That kernel stands under one of the 65 entries of the test's table whose kernels' local memory the test prints and does not check; the test also prints, by name, each kernel under no entry of its table that has local memory, and checks none of these. By the test's own table, the machine code of a few of the others has been read, among them one instance of a kernel that hashes leaves with their salts (its frame holds words of a column's running hash state before the salt: hidden values); for the rest at most the source was read, so it is not known which of the objects that it names the compiler keeps in the frame.
No test records from outside which GPU operations a whole program asks for, to show them equal for failing and healthy requests, other weights or other random values.

Two GPU tests run `cp_prove` twice on one request and one secret key directory, so that the two runs differ in their random values (and in the stored count of opened columns; in the first test also in two test variables that this build must ignore), and both compare little (each at one small configuration, on synthetic weights). One, on the production build, requires the same reply, the same file names, the same printed lines once every number is blanked out, and two proof files that are not equal byte for byte. The other, on a test build under a test seed, requires that both proofs are accepted, that the two files differ, and that each differs from a third proof made under fixed test randomness. Neither compares the two proofs' lengths, which can vary for one request. Neither looks whether each masked part of a proof differs, or records what the program asks of the GPU: one differing byte is enough, so a program in which only some of the random values were fresh would pass both. Held near it: by two tests that are part of this repository, two runs of `cp_commit` under drawn seeds must give other bytes in the key file and in the leaf file; and, by a test that is not, in the key file no sent entry may stay the same when the random values change (a test build, one small configuration, synthetic weights). The first of the two tests is part of this repository; the second is not.

A test compares every line format that the production build's `cp_prove` can print after it has begun to read secrets, and every word of its last line, with the sources. No test reads the page that lists these lines, and none shows that the output is the same when a request fails. Nothing keeps that page from falling behind the sources: in one comparison it lacked three lines that the sources print (by report; which three is not known). In one reading, each of 13 of the tests' line patterns had its line in the page's table (prover/tests/closed_front_lines.txt holds 14 patterns). The names that can follow "end 1" and "end 9", and the page's other tables (the lines before the close, the file names), were not compared. Of these tests, two GPU tests that compare real output with the patterns are part of this repository; the test on the sources is not.
Of three guards on the plan that `cp_verify` makes for itself, one is exercised by no test and two on synthetic lists only.
No test exercises the rejection that `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` attach to a parameter file that misses a condition for hiding; no such file is in the repository.
On `cp_verify` the rejection of a parameter file that misses a condition for hiding has been seen under two of the ten conditions only; under the others another check of the file rejects first.

By the programs' rule no word of a leaf table's drawn columns is to be written before every drawn position's node is made again and found equal; untested on a whole `cp_prove`: one flipped bit of a column in GPU memory, the column beside it, a slipped position, a TERM, SEGV or KILL while columns lie in CPU memory, a batch of several requests.

A leaf table's random entries and salts are fixed when the table is made, and at every opening `cp_prove` works the drawn columns out again from the weights in its memory and from those entries. A fault while serving (other weights in memory, one changed bit) would therefore put the same random entries under another table, and by the sources' own word hiding rests on that never happening. What guards against it inside the opening is a comparison: the tree node above every drawn position is made again from the columns and compared with the stored node before a word is written. The symbols that then go out are not themselves compared with anything: they are fetched from the columns a second time, by another GPU routine, into memory that is zeroed first; the salts are compared with a second derivation in the array from which the sent ones are then fetched (read in the code, not run).
Three stops of the random-value library, which draws the sub-proofs' pads, are exercised by no whole program: a cell drawn twice, a rejected launch, a state without the batch's key.

`cp_prove` has a check on each entry it takes from a request's table of masks, as well as a check on the whole table. Two cases of a GPU test that does not ship reach the check on each entry, in a test build at a small configuration with a test seed, but no run of them is known.
The test build that counts how often each pad slot is filled counts the sub-proofs' slots only, not those of the unit that opens the weight table; a pass does not show that a mask hides anything.

No test calls the unit that opens a leaf table out of order, and none shows that a batch's shared opening depends only on the leaf table and the key. That a rejected second start keeps the first start's seed is known from reading only.

Some start-up rejections of `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` are met by no test: `cp_commit` without a verifier beside it; a directory in which `cp_commit` cannot create its two directories, and a spool directory that `cp_prove` cannot write; a parameter file for a model with experts that lacks the digests of the four public tables, for either program; and `cp_prove` on a busy GPU. Tests exist for `cp_commit` on a busy GPU and, for `cp_commit`, on synthetic model files under `-public-weights`, for integers that differ from the sums file; both have passed, not on the released programs.

No test kills or signals `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` or a service on purpose at a parameter file that asks for proof of work, which the default does. The search for a nonce is one GPU kernel that ends only when a nonce passes or 2^63 - 1 have been tried (rows C1.2, C2), and what is left behind when the process is killed inside it has not been tried.

Neither `cp_commit` nor `cp_prove` has an ending for a challenge of a proof's hash chain that comes out 0: by the chain's rule a challenge may be 0, nothing is flagged at the draw, and the run goes on; in the library and in `cp_verify` alike a challenge comes from the hash chain and is drawn from the whole extension field, 0 included, unless the round asks for a nonzero element (two kinds of round do: the factor on a sample's pad and the last challenge of a masked sumcheck); where 0 would help a cheat (as in the masked sumcheck's first challenge) it is counted in the round's error, 1/|E| a draw. `cp_verify` rejects a 0 at one such challenge, the first of the sumcheck over tokens in a feed-forward segment, by which it divides (`NO: coin-zero`): there an honest proof is rejected with that small chance. No test is known to bring a whole program to such a draw (reported, not searched).

By a search of the tests, none names any of the three rejections with which `cp_commit` stops, before its long work, at configuration files under which no call of `cp_verify` could be a verification (no layout file; the verifier cannot plan a request at the bits asked for; the files are outside the standard parameter form), so no test is known to show the whole `cp_commit` such files, in the production build or in a test build at 128 bits. The routine that puts the question to the verifier has a unit test, which is not part of this repository and meets the third answer only with stand-in scripts in the verifier's place; by the source's own comment, without that stop a run could end well and leave a commitment under which no request's check is a verification.

`cp_prove` rejects at its start a `seed.bin` that is not a plain file of 32 bytes for its owner alone (`hc-key-file`) and, outside a test's run, one that holds a seed written in the sources (`hc-key-test`). Of the first, one case is tried: a file open to its group (prover/tests/refused_at_the_start.sh). The second no test tries on `cp_prove`, which has its own text of these rules (prover/prover/isk.cuh).

In the public test prover/tests/refused_at_the_start.sh the case answers-two (a parameter file that says two answers) is rejected by the parameter file's reader (`parameter-range`), and the case record-made-up (another example's parameter file in the place of the commitment's own, on synthetic weights) as `ranges-not-guarded`: the line `ranges` holds the digest of other configuration files. What no run is known to have tried of the refusal of more than one answer: row LIM-42.

At a start `cp_prove` walks the paths of the spool directory (`-spool`) and of the secret directory (`-isk`) from the root, part by part, before it touches anything. It rejects a name that does not begin with /, a part that is a link, and a directory on the way that belongs to an account other than root and the caller or that its group or others can write; a directory with the sticky bit, as /tmp, passes if the part in it is root's or the caller's. Under sudo (the caller is root by its real and by its effective account, and the variable SUDO_UID holds an account's number) the account that typed sudo counts on the way as root does, also as the owner of a part in a sticky directory, and the spool directory itself, and the directory named with `-clear`, may be that account's own; the secret directory itself must be the caller's own, closed to group and others: under sudo, root's. What a run under sudo makes belongs to root. The directory that a single batch names with `-out` is walked in the same way, before it is made and again after that. A name given with `-out` that does not begin with / is rejected, and nothing is made. Not walked so: the directory that a single batch names with `-in`, which `cp_prove` only reads: it opens it by the full path and follows links in the directories above it (read in the code). So an account that can write to a directory above it can make `cp_prove` read its requests from another place. The creation of the output directory itself goes by the full path, on a path that has been walked.

column3: A known fault: at a start behind your own `sudo`, a server of the vLLM integration that runs as root can be led to send out closed files of root's. Every process of the integration opens each directory that its config file names once, where it loads that file, makes its checks on the open directory and keeps it open: so a link or another directory put under a name leads a running server to no other file, with one exception: the check that the middleware makes of each batch with `cp_verify` (duty 6: docs/limits.md#the-conditions) reads the public files by their names, so after a swap it can read other files than the server serves (integrations/LIMITS.md#the-middlewares-check). A swap under a running server can at most part the server from whatever goes by the name later, lead that check to other public files, put a policy on hold, or end a hold that was put only in the directory under the name (by reading). Run as root, a server also looks above its config file, the public key directory and the parameter file's directory. Run as root, it keeps other accounts out by that look, but for the look's gaps, among them: it reads owners and modes, not access control lists, and it is one look by path, which another account can race (integrations/LIMITS.md#the-look-above); seen, not on the released programs: a published folder inside a third account's folder was refused at the start. Behind your own `sudo` the scripts do not defend against a process that already runs under your own account. That look trusts the directories of the account that typed `sudo`: where the configured directories lie in your home, every process of that account can, ahead of a start or of a command, by a link or by renaming alone, bring a closed directory of root's under a configured name (`clean`, `hold` and `lift-hold` then act on whatever of root's stands under the names at that moment); that holds at each start of each server process, also one that a supervisor makes with nobody looking on, as long as it carries `SUDO_UID`. The server then sends a closed `key.bin`, leaf file or `layout.txt` of root's that lies there, and the numbers of its parameter file, to anyone who can reach the server and has vLLM's API key, where vLLM was given one (how the example front end's middleware learns that key, and where it cannot: integrations/vllm/REFERENCE.md#the-operators-checklist; by reading, and by tests with a stand-in for vLLM's application, which call the routes that send these files too; the middleware has run under vLLM, not on the released programs, at toy size, and four times at full size, there with the key in `VLLM_API_KEY` alone, and of the files' routes only those of the published key.bin and of a leaf file have been called under vLLM, at no server led astray: row H11.2; where vLLM has a key that the middleware neither reads nor suspects, these files and numbers go out without a key unless the variable VLLM_API_KEY is set; what was seen, not on the released programs: row HW-275), for as long as that process runs, and nothing is logged. A server that was led astray at its start stays so until it is restarted, though the names are right again (integrations/LIMITS.md#above-a-public-directory). Because a running server keeps each directory open, moving or renaming a directory that it serves does not stop the serving (seen in the scenes that this row tells), and a hold does not stop it either (by the code, and one trial; no test). Removing the directory does (tests; but in the case that this row tells remove nothing); the middleware tells that by the directory's link count: seen on ext4 alone; on a file system that keeps no such count it does not notice a removal in that way (by reading). A restart does only if the directory no longer stands under its configured name: a server started again serves what it finds there (tests: a new middleware in one process). That stopping the server does is by the code, not tried; where a supervisor starts it again, a stop is a restart: hence the duty in docs/operators-duties.md, to stop the server for good: that loses no file. In the case that this row tells, remove nothing: the directory that the server holds open may be one of root's that was brought under the name. A server that is not root can be aimed, ahead of a start, at closed files of its own account, by whoever owns a directory above the configured directories or can write in one that is not sticky (by reading). If another spool directory had been given the configured name before the `hold` command was typed, the hold file lies in that other directory, and it holds the running server only while that directory keeps the name: after the names were put back, the server no longer found the policy on hold, and no message about the change was seen (one scene, run once behind a true `sudo` on files made for the test; it asked the program's own routine that lists the policies on hold and sent no client's request; that a client's request meets the same look is read in the code). How far "leads a running server to no other file" holds: that the middleware, but for that check and the look for a hold, opens nothing in any other way is by reading, and the rules have not been tried against every way of naming a directory. Three ways past the kept directories were found by reading, and the middleware is reported to guard against them; that there are no more is not shown. The walk that refuses a secret key directory goes by the path, just before the directory is opened: against a swap in that very moment it does not hold (not tried). The walk knows such a directory only by a file named seed.bin or isk.txt in it: one that has neither, or a copy of its sub-directories alone, is not known as one (by the code). A bad result, not on the released programs: where the scripts opened both public directories by path at every call, swaps made while the server ran brought root's closed files out, and nothing was logged of it (under a true sudo, in five set-ups, three times each; a test driver called the middleware). Keeping each directory open closes that way: a test tries such swaps under a running server (integrations/tests/test_proof_middleware.py, test_a_swap_at_or_above_a_name_moves_no_running_server), and so did the scenes that this row tells. One file of a secret key directory made for the trial also came out, where the parameter file's directory is itself called config: the copy of layout.txt in its config/ sub-directory, which by reading holds public bytes (one trial; a server as root, without a true sudo or vLLM). Keeping the directory open, and at a start the walk up the parameter file's path, close that way (tests; thirty swaps, with a server as root, without a true sudo or vLLM: no file of it came out). Tried: tests as root with `SUDO_UID` set by hand and without, and as an ordinary account; thirty swaps on a secret key directory made for the test, without a true sudo or vLLM; and 24 scenes, not on the released programs, as root and behind a true `sudo`, with up to three real accounts beside root, each scene once, on files made for the test, the server called by a test driver, without vLLM or a socket: under a running server no swap brought out a line of root's closed files; ahead of a start the account that typed `sudo` brought them out (by renaming: seen; by a link above: the open followed it; the rest read). Not tried with vLLM or with `cp_prove` (reported).

column3: What the programs lock, wipe and check on the provider's machine (docs/operators-duties.md, "Keys, seeds and machines", tells the duties). **The disk.** No program checks the file system type. From reading the code, `cp_commit` only tries, at its start, a few steps that it needs later ([`cp-commit-file-system`](faults.md#what-you-see-and-what-to-do)). Also from reading the code, `cp_prove` has to lock the secret key directory and its subdirectory `leaf`, which some shared and network file systems do not support ([`refused (cp-isk)`](faults.md#cp-isk)). **Memory.** `cp_prove` locks only the memory that holds the seed, and `cp_commit` only its own copies of the seed and the keys. From reading the code, the copy of a key that its random generator works from is not locked. If the lock fails, `cp_commit` warns and carries on, and `cp_prove` carries on silently. Other secrets in memory can be swapped out. **Core dumps.** The three programs switch their own core dumps off when they start. That is known from reading the source and has not been tested. **The check of GPU memory.** Each program checks only once, when it starts, so neither notices a process that starts later, or one that has not allocated its memory by then. `cp_commit` plans its work around the free GPU memory, so if another program shares the GPU, either of them can run out of memory partway through. **What stays in GPU memory.** No exit wipes the GPU engine's own memory pool, the kernels' per-thread memory, or what the CUDA libraries hold. After a GPU fault the wipe can zero no GPU memory at all, because the process can no longer reach the GPU ([what you then see](faults.md#what-you-see-and-what-to-do)). **Untrusted code.** Code that shares a processor with a process can learn about its branches and memory accesses from caches, branch predictors and performance counters, without reading its memory. Any user also sees the GPU's load and memory usage. **Time to stop.** Let the service manager wait more than 600 seconds before it sends KILL (systemd: `TimeoutStopSec=`), because that is how long the wipe may take. Allow extra time, because that period starts only after `cp_prove` has finished its current step. From reading the code, that period covers only the wipe, and at full size even a clean end takes a while ([how long](../prover/docs/ends-in-short.md#how-long-an-exit-takes-at-full-size)): allow for that in the timeout too.
column4: Keep the duties in docs/operators-duties.md, "Keys, seeds and machines".

column3: Host memory at full size. At full size, `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` each need several hundred gigabytes of host memory. The need grows with the weight files: from reading the code, at a start the programs can take up to twice the files' size ([A slow start at full size](quickstart.md#a-slow-start-at-full-size)). Neither program checks first how much is available, so a run that exhausts memory can make the kernel kill other processes too. From reading the code, both ask the operating system for huge pages for the host copy of the weights only with `-huge-pages`, which is off by default; without it the machine's own setting decides. What the option gains or costs at full size has not been measured on the released programs. The example scripts check before they start a program, each against its own limits: `prover/examples/run_target_example.sh` for synthetic weights (only for a configuration larger than the small examples), `examples/maverick/run.sh` for the real ones. If you run the programs yourself, nothing checks. From reading the code, `cp_commit` can need more host memory than a service: in its first phase, the check of the weights, it holds up to six buffers, each as large as the model's largest tensor unpacked to integers. So size the machine for the larger of the two. The check of duty 6 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions) takes memory and CPUs of its own beside the service; how much, in one run: row RES-32. How host memory behaves in a longer service is not known. See also row P3.4.2.
column4: Do not run `cp_commit` at full size beside other people's work on one machine.

column3: What the programs check of the places that an operator names, and what they miss (see also rows R24 and R25). `cp_prove` rejects a secret key directory that the service account does not own, or that is open to group or others. Both programs reject a count file for the same reasons. At every start `cp_prove` also checks the path to the directory, and rejects a link or an open directory on that path ([step 13](operators-duties.md#from-nothing-to-the-first-proof) has the rule). From reading the code, `cp_commit` checks the paths to the places named with `-isk`, `-ivk` and `-worst-case-table` in the same way at its start, but not the paths given with `-config` and `-weights`. It does not check the paths given with `-config` and `-weights`, and it follows symbolic links there. So anyone who can write to a directory on one of those two paths can point it at other input files. Unlike `cp_prove`, it accepts a relative path for these three, and completes it from the current directory first. `cp_prove` checks the secret key directory again at every start. So a place that is opened to others after `cp_commit` has checked it shows up only then, when the commitment may already be in doubt ([`refused (cp-isk)`](faults.md#cp-isk)). The programs look only at these permission bits, not at who is in a group. `cp_commit` does not accept one key directory inside the other, but the programs do not check where they are moved afterwards. `cp_commit` starts the `cp_verify` next to it without checking who owns it; the `cp_verify` of the check of duty 6 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions) is yours to guard. So anyone who can write to that directory or to the checkout runs code as you. Once the commitment exists, an account that can write to a directory above the secret key directory can move the whole secret key directory, or swap it for another of yours with a lower [count](operators-duties.md#the-count). Even so, it cannot read the [seed](glossary.md#seed) or the weights this way. From reading the code, `cp_commit` accepts a directory it has just created only if that directory is yours, private and empty. For a single batch, `cp_prove` opens `-in` by the full path, without checking the directories above it ([service](service.md#one-batch-without-a-spool-directory)). The tests' `make_model` creates its new directory by the full path too. So anyone who can write to a directory above such a path can make them read or create something elsewhere, or have another empty directory removed instead ([limits](limits.md#the-tests-and-your-files)). `cp_prove` checks the `-out` path as it checks `-spool`, and it rejects an `-out` directory that already exists and leaves it untouched. The one exception is a directory that holds nothing but what an earlier batch staged: `cp_prove` takes it over, and first overwrites and removes what is staged there (the conditions: row R35). `cp_commit` runs a path check at its start, on the paths to what it creates. It keeps its two working directories open while it runs, so that renaming or replacing a directory mid-run does not redirect what it creates, renames or removes. There are gaps. After a working directory is created and before it is opened, it can be replaced with another empty private directory that the caller owns. A similar gap lies before a deletion and before each of the last two renames. What this says of `cp_commit`'s check and of `-out` is from reading the code. Attacks on these guards ran only through test drivers ([limits](limits.md#path-names)). **Under `sudo`.** If you serve as root through `sudo`, the account that ran `sudo` controls where the path to the secret key directory leads. The path checks of `cp_prove` (for `-isk`, `-spool`, `-clear` and a single batch's `-out`) and of `cp_commit` trust directories owned by that account as they trust root's, and that account may own the directory itself that `-spool` or `-clear` names. On its own, without `sudo`, it cannot read, open or alter the secret key directory or any count in it. All this is from reading the code. What that trust can lead to with `-out` and `-clear` was tried in six tests, each run once, under a real `sudo`, on synthetic files, not on the released programs. `cp_prove` itself was not run: two short host programs called the routines of `prover/prover/spool.h` that `cp_prove` uses for `-out` and `-clear`. A helper held the program for four seconds at one file-system call, and in that pause the account, without `sudo`, exchanged one part of the path. With `-out`, the account put a link to a closed directory of root's in the place of a directory of its own: the program rejected the path and ended with status 1, but it had already made an empty directory, owned by root, inside root's closed directory. With `-clear`, the account moved another directory of its own, with other staged files in it, to the name: the program reported success and had cleared that other directory, and the staged files in the directory that had been named were still there. How often the moment is met without the pause was not tried, and an account that may run only these programs with `sudo` was not tried. The outcome seen is one empty directory, or the loss of files that `cp_prove` had staged and not released. It takes an account that may run the program with `sudo` and owns a directory on the path.

column3: The two commands in docs/operators-duties.md, "Public weights", that write a `.weights-are-public` file. **The first command** creates the file in one atomic step. If anything with that name already exists, whether a file, a directory, a pipe or a link of any kind, it fails with `FileExistsError` and writes nothing. So no one can slip in a link for it to write through, however they time it. If the command fails after that step, for example on a full disk, it leaves an empty file behind (the next command replaces it). The file gets mode 644 less your `umask`: under `umask 077`, which docs/operators-duties.md asks of the service account, only you can read it. Whether `cp_commit` then fails for another account that commits to the same public weights has not been tried. **The second command** creates a new file next to the old one, under a random name, and renames it over the old file, so you do not remove anything by hand. It writes through no link, and an account that still has the old file open cannot reach the new one. Narrowing the old file's permissions instead is enough only if no other account opened the file while it could still write to it. Such an account keeps the file open for writing and can still change what the file declares, and `cp_commit` does not see that: it checks the file's permissions, not who has it open. In a directory that another account can write to, that account can exchange the entry between the check and the renaming. The command can then end without an error although the file under that name is not the one it wrote. `sha256sum` also follows a link under `NAME.gguf`, so the new file would then declare another file public. If the command is cut short, a file whose name is the old one's plus a dot and eight random characters can stay behind. No program reads it, and it does not block a second run.
column4: Run the second command only in a directory that no other account can write to.

column3: `-public-weights`: what the programs check, and what they cannot catch. This is the only option that lets the programs use real model files with a seed that is not random. `cp_commit` then derives the seed from the 32-byte file, and no fresh randomness goes into any file that it writes. So, by design, anyone can regenerate the same commitment and compare its ID with a published one. All they need is the weights directory (the model files with `wsums.txt` and `fold.txt`), the configuration files and the 32 bytes. **Proofs under this option.** With this option anyone can compute the seed. A batch's key is derived from the seed and from 32 fresh bytes, which `cp_prove` samples for each batch and does not keep anywhere. So a proof, unlike the commitment, cannot be regenerated. But no argument shows that the requests of one batch stay hidden from one another. **What the programs check.** `cp_commit` computes each model file's SHA-256 itself and rejects the call if it does not match the `.weights-are-public` file (`cp-public-weights-marker`). `cp_commit` rejects a `.weights-are-public` file that is a symbolic link, has more than one hard link, or is writable by group or others. It also rejects one that belongs to anyone but the account that runs `cp_commit`, the model file's owner or root. The message says what is wrong and, where there is something to do, what to do or where to read it. That last rule is tested only in the two routines that apply it (the public test `prover.public_weights_test` of SUITE.md, which gives real files to another account only where it runs as root); not on the released programs, they rejected real files owned by another account. It has never been tested in a full `cp_commit` run. `cp_commit` rejects the option together with `-keep-for-the-audit`. `cp_prove` serves such a commitment only with the same option and the same file ([`cp-isk-seed-public`](faults.md#what-you-see-and-what-to-do)). It does not read the `.weights-are-public` files. **What they cannot catch.** If you, the model file's owner or root create a `.weights-are-public` file for weights that must stay hidden, `cp_commit` with the option accepts it, and so accepts those weights. With this option the weights are not hidden. `cp_commit` does not check the permissions of the directory itself, so public weights can live in a shared directory. It also does not notice that a `.weights-are-public` file is some other file that was renamed to that name. So anyone who can write to the directory can rename a file into place, if it belongs to one of those three accounts and begins with the right 64 hex digits. Nor does it notice a model file that is modified in place while it runs. A mount or a container that maps several accounts to one, or a file system that lets an account give its files away, can get another account's file accepted. That has not been tested.

column3: Shared machines: the directory in which you stand, and `TMPDIR`. Python looks in the directory in which you stand first for the modules that a `python3 -c` command imports, so a file that another account put there can run as you. One test file is known to start such a command in your current directory: `tools/confine_test.py`, `import multiprocessing` (read in the code, by a count through the whole tree; that such a file is taken in the library's place has been tested on files made for the purpose, not through this test; the list may not be complete). That matters only if you start such a test by hand while you stand in a directory where another account can create files: under `run_suite.py`, or from the repository's top, as these pages print it, it does not apply. Two further test files of this project, which are not in this repository, started Python in that way; tried with files made for the purpose, once, as root, Python 3.13, both took them. The second place is `TMPDIR`, or `/tmp` if `TMPDIR` is unset, because some scripts create their working directory there without checking what lies above it. From one reading of the scripts, with nothing tried, the GPU quick start, `examples/maverick/run.sh`, the build scripts, `run_suite.py`, the audit scripts and `integrations/vllm/integer_model/examples/serve.sh` do not depend on this. Under `sudo` the audit scripts, the Makefile in `blocks/`, `scales/calibrate.py` and `examples/maverick/run.sh` each reject a work or output directory that your own account made ([tools/audit](../tools/audit/README.md), [blocks](../blocks/README.md), [scales](../scales/README.md), [maverick](../examples/maverick/README.md)).
column4: Start scripts and tests from a directory that no other account can write to.

column3: The build, for an operator. The script builds in a new work directory, and each program is renamed into place only after its own steps have passed. So after a failed or interrupted build the directory can hold programs of two builds, or no `cp_verify`: build again. `cp_commit` starts the `cp_verify` next to it for every check of its files, so build only while no program from that directory is running. As a rule the programs load the CUDA libraries from the toolkit that built them, no matter who runs them or where they are copied. So anyone who can write to the toolkit's directory controls code that runs with access to the seed and the weights. If the build prints a line that begins `build.sh: note:` and names the CUDA libraries, part of that directory does not belong to root. If it prints `build.sh: warning: the programs get no rpath`, they start only where the system's loader finds the libraries by its own configuration. A `build.sh: note:` that names `OUT` says that another account may be able to change the output directory or a directory above it. If you set `OUT` yourself, the script will not build in such a place. The `sources` line of a `<program>.build` file is the digest of the sources the program was built from. Enter it in your record, even though no digest is published to compare it with.
column4: Follow step 5 of docs/operators-duties.md, "From nothing to the first proof".

column3: Which token IDs a request holds. A proof covers token IDs, not text, and tokenizing the text again can give other IDs. A proof on other IDs is a proof of another reply. Neither the commitment ID nor a proof covers the tokenizer, the chat template or the end-token IDs ([what a client brings](verifying.md#what-you-need-and-where-it-must-come-from)). From reading the code, the example front end never tokenizes: it uses the IDs that vLLM reports in its reply, with padding after them, outside the checked range. The client has to ask for them (`"return_token_ids": true`), and where a list is missing or malformed there is no proof. `integrations/spool.py make-request` builds a request from whatever two files of token IDs you give it, so there this duty is wholly yours.
column4: Take a request's prompt and reply from the inference engine itself.

column3: The audit with the key: particulars of the operator's duties. The scripts erase a kept file only if their last word is `--erase-kept-files`. With `--rehearsal` they run the same checks and erase nothing, and without a last word they reject the call. Together with the seed, the kept files reveal every mask and salt of what they cover. Until the audit has erased a batch's kept file, hiding does not hold for that batch. After any ending other than NO or NOT WHOLE, fix the cause and run the audit again. That covers a passed rehearsal, a mistyped word, a missing helper, a kill, and a stop that touched no kept file. If the audit finds nothing kept after a YES, there is nothing to do. The ban after NOT WHOLE has one exception, from a known fault of the scripts. Under `sudo`, on a commitment or a batch that your own account made, the audit ends NOT WHOLE even if nothing is wrong with the files. It then says `isk/audit/ is not a folder of mode 0700 that belongs to the caller`, and erases nothing. After a NOT WHOLE with these words under `sudo`, run the audit again as the account that ran `cp_commit` and `cp_prove`, with a work directory that does not exist yet, and go by that verdict ([Under `sudo`](../tools/audit/README.md)). Until then nothing of that commitment leaves the machine. A NOT WHOLE with other words is no exception. This is from reading the code. `cp_prove` does not start while anything is in `audit/` (`cp-kept-for-the-audit`). But it checks only whether that directory is empty, not whether the audit has said YES. It also checks only at startup, so a service that is already running carries on while a kept file is there. `cp_prove` never erases a kept file. Even a YES covers only part of the system ([what it does not cover](../tools/audit/README.md)).

Single rows of the tables in docs/faults.md: what the short cells leave out. **`asked-to-end`.** That the machine's memory still holds weights and masks matters only if the GPU or the machine then goes to another account. The batches in progress were never finished, so an exit after a signal does not rule out a failed self-check. But nothing from those batches was released, and a persistent fault faces the same self-checks on the next run, so that is no reason for a hold. In its very first moments, before it holds any secret, a signal still terminates `cp_prove` without a last line. **`cp-prove-kept-not-written`.** From reading the code, that audit cannot end in YES, because there is no proof to compare. **`cp-weights-files`.** From reading the code, at the first start on a new commitment the cause can also be model files of a storage type that `cp_prove` does not accept although `cp_commit` did. **`write-failed`.** From reading the code, `write-failed` can also mean that the file of a response that was not released could not be overwritten. It is still removed, so its bytes can stay on the disk under no name, and no line on the wipe need come. **`not-all-wiped`.** Even when the wipe was given up at its time limit, the last line keeps its usual name if the exit code is 9. **The line before the last.** Once `p258 closed` has been printed, `cp_prove` prints the line that begins `p258 not every step of the wipe ran` if the wipe skipped a step, failed in one or was given up at its time limit, and after a crash, when no wipe runs. **An empty policy.** With a parameter file where `theta` equals `C` and `cap` is 1 or more, `cp_verify` would call the policy empty for any request with no more checked tokens than `cap` (row R16.3). **`cp_commit`.** A signal that arrives before it has made anything also stops it without a line. **A later call on the same `-out`.** From reading the code, a later call that names a single batch's `-out` directory again also clears it, on two conditions. The directory holds nothing but `.tmp`, and `.tmp` holds a well-formed `mark.txt` and otherwise only what `cp_prove` staged. That is the state after a batch that was killed or crashed, or could not remove what it had staged, and had released nothing. And the call has to get that far: one that is rejected earlier, as after a batch kept for the audit, clears nothing. After any other failed batch `.tmp` is empty and has no `mark.txt`, so name a new directory. **The alarm `unreadable-request`.** The file stays in `in/` and gets no response as long as each scan's try to open it fails with `Permission denied`. A file that the service claims and then cannot read is removed, unanswered (seen once, in a test with two accounts), and a production build names it nowhere. From reading the code, a scan first tries to open a file that is not the service account's own, and leaves it as long as that try fails with `Permission denied`. After any other error it still takes the file. Once the file can be opened, the scan takes it like any other. A file that is that account's own and has the owner's read permission is taken untried: if it still cannot be read, it is removed, unanswered. A request that is lost in this way can be sent again by whoever still has it. **`cp_prove -clear`, exit code 0.** Exit code 0 means nothing staged is left, also where nothing was staged. An `-out` directory keeps `.tmp/`, and the `mark.txt` in it if there was one. **`cp_commit`, exit code 4.** Exit code 4 has several causes: an internal error, an uncaught exception, or a file that could not be created; a working directory that cannot be locked, or that someone replaced during the run; a key file or leaf file that `cp_verify` did not pass. **`refused (cp-isk)`, a directory on the path that others can write to.** The commitment is in doubt unless you know that no other account has been able to write there since you committed. You would know that if, for example, the only write permission is for a group whose only member has always been you. **`cp_commit`'s checks at a terminal.** From reading the code, on a terminal set to `stty tostop` a check's first printed line stops the check. `cp_commit` then waits in silence until that limit, prints that the check gave no answer and is asked once more, and waits again.
column4: Look up the exit code and the last line in docs/faults.md.

column3: The service's directories: particulars that docs/service.md tells in short (see also rows R18, R18.1, R18.4, R24 and H26.1). **At a start.** `cp_prove`, clearing `out/.tmp/`, leaves every other entry untouched, and also a staged file that has a second hard link or that its own account does not own. If anything is left, it does not start. A start that succeeds prints nothing about what it removed from `out/.tmp/`. By the time that it looks for unexpected names it has created whichever of the five subdirectories were missing, and they stay. These checks see only the top level of `work/` and `out/.tmp/`, and pass over the name `.tmp` there. A file in `in/` whose name is not the hash of its bytes is deleted, and nothing ever appears in `out/`. `cp_prove` prints how many such files it deleted. A production build prints that line only at startup. **`cp_prove -clear DIR`.** It also touches nothing if `DIR/out/.tmp/` or `DIR/.tmp/` holds, at its top, a name that `cp_prove` never uses there: it then lists up to twenty such names, for both together, and what was staged stays, unlisted. An empty one without `mark.txt` is left as it is. If `mark.txt` is missing beside entries, or is wrong, nothing is listed. Where it does clear, it lists for each marked one the entries it leaves behind: up to twenty that it could not clear and up to twenty that it did not touch. **Under `sudo`.** The spool directory itself may belong to the account that ran `sudo`, with mode 0700. You then trust that account as much as root, because the directory's owner can rename or replace `in/` while a request is being written. If the run under `sudo` wrote `mark.txt`, only root can read that file: the message then names the cause, and a front end without `sudo` cannot read the file either. If a front end had written `mark.txt` before, the message names the directory inside the spool directory that cannot be opened, and the cause (`Permission denied`). It says whose that directory is and whose it would have to be. Where that directory is not yours, it gives two ways on: a new, empty spool directory of your own, or every step the same way, with `sudo` or without. **A single batch.** `cp_prove` checks the `-out` path by the rules for `-spool`, before it creates the directory and again right after. Under `sudo`, the account that ran `sudo` is trusted along that path, and can still redirect it through a directory that it owns. **The example front end's library.** Three kinds of library function in `integrations/spool.py` check less (read in the code). `request_stop()` without a commitment ID checks only the file's format, so it writes `stop` into any commitment's marked directory. The functions that take an open directory check no mark. Nor do those that only read. **At an exit.** The rule on names by which an exit clears `out/.tmp/` is tested on the spool's own code on a CPU, by a test that is not in this repository (reported). The rest is read in the code. None of it was seen in a run of `cp_prove`.
column4: Keep the spool directory for cp_prove and the front end alone, under one account.

column3: That `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` need no root rights is known from reading their sources and from some runs. By two searches of the sources (tests apart): one `mlock()`, on the seed's 32 bytes, and a failed call goes unnoticed; no `mlockall()`, and no limit is raised; pinned host memory is asked of NVIDIA's driver, which any account that may open the GPU may ask (from NVIDIA's documents and common use: not tested); `-huge-pages` is a hint and needs no privilege; the programs only lower limits, set their own CPU affinity, and read the effective user id only to check who owns a directory of mode 0700; they call nothing that changes the user, an owner, a mount or a priority. The GPU's device files must be open to the account: the driver's installation decides that. Runs, not on the released programs: the summaries of ten full-size runs of `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` and `cp_verify` name an ordinary account (uid 999) as the job's user, and so do the summaries of eight sets of runs behind tests of hiding, in which these programs and the two audit scripts ran; for other runs on GPUs, the GPU tests through the suite's runner among them, no line prints the account (there the folders that the runs made belong to that same account: an inference). The CPU tests' reference runs, with `verifier/build.sh`, `weight_sums/build.sh` and `cp_verify`, ran under such an account too; one test that runs only as root was left out there. The build scripts (`prover/build.sh`, `verifier/build.sh`, `weight_sums/build.sh`, `blocks/Makefile`) ran under an ordinary account in every build behind these runs (by report). The quick start's build and small example ran once under an ordinary user account, not on the released programs.

column3: Two helps that docs/quickstart.md tells shorter. **Route 2, a message that the toy script's proof was not made or not accepted:** a step failed, or the program accepted an altered copy or rejected an honest file; for exit code 2 the line above counts both. **A call of `nvidia-smi` that hangs while a full-size program ends:** So give a monitoring script's call a time limit, do not wait for a call that outlasts it, try again later, and do not take one hung call at a program's end for a fault of the GPU.
