column3: `cp_prove` is given no commitment ID and knows none. Any well-formed mark.txt fits, so a service for one commitment starts on a spool directory that another commitment's front end has marked; and where `cp_prove` started first the mark holds 64 zeros for good, so that every commitment's front end takes that directory, and its clean-up can remove responses there. `cp_prove` does not tell one commitment's secret key directory from another's. It reads no `key.bin`, so damage to that file is not found. It does not compare what it reads of the public files with the verifier's reading, and it does not check that they reach 128 bits; `cp_commit` does both. A changed configuration file is caught by one guard alone (`ranges-not-guarded`): it compares a line of `isk.txt` with a digest of the three configuration files in the same folder, and whoever can write those files can write the line. So a service can start on the wrong directories: requests go to the wrong service, its proofs fail at the first `cp_verify` that is given the right commitment ID, and the requests use up a leaf table's count of openings.
column4: Keep one spool directory for each commitment, and give the check of duty 6 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions) the commitment ID from your own record.

column3: Where a configuration asks for proof of work, the tests' altered requests are rejected at the first nonce, which a forger would compute again; no test makes the nonce again after the change, so these tests do not show what the verifier does behind that first rejection. Where a configuration asks for no proof of work, a test sets words of the request and of the reply to other values and counts that every such call is rejected; it does not ask at which check the verifier stopped, so the tests do not show how far the verifier goes with a changed request either.

No test runs the whole `cp_commit` to check which files it leaves, that it publishes the bytes its verifier accepted, what it does on a rejection, or that it never writes through another account's link or directory.
column4: Inspect its output; keep its directories closed to other accounts.

column3: Two things about files that no test shows (searched). The first: that each program opens each of the three configuration files (policy.txt, KL.bin, layout.txt) once in a run and works from the bytes that it read then. Read in the code, not run: `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` and each call of `cp_verify` have one place that opens each file, and what comes later takes the bytes from there; `cp_commit` writes these bytes into the secret key directory. No test counts the openings or changes a file while a program runs. The rule holds inside one process only: `cp_commit` starts `cp_verify` as a program of its own, and its calls on a key file or a leaf file open the copies in the secret key directory again, by their paths. The second: that `cp_prove` creates, opens for writing or removes nothing in the secret key directory but the leaf tables' counter files. No test runs it where it may write these files alone. Read in the code: what it writes there is a leaf table's counter file and, with `-keep-for-the-audit`, one more file, in a directory `audit` that it creates there if it is missing. The two nearest tests list the regular files of a work directory that holds a copy of the secret key directory, before and after a good run of `cp_prove`, and ask that none is gone and that only the counter file has other bytes; the first also asks that nothing is new but the response's two files. Both look after the run has ended, so neither sees a file that comes and goes during it. The first runs a test build under a test seed, the second the production build; both use a small configuration and synthetic weights.

No test gives `cp_commit` a parameter file that its own reader admits and the verifier rejects; by reading, `cp_commit` stops such a file before anything is sampled. `cp_prove` asks no verifier: it would serve under such a file wherever isk.txt's line `ranges` fits it (row R40), and no test gives it one.

With overlapping batches only a wait at each hand-over keeps one batch's late GPU kernel from the other batch's failure word and lent memory; a test that is not part of this repository reads the waits in the source text, and the test that compares bytes, which is not part of it either, would most likely still pass with one wait taken out: it checks by the program's own lines that each batch's opening rode on the next batch, but delays no kernel, so a wait that is taken out would show only if a late kernel happened to collide in that run (read).
column4: None: the two options are rejected on a model's files.

column3: `cp_prove` queues part of a request's GPU work on side streams. That work must be over before the request's failure bits and its state are stored: by the source, a failure bit that is set later counts for no request, so that the whole batch gets no responses, or for the next request, and a late write lands in memory that the next request uses. By reading, in each of the three files that queue work on a registered side stream (two of them register the streams) the main stream is made to wait for it; whether these are all the waits that are needed was not followed. As a backstop the routine that stores the bits first waits for every registered side stream. Which streams must be registered was decided by reading. No test delays a kernel on a side stream: the backstop's calls, and the list of places that create a stream, are only compared as text, by a test that is part of this repository, and no test looks at the sub-proofs' own waits.

One GPU test, which does not ship, compares the prover's whole public table of exponentials with a second implementation of its recurrence, at two of its settings; nothing compares `cp_verify`'s table so. The other check reads a few constants and two rounding rules in the sources as text and runs no program; for the seven tables of the policies that score tokens that script is all there is.

Published attacks on arguments made non-interactive by hashing (ePrint 2025/118 and 2026/1838) have not been examined against the released programs or their format, and a technical report that is not public and not refereed, on whose argument rows SO-32, SO-32.2, SO-52, SO-62 and SO-65 lean, does not discuss them. Not every value that a proof uses is committed: lookup keys, inner nodes of product trees and one vector of the attention sub-proof are not.

Two published attacks on Fiat–Shamir-compiled proof systems ([KRS25], [Fen26]) have not been examined against this protocol or these programs, and a technical report that is not public and not refereed, on whose argument rows SO-32, SO-32.2, SO-52, SO-62 and SO-65 lean, does not discuss them.

GPU kernels keep values in per-thread local memory, which belongs to the CUDA runtime and which no code of the programs can wipe. Of the 231 kernels that draw, place, use or erase a mask, pad, salt or random value, 50 had such a stack frame on test builds, under two versions of the compiler alike but for two kernels; two of the 50, which take a key, have none by a test's listing, not on the released programs (rows H39.2 and H39.3), and a test that is not in this repository prints the frames' sizes of the listed kernels at every run and asks nothing of them; the count has not been made on the released programs. (A second count, on a production build, not on the released programs, with a list of 211 such kernels, found a frame in 49 of the 203 that the build holds.) No way is known for a client to see this memory in a run without a fault (a report that bears on it, reads of uninitialised GPU memory in a served batch, not on the released programs, is not fully explained: row T3.1), and no line of the programs is known to read it back; whoever can read the GPU's memory afterwards may. These readings and listings, here and in the rows below, are of the machine code for the H100 that the programs hold, and the compiler version that they name, nvcc 13.2.86, is the released programs' own; the programs also hold intermediate code, which a driver compiles where it finds no fitting machine code or is told to: kernels compiled so have not been read.

column3: Of the 33 GPU kernels of `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` through which a sub-proof's values are masked and sent (those that call a function of prover/hiding/sumcheck_door.cuh, themselves or through a function that they call: 33 as compiled, 32 in the source, where one is compiled twice), 23 have a stack frame. These 23 compute with values before masking: by the source, the objects that they work on include a round polynomial's coefficients and values before masking and, for most of them, a copy of the object in which the sumcheck's running claim is stored without masks (16 hold the copy in a thread's own variable, 4 in shared memory, 2 use the object in place, 1 only reads it). By one reading of the source the other ten work on such objects too; by the compiler's own listing they have no stack frame and spill nothing in the released programs, so what this row tells of frames does not arise for them. In the released programs, by the compiler's own listing, each of the 23 has a stack frame of 864 to 2,512 bytes per thread; on test builds of other sources (row HW-678) the compiler tools' listing of resources gives 864 to 2,544 bytes, alike under two versions of the compiler. In the released programs `kG_msg` has a frame of 1,904 bytes, and its spill instructions, its out-of-line functions counted in, move 628 bytes in stores and 636 in loads (row RES-54). None of these figures measures what a kernel leaves in GPU memory. One of the 23 (kG_msg, prover/head/claims_lib.cuh) has been read in machine code, not on the released programs (one reading; two more checked parts of it): a round polynomial's three coefficients, without masks, are written to one thread's stack frame, and no instruction overwrites 68 of their 72 bytes before the thread ends; from the coefficients and the public challenge the sumcheck's next running claim follows. Of that kernel's frame only 18 words and a few fields beside them were read, not the frame as a whole. The other 22 have not been read: which of these values the compiler places in their frames is not known. Whether these bytes reach the GPU's memory at all, or stay in its caches, has not been measured, and neither has what remains after the program ends. The reading holds of that machine code (nvcc 13.2.86), not of the released programs: which values a compiler places in a frame can turn with any build, and the machine code of 22 of the 23, `kG_msg` among them, differs between the two kinds of programs that row HW-748 sets side by side. No test checks the reading.

By a test that is not part of this repository, which reads it off built programs, none of the twelve kernels that are handed a secret key has a stack frame or local memory; it has run, not on the released programs (on which, and what it does not show: row H39.3). Many other kernels that handle hidden values do keep frames: on a production build, not on the released programs, of the 203 kernels of the two programs that are on a list of routines that handle masks, pads and seeds, 49 had one, of 24 to 2,544 bytes; they are listed in row H39.6. The sizes are known; what is stored there has been read in the machine code, not on the released programs, for one instance of one kernel; six further functions' frames have been read, not on the released programs (row H39.6), and one more is told in row H14.1; two readings, each with a bad result, are told in rows H39.4.1 and H39.8 (this list is not whole: the count of all readings is in row HW-213); for all that neither this list nor row HW-213 counts, it has not been read, and no test checks it.

On other programs (row HW-678), two of the kernels that take a key (k_chain_leaves and k_fibre_leaves, prover/hash_commitment/hf_tree.cuh) had a stack frame of 64 bytes; by one reading of their machine code it held hidden working values and not the key. On a second set of other programs, in which both are written so as to need none, a test that is not in this repository found no stack frame in any of the kernels that take a key (one compiler version; not on the released programs). In the released programs none of the twelve kernels that take a key has a stack frame or local memory, by the compiler tools' listing of resources of the programs themselves, and none spills, by the compiler's own listing. That is the listings' word, not the test's, and most of what the test does not show (below) they do not show either. The machine code of the twelve kernels that take a key has not been read in the released programs: the test reads the compiler tools' resource listing alone. What that test does not show, among other things, by its own list: its listing has no line for a routine that a kernel calls without inlining it, and one such routine, whose working words start as the key's, is not covered; a kernel that gets a key through a pointer, or inside a type that is not on the test's list of key types, is not found; another compiler release, or a driver that compiles the programs' portable code again, can decide differently; registers, shared memory, the constant memory with a kernel's arguments and the copies that runtime and driver make of them are not examined, nor whatever a driver saves when it interrupts a kernel.

On test builds of other sources (row HW-678), twelve kernels whose main work is to draw random challenges kept 1,032 bytes per thread in local memory (one 1,248), and eight more kernels 24 to 256, by the compiler tools' listing of resources, alike under two versions of the compiler; by the source most of the twelve work on a copy of the object in which the sumcheck's running claim is stored without masks, one works on that object in place (ft::k_bits_point), and one also reads and writes two unmasked hidden values (lookup_tie::k_join), and what their frames hold has been read for one of them alone: a bad result (row H39.4.1; of the kernels that mask and send, one has been read: row H39.1). In the released programs eleven of the twelve stand: by the compiler's own listing, the frames of 1,032 bytes have 1,000 and the one of 1,248 has 1,216. In the released programs one kernel that hashes leaves with their salts (`k_last_pass`, prover/engine/encode_kernels.cuh) has a stack frame of 56 bytes per thread, in all nine of its instances in `cp_commit` and all nine in `cp_prove`, by the compiler tools' listing of resources of the programs themselves, and the compiler spills into it: by its own listing the spill instructions move 84 bytes in stores and 92 in loads (88 and 100 in one of the nine; how such a listing is made: row RES-54). None of these figures measures what the kernel leaves in GPU memory, and what the frame holds in the released programs has not been read. By one reading of the machine code of one instance, in a `cp_commit` built under one compiler version, not on the released programs, the frame holds words of a column's running hash state before the salt goes in: hidden working values, but no salt, no random entry and no symbol of a table; the other instances were not read; the reading has not been checked independently, and no test checks it. By one reading of the sources (names followed, nothing run, not checked independently) the released programs launch this kernel at the default setting for the trees of oracle messages that the proof library's prover sends: in `cp_commit` where the key file and each leaf file are made, in `cp_prove` in every batch; not for the weight table, whose leaves another kernel hashes. What an oracle message's rows carry of the weights that reading does not tell, nor which of the nine instances such a run takes.

column3: A bad result (a heavier one: row H39.8): one of the twelve kernels of row H39.4 (ga::k_coins; a stack frame of 1,032 bytes) has been read in the machine code of a `cp_prove`, not on the released programs (nvcc 13.2.86; sm_90a); a second reading, made to break the first, worked out the machine-code side with programs of its own and could not break it. One thread copies the whole object in which the sumcheck's running claim is stored into its stack frame, and no instruction overwrites the 24 bytes of that claim before the thread ends. By the source alone (no value was seen), at the one launch that was followed they hold a sumcheck's true end claim, without masks: one field element made from the attention's queries and keys, a function of a request's activations and not a weight; a proof carries such values only under masks. Two things weigh the other way. It is a second copy: the same bytes stand in ordinary GPU memory before and after the kernel, which the programs could wipe (whether they do was not followed; row H39.5), while the frame's copy they cannot reach. And no other hidden bytes were found in that frame: the kernel does not compute with the claim, no branch or address depends on it, and the frame holds no key and no seed. "Stays" means that no instruction of the kernel overwrites the bytes: whether they ever leave the GPU's caches for its memory has not been measured. It is shown for one of the twelve: of the other eleven nothing has been read, and ten of them copy the same object, by the source. (In these sources eleven of the twelve stand, this kernel among them: of the other ten nothing has been read, and nine copy the object.) This machine code is not that of the released programs. There the kernel copies the object too, by the source, and its frame is in use: by a count over the programs' own GPU code it has 285 instructions that store to a thread's own memory and 426 that load from it. Their machine code for this kernel has not been read, so whether the 24 bytes stay there is not known, and there its frame has 1,000 bytes (row H39.4). No test checks the reading.

column3: The transcript objects, with the unmasked claim, are also in ordinary GPU memory between kernels. There the wipes reach them at a pass's end and when the program ends by itself. A request's running transcript state on the GPU, with the running claim of a sumcheck without masks, is not among what is kept between turns: it is built again from the CPU's copy at each stretch of rounds. What the last stretch left stays in GPU memory until the next stretch of the same place or the next restore: with two or more requests in step that is before the next turn; with one, at the next request's start or the pass's end. All this is known by reading only: nothing in a run checks that these buffers are zero afterwards, and after an abort, a kill or a crash nothing is wiped. Far larger is what no ending wipes: the GPU engine's memory pool, whose free memory holds table cells, unmasked inner products, salts and random values in every honest run.

A test that is not in this repository reads the local memory of the kernels on its own list from the built programs. It requires that there is none for the twelve kernels that take a key, two groups that hold weights in registers, three kernels written for tensors of type Q8_0, F16 or BF16, and one kernel that holds entries of a range check's matrix; one instance of one of these groups is excepted and its frame only printed: by one reading of the code it holds no weight, activation or sum, but two routing values, which are hidden values: they depend on the prompt and on the weights. Row H39.1's 23 kernels, those whose main work is to draw challenges and some others through which hidden values pass are on the list only so that every run prints their frames' sizes: nothing is required of them. Kernels on no entry are not checked. Some of them handle weights or other hidden values. A rule that allows no frame above 800 bytes in any kernel is tried only by a control on synthetic listings, so nothing checks the built programs against it. For the three kernels for Q8_0, F16 and BF16 the test of local memory has passed once, by report, under one compiler version, not on the released programs. It does not look at shared memory, where one of the three kernels for Q8_0, F16 and BF16 leaves decoded weights (row H46.2). A bad result, not on the released programs: five further kernels of `cp_prove` that decode weights kept fourteen working values in per-thread memory (a stack frame of 56 bytes), which no code of the programs can wipe; by three readings of the machine code, two of them made apart, these were hidden values: a block's scales, an element's code, and the decoded weight of the last element that each thread handled. Nothing was run, so what lay in that memory after a run is not known. These sources differ there: in GPU code these values are no volatile locals (by a reading of the code: mul_rn() and sub_rn() in prover/weights_blocks/fold_rule.h); the test requires that the five have no local memory, and has passed, under one compiler version, not on the released programs; and by a report of two listings made apart (nvcc 13.2.86; sm_90a), not on the released programs, the five have no stack frame and no access to local memory. The kernels of `cp_commit` that decode weights have no stack frame (not on the released programs). Not on the released programs, one compiler listing shows 100 GPU functions of the two programs with a stack frame or other per-thread memory, and the two listings made apart show 94 with a stack frame (68 kernels by name), of 8 to 2,544 bytes. What lies in these frames no listing shows: in most of the kernels whose machine code has been read, not on the released programs, hidden values are written there (row HW-213 has the counts; rows H39.4.1 and H39.8 tell two readings with a bad result, and the released programs' machine code has not been read for them), and most kernels with a frame have not been read. By a sorting, mostly from the source code, hidden values can pass through most of the others, and weights themselves through a few. No way is known for a client to see this memory in a run without a fault (reads of uninitialised GPU memory in a served batch, seen not on the released programs, are not fully explained: row T3.1); who could is another process on the same GPU afterwards, if the driver hands memory on uncleared.

column3: Of the kernels with a stack frame that row HW-213 counts, eighteen through which hidden values pass (weights, activations, lookup keys computed from activations, routing values, a sub-proof's values before masking) have a stack frame in the GPU's local memory, by a listing not on the released programs (nvcc 13.2.86; sm_90a), and no caller can wipe that memory. Four of the eighteen have been read in machine code, each read twice, the second time to break the first, not on the released programs (of one of them two of its four forms with a frame, of another three of its seven forms with a frame: row H39.8): in all four the frame holds hidden values (in one of them whole lookup keys; in one only in part), and for one of the four the guess from the source was wrong. For the other fourteen what the frames hold is guessed from the source and from their sizes, and their machine code has not been read (the guess has not been checked independently): by that guess in seven it is taken to be spilled registers, where the kernels' local values include hidden and public ones and which of them the frame holds is not known (for one of the seven it very likely holds hidden values, because its large local objects are all hidden); in seven its size is that of objects that hold no hidden value. No test of this repository looks at these frames. (The whole family, and what was read in machine code: row HW-213; two readings with a bad result: rows H39.4.1 and H39.8.)

column3: A bad result, the heavier of two (the other: row H39.4.1): a sumcheck kernel of the attention part (ga::k_s3_ri) leaves hundreds of bytes of hidden kind in each thread's stack frame, among them words from which single activations follow. Three of its seven instances that have a frame were read in the machine code of `cp_prove`, not on the released programs (nvcc 13.2.86; sm_90a); a second reading, made to break the first, held every count, offset and address that it tried with programs of its own and could not break it. What stays when a thread ends, since no instruction of the kernel overwrites it: in one instance 688 of the frame's 824 bytes may hold hidden values. Twelve words are made from three entries, five from one query entry, six from one key entry and one from another (16-bit activations, after the rotary embedding and the clamp), each word from its entry and one public number: where that number is negative the word gives the entry exactly, where it is positive only its sign (reckoned by hand and on synthetic numbers; not run on the kernel's own values); with signs close to fair coins one query entry would follow in about 31 of 32 launches, one key entry in about 63 of 64 and another in about 1 of 2, and then for every thread of the launch. 142 words are halves, mostly the high halves, of exact, unmasked sums over five to seven entries with public weights (reckoned, not tried: for two sets of seven key entries they would as a rule fix the entries; for twelve more sets they narrow them, and whether they fix them has not been reckoned). 18 words are the thread's own unmasked share of the round's three sums. In a second instance 88 of 200 bytes stay: both halves of two sums over three query entries, and the same 18 words. On the way 38 whole entries and one whole arg-max index pass through the first instance's frame and are overwritten later on every path: none of these stays. The third instance that was read is compiled and never launched, by the source. By the source the other two are launched once each in every run of the attention sub-proof's first part (at least once in a run that proves attention; how often has not been followed), where the head dimension (dh) is at least 128 and lg + lt at least 5; every parameter file under prover/examples/ has dh 128 and lg + lt 7 or more (searched), and by two readings of the source every example and the full size reach them; no run's record was read for it. What weighs the other way: these are a request's activations, hidden values that depend on the prompt and on the weights; not weights, keys or seeds themselves; but they are computed from the weights, and what exact activations would tell of the weights to somebody who also knows the request has not been reckoned; the same unmasked values also go to ordinary GPU memory, as the source says; the frames are register spills, which belong to one build and compiler and can move or vanish with any change, and the released programs' machine code has not been read for them; the memory is on the provider's own GPU, and no way is known for a client to see it in a run without a fault (reads of uninitialised GPU memory in a served batch, seen not on the released programs, are not fully explained: row T3.1). Whether the bytes ever leave the GPU's caches for its memory is not known. Not read: the kernel's four other instances with a frame (8 to 80 bytes; one of them is launched with the two, by the source). Beside the frames, told and not weighed: all loads of the key rows are at addresses made from the hidden arg-max index, a pattern of accesses and a matter of timing; and the shared memory in which each warp's unmasked sums are added is not cleared. Both kernels with a stack frame that were read in that same machine code (this one, and row H39.4.1's) gave a bad result, and more than fifty kernels with a stack frame have not been read: the list is not closed. No test checks the reading.

column3: A malicious prover that hashes the true request and makes the output head's sub-proof for other positions is stopped by one thing only: `cp_verify` works out for itself which positions are covered. Two tests come near it (a proof checked under another range; a lie at a position that is not covered). What is missing is a proof that is dressed for the false range, together with a control on a weakened verifier.

In `cp_prove` the lookups' error word is set to zero when the counting ends, and no later code stores to it, so the path from that word to a request's failure bits carries nothing: a multiplicity that overflows would go unreported. In its place there is a rejection made from the parameter file only, which bounds a group's number of keys. One kernel's subtraction of the padding's count has no test, and where a wrap would lead has not been followed.

No test tries a prover that lowers one multiplicity of a lookup below zero and raises another, so that their sum is right only modulo 2^32: the cheating cases of the tests take 1 from a count that is at least 1 or add 1 to one (these are not part of this repository), or raise one row's count and lower another's that a key has counted (in a unit test whose program is; the line of the test table that runs this case is not). By the format page's reading of the source, a multiplicity is 32 committed bits and the sum is asked in the field, where a stated size condition is meant to keep it from wrapping round, so such a pair should miss the claim on the number of keys; that is neither proved nor run.

In `cp_commit`'s worst-case check the small example configurations end with exit code 7 under their own scales: their synthetic scales leave places of the forward pass short of room. Copies with more room pass, and at the full-size configurations every place that the check bounds fits.
column4: At a small size, use the example configuration whose name ends in `_roomy`.

column3: One try in the search for a proof of work can cost a malicious prover somewhat less than one full call of the compression function: the nonce sits in the last words of the last block and the test reads one word of the output, so the work before the nonce and after that word can be spared; by how much at this layout has not been counted. The bound counts each try as one query to the random oracle, whatever it costs to compute.
Nothing has been examined for the case that the same weights are also committed under another commitment scheme: what the two commitments show together is not known.

How each weight tensor is stored in the model file (one of seven storage types) decides code paths, memory sizes and copy sizes in `cp_commit` and `cp_prove`. What an observer can learn from time or memory use has not been examined. Proof, key and leaf files have not been compared across storage types. The list of what is shown on purpose does not name the storage type: count it as not hidden.

The list says what is shown, not that showing it is harmless: what the items together tell about a secret model has not been weighed. Under a score policy, for example, the served-or-failed answers to many requests measure the model's hidden scores.
column4: With secret weights keep exact match; or, before serving under a score policy, let the front end store only requests that it has formed itself from a client's prompt and the reply that was served, set the checked tokens itself, and reject every parameter by which a client fixes or restricts the reply's tokens.

column3: Some comments in the source code state a guarantee more strongly or more widely than the code gives it; the comments were gone over once for such claims, and some stand unmended; no list of them ships, so none is named here by file and line. A comment is not evidence that a check is made — the code is. For what holds, read these limits and not the comments.

`cp_prove` stops if a sub-proof's part of the weight matrix could begin or end at an odd line of the matrix, because memory sizes would then show whether one particular token is in the prompt. No test exercises this stop: no configuration that the programs make has such a layout.

The programs' printed messages point to pages and sections of the documentation. One test, which is not part of this repository, checks pointers of one form only, and there only that the page and the heading exist; of a pointer in another form only the page is checked. So a message can send an operator to a section that is not there at all, or that does not say what the message promises, and no test would notice. That check found two pointers in the programs' messages that led to no heading, though a count made without a program had called all of them right.

No page of this repository outside lean/ gives an argument of its own that the field equations a proof checks give the integer model's output (what lean/ has is about Lean's own model, and in the compilation theorem (`innerCompiledVerifier_sound`) the hypothesis on what the claim means for the model is not proved); for the output head, docs/format/11-4-output-head.md sets out the argument of the comments in the programs' source and states no property of the protocol. For the programs' output head no proof is known (verifier/docs/parameter-file.md). The format's pages on attention, on the feed-forward segment and on the output head each say that they give no such argument. A technical report that is not public and not refereed states the step and argues it on paper for its protocol. Nothing is proved about the programs' own equations. The verifier tests the size conditions on every file.

The verifier's tests of the attention computation were written from an understanding of the code. No argument, let alone a proof, shows that these tests catch every false computation of attention; that is read, not proved: a reading of the code found no step inside the attention sub-proof that reads a later position, the causal mask enforced through a lookup on committed cells, and the clamp that its margin needs checked at every position by the layer sub-proof's lookup, on the same footing as every lookup key (the range check and the no-wrap conditions, whose step from the field to the integers is argued, not proved).
The comparison of each prover's own range tests with the model's table of range conditions has not been made on the released `cp_prove`, and nothing has been run for it.

Of whole runs of the honest `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` and `cp_verify` in which a value of the forward pass sits at the last admitted or at the first rejected number of a range test: the test cases that are written are not part of this repository; no such case exists for a key's entry, for the shared expert's gate and up projection, for the ends of the residual stream or of the norms, for a later layer, for a prompt of unlike tokens or for full size; and the cases show what the honest prover admits, not that `cp_verify` rejects a value outside a range.

The GPU unit test of the attention sub-proof's two kinds of closing sumcheck runs them on small synthetic arrays, each case also with two injected faults, and with the test's own host code as the verifier, not `cp_verify`. No test runs these sumchecks on arrays of extreme values, with many members or at the full-size configuration's shapes, and no whole run of `cp_prove` and `cp_verify` is known that is made to reach extreme values in them.

Inside a plan some numbers are taken on the calling routine's word, and nothing holds them at that round. The source names five kinds: the groups whose lists count at a sample or a batching; the smaller cubes of messages that share a seed; a lookup's table and keys; the list of the stage that follows, in a code switch's batching term; and the table's distances at every round that is priced from them. The last are true only of a table whose key was tested at the same distances, a test that is in another file's plan. The program's own count of such rounds includes them.

The commitment opens columns of a leaf table after one proximity test. The commitment's construction follows published ones (Ligero, Brakedown: PUBLISHED-WORKS.md). Neither the planner's `analysis` nor `check_key`'s one-time test takes a bound from Brakedown's counting argument. The count for an opened column after that test is a figure computed for these programs. A technical report that is not public and not refereed states, and argues on paper, its own form of the bound for this protocol. That form of the bound has not been checked independently. That the one test serves every later leaf table and proof is counted once for each leaf table and once for each proof.

`cp_commit` admits parameter files under which `cp_prove` can serve no request and ends at its start. Completeness is stated for the parameter files that `cp_prove` admits; the example configurations are such files.

column3: `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` let NVIDIA's libraries multiply 8-bit integers into 32-bit sums, through four library calls that the programs reach. Such a sum is exact as long as the sizes of all terms that are added into one 32-bit word, over all calls that add into it and with each call's multiplier, stay below 2^31 together; for plain products of two signed bytes that means fewer than 2^17 terms (the method, exact products of integer matrices through a numerical library with a bound on the sums, is public: J.-G. Dumas, P. Giorgi, C. Pernet, "Dense Linear Algebra over Word-Size Prime Fields: the FFLAS and FFPACK packages", arXiv:cs/0601133; PUBLISHED-WORKS.md). A sum that overflowed would give a wrong value without an error. By a reading of the code (nothing was run but one CPU test's two cases on the last rule), a test in the code bounds the length at every place that was followed: in the calling routine, or in `cp_commit`'s and `cp_prove`'s tests on the parameter file: the model width is at most 8,064, and the inner width must be below 2^16. (The sums over the inner width are the down projections of the forward pass, two calls into one word, and one product of a layer's proof.) `cp_verify` has no such rule: it takes files with an inner width of up to 2^20, under which these programs refuse to commit or prove. For one of the four calls, in the lookups' Gram passes, the bound was read at the call alone, and its callers were not traced. At two places in `cp_prove` only a tensor stored in 8 or 16 bits (Q8_0, F16 or BF16) reaches a library product, both through one of the four calls. The first is the routed experts' product where a routed tensor is stored in this way and its experts are handled one by one (prover/weights_blocks/experts.cuh; at set-up the same call is also made, whatever the tensors' types, on work buffers and not on a tensor). A comment there says that the length is not checked, and its upper bound is not tested there; but the caller ends the program unless the length is the model width or an expert's inner width, and the tests on the parameter file bound these at 8,064 and 16,384 (with experts an expert's inner width must be a power of two and the inner width twice it, and the inner width must be below 2^16: prover/common/parameter_file.h). The second is the pass over the rows of a layer's matrices of one kind, where every tensor of that kind in a group of layers is kept as blocks of these types (prover/weights_blocks/row_pass_blocks.cuh): the routine ends the program above 33,025 rows. By a reading of the code every such sum stays below 2^30 (at most 2^28 and about 2^29.01); nothing was run for it. The programs' own kernels that add byte products into 32-bit words stand under the same condition and were not read for this row; one of them says of itself that its caller's bound is not checked (prover/common/zfold_turned.cuh); by one reading of the code its length is bounded in code for its callers, at 8,191 columns with coefficients -1, 0 and 1 (prover/hiding/tail_f.cuh, tail.cuh).

`cp_commit` is compiled for the x86 SHA instructions (prover/build.sh hands the compiler -msha for the unit that holds its SHA-256), and it does not look at run time whether the CPU has them. On a CPU, or in a virtual machine, that lacks them it would be ended by the system at its first SHA-256, with the shell's bare words "Illegal instruction", exit code 132 and no message of its own; it does not catch that signal, so it would end as after a kill, and the weights in its memory would go back to the system unzeroed (a core file, which this signal writes by default, `cp_commit` has switched off at its first step). Every call of `cp_commit` makes a new commitment: it refuses to add to one that exists. On a model's files the first SHA-256 comes while the weights are loaded (with -public-weights: each model file's digest, before a tensor is read) or checked (the tensors' checksums, where the model's directory gives them), before the seed is drawn and before a working directory is made: by two readings of the source, made apart, the call has by then made no file that holds anything secret: at most one file, an empty one, which -worst-case-table names (what swap space can hold: row H28). On synthetic weights such a call reaches none of these instructions. All of this is reasoned from the build lines and the source; it has not been tried on a machine that lacks the instructions and has a GPU. The system ends make_model in the same way, and those unit tests, built by prover/build.sh and prover/tests/unit.sh with that option, that reach the SHA-256 code; that was seen, not on the released programs, on such a machine: make_model died of the signal for an illegal instruction and printed nothing, and three public CPU tests ended with exit code 132 and no word on the cause but the shell's, while the other nine that unit.sh builds passed. In these sources prover/tests/unit.sh names the cause: where a test dies of that signal and a one-instruction program dies too, it prints that this CPU cannot run the SHA instructions, and the test counts as not run (read in the script and in SUITE.md's rows). `cp_prove`'s own SHA-256 code does not use them: the one unit of it that includes that source is compiled without the option and takes the same function in plain C++; a second unit that is linked into `cp_prove` is compiled with the option and includes no SHA-256 source (read in the build script). A count, not on the released programs, found no such instruction in `cp_prove` or `cp_verify`, and in `cp_commit` only in that one function (host code alone; the libraries that the programs load were not looked at). Whether `cp_prove` runs on such a CPU was not tried; the production build of it also catches that signal and ends with its usual last line; the test build that prover/build.sh makes does not. `cp_verify` and the programs of weight_sums/ are not built with the option either (read; the same count found no such instruction in them). Two example scripts (examples/quickstart-gpu.sh, examples/maverick/run.sh) look for sha_ni in /proc/cpuinfo and stop where the word is missing: that speaks of the machine on which the script runs, not of another to which the programs are copied, and it can turn away a machine that would do: one virtual machine was seen that hides the word and yet runs the instructions.
column4: Run `cp_commit` on a CPU that has the SHA extensions. `grep -m1 -ow sha_ni /proc/cpuinfo` prints sha_ni where the system shows them; a virtual machine can hide the word and still run the instructions. A sure check that needs no GPU: `(D=$(mktemp -d) && ./run_suite.py cpu "$D/work" --only '^prover[.]hmac_sha256_test$')`, typed at the repository's top, passes only where they run.

column3: `cp_prove` has no front end for clients of its own: it separates no clients, serves every request file in its spool directory and writes all responses into one directory. The repository ships one example front end, a middleware for vLLM, which by its own page does not authenticate each client and does not hide timing or queue length: it knows proof IDs, not clients. Whoever builds or runs the front end sees every prompt and every response, and both weight hiding and the privacy of one client's requests from another's depend on it.
column4: Build a front end that authenticates clients, submits each request itself (so that it draws the nonce), gives a response only to the client that sent the request, lets no response leave before `cp_verify` has accepted every proof of its batch (duty 6: docs/limits.md#the-conditions), and shows no client a directory listing, a file's times, a tag, anything that is still staged, or the programs' output.

column3: What the Python package `integer_model` returns, and what its example scripts print, is computed from the weights with no mask. That covers the greedy choices, each token's logit gap and cost and, through `record`, every layer's arrays and the logits. The package's vLLM class hands on only the chosen token. Anyone who is given the other values holds exact numbers computed from the weights.
column4: Where the weights must stay hidden, keep what these calls return and what the examples print on the provider's own machine, and hand none of it out.

column3: The commitment ID covers every byte of the configuration files, but not the programs' own constants: these are represented only by a version word in the parameter file's first line, which is typed in, not computed, and checked for its form, not hashed from the sources. So an equal ID does not show that two builds of the programs have the same constants.

column3: A request's range names positions, counted from 0, and position t is about token t + 1: the range takes in the positions r to e - 1, so for a prompt of n tokens and m tokens received it is r = n - 1, e = n + m - 1. Whoever names the received tokens' own positions leaves the first of them unchecked. Where the range ends at the window's end, the next token, which is no token of the request, is checked beside them.

column3: Of the bits that the programs' own error accounting computes for a round, some are proof of work. The rest are meant to bound the chance that one cheating attempt passes the round, by the programs' own calculation and under results that are cited or assumed.
`cp_verify` has not been reviewed independently (what was tried on it: rows SO-15.5 and SO-15.7).

A round's value that leaves without its mask is tried, in a whole run of `cp_prove` before `cp_verify`, only for the first two values of the first sumcheck of a place where values are sent: 13 such cases, each of which must be rejected. Two unit tests on the GPU try it on a part by itself: on the product layer on wide arrays, at 1 to 17 variables, on the two values of the first round and on the second end value; and on the lookup argument, on its second and its 601st round value and on one end value. No test tries it on every round, and none on the product layer on 16-bit keys by itself. Of the other masked values the whole runs send seven without their masks, each of which must be rejected: five end values of sumchecks and two values that are sent alone; and both unit tests also let the prover take the challenge that multiplies the end values' masks to be 0, so that every end value of every sumcheck leaves bare, and require a rejection. In a whole run it is not tried on the round in a sumcheck's extra variable, on the tie of a lookup's two roots or on the values of the claims about the weights. The unit test of the product layer on 16-bit keys has no cheating build: like the wide layer's it adds one to each sent scalar and to each mask entry in turn, before the proof library's verifier routines, and requires a rejection. Of these tests only the unit test of the product layer on 16-bit keys, which has no cheating build, is part of this repository as it is told here. The two other unit tests are here in their plain forms alone, in which no value loses its mask; their cheating builds and the whole runs are not part of this repository. So no run in this repository sends a value of the GPU code without its mask to a verifier's routine, and a reader cannot repeat what this row tells of such values.

Two GPU unit tests on the proof's one hash chain were run once and passed, not on the released programs: a test changes the GPU's messages of a product layer value by value (816 scalars and as many mask entries), another those of the product layer on 16-bit keys (640 scalars and as many mask entries), and that test also requires that the honest proof, read with its rounds in the plain order, is rejected. The 16-bit layer's changed messages are read by the proof library's verifier functions alone, not by `cp_verify`'s own; the wide layer's by both. No test puts a fault into the data of the layer sub-proof's chain of sumchecks or of its batched inner-product sumcheck; the lookup engine is compared with itself in two of its ways of working, not in all; and the 13 ways of cheating at a product layer, in a test that is not part of this repository, alter some of a case's rounds, not every round.

End to end through vLLM at full size, at the default setting, not on the released programs: seven calls of one script, each on one H100, on the real, public weights (a third party's public 4-bit conversion of Llama 4 Maverick), under a seed that `cp_commit` drew. The script does not ship; it calls the repository's end-to-end demonstration with more options than its documentation prints. First `cp_commit` made a commitment. Then vLLM, with the proof middleware and the integer-model plug-in, served greedy replies from the committed integer model, one request at a time. Then vLLM was stopped, and `cp_prove` proved all the replies as one batch. Then vLLM was started again, and the example client fetched each proof and checked it with its check script. In every call 16 of 16 replies, to 16 synthetic prompts, served by vLLM from the integer model, were proved, fetched and passed by the client's check script (reported, not on the released programs). In every call 1 of 1 changed reply got no proof (why was not checked), and was rejected with the unchanged reply's proof (reported, not on the released programs). Each proof covers every token of one served reply, under exact match; no reply's end was checked. The prompts are token IDs made by a formula, under a word-list tokenizer that is not the model's, and a pass compares greedy choices, not scores. The engine and `cp_prove` did not run at the same time, so no proving service stayed up beside a serving engine. That the parameter file that ran was the default setting's rests on a comparison of its first 32 lines, by report. Each call was made once, on one machine, under one seed. The calls show no proving speed, nothing about ordinary serving at full size, and not whether the demonstration starts at full size without the script's extra options for vLLM. The masking was on as in service. The calls tested nothing about hiding, and they show nothing about soundness. Three of the seven calls ran a proof middleware other than the one that ships. In some of the calls other scripts of this repository also differed from those that ship: in printed texts, docstrings and comments, in how `ask_and_check.py` puts the words of one note together, and in when `end_to_end.py` prints one closing piece of advice after a failure of `cp_prove`. In the other four, vLLM was given its API key in `VLLM_API_KEY` alone, and on the middleware's routes no call without the key was tried. The calls show nothing about the known fault of a proof server that runs as root.

column3: Ordinary serving has run at a small size (64 tokens a request, a vocabulary of 512), on a synthetic model, not on the released programs, in one scripted run made seven times, at two small test configurations, each with counted proof of work: ordinary serving under the clipped gap at the one, integer serving under exact match at the other. It ran on one machine, over the loopback address; in two of the demonstrations vLLM was stopped while `cp_prove` ran. The prompts are synthetic token IDs, not text. The three demonstrations served, and proved, the same replies, and each demonstration's eight requests were proved as one batch, with no standing proving service beside the engine. Each time 24 of 24 replies, to the same 8 prompts in each of 3 demonstrations, that vLLM 0.29.0 served were proved under a clipped gap and accepted (reported, not on the released programs). Each time 3 of 3 changed replies (one in each of 3 demonstrations) got no proof, and were rejected with the unchanged reply's proof (reported, not on the released programs). "Accepted" means within limits: the policy bounds a mean and a count over the checked tokens, not each token, so it does not say that a token is the model's top choice. The limits were fitted to the run's own pair of small models, and the run does not show whether their slack was needed. The changed reply was the same one each time, with every token replaced, and the run did not show why it got no proof. Its rejection shows at most that a proof is bound to its request, and nothing about the policy. That each check ran the verifier on the proof rests on the scripts' source and not on the run's record. The record has no log line for each request that vLLM served, because the demonstration turns that log off. That the directory that was served holds a floating-point copy of the committed synthetic model rests on the script's source. That the requests asked for greedy replies rests on the scripts' source, not on the runs' records. One demonstration uses the test build. None of the seven times used the scripts and the proof middleware exactly as they are in this repository: the middleware that the run used made no check of its own by `cp_verify`, which the one that ships makes (integrations/LIMITS.md#what-has-never-been-run; the scripts and the middleware are no part of a build of the programs). The fourth time it ran without `sudo`. None of this shows anything about the known fault of a proof server that runs as root. In some of the seven runs some steps were left out, the package's tests among them. The run shows nothing about weight hiding, soundness or speed, and a pass at a test configuration carries no security claim.

column3: Proofs under fitted limits, at full size, on the real, public weights, not on the released programs: one script, run twice on one NVIDIA H100, at the default setting (reported: of one run, the first 32 lines of the parameter file that ran are those of the shipped full-size file; of the other, by the run's own look at that file, its lines `answers` and `record` and those on proof of work are the default's), under a seed that `cp_commit` drew, with no test option and with a clipped-gap acceptance policy in place of the default's exact match; nothing was served in these runs. Each time 48 of 48 stored replies got a proof that the verifier accepted as within limits (reported, not on the released programs). The control, in which no reply should get a proof: each time 0 of 48 replies set after another prompt got a proof (reported, not on the released programs). That is a gross change: it is no test that catches a changed model or a changed token. That honest replies get a proof does not show that the limits tell models apart, or that a reply that passes was served by the committed model. The committed model is a third party's public 4-bit conversion of Llama 4 Maverick, as integers. The replies are stored ones: greedy, at most 500 tokens, served by a stock engine (vLLM 0.29.0) from the model's 16-bit checkpoint, to prompts of 524 tokens of WikiText-2. There was no other kind of prompt. The limits were fitted by `fit_limits.py`, under its default rule, on 48 of these replies; the fitted values are not published. The 48 other replies had been scored once before the fit. A proof checks every token of its request's reply, and `check_proof.py` checked each proof by calling `cp_verify` with the limits named. A request that misses the limits gets no proof. Weight hiding was not tested, and the architecture is shown. Each answer tells the client at least one yes-or-no fact about the model's hidden scores, and so about its weights, even if the masks hold; no statement bounds how much. By the loader's lookup before each of the two runs, the programs took a CUDA runtime and cuBLAS that by their checksums are, by the project's own account, 13.2.86 and 13.4.1.3: the pairing that a user's own build by the quick start gets (reported; the records give no version). Which files the running programs opened, the records do not show. One result of 48 of 48 does not bound how often honest replies are declined: limits fitted on the first 24 fitted replies alone are missed by 3 of the other 24, all honest replies of the same engine. The run does not show that the limits tell models apart in general: it tried one smaller model of the same family, with 24 greedy replies. The run shows nothing about another setting of the declared model, or about edited replies, which another scoring run, not on the released programs, found to pass often. The runs give no speed, and they were not a service. Each time 0 of 24 replies of that smaller model got a proof (reported, not on the released programs). The two runs share one set of stored replies and the same limits, so they are no second sample and no rate of acceptance. Under this policy which requests get a proof tells something about the model's scores. No test in this repository that runs on these programs shows `cp_verify` refusing a proof whose reply misses a clipped-gap policy's limits; the one test written for that is not part of this repository and has not run on these programs.

column3: The attack tests, each with what it does not cover. Stored replies of a stock inference engine, honest and altered, up to 500 tokens long, were scored, not proved, on the public weights of Llama 4 Maverick against clipped-gap limits that were just loose enough for the worst of the honest replies to 48 prompts to meet them, in one run of the integer-model package (not on the released programs). In each pair of counts the first is under limits fitted to the 16-bit engine's replies, and the second under limits fitted to the FP8 engine's. With one token replaced by the model's second choice, 28 and 24 of 32 replies met the limits; with one token at a random place replaced by a random one, 27 and 21 of 32; sampled at temperature 1, checked against limits set on greedy replies, 49 and 23 of 96; with four tokens replaced by the model's second choices, 1 of 32 under each (the others were refused by the cap, the limit on the number of costly tokens, not by the limit on the mean); each engine's own honest replies, to prompts that did not set the limits, 95 and 91 of 96; replies to another prompt, 0 of 96 (docs/limits.md#within-limits). The run ended at its time limit: of its eight sets of replies with 4 or 16 tokens replaced it had scored one, and it did not check the loaded weights against their checksums. Under exact match, none of the 96 honest replies would pass. Not covered: any proof; replies of a cheaper model, or of a model with altered weights; an adversary who picks the place; prompts from a corpus other than WikiText-2; short replies. Replies of a nearby, altered model, and replies with tokens replaced, were scored, not proved, on a small synthetic model, by the integer model's package on a CPU, against clipped-gap limits that were fitted to the honest model (not on the released programs). 60 of the altered model's 64 replies differed from the honest model's. 47 of the altered model's 64 replies met the limits when served in bfloat16, and 54 in float32; of the honest model's, 63 and 64 of 64. Under stricter limits 18 of the altered model's 64 replies met them, and 58 of the honest model's 64. With one token replaced by a random one 3 of 64 met the limits, with one token replaced by the model's second choice 5 of 64, and with four or more tokens replaced none (docs/limits.md#within-limits). Under looser limits all 64 replies from a slightly altered model passed, and for 40 of them only a written report is kept, not the data. Not covered: any proof; a real model; full size; a second altered model; a second seed. 80 altered copies of the files of a full-size run and 3 altered calls, on synthetic weights, were all rejected by `cp_verify`, at the default setting (not on the released programs). None of the 64 altered places in the key file and the leaf file was among the bytes of the out-of-domain (OOD) answers (masked sums of the weights). An altered copy of an honest file is not a deliberately constructed false proof, so forgeries are not covered. The committer stores the weights as a table encoded with an error-correcting code. `cp_verify` samples columns, so it can only be expected to catch a table that differs from every valid one in more than a fixed fraction of positions. A proof made from a tampered secret key directory, at full size, under a production build's own secret seed: by report, that run's own check before release rejected it (not on the released programs). Not covered: more than this one case; a batch of 24; a serving session. (See also row LIM-5.3.)

column3: One call of the prover on 64 requests, on synthetic weights, can fail at full size on an 80 GB GPU (an NVIDIA H100). In the timed runs, on synthetic weights at the default setting, a service of five batches of 64 failed in its first batch (64 requests taken, 256 waiting), and one call of the prover on 64 requests at once failed: none of their 320 and 64 requests got a proof and none was marked as failed; in both `cp_prove` ended with exit code 1 and the last line `p258 end 1 cuda-call`, the GPU's memory was nearly full (81,053 of 81,559 MiB at the largest sample), each used up one batch's share of the commitment's one leaf table, and no cause is shown. They ran on one machine and card, the call behind the service, on one commitment, so the two are not independent of each other. No batch of 64 has been proved on synthetic weights: every attempt on record failed, eight in all, six of them on other programs (row HW-678). Not on the released programs, at the default setting, the call was made once, on a directory of 64 request files, not as a service: it ended with exit code 1, at a failed CUDA call; no request was marked as failed, and 0 of 64 got a proof. The prover's last line named a failed CUDA call and nothing more: once the program has begun to read its secrets it prints only fixed lines, by its own design, so which CUDA call failed, and with which error, is not known. Not on the released programs, a service of five batches of 64 on synthetic weights was attempted once, on another machine: 0 of 320 requests got a proof; 64 had been taken into the first batch and 256 were still waiting when the prover ended with exit code 1, at a failed CUDA call, and none was marked as failed. Whether the same CUDA call failed is not shown. The card's largest sample was 81,053 of 81,559 MiB in each. Each used up one batch's share of the commitment's one copy of the committed table. The cause is not known, and one run gives no failure rate. The attempt is not like for like with the services at 64 on the real weights, which ended well. The same failure was seen in one batch of 64 full-size requests on synthetic weights on one such card (reported, not on the released programs). In the run of that batch, not on the released programs, `cp_prove`, the default build, was called once with `-in` and `-out` on a directory of 64 requests, not as a service, on a commitment made under a drawn seed, without `-public-weights`, with `-in-step 6 -memory lean,tensor-rooms=8`; it was that call's only batch. After 474 seconds it ended with exit code 1 and the last line `p258 end 1 cuda-call`, and left no response; one leaf table's count still grew by the batch's columns. The GPU's largest sample was 81,047 of 81,559 MiB. That it was want of GPU memory is a reading of that sample: the last line is the same for every failed CUDA call. column3: The GPU engine, whose trees both programs use, by its source zeroes both arrays of a tree's digests when it takes them from its pool, so that the place of a digest that is never stored should go out as 32 zero bytes; a unit test holds that for a leaf's digest (the public test `gpu.tree_arrays_cleared_test`). No run of the test leaves that clearing out; a control fails the test if a fresh buffer of the same size is zero in all four states of GPU memory in which it runs. The committer's own tree over a leaf table is zeroed first too. By one reading of the code, which has not been checked independently, `cp_commit` also builds trees of the GPU engine while it makes an entry (a leaf file). By the same one reading the clearing is the same code. At an opening the GPU engine's result buffers (the opened symbols, the salts, the sibling digests and the part of a tree that is made again) are taken from its memory pool and not cleared first: a kernel launch that was accepted and never ran, or a lost store, would leave old bytes of that pool in the proof's bytes. By one reading of the code the tree's root is fixed by then, so such a proof does not verify; `cp_prove` releases it all the same, with the old bytes in it (row H26); nothing was run. The lost digest itself is noticed by nothing where no opened position is below it.

The committer's own hash tree over a leaf table is built, level after level, in a buffer that has just held the table's last encoded symbols, and its kept levels become the stored nodes from which later openings take the digests that they send. That buffer is zeroed first, as the GPU engine's trees are: if the GPU silently lost a store there, the place would hold zeros or a lower level's digest, never a symbol of the masked table's codeword. The lost store itself is noticed at the kept level only when a drawn column lies under that place (`cp_prove` then ends the opening, `hc-own-node`); until then such a place can go out as a sibling for as long as the leaf table is in use; one above it is noticed when the stored nodes are next loaded; whether `cp_commit`'s own openings in the same run could carry such a place into the key file or a leaf file has not been followed. This is a reading, not a run: no injected fault has been run on the committer's own hash tree.

The GPU routines that put digests into memory were surveyed by a reading of the code: three build a tree and two rebuild a part of one at an opening. Of the three that build a tree, the GPU engine's and the committer's own are cleared first, and nothing calls the rest. Of the two that rebuild a part, one zeroes its whole room first and compares its result with a kept node before a word leaves (what is written comes from a second read: row HW-574). The other, where the engine makes the lower part of a tree again at an opening, takes two work buffers that are not set first: a lost store there would put 32 stale bytes into a proof file. By reasoning, not by a run, that is noticed only where a verifier is run: the root is fixed by then, so a verifier rejects the file; `cp_prove` runs none, and releases the file with the stale bytes in it (row H26). A kernel that hashes in another way under another name would have escaped the survey.

What these pages say about weight hiding does not cover a commitment made from weight files in which any tensor is stored as Q8_0, F16 or BF16 (here: weight files of 8 or 16 bits), or the proofs made under it. The machine code of the three kernels written for such files was read twice, apart, on test builds, for what the kernels leave behind on the GPU (rows H39.6 and H46.2) and for branches, addresses and indices that depend on a weight or a gain. What lies around these kernels has not been read in machine code: the roads that only such files take, on which the decoded weights go to work buffers and a closed library's kernels multiply them, and the other GPU functions that the code for such files changes, at least eight by a count of the compiler's resource lines. The code for such files lies in the 384 files that were read whole, once and fast: no branch that skips a mask on such files was reported, and the road of such files was no reading's task (row HW-745). No test has injected a fault into the programs on such files; and no search for leaks has run on files made from them.

With a weight file of 8 or 16 bits (for the routed experts the code goes by each routed tensor's own stored type, Q8_0, F16 or BF16, not by the file) the prover skips the two tensor-core kernels in prover/weights_blocks/ and handles the routed experts one by one: in each layer that has them, and for each of its three routed tensors, it decodes one whole expert and makes three or more launches for each expert that got tokens. So the number and sizes of its GPU calls depend on which experts got tokens and on how many each got. The routing is a hidden value: it depends on the prompts and on the weights. Whoever can watch the prover's timing, as every client can for its own batch, or its GPU calls can learn something about the routing (how much has not been measured), and whoever can watch its timing or memory can tell which type of file is in use. Timing is not hidden.

With a weight file of 8 or 16 bits (for the routed experts the code goes by each routed tensor's own stored type, Q8_0, F16 or BF16, not by the file), decoded weights of the routed experts and values of a request lie in four work buffers in GPU memory where a 4-bit file puts none of them. The loop that handles the routed experts one by one writes an expert's decoded weights into a buffer that with a 4-bit file holds only other matrices' decoded weights, and which expert's weights stay there follows the routing; it writes its tokens' activations into a second buffer, which with a 4-bit file holds weights alone, and the sums of their products into a third. Another kernel written for such files runs for every routed expert that a pass covers, whatever the routing: it writes the expert's decoded weights to a fourth buffer, unmasked sums made from them are written beside them, and the last expert's stay after the call. With a 4-bit file one kernel does that work and keeps all of it out of GPU global memory. By three readings of the source code, made apart (two for the buffer with the sums), the four buffers are zeroed at a request's start, before each turn if more than one request goes in step, at the end of a batch's pass, and when the prover ends by itself or through exit(); they are not zeroed after a fault signal, an abort, a kill or a GPU fault, or if the wipe is cut short, as with a 4-bit file. Three of them are lent to no other part of the programs; the one with the sums lies in memory that is zeroed when it is lent. That the zeroing between requests takes the buffers in rests on their being all zeros at the end of set-up, which is concluded, not seen; nothing was run, and no test of what stays in memory has run on such files (row H6 tells what is known of GPU memory in general). That other kernel also ends with decoded weights in GPU shared memory, which nothing clears, and it runs too for the other weight matrices that the prover keeps in the file's own form. For those other matrices the kernel for 4-bit files ends with decoded weights in shared memory too, the same amount per thread block (by two readings of the machine code of test builds, made apart: 8,192 whole weights, 16,384 bytes). But with 4-bit files no such kernel runs for the routed experts, so with a weight file of 8 or 16 bits this happens more often: for each routed expert, in every pass of that kind.

While `cp_prove` loads the weights, five kernels decode them and round them to integers. With an F16 file the decoding branches on the exponent bits of the weights; with a Q8_0, Q4_K, Q5_K or Q6_K file, on those of the block scales. For every type, BF16 too, the rounding tests each weight's size and whether it lies halfway between two integers. So the time of a start can depend on the weights (row HW-530 tells this in general). This is from the source code: whether the compiler keeps the branches has not been read, and nothing was measured.

Rows H21 and H21.1 tell what somebody who can write the provider's files, but not read them, can learn from how starts of `cp_prove` end. With a BF16 weight file this reached single weights: not on the released programs, at a small size, on synthetic weights, somebody who could write that file but not read it learned the magnitudes of two neighbouring weights of their choice in about 32 starts (by the run's report; its log was not read for this row). It has not been tried on the released programs. The vLLM package's reader has not been checked for it.

The three GPU kernels written for weight files of 8 or 16 bits (Q8_0, F16, BF16) have no test among this repository's public tests. One test that is no row of SUITE.md ships with this repository (integrations/vllm/integer_model/tests/test_against_the_prover.py): it runs cp_commit and cp_prove on one small synthetic model stored as Q8_0, F16 and BF16, one window for each type; by reading, it reaches two of the three kernels; whether it reaches the third is not known; no run listed the kernels launched; it tests nothing about hiding. The project's other tests of that code are not part of this repository.

The key file and every leaf file hold, for each row of a weight table and each stored answer, a sum of the row's weights with public factors, masked by a random pad alone, and they are published for good. No verifier can see whether the pads are there or are random. Where weight hiding stands: [docs/limits.md](limits.md#the-verdict). The judgement told there does not cover 2, 3 or 4 OOD answers a row. On a model's files `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` take a parameter file that says `answers 1`. `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` refuse a parameter file whose `answers` is not 1, on synthetic weights and under `-public-weights` too (`parameter-range`). Under `-public-weights` `cp_commit` derives the seed from the option's file of 32 bytes, whoever has that file can compute every pad, and nothing tests that this file, or the weights, are public. According to the written proof, published OOD answers, one such sum for each row, hide the weights as long as every pad is fresh, random and used once and the table stays within its limit of use (a further condition, on the sample points: row HW-584). The written proof covers one OOD answer a row, so two to four OOD answers a row are outside it. That proof is about the protocol on paper, whose pads are drawn fresh (with pads derived from a secret seed, as the programs' are, only under four conditions that have not been shown of the programs), and it is no firmer than the whole written proof, which its authors call "complete but not settled" (what that means: row PS-23). These programs derive the pads from a secret seed, so that rests on an assumption about the cipher that derives them (docs/limits.md, "derived pads"). What these pages say about weight hiding has been checked for the default setting only in part (which runs were at that setting, and what has not been tested there: row HW-584). (Among which matrices the written proof hides: row PS-28.)

Each program's parser refuses a parameter file that says 2, 3 or 4 answers, and that is what stands between any weights and 2, 3 or 4 published OOD answers a row.

By a reading of the code, one self-check in `cp_commit` (`own-test-pads`) is all that stands between a fault that loses every pad and a public file without pads. The programs' self-checks only compute each pad again, with a second implementation that is not an independent one, so a misreading of the rule that both share goes unseen. The published answers themselves are computed once. A bad result: in a trial on a test build (without proof of work, which the default setting counts), with that check switched off, a commitment without pads passed everything else that `cp_commit` does. The audit tool recomputes none of the answers: a committer that leaves the pads out gets its YES, and each published answer is then one exact linear equation on a row of the weight table.

What has compared the OOD answers by value: one test written apart from the programs, which is not part of this repository, computed each published answer again from the secret seed, on a test build, under a test seed, with all weights set to 0: at small size all 768 answers were the public factor times their own pads. It shows that each answer has its pad, not that the answer is right; with weights that are not 0 that rested, in that test, on reading the code; a run told in this row shows it at small size; that test says nothing of pads under a drawn seed; that run was under two drawn seeds. At full size that test's comparison has not been run; a partial audit met by value all 4,096 answers of one full-size commitment, once, on synthetic weights (not on the released programs). Its records have not been checked independently, and it says nothing on whether the masks hide. The sweep of injected losses on which other rows rest ran on test builds of other sources (rows HW-678, LIM-63.2), at the default's small form, but no case of it loses one of the pads on the OOD answers (row H3.1). Other tests, which are not part of this repository, do inject losses of pads: on test builds, at small size, under a test seed, with all weights 0, eight such losses were each ended by `own-test-pads`, with exit code 4 and no public file; all eight strike the key file's table. At the default's small form, on synthetic weights, on the released programs: a separate program, written mainly from these pages, computed the published answers again: 1,536 of 1,536 answers of two small commitments, each under a seed that `cp_commit` drew, were the row's weighted sum plus the public factor times the row's own pad; no pad came twice, none was 0. In two runs, not on the released programs, OOD answers were made from a real model's files, each time at full size, from public files of the model's weights, with `-public-weights`, under which nothing is hidden; in each run `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` on one request and `cp_verify` ended with exit code 0. One of the two read a third party's public 4-bit conversion of the model's weights. They are not the only such runs: rows HW-747 and LIM-63.2. The comparison by value has also run on the released programs at full size (rows LIM-63.2 and HW-747). No run is known that made OOD answers from a model's files that are to stay hidden: by a reading of the code, without `-public-weights` the programs take a model's files where the parameter file says `answers 1`.
