The OOD sample's own round has no proof of work, and must have none: a nonce in it would let two nonces give two points on one set of pads, and so one exact equation on each row's weights. No named condition says so: it holds by the code's shape and by one unit test, which asks it only where work is counted on positions.

At a failed CUDA call, an abort or a signal the pads' buffer in host memory and their copy on the GPU are not wiped; the host buffers can be paged out. What stays of the pads at `cp_prove`'s exits is told at length in rows H6.1 and R7.1.1.

`own-test-pads` also ends a run at pads that are all 0, where the table has no key, and where the key's second copy is missing or all zeros, and `own-test-zero-key` at no key or a key of 32 zero bytes. For two events of chance among these, pads that are all 0 and a key of zeros (the key or its second copy), a technical report that is not public and not refereed gives a term, as a formula that it does not evaluate; its corollary on derived pads, as worded, speaks of the first alone. A key or a second copy that is missing is a fault of the run: its chance has no bound, so the report does not cover a stop there (row PS-34). A second copy that differs cannot occur on paper: two copies of one key are equal in every run, so the report counts a program that compares the two copies as the program that does not, on two conditions: one committer or prover holds both copies, and what is computed only for the comparison goes into nothing else. That the programs' self-checks are of these kinds is a reading of the code, not a statement of the report. The report covers a stop only where it has a small bound on the stop's chance. Another self-check on pads need not have such a formula (rows PS-34, LIM-44). The report claims no term for two kinds of self-check: one that reads both a pad and a key and does not end alike in every run, and a comparison of the keys of two different tables; by two readings of the code one routine of the committer makes a comparison of the second kind.

What row E4.4 says of the stored weight tables' random entries holds for the pads on the OOD answers too: no test looks from outside a whole `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` at them as they lie in GPU memory. And no test of this repository forms the published OOD answers again from the weights and the pads (rows H47.2 and H47.3). (See also row H47.7.)

Whether the programs print a secret. By a reading of every print call of the production builds, with nothing run, neither program prints the seed, a key, a pad or a sum without its pad. A second reading, by patterns, found the same of what `cp_verify` prints when `cp_commit` starts it on a file that is not yet published. Not read: CUDA's and cuBLAS's own output; `cp_prove`'s calls behind the close, one by one. Nothing in the programs or the repository's two audits computes a published sum a second time, and one self-check in `cp_commit` is all that stands between a fault that loses every pad and a public file without pads. The rest of what has been checked of the OOD answers is in row HW-584.

column3: One salt at the start of a hash chain. The source is Chiesa, Orrù, "A Fiat–Shamir Transformation From Duplex Sponges", Cryptology ePrint Archive 2025/536. There the prover absorbs one random salt into a duplex sponge at the beginning and sends it with the proof. Zero knowledge is proved by showing that every later query is unpredictable, with a term for guessing the salt. There the state is that of a sponge over an ideal permutation; here it is a chain of hash values. That one salt would also suffice for a hash chain is said in Remark 2.2, without a proof. So for the chain here this step is argued, not proved.

column3: Hiding and soundness, object by object: At the one proof format and model size that `verify` takes, Lean proves that what is shown of the committed tables, within a budget of opened columns, has the same distribution whatever the weights (Lean's encoder, fresh pads, full size, before any hashing). For the protocol's own honest provers, as Lean definitions, zero knowledge is proved after hashing too, in the random-oracle model, against any verifier within a bound on its hash queries and replies, with one bit per request revealed (in a corollary, one label of three). That is proved at the exact-match policy, for one request to a proof, not for batches, and for one commitment with one leaf table ([where it stands](limits.md#the-verdict)). No theorem covers the programs, or the out-of-domain (OOD) answers (masked sums of the weights) as the programs make them ([what Lean proves](limits.md#what-lean-proves)). What Lean has for the link proof's prover by itself: docs/limits.md, 'What Lean proves', item 2. The programs derive their masks from a secret seed, which no Lean theorem covers. Lean has a soundness theorem for its own verifier, `verify`, not for the C++ program that users run: [what it says, and what it does not](limits.md#what-the-lean-proofs-cover). The theorem's scope is one format and one size: the format's default setting at full size. That the library's written copy of the full-size public files is the shipped files' is held by no theorem (a program beside the library, `lean/scripts/check_stored_examples.py`, compares them from outside). The compilation theorem (`innerCompiledVerifier_sound`), on `innerCompiledVerifier`, a verifier written in Lean, covers the committed tables, but under named hypotheses, and, at the library's descriptions other than `theDescription`, those on which soundness turns are not proved: it reduces soundness to these, it does not prove it. The 16 named hypotheses are not all that the compilation theorem needs: its inputs also carry laws in their types, which are counted nowhere. The soundness theorem does not go through the compilation theorem. It goes through a form of the compilation theorem at `theDescription` (through a coding of the hash queries that depends on the hash function's own digests: `lean/GAPS.md`, 28 (a); not the theorem under a policy of [lean/THEOREM.md](../lean/THEOREM.md), which is about files under another policy), and each condition that this form asks is supplied by a theorem, so the soundness theorem has none of them as a hypothesis. The sixteen conditions on the public files are tests inside `verify`, not theorems. The compilation theorem is a theorem about every description; two are given, one at each of the default setting's two sizes, as typed: the entry file and the OOD answers' seed and code as values, the key and proof files written at open parameters, the rest open parameters. The bound is a formula in open parameters: no number; at some settings of the open parameters the statement says nothing. Not the shipped files' bytes: no theorem ties them. `verify-on-bytes` (row L22) is a Lean text from which this repository builds no stand-alone program; one test (tools/accepts/) compiles it and has Lean load the compiled code while it evaluates files of lean/Ask/. No theorem on soundness is proved of what a program built from it accepts. That text follows `cp_verify`'s source, and follows that setting. **The spot check of four values.** By a reading of the code, when a sample has one element, as most do, the spot check reads a temporary copy.

**CPU machine code.** It has not been compared between the test and production builds.

In other sources (row HW-678), under a test seed twenty checks are off or milder, by two readings of the code, and in a production build all are on, but for one that, by a reading of the code, the option `-public-weights` lets go. So, apart from the audits of production-build commitments and of small production-build batches, the evidence by value has never taken those branches.

The tests ran the audit on honest files only, through kept bytes that are all zeros, so they never showed it finding a loss. Another test also makes a commitment under a sampled seed, whose kept bytes are not zeros. It builds no loss into a program for the audit to find.
The audit tool can share bugs with the programs that it audits. The order of its random samples comes from the prover's source, and some parameters come through the verifier's own code.

On other programs (row HW-678), if the audit tool's two routines that rebuild the trees of random values and recompute the sample answers stopped running, nothing would say so. In the tool in this repository, by two readings of these sources, with nothing run, and by its own page (tools/audit/README.md), the audit would report it if one of these trees or answers were skipped: not at `--level=0`; under `--batch`, only those in proofs; under `--drawn`, none. One kind of such tree is outside that, by the tool's own comment (tools/audit/level1.py: "a BASE mask that is sent alone"): the audit does not rebuild it; it compares its opened symbols, and not an unopened leaf's salt.

**Advice that the programs print.** By a reading of the code, each of the 58 pieces of advice that the programs print was followed, in the worst place for it. Several of these messages differ in the released programs. `cp_commit` says of leftover working directories that nothing has to be removed. `cp_prove` sends the operator to its own `-clear` call, not to a removal by hand. Of the 58, 42 lose nothing, and none sets a count back, repeats a random value or asks for a copy of a secret key directory. Five can do harm, in four ways: two ways lose a secret key directory that is still needed, and two can give a seed file to a hostile second account. By two readings of these sources, made by searching printed text for words (remove, rm, chmod, chown, delete and move in the sources and scripts outside tests; restore and copy too in seven source files), no message of `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` tells an operator to remove a secret key directory or to change the owner or mode of a seed file. These readings did not follow the 58 pieces of advice. Which of the ways the released programs have is not known. Nine more lose only the caller's own throw-away files, and two could not be followed to an end.

**The written proof (not public: row HW-763) on derived values.** The written proof has a statement on derived random values, in the proof that its authors call complete but not settled, for a prover that the written proof specifies, with a term for the generator for which no figure is known. The written argument treats random values that the prover derives from a stored key through one definition. Read literally, one item of that definition excludes every way of deriving them that relies on fresh random bytes for some of them, including the natural one and the one that the released programs are described as using for the random values of a request's proofs. So, read literally, the written statements on derived random values, among them the one that carries hiding over to the prover as specified, do not speak of the way of deriving that the released programs are described as using. In no reading are they about the programs: in one that takes in that way of deriving, they are about the protocol on paper with that way of deriving as it is described. The bound on the chance that two derived values come from the same bits is stated only for ways of deriving that have a property which the written proof names, and that property is proved of no released program. Read literally, that way of deriving as it is described also fails some of the conditions under which the bound is stated, and the written proof does not claim that these conditions are enough. The written proof says itself that, read literally, its definition and some of these conditions exclude that way of deriving as it is described, and it leaves both as they are.
Every cell of the weight table is in -128 to 127.

A weight tensor's storage type is one of seven, and it decides code paths in `cp_commit` and `cp_prove`: decoding branches, the forms of kernels, and the sizes of memory and of copies. So time and memory use can show it, and the list of what is shown on purpose does not name the storage type: count it as not hidden (row H41). Proof, key and leaf files were never compared across storage types.

The largest entry that the fitted scales show is that of a weight matrix after the normalisation gains and a fixed factor are multiplied in. For the routed experts it is one number for all experts of a layer.

Without a clock, a client that always has enough requests waiting to fill a batch learns how many requests of other clients a batch held, from how its own proofs group. That is reasoned from the code and has not been run.
A "failed" for an invalid request file is released with the batch before it, so it shows when that batch ended.

Only two bits of a request's failure word put substitute values into the forward pass, and so can change the routing and the time. At least two more depend on the request's hidden values (the range check's window, the policy's result). By a reading of the code of other programs (row HW-678), and by these sources' own comments (prover/prover/ends.h; prover/common/slot_flags.h; rows C3.1 and C3.1.1), `cp_prove` runs on through the same stages after a recorded failure, on substitute values where necessary, so that its steps do not show where it fails; within a stage the GPU launches can differ, and whether the running times are equal has not been measured. That rule has exceptions. At failures that depend only on challenges the host takes other branches, and after one of them it makes fewer hash calls, in the one case that was found. Which exceptions hold of the released programs was not gone through.
One key file belongs to one set of weights.

**How another request reaches a proof's bytes.** By the lines of the code that were read, without the bodies of the GPU kernels, another request of the batch reaches the bytes of a proof only as a salted leaf at a uniformly sampled place, and through the batch's key. The challenges of the batch's shared part, and of the client's own last part, depend on that leaf. That the shared part takes nothing of a request but the root of the batch's hash tree rests on reading alone. The programs compute over the field 2^64 − 2^32 + 1.
The small model has windows of 64 tokens.
The CPU code differs between test and production builds on purpose. It sets which GPU functions run, their order, memory and arguments, keys included.

On a real model's files, the proofs of two sets of programs cannot be compared byte for byte, because `cp_prove` samples fresh bytes for each batch. For a model whose weights are public, `cp_commit`'s files can, if both sets form the commitment ID by the same rule: with the option `-public-weights` and the same 32-byte file it makes the key file, the leaf files and the commitment ID again, byte for byte. No injected fault shows the outside count of opened positions at work.
By a reading of the code, a batch's shared part takes nothing of a request but the root of the batch's hash tree, over a hash of each request (row HW-16). That rests on reading alone.

It was found in a benchmark, where other shapes came out right, not in a run of the programs. **A gap in the design.** The prover and the verifier follow the same rule, so checking one against the other may not reveal a gap in the design. Some shared mistakes make every verification fail and so show at once, but others would not.

**What the audit leaves out.** The audit does not check masks inside tables of real values, the columns of the stored (masked) weight tables, or unopened leaves, whatever the parameter file. At the default setting one search for leaks is known, at small size, which by its own word is worth little (docs/limits.md#the-verdict), and none at full size. Such a search finds no leak that comes from the protocol's rule itself.

For the default setting's parameter file only docs/format/FORMAT.md, 16.1, is known to count the ten conditions on hiding that the programs test at every start, by its own formulas. The range checks on which `cp_prove` tests them and those on which the verifier does are compared by value only by a public tool (row H19.3; the public test `gpu.frame_readings`: SUITE.md), on the six small configurations that ship: no proof fails if they differ, a provider's own configuration is compared only if someone runs the tool on it, and the tool does not test that these are the lists on which `cp_prove` tested.

**Duty 3.** Duty 3 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions) guards against repeated random bytes, and it applies to the `cp_commit` machine too. If a saved state is started again, the original's own continued run counts as one of the two runs.

**Duty 3 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions).** By two readings of these sources, with nothing run, in a production build a batch's own private randomness follows from the seed (with 32 system bytes drawn once at the batch's start), the configuration digest, a constant of the program, the numbers of leaf tables and slots, the first live table's number, the requests in their slots, and the chosen table's name and answers. Two runs that continue from one state saved after that draw, with the same requests, have the same keys, and no input guards against it. Only a batch with the same requests on the same leaf table gets the same masks, and two runs that are equal in every byte show nothing new. Two such runs can differ: by a fault or a flag in one place, or by an input outside the key's digest. The same masks then lie over different data, the two runs' files can be subtracted, every proof still verifies, and nothing guards against it. The equations that follow reach the weight tables' long-lived masks as well as the weights, and no counter counts what is shown in this way. That the files can then be subtracted, that every proof then verifies, and how far the equations reach is reasoning, not a reading, and is not known of the released programs.

**Duty 3 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions), a machine booted from an image.** A machine freshly booted from an image does not break duty 3, if the system seeds its random generator freshly at every start and the image holds no secret key directory. The whole weight lies on that "if": no program can check it, nothing notices a source that repeats, and no operating system has been examined for it. "Booted" does not cover a machine resumed from a snapshot, a process restored from a checkpoint, or a clone made after the boot. A container shares its host's random generator, so what counts is how the host was started. An image can also carry a saved seed file for that generator, and two machines booted from it then begin alike unless each adds randomness of its own at boot.
**Duty 7 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions).** Under duty 7 the production build is made from the published sources, but the programs reject only some misuses of test options.

**Duty 12 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions), the commitment ID.** `cp_prove` is given no commitment ID: the check of duty 6 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions) gives it to `cp_verify`. It protects only if its value comes from somewhere that an attacker with write access to the secret key directory cannot write. Even then it does not cover the counters, the seed file or the lines of the directory's text file. Nor does it help against whoever can change the command line or script that runs that check, or write the directory of the `cp_verify` that it runs. It does not help against settings changed before the commitment was made, or a change to the model directory of an inference server beside the prover. By a reading of the code, nothing from outside the secret key directory is held against it when `cp_prove` starts: of the key file it reads nothing, of a table's kept entry, at a batch's start, only the first part, by form, and it compares the three configuration files only with the line `ranges` of `isk.txt`, which no key protects. So a writer of that directory who changes a configuration file and that line together passes the start. Such a service is stopped, by one of two self-checks on the stored tree (`hc-nodes-root`, `hc-own-node`), at the latest at the end of its first batch, which is by then taken and counted: every request of it gets "failed", no proof and no token leaves, and `cp_prove` ends with exit code 1; each new start repeats that (by a reading of the code, not run; no test plays it). If the writer also fits the stored nodes' file and the entry's root to each other, one check alone is left, the comparison at the opening (inferred); files in the weights' directory that lie outside the three configuration files and their digest were not looked into, nor were the options `-overlap` and `-overlap-two` gone through. Another commitment's whole directory is taken as it stands, and its proofs fail at the first `cp_verify` that is given the right commitment ID (rows H21.15 and R40). By two readings of these sources, with nothing run, `cp_prove` compares a changed OOD answer in the first part of a table's kept entry, its form kept, with nothing that can fail on it and serves on: each batch still spends the table's columns, and each such proof is bound to other answers than `cp_verify` binds, so that, by inference from the hash, it fails in the request's first chain, against the public leaf file; such a proof lacks no mask and shows no more than an honest one (by readings of the code, not run, in part); which test speaks first was not followed, and no test plays it. column3: **The read-back, first half.** The first half of the read-back check compares what is stored at a mask's place with what was sent to the write.

**The read-back, second half.** The second half of the read-back check keeps each mask as sampled, works out the GPU engine's address of its place again, for itself, and compares what is stored there with what was sampled. The place's index comes from the same routine both times, and a fault in that formula is not seen. A third comparison holds each mask that is read back against its sampling worked out a second time.

**What the audit of proofs does not check.** The audit of proofs by value does not check masks inside tables of real values, the columns of the stored (masked) weight tables, or unopened salts. No injected fault has been tried on a batch that a production build made. Each request has 45 or more masks inside tables of real values, and how many of them the audit can reach has not been counted.

**Exit code 9.** Exit code 9 means that a self-check on secret random values or keys has failed, and the last line names the check. One name, `own-test-coin-library`, can also mean that the operating system gave no memory page that a fork wipes: then no self-check has failed (docs/faults.md).
**After a fault.** Where its hold is not set, the example vLLM middleware keeps handing out earlier proofs after a fault (integrations/LIMITS.md).

**The seed.** Whoever reads the seed can strip the masks from every shown column of the anchor and can test a guess at the weights. Each unmasked column is one exact linear equation in a row's entries (an entry is one byte-sized digit of a weight), the same for all leaf tables, so the equations add up over batches and leaf tables. After enough batches under one commitment there are as many equations as unknown entries, and the weights then follow by interpolation: that limit holds at every parameter file. At full size it lies at about six million batches, at the default setting (a count from the design and the planner's numbers, not from a run: an upper mark, no margin). One leaf table's whole life gives about a ninth of that count, and fewer are needed if part of the weights is known. That is a count of linear equations, an upper mark on what is needed, not a margin of safety: because the entries are small numbers, far fewer equations may already fix them in principle, perhaps within one leaf table's life. Trained weights have less entropy than their public ranges, by an amount that is not known, and that can only help the seed's holder. For a small fine-tune of a known model no floor is claimed. No practical method is known for that, and none is ruled out. This is a count from the design, and none of it has been tried. It counts columns that the reader of the directory holds: a batch's columns are in the proofs that went to that batch's clients, and only those in the key file and the leaf files are public. Whoever reads the seed (for a leaf table: with that table's own secret, kept in the same directory) can also open every weighted sum that the commitment publishes, with no proof served. By design only the provider holds the seed, which no program can enforce, and no verifier needs it. Under `cp_commit -public-weights` the seed is derived from a file of 32 bytes that is given with the option, whoever has that file can work out every mask used for the key file, for the leaf files and for the stored tables' columns that proofs open, and the weights are not hidden.

**Where the hard link fails.** Where the system protects hard links (`fs.protected_hardlinks = 1`), or the attacking account can create no name on the weights' file system, that account gets no link. The setting must hold on every host that mounts the file system, from before the weight files are put there: a hard link made earlier passes every check. The setting itself was tried once, at the system call alone, on one machine, with one kernel and file system: never with the programs, with two accounts there, or switched off as a control. It does not stop code that runs as the files' owner or with `CAP_FOWNER`, or an account that can read and write the file.

The same values were in the programs' own GPU buffers at that moment, so a frame added a copy that could not be wiped, not a new kind of secret.

In three separate readings, every store to per-thread memory in it was followed, with controls in which a key put into a frame on purpose was reported, and nothing of the key was found. The readings were of other programs (row HW-678) and of code from the released programs' compiler, not of the released programs as linked (HW-213 tells what the listings show).

The key in a launch's constant memory or in uniform registers, and what a driver saves when it interrupts a kernel, were not looked at.

**One more frame.** In the released programs one kernel that hashes leaves with their salts (`k_last_pass`, prover/engine/encode_kernels.cuh) has a stack frame of 56 bytes per thread in every instance, and the compiler spills into it, by the tools' and the compiler's listings. What the frame holds there has not been read. By one reading of the machine code of one instance, not on the released programs, the frame holds spilled words of a column's running hash state before the salt goes in: hidden working values (the figures, the reading and its bounds: row H39.4).
**Count on less.** The service stops at the first full leaf table, even if others have room. Tables are picked at random, so the fullest runs ahead of the average and some batches are never used.

**The counter file.** Each weight table in the secret key directory has a counter file, `count.bin`, whose length in bytes is the number of columns counted so far. By a reading of the code, all of a batch's columns are counted before the batch's opening begins, so the count errs on the high side.

**A missing counter.** The programs never take a missing counter for 0, so a table whose count is lost is not served again. A counter that has been set back, by a rollback, a restored copy or a shortened file, is served: no program can detect that. The file system's append-only attribute (chattr +a, root's) is the one thing named here that stops a shortening, and no code of these programs sets it.

**A further commitment.** A further commitment to the same weights, under the same configuration files, lies inside the judgement on weight hiding, on thin ground and on conditions of its own (docs/limits.md#a-further-commitment). No leak is known in the programs where each commitment draws its own seed. A further commitment has a new seed, so all its masks are new, provided the random source does not repeat (rows HW-189 to HW-191). That does not hold under `cp_commit -public-weights`: there the same file gives the same seed, and the weights are not hidden. What two commitments to the same weights show together is covered by the written proof (not public: row HW-763) only on conditions that no program checks; Lean's theorem assumes one commitment, and no test has searched two together.
**Two commitments together.** No test has searched two commitments together. What happens to the same weights under another commitment scheme has not been examined at all.

**If the seeds are not independent.** After a machine image has been started twice with one seed, on changed weights under the same three public files, no column need be read: the two commitments' public files alone give exact linear equations in the two sets of weights (how: row HW-584). One column read under both commitments shows, for each row, one symbol of the encoded difference between the two sets of weights, without any mask, and a common column is not even needed: the two tables share their random tails, so the limit on opened columns holds for both together, and nothing counts them together. Over the same weights, which is the case at a renewal, a repeated seed gives the same key file's table and the same ID again; where the leaf tables' own random bytes repeat too, the second commitment is the first again with its counts at zero, and its masks would then be used beyond the limit for which they were sized. With another configuration, equal system bytes still give other random values. Two starts of an image give one seed only if the system's random source repeats or the image is a saved state. Under `cp_commit -public-weights` two commitments made with the same file also have one seed; there the weights are not hidden.

**Which policy fits.** The exact match policy fits when the integer model itself serves the replies. If a floating-point model serves them, a single token that is not the integer model's top choice means that no proof can be made.

**Under clipped gap: the start-up tests.** At every start all three programs test ten conditions on the parameter file, and reject a file that leaves too few random values. The ten look at counts, not at values, are not shown to be the right ten, and have not been seen to stop `cp_commit` or `cp_prove`. These tests have not been traced to the end under the clipped gap policy.
Audits apart (rows H13.7 and H13.8), no test of hiding ran under a score policy.

**Fitted thresholds.** What a threshold fitted on a model's own replies reveals has not been worked out. By a reading of the code, such thresholds are exact statistics of the model's own costs on chosen replies (one cost, the largest mean, a count). By the repository's own pages and a search of its policy files, the release does not include an example policy file whose thresholds were fitted on a real checkpoint; one example has thresholds fitted on replies of a model exported from synthetic weights. A search for the two values that have been fitted on a real checkpoint's replies covers blocks/, docs/, prover/, scales/, tests/, tools/, toy/ and verifier/, and found neither there; it does not cover examples/ and integrations/. But the four policy files under examples/ are, byte for byte, files under prover/examples/, and the one under integrations/ has the exact-match lines (`C 256`, `theta 256`, `cap 0`). Nor does the search cover guide/, README.md, AGENTS.md, docs/README.md and docs/figures.tsv. Apart from it, 25,856 and 512, the full-size clipped-gap example's `C` and `theta`, were set beside the thresholds fitted on a real model's replies, and neither equals any of them (`cap 1` was not searched for). Other lines of the example files depend on a real model's public weights, or may; the pages name Llama 4 Maverick and Llama 2 7B (`THIRD_PARTY.md`, "What depends on Meta's models").

**For the programs.** For the programs, hiding also assumes the hash and the system's random bytes. The random generator adds at least one assumption: that ChaCha20's block function is a pseudorandom function under a secret key. It is a computational assumption, and its standing rests on cryptanalysis only. That assumption does not bring the programs' way of deriving random values under the written argument (HW-6). The chain of calls by which a key of the prover's private random values is derived, each call taking a key and four words to the next key, is the cascade construction of a paper of 1996 (Bellare, Canetti, Krawczyk, "Pseudorandom functions revisited: the cascade construction and its concrete security", FOCS 1996), which treats inputs none of which is the beginning of another. The form of that paper's bound, of the order of ε · n · q for q inputs of n blocks of which none is the beginning of another, where ε bounds the advantage against the function that is chained, is as the abstract of Pietrzak, "A Closer Look at HMAC" (Cryptology ePrint Archive, Paper 2013/212), renders the result; it is taken from that abstract and not from the 1996 paper itself. The 1996 paper's argument has not been written out for this chain. The service also uses SHA-256. A request ID is the SHA-256 hash of the request and a secret nonce of the front end, and the IDs order a batch's places. That order is independent of the requests' content only if SHA-256 is modelled as a random oracle. A response's tag is HMAC-SHA-256 under a key made from that nonce, and no listed assumption covers HMAC-SHA-256. Nor does a listed assumption cover SHA-256 as a random oracle. The nonce is drawn from the system's random bytes, and none of the three routines that draw it (driver/spool.py, integrations/spool.py, prover/prover/spool.h) checks the bytes.

**A later break.** If one of the assumptions listed here is broken later, everything published by then can be unmasked or tested against guesses. That includes the hash, because published proofs hold salted digests of unopened leaves.

**The value without its own mask.** In each sub-proof with weights, one value has no mask of its own, and an entry of the request's table of masks covers it. If the GPU's copy of that entry is lost, and is still lost after the sub-proof's last kernel, no request of the batch gets a file: if the kernel read it before it was lost, a self-check by value (own-test-slot-pads) ends the run; if not, a guard of the proof library does. If the kernel read that entry wrong from a cell that is right again at the self-check, no self-check by value sees it: the value is then formed under a wrong cover, or, with the entry read as 0, under none, and it is a linear form of the weights. It does not leave the prover. At the request's end, before any file of the batch is written, `cp_prove` proves its claim on that value with the host's copy of the entry, and a guard of the proof library on the prover's own sumcheck (blocks/iop/psc.h) then fails: `cp_prove` ends with exit code 1 and the name `guard` (not a self-check's code 9), and no request of the batch gets a file. The guard does not see a fault that the host's copy shares: if the draw and its second implementation share one, all copies agree, the proof verifies, and the value is sent unmasked. Nor does it see what happens to the bytes after it. By reading the code, not run: no test of this repository plants such a fault in `cp_prove`; blocks/iop/tests/psc_stops_test.cpp triggers the guard at toy size. What it costs that this value has no mask of its own has not been worked out.

**Other losses of that entry.** If the CPU's copy is lost after the table is sent, a self-check (`own-test-index-mask`) stops it when a sub-proof takes that entry, with exit code 9. Of the table's other entries, which the test on the weight table reads as masks of sums that are linear in the weights, no check after the one at the sending has been found, by readings of the code: a loss there, after the sending, is stopped by nothing in `cp_prove` that has been seen. By the like reasoning the proof is then false, with such a sum under a wrong cover or under none. It leaves the prover, and only `cp_verify`, run before the response leaves the provider, keeps it from a client (duty 6: docs/limits.md#the-conditions; row H26). Read, not run. Only after a loss in the table itself, between sampling and sending, would the proof still verify, and a check of the whole table looks for that and ends `cp_prove` with exit code 9.

**Worst-case step.** `cp_commit` computes worst-case bounds from the weights and the scales, into a table that is to be kept as secret as the secret key directory. The fitting tool's worst-case step reads that table and makes each scale that falls short coarser by the number of bits by which it is short. So the public scales then depend on the norms of the weight matrices' rows, but they do not hold the bounds.
**Evidence.** The figures on fitted settings come from the fitting tool's formulas. No file fitted to full-size weights was examined.

**Testing a guess.** A guess at a request's tokens can be tested by whether `cp_verify` accepts, but only for all the tokens together. Whether a guess at fewer tokens can be tested against a proof file in some other way has not been examined.

**Window, checked range, next token.** The model and its range checks run on the whole window, but the acceptance policy looks only at the checked range, from one token up to 1,023. A proof covers the next token, the one after the window, only if the checked range ends at the window's last position.

**What a failed self-check does.** The self-checks whose name begins `own-test-` look at secret random values or keys; each prints its name in `cp_prove`'s last line and ends `cp_prove` with exit code 9, most of them at once and a few at the next end of a batch. A few checks on random bytes, keys or counters end it with exit code 1, at least two of them without a name. A few others, on data and not on random values, fail while `cp_prove` goes on, and most of the rest end it, so its batch fails.

**The wait after a failed self-check.** The clients whose requests were in progress hear nothing until the next start, which answers "failed"; a comment in the code and the runbook (`docs/operators-duties.md`) say so. One of the authors' GPU tests asks for exactly this; no run of it on the released programs is known.

**What a failed self-check can reveal.** Some self-checks read hidden values, and a partial reading of the code of other programs (row HW-678) found none that fails for some weights and not for others, unless a value leaves its range. It read the proof library's roughly 770 conditions once and did not always open a helper that a condition calls. It read the prover's own stops in part, and the GPU engine's checks not at all. By a reading, also of the code of other programs, a value out of range fails only its own request and does not end `cp_prove` (in these sources: prover/prover/ends.h; row C3.1.1). Readings, also of the code of other programs, found no way for a request to end `cp_prove` with exit code 9, but for the self-check on one-time masks that rests on no kernel writing into their memory at an index that depends on data, which is not fully established. It has not been shown that the end of a process tells nothing about the weights.

**A request that a verifier rejects.** Two readings, made apart, of the code of other programs (row HW-678) found no request that can make a verifier reject a response or run long. That was not tested, and the readings do not close one lever: memory that moves with what the requests hold. One such request was nevertheless found, under one kind of clipped-gap parameter file (row HW-412). By another reading, also of the code of other programs, `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` reject such a file at their start (the rule stands in these sources: prover/common/parameter_file.h; row R16.3). The programs have not been run on such a file; the routine that reads it was tried on 144 parameter files on a CPU. Not known: whether a client can make a verifier reject a response at will in some other way, which would cost the whole batch, and at the vLLM integration a hold on that policy until a person lifts it.
**A request's own failure.** No hiding test looked at a batch in which a request failed.
**Not known.** Whether a client can make a self-check fail in some other way, or change memory use; whether the verifier's time depends on the number of checked tokens, which the client chooses.

**Sizes that depend on content.** Only some memory allocations have been checked for dependence on hidden values, and three sizes depend on content. Two are fixed at the end of set-up, but the third, a small list of address ranges, is allocated again inside each batch, and a failed allocation there ends `cp_prove`.

**How content gets in.** Each 256 KiB piece of recorded GPU memory that is not all zeros gets a second copy; the weights themselves are excepted, and the size on the GPU is capped. Tables made from the weights may be among that memory, and which of them, if any, has not been followed. Of three readings of the code, two could not trace what the memory holds. The third found only configuration values for one of the two kernels, and could not finish for the other.

**Two synthetic models.** The model server's reply times told two synthetic models apart. That was with no prover behind the model server, at full size, for a tester on the server's machine who held both models and chose the prompts. One model was a copy of the other with one of its 24 routers redrawn, and the tester told them apart in all 24 groups of five request pairs. The model server was the engine that serves the integer model (`integrations/vllm/integer_model/`), and that engine does not hide its timing. By its time two synthetic models have been told apart, at full size on a form of the engine that is not in this repository and at a small size on another such form, nearer to the released one, each time by somebody who knew both models and chose the prompts. Solving for weights from it has not been tried, how much it tells of a model's weights is not known, and no statement bounds it.

column3: **Kernels.** By readings of the source code, 110 of 611 GPU kernels have a memory address, an atomic operation's address, a branch or a loop count that follows a hidden value. In `cp_prove` these follow not only the routing, but also attention scores, the position of a row's largest score, the logits and their histogram, the checked token, lookup keys computed from activations, and each norm, in the loops of its square root. So time and memory traffic can depend on these hidden values too. In the output head's kernels, branches, loads and a loop's bounds follow a request's two range numbers, and the embedding's loads follow its tokens; so time and memory traffic can follow another client's checked range and tokens (by a reading of the code; both kernels stand in the sources, by a search). All of this holds in honest runs, when nothing fails, in kernels of the forward pass, of the lookups, of the sub-proofs and of `cp_commit`. By the same readings, CPU code follows the secret arrangement of a batch's hash tree, but CPU code was read only to find launches and to trace operands. Of the 499 other kernels that were read, 274 have a condition of a kind that the readings' rule left out, the field's reduction among them; no count of those in which the value is a hidden one is known. Nothing was compiled, run or measured. The count may be incomplete, and it has not been made on the released programs. It does not cover the 83 kernels of the GPU engine (`prover/engine`), and, by a reading of the code, at least one of those has such a dependence on the weights. It leaves out one known kind, kernels in which a request's place in its batch picks the memory regions: these were neither listed nor counted, and that part of the released programs has not been read for this count.

**Counting leaf tables.** No public file states how many leaf tables a commitment has (a file in the secret key directory does), and neither the configuration's digest nor the commitment ID covers that number. They can still be counted, because `cp_commit` writes one public file for each and a proof's head carries its leaf table's number.

**File times.** `cp_commit` zeroes its public files' access and modification times, but not their change times or the directories' times. The differences between the files' change times therefore show how long each step of the run took. A first read can move a file's access time.

**Who can read a change time.** The change time of one of `cp_commit`'s public files is visible only to someone who gets the files' metadata from the directory that `cp_commit` wrote, through a share, a hard link or a copy that keeps times. A client who is handed copies of the bytes cannot read it.

**The embedding.** `cp_commit`'s check that every weight is in its declared range makes an exception for the embedding, whose entries may have any magnitude below 2^30, whatever its declared width. By a reading of the code, with nothing run, `cp_commit` prints whether the embedding is wider than its declared width, which is one bit about the weights. It also prints the seconds that its checks of the weights took, which follow the weights. What these lines tell beyond that has not been examined. On other programs (row HW-678), `cp_commit` printed, with the worst-case check, a short table computed from the weights, and nothing in the program kept it back (one of the five ways that row HW-576 tells). That was noted on public weights, and never seen on secret ones. As reported, the table was printed by those programs as built by default, which is not their serving build, and with secret weights the print would have been a leak; their serving build did not print the table. By one reading of the code, a short table computed from the weights goes only into a file that the operator names. One fast reading of these sources found all three as told here: the line on the embedding's width, the seconds, and the table that goes only into the operator's file.
