column3: **A failed request's leaf.** A request that fails because of a range check or a wrong token, once it has got as far as its seal, keeps its real leaf, a salted hash of its own state, in the batch's hash tree. A place in which no request was seated (a malformed file) gets a random leaf. Only the hash and the salt, 40 random bytes that are never sent, separate that state from a neighbour in the batch. That a leaf's salt is used in that leaf alone has been traced in part of the code only. What such a digest shows has not been worked out: that it reveals nothing is argued on paper but for the last step, and not for the programs. The published theorem on hiding through salted hash trees is proved for salts of twice a digest's length, here 64 bytes. By a reading of the code, the programs' salts have 40 bytes by default, so that bound cannot be claimed for them. By a note of this project, which was not checked again, the theorem's error term is also far too loose at hash trees of this size: it gives the method, not a bound.

**Anyone who holds the secrets.** A digest of all the requests in a batch goes into the batch's key, so anyone who holds the seed and the batch's fresh bytes can test any guess at the other requests against a proof file. Fresh bytes are random bytes sampled again for each batch, and, run as a service or on a model's files, `cp_prove` keeps them nowhere.

**An assumption of the argument.** The hiding argument assumes that honest clients do not act on the bytes of their proofs. What they ask next may depend on the weights, on public data and on what the colluding clients see, but not on bytes of a proof that those clients do not see. What the other clients send, and when, is theirs to decide and can depend on what they received. A client that continues a conversation, or sends the prompt of a failed request again, changes how many requests later batches contain and when they are taken. So the grouping and the time of release can carry something of another client's outputs and failures too.
**The front end.** `cp_prove` has no front end of its own and does not keep clients apart, and anyone who runs a front end sees every prompt and every response.

**The example vLLM middleware.** With the example vLLM middleware that ships, whoever has a proof ID, and has the shared key where vLLM was given one that the middleware can read (how the middleware learns that key, and where it cannot: integrations/vllm/REFERENCE.md#the-operators-checklist), can fetch that one proof, delete it, and test guesses at its prompt and reply. The middleware does not authenticate each client. The routes stay open where vLLM has a key that the middleware neither reads nor suspects (for instance another vLLM than the pinned 0.29.0; the cases: the same checklist). There, setting VLLM_API_KEY closes them. Count on no warning: try one call without a key. That its routes ask for vLLM's API key, however vLLM was given it, where the middleware can read it, and that the variable closes them elsewhere, is by a reading of the pinned wheels, and by tests with a stand-in for vLLM's application: the middleware has run under vLLM, not on the released programs, at toy size, and four times at full size, there with the key in `VLLM_API_KEY` alone (what those runs called, and what they did not: row H11.2). The few runs that joined the middleware to the programs: integrations/LIMITS.md. A fault that these sources do not have: a form of this middleware that is not in this repository knew `VLLM_API_KEY` alone, and left these routes open at a start with `--api-key` alone: in a run at toy size, not on the released programs, calls without a key were given the list of policies, a job's state and its whole `proof.bin`. The released middleware takes the keys that vLLM asks for; in a run at toy size, not on the released programs and not with the middleware exactly as it is in this repository, such calls got status 401 (integrations/LIMITS.md).
**Builds outside the comparison.** The comparison of the test and production builds does not cover test builds with one more switch.

**Test seeds.** Some checks are off under a test seed, so the tests that recomputed a proof's masks under a test seed did not run the production build's code paths, and nearly every check of a proof's masks by value ran on a test build. A proof of the production build can be checked that way only in a batch made with `-keep-for-the-audit`, outside a service, on synthetic weights; a few such batches have been audited. The repository's own audit compared less than a quarter of the proofs' bytes by value where the share is known, and has never been shown a faulty public file of full size (rows H13). No injected fault has been tried on such a batch.
**The audit with the provider's secrets: what it does not check.** The audit does not check the weight tables' columns, or unopened leaves of trees that hold real values.
**A client's files under two neighbours: not compared.** No test in the suite compares one client's files under two different honest neighbours.

**The main self-check.** In a one-request batch it compares the random entries of GPU-made encoded rows alone. The rest of the random values are words of salts that are not kept. By a reading of the code, a further comparison looks at them (HW-344).
**Silent losses at full size.** No test at full size injected a loss that leaves a proof which verifies.
**The worst-case check: not shown.** It has not been shown that the list of kinds is complete, that the bounds are right, or that the prover's integers are the same as those that this check bounded.

**The worst-case check: the verdict and the served weights.** Only the run of `cp_commit` that checked and committed the weights writes the line that records the verdict. `cp_prove` does not start without that line, and no proof is released on other weights. But that line is plain text under no key, and nothing in it depends on the weights, so whoever can write the secret key directory can set it, and nothing in a proof shows that the check ran. No test tries that.

**The worst-case check: arithmetic.** The bounds assume that the GPU library computes the classical matrix product in IEEE binary64. Two guards test this in every run, and if one fails no commitment is made.

By a reading of the code, a self-check compares part of a folding step's mask with a second derivation (HW-497). Whether that self-check would stop a re-used mask in the GPU programs has not been tried.
**The sending routine.** The library's sending routine cannot tell mask rows that hold fresh random values from those that hold data.

**The ten tests at start-up.** The fault: too few random values in the parameter file. The check: ten tests at start-up, in all three programs. Its blind spot: not shown to be the right ten, and passing them proves nothing by itself. Nor do they guard the numbers that they are tested on (row LF-18). Never seen to stop `cp_commit` or `cp_prove`.

**The self-checks by value after the hashing, and the provider's check.** The fault: a value lost after it was hashed in. The check: on private random values that the host keeps (mask rows and their random tails, the masking word of a proximity test's last step, a fold's mask, those entries of the index-mask message that a sub-proof takes; the others: row HW-245), self-checks by value compare them with their draws again after the hashing, at their next use, and end `cp_prove` with exit code 9. On an opened column of the stored weight table, its salts are made a second time and its hash is held to a stored node, and nothing is written where either fails (row HW-574). These see neither a value that is overwritten after them nor the copies that the engine has encoded. (By a reading of these sources, not run.) On any other value, on a value lost in GPU memory, and on a salt or word of an opening of a run's own trees, none in `cp_prove`: the file leaves, and the provider's check of the whole batch with `cp_verify` (duty 6: docs/limits.md#the-conditions) is what rejects it. That check's blind spot: that `cp_verify` rejects every such file is argued, not proved. For many faults it is the only check.

**The second implementation, on a leaf table's masks (row HW-685).** The fault: a leaf table's masks, when it is made. The check: second implementation. Its blind spot: first group of parts only. Salts are not compared then.

**The recomputation at every opening, on a leaf table's masks and salts (row HW-685).** The fault: a leaf table's masks and salts, at every opening. The check: other GPU code recomputes each opened column, which must fit the stored tree. Its blind spot: a salt at a column never opened, and the few routines that this check and the second implementation share.

**The second implementation, on a leaf table's masks, when the table is made (row HW-685).** It compares every mask of every row, in the production build too. Later groups of parts make the same masks again without a comparison.

**A leaf table's own masks or salts (row HW-685): later losses.** By a reading of the code, a later loss ends in a visible failure at an opening (a failed batch) and unmasks nothing. A loss only among the later groups, or only at an opening, has not been tried.

**The second implementation, on sub-proof masks (row HW-686): further comparisons.** It also compares two of the key file's tables of masks and their random tails, and the random tail of each request's table. No test is known that makes the comparison of a request's tail fire.
**Shared code.** Several checks share a routine or a number with what they check.
**Known-answer self-tests.** The known-answer tests at start-up have been checked only by reading the source, and no whole program has been seen to stop at one.
**The production build.** No self-check on a lost random value has been seen to fail there, because no fault can be injected into a production build.
**One lost mask.** One lost mask can give away at least one exact linear equation, in the weights, in a table's random entries, or in the client's own internal values.
**A value lost in CPU memory (row HW-689): the audit.** The audit tool, which holds the provider's secrets, can find a bug that shows in every run, but never an accident of one real run.

**A value lost in CPU memory: the key file's second table.** Two of the key file's tables of masks are compared right after they are sent. That comparison does not see the copies that are handed to the engine for the encoding, or a fold mask's own table.
**Salts at unopened leaves: a lost salt.** A lost salt lets someone test a guess at its leaf. Whether testing such a guess is feasible has not been worked out.

**Salts at unopened leaves: compared, by reading.** By a reading of the code (prover/hiding/engine_coins.cuh, prover/engine/stream_coins.cuh), `cp_prove` compares every word of every leaf's salt of the hash trees that its GPU engine builds, as it lies in GPU memory after its tree is made, with the generator run again. It is judged only at the end of the request and of the batch. By a reading of the code, each verdict comes before the parts that it judges are staged. But a request's first part is staged, under no final name, while the salts of the shared part and of the request's second part are still unjudged. Unseen: a fault that both sides share, a hashing kernel that misreads a salt, and, by this comparison, the salts that are made again for an opening (only the verifier's path check tests those, outside the prover). The salts of the tree that ties a batch together are not compared. Under a generator other than the GPU's own the salts are not compared at all, and nothing says so; by the same reading another check then ends `cp_prove` later.

**Left-over values.** The matrices of a request's sub-proofs end in filler cells, whose content the verifier does not fix; `cp_prove` sets them to zero twice and counts the zeros before it commits, and a request whose count is off gets no proof. By a reading of the code, the count covers the filler cells of twelve matrices only. The two matrices that hold the residual stream going in and coming out are not among them (HW-570). By a reading of the code, the second write only repairs: it checks nothing and tells nobody. Where it makes up for a lost launch, the run gives the honest files and no line, so the operator never learns that the GPU lost work. Whether a value that got into such a cell after the count would be masked like any other cell has been argued only: no proof and no run shows it. A left-over in a place that must itself be random is a lost mask.

While a hash tree of the GPU engine is built, nothing detects a store that is lost (prover/engine/tree.cuh, `begin()`; what clears the trees before use: row H45; the two checks that come later: row HW-458).

**A rejected GPU launch: noticed, not tested.** By a rule of the code, which a test that reads the sources checks, the programs notice a rejected launch before anything is released. No run shows that on a whole program. A silent loss shows only as a false proof or a lost mask, and a false proof can leave the prover (row HW-491). No test rejects a launch in a whole `cp_commit` or `cp_prove`.

**A rejected GPU launch: an assumption.** One library call is known to reset the status that records a rejected launch. It is assumed that no other does, and that was checked only on CUDA 13.0, which the build rejects. The programs make that one call only through a macro that reads the status directly before it, and a test reports the call's name anywhere else.

**A batch's fresh random bytes.** The only test on a batch's 32 fresh bytes is that they are not all zero. Any other constant, public or repeated key is still taken. No test compares responses of different batches.

**Repeated randomness: roll-backs.** A machine or process rolled back to a saved state can bring a batch's masks back, if the state was saved after the batch's random bytes were sampled or the system's random source repeats (by a reading of the code a rolled-back directory alone does not bring a batch's masks back: row HW-429). A rolled-back secret key directory brings a leaf table's masks back under new columns.
**Full size.** No test in the suite runs at full size or reads the production build's randomness (runs at full size outside the suite: row HW-461).
**Secrets in files.** No test in the suite searches the published files, or what a run leaves on disk, for the values of secrets.

**The clearing's test.** The test that ships with the clearing of a hash tree's memory checks one case: a leaf digest that is left unwritten must go out as zeros. That test does not try a lost store higher up in the tree, and the lost block itself may still go unnoticed. What a store that is lost in such a tree leaves, by a reading of the code: row HW-458.

A lost GPU launch is a cause of the faults that no check has been seen to catch, not a further kind. No test leaves out a GPU launch in the sums that mask the normalisation, so what such a lost launch would show, and whether a self-check would notice, is not known from a run. In a batch with other requests, no test injects the loss of a copy of a mask, only of its sample. Nor does any give one place in the batch another place's one-time masks, or inject a loss in a process's second batch alone.

By a reading of the code, no service starts without the line of `cp_commit`'s worst-case check, except under a test seed on synthetic weights. The GPU compiler's fault that was seen in a test appeared with nothing tampered with. The build tests for that fault on one small kernel only, and runs the test only where a GPU is present. That says nothing about any other kernel.
A biased mask has not been tried.

Several rules on what the GPU programs read, write and print are checked only by tests that read the source. Of two other tests of that kind, on the random generators' keys, one missed most of the changed spellings that were tried. The other, in a form that is not in this repository, was got round in 21 tries of 21, and those kinds of change are among the breaches that it must catch.

column1: # PS-1 to PS-22 and PS-33: where the programs differ from the protocol of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, as far as the report does not fully cover the difference. In these rows the basis opens with a mark of that report's (covered, covered in part, not covered), which is about that one difference. Covered means that the report also has a statement about the protocol on paper with this one change. It does not mean that the programs are proved, or that all the changes are covered together. A few of the report's results take several differences together, but none takes all of them. The kind names the property that the difference might affect. A property that is not named means that the comparison named no effect on that property, not that it ruled one out. Such a mark can differ between parts of a difference. Covered under an assumption means covered, but under a named assumption beyond the random oracle. After covered in part, the basis says which part. A plain covered in this table comes with a condition that is known only from reading the source. Not covered means that the report's theorems are stated only for the protocol as the report defines it.

column3: Where identities are tested. Four identities are tested at a point that the segment's lookup has sampled. These tests have no round and no error term. The statement for these tests, in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, has three hypotheses; that the programs meet them is known only from reading the verifier's source. Where the three can be read here, under the word "conditions": a comment in prover/prover/plan_rounds.h ("Three conditions must hold") writes them out for one of the four tests; docs/format/FORMAT.md, 13.6, names that comment and two more; the comments argue the bound without proof, under the same three conditions, which no program checks.
column5: Covered in part; not covered: the step from the conditions to the model's reply. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that report's own, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67).

column3: A segment's zerochecks. The first segment has two zerochecks, in three verifier messages: two of the three hold the two parts of one point, for one family of identities. An attention segment puts the points of two zerochecks in one verifier message. It has two further messages of one element each, whose powers are the coefficients, each before its sumcheck. A third such element is no coefficient of a zerocheck: it batches the closing claims of a sumcheck at one point; one more element batches two sum predicates. The last segment has the form of a segment of layers: a point alone, with the identities of the normalization one by one, until a later element batches all claims. In each attention segment (12 of the 25 segments at full size), the points of two zerochecks are drawn in one message, before the coefficients that batch them. The programs charge each later draw a round error of its own. A technical report that is not public and not refereed has a lemma on a message that holds points alone, which has the points of two families in one verifier message as a case. That the programs meet what the lemma asks is a reading of the verifier's code, and the lemma is carried to the programs' order by an argument in prose. What the lemma asks was gone through only briefly, for another form of the same row, and not at an attention segment. Missing is a statement that the programs' identities are the summands of a partition of the model's conditions, and that has not been looked at. Which identities each of attention's two points serves was traced by a brief reading of the verifier's code, not on the released programs; nothing was run, these steps were not attacked by a program, and the reading has not been checked independently.
column5: Covered in part: several zerochecks, the further elements and the points of two zerochecks in one message; not covered: the step to the model. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that report's own, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67).

column3: Sumchecks on a product of two maps. Attention's sumchecks on products of two maps reveal both maps. Such a sumcheck also proves the sums of squares of a normalization, and the entry-by-entry product of a feed-forward block's gate and up projections. After some of these sumchecks one element is sampled that nothing reads. The conditions are that the sumcheck's degree bound and its mask entries fit what it reveals. By a reading of the source there is a mask entry for each revealed value. For soundness, these conditions were read one by one, in readings of minutes each, against the verifier's code, for every sumcheck outside the lookups, from one list of questions that was shorter than the hypotheses and had no question on one of them; no condition was found to fail (not on the released programs). That rests on reading alone: no program was built or run, these rounds were not attacked by a program, and the readings have not been checked independently. The code that tests, at a segment's end, the one equation into which these claims are batched was read at single places only, in few of these readings, and that the range check ties the reads to the cells was taken as given. By the same readings every round runs a degree bound that is at least the one asked. For hiding these readings say little: they mostly could not tell whether the mask entries are uniform. "Reveal" here means that what is sent for each map is its end value under a mask entry, not the bare value.
column5: Covered in part: each sumcheck by itself, on one condition; not covered: that element, and the lemma on the model's segments, in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, with these sumchecks. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that report's own, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67).

column3: Maps that a sumcheck does not reveal. One sumcheck of a layer's segment reveals only some of its maps, and its closing claim enters the next sumcheck's target. The conditions are that its degree bounds, its mask entries and the maps that it does not reveal fit. For soundness, these conditions were read one by one, in readings of minutes each, against the verifier's code, for the two sumchecks, from one list of questions that was shorter than the hypotheses and had no question on one of them; no condition was found to fail (not on the released programs). That rests on reading alone: no program was built or run, these rounds were not attacked by a program, and the readings have not been checked independently. The code that tests, at a segment's end, the one equation into which these claims are batched was read at single places only, in few of these readings, and that the range check ties the reads to the cells was taken as given. For hiding these readings say little: they mostly could not tell whether the mask entries are uniform.
column5: Covered in part: if these conditions hold; soundness and hiding both rest on these conditions. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67).

column3: A lookup's claim on its keys. No sumcheck reduces the claim that a lookup leaves on its keys. Instead the verifier sums out that claim's variables itself, with weights that it computes. That the programs' sum is the same is known only from reading the verifier's source. By a reading, not on the released programs, in each kind of segment the sum which the verifier forms is the one that the lookup leaves, given that each entry of the reads' message is the read that its place stands for. That finding has limits. It holds only for parameter files that pass certain tests of the verifier, which rejects the others. It is about the table of keys that the verifier's own weights and forms define, and that table was not compared with the key maps of the lemma on the model's segments in a technical report that is not public and not refereed. It rests on the parts of a lookup and the columns of a part lying at aligned places, which follows from how the programs place them and which no line of code tests. Some points that bear on these terms were not asked: whether the summand that is taken, the numbers of variables, the addresses and the places of the values sent under a mask entry are public parameters; what form the targets of shown values have; whether the state gives the weights of a read; which virtual maps a summand that is taken may have; and whether a variable that is summed out is read by only one map. Each of these was gone through only in part, the public parameters only in passing. The conditions are what that report's result asks of such a sum (among other things degrees, mask entries, the maps that the sumcheck does not reveal, and the next token); soundness and hiding both rest on these conditions. For soundness, these conditions were read one by one, in readings of minutes each, against the verifier's code, for every sumcheck outside the lookups, among them those that take up this sum's inner sums, from one list of questions that was shorter than the hypotheses and had no question on one of them; no condition was found to fail (not on the released programs). That rests on reading alone: no program was built or run, these rounds were not attacked by a program, and the readings have not been checked independently. The code that tests, at a segment's end, the one equation into which these claims are batched was read at single places only, in few of these readings, and that the range check ties the reads to the cells was taken as given. For hiding these readings say little: they mostly could not tell whether the mask entries are uniform.
column5: Covered in part: for a sum that is the same. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that report's own, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67).

column3: A segment's lookup tables. The keys of all of a segment's lookup tables go into one lookup, with padding. In the last segment that lookup can read entries that count as padding. This happens if the vocabulary does not fill the last block. The programs arrange the last segment's columns, one for each token of the vocabulary, in blocks of equal size, and entries beyond the vocabulary count as padding. At the full-size example's vocabulary of 202,048 tokens it does not happen: the vocabulary fills its blocks.
column5: Covered in part: the lookup; not covered: a whole request with such entries. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67).

column3: A request's digest. The programs compute it with a second hash function of their own, which calls BLAKE2b's compression function directly. The request file's own words stand beside that digest, byte for byte, in the first BLAKE2b query of a proof's first chain. The same function also makes digests of public lists and tables that enter a proof's first hash query, and a technical report that is not public and not refereed treats these values as public parameters.
column5: Covered under an assumption, for the protocol of a technical report that is not public and not refereed; the released programs are not covered. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that report's own, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67). That report's bound is stated under the assumption that the two hash functions act as one oracle. Beside it: with the public files fixed beforehand, soundness against a prover rests on BLAKE2b, and on the weak assumption that the second hash function does not disturb its standing as a random oracle (by a reading of the code, not on the released programs; no formal proof); which four tables, bit for bit, a parameter file names hangs on the second hash function alone, on its collision resistance (docs/limits.md#what-the-theorem-assumes).

column3: Randomness. The programs generate all masks with ChaCha20, from one secret seed and random bytes from the operating system. Under `-public-weights` the seed is computed from a 32-byte file that the provider names, which need not be secret. Then no random byte from the operating system goes into a file of the commitment, but each batch still draws its own. A technical report that is not public and not refereed treats random values that the prover derives from a stored key through one definition. Read literally, one item of that definition excludes every way of deriving them that relies on fresh random bytes for some of them, including the natural one and the one that the released programs are described as using for the random values of a request's proofs. So, read literally, the written statements on derived random values, among them the one that carries hiding over to the prover as specified, do not speak of the way of deriving that the released programs are described as using. In no reading are they about the programs: in one that takes in that way of deriving, they are about the protocol on paper with that way of deriving as it is described. The bound on the chance that two derived values come from the same bits is stated only for ways of deriving that have a property which that report names, and that property is proved of no released program. Read literally, that way of deriving as it is described also fails some of the conditions under which the bound is stated, and the report does not claim that these conditions are enough. That report says itself that, read literally, its definition and some of these conditions exclude that way of deriving as it is described, and it leaves both as they are.
column5: Covered in part: under an assumption, for a prover that a technical report that is not public and not refereed specifies, and not for what the note tells of derived random values; under `-public-weights`: not covered, neither for the weights nor for the other requests of a batch. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that report's own, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67).

column3: Derived randomness. The main results need fresh, uniform randomness. The programs derive theirs with ChaCha20 from a secret seed and fresh system bytes, so their hiding is computational at best. It rests on an assumption about ChaCha20 for which no figure is known, and a later break or leak exposes what was already published. A technical report that is not public and not refereed treats derived randomness, under that assumption and for a prover that it specifies itself. But, read literally, the written statements on derived random values do not speak of the way of deriving that the released programs are described as using. In any reading they are about the protocol on paper, not about the programs. That report says this and does not correct it (row PS-8). That the operating system's generator gives uniform bytes is a further assumption.

The search for a proof of work. The prover sends the first value, in order, that passes, but it also tries later values along the way and so makes more hash queries. For a proof that is released, what the search reads is public, and the value that it finds is fixed by what it reads. That the programs' search returns the first value that passes, and that it uses of a later answer only whether it passes, is known only from reading the source. The cover, in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, rests on one sentence of a remark, which has not been checked independently. What the prover does at the search's cap must depend only on that fact, and nothing in the programs checks that it does. From reading the source, the programs' only cap is 2^63 - 1 tries, at which the program ends.
column5: Covered, up to the cap on the tries; outside: the time of the search, and a search that does not return the first value that passes. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that report's own, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67).

column3: Roots in a hash query. Under the rule that places messages in trees, a hash query holds at most three roots at the configurations that were compared, but no program checks the count.
column5: Covered, if the count of three is right. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67).

column3: Further hash queries. The programs make further hash queries: for the sources of the randomness, for digests that are printed or kept, and, in the verifier, for a digest of the parameter file that nothing reads. None enters a decision of `cp_verify`.
column5: Covered in part: those for the randomness, as far as row PS-8's limit allows; not covered: the others. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67).

column3: A request that cannot be served. The programs mark the request, run it to the end of its batch on substitute values and answer "failed". The other requests are answered. The programs learn that a request cannot be served only while they prove it. What a technical report that is not public and not refereed proves is for another kind of prover. For it, a public rule that looks only at the weights and the request decides which requests cannot be served. It forms no proof and runs no verifier for such a request. In all else it does what that report's prover does, under five conditions that the report names. It has not been shown that the programs are such a prover. Any client can send such a request at will, and for the other proofs of that batch there is then no statement about the prover as the programs implement it. No result bounds what the answer "failed" itself tells about the weights (row PS-49). A request can be served if the integer model runs to completion on all its tokens and the checked tokens meet the policy.
column5: Not covered for the programs; covered for a prover for which a public rule decides which requests cannot be served. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that report's own, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67).

column3: A proof that the provider's check rejects (duty 6: docs/limits.md#the-conditions). Nothing of its batch is handed on. (A check that comes to no verdict: rows PS-34 and PS-53.)
column5: Covered in part: a rejection; not covered: no verdict in time. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67). The code that was compared lets the prover itself have its proofs checked by the verifier. In the released programs `cp_prove` makes no such check, and the serving scripts that ship make it for a whole batch (duty 6). The serving scripts were not read for that comparison as the code was (row PS-62), so the mark does not come from a reading of this check. By inference it fits all the same: the report charges the event itself, so it makes no difference who holds the batch back. (What the bound charges where a whole batch is withheld, as that check withholds it: rows PS-31 and PS-32.) The report's statement is about one prover, not about a prover with a script beside it.

column3: What the prover counts. A technical report that is not public and not refereed counts batches, but the programs count, in a file, the columns that each leaf table has revealed. After a loss of power, a batch that was begun and has revealed no column yet may lose its place. By a lemma of that report, whose proof its authors call "complete but not settled" (what that means: row PS-23), for the interactive protocol with an honest verifier, every run begun on a leaf table counts in full. For a batch that is broken off further conditions apply: among them, the round at which it stops may depend only on what has been revealed and on randomness drawn anew for that decision, never on the weights, a witness, a request that is not revealed, or the committer's or the prover's secret random values. Whether one of the programs' own stops fires for some weights and not for others was not gone through stop by stop (rows HW-745, HW-256; what the written bound charges where the prover stops a batch: rows PS-31, LIM-44).
column5: Covered in part: as long as no counter is lost; not covered: a prover that loses one. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that report's own, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67).

column3: The last segment's conditions. The last segment always runs the equations of the clipped gap policy, even under exact match. The programs write some of the clipped gap policy's conditions differently from a technical report that is not public and not refereed, and one identity differs where the last segment has more columns than the vocabulary. A second matter: that report does not write out a complete layout for either version of the last segment, its own or the programs'. That is a gap in what has been shown, not a known fault (docs/limits.md#how-the-programs-count). For both versions it does write out and check the model's arithmetic and the numbers behind the error bounds.
column5: Covered in part: the conditions as a technical report that is not public and not refereed writes them; not covered: some that the programs write otherwise, and one identity. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that report's own, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67).

column3: The public parameters. The provider writes them in the configuration files, and the commitment ID commits to them. Only for the conditions on sizes is it argued on paper, in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, that the constants listed as the programs' and the tests listed as the verifier's imply them, with exceptions (row PS-18). That the programs have these constants and make these tests is a reading of the code, not a proof. The hypotheses on layout and on proximity have not been shown to hold for any file that `cp_verify` accepts, though the programs test the arithmetical ones on every file.
column5: Covered in part: if every choice meets the theorem's hypotheses; not covered: whether every accepted file meets them. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that report's own, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67).

column3: Configurations and the theorems' conditions. A configuration file can pass all of the verifier's checks and still fail one of the theorems' conditions, and that can break soundness. No complete set of parameters is known to meet all the conditions; a technical report that is not public and not refereed does not claim that one exists, and its list of the conditions is not proved complete either. The layout conditions, which say how data is arranged in messages and trees, have not been checked. The provider writes the public parameters (rows PS-17, PS-19). The theorems hold if every choice in the files meets their hypotheses. Whether every file that the programs accept does so is not covered. This is argued on paper for the conditions on sizes only: that report lists constants as the programs' and tests as the verifier's, and argues that these imply the conditions, with exceptions. That the programs have these constants and make these tests is a reading of the code, not a proof, and that reading itself finds a departure in one number (row PS-18). It has not been proved that the conditions suffice for the programs' own forms. Configuration files can also make the programs use other versions of some steps, and `cp_verify` can still accept (docs/limits.md#who-chooses-the-model).
column5: Reported: that report's own account, from its comparison with the programs' source code.

column3: Size conditions on the model's parameters. `cp_verify` tests its own inequalities on the configuration files before it checks a proof. A technical report that is not public and not refereed lists constants for the programs and argues on paper that these and the row's tests imply the size conditions, except for one clause that only completeness uses. That the programs use the constants and run the tests is known only from reading the source. One number differs in how its digits are written: a 23-bit part of a square root, written in three digits. That report puts the short digit on top and the programs put it lowest, which proves the same range.
column5: Covered in part: the tests imply the size conditions, but for one clause; not covered: the digits of one number. Read, and argued on paper: the mark is that report's own, from its comparison with the programs' source code, not on the released programs (what a mark means: row PS-67).

column3: Versions set by configuration. The configuration files can give the programs other versions of some steps, and `cp_verify` can still accept. A layout file can keep a segment's oracle messages longer or split them differently. A layout file can also leave places in the main rows of an oracle message that belong to no matrix. `cp_verify` tests that every entry of every matrix has exactly one place and that no place is taken twice, not that every place is taken. The shipped layout files leave places that belong to no matrix, in every oracle message that they place. No claim reads these places, and a technical report that is not public and not refereed has no statement for that form. By a reading of the prover's source it writes zeros there, the pad's own entries aside; nothing was run to show it. What that means for hiding has not been worked out. By readings of the source, with nothing run, the zeros are there only because each band of GPU memory is cleared before it is filled (prover/engine/lay.cuh). By one of these readings, stale GPU memory would be committed there if such a clearing were lost, and nothing would notice except at a pad's own entries. For soundness the zeros change nothing: a malicious prover may write what it likes there. Whether such places can help a false proof pass is not settled by any statement of that report, and no road to it has been found by a reading, not on the released programs. The tool that packs a layout leaves them by design. An oracle message's out-of-domain samples do weigh such places. column3: The written proof of weight hiding, in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, is what its authors call "complete but not settled": the proof is written out in full, but the checking that it has had is not enough to rely on it. Sentences of it were found false as worded, and it is not claimed that all of them are corrected. The correction of one lemma (on masks that are sent in advance) failed several times, and some of the failed forms had passed a reading; one of them had passed at least three readings, its writer's among them. The lemma as it is worded has not been read for the judgement on weight hiding. No reading under which the lemma as it stands is false is known. Readings name two points at which one hypothesis of the lemma is wanting: it lacks a clause that the proof uses (row RES-66), and it does not say what it asks of a run that fails. So, read strictly, one use of the lemma in the proof of hiding lies outside it: the use for the range check, when that check fails. So does the use that repeats it for the protocol on paper taken in the programs' order of messages. That the proof covers a failing range check all the same is the word of two of the three readings that found the point, after minutes each. Whether the lemma as it is worded holds is not known: it is not claimed that either point on its hypothesis is answered (row HW-763). Whether its conclusion could be had by another route if it failed cannot be said. Not every find has been traced. In the reading in shares that came nearest to reading the report whole (the report divided into shares of eleven to twenty-seven pages, a share read in ten to twenty minutes; that a share was read in full is its reading's own account), faults in four statements on which the proof of hiding rests were passed. A second reading of the same text found three of them, and the fourth was found only afterwards. Three of the corrections narrow what is claimed, and in one the claimed bound did not hold in a case that is excluded. Each correction had a single reading, of minutes. Other readings took some statements whole with their proofs and of others the changed places alone, in six to some thirteen minutes each. Six places were found loose: each was true as read, one of them only under the kinder of two readings, but said more or less than its ground gave, or could be read wrongly. The remark that holds two of the six has not been read whole as it stands. The forms that stand were read briefly and in few readings, some by their changed words alone or by their writer alone, and one change has not been read where it stands. Most changes, not all, were read by their changed words. How many changes have been read again only by whoever proposed them is not counted. Four of the six bear on the proof of hiding; one of these stands word for word, and the report lists it among the points that are left as they are. In one paragraph of proof one more sentence is loose, not false; the report says so and leaves it as it is. The definition of zero knowledge for the interactive protocol had an error: read to the letter, a condition was met by no environment that asks for a session. The error was recognised only after the statements had been closed to change, and it had passed at least four readings, among them that reading in shares. With the correction the definition asks more than its letter did, so the statements that conclude it say more and those that assume it assume more. The correction was read only briefly, and it has not been checked independently. The appendix on the programs was not held against the source code in its later readings: a clause on what the programs do stood through them, and was struck as never true of them. Some corrections were put in as given, and not all of these have been read. One change, in one statement's item on zero knowledge, has been read once where it stands and found true, without going through the places that cite it. That reading in shares did not cover all of the text as it stands: it covered nothing that was written or changed after it. It did not cover: the subsections on batches that overlap and on derived random values for the published OOD answers, what the report says on published OOD answers, the widening of one lemma on the parts of a session, the new form of the bound on repeated derived values, a paragraph in the corollary that puts the hiding argument together, one sentence of the main theorem on hiding, one of the remark behind it, and all of the last changes. The paragraph, with its proof, is about a third of the corollary's statement and over two fifths of its proof. A first wording of it was found false; the text that stands has had two readings. column3: What the results on hiding of a technical report that is not public and not refereed do not reach. How long a call runs, and how much memory it uses, is outside the definition itself. Among what lies outside the results are the following; the list is not whole, and more stands in rows PS-8, PS-9, PS-13 to PS-15, PS-31, PS-32 and PS-40. Random values that repeat for a reason outside their distribution, as when a machine image is started twice. (Whether a generator of random values that keeps state from one call to the next meets the definition's conditions, no sentence of the report says.) A prover that uses the first part of one request's proof again in a second batch: the tables that this part commits to would then be opened at the positions of two batches, while their randomness is sized for one. A prover that itself runs a withheld request again in the same call. A stop whose chance has no bound, such as a fault of a machine, with what its fact or its moment shows. A count that is copied or restored, or that is not one count for all processes, tested and raised in one step. A rule for choosing the table that reads more than the earlier choices. A count that is lost at a loss of power, for a prover with derived randomness and stops, as the programs are by a reading of their source. The results do not cover a proof file that was not among those meant for the attacker in its batch, or that was withheld, and that the attacker obtains only afterwards, or a check by the provider (duty 6: docs/limits.md#the-conditions) that gets no verdict in time, so that its batch is withheld. A proof that is meant for the attacker and is only handed over late is covered on paper, by one lemma (row PS-53). No Lean statement says anything about a batch with a failed or rejected request. On paper, the privacy of a batch's other requests is argued in a proof that its authors call "complete but not settled" (row HW-763). That argument covers batches in which every request is served. A rejected request is not served: to a batch that holds one the argument applies at most for a prover that the report itself defines, which rejects by a public rule on the weights and the request (row PS-13), and nothing shows that this is the programs' prover. Covered by the written proof (its authors call the proof "complete but not settled": row HW-763), for the prover that the report defines and under one commitment, are the following. Serving on after a failure, at a price in the bound; a failure here is a failed range check, a search that finds no value, or a rejection by that prover's own verifier, not a fault. A provider that checks the key file that it has just made and, if the check fails, makes another. The published key file has then passed a test, and is not drawn as the proof supposes. A provider whose counter of how often a leaf table has served loses counts, for example at a loss of power, so that a table can serve beyond its limit. The proof that the committed weights are well formed, or the proof that ties a leaf table to the first table, made a second time on existing tables. Each time it is made it opens further positions, and the limits leave no room for a second. Leaf tables that are made and published after the key file is out. By a reading of the code, not on the released programs, `cp_commit` rejects an attempt to add leaf tables to an existing commitment. When they are used up, a new commitment is made, which is the case of several commitments. For a further commitment to the same weights, under the same configuration files, that the weights stay hidden rests on [conditions of its own](limits.md#a-further-commitment): a count over two small commitments, not on the released programs, found no derived random value twice (a check for gross faults only), and no test has searched two together for leaks. Commitments under different configuration files. A provider that answers "no proof" to a request that could be served, marks the batch or runs it again because another request of the batch cannot be served. That shows a client one bit about the weights on a request that may lie outside what that client sees; the simulator is not given this bit, and whoever sends requests decides how often it happens. A written proof in a technical report that is not public and not refereed covers several commitments only under conditions that no program checks. Even then it leaves out cases, among them a request that is marked and withheld (row PS-40). No test has searched two commitments together. This part's status is no higher than that of the whole proof.

A request is bound by its own words. The first BLAKE2b query of a proof's first chain takes the request file's words (the tokens, then the two numbers) byte for byte, beside their digest under the second hash function (row PS-7). So distinguishing two requests rests on BLAKE2b, and on the weak assumption that the second hash function does not disturb its standing as a random oracle, with the public files fixed beforehand (a reading of the code, not on the released programs; no formal proof).

column3: What a mistake in code that was not read can do. A mistake in code that was not read can do three things. It can make a proof fail, and the verifier sees that. In the shared arithmetic it can weaken soundness, and no run reveals that. It can weaken hiding, for instance by losing a mask. `cp_verify` gives each masked value of a sub-proof an entry number of its own. From reading the code, the verifier ends without a verdict (`NOT CHECKED`) if its own code gives one place two values, and through the segment's equation it rejects a number that was sent under another entry than its own, or under none. But it would not notice an entry that is 0, or two entries to which the rule that derives the entries from the batch's key gave one value: these give a proof that verifies (row HW-581). Nor is it proved that under one key no two mask entries come from the same input of the keyed function. The programs' own checks catch a lost mask only in part. That is why comparing the programs with a technical report that is not public and not refereed says less about hiding than about binding.

What an answer tells. But for what it says of the programs by name (one sentence near its head, and its last three), this is said of the protocol of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, with its own scored last segment and a prover that it defines. Two numbered statements stand behind it: the corollary on hiding under a policy, which is for requests that can be proved, and the lemma on refused requests, whose simulator is given a shown request that is refused, with a mark, and nothing else about it. What the one fact says under each policy, and that nothing bounds many together, stands in remarks and running text, in no theorem. All else that this row says of the protocol stands in remarks and running text of that report, in no theorem. On paper each answer, a proof as much as a rejection, is one yes-or-no fact about the model's hidden scores, and so about its weights: whether the request can be proved; no statement bounds what many such facts tell together. For the programs one fact is no cap: each answer tells the client at least one yes-or-no fact about the model's hidden scores, even if the masks hold; no statement bounds how much. Under exact match the fact is that the model has an output and the checked tokens are its top choices. Under the clipped gap it is whether three things hold together: the model has an output; a sum of clipped gaps between the model's hidden scores is within a public bound; and the number of gaps above the clip is within its cap. A client that may choose the checked tokens, and sees which requests are proved, learns this bit for each request, and can narrow down differences of scores, up to the clip, by repeated requests. No statement bounds what these bits tell about the weights, and that report states no ceiling on it. The protocol does not prevent this: it limits the number of requests only by the number of sessions that a key serves. A provider can narrow it only outside the protocol, by proving only replies that it has served; even then the prompt before the checked tokens, the tokens after them and the range stay the client's choice. One lemma says that key and proofs add nothing to these bits; it does not bound what the bits tell. A policy that is fitted on the costs of honest replies under the committed weights is a function of the weights, and what it tells is not hidden. Of the programs: by that report's comparison with their source code they score under every policy, in a form that differs from its own in points of form. That the same narrowing is open to a client of the programs, wherever it may choose the checked tokens, is an inference. No sentence of that report compares the programs on this point.

column3: By default the service overlaps batches in time. With no option set, `cp_prove`'s service takes the requests of the next batch before the finished batch has its final names, and counts and proves it after that; a front end that keeps duty 6 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions), the vLLM integration among them, checks a finished batch while `cp_prove` goes on, so its clients can have a batch only after that check, whatever `cp_prove` has counted by then: nothing in `cp_prove` ties how many later batches it takes, counts and proves to whether a client holds an earlier one. In one process, by default, the proving itself does not overlap: a batch is proved whole before the next one is taken. That was read, not run. In the main experiments of a written proof, in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, a batch's proofs are handed over before the next batch is chosen. By default the service takes the next batch before it hands out the last one, and no proved statement covers the service as it runs that way. By one lemma of that proof the order by itself is not the cause: in its experiments a client that must choose blind, or sees proofs late or never, learns no more than in the plain order (the lemma has not been checked independently). The lemma has no item on stops or broken runs. The reading in shares that came nearest to reading the proof whole (row HW-579) did not cover the subsection on batches that overlap (row PS-23). What stays outside: in the service the machine's timing decides the order and who shares a batch, and an end of `cp_prove` can withhold one proved batch (row C3); with `-overlap` or `-overlap-two` a stop in a later batch can withhold earlier ones; and a rejection at the provider's check (duty 6) withholds that whole batch; the vLLM integration also wipes it (narrow exceptions, none open to a client: [integrations/LIMITS.md](../integrations/LIMITS.md#narrow-exceptions)). The lemma's "no more" is exact for fresh randomness only: with derived randomness it gives the plain order's error against a larger running time (what that proof's statements on derived random values do not reach: row PS-8). What is not covered is hiding. Each batch draws 256 fresh bits of its own, and its random values are derived from these, from the one stored root key and from its requests. They are the batch's own only if the deriving function is pseudorandom and the fresh bytes are uniform and never repeat. The deriving functions were not read for this, and every batch that draws a leaf table shares that table's masks by design. By readings of source code, and by an inference from them, the service as released meets neither the third nor the fourth of the four conditions of that proof's corollary on a service whose batches overlap, and that it meets the first has not been shown. Of the second no statement is made here. Who checks the proofs does not decide whether the service meets the third and the fourth. `cp_prove` works on a directory, where responses and "failed" answers appear unasked; the third condition, in its plain form, lets colluding clients get only proofs, at their asking. It takes a batch whenever it is free, which depends on hidden values (docs/what-is-not-hidden.md#time); the fourth lets only what those clients have seen decide that moment. A provider's check (duty 6) changes neither. The readings are of code whose prover checks its own proofs (row PS-14); of the released service this is inferred. That corollary gives a service nothing unless it is shown that the service's run, with each batch's computation moved back to the moment at which the batch was taken, is the corollary's experiment, and the four conditions as they are numbered are not claimed to be enough by themselves. No attack is known: three readings looked for one, minutes each, one of them in the source code of other programs (row HW-678), with nothing of the service run. The following is not certain. First, from reading the code: on one machine a second `cp_prove` that would serve or prove from the same secret key directory is rejected at its start, whether it comes as a service or for one batch: each such `cp_prove` locks the directory at its start and holds the lock until the process ends. Not caught: a `cp_prove` on a copy of the directory, and one on another machine that shares the directory, unless the file system applies the lock between machines. The lock may also miss one that reaches the directory by another route on the same machine (through a container's layer, from a virtual machine, or by a second mount). In all these cases nothing rejects the second process, nothing orders what the two release, and no statement on hiding is made. No attack is known, and none has been looked for in these cases. Second, if a batch does not pass the provider's check (duty 6), it is not handed on; in the vLLM integration, at a rejection the policy under which the batch was proved goes on hold and, where that hold can be written, only a person lifts it (row H26); at any other end the batch stays back, the check is tried again, and the policy can go on hold too; `cp_prove` learns nothing of it and goes on with the requests that it holds. That proof can be read as allowing this after a broken run, at the price that it states for such a run. One step of that reading is taken by no sentence of it: its statement is about one prover that checks its own proofs, not about a prover with a serving script beside it. And the reading holds only where that proof's own verifier would say no. `cp_verify` refuses more, and where a batch is kept back for such a no, or because the check came to no verdict, that is no broken run, and this reading does not apply (row PS-34). Third, a failed request that is sent again at once is, read literally, a case that the proof lists as outside its results. What that proof says about a client that sends a failed request again does not reach a request that is sent again to the service, at once or later. Fourth, the order in which a front end passes the files on to clients has not been examined. Nor have the two options, `-overlap` and `-overlap-two`, under which the prover proves several batches at once, been examined; `cp_prove` rejects `-overlap` on a model's files, and `-overlap-two` likewise. A production build takes both options on synthetic weights, and the rejection hangs on one line of `isk.txt`, a plain settings file in the secret key directory. No key protects that file, so the program cannot tell whether a line was changed. What would follow from a changed line has not been traced, except for the line on the weights' source. There, by a reading of the code, the prover then generates weights, opens no file of the model, and its first batch fails a self-check before anything is released (read, not run). Fifth, at its next start the service withdraws a response that already has its final name, if its request is still among those in work, and answers "failed". So a proof that a front end may already have passed on can be followed by "failed" for the same request. That does not touch the order of the batches; it touches what "released" means.

The numbers in a parameter file, such as code lengths and how many positions a test opens, differ by setting: each setting has its own list of places where they depart from the values behind that report's figures. The released programs differ from the code that was compared, among other things in five places, four of them in what is hashed: the request file's words also enter the first hash of a proof's first chain; a proof's shared and second chains bear labels of their own; a step that seals a hash chain bears no proof of work, which the planner checks; the commitment ID's hash also takes in the OOD seeds; and the key behind a batch's private random values also takes in a number, the prover's revision. Their lines have been read, each difference by itself. The comparison does not cover these differences, and nothing is proved about them. Of the other code differences of which that report tells, only the lines that differ were read, for minutes each, and two files of GPU code that computes values could not be compared by their differences. Of the differences of which that report tells, source files that are not in the code that was compared were read in full. A code difference of which that report tells nothing lies outside the comparison. One such: `cp_prove` runs no verifier, while that report's prover, like the code that was compared, checks its proofs with the verifier (rows PS-14, PS-34); the lines of this difference have had no reading against that report. The readings of code differences did not go through the table of differences row by row, and no row was compared under a parameter file that `cp_verify` admits. Tools, integrations, tests and differences in comments alone were left out. These readings were made to keep that report true, not as a review of the code for faults, and none attacked anything. Not done at any step. No script around the programs was read as the code was. None of the three programs was built or run for any of these comparisons, except to get the numbers that the programs compute from their parameter files. That report's table of the differences was reviewed once, without opening any source code. Its appendix on the programs lists what else is the same, as far as the source was read. That is that report's own account, which cannot be checked here.

column3: What Lean's results on weight hiding leave out. Completeness, where the model has a result, and zero knowledge are proved in Lean for the protocol, at full size and at the exact-match policy, each up to a small stated error, with fresh random masks; after compiling, both are on one leaf table. The honest prover in these theorems is a Lean definition, not the CUDA prover: nothing is proved for the programs. (What Lean proves on hiding: docs/limits.md#what-lean-proves.) Completeness is proved on served requests: the requests that can be served (`CanServe`) whose claimed output is the model's own (`finalComplete_iff_completeOn`). Zero knowledge after hashing is stated at every request, well-formed or not (`zeroKnowledgeAtEveryRequest`); whether a request is served depends on the weights and is revealed, not hidden: the simulator is told it. The corollary with a label shown is stated at every well-formed request. The programs derive their masks from a secret seed, which no Lean theorem covers. Behind the programs' counter no Lean theorem stands: nothing in Lean keeps count of the columns that a table has opened. (Row PS-64.) Of batches, which are what the programs serve, Lean's results on hiding say nothing (row PS-65). They model no size, time, memory or restart, and no proved statement on hiding covers a prover that stops a batch; at a request that is not served the Lean prover hands out the empty proof (a reply that holds no proof) and nothing else; a label beside it is a service's choice. The programs' service answers "failed" for every request that it does not prove, whatever the cause; a client can partly tell the causes apart (row HW-532). That answer is neither the bit that the simulator is told for each request (whether it is served) nor the corollary's label "failed", and no theorem ties it to what the Lean prover hands out. The theorems do count a stop of the honest prover at a served request: as a value of the proof; the chance of a stop for a private reason is a term of the error. They also leave out faults, the order of work and what the proofs of one batch share, so they say nothing about them either. Lean's theorem on zero knowledge is for exact match: under a clipped-gap policy no Lean theorem covers what a whole proof reveals (row LIM-27). A kept row's 219 random values are argued on paper only, and the count has no slack (rows LIM-64, HW-762). The scales (fitted from the weights), all sizes and all look-up tables are public. In Lean's results on hiding "the weights" are the weight matrices (one matrix in which they lie). The three public files stand outside: the scale file and some lines of the parameter file are fitted to the weights, and what they tell lies outside every statement on hiding; the sizes are those of one fixed format and model size, and the look-up tables are recomputed from the public files. Lean checks proofs; whether a statement says what these pages say of it in plain words is judged by a reading, not by Lean. Whether a request can be served is not hidden, and it depends on the weights (rows PS-13, PS-49). Nothing shows that a request that the programs serve is one that can be served in Lean's sense, and no theorem in the Lean library shows that any request to a real model is one on which the integer model passes all its range checks on all 1,024 tokens. A search for such a theorem found none, which is weaker than showing that none exists. Every theorem found that concludes this of a request either uses weights made up for the proof or takes it as a premise. The search was made on a library other than the Lean files in this repository. It went by script over every Lean file for a list of names, and some of the matches were read. Lean itself was not queried, and a search by name misses a statement put in other words. A theorem states that requests that can be served exist (`canServe_exists`). The statement names no weights, and the weights in its proof are all zero, made up for the proof. A theorem shows valid weights, constructed, not a real model's, at which no request can be served at the default setting's model parameters (`canServe_nowhere_atHaltingWeights`). These weights do not pass the first of the Lean library's two worst-case checks (`not_passesWorstCaseCheck_atHaltingWeights`). At weights that pass the first worst-case check, or the least-bound check with numbers that hold, the model has a result on every well-formed request (`modelNeverFails_of_passesSomeWorstCaseCheck`). These are the Lean library's own checks; neither is `cp_commit`'s worst-case check: no theorem relates either to a check that any program makes. The weights that are shown by name to pass the first check are made up; no theorem says whether a real model's weights meet that premise, and nothing in a commitment, in a proof or in what a verifier does shows that the committed weights meet it (guide/what-is-proved.md, "Completeness"; lean/LIMITS.md, L27, L93). By the word of a Python program of this project that mirrors the Lean checks, Llama 4 Maverick's public weights, at settings fitted by this project, of which by its word they are valid weights, fail the first worst-case check and pass the least-bound check. It is not a Lean evaluation, no theorem joins the program to Lean, and the program is not in this repository; each check was run once, and some margins are thin. That the honest proof is accepted at these weights is not shown. That these settings are valid settings is not shown either. (lean/LIMITS.md, L7, has the whole.) The theorems at weights that pass the first worst-case check, or the least-bound check with numbers that hold, are of neither kind: their premise is a condition on the weights, which no theorem shows of a real model's weights. By the Lean library's own headings, its reference table of scales does not fit any real weights. But by `THIRD_PARTY.md`, "What depends on Meta's models", that table's numbers may depend on a real model, and one value in the library goes back to another real model.

column3: The programs' limit of use. (A leaf table is a further masked copy of the weight table, with its own secret and masks.) The programs count batches of up to 64 requests for each leaf table by itself, and stop when one is full. At the default setting, at full size, the programs' limit is planned as 688,127 batches for each leaf table; the verifier's own planning call prints it at the full-size file, and no run has come near it. Behind the programs' counter no Lean theorem stands: nothing in Lean keeps count of the columns that a table has opened. (What Lean proves on hiding: docs/limits.md#what-lean-proves.)
