column3: Lean and batches. Of batches (of up to 64 requests), which are what the programs serve, Lean's results on hiding say nothing: nothing of what the proofs of one batch share, of a batch's other requests, or of somebody who gets hold of a further proof of a batch. These results do not extend to batches (docs/limits.md#the-verdict): the definition of index privacy that these pages cite (docs/glossary.md#index-privacy) has no batches. (Lean's results on hiding with numbers: docs/limits.md#the-verdict.) Of its numbers: they are for one commitment with one leaf table, one request to a proof, up to 688,127 replies and 2^64 hash queries; committer, provers and simulator are Lean terms, tied to no program.

A real model's scales and weights against Lean's definitions. "Lawful" does not say that a table is sensible (`lean/LIMITS.md`, L7 and L29). As far as its pages say, no table of scales in the repository came as a whole out of a fit to a real model. But one value of the full-size table, its attention shift, very likely goes back to a real model, and others may. Single values in the example and test files and in the programs depend on a real model's public weights, or may. At least one such value stands in the Lean library too, and that library's reference table of scales may depend on Llama 2 7B (`THIRD_PARTY.md`, "What depends on Meta's models"). The pages name Llama 4 Maverick and Llama 2 7B. Where each of the other entries comes from is not known entry by entry (`THIRD_PARTY.md`, "What depends on Meta's models", has one row for each table as a whole; examples/full-size/README.md tells what is known of that example's files). A real model's weights. That a real model's weights, quantised and arranged as the repository's documents describe, count as committed weights in Lean's sense has not been confirmed by reading source code or real weights.

The table of differences of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, in counts, and the differences that have no row of their own here. That report's theorems do not apply to the programs as they stand. A program can contain a bug that none of these theorems would catch. The programs differ from its protocol, and it does not fully cover most of the differences that were found. No attack that exploits any of them is known, but none has been ruled out, and the list may be incomplete. "Covered" means that the report also has a statement about the protocol on paper with this one change. It does not mean that the programs are proved, or that all the changes are covered together. The table describes other sources (row HW-678), and reaches further only by readings of the lines of code that differ (row PS-62). Of five differences between those sources and the released programs (which: row PS-62) the table says nothing: no row was read for them, and its mark "covered" for the row on the key does not stand for the commitment ID as the released programs form it, which no statement of that report covers (by its own account); by the same account the programs differ from its protocol at two places more: what a proof's first hash takes in, and the labels of two of a proof's chains. These five are the report's own list, which does not hold every difference (row PS-62). Where the programs differ outside that list, the table says nothing either: a mark there is the report's word on the compared code. Row PS-14 is such a row, and says how far its mark fits the released programs. No row of the table was compared under a parameter file that `cp_verify` admits. Whether a comparison that was made with one parameter file holds at another was not walked through the rows: where the code that was compared depends on the file, a row made with one parameter file says nothing of another. That each linear claim of the sub-proofs reads the entry of the reads' vector (`U3`: docs/format/FORMAT.md, 11.1) that it is meant to read has not been checked entry by entry (row SO-17.1.1). 22 differences, which stand for 25 rows of that table, have rows of their own here. That table also covers only in part eight further differences, which bear on hiding (rows PS-54 to PS-61). What is not covered in them is zero knowledge or index privacy, that report's two names for what guards the weights against clients. Nor does that report fully cover four more. Two are acceptance policies and stops at rare challenges, told in this row. The others are the overlap of batches (row PS-53), and numbers on which many rounds' errors are priced and that no check ties to the run at that round (row SO-4). For rows PS-53 and SO-4 its table says "No statement." If you plan to rely on a proof, two matters weigh most: that the provider writes the public parameters (rows PS-17, PS-17.1, PS-19), and the inner steps of a segment (row PS-38). The marks here follow that table, except for rows PS-9 and PS-11. The table calls these two "covered" within limits, and these rows state those limits as conditions. Each of the 22 differences has one of four marks. Two are not covered: a request that cannot be served (row PS-13) and versions set by configuration (row PS-19). Seventeen are covered in part. Two are covered only if a condition holds, and the only evidence that it holds is the source-code comparison. One is covered under a named assumption beyond the random oracle. Where to find them. The 22 are rows PS-1 to PS-9, PS-11 to PS-22 and PS-33 of the table of all rows. Each row states what the programs do, the property that it bears on, a mark and a note. The rows use that report's terms and assume that you know proof systems of this kind. That table gives other differences the mark "covered". Among those that it covers only in part are acceptance policies, where completeness is not covered, and the stops at rare challenges. Differences found in readings of code that differs have no row and no mark of their own. Most of the covered ones concern single steps of the protocol, such as testing some groups of messages earlier, and are not listed because they mean little without that report. Three need a comment: At a rare challenge of the range check, a request gets no proof: the programs mark that request, finish its proof and withhold it. The other requests in the batch are served, and their proofs take in a salted digest of that request's state (docs/what-is-not-hidden.md). For a prover that it defines, that report has a statement on a proof that is withheld, for one commitment only, and under conditions that the programs are not shown to meet (row PS-40). `cp_verify` gives other answers besides "accept" and "reject". docs/verifying.md, "When to accept", explains how a person or a script should read them. Covered only in part: at some rare challenges the prover or the verifier stops. That report's bound for hiding, whose proof its authors call "complete but not settled" (row PS-23), has terms for such stops. Such a term can be the largest in the bound, and for some of them that report does not prove a value. Where only one request is marked and withheld, nothing stops at that point. But a later test that ends a batch or the service, and fires because of what a marked request computes, is again such a stop, with a term of its own. For the verifier's stops, see docs/limits.md#an-honest-proof-can-be-rejected.

`cp_verify` and a stand-alone program built from `verify-on-bytes` (row L14), which this repository does not build as one. That program was run beside `cp_verify`. No theorem ties it to `cp_verify`, and the soundness theorem for the Lean verifier is not about it. It follows `cp_verify`'s source text, so the two programs are not independent: where they agree, that is not independent evidence. It follows the default setting as a program. No theorem bounds the chance that `cp_verify` accepts a false file. No theorem bounds the chance that that program accepts a false file, at this or any other setting. That `verify` hashes what the programs hash is proved only at queries that pass the coding's own tests; three groups of calls go round that coding; and in the one comparison, on one stored proof, the two logs of hash calls were not equal call for call. That program and `cp_verify`: tested, not proved; known to differ. The calls told in this row were made on Lean files that differ from those in this repository. How many calls gave both programs the same files, at which parameter files, and how they ended is told in `lean/OnBytes/LIMITS.md` ("Tests"); what is known to differ is told there too ("Known differences from cp_verify"). That program is a port of `cp_verify`, so a mistake that both share would not show. By a reading of the code it asks less in a few places; none is known to let a false claim through or to bear on hiding. The compilation theorem (`innerCompiledVerifier_sound`; row L14). It has 16 hypotheses; four are unproved — `keySound`, `proofSound`, `commitment`, `sound` — so the interactive protocol's own soundness is a hypothesis of that theorem, not proved there. At the library's descriptions other than `theDescription` (`innerCompilerInputFromDryRunAtFullSize`, `innerCompilerInputFromDryRunAtSmallSize`), four of the sixteen are not proved: `keySound` and `proofSound` are marked "may be false", `sound` "a definition to read", and `commitment` "not proved, in no file of this library" (`lean/LIMITS.md`, V3; V9 to V11). The weight of the theorem lies in the four; what the others are, and how far they hold: `lean/LIMITS.md`, V3. The 16 are not all that it needs (`lean/LIMITS.md`, V4). Nothing shows that these descriptions are the prover's protocol, and the theorem is stated at no setting of its own. What of `innerCompiledVerifier` has run at these descriptions, and what no theorem shows of it: `lean/LIMITS.md`, V6. If one of the four is false the theorem says nothing. Of `keySound`: at these descriptions nothing of the key protocol's soundness is proved at the default numbers (`lean/LIMITS.md`, V10; at `theDescription`, through which the soundness theorem on `verify` goes (row L14), the key file's soundness is a theorem where the tests on the public files pass). For the compilation theorem Lean gives no number of bits. The soundness theorem on `verify` does not go through the compilation theorem. What the compilation theorem assumes of the hash: two assumptions: that BLAKE2b may be treated as a random oracle, and that the second hash function resists collisions and does not disturb that (`lean/LIMITS.md`, V3; row L8).

From a proof's claims to the model. For its protocol, a technical report that is not public and not refereed has a lemma that the claims of a segment's sub-proof imply the integer model's step. For the programs, the comparison with that report found that step not covered (rows PS-1, PS-2, PS-3, PS-16, PS-18, PS-20, PS-21), and the file-format docs do not offer an argument of their own. The step that rewrites a weight claim summed over a tensor's indices as weights on the committed matrix's rows and columns, by the layout's rule, has no written proof (row SO-17.14).

column3: Three things to know before you use the programs. `cp_verify` can accept a configuration that the theorems of a technical report that is not public and not refereed do not cover. The provider, who serves the model, writes the configuration files, which hold the protocol's public parameters. That every file that `cp_verify` accepts meets the theorems' hypotheses has not been shown. See rows PS-17 and PS-19, and docs/limits.md#who-chooses-the-model for what a client can do. A client holds a 32-byte commitment ID, not the whole verification key. That report has a statement for such a client of its own protocol, not for a client of `cp_verify` as it stands. See docs/verifying.md#what-you-need-and-where-it-must-come-from for what the ID covers and what it does not. What an accepted proof says depends on the acceptance policy. Under exact match, an accepted proof says that each checked token is the committed integer model's top choice, up to the error bound. That is argued on paper, for that report's protocol, given results that it cites or assumes; whether the same holds for the programs is not known (rows PS-1 to PS-22). The integer model is not the floating-point network that it was made from, and nothing bounds the distance between the two. Under the clipped gap policy, the checked tokens' scores only have to meet limits that the configuration sets, so another model's replies can be accepted. Do not mistake one policy for the other (docs/verifying.md, "Acceptance policies").
column5: argued on paper (the report's protocol); read

column3: What "the programs" are, and what is proved of them. "The programs" (elsewhere "the code") are the programs in this repository as they are built and run, above all the committer and the prover (`cp_commit`, `cp_prove`), which handle the weights. What is proved is about something else: the written proof of hiding (in a technical report that is not public and not refereed; its authors call the proof "complete but not settled": row PS-23) is about the protocol on paper. Completeness, where the model has a result, and zero knowledge are proved in Lean for the protocol, at full size and at the exact-match policy, each up to a small stated error, with fresh random masks; after compiling, both are on one leaf table. The honest prover in these theorems is a Lean definition, not the CUDA prover: nothing is proved for the programs. (Row PS-63.) Nothing proves that the programs do exactly what the protocol says, that every mask is drawn, is fresh and goes where it belongs; and in other things they are known to differ from it (rows PS-1 to PS-22). A written proof of soundness, in the same report, is about the protocol's verifier as it is defined on paper, and Lean has a soundness theorem for its own verifier, `verify`, not for the C++ program that users run. Nothing proves that `cp_verify` makes exactly those checks, or only those. By that written proof's own account no proof covers five differences between the code that it compares and the released programs (row PS-62): none of soundness or of binding, and none of hiding. The five are the report's own list. Of differences outside it, such as that `cp_prove` runs no verifier on its proofs (row PS-62), it gives no account. Of the Lean library's six top-level statements (`lean/VerifiableInference/Statements.lean`) `Sound` alone is had of the system of `verify`, the Lean verifier, in a restricted "nearest form" (`NearestSound`, `lean/Ladder/Package.lean`): `Sound` at the files that ask for exact match. Of the compiled system (the same verifier, `verify`, with the honest committer and prover that the compiler yields) Lean proves the final statement's six fields at all public files in use (in scope, readable, at the exact-match policy, and passing the verifier's first test); completeness and zero knowledge are proved in other forms than the top statements as written. The restriction of `Sound` is this project's own; whether it is the right form of the soundness goal is not known (lean/THEOREM.md).

The sources hold code that nothing reaches. A search by name over other C, C++ and CUDA sources (row HW-678), with one more found by reading, gave 36 functions that nothing in this repository calls: 226 lines in 20 source files, not counting the comments above them (35 of the functions are in prover/, 1 in blocks/ and none in verifier/; 1 of the 36 lies in a tests' directory). Ten more have no caller (27 lines in four files): eight of the 50 functions that do nothing (row E29.1) and two helpers of tests. Some of them are called by tests that are not part of this repository. A further 75 functions (583 lines) outside the tests' directories are called by tests only. The true number of uncalled functions is higher: the search leaves aside the functions that share their name with another and that it cannot tell apart (nearly a third of all definitions) and all constructors, destructors, operators and virtual functions, and it counts a function as called wherever its name stands a second time outside a comment, also in a caller that is itself never called. This is known by name and by reading: no build shows it.
column4: None: as far as a search by name can tell, no run of the programs reaches such code; some of it is nevertheless compiled into them.

column3: Test code that a production build never compiles stands in the sources: 614 lines in 24 of the files that a build of the programs reads are compiled only without `SERVING_BUILD`, and code that can inject a fault in every build but the production one is among it; two macros choose between test and production code without a conditional, and other tests' switches stand there too; the hooks of cheating code that is not part of this repository are 50 functions that do nothing (they are empty, return a constant or hand their argument back), the 166 places that call them, and 94 lines that can never run (the lines of most consequence among them stand in `prover/prover/opening_in_process.cuh`: row E29.1.2). The 50, the 166 and the 94 are counted by text, not by a compiler, in the 475 files that a build of the programs reads, of other sources (row HW-678); no count was made in these sources. That the functions do nothing and that the lines can never run is known by reading them, not from a compiler or a run. Of the 94 lines, 50 are lines of small functions that nothing calls. The other 44 are the lines of 14 statements, counted from each one's `if`: the condition in that first line is still evaluated, and what depends on it never runs. Counted by program, by a search for each namespace's name before `::` on lines of code, comments left out, over the 439 C, C++ and CUDA sources that lie outside the tests' directories: one preprocessor block on a name that holds CHEAT (`prover/hash_commitment/commit_lie.cuh`:31-33, which only gives `COMMIT_CHEAT` its default: 2 lines in 1 file; none in verifier/src). 163 lines in 31 files call into five namespaces of test hooks: 139 of them into two whose functions do nothing, and 24 into three that can inject a fault in every build but the production one (two of the 24 call nothing: one sets a flag, one reads one) (`lost_coins_door`, `lost_copies_door`, `cert_doors`: faults of hiding: they zero private random values or copies of them, leave out a kernel launch that copies, adds or checks such values, or derive the key of the key file's random values from another seed; each acts only in a run on synthetic weights under a test seed; by a search, no test of this repository sets a variable that they read). These three are not all the faults of hiding that such a build can inject: outside the five namespaces, and so outside these counts, `cp_commit`'s own code zeroes a weight table's masks or pads, or hashes the salts of a fixed public key into the leaves of its tree in place of its own, under the test variable `ROWS_TABLE_FAULT` (prover/hash_commitment/hf_commit_table.cuh), and can shorten the count of opened columns under `ROWS_COUNT_FAULT` (prover/hash_commitment/hf_commit_once.cuh): in no production build, only on synthetic weights under a test seed, and no test of this repository sets either. Further test variables of such a build were not read for what they do to hiding. (The 166 count calls, not lines, of all 50 functions that do nothing: 147 of them stand on these 139 lines.) Messages that name switches which are not in these sources: row E29.1.3. In the production build the hooks are inline functions that hand their argument back, say no or do nothing; some of these files are empty in that way only under the production build's own macro, and are working code in a test build (read in the code). A switch of blocks/fence.h's list, which holds twelve switches, all of them tests', on the build line of the production build does not compile; a switch that a source defines behind its first include is not seen by that file's list. No code in this repository is switched on by a malicious prover's or committer's switch: a build line that sets one compiles, and switches nothing on (from reading and a search; not compiled). `COMMIT_CHEAT`, the malicious committer's switch, is on no such list: on that build line it compiles and switches nothing on, because the code that it would switch on is not part of this repository (shown by the preprocessor's output; not built). That is said of switches on a build line. One test variable is working code in every build but the production one, and can do a part of a malicious committer's work: `FORMF_PLANTED_INTEGER` (prover/hash_commitment/hf_commit_doors.h) puts a value that the caller names in the place of one committed integer; with `:past-the-scan` behind it, the pass of `cp_commit`'s range scan does not get that value, so that a value outside the declared range passes the scan and is committed to. By the source's own comment such a run is expected to fail all the same, at one of `cp_commit`'s own checks while it builds the key file, or where `cp_verify`, which `cp_commit` runs with `-key`, rejects that file's range proof; nothing was run to show it. The variable acts only in a test build, in a run with `-test-seed` on synthetic weights: in every other run `cp_commit` ends with exit code 2 where a test variable is set. In the production build the hook is a struct whose functions do nothing, and by that header's comment prover/build.sh installs no production program that holds one of the hook's strings, which prover/tests/serving_build_words.txt lists. No test of this repository sets `:past-the-scan`; the one test that names the variable asks that `cp_commit` refuse it (prover/tests/public_weights.py). Where the committed matrix is read in cuts of the stored tensors a test build's `cp_commit` refuses the variable (exit code 2), so the lines that would apply its value there (prover/hash_commitment/hf_commit_windows.cuh) never act; most of them are compiled in the production build too, where their flag stays false. They are not among the 94 lines told above. (All that is said here of `FORMF_PLANTED_INTEGER` rests on a reading of these sources and a search; nothing was compiled or run.) prover/build.sh also searches `cp_prove` and `cp_commit`, before it installs them, for five strings that mark a build under a malicious prover's or committer's switch or one of the tests' switches (one of the five stands in the code of a source that ships: the mark of a build with one of the tests' switches, in `blocks/fence.h`; the code with the others is not part of this repository), and holds every printable string of four characters or more of the production build's `cp_prove` and `cp_commit` against a list of words (so it cannot see the list's one line of three characters, `LIE`); a hit stops the build. **Lost random values.** The released programs have no check that recomputes every random value that the CPU samples. For the loss of a batch's salts a lemma of the written proof leans on the lost value alone. column3: At the shipped files' own number of masks no test has crossed a leaf table's limit of use.

A self-check recomputes every random entry of the encoded rows that the GPU makes, right after their hash tree is made. No test in this repository injects a fault that leaves an encoded row too few random entries. That self-check does not see values that the CPU samples, or a kernel that reads fewer entries than are there.

**What clients hear when the service stops.** When `cp_prove` exits, a request that it had already taken is answered "failed", at the latest when the service restarts. A request that was still waiting gets no answer until then: it stays in the queue for the next process. The runbook says so.

**A full disk.** Nothing in the service keeps a client's unfetched responses from filling the disk. If they do, a failed write ends `cp_prove`, and every later batch ends the same way until someone frees space. This was read from the source code, not tried.

**A proof-of-work search that finds nothing.** If the search for a proof-of-work number finds none, `cp_prove` exits: the whole batch stops, even where the search fails in one request's own part. The search has 2^63 - 1 tries, so the chance of that is negligible. This was read from the source code.
The audit recomputes published random values from the provider's secrets.

How the test build and the production build are tied. By program, on other programs (row HW-678), their GPU code is the same, function by function, but for two test functions. They differ on purpose in lines of CPU source. These lines were put on three lists, which are not in this repository, and no test in this repository looks for a new differing line. Each listed line was read with one question: can it change what is sampled, masked, sent, counted or wiped in a run without test options? The answer was no for each. Some lines had fewer readers. In `cp_prove`'s list, 60 lines and 12 more were read only by their writer, and 6 and 7 more by their writer and one other reader. Row H13.5 counts these readings differently (85 and 6); which count is right has not been settled. In `cp_commit`'s list, the 7 calls that open a model's files were read by readers, two of whom had not written them. 194 more lines there, of the option `-public-weights`, and 6 in the third list, were read by readers, some of whom had not written them. Some 60 lines of the option `-public-weights` are on no list: both builds have them, and they act only if the option is given. The CPU machine code has not been compared, and a run under a test seed takes branches that neither the comparison nor the lists cover.

**The example front end's proof ID.** In the example vLLM middleware a proof ID is 256 random bits that are sent once, only to the client that asked. It works like a secret link. It travels in the URL of the later calls, so a proxy's log can record it.

**A request that fails by bad luck.** An honest request can fail by bad luck in a random sample, with negligible probability. For one such failure, a failed range check, the chance depends on hidden values. Each configuration states a bound on that chance over all the requests that a key can serve (2^-128 in the examples), and all three programs reject a configuration that does not meet it. This is read from the code.
**One commitment for each machine.** Each machine that serves needs its own commitment.

**The line that records the worst-case check's verdict.** Someone who can write to the secret key directory could put the line that records the worst-case check's verdict there, and nothing in a proof shows that the check ran.

**The weights' declared range.** `cp_commit` checks that every weight is in its declared range. Outside the embedding, for instance, the range that the key file states, and that the range proof shows, is -4,096 to 4,095. `cp_commit`'s own scan of the committed integers is narrower by one value: it compares a weight's absolute value with 4,095, so it admits -4,095 to 4,095 and rejects -4,096. For the embedding its limit is 2^30 - 1. The scan's kernel and its two limits are by a reading of the code, which did not trace call by call that the printed verdict comes from that kernel's count.

**Why a proof's length varies.** Two causes are read from the code: a position that is sampled twice is opened once, and a hash-tree path leaves out what follows from the opened leaves. Whether these two account for the lengths that were seen (row RES-61) has not been worked out.

**A request that is proved and that the verifier rejects.** Under a clipped-gap parameter file whose threshold equals its ceiling and whose cap is 1 or more, a request whose checked range covered at most as many tokens as the cap was proved, and then the verifier rejected it. On other programs (row HW-678) that ran `cp_verify` on each response themselves, the whole batch then failed and `cp_prove` exited. By a reading of these sources, `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` refuse such a file at their start (prover/common/parameter_file.h: row R16.3), which has not been run, and the vLLM integration's middleware refuses to start on it (integrations/proof_middleware.py; read, not run); were that rule passed, nothing in `cp_prove` would stop the response (what that would cost a provider that keeps duty 6: row HW-257). No parameter file in the repository is of this kind, and the rejection says nothing about the weights.

**How a guess at an earlier batch's requests would be tested.** If a batch's random bytes repeat, a client fills the other places in the later batch with its guesses, and its own proof contains the same salted digests exactly when the guesses are right. The method tests whole guesses and does not read a request. This is reasoning only and has never been tried.
**Which policy the tests of hiding used.** Every test of hiding used the exact match policy; none used a score policy such as clipped gap (audits apart: rows H13.7 and H13.8).
**A batch's fresh bytes.** For each batch `cp_prove` samples 32 fresh random bytes from the operating system. With the seed they decide every mask, one-time mask and salt of that batch's proofs.

**A failed request's leaf after a failed self-check.** By a reading of the code, the batch's other requests are not released after a failed self-check on secret random values. After one of the few self-checks on data that fail a single request, by one other reading, the batch's other requests are released. By two further readings, the failed request's leaf is still sent: a request that ends puts its digest into the tree whatever failure it has met.

**A checked token's cost under clipped gap.** Under clipped gap each checked token has a cost, which grows with the distance of its score below the best score at its position. A cost above the ceiling `C` counts as `C`.
**The random generator under a known key.** Masks and salts are derived from the programs' random generator. How it behaves with a secret input under a known key has not been examined.

**A counter, and what the programs check.** A counter is a file whose length counts the columns that a leaf table has shown. The programs detect a missing or malformed counter, and check some of the file permissions and some of the build.

**Testing a guess without the seed.** By design, no one without the seed can test a guess offline against the published files, but that is not proved for the programs, and it holds only while every mask is there: an unmasked value is an exact equation, against which a guess at the weights can be tested (reasoned; not tried on the released programs). Under `cp_commit -public-weights` whoever has the option's file can work the seed out.

**Who can set a counter back.** By a reading of the code, the programs do reject a counter that does not belong to the service account. That leaves four routes: the service account itself, root, swapping a file between two checks, and exchanging two tables' counters, which has not been tried.

**How a leaf table is used up.** Each batch of 1 to 64 requests shows a fixed number of columns of one leaf table, picked at random. That these picks can stand for uniform and independent ones is argued, not proved. While a batch's fresh bytes stay the same, the pick is a fixed secret function of the requests. Whether that can be used to steer which table's limit is spent has not been worked out. The parameter file sets how many batches a table serves, and `-M` sets how many tables there are.

**Why a further commitment is needed, and what it does not mend.** A provider needs a further commitment because a full leaf table stops the service until a new commitment is made. A further commitment to the same weights, under the same configuration files, lies inside the judgement on weight hiding, on thin ground and on conditions of its own (docs/limits.md#a-further-commitment). No leak is known in the programs where each commitment draws its own seed. A new commitment does not undo anything that was published. It resets only the count of opened columns. Each proved request's share of any bound on hiding, and what the served-or-failed answers give, run on over the weights' whole life, across commitments.

**A batch's fresh bytes.** By a reading of the code, each batch begins with 32 fresh random bytes, so a retry, a restart or a rolled-back directory does not bring a batch's masks back (a machine or process rolled back: row HW-357). The only test on those bytes, though, is that they are not all zero. `cp_commit` takes 32 fresh bytes of its own each time it makes a table (prover/hash_commitment/hf_commit_keys.h, `Make::a_copy`), except under a test seed or `-public-weights`. Without them a table that is made twice has the same masks, with no fault.

**Hard links.** One text file in the secret key directory has a line that names the directory of the weight files. An account that can write the secret key directory can point that line at a directory of its own, which holds a hard link to a committed weight file (what such an account can learn: row H21). A hard link that another process creates and removes in a tight loop while the files are opened can pass both of `cp_prove`'s checks on a weight file; no bound on the rate is known. No change to the code that reads the weight files helps against the re-pointed line. Keeping `fs.protected_hardlinks = 1` on every host that mounts the file system, from before the weight files are put there, blocks the route by the re-pointed line, by reasoning and not by a run. The setting itself was tried once, at the system call alone, on one machine, with one kernel and file system: never with the programs, with two accounts there, or switched off as a control. It does not stop code that runs as the files' owner or with `CAP_FOWNER`, or an account that can read and write the file. On the released programs that route has not been tried.
column4: Keep fs.protected_hardlinks = 1 on every host that mounts the file system.

column3: **What the two tensor-core kernels leave behind.** The two tensor-core kernels end with hidden values in shared memory and registers: sums and scale pairs in one; decoded weights, activations and sums, up to 231,936 bytes a thread block, in the other. These two are not the only ones: other kernels that multiply on the tensor cores also end without clearing their shared memory (by a count from the sources, not checked: twelve in all, in eight files).

**One batch's kept bytes: the option.** `cp_prove -keep-for-the-audit` writes one batch's 32 fresh random bytes into the secret key directory. The option is in every build, the production build too, and can be given on the command line alone. By a reading of the code, it is accepted only on synthetic weights: it is rejected on a model's files, in a service (`-spool`), and while an earlier kept file is still in the directory.

**One batch's kept bytes: how long they stay.** The file that `cp_prove -keep-for-the-audit` writes stays until the audit erases it, even if `cp_prove` dies. Until then every new start is rejected, though a running service carries on. `cp_prove` releases a batch's responses once all of them are staged, before any audit. So handing them out only after the audit has passed is a person's duty, and no program enforces it.
**How many requests shared a batch.** A batch's time depends on the number of requests in it, so it shows a client roughly how many requests the batch held.

**What has run, and on what.** No run of a test of hiding on a build made by an nvcc later than 13.2.86 is known (what has run under CUDA 13.4's compiler: rows P4, P4.5). The version check in the prover's build lets a later nvcc through, but a later toolkit is not supported. Of the tests of hiding that these docs report, those under the judgement on weight hiding (docs/limits.md#the-verdict) have run at the default setting, in whole or in part (which of them on the released programs: row LIM-63.2), as rows LIM-63 and LIM-63.2 tell. Unless a result in these rows on hiding says otherwise, it did not come from the released programs. Limits of the repository's own audit: rows H16.1, HW-183 and HW-201.

The usual conditions of a trial, and sizes. Unless a row says otherwise, a trial was one run, at small size, on synthetic weights. Small size is 8 layers and windows of 64 tokens. Full size is Maverick's shapes.

A mask that is never written to its position. `cp_verify` cannot see most masks, so the file verifies if the loss happens before the prover commits to the table. A loss in a proof is visible to that proof's client or, in the part that a batch's proofs share, to every client in the batch. A loss in a public file is visible to everybody, permanently. No search of many honest proofs for a lost or zero mask has run on the released programs; the two audits with the provider's secrets ran on them, once at small size, on synthetic weights, and once more under a clipped-gap policy (rows LIM-63.2 and H13.8). In another program of this project, which is not in this repository, a compiler fault did drop writes (row HW-550). The read-back check looks for this fault. The audit with the provider's secrets reaches a commitment's public files before they are handed out, on synthetic weights only, so no tool in this repository checks a provider's files for a real model by value (what the audit tool's program sees there without a secret: row HW-747).

What one lost mask is worth. Any lost mask can give away at least one exact equation in hidden values. What a client could learn from one has not been tested. A fault that strikes every proof alike gives such equations proof after proof; whether a client could solve for weights from them on the released programs has not been tried.

The read-back check: its first two parts. The first part compares what is stored at the mask's position with what was sent to the write. The second part keeps the mask as sampled, finds its position by a different route and compares what is stored there. No run at the default setting is known in which it fired (row HW-457).

The read-back check guards one-time masks only, and three cases get past its first two parts. (1) A mask lost in the few instructions between its sampling and its first copy. A third part of the check looks for this case. After each message is sent, it reads each one-time mask back from the table and compares it with a second derivation. By the repository's own page on that second derivation (`prover/second_writing/README.md`), an agreement guards against a slip in one of the two texts. It does not guard against a shared misreading of the rule, or against a slip that is in both. The part guards one-time masks only. (2) A mask written one position off, at one spot in the proof library. (3) A mask overwritten after the check. By a reading of the code, here too the proof is false: it can leave the prover, and a `cp_verify` outside the prover (the provider's check of the whole batch, duty 6: docs/limits.md#the-conditions, or the client's own, but by then the client holds the file) is what rejects it.

The self-checks compute most random values twice: a fault that both computations share can pass them, and so can a fault in a value that no check recomputes. Two faults at once may also pass. So can a wrong read that does not last: a routine once reads a correct one-time mask wrongly, and the check then reads it correctly. The cases of the start-up self-test with known answers (`own-test-coins`) are not independent of a list of faults that were injected into copies of these sources, so those faults are no blind test of it.

The last random entries of every row set to zero. The test that the released programs run at start-up (it is no test for a row with too few random entries: row HW-457) ignores the entries' values, so it would pass that fault, and their other self-checks have not been tried on it.

Faults that no check has been seen to catch. By a reading of the code, four more kinds of fault are expected to go unnoticed. One is a bug in the few routines that every computation of a weight table shares. One is a buffer of masks that is wrong from the start, beyond four spot-checked values. One is a lost salt at a tree leaf that no proof opens. By a reading of the code, a further comparison looks at `cp_prove`'s own salts at such leaves (HW-344). A stored table's salt at a column that is never opened stays unseen (HW-482). One is a left-over value in a table cell that no check reads. This list may not be complete.

What the programs' own checks miss. Masks kept in GPU memory are recomputed in full (row HW-684), but by the same GPU code, so that check cannot see a fault in the compiler or in the generator's core routines. Some other self-checks fail a request without ending the service.

The twelve self-checks. Each of the twelve compares a secret random value with a second derivation of it. No self-check on a lost random value has been seen to fire in a production build, which has no option for injecting a fault. By readings of the code, they do not see the following. The main self-check compares the random entries of GPU-made encoded rows alone; the rest of a batch's random values are words of salts that are not kept, at which a further comparison looks (row HW-344). Only the checks that use a second implementation could notice a fault of the compiler: the other comparisons set GPU code against the same GPU code (row HW-456). The count of zero filler cells does not see a write that comes after it and before the commitment (rows HW-570, HW-692). Nothing counts what a lost random value shows against a table's limit of use. The released programs have no start-up test for a row with too few random entries, and that fault has not been tried on them. Whether the released programs have a buffer of one-time masks that are sampled on the CPU and that nothing derives a second time was not traced. No run at the default setting is known in which the read-back check (row HW-687) or the comparison of `cp_prove`'s salts (rows HW-344, HW-690) fired, and none that shows that the self-check on messages with mask rows (row HW-686) was reached.

In these sources the arrays of a hash tree of the GPU engine are zeroed before anything is written to them (prover/engine/tree.cuh, `begin()`; read, nothing was run; for a leaf's digest a unit test of the engine's routine holds it, the public test `gpu.tree_arrays_cleared_test` (SUITE.md), which has passed: row H45), so that a store lost there leaves 32 zero bytes. By a reading of these sources, with nothing run, the vertices above such a digest are hashed over the zero and the root is taken from the array as it stands; an opening whose drawn positions do not lie under that vertex passes a verifier's path check and carries those 32 zero bytes where the digest belongs, and one with a position under it fails (prover/engine/tree.cuh: k_tree_nodes(), finish(), open()). What that means for the truth of an accepted file has not been examined beyond this reading. What goes out in that place is 32 zero bytes, not what the memory's last user left there. (What an accept warrants in general, whatever the prover did: rows SO-1 ff.; verifier/README.md, "What a YES does not say".) Beyond that unit test no run is known that bears the reading of `begin()` out, and no program without the clearing ran beside it as a control. By a reading, also of the code of other programs (row HW-678), `cp_commit`'s own hash tree over a stored weight table is cleared too (row H45; the public test `prover.guards_stand` (SUITE.md) checks, as text only, that the line which clears it is in these sources, not that it works or is reached), but no injected fault has been tried on it. No trial of one on the engine's trees as `cp_commit` builds them is known. By one reading of the code, not checked, `cp_commit` also builds trees of the GPU engine while it makes an entry (a leaf file). Two work buffers of the GPU engine, in which the lower part of a tree is made again at an opening, are not cleared. A store lost there could put 32 old bytes into a file. By another reading of the code, the same holds of every GPU buffer out of which the engine fills an opening of a run's trees: nothing clears them. One lost launch or store there leaves old GPU words where a digest, a symbol or a salt belongs, and they go into the opening's bytes. Such words can be partly encoded rows or unsalted chaining values. By the sources' own comment GPU memory holds what its last user left there, such as masks, salts or the model's inner values, and the clearing of the trees does not cover the buffers of an opening (prover/engine/tree.cuh, `begin()`). No self-check detects the loss. By one reading, also of the code of other programs, with nothing run, the tree's root is fixed by then, so the file does not verify: it leaves the prover, and a `cp_verify` outside the prover (the provider's check of the whole batch, duty 6: docs/limits.md#the-conditions, or the client's own, but by then the client holds the file) is what rejects it. The other reading did not follow the file to a verifier. So this rests on that verifier alone. Not known: whether other GPU kernels that build hash trees write into cleared memory. While a tree of the GPU engine is built, nothing detects a store that is lost (prover/engine/tree.cuh, `begin()`). Two checks come later: in `cp_commit` alone, a tree that is made again is held to its first root (row HW-745); and before a column of a stored table is opened, the node above it is computed again and held to the stored node.

The compiler. nvcc 13.0.88, which compiled other programs (row HW-678) on which tests told here ran, has two faults that can make a program silently compute a wrong value, and a wrong mask still verifies. One showed in a sample kernel and in the unit test of a single routine of the prover, not in a program. The programs do nothing against it. Their build tests for it on one small kernel only, and runs the test only where a GPU is present, which says nothing about any other kernel. Whether the released programs' nvcc has it is not known. The other is a published bug, which NVIDIA lists as fixed in nvcc 13.2.86, the oldest version that the build accepts. No run of a test of hiding on a build made by an nvcc later than 13.2.86 is known. That fix has not been checked by a test here. Almost none of the compiled GPU code has been read, and of some programs only a few kernels' per-thread memory has been (row HW-213).

Test results do not carry over to the released programs unless the tests are run on them (docs/limits.md#what-was-run-on-these-programs). The reading of the sources of `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` was of a text from which these sources differ in code in 68 of 384 files, and in 136 more in comments, names and the wording of messages alone (row HW-745). It read that text whole but for `cp_verify`'s own files, once and fast. That reading found no leak beyond the declared list in a correct build. Nothing was built or run, and the arithmetic was not checked. The class that feeds and finishes BLAKE2b stands in these sources in another form than in the text that was read, and it has been read twice for hiding (row HW-748).

The default setting. It counts proof of work toward its soundness figure. Every commitment publishes OOD answers. Of the tests of hiding only the test of the OOD answers by value and the audits have run at the default setting's full size. The test by value ran there on the released programs, once on synthetic weights and once on a real model's public weights, and on other programs (row HW-678) on both kinds of weights too (rows LIM-63.2, line 1, and HW-747; one further trial there, on other programs, ended with a failing status of its own controls: row LIM-29). The audits ran there on other programs: both once, and in another run both once (their exit codes alone are told; no false kept bytes); the commitment's audit once more (row LIM-63); and a separate audit, once, in part, on synthetic weights (further such audits: row LIM-63.2, lines 6 and 7). In the timed runs (docs/limits.md#the-timed-runs), on the released programs, the commitment's audit, and not the audit of a batch, ran there too, behind three honest commitments, which is no negative test (these, and one more run of both on other programs: row LIM-63.2, line 5). At its small form tests of the OOD answers and both audits also ran, the test by value and both audits on the released programs (row LIM-63.2, lines 1 and 5). Of the other tests of hiding the sweep of lost random values ran at this setting, at its small form, as reported, on one fixed sample, on more than one set of test builds of other sources, whose tie to the released programs has not been shown, once on each, each time with the same outcome, loss for loss (rows LIM-63 and LIM-63.2, line 3): no second witness (docs/limits.md#the-verdict). 30 of 165 losses in CPU memory went unnoticed: no rate. Of the others, the riskier losses were replayed there in kind, both audits were run there, and a separate audit, once, in part, on synthetic weights (docs/limits.md#the-verdict; further such audits: row LIM-63.2, lines 6 and 7); no other test is known there but for the count over two small commitments (row LIM-63.2, line 12).

It is assumed that test and production builds apply masks in the same way. That rests on a comparison of their GPU code, on other programs (row HW-678), and on one reading of their CPU code (row HW-116). It does not cover test builds with one more compile-time switch, which injects a fault or adds a hook, and nine tests that look at values ran on such builds.

The audit with the provider's secrets. It recomputes a proof's masks from the batch's random bytes. A test seed fixes these, but a service does not keep them, so in a served proof only the stored salts can be recomputed. The audits of commitments' files and of single batches used this tool or a part of it, but none was of a served proof.

**The tests that `cp_prove` makes on the model's files at its start.** The tests found by reading are on the files' form, on their fit to the parameter file's shape, and on whether every weight and every normalisation gain is finite and in its range. Only the last says anything about hidden values, and its ranges have not been compared with those that the key file states. Whether the files hold the committed weights is tested at each batch's opening, not at the start. This is by a reading of three of the loader's source files, and nothing was run.

Many of the results in these rows are of other programs (row HW-678) or other sources. Among the differences from the released programs are self-checks, the clearing of the GPU engine's hash trees, an option of the audit's that keeps a batch's random bytes, and the compiler.

What happens when a self-check fails. A self-check is a check that `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` runs on its own work in every run (some checks are off under a test seed: row HW-277), and some compare a secret random value with a second derivation of it. By two readings of these sources, of the default service (prover/prover/prover.h; row C3), if one of these fails, `cp_prove` ends (a few only at the next end of a batch: row HW-501) and the output of the batch in hand is held back; an earlier batch already has its names. A few other self-checks, on data, fail one request or one batch while the service goes on.

**The assumption on ChaCha20.** The programs derive their random values from the seed and from fresh system bytes, so they assume that ChaCha20's block function is a pseudorandom function under a secret key. It is a computational assumption, and its standing rests on cryptanalysis only. No figure has been put on that assumption. Under `cp_commit -public-weights` that key is not secret.

**What the marker files of `-public-weights` do not catch.** A marker file that was made for weights that should stay hidden passes like any other. A model file that is changed in place after its header was read is not caught. `cp_prove` reads no marker at all. This is what the code's own comments say.

**Responses left behind after a kill.** By a reading of the code, not from a run: after a kill (SIGKILL) or a loss of power, whole responses that have not got their final names stay, unchanged, in the staging directory (`out/.tmp` under `-spool`, `.tmp` under `-out`). Such a file can hold unmasked values. Under `-spool` a next start whose requests have the same length as those left in `work/` overwrites what is staged with zeros and removes it itself (a file that it cannot overwrite stays, and the service does not start; at an ending it is removed all the same: HW-491); if no such start comes there, run `cp_prove -clear` on that directory, and name no other, before you give it up. Under `-out`, by another reading of the code, the same `cp_prove` call with `-out`, made again, takes the directory, and first overwrites and removes what is staged, if the directory is the caller's own, closed to others, and holds nothing but `.tmp` with a `mark.txt` and names that `cp_prove` stages, and if the call gets that far: one that is rejected earlier, as after a batch kept for the audit, clears nothing. If it cannot remove all of it, the call fails and the rest stays. In every other case no later start touches the staged responses: only the call `cp_prove -clear` does, and the usage text asks the operator to run it after every exit code other than 0, a kill or a loss of power. That call does not reach a staged file that has a second name: the file stays, and `-spool` then does not start. By a reading of the code, the call works only in these two staging directories, follows no link in the path that it is given and needs directories that are the caller's own. It removes nothing unless a `mark.txt` says that the staging directory is `cp_prove`'s; in a marked directory it goes by names alone. If that directory holds, at its top, a name that `cp_prove` never uses there, the call touches nothing and what is staged stays, until the operator moves that entry out.
column4: See what `cp_prove`'s usage text says on `-clear`, and the runbook, before you start again. If under `-spool` no next start comes whose requests have the same length as those left in `work/`, run `cp_prove -clear` on that directory, and name no other, before you give it up.

column3: **Smaller limits that the code's own comments state.** By one reading of the code, not from a run: `-in` is opened by name; by another, a single batch's `-out` is walked from `/`, part by part, as `-spool` and `-isk` are, with two gaps: the directory itself is made by its full path between two walks, and under `sudo` the walk trusts the account that ran `sudo`. By a reading of the code: `cp_commit` starts its own runs of `cp_verify` under a supervisor, in a process group of their own, which is killed at a fixed time limit of 30 minutes and when `cp_commit` dies. By two readings, the supervisor holds the same bytes that are still to be judged as `cp_verify` does, and no seed, key or random value reaches it. `cp_commit` has these gaps: a `cp_verify` stuck in a system call; a supervisor that is itself killed; and the next start looks for no check that was left behind.

The stored weight tables' own random entries and salts, by a reading of the code. A fault that strikes alike the GPU kernels that make a stored table and those that open it would go unnoticed: the file would verify, and it would leak. Also unchecked are a salt at a column that is never opened, and all but the first of `cp_commit`'s rounds over a table.

A limit on all evidence by value that was gathered under a test seed. Under a test seed each file's 32 fresh random bytes are zeros. So such evidence does not show that these bytes enter the keys. Only the audits of production builds show that.

A salt partly lost at a leaf that no proof opens. A lost salt lets a guess at its leaf be tested, and whether that is feasible has not been worked out. That holds of a salt lost whole. With 8 of a salt's 40 bytes lost, 32 random bytes still enter the leaf's hash, so a guess cannot be tested (by a reading; no test has shown it).
The audit's check that needs no secrets looks only for a zero or a repeated value.
The programs' own list of conditions for hiding (the head of `hiding_conditions.h`) names sixteen groups of conditions that only tests of the code can check.

No program holds a commitment ID back until the audit has said yes: that is a rule of the runbook alone. A bad result: in one run at full size that rehearsed the runbook, the job sent out the commitment ID a minute before the audit said yes, against the very rule that it rehearsed, and nothing stopped it. The runbook's steps for a lost or doubtful count and for the hold after a bad exit have not been tried.

**What waiting shows.** How long a request waits before its batch begins shows its sender how much other clients are asking for. An answer "failed" to a file that is not a request that can be served is released together with the batch that was proved before it, so its sender learns when that batch ended. Both are read from code that is not known to be these sources. A release is not one step either: by one reading of the code, it names the staged responses one after another in the order of their request IDs, the "failed" ones among them. So the instant at which a client's own response appears also depends on how many requests of that release have a smaller ID. Another reading of the code saw that sorting.

**A response that a verifier rejects.** `cp_prove` runs no verifier, so a response that a verifier would reject, unless a self-check or a guard ends the process first, leaves the prover like any other, so no response may leave the provider before `cp_verify` has accepted every proof of its batch (duty 6: docs/limits.md#the-conditions). Such a response can hold unmasked values. A client that gets one holds them, and so can whoever can read the provider's output and staging directories, or a place where a front end keeps rejected responses. Of bugs and hardware faults of this kind `cp_prove` notices only those that a self-check, a guard of the proof library (row HW-244) or a check on its own data meets, and none of these verifies a proof (by a reading of these sources, not run); past them it goes on serving until a self-check fails or a person stops it. By a reading of the code, not from a run: overwriting the staged files is the last step of `cp_prove`'s wipe, and only an ending that gets that far reaches it. Only a regular file of the same user with one name is written into. A file that was not overwritten or not removed, or a lock still held after two seconds, counts as not all wiped: `cp_prove` then prints a line that begins `p258 not every step of the wipe ran` (docs/faults.md). On one road that report can be missing. Where a request fails together with its batch after parts of it were staged, and one of them cannot be overwritten, it is removed all the same, `cp_prove` ends under the name `write-failed`, and that ending need not count as not all wiped. At an ending, a staged response's file that `cp_prove` cannot overwrite is removed all the same, so its bytes stay on the disk, beyond the reach of a later start or of `cp_prove -clear`. As reported, on other programs (row HW-678), a response or a leaf file that `cp_verify` rejects can also show columns of a stored weight table that no counter has counted, and the masks are reckoned for the counted columns only. By another reading of the code, all of a batch's columns are counted before the batch's opening begins, in full, whatever becomes of it. `cp_commit` keeps a rejected leaf file nowhere.

The audit with the provider's secrets. On a served proof, whose batch's random bytes a service does not keep, it can check only the stored tables' salts, and only on synthetic weights. By a reading of the code, the released programs do not let it run on a real model's files.

**Who can write beside the weights.** By a reading of the code, not from a run: `cp_commit` compares the weights with a side file of checksums, `wsums.txt`, which it reads from the weights' directory. It prints how many tensors match, and exits with code 6, writing nothing, if not all do. A run that fails can name a tensor. So an account that can write that file and see `cp_commit`'s output learns how many tensors match, and so, with one line changed per run, a yes or no for each tensor, and by the exit code alone whether all do, on a guess at the checksums of weights that it cannot read. Each try takes a whole run of `cp_commit`. It is a test of a guess, weaker than what a reader of that file can do, and no client or holder of proofs comes near it.
column4: Let no other account write to the directory that holds weights that must stay hidden.

column3: **Who shares the machine.** The claim on hiding assumes that no untrusted code shares the physical machine, under any user or in any virtual machine. Caches, branch predictors and counters can show other code on the machine something of which branches the programs take and which memory they touch, and any user sees the GPU's load. Whatever runs under the service account, a front end too, is fully trusted. Whatever else holds the weights, such as the engine that serves the replies, must protect them by its own means.
column4: For secret weights use a machine, a GPU and disks that you share with no one.

column3: Which random values that the CPU samples are compared with a second derivation, by kind, by a reading of the code. These are compared. One-time masks. The mask rows and random tails of the messages on the index masks, in a request and in the key file, and of the key file's message on the ranges. Three of the four masking vectors in the last step of every proximity test. The mask tables and tails of two messages in the test on the weight table. These kinds are compared in part. The masks of a folding step: by a reading of the code, a self-check compares one copy of a mask's coefficients and of its tail with the same draws made again, at the fold. It does not compare the mask's table, the copy that the engine encodes, or the copies from which the sum and the rounds are computed. The proof library's other messages with mask rows: by a reading of the code, a self-check looks at each just before it is opened. It compares each value of the rows' random tail with a second derivation, and the table of masks only in part. Among what it does not see: a committed table's own columns, a message that is never opened, a message that another part of the proof sent, the engine's encoded copies, the pads on the OOD answers, and a fault that both derivations share. The following are compared with nothing. The other message inside the test on the weight table. Of every message inside the proximity tests but the last step's, all but the random tail of its mask rows. Among what is left are the single random values that fill the free room of each stage's message. The filling of a re-encoded row. The salts, the arrangement and the free leaves of the tree that ties a batch together. The 32 bytes at the head of each part.

**What the worst-case check's verdict gives.** The check serves hiding alone, and soundness does not rest on it. After it passes, `cp_commit` writes one line, `ranges`, into `isk.txt` in the secret key directory. `cp_commit` itself writes it only after the check has passed, and the production build always runs the check when it makes a new commitment. But the line does not show that the check ran on these weights: it holds only a digest of the three public configuration files, no key protects it, and a line copied from another commitment under the same files fits as well. It is the one tie of these files to the commitment at `cp_prove`'s start; a change of a file and of the line together is stopped later, in the first batch (read, not run; its bounds: row HW-193). The check's bounds on matrix norms hold if a vendor's library computes the classical matrix product in IEEE binary64, which the check asks for and spot-checks in every run but does not prove. Most of the rest of its arithmetic is rounded upward, assuming IEEE rounding with no fused operations. The build sets no compiler flag for that, and the whole file has not been searched for an expression that a fused operation could harm. That the program computes its bounds correctly is not proved either. A list ties each line of the prover that raises a range failure to a line of the check's table, and a test compares that list with the source text: 16 such lines, 19 lines of the table, none unaccounted for. Neither is in this repository, the ties are a reading of the code, and a range test of another form would not be seen. Documents on other programs (row HW-678) say that the prover's own test of a range is in places looser than the range, or missing, which does no harm while no window leaves such a range. By the same documents, a window might leave such a range because one of the worst-case check's conditions fails or because that check does not cover the range. They add that it is not established that the request would then be stopped, and what its files would show of hidden values, if they left the provider, has not been worked out. That the bounds are not proved correct comes from those documents too. The rest is by readings of the code, one for each part.

What a failed check does to the service. By two readings of these sources (prover/prover/prover.h; row C3), a failed self-check on secret random values or keys ends `cp_prove`: most with exit code 9 and a name that begins `own-test-`, a few with exit code 1, at least two of them without a name. A few end it only at the next end of a batch. For those few, the release of responses is blocked only once the service has read the failed check's result, so until then an earlier batch's responses can still be released. By a reading of the code of other programs (row HW-678), what fails one request or one batch while the service goes on is not a check on secret random values. It is a sample from hash output that gives no result, a few self-checks on data, a value out of its range, or a request above the policy's bounds. By a reading of the code of other programs, one of the stops without a name, the one at a counter that is not above the largest used under its key, is the only guard against repeated masks. Nothing was run for these readings.
No test checks what a request leaves in `cp_prove`'s own GPU memory.

With `cp_commit`'s option that keeps random bytes for the audit, the key file's and the leaf files' random bytes lie beside the seed. With the seed, they open every mask in the key file and the leaf files. An audit that says yes destroys them. After a no, or with no audit, they stay. By a reading of the code, `cp_commit` rejects the option on a model's weight files, so such bytes exist only beside synthetic weights.
Where only a test looks for a fault, nothing guards a real run. The programs themselves do not catch such a fault, or catch it only in part, and a test protects no service.

**Columns beyond the count.** By the written argument's count, each stored table carries just enough randomness for the columns that proofs may open, and the count stops there. If someone got at further columns in some other way, nothing would cover them. Columns that no proof has opened are protected only by the salts at the hash tree's leaves. For the hash trees that every proof of a leaf table's life reads, the main bound on hiding of the written proof (not public: row HW-763) has a term of its own: it holds for the key and a stated number of full batches together. It gives nothing beyond that number of batches on a table, and nothing for vertices of a tree that no proof opens. It is about the written proof's protocol and a prover that the written proof defines. The written proof's authors call the proof "complete but not settled" (row HW-763), and nothing of it is about the programs.
**After a loss of power.** Which batches had begun and were not yet counted on the disk when the power failed may show to a client. What that tells has not been checked for the programs.

**Real clients' requests and a test build.** A test build can take a batch's random bytes from a file and can list what it samples. Whoever knows those bytes can work out the folded row, with the folded masks in it, from an opening's files. The masks in that row are reported to be combinations of long-lived values, the same masks in every opening. So real clients' requests must never be sent to a test build.

**Which lines are fitted.** Of the parameter file's lines the tools in `scales/` fit two from the weights and the calibration set, `MF` and `s`. They compute the six lines of eps1, eps2 and epsF from the width, the model's norm epsilon and e_res, and rewrite 15 lines (`scales/README.md`). By two readings of this repository's files, the other seven lines, `theta0_lo`, `theta0_hi`, `KF`, `S`, `rx`, `cs` and `wb_emb`, are not fitted. A provider may choose more after a look at the weights: e_res, the clamps, the number of limbs and the policy's three bounds.
**Equal scores.** Of tokens with equal scores, the one with the lowest token number counts as the top choice.
**Other requests.** What a client learns about the other requests in its batch has been looked at little, and at small size.

**Real weights.** Only one of the five tests behind the judgement on weight hiding has run on a real model's weights, in four runs, one of them on the released programs (row HW-747), and the programs do not let the repository's own audit with the provider's secrets run on them. Every test of hiding that these pages tell of outside that row used synthetic weights.
**The first compiler fault.** The first fault of nvcc 13.0.88, the one that is not the published bug, is in no release note (the two faults: rows HW-459 and HW-293).
**Runs outside the test runner.** Many of the runs behind these pages' figures were made outside the test runner, and their records are often not in this repository.
**A scan that no tool makes.** No tool in this repository scans for masks lost from the equations that hold masks only.

**When the audit erases a batch's kept bytes.** A batch's audit erases that batch's kept random bytes only when told to: `audit_batch.sh` asks for a sixth word, `--rehearsal` (nothing is erased) or `--erase-kept-files`. With the second, each verdict erases them. The erasing itself can stop, or leave the file as it is. The audit's last lines then say so, and a yes becomes "not whole".

**The wipe after a self-check ends `cp_prove`.** The production build's last line does not tell how far its wipe got. By a reading of the code, the production build prints a fixed line before its last line if not every step of the wipe ran, and does not say which step. On a GPU that fixed line has not been seen. If the program had begun to read its secrets, and the last line is there and that line is not, the program has counted every step as run; even then secrets can still be in memory. By one reading's table of the self-checks, a few checks can end either way. By the source, what is left out is the erasing that the code which holds the leaf table does itself. Until the process is gone, the 32-byte key of that table's masks, salts and pads on the OOD answers, in two copies, any pads already made from it, and a combination of its rows, an exact linear image of the weights, the masks and the pads, then stay in CPU memory. After a trap the GPU is unusable, so the wipe at the program's end fails. The GPU code has traps. In three runs of one test, a test build, at small size, on synthetic weights, under a checking tool for GPU code that reported an internal error of its own, ended after an illegal memory access on the GPU. `cp_prove` printed that GPU memory could not be zeroed, and the test build's last line said that not every step of the wipe had run.

**Time, the masks and the seed.** The CPU part of the prover computes on hidden values before they are masked, and on the masks themselves. The source code writes the field's reductions there as conditional expressions, and the machine code that the compiler makes of them has not been read. So the time of a response may follow the masks and the seed, as well as the weights and the requests. A leaf table's masks serve for the table's whole life, and the same masks are computed again in every batch, so whatever time tells about them adds up over all its batches and cannot be taken back. How much that is has not been estimated. This is by a reading of source code. By two readings of these sources, of one file (blocks/field/gl64.h), the field's addition, subtraction, negation and last reduction are written as conditional expressions, and the two corrections inside the 128-bit reduction are written with bit masks, without a condition; other CPU code on field elements was not read for this. Nothing was compiled, run or measured.

**What `cp_commit`'s time can follow.** While a weight table is built, a weight cell that is 0 skips a multiplication and an addition. While the file for the range check is made, a weight's byte or its two digits pick the memory cell of an atomic addition, and the scan of the ranges branches on a weight's size. So `cp_commit`'s time and its memory traffic on the GPU can depend on the weights' values. At `cp_prove`'s start, kernels that decode and round the stored weights have branches on the weights' values. How much the time of a commitment or of a start tells about the weights has not been measured. Only the time of a rejected start was measured, in one study, not on the released programs, at small size, without a settled result. In one pass on a shared GPU, the times of 92 rejected starts differed with the answer that each of these starts had earlier given, which a rejection hides. Nineteen passes alone on the machine showed no steady difference. No log of those passes is in this repository. The time of a run of `cp_commit` is on no declared list, and no written statement on hiding counts it. This is by a reading of source code. By two readings of these sources, the skip at a zero cell (by the source's own comment), the atomic addition and the branches at `cp_prove`'s start stand as told here; the scan of the ranges was not looked up. In these readings nothing was compiled, run or measured.

**When a service stops or restarts.** Clients see a stop, a restart and a withdrawn response. No statement on hiding in these pages covers a "failed" that the provider itself brings about, by its load, say, or by a signal (HW-568), and no statement of the written proof (not public: row HW-763) covers what an end of `cp_prove` withholds, whoever causes it (HW-583). Whether the written proof covers a finished response that the next start withdraws is not known (row PS-53). Whether the written proof covers a stop or restart that the provider itself brings about is not known. By two readings of these sources (prover/prover/arguments.h), `cp_prove` has no option that answers a chosen request "failed" (variables of the environment were not looked at), but no program stops a provider or its front end from doing so, and none of the thirteen duties forbids it. So a provider should not let the moment of a stop or a restart, or an answer "failed" of its own making, follow anything that must stay hidden. After a restart the next process may withdraw a finished response and answer "failed" in its place.

**Telling the causes of "failed" apart.** Every cause gives the same answer, "failed", but a client can partly tell the causes apart. An ill-formed request fails sooner. A request that is sent again runs under new random bytes: a failure by chance goes away, and one caused by the weights returns. And no clock is needed to tell tokens above the policy's bounds from a value of the integer model that is out of its range. What a client learns from that last difference has not been worked out. All this was reasoned and read. Nothing was run, and the third point has not been checked on the released programs.

**A model file whose header is wrong.** By a reading of the code, never run: if a model file's header names more tensors than the file holds, `cp_commit`'s reader goes on into the tensors' bytes and takes them for a tensor's name and numbers. Where the call stops then depends on the weights. Its line on standard error gives one of the reader's fixed sentences, the file's path and, at the places that reject an entry of the tensor table, that entry's number. Which sentence and which number depend on the weights. More widely, which message `cp_commit` prints, and a few small numbers in it, can depend on the weights. The line holds none of the bytes that were read; no test of this repository checks that. `cp_prove`'s production build prints only its fixed lines. Such a header is a damaged file's, or the work of somebody who can write to that file. `cp_prove`'s own reader has two rejections with numbers from a model file's header (the number of blocks and the embedding length; a tensor's size in bytes). Its production build shows neither.
column4: Keep `cp_commit`'s standard error as secret as the weights.

column3: **The kernels of the lookup argument.** A survey of GPU kernels listed those whose addresses, branches or loops follow hidden values. The kernels of the lookup argument that run by default in every build are in none of the readings behind that survey, and they are not known to be in its counts. Their compiled code has not been read, but for a listing of each kernel's per-thread memory. As reported, some look a hidden key up in a public table, so that an address depends on it. They hold keys, tree nodes and digits in shared memory. Some have a per-thread frame of 16 to 368 bytes. Nothing wipes any of these.

**What the fitting tools print.** By a reading of the code, never tried: for some layers the tools in `scales/` print by how many bits the fit made an expert's down projection coarser. These are small integers, up to 24 of them by that reading's count, and the two public files do not give them.
column4: Keep the tools' output as secret as wsums.txt and the other fitting files, and show it to no one.

column3: **A mask key as a launch argument.** By two readings of these sources, nothing run: every kernel that makes a weight table's masks or its columns' salts is handed that table's long-lived mask key as a launch argument, and no code erases launch arguments. What the CUDA runtime and the driver do with launch arguments is not known. Copies of small arguments on a thread's stack and with the driver are recorded nowhere and stay after every exit, and words of a batch's key can stay in dead stack memory: that is not known to hold of the released programs. Only two readings of the call sites judged whether such copies hold secrets, and the tests on per-thread memory do not examine them. By the two readings of these sources, the wipe reports whether its steps ran and none failed; that it checks only that, and never reads memory back, is not known to hold of the released programs.

What a lasting fault could give away. Suppose that a fault leaves values of a sub-proof's lookup argument unmasked in proofs that still verify. Whether a client that sends one request again and again could then read off that lookup's whole hidden table of counts (its multiplicities), not just single values, has not been tried, and the released programs' code has not been read for it. What those counts tell about the weights has not been worked out.
