**No test has copied a running machine.** No test has copied a process or a machine in the middle of a batch. The programs' own guards against a one-time value that answers twice look at one process only.

**A prover started on the wrong files.** A `cp_prove` that is started on the wrong seed, weight files or shape would make table columns that `cp_verify` rejects but anyone could read. Only its comparison with the kept tree nodes keeps such columns in; past it they leave in the file, and a `cp_verify` outside the prover (the provider's check of the whole batch, which is duty 6 at docs/limits.md#the-conditions, or the client's own, but by then the client holds the file) is what rejects it. This rests on a written account of other programs (row HW-678); by one look at the code of a different set of other programs, the comparison stood there too (a wrong seed and another commitment's leaf file are scenes of the public test `gpu.refused_at_the_start.serving` in SUITE.md, which ran on the released programs; none has wrong weight files or a wrong shape).

**What the keys' labels do not tell apart.** By a reading of the code and its page on keys: the labels under which keys are derived hold the version word and no more of the build. So another build with the same version word samples under the same labels. For a batch, the key under those labels also takes in a number that stands for the state of `cp_prove` (`the prover's revision`); it is raised by hand, and row H4.5.1 tells what follows where it is not. None of `cp_commit`'s keys takes in such a number, and what would follow there has not been worked out. The way keys are derived does not help against a weak seed either. The list of ways in which one mask seed can come to serve two tables may be incomplete.
**What the start-up self-tests cannot show.** The start-up self-tests run under public keys, on cases that were chosen for them. So they say nothing about a fault that shows only under the real key.

**Serving as root through `sudo`.** By a reading of the code: if `cp_prove` runs as root through `sudo`, any process of the account that typed `sudo` can, between two starts, move root's secret key directory away and put another directory that root owns and no other account can open, taken from among that account's own directories, under that name. An older copy, or another commitment's directory, is then taken without a word; an older copy comes with its older count, so that a leaf table can serve past its limit and clients get exact equations in the weights. A trial on a CPU bore out that the copy is taken. That account cannot read, forge or open the directory, or change a count by itself. If the spool directory is that account's, it can see the times of the spool's directories and move them, but cannot list or read them. It can also replace the directory for incoming requests while root writes a request there, which puts a client's prompt at risk, not a weight. These last two are from reading alone.
column4: If you serve as root through sudo, you trust the account that typed sudo with the place of the secret key directory.

column3: **A second derivation that checks no real value.** The sources hold two second derivations of the proofs' private random values. The one in `prover/hiding/coins_by_value.cuh` runs only in the programs' start-up self-test, under public test keys. No value that goes into a proof or a commitment is compared with it. Where real values are compared, it is with the other one, `prover/second_writing/`. This is from a search for the file's callers, not from a run.

**What the key file's range proof commits to.** By design, the range proof in the key file commits to counts of how often each table row occurs among the weights' digits. These counts are as secret as the weights. They are committed in masked form and not shown, and the key file stays public for good. They are at risk if a mask in the key file is lost. This is from the format's own page: no code was read for it.

**What the worst-case check bounds.** `cp_commit`'s worst-case check bounds the internal values of the model's forward pass, not the values that the acceptance policy computes. Its verdict holds only for the configuration files for which the check was made. About a prover that runs under other values it says nothing. These three points are from a chapter on other programs (row HW-678), and they were not looked up in the released programs' code. After the check has passed, `cp_commit` writes one line into the secret key directory. By that chapter, and by a reading of the code of other programs, a production build's `cp_prove` rejects a start unless that line holds the digest of the configuration files that it reads itself (a missing line and an altered one are scenes of the public test `gpu.refused_at_the_start.serving` in SUITE.md, which ran on the released programs). The line is under no key. It is the one tie of these files to the commitment at `cp_prove`'s start; a change of a file and of the line together is stopped later, in the first batch (read, not run; its bounds: row HW-193).

**One mask entry over two values.** A one-time mask has no margin. If one mask entry covers two sent values, their difference gives the difference of the two hidden values at once. Where a hidden value is itself public, the sent value gives its mask away, which is harmless only while the masks are independent. This is a property of any one-time mask.

**What the written argument covers of a service.** By the letter of the definition of hiding of the written proof (not public: row HW-763), a rule for forming batches that hangs on nothing but the weights and what clients have seen is inside it. The written proof does not say so of a service, and no comparison of the programs' rule for forming batches with that letter is known. What readings of the code say of the service is told in HW-553. A rule that hangs on random values of the prover that are not shown, for example on how long an earlier batch took, is outside it. By default `cp_prove` takes the next batch's requests before the last batch's responses have their final names, and counts and proves the next batch only afterwards. A client gets a response later than that: this repository's vLLM integration first runs `cp_verify` on the whole batch, once a job of that batch has been asked for, while `cp_prove` is already at work on the next one. So, as a client sees it, the next batch can be taken, counted and proved before the last one reaches it (inferred). In the written proof's main experiments a batch's proofs are handed over before the next batch is chosen. No statement with a proof covers the service as it runs by default (HW-553). One key serves all requests of a batch. The argument is meant to cover that for the hiding of the weights, if the seed is secret and used only as a key, each batch's fresh random bytes are independent, and the keyed function behaves like a random one, for which no figure is known. Read literally, the argument's definition of derived random values excludes every way of deriving them that relies on fresh random bytes for some of them, and so the one that the released programs are described as using (row HW-6). For the batch's other requests it gives less: only one corollary of the written proof could apply, with limits of its own (it leaves out a client that sends a request again because it got no proof). In the written proof, privacy between the requests of a batch with random values derived from a key has not been gone through as far as the OOD answers, which every commitment publishes, bear on it (HW-584). Random values that repeat are outside the argument. A first part of a proof that is used again in a second batch is not covered. The argument is about the written proof's protocol and a prover that the written proof defines. The written proof's authors call the proof "complete but not settled" (row HW-763), and nothing of it is about the programs.

The host compiler's fault. By the build scripts' comments, g++ 13.3.0 can silently drop writes to memory: the writes that fill an object passed by reference. That is one way in which a random value could be lost in CPU memory. It was seen once in this project, in a CPU reference prover (a program that is not in this repository) built with other options, where a self-check stopped it. It has not been seen at the options that the build scripts use, or in `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` or `cp_verify`; no examination of these three for it is known. The build switches the faulty optimisation off with a documented option, `-fno-ipa-modref`, in every compile line that a reading found. Whether that removes every case, and whether another version of g++ is free of the fault, is not known.

**A whole batch that fails while the service goes on.** A whole batch can fail, with the service going on, for a cause that is no single request's. By a comment in the source code, such causes can depend on hidden values. Two readings of the code, made separately, name two such causes: a flag that belongs to no request, and a table of set-up constants that a run has changed. No working-out of what a client learns from such a failure is known.

**Overlapping batches.** By default `cp_prove` takes the next batch's requests before the last batch's responses have their final names, and counts and proves the next batch only afterwards. A client gets a response later than that: this repository's vLLM integration first runs `cp_verify` on the whole batch, once a job of that batch has been asked for, while `cp_prove` is already at work on the next one. So, as a client sees it, the next batch can be taken, counted and proved before the last one reaches it (inferred). In the written proof's main experiments a batch's proofs are handed over before the next batch is chosen. No statement with a proof covers the service as it runs by default. By one lemma of the written proof the order by itself is not the cause: in its experiments a client that must choose blind, or sees proofs late or never, learns no more than in the plain order (two readers, once each and under half an hour, read its whole subsection, found no fault in the lemma and computed it on small cases). One item of the lemma's proof has been corrected; for that item they counted runs and computed no bound, and the lemma has no item on stops or broken runs. The reading in shares that came nearest to reading the proof whole (row HW-579) did not cover the subsection on batches that overlap (row PS-23). What stays outside: in the service the machine's timing decides the order and who shares a batch, and an end can withhold the batch that is staged and not yet named; with `-overlap` or `-overlap-two` a stop in a later batch can withhold earlier ones. The lemma's "no more" is exact for fresh randomness only: with derived randomness it gives the plain order's error against a larger running time (what the written proof's statements on derived random values do not reach: row PS-8). Time, stops and who shared a batch are on the list of what is not hidden, and no limit is known on what time or a stop reveals. No attack is known: three readers looked for one, minutes each, one of them in other sources (row HW-678), with nothing of the service run. The judgement on weight hiding takes that overlap in on this thin ground alone (docs/limits.md#the-verdict). That each batch has random values of its own holds only if the function that derives them is pseudorandom and the batch's fresh bytes are uniform and never repeat. A corollary in the written proof (not public: row HW-763) states weight hiding for a service whose batches overlap, on four conditions. It gives a service nothing unless it is shown that the service's run, with each batch's computation moved back to the moment at which the batch was taken, is the corollary's experiment, and the four conditions as they are numbered are not claimed to be enough by themselves. By readings of source code, and by an inference from them that row PS-53 tells, the service as released meets neither the third nor the fourth, and it has not been shown that it meets the first. Of the second no statement is made here. Readings have found the corollary false as worded many times. The corollary has not been read for the judgement on weight hiding. A leaf table's masks are shared by design by every batch on that table. In one run, on a test build, not on the released programs, a second `cp_prove` on the same directory was rejected at its start. That was a single run of a test that is not among this repository's public tests, on one machine, under one account. That a second `cp_prove` is rejected wherever one running operating system treats the directory as the same one is by a reading of the code. By that reading it holds whether the second comes as a service or for one batch. Each such `cp_prove` locks the directory at its start and holds the lock until the process ends. Not caught: a `cp_prove` on a copy of the directory, and one on another machine that shares the directory, unless the file system applies the lock between machines. The lock may also miss one that reaches the directory by another route on the same machine (through a container's layer, from a virtual machine, or by a second mount). In all these cases nothing rejects the second process, nothing orders what the two release, and we make no statement on hiding. Nor does the lock hold off the audits or `cp_prove -clear`. Read literally, the written proof also leaves out a failed request that is sent again to the service, at once or later. Holding such a request back at a front end does not change that, since time still decides who shares a batch. That is inferred, and nothing was run. No harm is known from the wait, and none has been looked for. No attack through such a request is known, and no search for one is known. The time at which a response is released also tells about the batches next to its own, which hold other clients' requests. With either of two options, `cp_prove` also proves several batches at once, and, by a reading of the code, it rejects both options on a model's files. A comment in the source code gives the reason: by its count, a failure that no request caused or an exit then costs one or two more batches, and a response's time shows more of a neighbour batch's size and arrival time. By a reading of the code, with nothing run, both kinds of cost also hold of the service as it runs by default. The count is the comment's, of the two options. In the default service, by another reading of the code, with nothing run, an end of the process can withhold the one batch that is staged and not yet named, though it was proved whole. By the same reading, an end of the process can leave the requests of the next batch, which is taken before the last has its final names, without an answer until the service is started again, and they are then answered "failed". So the rejection of the two options does not end that leak. How the two options work inside has not been read in the released code, but for the waiting batch's buffer (row HW-92). By two readings of these sources, with either option the routed experts' weights that a waiting batch's pass has decoded last and other unmasked values, among them that pass's sums, the masks' shares and the opened columns, lie in the waiting batch's own GPU buffer through the turns of the later batch on whose pass it rides, and no wipe between turns touches that buffer. By the same readings the decoded weights are zeroed when that pass over the weights ends, the sums, shares and columns last the opening (with `-overlap-two`: through two later batches), and the whole buffer is zeroed when the opening ends. The other weights, which `cp_prove` decodes between turns into the sub-proofs' scratch memory, are zeroed by the restore before the next turn. Nothing was run for these readings, and no test has looked at that memory. At its next start the service withdraws a response that already has its final name, if its request is still among those in work, and answers "failed". So a proof that a front end may already have passed on can be followed by "failed" for the same request. That is by a reading of the code, and nothing was run.
column4: Do not run `cp_prove` on a copy of a secret key directory, or on one directory from more than one running system. Even then no statement with a proof covers the service as a whole. Do not rely on holding back a failed request that comes again: by a reading of the written proof the wait brings that request under no statement of the written proof, since time still decides who shares a batch.

column3: **What `cp_commit`'s log holds after a rejection.** When `cp_commit`'s own run of `cp_verify` rejects a key file or a leaf file, the file is written nowhere. But the log already holds `cp_verify`'s lines (the parameter file's values and the name of the failed check), the rejected file's length, and `cp_commit`'s lines with the time of each phase. What these tell about the weights has never been worked out. This is read from the source code, not run.

**Where `cp_commit` ends.** `cp_commit` ends wherever it finds a cause, and some causes depend on the weights, on the seed or on sampled values. Its exit code, its lines, its timing and what it leaves on disk show which. Whoever can write the two unsigned files beside the model (`wsums.txt`, `fold.txt`) and see the outcome learns, among other things, each tensor's largest product of weight and gain to within a factor of two, and whether a value is not finite or a norm's gain is too small. What many runs together show has not been examined. All of this is read from the programs' own page on how they end (`prover/docs/ends-in-short.md`), and holds in the main by two readings of these sources; what else `fold.txt` sets was not followed.

**A token whose embedding row is zero.** Under clipped gap, if a token's row of the committed embedding table is all zeros, then at every position up to which a window holds only such tokens every score is zero, whatever the other weights are. So a token checked there has a publicly known cost: the lowest possible cost for token 0, and one more for any other token. A client that knows such a token has positions of known cost to measure other costs against, without knowing or searching for the model's top choices. This is worked out from the model's formulas and a reading of the code, and nothing was run. No examination of what such prompts give where the front end follows duty 11 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions) is known. No model's table was looked at, so this does not say that any model has such a row.

**Where measured scores lead.** Under clipped gap, a checked token's cost is the distance of its score below the top score at its position, plus a constant. So the measured costs of chosen tokens after one fixed context give that context's scores relative to one another, as far as they lie within `C` of the top. A cost above `C` shows only that it is above `C`. Published work recovers a model's last layer, up to a linear map, from many such score vectors (N. Carlini et al., "Stealing Part of a Production Language Model", arXiv:2403.06634). This has not been tried on these programs. How many requests one measurement takes has been worked out, by arithmetic alone, for the small example that ships with a clipped-gap policy, on limits that are not shown to be those of the example as it ships. A client that chooses tokens and range, and knows the model's top choices at the other checked positions, has 58 exact thresholds there. So six requests place one token's cost in one of 59 classes. No working-out of how many requests the whole recovery would take is known. The cost's formula comes from a reading of the code.

By two readings of these sources (prover/engine/engine_gpu.cuh; nothing was run), `cp_commit` compares every salt that it keeps in GPU memory with its generator at each commit of a hash tree by its GPU engine; a tree that is made again gets no such comparison, and there the new root is held to the first root. Of a stored table's own tree it compares less: row H3.17.1. By a reading of the code of other programs (row HW-678), where a comparison fails, `cp_commit` stops without leaving a file. `cp_prove` keeps no salts. By a reading of the code, `cp_prove` compares every leaf's salt of the hash trees that the GPU engine builds with the generator run again (HW-344). The salts of the tree that ties a batch together are not compared.

By a reading of the code, `cp_prove` compares a request's whole table of masks with a second derivation right after sending it, and each entry that a sub-proof takes again when it takes it (the table's other entries: row HW-245). It leaves out the places of one-time masks, at which the read-back check looks.

Encoded rows' random entries. By a reading of the code, the GPU engine compares every such entry of the rows that the GPU makes with its generator after the row's hash tree is built. It compares the buffer of random entries, not what the encoder read. So it misses a kernel that reads fewer entries, and two rows that are given one row's entries. The proof library itself has no such check, so this holds only for the GPU engine that the programs use.

**A second way in which a stop could follow hidden data.** A failed comparison of the sub-proofs' one-time masks ends the service. By a comment in that check's source file, an overwriting of the masks that depends on hidden data can be the cause, and that the service ended then tells something about weights or tokens. By the same comment, it is not ruled out that a kernel writes into the masks' array at an index that depends on data. No such write is known, and no kernel was traced. Such a write would stand in the published source code itself, so, by inference, none of the list's four conditions excludes it.

**What a client sees of a stop.** A client sees that the service stopped, when it stopped and how its own request was answered. The answer differs with the kind of stop: after exit code 9, and after most ends with exit code 1, clients with a request in progress hear nothing until the next start; where a batch meets a full leaf table or a like fault, it is answered "failed" first; after a no at the provider's check the clients of that batch get "failed"; at the vLLM integration's check every submitted job of that policy first gets 503, until a person lifts the hold. So one stop may tell more than one yes or no. How much it can reveal about the weights has not been worked out, and no argument on that is written in this repository.

**The order of a job's states in the example front end.** Through the example front end, the order of a job's states can tell a rejection at the vLLM integration's check (503, then no proof) from a failed self-check or a crash (a wait, then no proof), unless whatever starts `cp_prove` lays the hold at a bad exit and starts it again before the hold is lifted. Rule 1 for front ends forbids passing that on. It bears on faults and on secret random values, and no use of it against the weights is known. This is inferred from the code, not run, and a race decides which order a client sees.

**The seed alone, and a leaf table's own secret.** No written statement covers the case in which the seed is known and a leaf table's own fresh bytes are secret, nor the case in which those fresh bytes are known and the seed is secret: a sentence of the written proof (not public: row HW-763) on that second case was found false as worded, and was struck. The written proof speaks only of someone who holds both, for whom every stored table is opened. The first case would need an assumption on the keyed function when its key is known, and the written proof makes none. No examination of that property is known. What the written proof says of that case is about the written proof's protocol and a prover that the written proof defines. The written proof's authors call the proof "complete but not settled" (row HW-763), and nothing of it is about the programs.

**Weights fixed before the seed.** What is said of hiding supposes that the weights were fixed before the seed was sampled, so that no weight depends on a mask. That is a condition on the provider, and no program or verifier tests it. One run of `cp_commit` reads the weights and samples the seed, so for a first commitment it holds by the order of the run. By reasoning, it fails where a seed is kept, or comes again from a random source that repeats, and the weights are changed afterwards.

**What a YES does not say.** A YES from `cp_verify` does not say that the weights were hidden. For hiding, `cp_verify` tests ten conditions on the parameter file at every start (HW-228), which look at counts, not at values. No verifier can tell how masks and salts were produced, or whether a leaf table is retired or past its limit.

**A "failed" that the provider decides on.** No statement on hiding in these pages covers an answer "failed" that the provider itself decides on, for instance to shed load, or causes by terminating `cp_prove` with a signal. Such a decision can depend on load and time, and therefore on hidden values. That is inferred: no leak was shown or measured. By two readings of these sources (prover/prover/arguments.h), `cp_prove` has no option that answers a chosen request "failed" (variables of the environment were not looked at). But no program stops a provider or its front end from doing so, and none of the thirteen duties forbids it. A "failed" that follows a no of `cp_verify`, or no verdict, in the provider's check of a batch is not of that kind: the check decides it, not the provider, and by the runbook it is told, once the hold is lifted, to every request of the batch, in `cp_prove`'s own form. No statement on hiding in these pages covers it either: after a fault, whether a proof verifies can follow a hidden value (row HW-577), and whether the check gives a verdict can depend on load and time. At the vLLM integration's middleware the answer to a rejection comes only after a person lifts the hold, and until then every submitted job of that policy gets 503, by which a client can tell it from `cp_prove`'s own. Where the middleware's check gives no verdict it hands on nothing of that batch, wipes nothing, tries again at a later call, and if the same cause stands at that next try (or at the tenth try, whatever the causes) puts the policy on hold, and tells no one "failed".
column4: Tell a client "failed" only where `cp_prove` wrote `<id>.failed`, or where `cp_verify`, in your check of a batch, rejected one of that batch's proofs or gave no verdict on it: then, once the hold on the service is lifted, tell it to every request of the batch, in the same form. Stop the service with its stop file, which first answers what it has taken.

column3: **A table stored twice.** No verifier can tell whether one leaf table is stored under two numbers. By a page on the verifier, a "leaf table" that is the very table which `cp_commit` makes with the key file, before any leaf table, passed, and that was accepted by design. By two readings of these sources, no test in `cp_verify` compares a leaf table's root with the key file's table or with another leaf table's, so one table under two numbers, or the key file's own table as a leaf table, meets no rule against it. Whether the released `cp_verify` accepts such a table has not been followed through its code or run.

The count of filler cells. By a reading of the code, the count covers the filler cells of twelve matrices only. The two matrices that hold the residual stream going in and coming out are not among them. By a reading of the code, they lie outside the shared scratch memory, so their filler, where they have any, is never written a second time and is not zeroed between turns. Three or four lost GPU operations together can pass it when several requests are advanced in step. It also misses a filler cell that the program's own layout numbers place wrongly, and a true cell that the forward pass does not write. That the count does not fail in a run without a fault is a reading of the forward kernels alone, not of other code that writes to GPU memory before the commitment. Its start value recurs after 255 begun requests. In a run with a fault the outcome itself can also depend on hidden values: the request fails if a byte that was left in a counted cell is not 0.

Left-over bytes, and the written argument on hiding. Where an entry of a message or of a file is meant to hold nothing, the argument of the written proof (not public: row HW-763) covers no left-over bytes there. Left-over bytes of the prover's keys, or of salts that are not shown, are not covered by it either. That argument is of the written proof's protocol and a prover that the written proof defines. The written proof's authors call the proof "complete but not settled" (row HW-763), and nothing of it is about the programs.
No search of the released programs for a place where a value is stored without its one-time mask is known.

**The check on opened columns.** Read in these sources (prover/hash_commitment/hf_tree.cuh); nothing was run. Before the routine that writes opened columns writes a column of a stored table, it hashes the columns that were made again, in GPU memory, up to the lowest stored node and holds that one hash to the stored node. The symbols that it writes come from a second read of the same GPU buffer, and nothing in `cp_prove` hashes them again. So a second read that is lost in part, in which the hash arrives and some symbols do not, passes the comparison. The memory that takes that read is zeroed first, so the lost places hold zeros in the file, not values that were left there. A second read that is lost whole fails the comparison, and nothing is written. Such a column should fail the hash path that `cp_verify` computes, which a `cp_verify` outside the prover (the provider's check of the whole batch, which is duty 6 at docs/limits.md#the-conditions, or the client's own, but by then the client holds the file) runs; that was not traced for this case, and no test plants this fault.

How short a salt may be. Not known: which bound on an attacker's hash queries is meant for hiding, and so the least length of a salt (the hash library's own page: blocks/hash/MODE.md, "What this page does not decide").

**The scripts around the programs.** The scripts around the programs in `driver/`, `integrations/`, `scales/` and `examples/` were read once, in part, in a text from which the released scripts differ. Not read: the tests' directories, most of the two clients' tools, the integer model's arithmetic and vLLM's own source. Read only where they write files: all but one of the tools in `scales/`. Read only in part or by searching them: the scripts in `examples/` and three further tools. The audit tool's scripts (`tools/audit/`) were not part of that reading. What differs from that text has been read by difference alone, not up to the released scripts, for minutes; no way to a leak was found. Only what differs was read, and in two stretches of it only what differs in code. Nothing was built or run in any of these readings. The commands that the pages print were read by difference, in eleven readings of minutes each, not up to the released pages. The reading took in the command blocks of the pages and the commands in the tables of tests. Commands that stand inside sentences were read only in part: the program that cut the commands out of the pages is known to have missed some of them, and nobody but its writer has read it whole. A reading by difference also does not show a command that stays while a protection around it goes. Readings of the scripts and pages found five ways by which a secret could reach another account, a log or another machine: `serve_gguf.sh` put the SHA-256 of `wsums.txt` and `fold.txt` on vLLM's command line; its working directory could lie where others can write, or could first be made by them; the runbook had `cp_commit`'s whole output kept on another machine; one page's advice could leave a copy of the weight files readable by other accounts; and `cp_commit` printed a short table computed from the weights (row HW-270). By readings, not up to the released scripts and pages, the first way is shut in `serve_gguf.sh` alone, the second not wholly, and the other three are shut. By two readings of these sources, the package beside that script takes such digests in vLLM's option `--model-loader-extra-config`, so on its command line; integrations/vllm/integer_model/OPERATING.md warns of it. By two readings of these sources, made by searches for words over the pages and not of every command, the one printed command that the searches found to copy weight files makes the copy in a new directory of mode 700 under umask 077, and the page warns of commands that keep the source's modes. By a reading of the code, `cp_commit` prints no name or string that it has read from a model file, and the runbook keeps its error output apart. Which message it prints, and a few small numbers in it, can depend on the weights. The reading of the scripts found nothing new that a client or a verifier sees, and no script that opens, copies, lists or removes the secret key directory. The example script `serve_gguf.sh` takes and writes no digest: it gives vLLM the path of the directory with the reference copies, and the loader takes the digests there, in memory (read, at its head and its lines; run only before a stand-in for vLLM). The SHA-256 of `wsums.txt` and `fold.txt` lets whoever already holds a whole candidate model test it, and the duties say to keep it as secret as the weights. A check made once, on the path as given, leaves a short window for a swapped link, through which another account could take over the directory (that it could so run code as the operator is reasoned, not tried). Tries got through that window a few times in a thousand. The script checks `TMPDIR` as given and its real path before it makes its directory, and stops if another account could change either. By a reading of the code alone, this shuts that one window; the page says of every such look but the demo's that it is "one look by path, which another account can race" (integrations/LIMITS.md, under "Smaller limits": "The look has gaps"), and of this script that it "works in a new directory that it has made in the real path that it checked" (the entry behind that one, "The other scripts have less behind the look"). Three limits are known. The first is inferred, not tried. The script's look goes by owners and modes alone, not access control lists, and a file system that another account serves (FUSE with `allow_other`) can report any owner and mode (that page's entry "The look has gaps"). So another account can receive what is written in the directory that `TMPDIR` names, on three conditions: the directory lies below one that all can write in and that is sticky, such as `/tmp`, which the look lets pass; that account has made it first and serves it in that way; and the system has `user_allow_other` set (off as installed). The server's `HOME` is made inside that directory: that the account could so run code as the operator, beside the weights, is reasoned, not tried. Second, nothing removes the working directory: it stays after the server has ended, with vLLM's own files in it, and what they hold has not been looked at; it is readable by the caller and root alone, and every start makes a new one. Third, some twenty other scripts and tools that ship use the same check or a copy of it, by a search for its name that has not been read through. Eight of their calls, in seven files, were read: each checks once, on the path as given, which leaves that window, unless differences that were not read bear on it. There that reading saw no value that follows from hidden weights and is not published anyway, but followed none to its end; no reading of the rest for this is known.
column4: Run `serve_gguf.sh` with `TMPDIR` unset, or set to an existing directory that is your own and that only you can write in. The script's working directory stays after the server has ended, with vLLM's own files in it, which have not been looked at: keep it as secret as the weights. Its path stands in the line that the script prints when it starts (`The server's working directory, TMPDIR and HOME:`). Once the server has ended, or has failed to start, that one directory can be removed, whole, by the exact path that was printed, with no wildcard and no guessed name.

column3: **Time, stops and failures in the written argument.** The written proof (not public: row HW-763) puts the prover's time and memory outside what an adversary sees. So none of its results hold for an adversary that sees time. Whatever else depends on the prover's random values or on challenges is treated in one of three ways. Some of it is counted in the error bound with its whole probability: a range check that fails in an honest run, a failed search, a proof that the prover's own check rejects, a whole batch stopped at a rare challenge. The written proof's prover checks each proof that it makes with the verifier; `cp_prove` does not, and the vLLM integration that ships does so at the front end, once a job of the batch has been asked for. A proof that the written proof's own verifier would reject is charged in the bound whatever is done with it. The term for a whole batch stopped at a rare challenge is the price of stopping there: it is paid where the provider's check (duty 6: docs/limits.md#the-conditions) holds the batch back, and by `cp_prove` itself if a run gets to the stop in its own sumcheck code (row C2). That this holds of the programs is inferred. A failed search is counted so only where it fails in the part of a request that cannot be served, or of a marked one. There the written proof gives that term's form and no value, for the prover of the written proof's own paragraph, and whether the programs meet that paragraph's other conditions is not shown. Elsewhere it treats such an end as a broken run, with a lemma that asks nothing of the prover afterwards. Its term for stops at tests on keys and fresh random bits depends on a count that the written proof takes over unchecked, and what its term for the listed values supposes was not compared with the programs (row PS-61). Some is handed over: one proof withheld by a public test on that request's challenges has no term of its own. Some is listed as not covered: a stop at a time limit, a fault of a machine. After a fault of the machine, a self-check of `cp_prove` can fire or not, and a verifier outside it can reject or not, according to a hidden value, so the batch's failure, or that verifier's no, is then a signal about that value. By the written proof's appendix, the released prover also ends at checks of its own that read random values it has drawn. The appendix names three. The written proof places them under none of its statements and gives no bound for them; by reading, no way was found for two of these to end a run on a sound machine, and of the third it does not say. (Ends at a count of draws are another matter: row PS-61.) It also learns only while proving that a request has no valid answer, for which the written proof has no statement. So the written proof states no level for the programs. Its results are about the written proof's protocol and a prover that the written proof defines. The written proof's authors call the proof "complete but not settled" (row HW-763). The start-up test that bounds how often an honest range check fails counts every table that a key can serve.

**The key file's own proofs.** The proofs that the key file itself holds are inside the main statement on hiding of the written proof (not public: row HW-763): the key is part of what the adversary sees there. That statement is about the written proof's protocol and a prover that the written proof defines. The written proof's authors call the proof "complete but not settled" (row HW-763), and nothing of it is about the programs. The programs' proofs in the key file differ from those that the written proof describes. By the written proof's appendix on the programs, each of two lookup tables is looked up through several key maps, and so further values leave under masks into the key file, which is public for good. Among them are the two last values of each key map, which are linear in the weights. The GPU code that computes the values under these masks was read, for the written proof's comparison, at its interface alone, and the GPU code that encodes and commits the two oracle messages not at all. In three other sets of readings these files were read whole, once and briefly, for hiding, as they stand in other programs (row HW-678): every file in at least one set, some in all three; none reported a way, beyond the list of what is not hidden, for a hidden value to reach a client in a correct run (a further reading: row HW-745). That is these readings' own account, known only from short written accounts. Which files hold that GPU code is taken from a list made for these readings. For these readings no program of the prover or of the committer was built or run, and they are not a comparison of the code with the written proof. By a comment in the source code, the committer's checks on itself do not see a value that is lost in the copy of the mask row or in its encoding (row PS-59).

**How far the written proof of hiding goes (not public: row HW-763).** The written proof is about its own protocol and a prover that it defines. The written bound on hiding is explicit, and every numbered statement on the way to it has a written proof. The bound is small only for a bounded number of sessions on one commitment (a session is one call of the prover). Only a part of the bound is evaluated, by computation, for the written proof's own order, for fresh randomness, and for settings of which no complete example is written out. The term for the keyed function has no known number; that function turns a stored key into the prover's random values (rows HW-6 and HW-538). The written proof leaves the terms for stops to be bounded for the prover at hand. A stop: the prover ends its run, or holds a whole batch back (which stops have a term: rows HW-577 and HW-740). The proof has been read in parts, mostly briefly. Some passages were read by their writer alone, and some by nobody. As far as is known, the proof as it stands has never been read as a whole. The nearest to that, one reading in shares, each share of eleven to twenty-seven pages read in ten to twenty minutes, did not cover all of the text as it stands (rows PS-23 and PS-35.1). Every time but one that a whole part was read, further sentences were found that were false as worded. A reading of the chain of statements on which hiding rests found one sentence of that kind. That reading went in parts and took only what had changed: some statements whole with their proofs, of others the changed places alone, in six to some thirteen minutes a part. One reading named one wording slightly more favourable than its ground; that wording stands in one subsection, on whose corollary no claim about the programs relies. Of the fixes to the four statements of row HW-763, three narrow what is claimed, one of them because an error bound was wrong in a case that is excluded. The error in one of the four had passed two readings of the same text. One reading of the proof does not agree to its remark on batches that overlap, taken as a whole. The same reading does not agree to one clause, on fresh random bytes, of the definition (row HW-6) of random values that the prover derives from a stored key. The same reading does not agree to two passages of the running text. The programs differ from the written proof's protocol at three places beside those that its table of differences lists (row HW-763). The three, where "a proof" is what the prover puts out, are what a proof's first hash takes in, the labels of two of a proof's chains, and how the commitment ID is formed. The written proof does not cover five differences between the programs and the sources that its table describes, these three among them (row PS-62). No one statement covers all the points in which the programs differ from the written proof's prover. The first correction of one theorem had a fault of its own; so had that of the lemma of row HW-763, whose correction failed again. The fixes have been read briefly. Beside the fifth error of row HW-763, a further gap was found in the definition of zero knowledge. The fifth error of row HW-763 came with a gap in one proof, that of the lemma on several commitments. A reading that met the fifth error of row HW-763 in a proof that uses the definition graded it as light, and at least four other readings of the definition did not see it.

**A way in which a verifier's no could follow hidden data.** That every response which `cp_prove` serves also verifies supposes that, wherever `cp_verify` would reject a response because of a request's data, `cp_prove` has already failed that request. It has not been shown that this holds in every case. A partial table, made by a reading of the code of other programs (row HW-678), sets each rejection by `cp_verify` that can depend on a request's data beside `cp_prove`'s own test for it, and found none without one at two of this repository's three model shapes. For some of them it could not tell whether an honest run can meet them at all: that hangs on `cp_commit`'s worst-case check, which was not read for it, nor were some GPU kernels. The table is not in this repository. If a request's hidden data made `cp_verify` reject a response that `cp_prove` had not failed, the response would leave the prover as served, and a verifier would reject it. So one request's hidden data could show as a served response that does not verify, an outcome beside "served" and "failed"; the vLLM integration that ships lets nothing of that batch out: there it shows as a hold on that policy, 503 for all the submitted jobs of that policy, until a person lifts it, and then as a "failed" for every request of the batch (narrow exceptions, none open to a client: integrations/LIMITS.md). What such a response shows beyond that no has not been worked out. At those two shapes no such case is known; no reading at the third shape is known. The table named one such case, in models far wider than these shapes, whose dense feed-forward layers have 116,509 or more hidden units: a 32-bit sum that can wrap under contrived weights. By a reading of the code, `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` reject a parameter file of such a width, which shuts that case.

In every proof some mask entries can be worked out by anyone, because they cover a public constant or nothing at all. By the written proof, which is about the protocol on paper and is graded "complete but not settled" (row HW-763), that shows nothing of the weights as long as each entry covers one group of published numbers only. If a bug made such an entry cover a second number by itself, everyone could read that number. In every build the prover stops if a sub-proof's sent numbers and mask entries differ in count, if these numbers do not fill one unbroken run of places, or if its steps are called out of order. A self-check compares each mask entry that covers a sent number with the value that the batch's key gives; the unused entries and the random tail of a segment's mask row are compared with nothing. By a reading of the code, the verifier ends without a verdict (`NOT CHECKED`) if its own code gives one place two values, and through the segment's equation it rejects a number that was sent under another entry than its own, or under none. None of these would notice two entries to which the rule itself gave one value. By the appendix on the programs of the written proof (not public: row HW-763), in the production build nothing counts how often a number is written at each place, and so how often each mask entry is used. What guards it was read at the lines of the code, the prover's stops and the self-check in one reading and the verifier's part in another, and was not run for this. The verifier's part guards hiding only where the provider's check of duty 6 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions) holds the file back: past the prover's stops and the self-check, nothing in `cp_prove` would notice (but for the value of row HW-244). That the verifier then ends without a verdict was read in a further reading.

**Every end of the process reaches back.** Every end that `cp_prove` makes itself first stops the release of responses and removes what has not yet got its final names. Where a failed check ends the program through exit(), the C library first runs the exit handlers that were registered later; the release is stopped only after them, but still before the wipe's first step. In that time a staged response can still get its final names (read in the code). A self-check that fails later takes back no response that has its final names; the next start removes it only if its request still lies in `work/` (what that means for hiding: row C3). By one reading of the code, a kill, a fault signal or an abort does neither, but after such an end nothing gets its final names either. So an end of the process can withhold the one batch that is staged and not yet named, though it was proved whole; by default all that has happened of a later batch then is its taking. A response that is named and not yet synced can go the same way: the next start deletes it and answers "failed"; no bound on how many is in the code, and in the ordinary case it is the last batch at most. If one naming fails partway, the responses named before it stand in `out/` under their final names, their requests stay in `work/`, the next start deletes them and answers "failed", and the rest of the batch is removed; the shipped front end shows none of them. That batch, and with `-overlap` or `-overlap-two` earlier ones, can be withheld so at every end, not at a stop rule alone: a fault, a failed self-check, an operator's signal or a kill. By another reading of the code, a few failed self-checks end `cp_prove` only at the next end of a batch. For those few, the release of responses is blocked only once the service has read the failed check's result, so until then an earlier batch's responses can still be released. For none of these is a probability bounded anywhere. No statement of the written proof (not public: row HW-763) covers that for the service. All this is from readings of the code, and nothing was run.

**The OOD answers.** Every commitment publishes OOD answers (the parameter file's line `record 1`; its separate line `answers 1` says how many a row). The OOD answers are, for each stored table, one weighted sum of each row's weights, hidden by a random pad of its own; they are published in files that every client downloads, for good. Each published value, called an answer, is a row's weighted sum plus a public factor times its pad. It is hidden only as long as the seed stays secret and ChaCha20, the cipher that derives the pads from it, is not broken, while the file is public for good. The anchor's sums are in the key file, and each leaf table's are in its leaf file. According to the written proof (not public: row HW-763), published OOD answers with one such sum for each row hide the weights as long as every pad is fresh, random and used once and the table stays within its limit of use, and under a further condition, on the sample points. The proof has one OOD answer a row, so 2, 3 or 4 OOD answers a row are outside it, and no review covers them. That proof is about the protocol on paper, whose pads are drawn fresh (with pads derived from a secret seed, as the programs' are, only under four conditions that have not been shown of the programs), and is graded no higher than the whole written proof, "complete but not settled". These programs derive the pads from a secret seed ([how, and what that assumes](limits.md#derived-pads)). In the written proof, privacy between the requests of a batch with random values derived from a key has not been gone through as far as the OOD answers bear on it. By a reading of the code, `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` take a parameter file that says `answers 1`, and by two readings of these sources every parameter file with a line `answers` says 1. Nothing stands between a model's files and one published OOD answer a row: `cp_commit` prints a note and goes on. By a reading of these sources, they refuse a parameter file that says 2, 3 or 4 answers, which no written proof and no review covers, under `-public-weights` too (`parameter-range`): a scene of the public test `gpu.refused_at_the_start.serving` (SUITE.md) tries `cp_prove`'s refusal at `answers 2`, on synthetic weights. By that reading, each program's parser refuses such a file, and that is all that stands between any weights and 2, 3 or 4 published OOD answers a row. On other programs (row HW-678), which refuse such a file by a rule of their own (2, 3 or 4 OOD answers a row on a model's files, without `-public-weights`), that rejection was tried by runs, not on the released programs, once each, at small size, with two answers a row alone, and, as reported, held: `cp_commit` on a small synthetic model's files and on a stand-in with one empty model file, `cp_prove` on such a stand-in alone. No test of this repository tries `cp_commit`'s refusal. No run that tried either program's refusal under `-public-weights`, or at 3 or 4 answers, is known (the shared parser has a unit test: row LIM-26.1). The programs take every parameter file that passes their checks, not the default setting's alone. Beyond its line `answers`, no reading in this row opened the default setting's parameter file. The judgement on weight hiding does not reach a real model's weights, or what a fit to them writes (a parameter file, a file of scales): only one of the five tests behind it has run on any, in four runs, one of them on the released programs (row HW-747). That judgement does not cover 2, 3 or 4 OOD answers a row. No verifier can see whether the pads are there, or are random. By a reading of the code, one self-check in `cp_commit` (`own-test-pads`) is all that stands between a fault that loses every pad and a public file without pads. By that reading, that check holds every pad of every row, in each of the four buffers in host memory that use the pads, each user its own, against a reference derivation: it never looks at an answer or at a byte that is written. The self-check counts its comparisons only against floors (two while a table is built, one for each table that a run opens), not for each user of the pads by itself. For a loss in one to three of the four buffers there is a second net, by reading; no run has shown it: the inner `cp_verify` ties the answers to what lies under the root. For a loss in all four alike that check stands alone. In a trial on a test build, with that check switched off, a commitment without pads passed everything else that `cp_commit` does. Without its pad, each published answer is one exact linear equation on a row of the weight table. The programs' self-checks only compute each pad again, with a second implementation that is not an independent one, so a misreading of the rule that both share goes unseen. The published answers themselves are computed once. By a reading of the code the pads lie in host memory that can be paged out and is not locked, while the keys' memory is locked if the system allows it. While a proof is made, the pads of the table in use lie in ordinary host memory that the wipe at exit does not reach ([details](../prover/docs/ends-in-short.md)). With its published answer a pad gives one exact equation on a row's weights, so treat the prover's machine and its memory as you treat the weights. One of the two implementations against which the pads are held has a copy of the cipher that is near in text to the first. Whoever gets the seed (for a leaf table: with that table's own secret, kept in the same directory) can open every published answer, at any time, with no proof served; each is then an exact linear equation in the weights. So the seed of a commitment has to stay secret for as long as the weights do, also after the commitment is no longer used, in backups too. The danger ends only when the seed and the leaf tables' secrets are gone, backups too, and the programs have no tool that destroys them (row H9.4). If `cp_commit` repeats its random bytes on other weights (a random source that repeats, or a machine image started twice), the two commitments' pads are equal. The two commitments' public files alone, with no proof ever served, then give, for every row of each table and each stored answer, one exact linear equation in the two sets of weights, for good: in the weights themselves, if one of the two sets is known. The anchor table's pads hang on the seed alone, and no table's key reads the weights. To end this in the code, every table's key would have to take a digest of the weights as they are committed: a change of the key schedule, not of a parameter. By a reading of the code, with nothing run, every fresh draw is one call for 32 random bytes with nothing mixed in, and nothing notices a repeat. Reasoned and not shown by a run, three more things must hold, because a pad is also stored inside its row, under the root of the table's hash tree. Each proof's own masks must hold: every proof commits to a random combination of the table's rows, pads included. Once about a third as many independent combinations have leaked as the table has rows, they give the pads (683 for 2,048 rows; reasoned, not run). So a lost mask also counts toward the pads: once the pads are known, each published answer is one exact linear equation on a row of the weight table. A table must stay within its limit of use (that holds of every stored table; for the first one the committing program alone counts, in its one run): beyond it the opened columns give exact equations in a row's content, its pads included. And the answers' points and factors are a hash of that root, which depends on the pads: that the pads are independent of them needs an argument, without which it is not proved that a pad hides its answer. The same argument must show that the root itself, the published upper layers of the tree and the neighbour hashes in opened paths tell nothing of the pads. No program can settle either matter. For the first the written proof has an argument, in the proof of its theorem on published OOD answers; it is not settled, and no whole reading has taken it in. On the published upper layers a reading found no word in the written proof. With `-public-weights` nothing is hidden. By a reading of the code, under `-public-weights` the seed is derived from the option's file, which is meant to be published: whoever has that file can compute every pad, and each published value is then an exact linear equation in the weights. Nothing tests that this file, or the weights, are public. A client cannot tell from the public files that a commitment was made to hide nothing ([details](what-is-not-hidden.md#public-weights)). With `-public-weights`, under which nothing is hidden, OOD answers have been made from a real model's files at least twice, not on the released programs (row M1.4), each time at full size, from public files of the model's weights; in two such runs `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` on one request and `cp_verify` ended with exit code 0 (reported). One of the runs read a third party's public 4-bit conversion of the model's weights. The public test `gpu.record_on_public_weights`, which ran on the released programs, makes and serves a commitment under a sampled seed, and another with `-public-weights`, on a synthetic model in files of the model format, made by the repository's own tool, not a real model's. It tests nothing of hiding. Only one of the five tests behind that judgement has run on a real model's weights, in four runs, one of them on the released programs (row HW-747). That judgement does not reach them ([Not covered](limits.md#the-verdict)). What these pages say about weight hiding has been checked for the default setting only as far as [that judgement](limits.md#the-verdict) tells. At the default setting hiding has been tested in those of the runs in this row that say so, in the runs of the sweep at its small form (row HW-660) and in the runs listed with [that judgement](limits.md#the-verdict), and in nothing else. In none of them was anything truly secret: the weights were synthetic, or a real model's public weights. On the synthetic weights the last token almost determines the next one, so the proofs accepted under exact match show that the pieces work together at full size, but say little about attention, routing or the scales. column4: The judgement on weight hiding covers two kinds of parameter file only: the default setting's, and one that differs from it in a clipped-gap policy's three numbers alone, the latter on less evidence. That judgement covers no other file that the programs take. Before you hand out public files, know that OOD answers cannot be called back. Make the commitment on a machine that was not cloned or restored from a saved state; hand the public files out only after `cp_commit` has ended with exit code 0; keep the secret key directory secret for as long as the weights matter. If you doubt a public key directory (a saved state used twice, a fault, a seed that got out, programs that are not a production build of the released programs) and have not handed it out: give it to no one, and make a new commitment. If the example front end's proof server is running on it, stop the server for good (removing the directory that the server opened ends it too, which was tested on ext4 alone: details, and what to look at first: integrations/LIMITS.md). Moving or renaming the directory, or a hold, does not stop it, and a restart alone, the directory still under its name, serves it again (details: integrations/LIMITS.md#above-a-public-directory; row R25 says what of this was seen or tested). Prefer stopping: it loses no file. Whoever removes instead: what counts is the directory that the server opened at its start; if it has since been moved or renamed, that is the moved one, not what stands under the name by then (removing that takes nothing back). Everything in it is lost, so list it first. If the server was led astray at its start, that directory is another of root's. Do not remove it; stop the server. If a public key directory with 2, 3 or 4 OOD answers a row on real model files exists anyway, do not give it to anyone. If the public files have been handed out already, they cannot be taken back: tell the person in charge of the weights. Whether these steps are enough for weights that must stay hidden is each provider's own decision. A retired commitment stays dangerous. The programs have no tool that destroys a seed, so keep the seed and the leaf tables' secrets as secret as the weights for as long as they exist, backups too (docs/operators-duties.md#backups-and-restored-copies, step 5).

What share of all draws the kinds of these 30 make up has not been reckoned for this sweep. What an unnoticed loss exposes this test does not show. **A sweep of lost random values at the default setting's small form, and the readings of its 30.** At the default setting's small form the sweep of lost random values ran, as reported, under a test seed, on synthetic weights, with one request, on one fixed sample, on more than one set of test builds of other sources (row HW-678), whose tie to the released programs has not been shown, once on each, each time with the same outcome, loss for loss (rows LIM-63 and LIM-63.2, line 3): no second witness (docs/limits.md#the-verdict). A bad result: of 165 losses injected in CPU memory 30 went unnoticed and after 12 more the files were byte for byte those of an honest run. All 130 in GPU memory were stopped by a self-check. That is no rate. A loss is one sample of random values overwritten with zeros right after its sampling, at the first and the last sample of each class of the four generators on the sweep's list and at a few more in large classes, not at every sample: a class in which these were stopped may hold one that is not. No case of the sweep loses one of the pads on the OOD answers, a sub-proof's mask or a weight table's random entry, which come from other generators. Random values that are no samples of these four generators were not tried: the seed, each batch's 32 bytes from the system and the keys derived from them, the sub-proofs' masks, and the leaf tables' random entries and salts. "Unnoticed" means that the verifier program of the same build accepted: a whole call for the 19 altered proofs, and its two calls on the key file and a leaf file alone for the 11 altered commitments. What an unnoticed loss exposes this test does not show. 122 of the 130 were stopped by one self-check alone. The 295 runs struck 189 of 73,177 draws, and the 30 are 27 different draws. What share of all draws the kinds of these 30 make up has not been reckoned for this sweep. Other losses outside the sweep go unnoticed: 9 of 9 at neighbouring draws that no self-check covers, and far more draws of their kinds are covered by no check (row LIM-63.2, line 4). By two readings of the code of other programs, apart, about ten minutes of reading each, with toy computations and nothing run on the programs, none of the 30 exposes anything of the weights by itself, as long as every other random value is there, except for one case, for which that is not known: the loss of a batch's salts. No pair of losses was tried or computed for these 30. 16 are spare random entries of mask rows, which no sent value needs (four more readings judged these 16 and agree). Nine of these 16 are the heads of stretches of 58 to 5,116 neighbouring draws, 14,970 in all, of which the head alone was struck. The spare entries are the only reserve for a lost pad or tail entry of their rows, and at full size one stage has 4 of them. 5 are bytes that stand in the file anyway. 7 can show a fact about the batch (that a slot is free; something of the order of arrival). 2 are the draws of a binding tree's salts: the key file's, whose one salt is written in the file anyway, and a batch's, whose loss lets a guess at a 32-byte hash be tested. For the loss of a batch's salts a lemma of the written proof leans on the lost value alone. At stake there is a test of any guess at what of the weights enters a failed request's part of a batch, for whoever holds its neighbour's proof. Not known, for these 30: whether that case exposes anything of the weights. No checked repair is known for the prover that the written proof (not public: row HW-763) specifies, and no statement says that the released prover is that prover. In small computed examples a prover that fills that part without fresh random values leaked fully. That the released prover fills it freshly and hands out nothing of it rests on brief readings of the code of other programs, with nothing run (row C3.1.1). In those small computed examples some pairs of losses did leak. None of this is proved or checked. The written proof of hiding counts some of the 30, or values of their kinds, as random or fresh: a run that has lost one lies outside what that proof is stated for, and what that costs is not settled.

**Weight files of 8 or 16 bits.** These are weight files in which any tensor that the programs read is stored in 8 or 16 bits (Q8_0, F16, BF16). Random values kept in GPU memory are lost before they are hashed in. What looks for it in every run: A self-check recomputes them in full. What that does not see: It uses the same GPU code, so it cannot see a fault in the compiler or in the generator's core routines. It misses a kernel that reads fewer of the values, and two rows that are given one row's entries. What trials showed: The sweep at the default setting's small form: row HW-660.

column3: A stored weight table's own masks or salts are lost. What looks for it in every run: When a table is made, a second implementation compares every mask. At every opening, other GPU code recomputes each opened column, which must fit the stored tree. What that does not see: Later groups of parts make the same masks again without a comparison, and none of the table's salts is compared when it is made. A salt at a column that is never opened. The pads on the OOD answers, which every commitment has, and which have a self-check of their own. With a fault in the few routines that both checks share, a proof would verify and leak. What is written comes from a second read of the column, not from the read that was hashed: row HW-574.

Sub-proof masks or a table of masks are lost. Every value that they should hide can then go out unmasked in a proof that verifies; such a loss has not been tried on the released programs. What looks for it in every run: A second implementation compares sub-proof masks and a request's table of masks. It also compares two of the key file's tables with their random tails (their random entries), and the random tail of each request's table. What that does not see: Its own comparison skips the one place in a request's table that holds a one-time mask. The read-back check looks at that place. The second implementation compares these tables only. It does not compare the cells in which a round's sum of sub-proof mask entries waits (row HW-746). Of other messages' tables of masks and their random entries, the two further checks (row HW-619) compare some with a second derivation, and the others are compared with nothing after their sampling (see row HW-689). By a reading of the code, a self-check looks at each of the proof library's messages with mask rows just before it is opened. It compares each value of the rows' random tail with a second derivation, and the table of masks only in part. Among what it does not see: a committed table's own columns, a message that is never opened, a message that another part of the proof sent, the engine's encoded copies, the pads on the OOD answers, and a fault that both derivations share. No test is known that makes the comparison of a request's tail fire.

A one-time mask is not written where it belongs. What looks for it in every run: The read-back check. What that does not see: A mask that is overwritten after the check has looked. By a reading of the code the proof is then false: it can leave the prover, and a `cp_verify` outside the prover (the provider's check of the whole batch, duty 6: docs/limits.md#the-conditions, or the client's own, but by then the client holds the file) should reject it (argued, not proved).

A mask is never generated, or one random value is used in two positions. A value whose mask is never generated can go out unmasked in a file that verifies; what one value in two positions would give away is told in row H22. One mask entry that was the only mask of two sent numbers would give away one known linear combination of the two hidden values, their difference where both are masked in the same way (plain arithmetic). Neither fault has been tried on the released programs. What looks for it in every run: Nothing that a run has shown. No injection of either fault into any program that has the two further checks (row HW-619) is known, so no run shows whether these checks reach these faults. By a reading of the code, a self-check compares part of a folding step's mask with a second derivation. Whether that self-check would stop a re-used mask in the GPU programs has not been tried. What that does not see: The audit tool, which holds the provider's secrets, reports them only with all the secret bytes, which for a proof exist under a test seed or with the option that keeps a batch's random bytes.

Another random value (other than those of rows HW-684 to HW-688) is lost in CPU memory before it is hashed in. What looks for it in every run: For one-time masks, the read-back check's later part. For some other values, the second implementation's comparisons (row HW-686) and two further checks (row HW-619), which compare them with a second derivation. What that does not see: Most such values are compared with nothing after their sampling. What trials showed: The sweep at the default setting's small form: row HW-660 (of 165 losses injected in CPU memory 30 went unnoticed).

column3: One of `cp_prove`'s salts is lost at a leaf that no proof opens. What looks for it in every run: By a reading of the code, `cp_prove` compares every word of every leaf's salt of the hash trees that its GPU engine builds, as it lies in GPU memory after its tree is made, with the generator run again. It is judged only at the end of the request and of the batch. By a reading of the code, each verdict comes before the parts that it judges are staged. But a request's first part is staged, under no final name, while the salts of the shared part and of the request's second part are still unjudged. What that does not see: a fault that both sides share, a hashing kernel that misreads a salt, and the salts that are made again for an opening, which this comparison does not reach (the verifier's path check tests those). The salts of the tree that ties a batch together are not compared. A salt lost whole lets someone test a guess at its leaf (lost in part: row HW-484). Whether that is feasible has not been worked out.

Old GPU memory gets into a hash tree. What looks for it in every run: In these sources the arrays of a hash tree of the GPU engine are zeroed before anything is written to them (prover/engine/tree.cuh, `begin()`; read, nothing was run; for a leaf's digest a unit test of the engine's routine holds it, the public test `gpu.tree_arrays_cleared_test` (SUITE.md), which has passed: row H45). What that does not see: Other GPU memory, and CPU memory (row HW-458).

column3: An old value stays in a table cell that no check reads. What looks for it in every run: `cp_prove` sets a sub-proof's filler cells to zero twice and counts the zeros before it commits. By a reading of the code, the count covers the filler cells of twelve matrices only. What that does not see: The filler cells of the two matrices that hold the residual stream going in and coming out, which the count does not cover and which are not zeroed a second time (row HW-570). For the host compiler's fault, the build switches the faulty optimisation off. What that does not see: Any other kernel. The full recomputation (row HW-684) compares GPU code with GPU code. What trials showed (the four faults, one by one: rows HW-520, H8.4, HW-45, HW-550): From the GPU compiler's first fault, a wrong value was seen in a sample kernel and in all 17 cases of one routine's test (nvcc 13.0.88; one run), never in a mask or a file. By its kind it gives files that do not verify, but no run has shown that, and such a proof file can leave the prover (row HW-491), though a key file or a leaf file meets a verifier first: `cp_commit` runs `cp_verify` on these before it writes them (by a reading of these sources, not run). column3: **How a failed self-check ends `cp_prove`.** By two readings of these sources (prover/prover/prover.h; row C3), a failed self-check on secret random values or keys ends `cp_prove`: most with exit code 9 and a name that begins `own-test-`, a few with exit code 1, at least two of them without a name. A few end it only at the next end of a batch. For those few, the release of responses is blocked only once the service has read the failed check's result, so until then an earlier batch's responses can still be released. By a reading of the code of other programs (row HW-678), what fails one request or one batch while the service goes on is not a check on secret random values. It is a sample from hash output that gives no result, a few self-checks on data, a value out of its range, or a request above the policy's bounds. Nothing was run for these readings.

**Four more kinds of fault that no check would catch.** Besides the losses that other rows tell, a reading of the code finds four more kinds of fault that no check would catch, but for part of one. All four are in rows HW-326, HW-685, HW-690, HW-692. They are what the second implementation and the recomputation at every opening do not see, what the spot check of four values does not see, a salt at a leaf that no proof opens, and an old value in a table cell that no check reads. But by a reading of the code, a comparison looks at `cp_prove`'s own salts at such leaves (see row HW-690). A stored table's salt at a column that is never opened stays unseen (row HW-685). A fault in the routines that the second implementation and the recomputation at every opening share strikes alike the GPU kernels that make a stored weight table and those that open it.

**Single findings on hiding.** What they tell as read was read in the code of other programs (row HW-678), and what they tell as run was not run on the released programs, unless the finding says so. (1) In the released programs `cp_prove` runs no verifier: a proof that does not verify leaves like any other (row HW-491). (2) In each batch `cp_prove` allocates a small list of address ranges whose size depends on what a part of the GPU's memory holds, and it exits if that allocation fails. Tables made from the weights may be in that memory. Whether they are is not known: three readings of the code did not settle it. (3) By documents and a comment in the code, a client can use up a leaf table's batches: a batch that was begun counts whatever becomes of it, and a full leaf table stops the service (item 8 of the list: docs/what-is-not-hidden.md#volume-and-schedule). (4) The stop at a table's limit has been tested only at small size, and on the released programs in one scene of the public test `gpu.serving_first_run` (SUITE.md), at a count that the test sets itself (the end that it waits for, `cp-copy-spent`: prover/docs/ends-in-short.md; that the test passed: row LIM-63; what lies past a limit: row H5.3). (5) On a served proof the audit with the provider's secrets can check only the stored tables' salts, and only on synthetic weights. (6) No full-size proof has been searched for leaks.
