**One term of the written bound on hiding: what the paragraph on resent requests of the written proof (not public: row HW-763) does not reach.** The term is one of the written bound's terms for stops (row HW-579): that of a prover that holds a whole batch back when one proof in it does not verify. It stands in a bound on paper: it is not a leak, and no attack through it is known (these docs' own words, not the written proof's; no search for one is known). `cp_prove` runs no verifier, but the vLLM integration that ships runs `cp_verify` and, at a no, hands out nothing more of that batch (narrow exceptions, none open to a client: integrations/LIMITS.md). On paper the two together are such a prover, so the term stays. A provider is free of it for that cause only if, at a no, it holds back no more than that one response and goes on serving, which duties 6 and 8 do not allow (docs/limits.md#the-conditions), and not wholly even then: `cp_prove` itself has a stop at one kind of rare challenge in its own sumcheck code (row C2), and whether a run gets there has not been followed. To be free of it also supposes that, at the rare challenges at which a verifier says no, `cp_prove` computes what the written proof's prover computes, and the code was not read for that. All this is inferred from the written proof, which does not say it of the programs. That term, by the written proof, can be much the largest in the bound. As reported, not shown, it is real and not an artefact of the proof. What it comes to rests on a count that the written proof does not write out or claim (row PS-31). The written proof's computed figures on hiding are for fresh random values alone and leave out several terms. One of them, that of the keyed function, has no number at all (row HW-579). The term told here is another, and it has no figure either: its input was not counted at the default setting (row LIM-44). For the released prover, which also stops at tests for which no bound is stated, the written proof has no bound at all. The written proof's paragraph on resent requests says that, for the weights, a client that resends a request because its proof was withheld adds no term of its own. That paragraph covers one commitment only, and a prover that loses no count. These programs can lose a count when the power fails. By a reading of the code, a batch opens no column before its count is synced to the disk. So on a disk that keeps synced writes, a loss of power by itself takes no table past its limit. No loss of power has been simulated. The paragraph also asks for a client that acts on nothing but whether it was answered and whether its proof was withheld: not on the bytes or the time of its answer. Where a provider passes on what a bare `cp_prove` made, a client can get a proof that its verifier rejects. A client that resends for that reason chooses by what is in that proof. Read literally the paragraph does not reach it, unless its request is one of those whose proofs the adversary sees. (Inferred: the written proof names no such client.) And the paragraph is one of the statements on derived random values that, read literally, do not cover the way in which the released programs are described as deriving them (row HW-6). Read literally, that paragraph does not reach a request that is sent again to the service, at once or later; the written proof leaves such a request out (row HW-553). By default `cp_prove` takes the next batch's requests before the last batch's responses have their final names, and counts and proves the next batch only afterwards. A client gets a response later than that: this repository's vLLM integration first runs `cp_verify` on the whole batch, once a job of that batch has been asked for, while `cp_prove` is already at work on the next one. So, as a client sees it, the next batch can be taken, counted and proved before the last one reaches it (inferred). How the batches follow one another is by a reading of the code, and what the written proof leaves out by a separate reading of the written proof; nothing was run.

**The orders on the front end (docs/operators-duties.md#the-front-end).** (1) The limits on waiting requests and unfetched responses matter for the front end too, because a client that fills the queue uses up a leaf table, and once a batch has started it is counted even if it fails. (2) **Send real clients' requests only to a production build,** never to a test build. In a test build a batch's random bytes can come from a file, and nothing checks whose requests it receives. (3) **During a hold:** Tell clients only that the service is down. Do not give them a cause, an exit code or a count. Do not send any response or `.failed` file that was made before the hold. Clients may see that the service stopped, but not why (this is an order and no finding: what a client can in fact see of a stop is item 7 of docs/what-is-not-hidden.md). The example front end tells them more than that: its answer says that the provider has put this policy's proofs on hold ([its limits](../integrations/LIMITS.md#after-a-fault-nothing-stops-by-itself)).

**On which programs and at which size the tests of hiding ran.** (1) Most of the runs that these pages tell were not on the released programs; where a run was, its entry says so. (2) Beside the runs that the judgement on weight hiding rests on (docs/limits.md#the-verdict), the sweep of lost random values (one fixed sample) and other tests of the out-of-domain (OOD) answers have run at the default setting's small form. The sweep ran on test builds of other sources (row HW-678), whose tie to the released programs has not been shown. These other tests of the OOD answers ran on test builds or otherwise not on the released programs. (3) A separate audit has run at the default setting too, at full size, once, in part, on synthetic weights (further such audits: row LIM-63.2, lines 6 and 7). (4) Taken together, the five tests that the judgement rests on (which of them on the released programs: row LIM-63.2) have run at the default setting, in whole or in part, nearly all at its small form, and beside them a separate small audit with every secret has run at that setting (what of each ran: rows LIM-63 and LIM-63.2). (5) The repository's two audits have run on synthetic weights, at the default setting, at small size and at full size (rows LIM-63 and LIM-63.2; tools/audit/README.md, "What has been run"), and said yes, but a yes says nothing of the pads on the OOD answers. At full size the fifth's two audits have run together only on other programs.

Code that keeps the language's rules but breaks the library's stated contract (blocks/chain/closed.h; among its clauses: naming no private member of the library; declaring nothing at global scope before its headers; keeping operator new) can still get `blocks/` to accept a false claim. By one reading of the code, the six ways found for ordinary code to do that are closed inside one process. By another, of 22 ways counted in other sources of the library (row HW-678; nothing was run for it), 15 are closed, 2 only in part, 4 only where one running program performs all the tests of a weight table, and 1 is open; counting two of the 15 that lean on the caller and the 4 as closed in part gives 13, 8 and 1. Two further ways for ordinary code stand outside the 22; they are closed inside one process only. The counts overlap and must not be added. "Closed" is said only of source code that breaks no rule of the language, defines none of the tests' macros and calls the library's own entry points. Of the ways that break that contract, one works at the 128-bit target at toy size. A second, an operator template declared before the headers, gave a wrong plan and, not on the released programs, a false acceptance at 128 bits; a program of that kind, run on the library in a process of its own at the same 128-bit target, at toy size on synthetic data, had a false claim accepted in 8 of 48 tries (0 of 48 without the declaration); nothing that closes this way has been added to the library. A third is closed in part only: for fourteen planning routines, and not for two further kinds of planning routines, the routines that run a proof or a plan's scope. The library is not offered as an interface, so a caller that passes mismatched configurations or tables may find more ways. For one way, the prover's and the committer's side have not been read to the end. What you can do: Call the three programs, not the library. Basis: read; run, not on the released programs; reported (the first way: of 16 tries 9 were carried through and all 9 accepted, in its harness on the library; the second: 8 of 48, control 0 of 48).

By design, a commitment made under a test seed hides nothing from anyone who knows the seed. Its public files carry no mark of the test seed, so someone who is handed them cannot tell. Only the production build accepts a real model's weight files. It also has four options that work only on synthetic weights, and it rejects them on a real model's files: `cp_commit -keep-for-the-audit`, and `cp_prove -keep-for-the-audit`, `-overlap` and `-overlap-two`. That rejection was seen on a GPU, at small sizes, not on the released programs, for all four except `cp_prove -keep-for-the-audit`: by the tests' scripts on a small synthetic model's files or on a stand-in for a model's folder, not on a real model's, and for `-overlap` and `-overlap-two` in a test build alone. The production build does accept a fifth option, `-public-weights`, on a real model's files, with a marker file next to each. With that option the weights are not hidden, and the public files carry no mark of that either. No test of hiding covers overlapping batches. Of the options `-overlap` and `-overlap-two` there is no argument either, and how they work inside has not been read in the code. No statement with a proof covers the service as it runs by default, with batches that overlap in time, that is, it takes a new batch before the last one has been handed out, and can have counted and proved that batch before the last one reaches a client (inferred). A corollary in a technical report that is not public and not refereed states weight hiding for a service whose batches overlap, on four conditions. It gives a service nothing unless it is shown that the service's run, with each batch's computation moved back to the moment at which the batch was taken, is the corollary's experiment, and the four conditions are not claimed to be enough by themselves; by readings of source code, and by an inference from them that row PS-53 tells, the service meets neither the third nor the fourth, and that it meets the first has not been shown (rows PS-53 and HW-553). Of the second no statement is made here. What you can do: Serve with the production build only; never reuse a test's seed or randomness file. Basis: run, not on the released programs; read.

No exit of `cp_prove` wipes all memory: its GPU compute engine's memory pool is never wiped. A crash (`SEGV`, `BUS`, `FPE`, `ILL`, `ABRT`, `SYS`, `TRAP`) or a `KILL` skips the wipe altogether. After a crash, a production build prints an ordinary last line, with exit code 1 (9 after a failed self-check). The wipe fails after a trap in a GPU kernel, and a wipe that takes longer than 600 seconds is abandoned as `not-all-wiped`. Either way, weights and masks may stay in GPU memory. The last line does not always say so (read). By the source's own comment, the limit of 600 seconds does not help while the main thread sleeps uninterruptibly in the kernel (row R7.1). `cp_prove` can exit while the service's thread is inside the code that holds the weight table. That is what happens when a check fails while the part shared by a batch's proofs is being built. Such an exit leaves the key for the leaf table's masks and salts, and an exact linear image of weights and masks, in CPU memory (read). The production build's last line does not report this. By the code, a line before it then says that not every step of the wipe ran, and not which (read; not seen in a run). What you can do: Treat the machine's memory as holding secrets after every exit. Basis: read; reported.

Four runs that were timed, at full size on a real model's public 4-bit weights, not on the released programs (row RES-19): one with sessions of batches of 24, one with batches of 8 and of 1, one with batches of 64, and one with batches of 24 under a clipped-gap policy on stored replies. A small helper that gives the weight files' cached pages back to the system ran beside parts of all four: beside each session's start-up and the beginning of its first batch, and in the run with batches of 24 beside the loading of the weights for the request proved by itself. In the other three it ran beside no counted interval. In the run with batches of 24 it also ran beside the first session's last four and a half minutes. Of that session's three counted intervals it touched only the third: its last 8 seconds, or 16 with the call that started the helper. It ran beside the whole last interval, which the steady rate leaves out and the rate from the start of the process counts. The same stretch holds the fourth batch's last 8 seconds, all but the first 62 seconds of the fifth's, and the end of one of the eight checks that those runs' programs made before a release, the shortest. That run's rates, waits, start-up times and overheads have it in them. So do the first-batch wait, 751.7 seconds, of the run with batches of 64, for its first 45 seconds, and the clipped-gap run's rate with the start-up counted.

This section distinguishes three things: the programs in this repository, the protocol as [a technical report that is not public and not refereed](glossary.md#technical-report) describes it, and the protocol as Lean describes it. Each entry below is about the programs unless it says otherwise, but what a `YES` means is stated for the protocol. A run is to be taken as made at the [default setting](glossary.md#default-setting) only where its entry says so ([kinds of evidence](limits.md#how-a-thing-is-known)); few kinds of test have run there ([what has run at the default setting](limits.md#few-runs)). The programs are known to differ from the protocol, and it has not been shown that the differences do not matter ([No theorem is about `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` or `cp_verify`](limits.md#which-verifier-has-a-theorem)). The report's proofs have not been checked independently: they have been read in portions only, not every portion in the wording in which it stands, and no single reading covered the whole argument ([how the proofs were read](limits.md#what-the-theorem-assumes)). A `YES` from `cp_verify` is meant to show that a reply matches the committed model's own output. The mathematics behind that claim is not about the three programs `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` and `cp_verify`. It is a written proof about the protocol on paper, with the hash taken as a random oracle, and theorems about the protocol as Lean describes it. For soundness and binding the written proof rests on a theorem on Reed–Solomon codes that is taken as given in the written proof, which cites it, and in the programs' accounting (what this repository's Lean library proves beside it, and what rests on reading: row SO-2). Lean has a soundness theorem for its own verifier, `verify`, not for the C++ program that users run: [what it says, and what it does not](../lean/THEOREM.md). [No theorem bounds the chance](limits.md#which-verifier-has-a-theorem) that a program of this repository accepts a false file. **What you can rely on.** The attacks ran mostly not on the released programs, and of the stronger kinds of attack few have run at full size: apart from the 57 lying proofs (24 for false replies, 33 with a planted lie) of `lean/THEOREM.md` ("What has been run"), no prover that itself sends a false value has, and, but for one cheating committer's false leaf file (a false copy's file) at full size, tried once through a form of the executable `verify` that is not in this repository and through a C++ verifier built from other sources (row HW-678), and rejected by both, in `verify` at that file's own check, by report (`lean/GAPS.md`, 14 (i) and 33), no malicious committer, and no malicious prover that alters a value but these lying proofs, has run at the default setting at full size; a cheating prover that, by report, alters no value and only goes on past its own test on the policy has, under the clipped-gap policy: its one proof of a true claim was accepted and its two proofs of false claims were rejected: the two rejected claims are false by the run's own sheets; neither rejection is shown to be owed to the policy's limits (each names a step of the proof file's check); one run, on test builds, evaluated, not proved; both verifiers gave the same three answers (`lean/GAPS.md`, 14; [what has run at the default setting](limits.md#few-runs)). The Lean verifier's three calls on that cheating prover's proofs and the executable form's one run on that false file were made over Lean files and sources of the parser that differ from this repository's.

By design, a commitment ID fixes the weights that its anchor decodes to, not the key file's bytes (which one is [the theorem on codes](limits.md#what-the-theorem-assumes)'s to give: [binding](glossary.md#binding)). A test, not on the released programs, ran at small size on synthetic weights, under the default setting's parameter file as the small example `target_small_f2_roomy` has it (proof of work counted). An edited committer (the edit is not part of this repository) made three key files from the weights of the honest key file. By a reading of the edit and by the edited program's own counts, their anchors differed from the honest anchor at 1, 16 or 256 of 8,388,608 positions a row, in all 256 rows. That gave three pairs with the honest key file: four IDs over one leaf table. By the files' own bytes the four leaf files are equal in head, root and stored answers and differ only in what follows these, the link's proof, while the four key files' roots and stored answers differ. The unedited prover of a test build, run once on each committer's files, wrote the same four proofs byte for byte, and the same test build's `cp_verify` accepted them under each of the three further IDs, in 12 full checks, each run once, as it did under the honest ID. Each commitment was made once, so this is for one try. That such anchors decode to the same weights is arithmetic and an argument on paper, which this test did not try; by report, no anchor built to decode to other weights was tried. These twelve are among the 24 full checks that row SO-15.7 tells, so the two counts must not be added. No statement about the weights is falsified by it. That rests on the same argument on paper (how that squares with these docs' claiming no binding for the released programs: docs/limits.md, "Soundness, in short", the point "Accepted, though the committer lied"). In another run, not on the released programs, at the small example's parameter file as it ships (by its checksum in the runs' logs), 22 of 40 further lying key files, each with a commitment ID of its own and an anchor altered at 257 to 524,287 of 8,388,608 positions, in all 256 rows, were accepted by an unedited cp_verify in all four of their full checks: the largest count accepted was 65,536, the least refused 8,192, and all 12 at 131,072 or more were refused, 3 of them at the leaf file only, after the check of the key file had passed (at up to 262,144 positions). There is no threshold: by the edited committer's own print a check passed exactly when none of its sampled columns was altered. Each commitment was made once, under one of four test seeds, so this is for one try; each YES stood beside the reply that the edited committer and edited prover gave with nothing altered; and by a separate program's count of the changed columns (BLAKE2b-256 taken as collision-free) every accepted anchor lies far inside the distance (3,899,392 positions) up to which a table is close to the honest codeword alone. That count measures from the table of the run with nothing altered; that this table holds the honest codewords was checked at all positions under one of the four seeds only (row SO-15.7). Small size; synthetic weights. That each altered table behind the 24 accepted full checks is close to the honest codeword alone is arithmetic and an argument on paper, and rests on a run as well. Eleven cases, at the small example's parameter file as it ships (by its checksum in the runs' logs), put before an unedited cp_verify, not on the released programs, a stored table that is another matrix's, or lies 1 or 256 positions from it, and it refused all eleven, each at the check that was expected. In each case the other matrix differs from the committed one in one weight. Behind the eleven cases stand seven different tables and nine different tries. No reply known to be false was among the eleven. At most one try a case; one seed; small size; synthetic weights. The runs' records have not been checked independently; no checksum of the parameter file was recorded for each commitment; for the eleven cases the jobs, not the cases, are tied to it. Row SO-15.7 tells these runs with their limits. An honest committer's two commitments to the same weights have two leaf tables as well, and share no proof. The ID does not cover the proofs inside the key file or the leaf files, which `cp_verify` checks when it reads them; row SO-8.3 says what the ID does cover. A theorem in a technical report that is not public and not refereed says that, in the report's protocol, soundness holds whoever made the key file and the leaf files, as long as they pass the protocol's checks. This too depends on the theorem on codes, taken as given, and, at the default setting, on counting proof of work. It has not been shown for the programs. By the design's intent a false leaf file can only make you reject an honest proof, and that has not been proved either. The proof of the report's theorem has not been checked independently.

column3: `cp_verify` compares three things with the values that you pass in: the commitment ID, the next token and the policy's values. It cannot tell whether those values are your own. Three more comparisons are left to you: the range, the end of the reply and the tokenizer. Skip them, and a `YES` can be about the wrong thing. The script `integrations/check_proof.py` makes some of these comparisons, using values that you state yourself (row SO-49 says how far it has been tested). It has not been checked independently. You have to make the remaining comparisons yourself.

Under a clipped-gap policy a passing check that covers a token of the request ends `WITHIN LIMITS`, not `YES`. It tells you only that the checked tokens' costs meet the limits you named: their average, with each cost counted only up to the clip, and the number of costs above the clip. It does not say that the reply is the model's. What it says about a single token depends on your limits, and can be nothing. A technical report that is not public and not refereed states what such a pass means in the report's own protocol, for its own output head (the model's last step as the report writes it), under its hypotheses, with a written proof. For the forms that the programs use, the report itself gives that step as not shown. The written proof has not been checked independently. The compilation theorem (`innerCompiledVerifier_sound`) claims that every output token is the model's first choice. No other acceptance policy is covered. (`lean/LIMITS.md`, V5.) That is said of this theorem. The theorem under a policy, beside the soundness theorem for the Lean verifier, does cover other policies, weakly, and of `verify`, not of `cp_verify`: for all public files in scope, an output that `verify` accepts meets the policy that the files state, at the weights that the protocol's own extractor returns, except on an event of probability at most the stated bound. By itself it bars nothing against a committer who commits to weights under which every output meets the policy ([lean/THEOREM.md](../lean/THEOREM.md), "The theorem under a policy: other acceptance policies"). The claim is about the weights that the extractor returns, not about weights that anybody has shown, and nothing says that they are a sensible model. The extractor's definition has to be read too; that its weights are an honest committer's, and that the commitment opens to no others, is proved of two committers alone: of an illustrative one written in Lean (lean/THEOREM.md, "What the commitment gives, as proved") and, at public files in use, which are at the exact-match policy, of the committer that the compiler yields from the Lean provers (guide/what-is-proved.md, "The commitment"). A policy can be empty of content, and the theorem on completeness is at the exact-match policy alone. Lean's theorem on zero knowledge is for exact match: under a clipped-gap policy no Lean theorem covers what a whole proof reveals.

column3: A reply that meets fitted limits says little about which of two similar models served it, but one that misses them says a lot. In one trial on a small synthetic model, scored on a CPU, not on the released programs, limits were fitted to the honest model, and 60 of a slightly altered model's 64 replies differed from the honest model's. The altered model's replies met the limits: 47 of 64 served in bfloat16, and 54 of 64 in float32 (the honest model's: 63 and 64 of 64); so did 3 of 64 replies with one token replaced by a random one, 5 of 64 with one token replaced by the model's second choice, and none with four or more tokens replaced. Under stricter limits 18 of 64 of the altered model's replies met them, and 58 of 64 of the honest model's. Under looser limits, in another trial, not on the released programs, all 64 replies from a slightly altered model passed, though for 40 of them only a written report was kept. The replies were scored, not proved, with one altered model and one seed. A trial on a real model also shows weaknesses. One run scored long stored replies, of up to 500 tokens, from a stock inference engine running Llama 4 Maverick's public weights, against limits fitted to the 16-bit engine's honest replies and against limits fitted to an FP8 engine's (the first and the second of each pair of counts here); the limits were just loose enough for the worst of the honest replies to 48 prompts to meet them. With one token replaced by the model's second choice, 28 and 24 of 32 replies still met the limits. With one token at a random position replaced by a random one, 27 and 21 of 32 replies still met the limits. So did 49 and 23 of 96 replies sampled at temperature 1 rather than decoded greedily. With four tokens replaced by the model's second choices 1 of 32 met each engine's limits. The others were refused by the cap, the limit on the number of costly tokens, not by the limit on the mean. Of each engine's own honest replies, to prompts that did not set the limits, 95 and 91 of 96 met them; of replies to another prompt, 0 of 96. Under exact match none of the 96 honest replies would pass. That run tested no cheaper model and no model with altered weights, no adversary who picks the place, no prompts from a corpus other than WikiText-2 and no short replies. It ended at its time limit: of its eight sets of replies with 4 or 16 tokens replaced it scored one. It did not check the loaded weights against their checksums. The replies were scored, not proved, in one run, with a model package other than the released one. The counts apply to the released programs' integer model only if its fitted scales are the ones the run used. A second scoring run used the same limits. Most replies that the same model sampled at another setting still met them: 86 and 70 of 96 at temperature 0.7, and 85 and 65 of 96 at temperature 1 with top-p 0.9. Greedy replies of Llama 4 Scout, a smaller model of the same family, met them in 4 and 2 of 96, and Scout's replies sampled at temperature 1 in 0 of 96. So these limits hardly tell another sampling setting of the same model from greedy serving. How loose they are depends on the single worst of the 48 replies that they were fitted to. With the threshold at the third-worst fitted reply instead, none of Scout's 96 greedy replies met either set of limits, 30 and 53 of 96 (temperature 0.7) and 21 and 34 of 96 (top-p 0.9) of the sampled replies still did, and the limits fitted to the 16-bit engine also rejected 5 of 96 honest replies of that engine and 11 to 17 of 96 honest replies of an FP8 engine. On how narrow the result on Scout is: row SO-26.1.1. The second run tested no model with altered weights either, and did not check the loaded weights against their checksums. It ended at its time limit, with two further sets of replies unscored. Its replies have up to 500 tokens and continue text from one collection, WikiText-2; they are not chat. Here too the replies were scored, not proved, in one run, with a model package other than the released one. **What to do.** When you get the commitment ID, read the limits in the parameter file that it covers. Decide before you send a prompt whether you accept them, and pass them with `-policy`. Do not take the values for `-policy` from files that came with a response. Read also the final norm's two exponents, the parameter file's lines `MF` and `KF`: `cp_verify` prints them in no line. How much a clipped-gap policy excludes depends on their difference as well as on the policy's three numbers. At a small difference, a policy whose threshold fits the file's line can exclude nothing, whatever the weights. That is a theorem about Lean's model (`Policy.exists_policy_of_close_scales`, lean/Policy/Front/MeetsPolicyIdleAtScales.lean), which Lean's kernel has checked; the kernel checks the proof, not that the statement says this. From reading the code, the programs accept every difference from 0 to 14, and no stage rejects such a file or changes the call's last line; nothing was run. If you cannot assess the numbers, accept only exact match. (See also rows T46, SO-26.1.1.)

column3: The presence of a test in the repository does not show that it has run on the released programs. No test has walked a real proof's fields behind the first answer to a draw of positions one by one, and no sweep over a proof's bits or fields has run at full size. See [attacks at full size](limits.md#few-runs). Rows: SO-19, SO-19.1, SO-19.2, SO-21.

**In short.** The programs print bounds on the chance that a false reply is accepted. The bounds are calculations on paper, and they rest on assumptions, on published results whose proofs were not checked for this project, and on proofs in a technical report that is not public and not refereed. The figures were calculated, and the proximity tests' per-round errors derived a second time, from the report's formulas (for the weight table's rounds, by the programs' own formulas: a second arithmetic); the added and compiled figures come from one planning call. They have not been checked independently. These figures are the programs' own arithmetic, on stated assumptions; they say nothing of the whole system or of an attack's real cost, so they are not a security level. Never quote "128 bits" by itself. By the programs' own calculation, at the default setting and full size every [round](glossary.md#round) of one call reaches the target of 128 bits, some only by counting up to 32 bits of [proof of work](glossary.md#proof-of-work); without that work the weakest round has 96.23 bits (reckoned by a planning call: `cp_verify -plan accounting` at the default's parameter file; the programs' own accounting, not a security level). These figures are per round, under exact match; [a whole call's figure is lower](limits.md#the-soundness-figure). A round's bits are not the chance of a forgery, which grows with every hash computed, the verifier's own included. Even those 96.23 bits rest on the theorem on codes, taken as given, on results that are cited, and on the hash, taken as a random oracle. None of the figures here is a security level. They are the programs' own accounting of the protocol's rounds, made by a planning call, not a bound proved for these programs. By the programs' own accounting, under exact match, at the default setting and at full size, a false reply is accepted with probability below about N/2^126 if proof of work is counted, and below about N/2^96 if it is not (reckoned by a planning call: `cp_verify -plan accounting` at the default's parameter file; the programs' own accounting, not a security level). A false reply is one that differs, at a checked position, from the committed integer model's next token. N counts all the hashes that the committer, the prover and the verifier compute. - After 2^64 computations that is one in 2^62 with the work counted, and one in 2^32 without. The bound counts computations because a malicious prover can retry until a challenge suits it.

column3: - The bound is for one key, with public parameters and a policy that are fixed in advance and not taken from the prover. - The numbers are the programs' own: `cp_verify -plan accounting` puts the round errors and hash counts that it prints into a bound of the same form as that of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, with one larger constant. The report's form: a malicious provider (committer and prover together) that makes Q hash calls in total, the verifier's included, succeeds with probability at most Q · ε + c · Q² / 2^256, where ε is the largest error of a single round, after that round's proof of work, and c is a small constant; it is argued on paper. The numbers are not figures of the report. - The bound assumes that [the results it rests on](limits.md#what-the-theorem-assumes) hold and that the hash behaves as a random oracle, against classical adversaries. - The report states, for the default setting with the differences that the report names, a corollary with counted proof of work and a proposition on what would remain without the theorem on codes; both have had one review, of the parts of each that concern soundness and no others, in readings of minutes each, and have not been checked independently (row PS-35). If that theorem failed, the programs' accounting would rest on one other cited bound, itself unverified and not wholly independent of it, and by a calculation on paper fewer bits than the target would then remain, for the truth of an accepted request and for binding alike; the report does not call that firm. The Lean verifier's own bound does not take the theorem on codes as given. None of these statements is a theorem about these programs, and no configuration of the programs is known to meet all the hypotheses of any of them. - Even if a cheater computes no hashes, N is not zero, because the verifier's own hashes count: 839,115 calls by the planner's count, which is no proved ceiling: it plans every opening at its largest and leaves out some hashing outside the rounds; in a checking run of a stored full-size proof on the released `cp_verify` the verifier counted 794,273, fewer than planned; hashing of public files and tables, and words that a draw skips, are planned nowhere, so no rule keeps a run's count at or under the plan; on the stored sets it stays under, because the plan counts every opened path whole and paths share vertices. For a cheater who computes no hashes, for one call, the bound behind these rounded figures gives 2^-108.3 with the proof of work counted, 2^-76.5 without crediting it, at the planner's count, calculated from the planning call's prints; printed by no program (reckoned by a planning call: `cp_verify -plan accounting` at the default's parameter file; the programs' own accounting, not a security level). N/2^126 is a looser summary of that bound, so dividing by hand gives a slightly weaker number. The program's printout names one key file's, one leaf file's and one request's proof, that is one call, as "the unit of all figures above". Row SO-3 says what holds for a batch, and under which interpretation. The two values for a cheater who computes no hashes apply to one call and are weaker for a batch: 2^-102.32 with the proof of work counted, 2^-70.55 without crediting it, at the planner's count, for 64 whole calls, calculated from the planning call's prints; printed by no program (reckoned by a planning call: `cp_verify -plan accounting` at the default's parameter file; the programs' own accounting, not a security level).

column3: Counting the [proof of work](glossary.md#proof-of-work) rests on [a separate assumption](limits.md#how-the-programs-count), so read both columns of the table at [docs/limits.md](limits.md#the-soundness-figure): with the work counted, and without. The binding of the commitment's files (its key and leaf files) depends on counting the work too. At the default setting the rounds that draw positions count 20, 28 or 32 bits of work. At full size all of them reach the target of 128 bits only with that work counted: 71 rounds across the proofs of the key file, the leaf file and the request (reckoned by a planning call: `cp_verify -plan accounting` at the default's parameter file; the programs' own accounting, not a security level). By the programs' own calculation, at the default setting and full size: The third row is one of what the printout calls "stricter readings of the same rounds, which decide nothing". Both columns rest on the same footing for the closeness rounds, the theorem on codes, taken as given, and in both the binding of the weights rests on that theorem too; the right-hand column only leaves the position rounds' work uncounted. No number in the table is a floor, not even in the right-hand column. Each still rests on [everything else that the bounds rest on](limits.md#what-the-theorem-assumes), and the bound weakens with every hash that a cheater computes. The truth of an accepted request and the binding of the weights both rest on the theorem on codes, and, at the default setting, both lean on counted proof of work in the rounds that draw positions. 71 rounds at full size reach the 128-bit target only with their proof of work counted (up to 32 bits); the rest reach it without. Proof of work is hashing that every attempt must pay, which is assumed to cost as much on the programs' hash chains as it would on a random oracle; without that work the weakest round has 96.23 bits (reckoned by a planning call: `cp_verify -plan accounting` at the default's parameter file; the programs' own accounting, not a security level). A provider can write a parameter file that combines these otherwise; the verifier's accounting lines, not its last line, print which applies, so compare the file with the shipped ones. The default leans on both at once: on counted proof of work in its position rounds, which rests on an assumption about grinding the programs' hash chains that is argued, not proved, and on the theorem on codes in its closeness rounds, the commitment's included ([what the bounds rest on](limits.md#what-the-theorem-assumes)). The whole bound "as one number", as `cp_verify -plan accounting` prints it, is 126.21 bits with the work counted and 96.23 bits without (reckoned by a planning call, at the default's parameter file; the programs' own accounting, not a security level).

column3: No configuration of the programs is known to meet all hypotheses of the theorems of a technical report that is not public and not refereed. `cp_verify` has been read and has not been checked independently. A review is the one fresh reading of large parts of it on record. A program can contain a bug that none of these theorems would catch. Some gaps are known; no attack that exploits any of them is known, but none is ruled out, and the list may be incomplete. The report's comparison lists four places where its statements on soundness do not cover what the programs do, or cover it only in part. They are rows PS-6 and PS-19, the form of one stage of the committer's one-time proof (its row stands under row PS-33), and the numbers from which a round's error is computed (row SO-4). For the last it has no statement. (Row PS-50 tells that stage.) The report's comparison does not cover one stage of the committer's one-time proof (how many mask rows its plan has there). At the default's file the plan gives that stage two mask rows, and not the four that the comparison left open (read off a dump of the plan of a verifier with added prints, not on the released programs; a planning call; no key was made); the stage itself has not been compared at the default's file. No row was compared under a parameter file that `cp_verify` admits. Four more (rows PS-2 to PS-5) are off that list only on a reading of the source code, with a lemma and sentences added and nothing more, as the report says of itself. These readings stopped short at places that are not named. All four rows are covered only in part: they are not covered for the step to the model (rows PS-2 and PS-3) or for hiding (rows PS-3 to PS-5). By rows PS-3 to PS-5, their soundness too rests on those conditions (degree bounds, mask entries), which have been gone through only in readings of minutes each, against the verifier's code, not on the released programs, with nothing run.

For two of the four (rows PS-6 and PS-19), the cases that were looked for do not occur in the example files that were examined. With one exception (row PS-19): the shipped layout files leave places that belong to no matrix, in every oracle message that they place. No claim reads these places, and the report has no statement for that form. By a reading of the prover's source it writes zeros there, the pad's own entries aside; nothing was run to show it. For soundness that changes nothing: a malicious prover may write what it likes there, and no statement of the report settles whether such places can help a false proof pass. What the zeros mean for hiding has not been worked out. For row PS-6 the files that were examined were only the full-size example's. But a provider can write files that contain some of the cases, and `cp_verify` accepts some such files. Every `YES` also depends on two parts of `cp_verify` that rest, wholly or in part, on a reading of the source. The first is a computation in the range check. A self-test in every call computes one part of it a second time, from the same sizes and places as the first, so an error in those escapes it. The rest has nothing to compare it against, and a fault there could let a false statement pass. The second is a shortcut that `cp_prove` takes too. From reading the code, the shortcut's condition is believed to hold for every parameter file the program accepts, but there is no check at that point and no test confirms it (rows SO-17.3.1 and SO-17.7 name both places). The prover and the verifier are also built on one library, `blocks/`. It holds the hash chains, trees, codes, sampling, proximity tests, the plan of every round and the error accounting, each written once for both ([source map](../verifier/docs/source-map.md)). They share more than the library. The rounds of each kind of sub-proof are listed once for both, in headers under `prover/`. And `cp_verify.cpp` is compiled a second time and linked into `cp_commit`. So comparing the two cannot reveal a fault in the shared code. `cp_verify` tests no-overflow conditions on the public parameters. They are meant to ensure that an equation that a proof checks modulo the prime also holds over the integers. For the report's protocol the report argues that its conditions suffice; that argument has not been checked independently. column3: In a [closeness round](glossary.md#closeness-round) a challenge combines several rows into one. **The theorem on codes.** That theorem is one of Ben-Sasson, Carmon, Haböck, Kopparty and Saraf, whose paper is published at STOC 2026; the theorem the programs use, Theorem 4.6 of its full version (ePrint 2025/2055), is not in the proceedings, which state the plain form up to the Johnson radius (Theorem 1.5); for its proof the full version gives an outline of one paragraph, and credits a proof of the property, up to the Johnson bound, to a note that it cites as a personal communication, which is public as a note (ePrint 2025/2110; the same note, by its citation; texts not compared). It is taken as given in a technical report that is not public and not refereed (what of the programs was compared with that report: rows PS-37 to PS-39) and in the programs' accounting. A statement on codes held to follow from that theorem, in its case of two words, is proved in this repository's Lean library, by way of another formalization's theorem and a comparison of bounds; the paper's own form of the bound is not proved there, and that the library's statement follows from the paper's, and that these programs' parameters meet the theorem's conditions, rest on reading, not on a proof (lean/LIMITS.md, L15; [lean/THEOREM.md](../lean/THEOREM.md), "What it rests on"). No proof of the paper's own form of the bound has been checked. This repository's Lean library has a statement written to restate its two-word case, which the library proves (that it is that case is a reading; no theorem says it); two theorems from which that statement follows, and the step from them to it, are proved inside the library, in files adapted from two public Lean libraries, ArkLib and Mathlib (`lean/ThirdParty/`), and in files of the project's own (`lean/Cb/Bridge/`). The paper's theorem has not been compared with later work; a correction to it may exist that is not known here. A public Lean library, ArkLib (Apache-2.0), has a theorem of this kind: mutual correlated agreement of Reed–Solomon codes on affine lines, for every radius below the Johnson radius (`ReedSolomon.mcaError_affineLine_johnson_le`: proved there, by a reading of its source, through the package VCV-io, which was not built; not among what was checked); the paper's own form of the bound is not proved there. This repository's library holds files adapted from ArkLib (from a copy marked as commit `2817d8c7d2f28d706b17f8de0f885880d0b2eb13`; that commit has not been looked up on ArkLib's public repository) and files adapted from Mathlib v4.34.0 (how many of each: `lean/ThirdParty/README.md`, "What is in it"; which: `lean/ThirdParty/TAKEN-OVER.tsv`), with proofs of the two theorems, a counting form of such a statement (`ReedSolomon.exists_johnson_line_exactCorrelatedPair`) and a bound on its count (`ReedSolomon.HiddenDerivative.johnsonExceptionCount_le_comparisonEstimate`). Not all declarations of ArkLib's files are kept, some of their proofs are changed for the older Lean and Mathlib, and in further places a lemma is called by its older name (`lean/ThirdParty/README.md`, `lean/ThirdParty/TAKEN-OVER.tsv`); the statements of two lemmas on the way are changed: each asks more of its premises than ArkLib's, and so says less; four more keep their sources' words yet ask more of a premise, because the older Mathlib means more by one of those words; the files adapted from Mathlib bring declarations of the newer Mathlib, some of them with a changed proof; and a file of the project's own, with one definition and one lemma, stands in for two names that ArkLib takes from the package CompPoly (`lean/ThirdParty/README.md` and `lean/ThirdParty/TAKEN-OVER.tsv` list the changes). From the two theorems the library proves the statement that it takes in the theorem's place, bound included (that statement's bound, not the paper's own form; `Cb.Bridge.bchks46`; at the library's two fields `Cb.Gl.bchks46At`; files of the project's own, `lean/Cb/Bridge/`); every theorem stated with that hypothesis keeps it, the statements of the compilation theorem (`innerCompiledVerifier_sound`) at the two sizes and the entry file's soundness among them (it is no premise of the compilation theorem itself: `lean/LIMITS.md`, L15); the compilation theorem itself does not apply the proof; second forms at the two sizes (`innerCompiledVerifierSoundFromDryRunAtFullSize_codes`, `innerCompiledVerifierSoundFromDryRunAtSmallSize_codes`) and the bounds on the entry file's closed check do. The soundness theorem for the Lean verifier rests on theorems on Reed–Solomon codes, above all mutual correlated agreement below the Johnson radius. As typed in this repository they are proved in this library, not assumed, from files adapted from ArkLib and Mathlib (`lean/ThirdParty/`). That says nothing on whether a published paper's theorem is formally verified. That the typed statement follows from the published theorem rests on readings alone, and the two have not been compared independently. The Lean files of this repository have the checksum 620d8930. One Lean file, with one definition and four theorems, which nothing else imports, was added after the runs reported here and checked on its own. Three of the check script's pinned values were changed and three of its stored lists were extended for it; nothing else in the script or the lists changed. (The file: `lean/AtFullSide/Face/ExecutableVerifierIsLeanVerifier.lean`; the full account: lean/CHECK-RESULTS.md.) Wherever these pages say that a run was made over this repository's Lean files, over a build of them or over the released Lean files, that file was not among them. Without that file and these changes, at the checksum c06b37e6, these have run: the build of the whole library with its two side libraries, with no error and no `sorry` (with Mathlib and the other packages compiled beforehand, the library's own files from nothing, in several calls of Lake, the last of them over all three libraries: lean/CHECK-RESULTS.md tells how); Lean's own print of the named theorems and of the axioms that each rests on; and, of the library's check, the steps on the files' text (tree, words, imports); and its audit of axioms and of the lists of names, inside the whole run of that check that is told below (10,772 names; 184 stored statements). The Lean verifier's reference run has been made over this repository's Lean files (row L9), and the independent checker has been run, on the soundness theorem's export and, in passes of their own, on those of three further theorems (`sound`, `repliesFit`, `refusedHandsOutNoProof`), as the exporter writes them over this repository's build; what the checker accepted: lean/CHECK-RESULTS.md. One whole run of the library's full check (`lean/scripts/check.py`) over the Lean library in `lean/` has the last line "All steps passed: tree, words, imports, build (kernel replay, audit). …", at the checksum c06b37e6. That line also says that no theorem got a verdict on binders or on `Classical.choice`: every line of `lean/scripts/top-theorems.txt` says "general" (the whole line: lean/CHECK-RESULTS.md). It is one run, on one machine. In its kernel replay 1,438 modules go by another call than `leanchecker`; Mathlib and the other packages are taken as they were compiled beforehand, and are not replayed (lean/GAPS.md, 81 (g)); the 13 files under `Ask/` are read by the text steps alone. The script runs no mutation tests and no second, independent proof checker. These runs were made on the project's own machines and have not been repeated outside it; the adapted files were compared with their sources by programs, without following the mathematics line by line. That the statement which Lean has accepted is the bound that the written proof uses, at the project's parameters, rests on readings alone. The programs' use prices many interleaved rows as a line through two words by a step that the report proves after a statement in the abstract of S. Jo (ePrint 2026/891; no refereed version has been looked for), at the theorem's M = 1, and the steps from the theorem are the report's own. No theorem says that the programs' tests combine Reed–Solomon code words on lines; that they do is known from a reading of the source code, not from a run on the released programs, and lies outside that report's comparison. The bound rests besides on steps that the report argues on paper for this protocol (no factor for the interleaved rows; a fold of 2^v rows counts v closeness terms; one list size more for the repeated mask code beyond a third of the distance), which have not been checked independently. That the parameters meet the theorem's conditions is the project's own reckoning, which has not been checked independently either; and the rounds that rest on it hold at the target with no bits to spare. The report's three further steps on codes are argued on paper and none is in Lean. For the interleaving step it follows a statement in the abstract of S. Jo (ePrint 2026/891) and gives its own proof; for the step on the generator that combines several words a published work (Bordage, Chiesa, Guan and Manzur; the report's reference: ePrint 2025/2051, CCC 2026) has the step for mutual correlated agreement and results of the same form, and the report proves a form of its own with the count of the theorem on codes; the two have not been compared line by line (this sentence rests on the report's own citation and on that work's version of February 6, 2026: none of its proofs was checked, its last revision, of May 19, 2026, was not seen, and its proceedings version was not compared); of the third step, on the repeated mask codes, the report gives its statement and proof as its own, with the pointer that the table in the paper's section "The sources of each part" gives (under `paper/`); no published equivalent has been searched for. All that is said here of the report's steps is an account that a reader of this repository cannot check. The entry file is what `docs/` calls the leaf file.

At the default setting every closeness round rests on the theorem on codes (the planner counts none on the bound within a third of the distance), and counts no proof of work. By a planning call of `cp_verify` at the full-size parameter file under `prover/examples/` the theorem carries 255 rounds in a request's proof, 63 rounds in the key file and 23 rounds in a leaf file (reckoned by a planning call: `cp_verify -plan accounting` at the default's parameter file; the programs' own accounting, not a security level). At the default setting, with the work counted, these meet the target by under 0.01 bit: 68 rounds: 25 of the range check and 43 with a closeness term, out of 67,383 entries of the plan, 62,421 of them with a verifier's message. Two of the entries, named `RECORD`, are the draws of the tables' OOD seeds and are no rounds: 67,381 rounds. 71 rounds hold only because their work is counted. So there are no bits to spare on the theorem's side: each of these closeness rounds rests on the theorem, and proof of work adds nothing there, since closeness rounds count none; nor do the 25 range-check rounds, which stand at exactly 128.00 bits with no proof of work. If the theorem's count were twice as large, each round with a closeness term that holds with less than one bit to spare would miss the target: 325 of the 341, by the programs' own accounting (`verifier/tests/known_answers/kit_rounds/target_full_f2.txt`). By the programs' own planned accounting the tightest rounds sit exactly at the target; any loss in the cited bound, however small, puts them below it, in a proof and in what the committer makes once.

column3: **The bound within a third of the distance.** By the rule of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, a repeated mask code's rounds that lie within a third of its distance take their error from the lemma of the paper this protocol builds on, which the report proves again in an adapted form. It holds strictly below a third of the code's distance. The report proves an adapted form of it and adds lemmas, proved in the report after published works, so this source too rests in part on proofs in the report. At the default setting no closeness round rests on it: the planner counts none on it. The lemma is proved in the paper that this protocol builds on; these pages claim no proof of it in this repository. The Lean library under lean/ also proves a statement of its own of that kind (`Cb.ld_mca_third`: mutual correlated agreement within a third of the distance, for any code that is linear as the protocol reads it (Lean: LdCode.Laws, lean/Cb/Ld/LdRel.lean: encoder and reading map linear, encoder injective, reading map reading only declared positions)); it has not been compared with the paper's lemma clause by clause, and no theorem ties it to the programs' count.

column3: **Counted proof of work.** Proof of work is counted in the rounds that draw positions, and in no other kind: 20 bits in a request's own rounds, 28 in a batch's shared rounds, 32 in the committer's. By the planning call at full size 71 rounds reach the target only with that work counted; without it the weakest, which by these counts is one of the committer's, has 96.23 bits (reckoned by a planning call: `cp_verify -plan accounting` at the default's parameter file; the programs' own accounting, not a security level). So every response passes only with the work counted, and so does the commitment: the key file's and the leaf file's position rounds count 32 bits. That counted work may lower a round's error is assumed, not proved, for the programs' hash chains ([how the programs count](limits.md#how-the-programs-count)). Each such round's term takes its list size from the Johnson bound, a proved counting bound; what the theorem on codes gives the rounds at the Johnson radius is the larger distance at which they sample, and so fewer positions, not the validity of their count. By a reading of the planner's lines no single round's term leans on both the theorem and the work; the bound, which sums the rounds, and the `YES` lean on both.

column3: **What the provider chooses.** What the provider's file picks, unseen in the verdict: how much work is counted (up to 32 bits a round; `cp_verify` rejects a file that declares more: `policy-work-most`). Of the closing lines, the `commitment:` line and the `accounting:` lines say which source the commitment's rounds rest on; `proof of work:` and `work=` show the work; neither the last line nor `result-v1` shows the source of a request's own rounds. `cp_verify` tests neither the work nor the source against a shipped setting: compare the first 32 lines of the file with the shipped ones ([which setting is it?](verifying.md#which-setting)). - *The cap.* `cp_verify` caps the work that is counted at 32 bits a round, and rejects a file that declares more. Up to that cap, unless the caller passes `-no-proof-of-work`, `cp_verify` does not test how much work is counted, and it never tests on which source a request's closeness rounds rest, which follows from the file's group lines (what these are: docs/format/08-parameters.md, 8.2; which files share the default's: row SO-15.6; how the source follows from the file's numbers: rows SO-2.7 and T7.1.13). A call with the option ends at best in `NOT-A-VERIFICATION` if some round meets the target only with its work. A `YES` under it says only that no round leans on work by the programs' own count. - *Where the source is printed.* `cp_verify -plan accounting` prints which source applies file by file, in the `footing:` lines. A checking call that ends in `YES` or `WITHIN LIMITS` prints it too, for its three files together, in the `accounting:` lines under `what stands behind it:`.

column3: - *What a provider's own file can still do.* A provider's own file can still do four things that the last line does not show (the work and accounting lines show some). It can count the full 32 bits in a request's own rounds and a batch's, where the default counts 20 and 28: by the formula a round that reaches 128 bits with 32 of them counted as work has 96 without it, so more rounds would then sit at 96; no planning call has been made at such a file. It can count work, up to the same 32 bits, in the other four kinds of round too, closeness rounds among them, where the default counts none. It can set the other numbers that a round's error is priced on and that no check ties to the run at that round (row SO-4), and shapes under which no honest file exists and nothing has been tried (rows SO-6.3, SO-6.3.1). It has not been shown that these are the only lines of a parameter file that go unchecked in this way. - *The target.* Up to the cap, these choices change what the bounds rest on, not the target. The file also states its own target. A call rejects a file whose target is below its [requested bits](glossary.md#requested-bits) (`NO: security-bits`): these are 128, and a call that asks for fewer is not an acceptance (`NOT-A-VERIFICATION`). So in an accepted call every round's error is at most 2^-128, but only by the programs' own calculation, with the bound of its source and the declared work counted.

column3: **A commitment publishes [out-of-domain (OOD) answers](glossary.md#record) (masked sums of the weights)**, so the binding of the weights, and not only the request's truth, rests on the theorem on codes, with no bits to spare, and on counted proof of work (binding in a modified sense, in which the hash itself supplies the OOD seeds; that sense does not imply the binding definition cited by a technical report that is not public and not refereed; the report's written argument for that sense covers a commitment ID whose hashed string does not take the OOD seeds: the released programs' string takes them, and that argument does not cover it, so these docs claim neither sense of binding for the released programs; even for the report's own ID that argument is stated for independent random oracles, and by the report's own account its carry-over to one hash stands in the report's running text alone, under further hypotheses, with one step that no numbered statement or printed proof holds). The report states, for the default setting with the differences that the report names, a corollary with counted proof of work and a proposition on what would remain without the theorem on codes; both have had one review, of the parts of each that concern soundness and no others, in readings of minutes each, and have not been checked independently (row PS-35). If that theorem failed, the programs' accounting would rest on one other cited bound, itself unverified and not wholly independent of it, and by a calculation on paper fewer bits than the target would then remain, for the truth of an accepted request and for binding alike; the report does not call that firm. The Lean verifier's own bound does not take the theorem on codes as given. Lean has a soundness theorem for its own verifier, `verify`, not for the C++ program that users run: [what it says, and what it does not](../lean/THEOREM.md). The theorem's scope is one format and one size: the format's default setting at full size. That the library's written copy of the full-size public files is the shipped files' is held by no theorem (a program beside the library, `lean/scripts/check_stored_examples.py`, compares them from outside). The theorem is soundness only, with nothing on weight hiding. The `commitment:` line and `record=1` in `result-v1` say on every accepted call that OOD answers are published; read them as the commitment's footing ([verifying.md, point 7](verifying.md#when-to-accept)).

column3: **Published OOD answers.** A commitment publishes [out-of-domain (OOD) answers](glossary.md#record) (masked sums of the weights). The rounds of the key file and the leaf file rest on the theorem on codes too, and the call can still end in a plain `YES`. So the binding of the weights, and not only the request's truth, rests on the theorem on codes, with no bits to spare, and, where the file counts work, on counted work too. Binding is meant there in a modified sense in which the hash itself supplies the OOD seeds; that sense does not imply the binding definition cited by a technical report that is not public and not refereed. The report's written argument for that sense covers a commitment ID whose hashed string does not take the OOD seeds: the released programs' string takes them, and that argument does not cover it, so these docs claim neither sense of binding for the released programs. A stand-alone program built from `verify-on-bytes` (row L14), which this repository does not build as one, follows the default setting as a program, and no theorem bounds the chance that it accepts a false file, at this or any other setting (rows L14 and PS-68). Of `cp_verify`'s four closing lines, only the `commitment:` line and the field `record=1` of the `result-v1` line show that OOD answers are published ([what a `YES` does not say](../verifier/README.md#what-a-yes-does-not-say)).

No single reading has covered the whole argument. Known faults may stand in the proofs uncorrected, and there may be more that are not known. column3: **Parameter files that no test covers.** `cp_verify` also accepts such files: - Files whose closeness rounds priced by the lemma would miss the target if counted by the theorem on codes' larger count. The default is not such a file, by what its file says. No one has made a key, a proof or a whole call under such a file. - Files in which a proximity test folds its message down to a single entry. Apart from planning calls (row SO-6.3.2), no test has given `cp_verify` a file of that shape, and no one has made a key file, leaf file or proof under one. `cp_verify` also accepts forms of a parameter file that have no row of their own among the differences between the programs and a technical report that is not public and not refereed. Two are known, from a list that is not complete: a weight table whose matrix has one row, and a table with room for the key's test or a link, but for no batch. The party that can use them is the provider, who writes the files. Both forms were read in other sources (row HW-678), and no such file was run (row PS-52 says what each form leaves uncovered).

column3: **Worst case:** Every setting also rests on taking the hash as a random oracle and on the round-by-round soundness of the proximity test's steps, which a technical report that is not public and not refereed cites and does not prove: they are taken as given, and no full proof of them on paper was checked. If either of those failed, no argument would be left at any setting, and the proofs and commitments already handed to clients could not be called back. The report's proofs of composition and compilation have not been checked independently. If one of these fails, the rounds' own errors may stand, but nothing ties them into a bound on the chance that a false reply is accepted, at any setting. A parameter file that fails a hypothesis of that report's theorem can break soundness too ([how the programs count](limits.md#how-the-programs-count)). In the other cases some rounds would have a weaker bound or none. No forgery is known. (What did pass, and that it is none by a reading alone: row SO-15.7.)

column3: - *The theorem on codes.* It is taken as given in a technical report of this project that is not public and not refereed and in the programs' accounting. A statement on codes held to follow from that theorem, in its case of two words, is proved in this repository's Lean library, by way of another formalization's theorem and a comparison of bounds; the paper's own form of the bound is not proved there, and that the library's statement follows from the paper's, and that these programs' parameters meet the theorem's conditions, rest on reading, not on a proof (lean/LIMITS.md, L15; [lean/THEOREM.md](../lean/THEOREM.md), "What it rests on"). What the report reckons would be left without it is told further on in this row. The bound on every closeness round, in a request's proof and in the commitment's files, and with them the binding of the weights stands or falls with that theorem. If that theorem failed, the programs' accounting would rest on one other cited bound, itself unverified and not wholly independent of it, and by a calculation on paper fewer bits than the target would then remain; the Lean verifier's own bound does not take the theorem on codes as given. That other bound is a further, weaker cited lemma (ePrint 2025/2051, Lemma 9.3), on which that report falls back, whose proof was not verified for this project and whose constant is in question; by that calculation it would leave fewer bits than the target, for the truth of an accepted request and for binding alike, and the report does not call that firm. At the default that fall-back would have to carry both claims at once: that an accepted request is true, and that a key binds one set of weights. Nor does it cover every way in which the theorem could fail. The fall-back bound (ePrint 2025/2051, Lemma 9.3) is proved by modifying a proof in a public note (ePrint 2025/2110): by its title, author and the place where the proceedings cite it (the two texts have not been compared), the note that the full version credits, as a personal communication, with the proof of the property up to the Johnson bound. So the two bounds may share the step to mutual agreement, and a fault there could touch both (an inference; that step has not been traced through both). What the report reckons: by the calculation of its proposition on what would remain (rows LIM-14.3 and PS-35), about 89 bits, counted in hash queries, would remain, with the cited lemma's constant as printed, and with the proof of work counted or not. That is for the report's own protocol at its own setting (the default setting with the differences that the report names), for independent oracles, with the verifier's own queries counted. It is for the truth of an accepted request and for binding alike, binding in the modified sense and for the report's commitment ID, not the programs' (row LIM-14.1). It is a figure of that protocol on paper, not of the programs, and a level in hash queries, a cheater's chance being at most about N/2^89 after N hashes computed, the verifier's own among them; it is not to be set beside the planning call's figures in rows SO-1, LIM-7.1 and LIM-7.2, nor beside the error of about 2^-89 that Lean proves for an illustrative committer's commitment (docs/limits.md#what-the-theorem-assumes, on binding), which is a chance at a fixed count of queries and does not take the theorem on codes as given, where this figure is for that theorem's failure; the report does not call it firm, and if the fall-back bound failed too, no level would be left for either claim. What the project states is told under [what the theorem assumes](limits.md#what-the-theorem-assumes): which form of the theorem is used, how that use prices interleaved rows, that the parameters meet its conditions by the project's own reckoning, and the project's own three steps. One thing more rests on that report: a lemma of the paper that this protocol builds on, proved again there: a group's error is at most the sum of its codes' errors (that proof has not been checked independently). - *One of this project's own steps fails.* These steps carry every closeness round that rests on the theorem: if the step for the interleaved rows, the count of closeness terms for a fold of many rows, or the repeated mask code's list size fails, those rounds lose their bound in all three files.

column3: - Counting proof of work rests on one step: that g bits of work may be counted as a factor of 2^-g in a round's error. The work makes each retry more expensive for a malicious prover. It does not lower the chance that a single challenge lets a false claim pass. For the protocol's own hash chains this step is a lemma with a written proof in a technical report that is not public and not refereed; that proof has not been checked independently. For the programs' own hash chains the step is assumed, as the program itself prints. No theorem ties the chains of that report or of Lean to them (what is known of how Lean's hashing differs from the programs': row PS-68; lean/GAPS.md, 22; lean/LIMITS.md, L21). One attempt at the work can also cost less than one hash call, so g counted bits mean fewer than 2^g calls. By how much has not been counted for this layout. At the default setting, up to 32 of a round's 128 bits rest on this step (rows SO-32 and SO-59). - At full size, hundreds of rounds get their error, in part or wholly, from a number that the parameter file or the program's own code supplies. Some of the numbers are checked later, but nothing checks at that round that the round runs with that number. Where a later comparison exists, it often takes the number from the same source, so it checks the form, not the value. The count of such rounds covers only plans that the library's own planners make (row SO-4). These are not the closeness rounds of [what the theorem assumes](limits.md#what-the-theorem-assumes), though a few rounds are in both groups.

column3: - At the default setting's full-size file one kind of round would miss the target of 2^-128 under a stricter count than the written arguments need: the range check's round (`smallness` in the printout) counts one column of the check's matrix, not all columns. (It is not the only kind: the 25 rounds in which a switch with kept members draws its positions count no factor for the list of 54 candidate code words: row SO-2.3.1. The range check's own 25 rounds too are counted with no factor for a list of more than one codeword (by the technical report, each sent message's out-of-domain sample singles out one codeword before any later challenge); with a factor for a list of 54 they would stand near 122.2 bits (paper/paper.pdf, Table 15).) Counted over all columns, that round would have 113.44 bits at full size, at the default setting (reckoned by a planning call: `cp_verify -plan accounting` at the default's parameter file; the programs' own accounting, not a security level). In the round that the printout calls LINK, the calculation takes the larger of two errors, not their sum. At the default setting LINK, as charged, has 129.57 bits with its proof of work counted (97.57 from the positions opened, 32 from the work: `verifier/tests/known_answers/kit_rounds/target_full_f2.txt`); counted as a sum it would read between half a bit and one bit lower: at the default setting's full-size file still above 128 bits with the work counted; at its small example configuration, where LINK as charged has 128.77 bits (`verifier/tests/known_answers/kit_rounds/target_small_f2.txt`), it may read below 128 bits (about 127.8 if its two errors are equal there). The proof that the smaller errors are enough exists on paper only, in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, for that report's protocol; it has not been checked independently. The program prints both counts for the range check's round.
