column3: **On paper.** The proof of hiding in a technical report that is not public and not refereed, for a prover that the report defines, is what its authors call "complete but not settled": the proof is written out in full, but the checking that it has had is not enough to rely on it (row HW-763). It covers one OOD answer a row: with pads drawn fresh, and with pads derived from a secret seed, as the programs' are, only under four conditions that nobody has shown of the programs ([an assumption](limits.md#derived-pads)). It concerns only the protocol on paper, not the programs, and it has not been refereed or checked independently (among which matrices it hides: row PS-28; what its results do not reach: row PS-34). That report also lists differences between its protocol and the programs, found by reading other sources (row PS-67); twenty-two of them leave hiding open. The written proof does not cover three more places at which the programs leave the protocol that its statements are about (what a proof's first hash takes in; the labels of two of a proof's chains; how the commitment ID is formed). Read literally, that report's statements on random values that the prover derives from a stored key do not cover the way in which the released programs are described as deriving them (rows HW-232, HW-233). By default the service takes the next batch before it hands out the last one, and no proved statement covers the service as it runs that way. By one lemma of the written proof the order by itself is not the cause: in its experiments a client that must choose blind, or sees proofs late or never, learns no more than in the plain order (two readings, once each and under half an hour, took in its whole subsection, found no fault in the lemma and computed it on small cases). One item of the lemma's proof has been corrected; for that item they counted runs and computed no bound, and the lemma has no item on stops or broken runs. The reading in shares that came nearest to reading the proof whole (row HW-579) did not cover the subsection on batches that overlap (row PS-23). What stays outside: in the service the machine's timing decides the order and who shares a batch, and an end of `cp_prove` can withhold one proved batch (row C3); with `-overlap` or `-overlap-two` a stop in a later batch can withhold earlier ones; and a rejection at the provider's check (duty 6) withholds that whole batch; the vLLM integration also wipes it (narrow exceptions, none open to a client: [integrations/LIMITS.md](../integrations/LIMITS.md#narrow-exceptions)). The lemma's "no more" is exact for fresh randomness only: with derived randomness it gives the plain order's error against a larger running time. Time, stops and who shared a batch are on the list of what is not hidden, and no limit is known on what time or a stop reveals. No attack is known: the search for one took minutes, by reading, with nothing of the service run. **What Lean's results on hiding leave out.** Completeness, where the model has a result, and zero knowledge are proved in Lean for the protocol, at full size and at the exact-match policy, each up to a small stated error, with fresh random masks; after compiling, both are on one leaf table. The honest prover in these theorems is a Lean definition, not the CUDA prover: nothing is proved for the programs. The programs derive their random values from a secret seed and keep their own count (row PS-63). **The judgement, and the tests.** Where weight hiding stands, with the project's judgement on it: [docs/limits.md](limits.md#the-verdict). Neither that judgement nor the tests and readings behind it have been checked independently. That judgement does not cover a real model's weights, or what a fit to them writes (a parameter file, a file of scales): only one of the five tests has run on any: the first, four times, one of these on the released programs (row HW-747). That judgement is given at target_full_f2's files and at the two small forms at which its tests ran, target_small_f2 and target_small_f2_roomy; it reaches the two _gap configurations on less evidence. It does not reach target_small_file_f2's parameter file, which differs in more than a policy's three numbers: of the tests of hiding the first alone has run at it, once on the released programs (row LIM-63.2, line 11). At target_small_f2 its tests ran on test builds under a test seed, which leaves cp_commit's worst-case check out. No such judgement covers any other parameter file that the programs take, but for a file that differs from the default setting's in a clipped-gap policy's three numbers alone, which it reaches on less evidence. A commitment publishes, for good, in files that every client downloads, for each stored table, one weighted sum of each row's weights, masked by a pad of its own, which the programs derive from a secret seed ([an assumption](limits.md#derived-pads)). No test of hiding has run on the released programs on files holding 8- or 16-bit tensors. Two commitments to the same weights have not been searched together. How `-overlap` and `-overlap-two` work inside has not been read in the released programs' code, but for the waiting batch's buffer (row HW-92). With `-public-weights` nothing is hidden. The main risk: a bug or hardware fault silently drops a random [mask](glossary.md#mask), and a file with an unmasked value can still verify. In a sweep of injected losses of random values at the default setting's small form, on test builds of other sources, 30 of 165 picked losses in CPU memory went unnoticed (12 of the 165 changed no byte of any file, so 30 of the 153 that could show anything), and none of 130 in GPU memory: no rate (row LIM-22.1). All 263 replayed losses of the riskier sort were stopped, on programs of other sources that held test-only code; 9 more, at neighbouring draws that no check holds, went unnoticed. Each sample of losses ran on more than one test build with the same counts, which is no second witness. What share of all draws the kinds of these 30 make up has not been reckoned for this sweep (what was counted of 16 of them: row HW-660). By two short readings of the code of other programs, about ten minutes each, none of the 30 exposes anything of the weights by itself, but for one case, where it is not known (a batch's lost salt beside a failed request); no run has shown that. No pair of losses was tried. In small computed examples some pairs of losses did leak; none of this is proved or checked (rows HW-660 and H17.3.1.1). Both tests (the third and the fourth of the five tests: the sweep of lost random values, and the riskier losses outside that sweep; docs/limits.md#verdict-runs) ran at small size, the third on test builds of other sources and the fourth on programs of other sources that held test-only code, on synthetic weights, by report; not every random value was struck, neither test reaches the pads on the OOD answers, and what an unnoticed loss exposes the tests do not show (all bounds: [Where it stands](limits.md#the-verdict)). Masked sums of the weights are public for good, a single self-check is all that stands between a fault that loses every pad and a public file without pads, and the seed must stay secret for as long as the weights matter. Nothing else that these pages say about weight hiding covers weight files with 8- or 16-bit tensors ([why](limits.md#files-of-8-or-16-bits)), and for the default setting it has been checked only as far as [Where it stands](limits.md#the-verdict) tells. Each provider decides whether all this is enough for secret weights. Only some of the tests on this page have run on the released programs ([which](limits.md#what-has-run)). By design, at least eleven things are not hidden ([the declared list](what-is-not-hidden.md)), among them each reply, whether a request was served or failed, the time that the work takes, the model's architecture and all its sizes, settings fitted to the weights, and [masked sums of the weights](what-is-not-hidden.md#record-sums). Faults in the compiler or the machine are part of the main risk. The programs take weight files with 8- or 16-bit tensors without a warning.

column3: - **What is not shown or not known?** The judgement on hiding is not a proof, and it has not been checked independently. Much else is not shown or not known ([the list](limits.md#what-hiding-rests-on)). One point: a reply can be checked in two ways, by exact match or by a score with thresholds ([the clipped-gap policy](limits.md#which-policy)). Under a score policy the outcomes themselves tell something about the scores: [item 2](what-is-not-hidden.md). Under it, each answer (served or failed) tells a client something about the model's scores, and so about its weights, even if the masks hold; no statement bounds how much. A client that chooses the checked tokens can measure the model's hidden scores over many requests. No theorem bounds this, no one has measured it, and none of these programs limits requests. A technical report that is not public and not refereed has a written corollary on hiding under a policy, which is for requests that can be proved, for the protocol on paper, with a proof that its authors call "complete but not settled" (what that means: row PS-23); it says nothing about the programs. The last sentence of its statement has been named as worded too widely, a point that was given little weight, and it stands so worded. The corollary names six statements, four of which were changed late; as reported, its proof was read against them once, briefly, in a text from which the report differs, and nothing false was found. That reading found its list of what is not hidden short by one case. The report's list has that case, and a reading found the case itself short. Of the five smaller points of the reading of the corollary's proof, two stand unanswered in the report as it is. Neither its statement nor its proof has been assessed for the judgement on weight hiding.

column3: Unless a result on weight hiding in the LIM- rows says otherwise, its run was not on the released programs. A fault of the code, told in the present tense, holds of the released programs, unless the sixth column says otherwise. - A *test build* lets faults be injected. A fault *went unnoticed* if the file verified and nothing stopped it. - An *audit* is a tool that makes part of the published bytes again from the provider's secrets and compares them; the rest it only parses and replays. For proofs it needs a *kept batch*: one whose random bytes were kept for the audit. On a served proof, whose batch's random bytes a service does not keep, it can check only the stored tables' salts, and only on synthetic weights. - *The default setting* counts [proof of work](glossary.md#proof-of-work) toward its soundness figure. A commitment publishes out-of-domain (OOD) answers (masked sums of the weights).

*What the judgement on hiding rests on.* First, a reading for hiding by difference between sets of sources, all of other programs (row HW-678): some 270 to 280 lines of code that differ, in 35 or 36 files, in the sources of the programs, of the audit tool and of the scripts that build and start them. Not read: the parameter files, the tests, and the integrations but for one file. In the lines that were read, no check, wipe or refusal that guards a secret is removed. One wipe does not reach every folder: at the end of a running service, a folder in the place where responses are staged is zeroed and removed only if it bears a response's name; a folder under any other name is left, the end counts as not fully wiped, and the next start is rejected. By a reading of the code `cp_prove` stages under responses' names alone, so nothing that it stages escapes the wipe ([the rule](service.md#how-the-service-ends)). And on a model's files a commitment publishes one OOD answer a row (`answers 1`): no refusal stands against that. Nothing was built or run for that reading. Much hangs on the code that makes, uses, checks and wipes seeds, keys, masks and pads, since at a provider with secret weights the code for the OOD answers handles them. Most of what the judgement on hiding rests on was read or run on other programs than the released ones, so it reaches these on less evidence (row LIM-63.1); other code (changed, or built otherwise) it does not reach.

column3: 3. *The sweep of lost random values*, at small size, on test builds of other sources (row HW-678), whose tie to the released programs has not been shown (row HW-660): 295 runs with a picked loss. In CPU memory 165: 123 were stopped, 30 went unnoticed, and after 12 more the files were byte for byte an honest run's, so these show nothing: 30 of the 153 that could show anything went unnoticed. In GPU memory 130: all were stopped, 122 of them by one self-check alone. column3: **What supports weight hiding.** - **Lean's results** ([docs/limits.md](limits.md#weight-hiding)). Completeness, where the model has a result, and zero knowledge are proved in Lean for the protocol, at full size and at the exact-match policy, each up to a small stated error, with fresh random masks; after compiling, both are on one leaf table. The honest prover in these theorems is a Lean definition, not the CUDA prover: nothing is proved for the programs. Nothing shows that a request that the programs serve is one that can be served in Lean's sense (row PS-63). - **A written proof.** A technical report that is not public and not refereed has a written proof of hiding for the protocol on paper. Its authors call the proof "complete but not settled": it is written out in full, but the checking that it has had is not enough to rely on it (row HW-763). It is conditional, and no complete configuration that meets all its hypotheses has been written out (among which matrices it hides: row PS-28). - **Its errors.** The written proof has not been refereed or checked independently, and readings of it have missed real errors. Four were in statements that the proof rests on, and a fifth in the definition of zero knowledge itself. More such errors have been found, and they have not been counted. It is not claimed that every known error is fixed. The fix of the lemma of row HW-763 failed several times, and some of the failed forms had passed a reading; that row tells more bad results on it. The lemma's proof has been read step by step, in tens of minutes a reading, which each reading had for this proof and two other tasks together, in a text from which the proof as it stands differs. Most of its steps were derived, some only with a step that the reading supplied itself, and the rest were followed. As it stands, but for one clause that was reworded afterwards, that proof has been read whole only in readings each of which took in some sixteen passages in about a quarter of an hour; in parts it has been read in six to some thirteen minutes a reading. No way of reading the lemma as it stands under which it is false is known (what was tried, for minutes, and what was not searched for: row RES-57). On that lemma (on masks that are sent in advance) some points are open. Readings name two points at which one hypothesis of that lemma is wanting: it lacks a clause that the proof uses (row RES-66), and it does not say what it asks of a run that fails. So, read strictly, one use of the lemma in the proof of hiding lies outside it: the use for the range check, when that check fails. So does the use that repeats it for the protocol on paper taken in the programs' order of messages. That the proof covers a failing range check all the same is the word of two of the three readings that found the point, after minutes each. Whether the lemma as it is worded holds is not known: it is not claimed that either point on its hypothesis is answered (row HW-763). Whether its conclusion could be had by another route if it failed cannot be said. The fixes have been read briefly, and have not been checked independently. Not every finding has been followed up. There may be more errors. The lemma as it is worded has not been read for the judgement on weight hiding (the errors: row HW-579; that lemma: row HW-763). - **Readings of the code.** They found no way for a client to learn more than the declared list. That is said of a build that does what its published sources say, and of a provider that follows the duties. These were quick readings of sources alone. Nearly all of the source files of other programs (row HW-678) were read from end to end, briefly. For about a fifth of these files that rests on one account alone, and that account is thinner than it said; of that fifth all the GPU code has been read whole, briefly, in such sources too. These readings looked at what is drawn, placed, zeroed, stored, sent or printed, not at whether the arithmetic is right, and none of the released programs was built or run for these readings. None found a way, beyond the list of what is not hidden, for a hidden value to reach a client in a correct run. That does not show that the programs hide the weights. One finding, in which no leak was shown: the number of events in a reply streamed by vLLM (integrations/LIMITS.md).

**What differs from the code on which most tests ran.** Many tests of hiding ran on other programs (row HW-678), which differ from the released ones in much code. By a program's count between two sets of such sources, 101 source files outside the test folders differ in code or are new, and 83 more files, test files among them, differ in comments or layout alone; scripts and documentation differ too. What differs further, up to the released programs, is not in these counts. Many of these differences bear on masks. What differs in the 101 files was read, each file once, for minutes in all, and nothing was built or run for that reading. By that reading, 36 of the files hold routines that make, place or check a mask, a pad, a random tail or a salt, and in 25 of these the code that differs touches such routines. Among the differences is what is compared: three self-checks are new or wider (which: row HW-497); many random values are compared with nothing; and one comparison shows little. The programs compute masks and salts a second time, with a second copy of the cipher, and compare. That copy's core comes from the same public-domain source as the first and is near it in text, so their agreement shows little. By a reading of the code, what checks these copies from outside is a set of stored known answers, all under public keys: under a real key they are compared only with one another. Other differences bear on hiding too, among them: - **Staged responses.** These are responses that have not yet got their final names; no verifier has run on them (nor on a response in `out/`, until the check of duty 6: docs/limits.md#the-conditions), and such a file can hold unmasked values. `cp_prove` removes them only where a mark file names the directory as its own, so without that mark they can stay longer. From reading the code, the last step of `cp_prove`'s wipe clears the staging directory itself, where the wipe runs to its end. And the same call again takes over a single batch's directory that holds nothing but what was staged, with a well-formed mark, and first overwrites and removes what was staged; if it cannot, the call fails and the rest stays (rows HW-83, HW-480).

- **What the programs print.** The line on a rejected model file holds no name read from the file, though which line is printed, and a few small numbers in it, can depend on the weights. Eight of `cp_commit`'s own lines on a model's files or on `wsums.txt`, and a ninth through the routine that reads a model file, do print a tensor's name. The program makes these names itself, from the layer's number and fixed words, and does not read them from a file; two of the eight come where a value read from the weights is not finite or is out of range. - **Scripts that ship.** The audits erase a kept batch's bytes only when told to. - **Published OOD answers.** A commitment publishes OOD answers, for good. The programs take a parameter file that says `answers 1`, and refuse one that says 2, 3 or 4 answers, which no written proof and no review covers, under `-public-weights` too (`parameter-range`; how that is known: rows LIM-42 and LIM-26.1). - **Weight files of 8 or 16 bits.** `cp_commit`, `cp_prove`, the tool `weight_sums`, the reader in `scales/` and the vLLM integration's Python package `integer_model` also take such files ([not covered](limits.md#files-of-8-or-16-bits)). The source code for these things has been read by difference between sets of sources, all of other programs (row HW-678); test files and documentation were not included. The readings were of source code only, each difference once or twice, briefly, and built and ran none of the GPU programs; they found no new way to a leak in what differs between these sets. Such a reading cannot show a fault in code that does not differ between them. Results on programs that lack this code do not cover it. Which tests have run on what is told under [what has run](limits.md#what-has-run).

**What is missing.** - No theorem ties what Lean proves to the programs. - By default the service takes the next batch before it hands out the last one, and no proved statement covers the service as it runs that way. `cp_prove` counts and proves the next batch while the provider's check (duty 6: docs/limits.md#the-conditions) still holds the last. A corollary of a technical report that is not public and not refereed, on a service whose batches overlap, gives a service nothing until it has been shown that the service's run, with each batch's computation moved back to the moment at which the batch was taken, is the corollary's experiment, and its four conditions are not claimed to be enough by themselves (row PS-53). - Read literally, the report's statements on random values that the prover derives from a stored key do not cover the way in which the released programs are described as deriving them. In any reading these statements are about the protocol on paper, not about the programs (what the assumption on derived values does not say: row LIM-43). - The widest gap in the evidence is how a production build samples, orders and applies a batch's randomness, which a few audits of a batch's proofs have narrowed but not removed. - The tests cover exact match only: audits apart, no test of hiding ran under a clipped-gap policy (risk 3). Exact match is the default's policy; ordinary serving uses the clipped-gap policy ([risk 3](limits.md#which-policy)). - A run is to be taken as made at the default setting only where its row, or a row that it names for that run, says so (row HW-584 tells some that were not). Of the tests of hiding told on these pages, those behind the judgement on hiding ran at the default setting, at its small form or at full size (which of them on the released programs: row LIM-63.2); the sweep of lost random values and tests of the OOD answers ran there too, at its small form, on test builds or otherwise not on the released programs. On test builds of other sources (row HW-678), 30 of 165 picked losses in CPU memory went unnoticed (12 of the 165 changed no byte of any file, so 30 of the 153 that could show anything), and none of 130 in GPU memory: no rate. The same sample ran on more than one set of such builds, by report with the same outcome, which is no second witness (rows LIM-63 and LIM-63.2). What an unnoticed loss exposes the test does not show. At the default setting these docs report one short search of honest public files for leaks: at small size, not on the released programs, which found nothing and is worth little ([Where it stands](limits.md#the-verdict)); none at full size.

column3: - **The OOD answers.** By a reading of the code, one self-check in `cp_commit` (`own-test-pads`) is all that stands between a fault that loses every pad and a public file without pads. In a trial on a test build (without proof of work, which the default setting counts), with that check switched off, a commitment without pads passed everything else that `cp_commit` does. column3: Breaking one of these duties can leak weights. No program can check most of them, so most breaches go unnoticed, and, a breach of duty 6 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions) apart, every proof verifies either way. Following them all does not show that the weights are hidden. What is published cannot be recalled, and a new commitment repairs nothing. The [runbook](operators-duties.md) gives the steps. The further requirements under duties 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11 and 13 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions), on [docs/operators-duties.md](operators-duties.md), are as binding as the duties themselves. 2. **Keep the directory on a local disk of the one serving machine.** Only the [count](glossary.md#counter) stops a leaf table at its limit, and two machines that share a directory can each keep their own (duty 1: docs/limits.md#the-conditions). 3. **Never let two runs continue from one saved state of a machine or process, because their masks can repeat.** That puts clients' requests at risk too. If the provider's random source repeats under other weights, as when an image is started twice, the two commitments' public files alone give, for every row of each table, one exact linear equation in the two sets of weights, for good. 4. **Let only one service account read and write the directory, and let no one else write to a directory above it.** Anyone who can write to it, even without reading it, can put every batch on one leaf table. Anyone who can read it can strip the masks (duty 13), and can open every published sum, with no proof served. 5. **Do not let a plain, unsalted hash or checksum of the weights leave the provider.** Anyone who holds it can test guesses at the weights, or at whatever part the hash covers, offline, as often as they like, and can tell whether two providers serve the same weights. After a file that `cp_verify` did not pass, `cp_commit`'s message points to `cp_verify`'s last line and prints a length. Both come under this duty: keep them inside the provider. To report the fault to anyone else, follow [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md): say in your own words what you saw and where the two programs come from, and send no line, length, exit code or count of that run. 7. **Serve only with the production build.** Under a test build's [test seed](glossary.md#test-seed) nothing is hidden, and no verifier can tell. **Never use `-public-weights` for weights that must stay hidden:** with it, nothing is claimed to be hidden ([details](what-is-not-hidden.md#public-weights)). 8. **Stop serving proofs on a machine after exit code 9, a response that `cp_verify` rejects, any other exit that you did not cause, or requests that keep failing. Do not restart there until you know the cause.** A fault that showed once can strike again where no check looks. Later responses may hold unmasked values, and so may earlier ones from the same process or machine. After any of the first three, hand on nothing more that this machine made, responses that already have their final names among them, until you know the cause. What a client already holds cannot be taken back. Exit code 1 can mean a like fault: the system's random source gave too few bytes or zeros, the seed file or a leaf table's key is zero or damaged, a column of a leaf table made again no longer fits its tree, or a generator's counter did not rise (by a reading of the code).

*Under duty 10 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions).* On a serving directory, do not run a program that opens a table's columns without counting them. A new or replaced counter starts too low, and columns opened without a count spend a table's random entries unseen. 12. **Give the check of duty 6 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions) the commitment ID from your own record, never from the secret key directory. Do not let anything restart the service automatically.** An account that can write to the directory and restart the service can learn about the weights from how each restart ends (risk 2: docs/limits.md#a-broken-duty). Keeping all thirteen does not by itself bring a use under the judgement on hiding. Conditions of that judgement, which are no duty of these pages: the default setting; neither `-overlap` nor `-overlap-two`; exact match, or a clipped-gap policy in a parameter file that differs from the default setting's in that policy's three numbers alone; for the check of duty 6, a `cp_verify` built from the same sources as `cp_prove`, which no program checks; and a seed that stays secret for as long as the weights do, also after the commitment is no longer used, and in any backup that exists despite the duty never to copy the secret key directory (the whole list: [Where it stands](limits.md#the-verdict)). None of the thirteen asks for these. A further commitment to the same weights has conditions of its own (docs/limits.md#a-further-commitment).

2. **A broken duty, or access to the provider's machine, can undo the masks with no fault in the programs.** Duties 1, 2, 4, 10, 12 and 13 (docs/limits.md#the-conditions) say what breaks in each case. What a breach gives away has not been tried on the released programs.

- No Lean theorem covers what the outcomes (served or failed) under a score policy such as clipped gap tell about the model's scores. Lean's theorem on zero knowledge is for exact match: under a clipped-gap policy no Lean theorem covers what a whole proof reveals, and, audits apart, no test of hiding ran under a clipped-gap policy. What a technical report that is not public and not refereed says of such a policy: row PS-49.

column3: - **Weight files of 8 or 16 bits.** What these pages say about weight hiding does not cover a commitment made from weight files in which any tensor that the programs read is stored in 8 or 16 bits (Q8_0, F16, BF16), or the proofs made under it. No test of hiding has run on the released programs on such files. Not on the released programs, one trial with a BF16 file ended badly (row H46.4): somebody who could write that file but not read it learned the magnitudes of two neighbouring weights of their choice in about 32 starts (small size; synthetic weights; by report). The three GPU kernels written for them have no test among this repository's public tests. One test that is no row of SUITE.md ships with this repository (`integrations/vllm/integer_model/tests/test_against_the_prover.py`): it runs `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` on one small synthetic model stored as Q8_0, F16 and BF16, one window for each type; by reading, it reaches two of the three kernels; whether it reaches the third is not known; no run listed the kernels launched; it tests nothing about hiding. The project's other tests of that code are not part of this repository. Two things change with such files: decoded weights of the routed experts and values of a request lie in four work buffers in GPU memory where a 4-bit file puts none of them (row H46.2), and time and kernel launches follow the routing more closely (rows H46 to H46.6, HW-213). Such files meet no rejection. `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` take them, and a mostly 4-bit file with a single such tensor, under a sampled seed like any other file, and no printed line says that one was read. So it is for the provider to know how each tensor of its files is stored.

- **Published OOD answers.** A commitment also publishes, for good, for each stored table, one weighted sum of each row's weights, under a random pad of its own. The programs derive the pads from a secret seed ([what that assumes](limits.md#derived-pads)). From reading the code, `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` take a parameter file that says `answers 1`, as every parameter file under prover/examples/ does. By a reading of these sources (row LIM-26.1), they refuse a parameter file that says 2, 3 or 4 answers, which no written proof and no review covers, under `-public-weights` too (`parameter-range`). column3: - **The pads on the OOD answers are derived: an assumption.** The written proof's theorem on published OOD answers draws each pad fresh. These programs derive it. By a reading of the code of other programs (row HW-678), with nothing run, a pad is one lane of a ChaCha20 block under that one table's key with the word "PADS". A published answer, one masked weighted sum, is a field element with three coordinates. With one answer a row, a row has three pads, one for each: three lanes of one block. By the same reading it is made exactly uniform by rejection. So a published answer is hidden only as long as the seed stays secret and ChaCha20, used as a pseudorandom generator, is not broken, while the file is public for good. Every other mask of the programs is derived in the same way. That assumption says that the values derived from the seed look random to anyone who does not hold it. It does not say that they reveal nothing about single bytes of the seed, which would be a further assumption that these pages do not make. This names a limit of the assumption, and reports no weakness of ChaCha20. A technical report that is not public and not refereed has a corollary for derived pads, under four conditions on the rule that derives them. It is written out in full, but the checking of it is not enough to rely on it, like the whole written proof. The report does not say that the programs' own rule meets them. The four conditions have been held against the code of other programs, by two separate readings of six minutes each. Neither found a condition that is not met at one answer a row in a production build without `-public-weights`; several of the conditions are met only with a rider, some parts could not be checked, and at five places the code is not to the letter of them. The five places: the number of answers, which the programs check; three tests or stops, for two of which the report gives a term, as a formula that it does not evaluate (2^-192 or less by a reckoning of these readings), and for the third no term; the report's own literal reading of its definition. The two readings differ in their counts, and how their findings were gathered has not been checked; the tree has not been searched for a further routine that draws under a table's key; beside the five places there is a cap on one sampler's tries. That corollary does not cover a self-check that reads both a pad and a key, unless the check ends alike in every run and keeps the two conditions told in row H47.8. Of which kind each of the programs' self-checks is, is a reading of the code, not a statement of the report. What the report says on published OOD answers has not had an unhurried reading. In any reading that corollary is about the protocol on paper, not about the programs ([what is missing](limits.md#what-hiding-rests-on)).

- **On paper, below 128 bits.** For a prover that stops whole batches, one term of the written bound on hiding in a technical report that is not public and not refereed comes out below 128 bits. The report's computed figures on hiding are for fresh random values alone and leave out several terms: one has no number at all; the one told here, that of a prover that stops a whole batch, can be by far the largest. `cp_prove` runs no verifier; the provider's check (duty 6) withholds the whole batch at a rejection, so the two together are on paper such a prover, and the term applies (inferred: row HW-740). That term lowers the figures, and its input was not counted at the default setting. For the released prover, which also stops at tests for which no bound is stated, the report has no bound at all. 129.5 is the report's computed figure for its own protocol and prover, without that term. None of these figures is a level for these programs. A term below 128 bits is not a leak, and no attack is known (row HW-740). These words are the pages' own, not the report's (row LIM-44.1). No search for an attack through this term is known.

**On paper: three figures, and two things that a technical report that is not public and not refereed leaves unsaid.** The report also prints what the term of row LIM-44 would be if one more event were charged like a stop of a whole batch: a zero row in the random matrix (entries -1, 0, 1) of a range check. By the report's reckoning one request meets such a row with a chance of about 2^-109.3 at the report's own setting, and by its account, from a reading of the code of programs other than the released ones, the prover then withholds that one proof and stops nothing else. Charged like a stop, the term alone would come to 83.9 bits as long as the whole commitment has served no more batches than one leaf table can serve, to 83.4 bits at a million batches, and to 64.5 bits over everything that one commitment can serve. By the report no statement charges this for a prover that withholds that one proof alone, by a public rule, and, with random values derived from a key, for clients that act only on whether they were answered and whether their proof was withheld or marked; by the report this does not reach the released service as a statement. By the report these figures are also the size of what is revealed where the adversary itself is told at which requests this happened. None of them is a level or a floor, for the report's protocol or for these programs. (These docs' own words, as in row LIM-44, not the report's: a term below 128 bits is not a leak, and no attack through it is known; no search for one is known.) Two things the report itself tells as left unsaid in its proof of hiding. Its definition of hiding, which compares what clients see with what a simulator makes without the weights, does not say how the hash and the parties' random values are drawn together. The theorem on the compiled argument asks that the honest committer's and prover's random values be fresh and independent of all else; how those of the adversary, and of the party that chooses the requests, lie to the hash and to each other, no sentence of the definition says. Draws that are tied to one another can meet these words: for such draws a small example has been computed, which is not the protocol, in which what is seen under two sets of weights is far apart. And the simulator's running time is part of no definition there, and no statement bounds it. None of this has been checked independently.

column3: **`cp_commit` needs a CPU with the x86 SHA instructions.** It is built to use them, and it does not check for them when it starts. On a CPU or a virtual machine without them, the system would end it at its first SHA-256, with the shell's bare `Illegal instruction`, exit code 132 and no message of its own. By two separate readings of the source, on a model's files that comes before the seed is drawn and before a working directory is made. The call would leave at most one file, an empty one, which `-worst-case-table` names, and the weights in its memory would go back to the system unzeroed. This has not been tried with `cp_commit` (row C5.2 has the rest). **What to do.** Some start-up rejections tell you how to fix the problem. If a program rejects your model, your files or your machine and offers no fix, the programs cannot serve them, so do not work around the rejection. Run `cp_commit` on a CPU that has the SHA instructions: `grep -m1 -ow sha_ni /proc/cpuinfo` prints `sha_ni` where the system shows them (row C5.2 has a surer check that needs no GPU).

column3: **Self-checks that end the service.** From reading the code, not from running it: every failed self-check on secret random values or keys ends `cp_prove`, so the service does not continue. Most end it with exit code 9 and the check's name, and a few with exit code 1; see [the table of endings](faults.md#what-you-see-and-what-to-do). A few of those with exit code 9 end it at the next end of a batch, not at once. For those few, the release of responses is blocked only once the service has read the failed check's result, so until then an earlier batch's responses can still be released, which arises with `-overlap` or `-overlap-two` alone. That is one of three exceptions: row C3 tells all three, and what such an end does not take back. No run is known that produced exit code 9 in a service, or in a production build, which has no way to inject a fault. Nor is any run of a production build known that shows `cp_prove` exiting with code 1 after a failed self-check. **Self-checks that do not end it.** A few self-checks on data, none of them on secret random values, merely mark one request or one batch as failed. Clients who act together and have two requests in one batch can tell whether a failure was one request's own or the whole batch's. Some of those share a failure flag with a check on the lookup argument, and these are non-fatal by design. If they stopped the service, a client would learn one bit about a request of its choice, and could end the service at will.

`cp_commit` and `cp_prove` guard against another account on the machine trying to redirect the paths they use. Attacks by a second account ran only through test drivers, not on the released programs, and the guards have several gaps, so follow the steps under "What to do" at [docs/limits.md](limits.md#path-names), which this row's fourth cell repeats. Row R2.6.1 tells a run of a built `cp_commit`, under one account; rows R2.7 and H21.13 tell two more. **What the programs do.** `cp_commit` keeps its working directories open, and it creates, renames and deletes files through those open descriptors. `cp_prove` opens the paths given with `-isk` and `-spool` one component at a time, and holds the [secret key directory](glossary.md#secret-key-directory) open (`prover/common/walked_path.h`). Without these guards a hostile second account with write access to the directory where `cp_commit` works could redirect what the program wrote and deleted, which in tests damaged the caller's files, and, by a reading of the code, could redirect `cp_prove` at start-up to another private directory of the caller's. In 32 cases run against `cp_commit`'s guard (not on the released programs), among them 22 attacks that damaged the caller's files without that guard, none damaged the caller's files, though in 2 of the 22 a directory's timestamps changed. **The gaps,** most serious first: 1. **`cp_commit` checks only the paths it writes to.** From reading the code: like `cp_prove`, it opens the directories that will hold its two output directories, and the one for the `-worst-case-table` file, one component at a time. It rejects a symbolic link on the way. It also rejects any directory on the way, the last one included, that belongs to anyone but root or you, or that group or others can write to (a sticky directory such as `/tmp` is accepted). Under `sudo`, a directory of the account that ran `sudo` passes too. It checks once, at the start: it does not see a later change of these directories' owner, mode or place (row R2.6.1). It does not check the paths given with `-config` and `-weights`, and it follows symbolic links there. So anyone who can write to a directory on one of those two paths can point it at other input files.

For a single batch, name `-in` and `-out` where no one else can write to any directory above them, or to `-in` itself. Under a sticky-bit directory such as `/tmp`, use a fresh directory from `mktemp -d`, never a name that others can predict.

column3: 2. **A single batch's `-in`.** From reading the code: `cp_prove` opens `-out` one component at a time, as it opens `-spool` and `-isk`, before it creates the directory and again afterwards. It opens `-in`, which it only reads, by full path, and it follows symbolic links in the directories above it. So an account that can write to a directory above `-in` can make `cp_prove` read its requests from another place. What it opens as `-out` must be a directory of yours that is closed to everyone else, and not a link. `cp_prove` creates the output directory itself by full path, and `.tmp` below it. By then it has checked that path one component at a time. 3. **A race on the working directories.** After a working directory is created and before it is opened, it can be replaced with another empty private directory (one that group and others cannot access, as with mode 0700) that the caller owns. The run then goes on in that directory, and a run that fails removes it (row R2.3). A similar gap lies before a deletion and before each of the last two renames. From reading the code: since `cp_commit` rejects a parent directory that another account can write to, only root, your own other processes and, under `sudo`, the account that ran `sudo` can do that. In a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, another account can put something under a name that is free. (A fault of this kind that these sources do not have: row R2.3.1.) 4. **The files that are only read.** `cp_commit` finds the files that it only reads by full path ([details](limits-further.md#r2.6)). (From reading the code, the directory of the file named with `-worst-case-table`, which holds numbers computed from the weights and which only its owner can read, is opened one component at a time, like the two output directories.) 5. **The path to `-isk` is trusted.** Any directory that you or root put on the path to `-isk` is accepted, even an older copy of the secret key directory, and no program notices ([details](limits-further.md#h21.15)). Under `sudo` the same holds for the account that typed `sudo` ([what to do about it](operators-duties.md#under-sudo)).

column3: 6. **Look-alikes after an interrupted call.** The next call to `cp_commit` reports what it found, but it cannot tell a dead call's directories from those of another commitment of yours. From reading the code, it sets apart a directory that another account owns, and tells you not to remove anything. If anyone else can write to the parent directory, what has a name can change after that look. One test, `commit.left_working_names`, covers that message, under one account only. It is a row of the public test table, 171 of whose 173 rows, this one among them, have run on programs that each test run built from these sources (most run test programs or scripts, not the three released programs themselves; eight run `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` as test builds: [docs/limits.md](limits.md#what-was-run-on-these-programs)). Two smaller points. The first, on directories made under umask 002, is in row H21.15.1. Second, the example script `prover/examples/run_target_example.sh` rejects a work directory below a directory that another account can change, but it looks once, at its start. If such a directory becomes writable to another account afterwards, that account can replace the new work directory, right after the script has created it, with another empty private directory of yours. The script does not notice, and creates its files there, the example's secret key directory among them. In a trial the swap succeeded every time, as root and as an ordinary user, in each of six rounds. The script was held at that moment, and the directory above was opened only then (row R2.10). Nothing is overwritten. The script goes on only if the directory in which it then stands is the user's own, closed to others and empty (it looks, right after it has entered it), so what it writes there is readable to no other account. That is read in the script; the trial tried only a directory of the user's own. - Name the example script's new work directory inside a directory that only you can write to, as the quick start's line with `mktemp -d` does, and do not change the permissions of any directory above it while the script runs.

column3: After a crash, a power failure, SIGKILL or any other signal that it does not catch, `cp_commit` deletes nothing. It leaves two working directories whose names end in `.making`, one of which holds the [seed](glossary.md#seed), and no tool deletes them. If it died in its very last step, the seed is under `<isk>`. What the call made is then under `<isk>` and `<ivk>.making`, or, partly or wholly, under both final names. After Ctrl-C, SIGTERM, SIGHUP or a broken pipe, or when it aborts itself, `cp_commit` deletes everything that the call has made. Even then, do not take the cleanup on trust: - The program's final status line can wrongly say that everything was removed. - From reading the code, the cleanup writes zeros over every file that the call has created before it removes it, the small secret files first. Four kinds of file are not overwritten: one with a second hard link, one that is not a regular file, one that cannot be examined, and one whose device and inode numbers are not those noted when it was made. Their names are removed, and nothing is said; a file that cannot be examined may also be left. A file that it cannot overwrite keeps its name, and a line says so. On flash storage the old bytes can survive an overwrite (row R3.2 says what else stays). - One gap: if an abort or a signal reaches another thread while the main thread is writing a file, that file can stay. - The file named with `-worst-case-table` can stay: a signal, an abort or an exit of the program's own early in the run can leave it behind. The file is then empty, partly written or complete. Keep it as secret as the weights ([faults.md](faults.md#a-killed-or-failed-cp_commit)). An abort left the seed's file on the disk in one run, not on the released programs.

column3: `make_model`, the tool that writes the tests' synthetic models, makes its directory by the path that you give and then holds it open. It creates its files through that directory and, if it fails, removes them through it, whatever has happened to the path since. It removes the directory itself by its path, only if the path still names it and it is empty. An account that can write to a directory above can choose where the directory is made. It can also swap in another private directory of yours right after that, which then gets the files, or another empty directory just before the removal, which is then removed instead. **After a run under `sudo`.** If the tests run under `sudo` in a clone that had no `bin/`, root owns what they leave: `bin/`, the programs built there and the work directory. The next run that is not root's then exits with code 1: the two tests that build into `bin/`, `build.verifier` and `weight_sums`, fail, and the tests that need one of them are not run. If the clone belongs to an account other than root, the test runner by default warns twice: during the run under `sudo`, if only root can write in the new `bin/`, and at the next run that is not root's. The build scripts of these two tests then build nothing and say that `bin/` belongs to root. That `bin/` is root's does not protect it: whoever owns the clone can replace it, `cp_verify` included. Under `sudo` the tests act as root on names inside the clone, so whoever owns the clone can steer what root does there, as with any program run by `sudo` from someone's copy. To go on with the tests, start again in a new copy of the repository. What root made there, only root can remove or give to another account. This page prints no command for that: whoever does it names each directory by its full path, and first checks that it is the one meant and that no part of the path is a link.

column3: **Worst case:** if the tests run as root, a faulty test keeps root's other powers: the confinement is a guard against a test's mistake, not against a test that means harm (row R1.1). It could still change any file's mode, owner or timestamps, and write to a device node that was already in its work directory. Where the machine allows it no separate mount namespace (root without `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, as in Docker's and Kubernetes' containers by default, or a filter that blocks `unshare`), it could also delete, overwrite or empty any account's files in `/dev/shm`. It cannot open a disk's device file under `/dev` for writing by its name (read in the tool; seen with a harmless device, not with a disk). Reading it, and `ioctl` on it, stay possible (read in the tool). As root, on a machine that allows that namespace, each test gets `/proc/sys`, `/proc/sysrq-trigger` and three more places of `/proc` read-only (seen for four of the five: row R1.1). A test that uses a GPU could get past that on `/proc/sys`, by either of two raw system calls (seen; nothing was written). No test with a GPU was run as root: the rule of --gpu was tried on machines without one. (Row R1.1.) On Linux 5.13 to 6.11, a faulty test running under any account can signal that account's other processes one by one, and one run as root any process of the machine. Under any account, before Linux 6.2 a faulty test can empty any file that the account may write. Under any account it can also create, write and remove files in the repository's `bin/` and in the run's shared directory (rows R1, R1.1). It can do the same in the machine's `/dev/shm`, unless it runs as root on a machine that allows it a separate mount namespace.

column3: Many of the tests and runs that these docs cite as not on the released programs used GPU programs built with nvcc 13.0.88, which the build rejects; far less has been run on programs built with nvcc 13.2.86. These programs are therefore not the ones that the build makes. nvcc 13.0.88 has two known bugs that can make a program silently compute a wrong value. One is published. NVIDIA lists it as fixed in CUDA 13.2 Update 2, whose compiler is nvcc 13.2.86. That fix has not been checked by a test of this project's. Whether the bug affected the programs that nvcc 13.0.88 built is not known. The other bug is of more concern. It has not been found in any release notes, and the build does not work around it. The build tests for it on one small sample kernel only, and with no usable GPU it skips that test and checks only the compiler's version. So it is not known whether the required version is free of this bug (row H8.2 says what was seen). The machine code has not been searched for either bug's pattern. Two more faults of this kind are known. One, in the compiler of CUDA 13.0, made one of the prover's own kernels compute wrong results. The code works around it, and nothing says whether the compiler that the build requires has the fault (row H8.2.2). The other is in the host compiler, which can silently drop writes to memory ([details](limits-further.md#so-37)). **Which toolkit.** Every build tested with nvcc 13.2.86 took the compiler from NVIDIA's Python packages, in sets that have no NVTX headers. CUDA 13.4 is not supported, though the build's version check lets it, and any later release, pass. NVIDIA's NVTX headers can bring a call of `getenv()` into `cp_commit`, which a check of the build's own rejects (the trial in which that happened: row P4.5); `prover/build.sh` compiles NVTX out of the programs' own code, and its check looks for it there; neither reaches the CUDA libraries that the programs load. CUDA 13.2 Update 2 as NVIDIA's installer or a system package manager installs it has those headers (for apt, by the index of NVIDIA's repository; for the installer, most likely), and a build with it has not been tried. Rows P4 and P4.5 tell these tries. If these docs give a test result that is not on the released programs, do not take it as a result for your own build.

column3: The limits of the integration and of the client scripts are in a separate document, [integrations/LIMITS.md](../integrations/LIMITS.md). A known fault, which these sources have: at a start behind your own `sudo`, the example front end's server, run as root, can be led to send out closed files of root's. Every process of your own account can, ahead of a start or of a command, bring a closed directory of root's under a configured name. `clean`, `hold` and `lift-hold` then act on whatever of root's stands under the names at that moment. A server that starts then sends a closed `key.bin`, leaf file or `layout.txt` of root's that is there to anyone who can reach it and has vLLM's API key, where vLLM was given one (how the example front end's middleware learns that key, and where it cannot: [the operator's checklist](../integrations/vllm/REFERENCE.md#the-operators-checklist); by reading, and by tests with a stand-in for vLLM's application, which call these files' routes too; the middleware that ships has run under vLLM at toy size, and four times at full size, not on the released programs, there with the key in `VLLM_API_KEY` alone, and of these files' routes only those of the published `key.bin` and of a leaf file have been called under vLLM, at no server led astray: row H11.2; where vLLM has a key that the middleware neither reads nor suspects, these files go out without a key unless `VLLM_API_KEY` is set; a fault of this kind that these sources do not have: row HW-275). Nothing is logged, and the server stays so until it is restarted, though the names are right again. Public files that you have not given to anyone are themselves to be guarded. Keep the directories, the config file and the checkout below directories that belong to root and that only root can write ([the way out, also for a server that is not root](../integrations/LIMITS.md#above-a-public-directory); row R25). A swap made under a server that is already running leads it to no other file (by report; row R25 says what the tests covered), with one exception: the check that the middleware makes of each batch with `cp_verify` reads the public files by their names, so after a swap it can read other files than the server serves ([the middleware's check](../integrations/LIMITS.md#the-middlewares-check)). At most a swap leads that check to other public files, puts a policy on hold, or ends a hold that was put only in the directory under the name. But moving or renaming a directory takes nothing back from a running server ([the runbook](operators-duties.md#a-record)). A server that is not root can be aimed, ahead of a start, at closed files of its own account, by whoever owns a directory above these or can write in one that is not sticky (by reading).

Three rates were counted in one run, at the same positions of the same texts. 6.81 %: at 5,779 of 84,893 positions in 216 texts the integer model's top token differed from that of the 16-bit weights evaluated in float32. 6.65 %: at 5,643 of the same 84,893 positions in the same 216 texts the top token of the public 4-bit files evaluated in float32 differed from that of the 16-bit weights evaluated in float32. No integer model and no fitted scale is in this rate. 3.11 %: at 2,638 of the same 84,893 positions the integer model's top token differed from that of the public 4-bit files, from which it is made, evaluated in float32. The three rates do not add up, and need not: each counts the positions at which two models' top tokens differ, and the 3.11 % and the 6.65 % are against different references. Since all three were counted at the same positions, arithmetic gives this much: at 4,392 or more of the 5,779 positions at which the integer model differs from the 16-bit weights, more than three quarters of them, the 4-bit files evaluated in float32 differ from the 16-bit weights too. So at the greater part of the positions behind the 6.81 % the step from 16 bits to the public 4-bit files, which a third party made, changes the top token already, before any integer arithmetic. The step to integers adds 136 positions net (0.16 points; with the texts as the units, these counts cannot tell whether that is more than chance), but that is not its size: it changes the top token at 2,638 positions, either away from the 16-bit weights' token (at 136 positions or more), or back to it, or from one differing token to another; how many of each was not counted. A differing top token is not in itself an error of either model, and none of the three rates says how good a reply is. The 6.81 %: measured three times, on three machines, not on the released programs, each time with new passes on both sides (5,779 in one, 5,778 in two, of which one against another public copy of the 16-bit weights; why they differ by one is not known); the run whose counts stand here was on integer weights and quantization scales fitted not on the released programs; the parameter file's other fitted lines were not compared; the weight files were not held to their checksums in that run. All its prompts were built on WikiText-2, and no task benchmark was run. The three rates are of one run: one pass of each of the three models over the same texts, compared at the same positions. The integer model was evaluated by a Python implementation, and both float32 passes by `scales/float_forward.py` (the 4-bit files read by `scales/gguf_weights.py`), neither as it ships; the programs that drove the three passes, read the 16-bit files, applied the output layer after the float32 pass and counted the differences are a study's own and are not in this repository. The 6.65 % was measured once. The 3.11 % was measured once as a whole; on the 192 replies among the texts (60,341 of the positions), other programs on both sides gave the same count, 1,521. What this row says of the integer weights, the scales and the parameter file holds of the 3.11 % too. None of the three has been run on these texts on the released programs. Another count, made once, on other data, in coarse bins: a share of the tokens in greedy replies generated with a third party's 16-bit copy of Meta's weights (taken to be the copy that a record of a fetching names as from RedHatAI's repository; that this count's replies came from that copy rests on their number alone; its files have not been compared with Meta's own) were not the integer model's [top choice](glossary.md#top-choice). That share has not been measured on the released programs ([details](limits-further.md#m1)). Programs were also compared, to see whether they compute exactly this integer model. That was done only at small example configurations and on synthetic weights, and the programs were not written independently (integrations/vllm/integer_model/OPERATING.md, "What has been run"). In one of these comparisons, not on the released programs, in one run, the programs proved, of seven requests, the three that `model.py` said meet the policy and none of the four that it said miss it. That compares which requests get a proof, not values. The others were not on the released programs either, as far as these docs tell. At full size, on real weights, only greedy choices and which requests get a proof have been compared, not scores, and the choices through the proofs' acceptance under exact match, not value by value (row M1.6). At full size on synthetic weights, which all but a few scripted runs used, the same two things were compared, not on the released programs; on such weights an agreement of greedy choices says little about attention, routing or the scales (integrations/vllm/integer_model/OPERATING.md, "What has been run"). Nothing has been compared where a range condition fails. In runs on a real public model's weights ([which](limits.md#few-runs)), the prover used less GPU memory than on synthetic weights of the same shape; the cause is not known. Memory use is seen on the provider's machine only, not by a client. Another account on that machine can see it. [THIRD_PARTY.md](../THIRD_PARTY.md), under "What depends on Meta's models", says, of the numbers in the example configurations that it names, on which model each depends or may depend, or that this is not known.

column3: **Scope.** At the default setting Lean proves that what is shown of the committed tables, within a budget of opened columns, has the same distribution whatever the weights (Lean's encoder, fresh pads, full size, before any hashing). For the protocol's own honest provers, as Lean definitions, zero knowledge is proved after hashing too, in the random-oracle model, against any verifier within a bound on its hash queries and replies, with one bit per request revealed (in a corollary, one label of three). That is proved at the exact-match policy, for one request to a proof, not for batches, and for one commitment with one leaf table ([where it stands](limits.md#the-verdict)). No theorem covers the programs, or the out-of-domain (OOD) answers (masked sums of the weights) as the programs make them ([what Lean proves](limits.md#what-lean-proves)). What Lean has for the link proof's prover by itself: docs/limits.md, 'What Lean proves', item 2. The programs derive their masks from a secret seed, which no Lean theorem covers. Lean has a soundness theorem for its own verifier, `verify`, not for the C++ program that users run: [what it says, and what it does not](../lean/THEOREM.md). The theorem's scope is one format and one size: the format's default setting at full size. That the library's written copy of the full-size public files is the shipped files' is held by no theorem (a program beside the library, `lean/scripts/check_stored_examples.py`, compares them from outside). `verify` accepts a false claim with probability at most about q/2^124 + 2^-101 after q queries to the random oracle, the committer's and the prover's added up. It is stated only for public files that ask for exact match, which `verify` does not test, and that are fixed before the hash function is sampled; no other acceptance policy is covered. The soundness theorem on `verify` is for one commitment, one prompt, one output, one proof and one call of `verify`. N proofs handed in at once under one commitment cost N times the error, taken at the whole list's hash queries, for a prover that has seen no honest proof; for proofs checked one after another no bound is stated. The bound is on the chance of a false accept ("accepted and wrong"), not on the chance that a given accept is false. Proof of work is counted in the bound: without their 20 to 32 bits of it the rounds that sample query positions have errors of about 2^-96 to 2^-110 (added up by a program, no theorem; bits of single rounds, not the chance of a forgery); each attempt is paid for in hash queries, inside q. Soundness after an honest commitment is proved with `verify` as the verifier only for an illustrative committer written in Lean: after its commitment to given weights an accepted output meets the files' policy at these weights, except with probability about 2^-88 + p/2^124 after p queries of the prover, on average over the committer's seed. That is never below about 2^-88, against 2^-101 in general, since the committer's own 2^35 queries are charged. No theorem ties that committer to `cp_commit`. That `verify` accepts the honest prover's proofs under the honest committer's commitment is proved of the compiled system alone, in the random-oracle model (the final statement's field `complete`). Of the Lean verifier's own system, whose committer is the constant committer (a committer that returns one constant whatever the weights, and so commits to nothing; the committer of the six lines (which six: docs/limits.md#what-the-lean-proofs-cover; the system that has it: row PS-71) is another: the one that `compile` makes (`lean/Johnson/Face/Compiler.lean`), which encodes the weights and hashes the key), nothing of the kind can be stated with content. The format's hash function is a random oracle, which committer and prover query classically, one bit string at a time: nothing is claimed against a quantum adversary, and of the real hash function the bound says nothing. A second, fixed hash function is taken as separate from the oracle. What is proved is the statement in Lean; these sentences are a gloss. (Rows L14, L37.)

Of the six lines (lean/LIMITS.md, L93) the independent checker has accepted `sound`, `repliesFit` and `refusedHandsOutNoProof` by name, over a build of this repository's files; over such a build the three on binding, completeness and zero knowledge have been checked by Lean's kernel alone. That the compiled files that these passes read were that build's is known from a report alone; Lean's own files were not compared with a list of checksums. The independent checker checks a text that an exporter of this project's writes, and its run cannot be repeated as it was made: the exporter is not in this repository (whether the public exporter lean4export would serve has not been tried). No test that changes the source has run on this repository's Lean files (row L25). A pass of the kernel, the full check or the independent checker does not show that the definitions beneath the statements, `verify`'s own text among them, mean what these pages say of them: that is a reading; nothing machine-checks it. (Row L43.)

column3: - **Further limits,** each told in full in [lean/LIMITS.md](../lean/LIMITS.md). The extractor takes the public files as an argument, beside the commitment and the committer's logged queries, and no theorem ties a commitment to one set of public files: one commitment may be accepted under two sets, with other weights extracted at each (a digest of the files' bytes is hashed into the ID, by reading; no theorem). It is a rule defined with choice, not a program with a running time. The model is the library's own integer program, and no theorem ties it to a real model (rows L29, L44). The format's hash function is a random oracle, which committer and prover query classically, one bit string at a time: nothing is claimed against a quantum adversary, and of the real hash function the bound says nothing. A second, fixed hash function is taken as separate from the oracle. The compilation theorem (`innerCompiledVerifier_sound`) too models the hash as a random oracle with classical queries, so it does not cover a structural weakness in the programs' hash function or a quantum adversary (row L8). No statement on soundness follows from the Lean functions on bytes in `Fmt/` and `Run/` (row L22). Soundness alone says little. Completeness, where the model has a result, and zero knowledge are proved in Lean for the protocol, at full size and at the exact-match policy, each up to a small stated error, with fresh random masks; after compiling, both are on one leaf table. The honest prover in these theorems is a Lean definition, not the CUDA prover: nothing is proved for the programs. (Rows L9, L13, L41.) column3: The masking is built in and on by default. **What is proved, and of what.** Completeness and zero knowledge are proved in Lean for the protocol, at full size, each up to a small stated error: first for the interactive protocol (IOP), then for the compiled (non-interactive) prover and the same Lean verifier, in the random-oracle model. The honest prover in these theorems is a Lean definition, not the CUDA prover. Completeness covers well-formed requests on which the model has a result and the claimed output is that result. Where the model has no result it says nothing. Zero knowledge holds against an honest verifier in the IOP and, after compiling, against any verifier within a bound on its hash queries and replies; the simulator's running time is not modelled. Both are at the exact-match policy, with fresh random masks, for one commitment and one request per proof and, after compiling, on one leaf table, not for batches. One bit per request is revealed (served or refused: a request is refused if it is ill-formed, if the model has no result on it, or if its result is other tokens), and it depends on the weights. A service that chooses to say "failed" (that is not the shipped programs' own "failed": docs/limits.md#narrower-than-what-runs) reveals one label of three in its place (served, failed or other tokens). Neither says anything of what the public files themselves tell of the weights, or of timing. In the code both are tested, not verified: every honest proof tried was accepted, and in honest runs of the released programs (what has run on them: docs/limits.md#what-was-run-on-these-programs) nothing beyond a declared list has been seen, though no test on them hunts for a leak. The Lean files of this repository have the checksum 620d8930. One Lean file, with one definition and four theorems, which nothing else imports, was added after the runs reported here and checked on its own. Three of the check script's pinned values were changed and three of its stored lists were extended for it; nothing else in the script or the lists changed. (The file: `lean/AtFullSide/Face/ExecutableVerifierIsLeanVerifier.lean`; the full account: lean/CHECK-RESULTS.md.) Wherever these pages say that a run was made over this repository's Lean files, over a build of them or over the released Lean files, that file was not among them. Without that file and these changes, at the checksum c06b37e6, these have run: the build of the whole library with its two side libraries, with no error and no `sorry` (with Mathlib and the other packages compiled beforehand, the library's own files from nothing, in several calls of Lake, the last of them over all three libraries: lean/CHECK-RESULTS.md tells how); Lean's own print of the named theorems and of the axioms that each rests on; and, of the library's check, the steps on the files' text (tree, words, imports); and its audit of axioms and of the lists of names, inside the whole run of that check that is told below (10,772 names; 184 stored statements). The Lean verifier's reference run has been made over this repository's Lean files (row L9), and the independent checker has been run, on the soundness theorem's export and, in passes of their own, on those of three further theorems (`sound`, `repliesFit`, `refusedHandsOutNoProof`), as the exporter writes them over this repository's build; what the checker accepted (the soundness theorem on `verify`, three further theorems, and what lies beneath each: row L25): lean/CHECK-RESULTS.md. The script runs no mutation tests and no second, independent proof checker ([what the full check is worth](limits.md#what-the-lean-proofs-cover)). A commitment publishes [OOD answers](limits.md#a-record). Lean proves, for the encoder as written in Lean and before any hashing, that what is shown of the committed tables has exactly the same distribution whatever the weights. That holds at the default setting, at the 400B model's shape, for each table's out-of-domain (OOD) answers (masked sums of the weights) together with up to 44,040,191 opened columns. *Its bounds.* It covers no message of a prover: the provers in its statement are fixed-message provers, which send the same messages whatever the weights and so show nothing of them. So it is not index privacy. At public files in use (row PS-71) the protocol's honest provers are other provers; they fall back on the fixed-message ones only where a function that makes an honest prover refuses. It supposes fresh random values (the pads, which mask these answers, and the rows' encoding randomness) and sample points that depend on nothing hidden. The programs derive the random values from a secret seed and get the points by hashing the table's root, so neither holds of them. It stops before any hashing: roots, salts and paths are outside it. What the provers' own messages add, and hashing, are covered by the theorems on zero knowledge ([where it stands](limits.md#the-verdict)). The 44,040,191 columns are the budget of a table's whole life. Nothing in Lean keeps count of it, and at one column more the single-table statement fails. The programs keep that count, in a file for each table. As a whole it is stated at that shape and nowhere else. As is usual, no theorem ties it to a program. In sum, no Lean theorem covers these answers as the programs make them (from a seed, at hashed points). After hashing, the hashed scheme in Lean too gets the points by hashing the root; its random values stay fresh. Lean checked the proofs; whether their statements say what these plain words say was judged by a reading, not by Lean. The programs derive their random values from a secret seed and keep their own count (what Lean's results on hiding leave out: row PS-63). It has not been established that the protocol as Lean describes it is the programs' step for step. A kept row's 219 random values are argued on paper only; no Lean result speaks of that number, and the count has no slack (rows HW-762, RES-58). Whether that is enough for weights that must stay secret is each provider's own decision ([where it stands](limits.md#the-verdict)). In a sweep of injected losses of random values at the default setting's small form, on test builds of other sources (row HW-678), 30 of 165 picked losses in CPU memory went unnoticed (12 of the 165 changed no byte of any file, so 30 of the 153 that could show anything), and none of 130 in GPU memory: no rate. No pair of losses was tried. In small computed examples some pairs of losses did leak; none of this is proved or checked (rows HW-660 and H17.3.1.1). Two commitments to the same weights, never searched together; batches that overlap in time, as they do by default: that judgement covers them on three short looks alone, one of them at source code, and that of other programs, with nothing of the service run and no test aimed at them (no proved statement covers the service as it runs that way); [a client that chooses the checked tokens](limits.md#which-policy). Each provider decides whether that is enough for secret weights. By design, every weight-dependent value that the programs publish is masked or salted, apart from a [declared list](what-is-not-hidden.md); with [`-public-weights`](what-is-not-hidden.md#public-weights) nothing is hidden.
