column3: **What was run on these programs, and what was not.** *In short.* The runs that this section reports as runs on the released programs were made on programs built from sources that differ from these in comments, names and the wording of messages alone; of the programs that these sources themselves build it reports three small runs and one at full size ("Which programs ran", below); the sources of `cp_verify` do not differ. In the test runs that cover all 173 public tests, most of which start none of the three programs, 170 passed, one passed in part, two were not run and none failed. On synthetic weights, the released `cp_verify` and the Lean verifier were given the same sets of full-size files, as reported: both accepted all 47 honest proofs, and neither accepted one of the 57 lying proofs; at 3 of the 57 the Lean command's parser refused the file, which is not a verdict. The Lean verifier also accepted 41 further proofs, on synthetic weights, as reported of the timed runs. One proof made at full size, on synthetic weights, by the programs that these sources build, as reported, was accepted by `cp_verify` and by the Lean verifier. `examples/maverick/run.sh` ran at full size on a real model's public weight files, without building, downloading or installing: its five stored values came out the same, byte for byte, and `cp_verify` ended with `YES`. In the timed runs on those weight files, at the default setting, all 1,851 requests were served, and all 1,851 proofs, each of the one token after the prompt, were accepted by the runs' own calls of `cp_verify`. The first and the fifth of the five tests of weight hiding ended as written down beforehand, the first also at full size, once on synthetic weights and once on a real model's public weight files. *What is left.* The 57 lying proofs are files made beforehand by test programs that this repository cannot build, all at one commitment and for three requests: no cheating prover was run against the released programs, and no refusal at the lookup checks themselves has been seen. At small size `cp_verify` accepted 228 replayed calls on altered stored tables: that is right if each table still decodes to the honest weights alone, which rests on counts of the changed columns: no decoder was run. Neither test of weight hiding shows that the masks hide, and the other three of the five were made on other programs; no run shows what the programs leave in host or GPU memory, and no audit with the provider's secrets has run on a commitment to a real model's weight files. Two runs at 64 requests on synthetic weights failed, and no cause is shown. The tests and scripts of those test runs differ from this repository's, a few in code; of the public tests that need a GPU or the CUDA compiler only two have been run on this repository's own files. The programs that ran and the runs' records are not in this repository, so a reader cannot check how they are tied to these sources. Nothing in this section is a proof about the compiled programs. *Which programs ran.* "The released programs" are `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` and `cp_verify` as the sources in this repository build them (the production build). The programs that made the runs that these pages tell as runs on the released programs, or on a test build of these sources, were built from sources that differ from these in comments, in the names of identifiers and files, in seven quoted texts that hold such a name and in the wording of eight messages (seven that `cp_commit` or `cp_prove` prints, one that a build script prints), and in nothing else. These pages tell a program built from those as built from these sources, a run on it as a run on the released programs or on a test build of these sources, and a reading of those as a reading of these sources; how far that tie is shown, and where it ends, is told under [What a reader can check](limits.md#what-a-reader-can-check). This rule speaks of `cp_commit`, `cp_prove` and `cp_verify` and of their test builds. How the tests' own files, the serving scripts and the other scripts of those runs differ from this repository's (they differ in code too) is told under "What these runs do not show", at "The public tests". Of the `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` that this repository's sources build, these pages tell four runs, three of them here alone: the first and the fifth test of weight hiding, once each, at small size, on synthetic weights, each ending as written down beforehand; and a comparison with the middle build told under [What a reader can check](limits.md#what-a-reader-can-check), on synthetic weights: under one test seed the test builds of both sides gave the same files, byte for byte, at small size, and so did both production builds of `cp_commit`, called with `-public-weights`, at small size. Not held: up to 31 zeros of padding behind a string or table, the program and section headers, and the entry point. A second reader derived every figure of the comparison's result anew, with a program of its own. Second step: a production and a test build of this repository's sources were compared in the same way with the middle build, without being run. `cp_verify`, `weight_sums` and `make_model` came out the same, byte for byte. The GPU code of `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` is the same, and the container of the GPU code is the same, byte for byte. In their host code every instruction of every function is the same, and each address in it points at the same thing. Of the data that the programs read, the quoted texts of those messages alone differ: eight texts, of the seven messages that the programs print, one of which is two texts. At this step, by a look beside the comparison, the entry point and the program headers are the same in all four pairs of programs (`cp_commit` and `cp_prove`, production and test), but for two headers of each `cp_prove`, which differ by 32 bytes, the difference in length of its read-only data. Not held at this step: where inside the container of the GPU code a pointer of the host code points. Faults were planted at this step too, 69 in all, and each was noticed: 60 on the host and GPU sides of the production `cp_commit` and `cp_prove`, 8 at the check of the texts that differ (2 for each of the four programs; none of these turns a byte of code), and one at the count of raw bytes. At 2 controls with nothing planted the tools stayed silent. The host and GPU code of the test builds was compared by the same tools with no plant. The result and the tools were each read a second time, by readers looking for a fault, with nothing run: they found no way for the comparison to pass wrongly, beyond what is told here as not compared or not held. Neither comparison ran anything. No reader of either comparison is an outside party. Apart from the comparison, under one test seed the test builds of both sides of the first step gave the same files, byte for byte, at small and at full size, on synthetic weights, and so did both production builds of `cp_commit`, called with `-public-weights`, at small size. At full size there was no control and no second run of one side; at small size each of six controls came out different, as a control must. Proofs of the production builds are drawn, so nothing is claimed of them by bytes. Equal bytes under one seed show that the two sides computed the same on those inputs; they are no test of weight hiding. The like run on both sides of the second step is the comparison with the middle build that "Which programs ran" tells: it was at small size alone; two runs of one side gave equal bytes, and each of seven controls came out different. *Programs outside the comparison.* Both steps cover `cp_commit` and `cp_prove`, production and test builds, `cp_verify`, `weight_sums` and `make_model`, and no other program: not the two helper programs that the audit tool (`tools/audit/`) builds for its own use, the programs of `blocks/`, the tests' own programs or the parser of `lean-verify`. The audits with the provider's secrets are runs of the audit tool. Its 14 scripts and the 2 sources of its helpers lie under neither digest. These 16 files, and the 118 sources that the helpers compile beside them (a list that a program drew from the `#include` lines, not a compiler's), have the same checksums in this repository as in the tree that the rows ran in; from which tree the audits' own copy of the tool came is not shown. One file that the tool imports from outside its folder, `docs/format/format_rules.py`, differs from that tree's: by a comparison of tokens, in docstrings, a comment and two string literals, both headings that it prints into a file. *What a reader cannot check.* The files of the programs that ran and the runs' records, the provers' build records among them, are not in this repository, so a reader cannot check these results against them. *Two builds of the sources of the runs.* Two builds of those sources were compared file by file, without running them: each, by the account of those who built them, from a fresh copy with nothing kept from another build, on one machine, at one path, with the same compilers. `cp_verify`, `weight_sums` and `make_model` came out the same, byte for byte. `cp_commit` and `cp_prove`, production and test builds alike, differ only in the name of a temporary file of the compiler, which, by a reading, holds a number that differs from build to build and stays in the program's list of symbols: a few bytes (6 and 11 in this pair; 5 and 12 in the test builds), at the same sizes. All their GPU code is the same, byte for byte. So the files of a second build of these two have another checksum. `cp_verify`, whose sources do not differ from this repository's, was also built on a second machine (Ubuntu 24.04, g++ 13.3.0), with the repository's own script: the same file, byte for byte. A third build of those sources, in the production build, in a fresh container on a GPU node, at the same path, with nvcc 13.2.86 installed at another place, was compared with the programs of the timed runs: `cp_verify` came out the same, byte for byte; in `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` no function differs, on the host or on the GPU, by a comparison function by function, but other parts of the files do. Each of the two differs from its counterpart in the same eleven sections of the host file, among them the container of the GPU code and the section that says which libraries to load and where to look for them, and in one note inside that container; none of these differences has been traced to its cause. That pair does not show what another build path does. Whether it was made on another machine than the programs of the timed runs, and which compilers made those, is not in the records that were compared. No test build was in that comparison. That comparison ran none of the three programs. It noticed a byte planted in a host function and bytes planted in the GPU images; the unpacking itself is not tested, and nothing was planted in the PTX. *How other sources differ.* How far the sources of other programs differ from these is told with each kind (row RES-39; the head of docs/limits.md). *Test code in the production build.* That a production build holds no test code is checked by a search for strings, which does not read code (row E17.2); at least 7 of the 93 lines of `prover/tests/serving_build_words.txt`, which it reads, stand nowhere in the sources of `prover/`, `blocks/` and `verifier/` outside their tests, so their absence shows nothing; that the search ran is shown by a build's records, not by a log. Counts of lines, files, kernels and functions on these pages may be off: no such count has been made on these sources, but for those that a row tells of the released programs (rows RES-39, RES-54, H39.1 to H39.4.1, HW-213 and HW-218). *Weight hiding and soundness.* What is proved, of what, and what is only tested is told on [guide/what-is-proved.md](../guide/what-is-proved.md) and [guide/weight-hiding.md](../guide/weight-hiding.md). Nothing in this section is a proof about the compiled programs.

column3: The five tests of hiding and what stands beside them, each by its conditions (which programs are "the released programs", and which kinds of result were got on other programs (row HW-678): docs/limits.md#what-was-run-on-these-programs). All under exact match, at the default setting, on synthetic weights, and each run once, unless a line says otherwise. Two of the five tests of weight hiding have run on the released programs: the first at small size on synthetic weights and at full size, once on synthetic and once on a real model's public weights, and the fifth once, at small size on synthetic weights. One of the fifth's two audits, the audit of a commitment, also ran on them at full size, in the timed runs (line 5). At full size the first test has also run on other programs, and the fifth's two audits have run together only on other programs. The second and the third ran on test builds of other sources, which hold the code that injects a fault, and the fourth on programs of other sources that held test-only code. A repeat of a test is no new witness. Each test's make-up and further bounds: docs/limits.md#verdict-runs. All figures are as the runs' own logs report them. 1. *The OOD answers by value.* A separate program, given the provider's secrets, computes the published sums again. On the released programs, three times at small size on synthetic weights and twice at full size, once on synthetic weights and once on a real model's public weights: at small size all 1,536 answers of two commitments in one run, all 512 of one commitment in a second, and all 512 of one commitment to a small synthetic model in files of the real files' form in a third (line 11), and at full size all 4,096 answers of the commitment's two tables, both times, each commitment under a seed that `cp_commit` drew, were the row's weighted sum plus the public factor times the row's own pad; no pad came twice, and none was 0; at full size none equals any of the some 112 billion random entries and salt values that the rules which the test carries give for the first table; all 8 faults that the program injected for itself were found each time. Beside that test, in each of the two full-size runs, the audit tool's program, run over copies of the public files alone (`--level=0`), reported nothing on them and stopped at each of three copies with one bit changed; a changed bit is no lost mask. At small size, beside the second and the third of the small runs, it read four honest sets of such files and reported nothing; no altered copy was put to it there. On other programs the first test also ran, several times at small size, and at full size twice on synthetic weights and three times on a real model's public weights, and ended the same way as on the released programs (one further trial ended with a failing status of its own controls: row LIM-29). The test's other call, on weights that the program makes itself: not run (not on the released programs, `cp_commit` made no commitment to such weights at the default setting's small form; not tried on the released programs). Bounds: it says nothing on what a sum gives away; the pads are derived from a secret seed; the synthetic weights' values came from the project's integer model; it reads the head, the root and the stored answers at the front of the public files, not the committer's proof chains behind them; it does not show that the masks hide, and it cannot show that a seed is random; the full-size synthetic weights are computed from a public seed in the parameter file, so nothing secret was committed there. The 8 faults show that the program's count on the pads can ring, not that each of its three counts (equal pads; equal single field values; pads that are 0) could have: no fault tells them apart, and that the program counts all three is read, not tested. Nor do they show that the search among the some 112 billion values would have counted a match with a pad: its control plants two values that are counted on a branch of their own, so that too is read, not tested. 2. *Lost pads.* On test builds of other sources, not on the released programs, at small size: all 8 injected losses of pads ended `cp_commit`, each under its self-check on pads and no other, and none left a public file; under a seed that it drew itself, the test build refused the switch that injects the losses. Bound: one self-check alone stands between a fault that loses every pad and a public file without pads; with that self-check switched off, on a test build without proof of work, a commitment without pads passed everything else that `cp_commit` does (one trial). The rejection of more than one OOD answer a row, on programs that refused such a file by a rule of their own, not on the released programs, once each, at small size, with two answers a row alone (as reported): `cp_commit` refused at once on a small synthetic model's files and on an empty stand-in, and made no directory; `cp_prove` refused at once on a secret key directory changed to two answers a row, wrote nothing and counted nothing. With three or four no run has tried it: there it is known from the source. 3. *The sweep of lost random values.* On test builds of other sources, not on the released programs, at small size: 295 picked losses, which struck 189 of the 73,177 random draws of an honest small run. In GPU memory 130 of 130 were stopped, 122 of them by one self-check alone. In CPU memory 123 of 165 were stopped, 12 changed no byte, and 30 went unnoticed: they pass the programs' self-checks and `cp_verify` (picked by kind: counts, not rates). For `cp_commit`'s 11 unnoticed runs, "unnoticed" means that `cp_verify` accepted in its two calls on the key file and a leaf file alone. Every run of the sweep is the same fixed sample under a test seed: no second witness. By two short readings of other sources, about ten minutes each, none of the 30 exposes weights by itself, but for one case, where it is not known; no run has shown that. With every secret of the honest run the shipped audit tool's files reported all 30 of the unnoticed ones, and nothing on the honest files (what that tool cannot see: rows E4 and H17.3.1); a script that does not ship started the tool's files and wrapped six of their functions, not the calls that these pages print. No such audit runs in service. 4. *The replay of riskier losses.* Not on the released programs: on programs that held test-only code, at small size: of 263 losses of draws that a self-check covers, 263 were stopped. In a control build without these self-checks 263 of the same losses went through under the verifier's yes, so it is the self-checks that stop them; 9 of 9 more, at neighbouring draws that no self-check covers, went unnoticed. Bound: single examples; far more draws of their kinds are covered by no check. 5. *Both shipped audits, with the provider's secrets.* On the released programs, at small size, once: with this repository's own audit files both audits accepted the honest files, and `cp_verify` accepted the four proofs of two kept batches, under two commitments, each under a seed that `cp_commit` drew; when a false file stood in turn for each of three kept files, under the tool's `--rehearsal` option, the audit said no each time; for a fourth kept file none was tried; no altered public file was put to them. On other programs, at small size, both audits also ran, several times, and said yes to the honest files each time. In the timed runs (docs/limits.md#the-timed-runs), on the released programs, at full size: the audit of a commitment alone, right behind each of three honest commitments under drawn seeds: it accepted all three (and a fourth, made under a clipped-gap policy: row H13.7). That is no negative test: no false or altered file was put to it; what the audit printed stayed on the machine, but for the fourth's last six lines, and the run's own script looked only at its exit code, at the form of its last line, at how many lines report a failed check and at how many kept files were left; that the audit's files in these runs were this repository's own, the runs' records do not print: they name the pack from which the files were unpacked, and hold it to its checksum; the pack's checksum was tied beforehand, on the machine that made the pack, to the tree from which the released programs were built. Not on the released programs, at full size, in one run, another than the one told at docs/limits.md#verdict-runs: both audits said yes, `cp_verify` accepted both proofs of the kept batch, and with a false file in turn for each of four kept files the audit said no four times of four, and nowhere else. Compared by value, on the released programs. At small size, under exact match: by the commitment's audit 33.00 % of the bytes of key file and one leaf file, and 29.27 % of those of key file and two leaf files; by the batch's audit, which takes in two proofs as well, 18.76 % and 17.87 %. At small size, under a clipped-gap policy, with one leaf file: 32.94 % and 18.78 % (row H13.8), and, by the commitment's audit in the making of a small example at the same configuration (row H13.8), 32.97 %. At full size: 10.18 % of the bytes of key file and leaf file, by the commitment's audit, once, under a clipped-gap policy (row H13.7). Under exact match no share at full size is known on these programs, and the batch's audit ran on them at small size alone. Not on the released programs, at small size, in one run: 32.99 % of 1,629,688 bytes of key file and leaf file (in another, whose policy is not told, 32.93 %: row LIM-63). Not on the released programs, at full size, in the run told at docs/limits.md#verdict-runs: 10.22 % of the bytes of key file and leaf file, and 7.66 % of those of two proofs, key file and leaf file; the account of the other full-size run, told above, does not say what share was compared. Beside the five, lines 9 (one of its four runs), 10 and 11 alone on the released programs. 6. *Audits by value of two small runs*, with a copy of every secret and programs of the audit's own: nothing differs outside a control. The key file and the leaf files were made again from the seed, whole but for their fixed form (39,919 and 39,872 claims, none differing); all 768 OOD answers of each commitment were met; of each run's eight proofs two could be made again (7,997,336 and 7,991,504 bytes met by value, none wrong). The kept proofs were made again with a helper, built from the verifier's code in other sources, which read those proofs to the end, so an error that the helper shares with `cp_verify` would not show. Limits: of all public bytes of a run 31.95 % are met by value, 54.30 % lead to a root by the hash alone, and 13.74 % are reached by no claim, all of the last two kinds in the proofs; the other six proofs of a run cannot be made again, so the search for a repeated random value over all eight gave no verdict; every control changes a thing in the audit's own computation, and no faulty file was tried; it shows that the files hold what the protocol's description says, in the parts made again, not that the weights are hidden. 7. *The like audits of one full-size run*: only a part of the public files could be made again (10.73 % of the 159 MB in one pass and 21.04 % in another; no total is given), with no difference. Six of the eight proofs can be made again only in part; 1,065,800 bytes of the key file are reached by no step; the helper program behind the larger pass is built from the verifier's code in other sources; of twelve kinds of controls on the parts of a proof that meet the weights, six were run at this size; the step that at small size checks the OOD answers and the two proofs whole was left out. The controls show that the comparison can fail, not that a faulty prover would be caught. column3: **A round's mask that waits in GPU memory.** By one fast reading of the sources of `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` (row HW-745; nothing was built or run): In several of the sub-proofs' sumchecks the constant that a round sends is covered by a sum of mask entries. These are attention's own sumchecks (two routines, one of which runs several times in a sub-proof), the layers' batched sumcheck and both merges of the claims on the weights. `cp_prove` computes that sum when the sumcheck begins, and keeps it in a cell of GPU memory until the round's kernel reads it (prover/hiding/psc_device.cuh:166, :306, :340). No self-check compares that cell. By a reading of the code one more value waits in GPU memory in the same way in attention's sumchecks: the challenge that multiplies the end values' masks. With 0 there the end values would go out bare, in a false proof. A flipped bit lays nothing bare. But if the cell came to hold 0 or a public value, the client could work out a true round value. If the store were lost, the cell would keep what was there before: zeros from set-up, a public value, or an earlier sumcheck's sum. Under an earlier sum one mask would cover two values, and whoever holds both could work out one combination of two true round values. In the two merges a true round value is an exact linear form in the sub-proof's weights, with coefficients that the client can compute. In the others it is a form of activations, or of activations and weights. By reasoning one such equation fixes no single weight. But it is true knowledge of the weights, and a way to test a guess at them. By arithmetic the proof is then false, but for a negligible chance, so the provider's check of the whole batch with `cp_verify` (duty 6: docs/limits.md#the-conditions) should reject it, once it has left the prover: it is the one net (the fault "a value lost after it was hashed in": row HW-322). Beside the class the two kinds' sources differ in 30 files, in comments alone. The two kinds' compiled programs differ in more than that class; the machine code that differs is not shown equivalent and has not been read. **That judgement.** For this class it rests on a reading of the class, on a reported comparison of the GPU code, on equal bytes at small size and on small runs of the first and the fifth test on the released programs (row LIM-63.2, lines 1 and 5). These runs are not aimed at the class: they show that what the two tests look at holds with it in place, and no more. The first also ran twice at full size on the released programs, once on a real model's public weights (row HW-747) and once on synthetic weights (row LIM-63.2, line 1), each time as written down beforehand. For this class that judgement rests on them no further than that. **What passes through the class.** In two readings, apart, for hiding alone, with its other form beside it, nothing was found against the class. By a third reading of the class, and of who calls it in `cp_commit` and `cp_prove`, no seed, key, pad, mask or weight is fed to it. The secret tables' leaves, rows and salts alike, are hashed by GPU kernels on three functions of the same file that stand outside the class and did not change; of these tables the class meets only the columns that a proof or a file opens, with their salts. What else passes through it: public facts (the parameters, the commitment ID); the lists whose digests enter the keys, which hold public facts and a batch's requests, in an object that is wiped; the transcript as it is sent; and the leaves of a binding tree (a batch's, and the key file's), each a seal with its salt, of 40 bytes at the default setting. Such a salt is drawn from the private randomness and goes out in its own request's proof, the key file's in that file; in memory it is not wiped. A batch's salts hide its requests from the readers of its other proofs, not the weights. The masks come from the seed by ChaCha20 alone. A wrong digest in a key's list would give other masks, not weaker ones, as long as the system's random bytes do not repeat; the list is there as a second safeguard against such a repeat. **What the class keeps.** What its callers lean on: all its state lies in the object, as plain data; the wipe behind a key's list covers the whole object; the bytes behind the last one filled are zeros. **Which text.** The class in blocks/hash/hash.h in this repository is, byte for byte, the one that these two readings had, by its difference from the one that was read whole. The comment in front of it differs from the one that they had in thirteen places, in words alone: one names the members that `init()` sets to 0, the buffer among them, where theirs says "the other members"; the other twelve are not on clearing, on what stays in memory or on what passes through the class. All thirteen have been read for hiding, once. What else of the 384 files of the reading of the sources whole differs: row HW-745. **The GPU code.** By a reported comparison every kernel that makes or hashes masks, pads, salts or secret rows has the same code, constants and shared memory in the two kinds of programs. That holds of the programs that it set side by side alone: in the released programs four such kernels (`k_fold_slab`, `k_join_runs`, `k_chain_leaves`, `k_fibre_leaves`) have other code than in either kind, by the sources. Of the 33 kernels through which a sub-proof's values are masked and sent (row H39.1), 22 carry functions of the transcript's family, by a look-up in that comparison's tables, and by the same look-up their machine code differs between the two kinds of programs. Each of them calls `tr_close`, one of the two out-of-line functions that hold the class, and a kernel's machine code carries a copy of the functions that it calls: it differs in the kernels that call one of the two: these 22, and 11 more, none of them among the 33, whose main work is to draw challenges (row H39.4 counts twelve, on test builds of other sources): 33 kernels by name, not the same 33 as row H39.1's; they are 41 where a kernel that stands in both `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` is counted once in each (the like count: row RES-39). The class was read as source; this machine code has not been read. **Equal bytes.** In the comparison of bytes the two kinds' programs wrote the same files, on synthetic weights: at small size their test programs under one test seed and their production `cp_commit`s under one public seed, with a control under another seed; at full size their test programs alone, under one test seed. At full size no control, no second run of the programs that hold its other form and no production `cp_commit` ran. So the bytes at small size speak for the production `cp_commit` directly; those at full size do not. For the production `cp_prove` the bytes, at either size, speak through the GPU code alone, which by the reported comparison is the test program's: its host code differs from the test program's on purpose and was not set beside it, and it draws fresh random bytes, so none of its proofs can be made twice. Of these comparisons of bytes that judgement rests on two reports, whose writer knew the test beforehand; not on the files. That no other start of either was made and laid aside is reported, not shown. The released programs' production `cp_prove` has also run: in the fifth test, at small size, and at full size in both full-size runs of the first (row HW-747; tools/audit/README.md, "What has been run"). In the fifth test, on synthetic weights, it proved two kept batches of two requests, which both audits and `cp_verify` accepted (row LIM-63.2, line 5). **One tool of the fifth test.** One of the fifth's two tools, the shipped audit of a commitment, ran at full size in the timed runs (docs/limits.md#the-timed-runs), as reported, by its lines in the three runs' summaries, on which that judgement does not draw: right behind each of the three runs' honest commitment to synthetic weights, under a drawn seed, and it accepted all three (and a fourth, made under a clipped-gap policy: row H13.7). That is no negative test: no false or altered file was put to it. What the audit printed stayed on the machine, but for the fourth's last six lines: the run's own script looked only at its exit code, at the form of its last line, at how many lines report a failed check and at how many kept files were left. That the audit's files in these runs were this repository's own, the runs' records do not print: they name the pack from which the files were unpacked, and hold it to its checksum; the pack's checksum was tied beforehand, on the machine that made the pack, to the tree from which the released programs were built. That judgement does not rest on it. **What this does not show.** *Nothing shows that less is left in memory.* The clearing of its buffer is ordinary stores and no wipe. In small programs, with call sites like the programs', the compilers (g++, and an nvcc other than the build's) deleted the last clearing, where the object dies with the call, as a dead store, and as many marked words of a salt or a request lay on the dead stack behind the class as behind its other form; the programs' own machine code was not read for this. On the GPU the frames of the kernels whose machine code differs, 22 of the 23 of these 33 that have a frame (row H39.1) among them, differ in size between the two kinds of programs; what they leave was not looked at. One printed line on GPU memory is lower with the test prover that holds the class in this form than with the one that holds its other form, in every run, by 0.027 GB with one request at a time, at either size, and by 0.161 GB with six proved in step; its cause is not shown, and it says nothing of what is left. What a program spills to the stack, to registers or to a GPU thread's own memory no run sees (rows H6, H39, HW-536). *On a GPU a guard of the class* whose condition does not hold ends the kernel by a trap: no such trap has been seen to fire, so that it works there is not shown. *The trap of `tr_open()`,* a guard of hiding in the transcript's functions, has not been run on the released code. *The first and the second implementation of the key schedule share the whole hash:* an error that the class took over from prover/second_writing/blake2b_plain.h would not be seen by the two self-checks that compare a key with that second writing (row E2.4). *That the equal bytes are right* is not shown, beyond the verdicts on them (56 at small size; 8 at full size, as reported, on the proofs of two single requests, one for the next token and one that covers 1,000 tokens, where the 24 proofs of the one batch went to no verifier but the run of `cp_verify` that the `cp_prove` of these runs made itself). *Equal bytes are equal on the inputs tried:* synthetic weights, a few seeds, and at full size one seed and the test programs alone. *The class's own push of the label* differs in text from its other form's: that it feeds the same bytes is shown on the inputs that were tried, not by the same text. *Three differences from its other form lie outside every digest, verdict and read state,* so equal bytes say nothing of them: the message with which a second finish aborts; an over-long push is refused by this class before the caller's bytes are read; and in an object that lives on behind `finish()` or `before_nonce()` its buffer holds zeros where the other form's holds the last block's words. *On other programs, or of other sources:* the second and the third of the five tests, on test builds, and the fourth; the audits at full size, but for the one told above; the reading of the sources whole (row HW-745), which saw the class in its other form. That the class's time does not hang on what it hashes is read, not measured.

column3: What a rate on these pages counts. The steady rate is a best case by its rule: a batch's requests times all 1,024 positions, divided by the mean interval between the releases of successive batches; the first batch has no interval before it; in the timed runs and in driver/measure_rate.py every interval behind it counts; start-up and commitment are not counted, and the quotient is cut after two decimals, not rounded. The rate counts all 1,024 positions of each request though each proof checks one token; a request's latency runs from its batch's start to its proof's release, and no verifier has run on a proof by then (row RES-32). The steady rate at 24 per batch is a best-case prefill rate, not a generation speed: each proof covers one pass of the integer model over a window of 1,024 tokens and checks only one token, the next one, which must be the top choice. A rate is requests × 1,024 / seconds: every position of a window counts, whether the proof checks it or not (one clipped-gap figure alone counts only the checked tokens). The seconds per request are a batch's time divided by its requests, not a waiting time; the two calculated rates with replies checked rest on the run's count of checked tokens and on the 524 prompt tokens that the requests' makers give; a gap such as 109.27 against 109.57 tokens/second (two single sessions, not on the released programs) shows nothing either way. In every timed service at most six requests went into each pass over the weights, and a steady rate rests on four intervals (five batches) or five (six batches); in both groups of runs not on the released programs that repeat the timed runs' kinds three times each (row RES-6), and in the two single sessions named above (109.27 and 109.57 tokens/second), each service's last interval is left out, so that a steady rate there rests on three of the four intervals between a service's five batches, or on four of the five between six. The session of 109.84 tokens/second (row T49), not on the released programs, also leaves its last interval out: its script, in a form that differs from the one that ships, counted the first three of its four intervals; with all four counted the rate would be 109.90. With 1 request a batch the steady rate is 17.41 ± 0.15 tokens/second (the timed runs: three runs, real public weights); and 1 is what cp_prove does unless -batch and -in-step are given, which are no part of the default setting.

The rate with every reply token checked (108.67 ± 2.8 tokens/second, n = 3, 105.41 to 110.41, all 1,024 positions counted) cannot be set against the project's target of 100 tokens/second or the steady rate at exact match: it was measured under clipped gap (a policy weaker than exact match), on stored replies with no inference engine, and a request's 1,024 positions are 524 of prompt, 31 to 500 of reply and then fill. That rate is no rate of serving: the replies were stored ones and no inference engine ran; and the setting is the default but for three numbers of the parameter file (the clipped-gap policy). From the first batch's start to the last release that rate is 107.95 tokens/second (sample standard deviation 2.8; least 104.77, most 109.63): above 100 in every run. With the start-up counted (61.2 to 64.2 seconds), over the five batches, that rate is 102.36 tokens/second (sample standard deviation 2.6; least 99.33, most 103.94): one of 3 runs under 100. The control with the start-up counted (77.0 to 80.5 seconds), over the five batches: 101.05 tokens/second (sample standard deviation 2.5; least 98.12, most 102.54): one of 3 runs under 100. If only prompt and reply tokens count and the filler tokens do not, the rate with every reply token checked is 94.7 tokens/second (calculated; sample standard deviation 2.5; least 91.8, most 96.2): under 100. If only the checked reply tokens count, the rate is 39.1 tokens/second (calculated; sample standard deviation 1.0; least 37.9, most 39.7). The three pairs of a service with whole replies checked and its control (105.41 | 105.57, 110.41 | 110.24, 110.20 | 110.37 tokens/second) do not agree in sign: they show no cost of the checking, and a cost smaller than the pairs' own spread would not show; the replies were stored ones, with no engine running; the hour and other containers' load may part the two sessions of a pair. Each control ran under its pair's parameter file, with the policy's limits in it: the pairs bear on the checking of the reply tokens, not on what the policy's setting itself costs. The rates under the clipped-gap policy cannot be made again with the script in this repository: they need stored replies and fitted limits, which the script does not make. Not on the released programs, in three runs (public 4-bit files, 24 requests a batch, clipped-gap policy), the steady rate with every reply token checked was 105.38 ± 4.6 tokens/second (n = 3, 100.07 to 108.24, all 1,024 positions counted), or 37.9 if only the checked reply tokens count (calculated; sample standard deviation 1.7; least 36.0, most 38.9), and the control's steady rate 105.26 ± 4.7 (99.94 to 108.96); with every reply token checked the whole machine's CPU pressure was 3.4 to 6.4 % of a session's length in these runs (in the timed runs 0.5 to 2.8 %: row RES-45). column3: The cost against plain inference: what the three multiples rest on. Proving is 71.4 times slower per GPU than plain prefill of 24 requests at once (65.2 to 76.4 over all pairs of the prover's 3 runs and the plain engine's 30 runs; calculated; full size, public weights, the timed runs). Proving is 93.0 times slower per GPU than plain prefill at the highest load tried (92.2 to 94.1 over all pairs of the prover's 3 runs and the plain engine's 8 runs; calculated). Proving one pass over the tokens is 20.1 times slower per GPU than plain decoding of as many tokens at the best load tried, 512 streams (19.7 to 20.5 over all pairs of the prover's 3 runs and the plain engine's 5 runs; calculated). The cost ratios are calculated, not measured side by side: from the prover's best case (the steady rate at 24 a batch, three runs) against another engine (stock vLLM) serving another format of the model (its FP8 release) on eight H100s, whose 30, 8 and 5 runs were not made beside the prover's. The baseline is another model format and another engine: stock vLLM 0.29.0 serving the FP8 release of Llama 4 Maverick on eight H100s, tensor parallel, greedy and warm, against the prover's one GPU on the 4-bit files. The plain rates are not the most that the machine can do, and a baseline that is too low flatters the prover. "Per GPU" counts only GPUs: the prover's one GPU comes with 24 CPU cores and host memory: in the timed runs, at 24 requests a batch on the public 4-bit files, 257.1 GB in its own process, 269.7 GB in its container (more on synthetic weights, and in the container at 64 a batch on the public files: row RES-24). The multiple on decoding compares throughput, not waiting time, and the proved pass yields one token that the proof checks where decoding yields as many served tokens. The baselines cannot be reproduced from the repository: neither the tuned settings nor a script for either baseline is in it. Two baseline measurements disagree: through the engine's HTTP server the plain rates at the highest load and in decoding were lower than through its Python interface with tuned settings; no run has shown why, and the two differ in more than the interface. The ranges of the second and third multiples cover the baseline through the Python interface alone (eight runs at the highest load on three days; five runs of decoding on two days), the stricter yardstick; against the baseline through the HTTP server alone they would read 85.7 to 87.5 and 18.8 to 19.1 times; the first multiple's range covers both baselines, its ends from the fastest and slowest of 30 runs (fifteen on text, fifteen on random token IDs, three days). One run of the plain engine at a further load, with as long a queue of prompts as some of the eight runs that are counted, with the same arguments for the engine and with VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1 exported, gave a higher rate than all eight; it enters no range, by a rule fixed beforehand: no run with that variable exported is counted in any multiple. Only this one of those runs would move an end of a range: with it the upper end of the second multiple would read 94.5 times (not on the released programs, in runs told below: 95.2 for the single runs and 103.3 for the 3 runs). By the engine's own lines it took its V2 model runner in every load on the last of the three days, on which that run was made, with the variable or without, so against the counted runs of the third day the run sets no model runner against another; which model runner the engine took on the first two days is not known. Not on the released programs, in 3 runs on other machines of the same kind, the three multiples are worse: 75.4 times (67.5 to 83.5), 98.2 times (95.5 to 102.9) and 21.2 times (20.4 to 22.4) over all pairs of runs; against the baseline through the HTTP server alone 88.8 to 95.7 and 19.4 to 20.9; with the highest rate of that further load the second's upper end would read 103.3. From single runs of the prover, not on the released programs, the same three ratios reach higher than in the timed runs: 66.5 to 76.9, 94.0 to 94.8 and 20.1 to 20.7 times.

column3: What a reader can and cannot repeat. The script that made these rates is not in this repository. driver/measure_rate.py measures by the same rule, so a reader can repeat the kind of measurement, not the runs; it has not been run on the released programs. On other programs (row HW-678) it has run, and none of those runs is shown to have used this repository's file. driver/measure_rate.py works under exact match only, and each proof that it has made checks one token, the one after the window. The printed route (the three lines of step 4 in guide/performance.md, "Reproduce the numbers") does not send the runs' windows: those 96 windows of text are not in the repository; the route sends the 32 windows of the calibration set, which are the windows on which the fit's scales were set, and from the 33rd request on the same rows rotated. A reader's run differs from the runs told on these pages: those had every program bound to 24 CPUs on the GPU's NUMA node, while the script binds nothing; it takes a batch's start from its own listing about ten times a second, so its start-up and waits can be a tenth of a second off. On another GPU model, driver or number of CPUs a reader's figure is that machine's own: it neither confirms nor contradicts the figure on these pages. No page prints the checksums of the programs that made the figures, so a reader has nothing to compare the SHA-256 sums that the script prints with. To measure at full size a reader needs: one H100 80 GB (driver 580.178.04 in the runs); 24 CPUs on the GPU's NUMA node (for one run on CPUs of the other node: row RES-9); 330 GB of available host memory for the commitment and 300 GB for the session, whose container had at most 269.7 GB in use in the timed runs at 24 requests a batch on the public 4-bit files, file cache not counted (278.3 GB on synthetic weights, and also at 64 a batch on the public files: row RES-24); the weight files, 232 GB; 10 GB of free room for the second commitment; 5 GB on a local disk for the session's 120 proofs. Typed again, the second line would empty the log from which the third takes the commitment ID, and cp_commit would refuse because its directories exist; so the first line unsets O if the directory is there already; in a new shell paste the printed O=… and type the third line alone; to start afresh take another name. The printed line that makes the second commitment calls cp_commit directly and does not look for the 10 GB of free room, as examples/maverick/run.sh commit does. One can also measure on route 4's own commitment, without a second one (the short route). That commitment is under the published seed, and with -public-weights nothing is hidden, so it is not the leading figures' case and no figure of the one case stands for the other; at 24 per batch such a measurement has not been made, at 64 once (not on the released programs); it too uses up five of its commitment's batches for good. The runs cannot be checked from the repository: it holds no record of any run that the pages report, timed runs included, and most attack tests are not in it either. Where a count of proofs is said to be counted from a run's record, what was counted is the record that the run's own script wrote, not the proofs, copies or calls themselves; the records are not in the repository, and that a record tells truly what the programs did rests on that script. Which programs the timed runs ran, and that they ran under a drawn seed and with no test option, is known from each run's own summary (the programs' checksums, the calls as printed, the file isk.txt), not from a check made apart from the run.

The 280 GB of available host memory that the full-size example's script (prover/examples/run_target_example.sh) asks for is a constant of the script: it is not taken from any run at the default setting. Three runs (synthetic weights, not on the released programs; at the default setting by docs/quickstart.md's word alone: no checksum of a parameter file is given, row RES-20) used up to 268 GB, file cache not counted. In the timed runs on synthetic weights, whose three parameter files are that example's by checksum, the container reached more, file cache not counted: 278.1 GB while cp_commit ran (the most of 3 runs; 265.2 GB in its own process), of which 12.3 to 12.5 GB were in use in the container before the program started. The script asks for 280 GB of available host memory before it starts. column3: The wait at 24 requests per batch, from a batch's start to its release, at its worst. At 24 requests per batch in the timed runs (full size, public 4-bit weights, default setting, three runs, one H100) a request waits 220.7 to 225.9 seconds from its batch's start to its release from the second batch on, and 227.0 to 230.3 seconds in a service's first batch: about four minutes, not the 9.2 seconds per request. In the timed runs cp_prove is called directly, and a response is released as soon as every response of its batch is written; cp_prove runs no verifier, so these are waits for a proof on which no verifier has run: the serving scripts run cp_verify on each response before they hand it on; that time comes on top and is not in these figures (docs/service.md, "The example front end"). On the released programs, in none of the timed runs, that check was timed by itself: the check by the vLLM integration's middleware (integrations/proof_middleware.py), on stored proofs, called directly, with no inference engine and no HTTP server around it. In every run of that check told in this row the scripts differ from this repository's in comments, docstrings and the texts of messages of integrations/proof_middleware.py alone; for one run the constant CHECK_THREADS was also set to 4. There was one run each of three arrangements, all on 24 CPUs of a 32-CPU machine with no prover beside it: at the middleware's default on 24 CPUs, six checks at once with one thread each, a batch of 24 proofs (synthetic weights, reported; exact match; 18.76 to 18.78 MB each) took 94.0 seconds from the hand-over of the proofs to the batch's release; with the middleware's constant CHECK_THREADS set to 4, where this repository has 1, 79.4 seconds; one proof alone 22.6 seconds. All proofs were released, and nothing was held, which is no negative test: no false proof was put to the check in these runs. What bounds these three figures: no spread is known; no prover ran beside the check, as one would at a provider's; the 24 CPUs lay on two NUMA nodes and were 16 cores, 8 of them with both hyperthreads (reported), so the gain from four threads is this machine's; no batch of 64 was tried; each check's call of cp_verify runs as four processes, the call itself and one for each of its three stages, so with six checks at once up to 24 ran side by side, for under two seconds at a time, and then 12, the half that runs longer, until they ended, after about as long as a check takes (21.22 to 23.23 seconds at the middleware's default with no prover beside it); 3.53 GB of memory is the most that any one of these processes held, and how much a check's four, or all the processes that ran side by side, held together was not measured. Before that call each check makes one short call, cp_verify -plan id, which runs as one process for about 1.1 seconds and holds at most 0.19 GB. The 94.0 seconds and the timed runs' waits were measured on different machines and under different loads, and their sum was not measured. Beside a serving cp_prove, on the released programs, in none of the timed runs, in one run on synthetic weights: while cp_prove served five batches of 24 at the default setting, the middleware's check was called five times, 225 seconds apart, on the 24 CPUs on which cp_prove served, each time on one batch of 24 stored proofs, at the middleware's default. A check took 88.74 to 89.15 seconds (mean 89.0); alone on the prover's machine it took 92.1 seconds before the services and 90.3 after them. The steady rate of the service beside which the checks ran (the run's first) was 109.64 tokens/second, and 110.11 in the same run's second service, with no check beside it: 0.4 % apart; in the timed runs on synthetic weights the two services of a run part by 0.1 to 0.7 % with nothing beside them, the first the slower each time, so no slowing by the check can be told, and one run cannot narrow that. A request waited 225.2 to 226.4 seconds from its batch's start to its release (232.3 in the first batch; the mean of the five batches 227.1). Reckoned from these two means (227.1 and 89.0 seconds), not measured end to end: about 316 seconds from a batch's start to a checked proof. The checks were started by a clock, 225 seconds apart, not when the prover released a batch, the first before any batch was released; each had ended before the prover released its next batch, and the prover released a batch every 224 seconds. The container's memory, file cache not counted, reached 298.4 GB in the service with the checks beside it and 278.2 GB in the one without; in the timed runs on synthetic weights the two services of a run peak alike (278.1 to 278.3 GB). What this run did not have: that prover's own fresh proofs (all seven batch checks, the five beside the prover and the two alone, read the same 24 stored files, proofs of another run of the same kind and size, warm in the file cache); the step from cp_prove's output to the middleware, which is in none of these times; an HTTP server or an inference engine; a false proof (all proofs were released, which is no negative test). What else bounds it: no spread over runs is known; the middleware's default alone was tried; the 24 CPUs were bound to the run, not reserved to it, and 36 to 39 of the machine's 96 CPUs were busy on average during the checks, the run's own among them; what else ran on the machine was not held the same between the checks alone and the checks beside the prover. The waits told in this row run from the batch's start. Before that a request waits in the queue: up to about one batch's proving time if the next batch takes it, longer if a full batch or more is queued before it (reasoned from how the service works: docs/service.md, "How a request becomes a response"). Not on the released programs: at 24 requests a batch a request waited 292.3 to 314.4 seconds, and 300.4 to 323.8 seconds in first batches (public 4-bit weights, n = 3 runs). The waits that are not on the released programs suppose a cp_prove that runs the verifier on every response before it hands it out; the released cp_prove runs none.

column3: `examples/maverick/run.sh` under `sudo` or as root. Under `sudo`, a new work directory below a directory that the caller's own account owns belongs to root, but whoever can act as that account can put another directory in its place while the stages run as root; the weights directory can be replaced in the same way. In a root shell, under `/var/tmp`, only root can replace these directories; elsewhere that holds only if every directory above them is root's too. With `sudo` or in a root shell, root runs what lies in the repository and in the Python environment, which the caller's account can change if it owns them. A work directory that the caller's own account made is refused under `sudo` (exit code 2), and one made under `sudo` is refused to that account. Some of the script's messages name `sudo`; that is no advice to use it.

column3: Three families of false claims against the library under the programs: what closes each in these sources, wholly or in part, and what the library accepted in test programs (rules R… are those of docs/format/FORMAT.md). (1) A public input that is in no query. Where the verifier reads a value that no query contains, a prover can choose it after a challenge. R0.4 closes it, and a routine of the library that runs on a channel takes a public input only out of a first query. By `blocks/chain/public.h` the types enforce that only where a value enters a chain: the lower steps in `blocks/iop/` take plain values, and there the caller must keep the rule. (2) A public fact that is stated twice, so that two public inputs can describe one thing differently. R0.5 and the comparisons of R14.9 (in a proof) and of R13.5 (in a key file) close it. (3) Public parameters under which a test says nothing: a lookup whose one digit has the weight 0, and a lookup all of whose keys are declared as padding. A prover does not choose these parameters. The rejections listed under R13.14 close it (`blocks/iop/wf.h`, `blocks/iop/lkp.h`); `blocks/iop/tests/wf_test.cpp` and `blocks/iop/tests/lkp_test.cpp` ask that parameters of the two kinds are rejected (row `blocks.tests` of SUITE.md). Bad results: false claims of each family were accepted in tests against the library, all at toy size and on synthetic data; none was an accepted forgery of `cp_verify`. Of family (1), with a cheating prover, in test programs that call the library directly, two false claims were accepted: the target of a claim in the test on the stored table, and the rows of a lookup's table. Of family (2), with a cheating prover, in test programs, six false claims were accepted: the cells of a lookup's padding and their number; where the digits of a smallness test are; the number of a matrix's rows, in two shapes; a lookup's number of key bits and its list of parts; the function to which a cell of padding belongs; and the same items in a request's first chain and in the shared chain, which nothing compared. At the worst a key file passed for a matrix with an entry out of its range, a cell of 1,000 passed under the bound 32, and a claim passed on another matrix than the committed one. Of family (3), in runs made on purpose, both kinds of public parameters passed every test that was made on them and left an acceptance empty: with a digit of the weight 0, the library's routines that make and read a key file accepted a key file for a matrix with an entry out of its range; with all keys declared as padding, keys that are in no row of the table passed. What a reader cannot run, and what is not tested: the cheating provers of families (1) and (2) are not in this repository and cannot be built from it, so a reader cannot run those tests; whether the check that is named for a family is what stops its prover is asked by a table of tests that is not in this repository either. No test in this repository puts a cheating prover to R0.4, R0.5, R13.5 or R14.9. A fourth family, a plan that was derived from other numbers than the run takes (how far it is closed: rows SO-5, SO-5.1 and T7.1.11); a second family of such plans: docs/format/toys/3-key-and-entry.md.

column3: *What a reader cannot repeat, on hiding.* No conditional in the sources reads a switch that builds a fault of hiding into a test program. What the sources do have are test hooks and test variables by which every `cp_commit` and `cp_prove` but the production build's can be told to inject a fault of hiding; those that were read for it act only in a run on synthetic weights under a test seed, and by a search no test of this repository sets one of them (row E29.1). What fails on purpose in a reader's copy are faults that a test injects into its own random values, fixture or generator, among them: the five negative controls of `blocks/tests/hiding/table_exact_test.cpp` and the three of `blocks/iop/tests/batt_hiding_test.cpp` (one of the three can be made in only four of that test's five cases); those of `psc_exact_test`, `lin_exact_test`, `link_exact_test`, `hull` and `exact_self_test`; and, for the prover's self-checks, those of `send_pad_test` (own-test-pad-kept), `fold_base_test` (own-test-fold-mask, own-test-base-mask) and `context_test` (own-test-mask-rows and the guards on opened positions). No run in this repository shows that `pads_fault()` (`blocks/iop/send.h`) reports a pad that is missing or used twice; that `salts_test` sees shared or zero salts; that `coins_own_test()` (`blocks/coins/coins.h`) catches a generator that rejects no word; that `fold_rounds_test` finds one value under two coefficients; that `toy_exact_test`, `rng_exact_test`, `lin_exact_test`, `link_exact_test`, `key_exact_test` or `hull` fails on a faulty form of the library's own prover; that `stream_coins_test` or `coin_keys_test` fails on a faulty build; that a verifier rejects a batch or a key under a second OOD sample on a table's pads, or that two such OOD samples reveal an exact linear equation on each row (`docs/format/FORMAT.md`, R4.12); that a request that is made to fail by one of three injected faults (a value inside the prover is pushed out of its range or window) samples its random values as the others do (`prover/tests/coin_contexts_listed.py`); or that a verifier's routines reject a value that the GPU code sends without its mask (row T40). Nor does any check show that the GPU library's products write every word that is read afterwards (row T3.1.1).

What the compiler's listing says of 41 kernels' own memory. A row is a kernel in one of the three compile units, which have 294, 101 and 735 in the released programs. All figures are by the compiler's own listing; of the released programs, from a separate run of its last stage (ptxas) on the intermediate code (PTX) taken out of the programs. Of the released programs the listing's registers and stack frames equal those read from their own images, row by row; that such a run gives functions with the programs' own bytes was seen on other programs alone (row HW-678), whose listing is line for line the same as the released programs'. The 41 GPU kernels (49 rows) are those that hold the routine named in row RES-39 and whose machine code differs from that of the programs described there. In the released programs the bytes that their spill instructions move, out-of-line functions counted in, are in sum 9,560 in stores and 17,528 in loads; in `kG_msg` 628 in stores and 636 in loads; in `tside::k_end` 448 in loads. How the programs of row RES-39 differ, by a listing from a compile of the same three units, whose functions had those programs' own bytes when that was compared: each stack frame of the 49 rows is larger there, by 32 to 448 bytes; `kG_msg` moves fewer bytes there (stores 520, loads 460), and so does `tside::k_end` in its loads (408). In the other 1,081 kernel rows, by compile unit, no frame and no spill figure differs; the registers of three rows do: `hfs::k_join_runs` has 32 in the released programs and 30 there, in two units, and `hf::k_fold_slab` 28 and 29, in one. The 14 kernels (21 rows) that those programs hold and the released programs do not are in no comparison. None of these figures measures what a kernel leaves in GPU memory, and this machine code has not been read for that (row H39.1).

Before it commits, `cp_commit` checks whether any prompt could drive a value out of range. That check can stop where a matrix or slice whose norm it bounds holds only zeros (one expert's up matrix, say): a scaling factor becomes infinite. No commitment results (exit status 7); only your own model can cause this. Every commitment without `-test-seed` runs the check. Read in the code, not run. (The check: rows H7 and H7.1.)
column4: If the check stops with "the matrix library's product is not a product in binary64, or the matrix or a slice of it holds only zeros", look for an all-zero matrix or slice in your model before you suspect the GPU library.

column3: Readings name two points at which one hypothesis of the lemma of row HW-763 is wanting: it lacks a clause that the proof uses, and it does not say what it asks of a run that fails. It is not claimed that either point is answered. No attack is known that uses either. Small examples that pass through one of the points were tried for minutes, and none breaks the lemma's bound. No search for an attack on the protocol itself through either point is known. Whether the lemma as it is worded holds is not known (row HW-763).

The clause that the hypothesis of the lemma of row HW-763 lacks would say that a step's verifier builds nothing new for the next step out of the encoded masks. One reading, of ten minutes, of a text from which the written proof of row HW-763 differs, went through the five proofs that apply the lemma. It found the clause met in each only if the clause does not count a message that is listed for several groups; in one of the five one message is listed for two. So, under a clause that counts such a message, that use would lie outside the lemma. In the two proofs on a request, according to it, only the order of the steps saves the clause. That reading was not aimed at refuting, ran no example, and checked neither the theorems on the steps nor any other hypothesis of the lemma. That the five proofs meet the lemma's hypotheses, as worded in the text that these two read, is the word of one reading, within thirteen minutes for all that it had to read, and of a second for two of the five. Both found them met but for the point on the range check and one or two lighter ones.

That each encoding is shown at as many positions as it has random entries, with no margin (219 and 219 at the default setting: row HW-762), is calculated, and read in other sources (row HW-678); it is taken from no run. No full-size proof, GPU run or encoding kernel was examined for it. By a reading of other sources, the programs test the number of opened positions for each tree at run time and do not add it up over a proof's new encodings of a row. That is enough only if each new encoding's random entries are fresh, and by the code's own list of conditions (`blocks/frame/hiding_conditions.h`, at `hiding_conditions_missed`) no function there tests that (what does look at such entries in a run, and what it does not see: row HW-398). That a row kept from one segment to the next is encoded anew, with fresh random entries, for each segment that holds it is read in other sources too, in readings of which one was aimed at finding a second opening.

A measured size is its run's, not the setting's: at one setting and on the same programs, the key file, the leaf file and the proofs differed in length between two runs. Each run made a commitment of its own under its own drawn seed, and as reported commitments under different seeds can differ in these lengths; why has not been looked into. By design every length follows from the three public files and, for an opening, from the sampled positions, which are public (docs/format/FORMAT.md; rows H32.1 and LIM-63); that the lengths seen in these runs follow that rule has not been checked. In the one run of both audits at full size (the run told in row LIM-63), not on the released programs, some public lengths differed from those of another full-size run, and the difference is not traced to that rule or to any other.
`cp_prove` and `cp_verify` each carry their own copy of a segment's step code; the library's copy, the one its unit tests cover, is a third; neither has been compared with it as a whole.

The tie of `verify-on-bytes`, a Lean text from which this repository builds no stand-alone program, to `innerCompiledVerifier` (`OnBytes.K.exit_innerCompiledVerifier`) is proved under six hypotheses. At least two of the six, as this repository states them, cannot hold once their parameters are set to the programs' values, and a third wherever the served statements do not pin the public files; so there the theorem is true but says nothing (lean/LIMITS.md, L22: proved at no input and may be false).
The check script was tested as row SO-66 says; no run has tried every documented answer and exit code of `cp_verify`, row by row of verifier/docs/output.md.
By report, the float64-exactness test was not run on the GPUs of the vLLM calls that these pages report; a pass elsewhere says nothing of them.
Clients that pool their proofs have not been tried, nor prompts chosen against the prover.

None of the five tests of hiding searches for a leak: they test that the masks are there and that a loss is noticed. Only the test of the OOD answers by value and the audits with the provider's secrets have run at full size (on which programs: row LIM-63.2), and only the test of lost pads, the sweep of lost random values and the replay of riskier losses inject a fault into the programs under test.
The sweep of lost random values (row HW-660). None of its runs was on the released programs, at full size, with two losses at once, or with a loss later than right after the draw.

Outside a trial, a code review found a fault: a mask never generated, in a routine that no program called. Not known: which routine it was, whether it is among these sources, and whether a released program calls it.

Of the five tests of hiding (docs/how-hiding-is-checked.md), the fifth, both audits with the provider's secrets, is in this repository: the two audit tools under `tools/audit/`, with their own test. So are the public tests (SUITE.md) that rows of this table name. By two readings of this repository's files, it does not hold the programs and scripts of the first four tests, of the audits by value beside the five, of the one short search for leaks (row LIM-29) or of the count of derived random values: a reader cannot repeat these from this repository. `cp_commit`'s range check is a check inside the program.
The list of faults that no check would catch is not complete (row HW-695). Where only a test looks for a fault, nothing guards a real run: a test protects no service.

**No program can detect that a secret key directory has been copied or rolled back.** Each copy and each rollback lets a leaf table serve batches past its batch limit; these pages give no ceiling on how many. What the batches past the limit give away (by reasoning: row H21.11) has not been tried on the released programs.

A proof shows its request's place in the batch's hash tree. That place is sampled uniformly, whatever the order of arrival, and free places hold random digests. If a run lost those digests, the salts or the arrangement, nothing would detect it, and a client would see the free places or a request's rank.
Even for a provider that follows the duties, it has not been proved for the programs that the counter keeps a table within its limit, or that staying below the limit is enough.

**At most, the design hides the following. This is a ceiling, not a promise.** A client cannot tell two sets of weights apart if they have the same configuration, give the same reply or the same "failed" for every request, and run the same numbers of batches and requests on the same schedule. A client is anyone who sends requests and holds its own replies and proofs and the public files. Clients who pool what they hold count as one.
As the programs run the protocol, the count has no slack: 219 random coordinates for 219 shown positions, so one further linear fact without a mask of its own would tell.

**The written proof of hiding.** A technical report that is not public and not refereed gives a written proof of zero knowledge against any verifier, batches included, for its own protocol with fresh masks, in the random oracle model, under its own bound and conditions. The written proof has not been checked independently, and its authors call the proof "complete but not settled": the proof is written out in full, but the checking that it has had is not enough to rely on it. Readings of the written proof of hiding have missed real errors (row HW-579): four in statements that the proof rests on, a fifth in the definition of zero knowledge itself, and more that have not been counted. It is not claimed that every known error is fixed: the written proof has known faults (row HW-767), some points in numbered statements are open, not every finding has been followed up, and there may be more errors. The proof rests on one lemma, on composing steps whose masks are sent in advance. Readings name two points at which one hypothesis of that lemma is wanting: it lacks a clause that the proof uses (row RES-66), and it does not say what it asks of a run that fails. Whether the lemma as it is worded holds is not known: it is not claimed that either point on its hypothesis is answered; no attack is known that uses either, and no search for one on the protocol itself is known (row RES-57). A failure of the lemma could point to a leak in the protocol. Lean's theorems on zero knowledge, which are of the protocol and its Lean prover, not of the programs, and cover one request to a proof and no batch (rows PS-65 and PS-71), rest on no statement of the written proof. Only a part of the bound is evaluated (row HW-579), and no result of the written proof is about the programs: for the released programs no figure and no level is stated. The report's table of differences is of other sources (row HW-678) and may be incomplete (row PS-67); beside what it lists, the programs differ from the written proof's protocol at three more places (row HW-579); no one statement covers them all. Without the lemma the whole protocol would have no written proof. Every figure drawn from the written bound on hiding would be without a written proof too. Because of the second point, read strictly, one use of the lemma in the proof of hiding lies outside it: the use for the range check, when that check fails. So does the use that repeats it for the protocol on paper taken in the programs' order of messages. That the proof covers a failing range check all the same is the word of two of the three readings that found the point, after minutes each. The lemma as it is worded has not been read for the judgement on weight hiding (docs/limits.md#the-verdict). Whether its conclusion could be had by another route if it failed cannot be said. Among the errors that readings have missed are errors in this lemma. The correction of this lemma failed several times, and some of the failed forms had passed a reading; one of them had passed at least three readings, its writer's among them. Read to the letter, five forms of one clause each admitted a prover for which the lemma is false. A further clause erred the other way and shut out the honest prover at one use, and more than one form of the restatement that followed had a fault too. Gaps were found in the lemma itself, and it is not claimed that the lemma as it is worded closes them. One more sentence of its proof was found false as worded. As reported, a reading of its statement under which it was false, which its finder rated as remote, was shut when the statement was reworded. As reported, another sentence of its proof that was false as worded, which five or more readings had passed, was replaced. No other way of reading the lemma under which it is false is known (what was tried, and what was not searched for: row RES-57). The lemma's proof has been read step by step, in tens of minutes a reading, which each reading had for this proof and two other tasks together, in a text from which the proof as it stands differs. Most of its steps were derived, some only with a step that the reading supplied itself, and the rest were followed. As it stands, but for one clause that was reworded afterwards, the lemma's proof has been read whole only in readings of about a quarter of an hour or less, each with more than this proof to read (row LIM-31). Lean proves a lemma of this kind (`Iop.goodT_seq_masked`, lean/Ior/KnowCollRulesMaskProofs.lean; stated in lean/Ior/KnowCollRulesMask.lean); nothing on these pages ties it to the written proof's lemma.

No statement, written or in Lean, covers what a prover computes or sends in a run that breaks off; it may depend on the weights. The programs hand out none of a failed request's proof: what leaves is the answer "failed" and, in the proofs of the batch's other requests, one salted hash (read in the code, not run).
No statement covers a proof of a batch that its owner passes on later. Of batches, which are what the programs serve, Lean's results on hiding say nothing.

The written proof (not public: row HW-763) nowhere says that the published sums (the OOD answers) are independent of the simulator's coins: if they were not, simulated OOD answers could differ visibly from real ones. No counterexample is known, with the pads, which mask these answers, as prescribed. That step was attacked or checked on paper, in two written arguments other than the written proof's, one of which has itself been read only in part, and it was not broken (as reported).

The written proof of hiding has known faults. One is in the definition of its claim: it does not say that what its two experiments draw is drawn independently (what draws that are tied to one another can cost, by a small computed example, which is not the protocol: row LIM-44.1). For one constructed block that the protocol does not have, a step of the printed proof fails by a computed example, and, as reported, the bound of the lemma of row HW-763 holds there too.

The widest gap in the evidence is how the production build samples, orders and applies a batch's randomness, which a few audits of a batch's proofs have narrowed but not removed (row LIM-63.2, lines 5 and 6).
Clients who act together and have two requests in one batch can tell whether a failure was one request's own or the whole batch's.

By a reading of the code, with nothing run, `cp_commit`'s clean-up does not touch what a finished step or a finished run has taken off its list. Where a new file's device and inode numbers differ between its opening and a later look by name, nothing is overwritten, not even the seed, and the printed line says only that the file is removed. A toy program built on the routine's own source has shown that for the seed's file. Not known: on which real file system the numbers differ.

The programs assume that ChaCha20's block function is a pseudorandom function under a secret key. It is a computational assumption, and its standing rests on cryptanalysis only. That assumption says that the values derived from the seed look random to anyone who does not hold it. It does not say that they reveal nothing about single bytes of the seed, which would be a further assumption that these pages do not make. This names a limit of the assumption, and reports no weakness of ChaCha20.
`cp_commit`'s worst-case check tests that no window can drive an internal value out of its range. That it covers the worst case rests on an argument and on reading the code, and is not proved.

Whoever holds a plain hash of the weights can test a guess at the weights, or at whatever part the hash covers, offline and as often as they like, and can tell whether two providers serve the same weights.
